question: In the book of Numbers, Moses gathered a wooden rod from the chief of every Israelite tribe, out in the desert after the escape from Egypt. The tribes kept challenging his brother Aaron's right to be priest, and God told Moses to lay the rods overnight in the sacred tent, the Tabernacle. How many rods did he lay there?
context: One rod for each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Numbers 17:2 -- 'Speak unto the children of Israel, and take of every one of them a rod according to the house of their fathers, of all their princes... twelve rods.' Source: Wikipedia, Aaron's rod; Numbers 17.

question: The chiefs of Israel's tribes each gave up a wooden rod to settle a challenge to the priesthood of Moses's brother Aaron, and the rods lay overnight in the sacred tent called the Tabernacle. In the morning only one was alive, budded and bloomed, and it was Aaron's. From which tribe of Israel did Aaron come?
context: Aaron is of the tribe of Levi (Numbers 17:8: 'the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded'). The rod-test settles that the Levites, and not any other tribe, are the chosen priestly line. Source: Wikipedia, Aaron's rod; Numbers 17.

question: Aaron, Moses's older brother and the first high priest of Israel, gave up his dead staff for one night in the Tabernacle, the movable tent-temple, when the tribes grumbled about who should be priest. By morning it had gone the whole way from bud to blossom to ripe fruit. In the book of Numbers, what fruit did the staff yield?
context: Numbers 17:8 -- 'the rod of Aaron... was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.' The almond tree is the earliest to bloom in the Holy Land, a fitting image of a first-fruits sign. Source: Bible Hub, Numbers 17:8.

question: The writer of Hebrews, a New Testament letter, placed Aaron's flowering rod in the Ark of the Covenant, a wooden chest covered in gold that the Israelites carried through the wilderness. He placed two other precious objects from those desert years in the Ark with it. What were those two objects?
answer: the pot of manna and the tables of stone
choices: the pot of manna and the tables of stone
the seven-branched menorah and the ephod
the incense censer and the breastplate
the scroll of the Law and the shewbread
context: Hebrews 9:4 lists 'the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant' inside the Ark. Later Jewish tradition disagrees on whether the pot and rod were literally in the Ark or beside it, but Hebrews puts them in. Source: Wikipedia, Aaron's rod; Hebrews 9:4.

question: The Israelites spoke against God and Moses further along the wilderness march: 'wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?' In the book of Numbers, God answered with a plague of biting creatures in the camp, and many died. What kind of creatures did God send?
context: Numbers 21:6 -- 'the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.' 'Fiery' probably refers to the burning venom of the bite. The people repent; Moses is told to make a bronze serpent on a pole, and any bitten man who looks at it lives. Source: Wikipedia, Nehushtan; Numbers 21.

question: King Hezekiah of Judah broke the bronze serpent in pieces, centuries after Moses had raised it on a pole in the wilderness. People in Jerusalem had begun burning incense to the old healing-relic as if it were an idol. Hezekiah gave the shattered thing a contemptuous nickname. What did he call it?
context: 2 Kings 18:4 -- 'he brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made... and he called it Nehushtan.' The name puns on the Hebrew nehoshet (brass) -- a merciless nickname meant to strip the object of the sacred aura Israel had wrongly given it. Baal-zebub, Dagon, and Molech are all real gods Israel encountered but were never nicknames for the serpent-pole. Source: Wikipedia, Nehushtan; 2 Kings 18.

question: In Genesis, God told an old man named Abram to leave a great walled city on a southern river and walk to a land he had never seen. Abram set out with his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot, about four thousand years ago as the story goes. From what city did he set out?
context: KJV Genesis 11:31: 'Terah took Abram his son ... and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan.' Nineveh is Jonah's Assyrian city; Haran was a way-station Abram stopped at on the road out of Ur; Babylon rose to power much later.

question: Abram walked hundreds of miles from his home city at God's command into a land he had never seen. At Shechem, in the hill country of Canaan, God appeared beneath a great oak tree and swore to give that whole land to Abram's descendants. What did Abram do at that spot to mark the promise?
choices: cut down the tree for firewood
set up a pillar of twelve stones
planted a vineyard and a grove
context: KJV Genesis 12:7: 'Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him.' Twelve-stone pillars belong to Jacob and Joshua later; the vineyard is Noah's after the flood.

question: Abram grieved that he was rich but childless, with only his servant to inherit. One night God brought him out of his tent and told him to number something no one could count, saying 'so shall thy seed be.' What did God tell him to try to number?
choices: the grains of sand on the shore
the leaves of the terebinth trees
the flocks on the surrounding hills
context: KJV Genesis 15:5: 'And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.' Sand on the shore is the promise given to Isaac and Jacob later; the other two never appear as the count.

question: God made a covenant with Abram in the book of Genesis, promising him countless descendants and the land of Canaan. As a sign of it, God changed Abram's name to Abraham, meaning 'father of a multitude.' On the very same day God gave Abraham's wife a new name too. What was her new name?
context: KJV Genesis 17:15: 'As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be.' Hagar was the Egyptian handmaid who bore Ishmael, Rebekah married Isaac a generation later, Rachel married Jacob two generations later.

question: Abraham was sitting in the door of his tent at the oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day when three visitors appeared. He ran to fetch a tender calf and cakes, and after they ate, one of them announced that in the coming year his wife would bear a son. She was listening from inside the tent, and what she did gave the boy his name. What did she do?
choices: she wept quietly in her veil
she sang a song of Miriam
she poured out a jar of oil
context: KJV Genesis 18:12: 'Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?' The son's name Isaac (Yitzhak) means 'he laughs' -- Genesis 21:6, 'God hath made me to laugh.' Miriam's song and the pouring of oil belong to Moses's sister and to the anointing scenes.

question: Melchizedek, the mysterious king of the town of Salem, came out to meet Abram on his way home from rescuing his nephew Lot from four raiding kings. He was a priest of God Most High as well as a king, the first priest named in the Bible. He brought out two things and blessed Abram. What did he bring?
context: KJV Genesis 14:18: 'And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.' The name Melchizedek means 'king of righteousness' and later became one of the most argued-over figures in Jewish and Christian tradition. Gold and myrrh belong to the visit of the Magi much later.

question: Lot fled the burning city of Sodom with his family as fire and brimstone fell on the cities of the plain. The angels had warned them not to look back. His wife broke that warning and turned to look at what she was leaving. What did she become in that moment?
context: KJV Genesis 19:26: 'But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.' Ancient travelers pointed to salt formations near the Dead Sea as her supposed remains; the moral of the story in the biblical text is about looking back at what one has been told to leave behind.

question: In the Roman poet Statius's telling, the sea-nymph Thetis heard a prophecy that her son Achilles would die young at Troy. To hide him from the war she sent him to the palace of King Lycomedes on a small Aegean island, in a disguise nobody would suspect on the son of Peleus. What disguise did she give him?
answer: A girl among the king's daughters
choices: A girl among the king's daughters
A shepherd boy tending the palace flock
A kitchen slave serving the king's table
context: From Statius, Achilleid Book 1 (1st c. CE). The disguise runs deep: Achilles takes a girl-name, lives among the princesses, and fathers a son on one of them (Deidameia) before he is ever unmasked.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles took a girl-name to match his disguise while he hid among the daughters of King Lycomedes on his Aegean island. It meant 'red-haired' in Greek, and his own son, born on the island, grew up called by a male form of it. What girl-name did Achilles take?
context: Pyrrha means 'red-haired'. Their son Neoptolemus ('new to war') was also called Pyrrhus, the male form of his father's alias -- a joke the Greeks did not forget. Source: Wikipedia, Achilles on Skyros; Neoptolemus.  (Legend.)

question: The seer Calchas told the Greek chieftains gathered at Aulis that Troy could not fall unless one specific warrior sailed with them -- and that warrior was hidden somewhere in the world, dressed as a girl. The chieftains picked a man to lead the search for him. Whom did they send?
context: The errand needed a trick, and Odysseus's tricks are why the assignment fell to him; in Statius's telling, Diomedes rides along as his companion. Source: Apollodorus, Library 3.13.8; Statius, Achilleid 1.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus spread his merchant's wares in front of King Lycomedes's daughters in the palace courtyard on the island: bright cloths, jewels, mirrors, ribbons. Hidden among the finery he placed two objects that had nothing to do with a girl's wardrobe. What were the two hidden objects that would betray the disguised Achilles?
context: In Statius's telling, and in Hyginus's, one 'daughter' ignored the pretty things and reached for these two -- and Odysseus had his man. Source: Statius, Achilleid 1; Hyginus, Fabulae 96.  (Legend.)

question: Apollodorus, the Greek writer, tells the unmasking of Achilles more simply. Odysseus tracked him down to the court of King Lycomedes and had one battle-signal sounded there, and the hidden young warrior gave himself away. What signal did Odysseus have sounded?
choices: A clash of shield on shield
context: Apollodorus, Library 3.13.8: Odysseus found Achilles living among the women and unmasked him by sounding a trumpet. Some vase paintings show the trumpet version rather than the shield-reach; either way, only Achilles reacts as a fighter.  (Legend.)

question: The Athenian hero Theseus, slayer of the Minotaur, came in his old age to the island of King Lycomedes, years before Thetis hid her son Achilles there. Lycomedes turned from host to killer and murdered his famous guest on the island. How did Lycomedes kill Theseus?
answer: He hurled him from a cliff into the sea
choices: He hurled him from a cliff into the sea
He poisoned his cup at the welcome feast
He set his hounds on him in the hunting field
He drowned him in the palace bath
context: The same court that sheltered young Achilles had already thrown Theseus to his death from a Skyrian cliff. Source: Wikipedia, Skyros; Lycomedes.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, the eldest son of Troy's old king led the Trojans out through the gates against the Greek army camped outside the walls. He was Troy's chief defender, and he killed many Greek captains. What was this Trojan prince's name?
context: Hector is the moral centre of the Iliad's Trojan side -- husband to Andromache, father to baby Astyanax. Source: Homer, Iliad; Wikipedia, Hector.  (Legend.)

question: Hector came in from battle in Book 6 of the Iliad, and Andromache met him at the gate with a nurse holding their baby son. When Hector reached out, the baby shrank back screaming from his helmet's horsehair crest. What did Hector do?
answer: Took the helmet off and laughed
choices: Took the helmet off and laughed
Sang the baby a battle hymn
Pressed the baby to the helmet plume
Handed the baby back and left at once
context: Iliad 6.466-473. One of the tenderest scenes in Homer; the emotional weight the death-scene later cashes in. Source: Wikipedia, Andromache.  (Legend.)

question: Hector stood alone outside the Scaean Gate to face the Greek champion Achilles, near the end of Homer's Iliad. His father and mother watched from the wall and begged him to come inside the city. When Achilles finally came on him in his new god-forged armour, Hector's nerve broke and he bolted. What happened next?
answer: Achilles chased him around the walls of Troy
choices: Achilles chased him around the walls of Troy
Achilles cornered him against the city gate
Achilles caught him within a single spear-cast
Achilles let him go and turned back to the ships
context: Iliad 22.136-207. The chase went three full laps of the city; Homer compares it to a hawk swooping on a trembling dove. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 22; Wikipedia, Hector.  (Legend.)

question: Hector stopped running only when a figure appeared beside him, promising to stand at his side: his own brother, come out from the city to help. It was not his brother at all. A goddess had taken that shape to trick him into turning to fight. Which goddess wore the disguise?
context: Athena took the shape of Hector's brother Deiphobus. When Hector reached for a second spear from his 'brother' after the duel began, no one was there. Iliad 22.226-247.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles came at Hector outside the walls and knew what he was looking at: his own old armour, stripped from Patroclus's body earlier in the war. He knew every joint of it and every gap in it, and he drove his spear into the single unguarded place. Where did the spear go in?
context: Iliad 22.324-329. The spear-point kept Hector alive just long enough to speak -- and to prophesy Achilles's own death. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 22.  (Legend.)

question: Hector lay dying at the feet of Achilles by the walls of Troy, in the final duel of Homer's Iliad. With his last breath he foretold Achilles's doom and named the two who would bring it, at that same gate: one a mortal Trojan, the other a god. Whom did he name?
context: Iliad 22.359-360. The prophecy comes true after the poem ends: in later tellings Paris shoots Achilles with a bow, Apollo guiding the arrow. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 22.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles refused Hector's dying plea that his body go home for burial. He pierced the tendons behind the dead man's heels, ran oxhide thongs through the holes, and tied the corpse to something that would drag it face-down through the dust while the prince's parents and wife watched from the walls. To what did he tie the body?
answer: The back of his own chariot
choices: The back of his own chariot
A litter borne by two horses
The mast of a beached ship
context: Iliad 22.395-405. The horses dragged Hector in circuits within full view of the walls -- and of Priam, Hecuba, and Andromache watching from the ramparts. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 22.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles hitched Hector's dead body up again the next morning and dragged it round the burial mound of his own dead friend Patroclus. He did not stop after one day, and even the gods on Olympus were sickened. Homer gave the exact number of days he kept it up. How many days?
context: Iliad 24.14-18. The gods on Olympus were sickened by the excess and finally forced Zeus to intervene. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 24.  (Legend.)

question: The mortal king Peleus married a goddess of the sea, one of the fifty Nereids, daughters of the sea-god Nereus, and their only son was the great hero Achilles. What was the sea-goddess's name?
context: Thetis is the sea-nymph mother; her wedding to the mortal Peleus is where the golden apple 'to the fairest' rolls in, and starts the chain of events that leads to the Trojan War. Source: Wikipedia, Achilles.  (Legend.)

question: In the telling of the Roman poet Statius, the sea-nymph mother of Achilles carried her baby son down to the underworld to make him proof against all weapons, and lowered him into the black water of the River Styx. The part of him gripped in her fingers was the only patch of skin the water never touched. Which body part did she hold him by?
context: The heel became the single un-dipped spot. Every language in the West now has the phrase 'an Achilles heel' for the single vulnerable spot in something otherwise proof. Source: Wikipedia, Achilles heel.  (Legend.)

question: Paris drew back the bow to shoot Achilles, and the arrow did not fly true on its own. A god stood at the archer's shoulder and steered the shaft, just as the dying Hector had warned. The god was a protector of Troy. Which god guided the arrow?
context: Iliad 22.359-360. Apollo, patron of Troy and of the bow, is the god Hector names in his last breath. Source: Homer, Iliad; Wikipedia, Achilles.  (Legend.)

question: Hector, dying at Achilles's feet, warned him that he too would fall in one particular place: the same great gate of Troy where Hector had made his last stand. Homer names this gate several times in the Iliad. Which gate was it?
context: The Scaean Gate is the western gate of Troy, facing the Greek camp on the beach. Hector waits there for Achilles in Iliad 22; Achilles falls there later. Source: Homer, Iliad 22.359-360.  (Legend.)

question: Aeneas, a young Trojan prince, fights in the streets of burning Troy on its last night, with the Greeks inside the walls through the trick of the wooden horse. His mother appears to him there, a Greek goddess, and tells him to save his family and flee. Which goddess is Aeneas's mother?
context: Called Venus in Latin. She warns him that the city's fate is sealed and the future of Troy must be carried out by him. Source: Virgil, Aeneid Book 2; Wikipedia, Aeneas.  (Legend.)

question: The old father of Aeneas cannot walk anymore and refuses to leave burning Troy on the last night of the war: he would rather die there than run. Aeneas has run home through the smoking streets, told by his goddess mother to save his family and flee. What is Aeneas's father's name?
context: Once Aphrodite's mortal lover; struck lame by Zeus for boasting about her. Priam is the king of Troy; Laocoon warns of the wooden horse; Antenor is another Trojan elder. Source: Wikipedia, Aeneas.  (Legend.)

question: In Virgil's Aeneid, the Trojan hero Aeneas begs his old father to flee on the last night of Troy, as the city burns. The old man will not leave, and Aeneas cannot force him. Then the family sees a sign: a small flame plays around the head of Aeneas's little son, and it does not burn him or his hair. What is that son named?
context: Also called Iulus, the name Roman tradition uses to link him to the family of Julius Caesar. Astyanax is Hector's baby son, killed in the sack; Telemachus is Odysseus's son; Orestes is Agamemnon's son. Source: Virgil, Aeneid 2 (Theoi); Wikipedia, Ascanius.  (Legend.)

question: Anchises, old and lame, finally agrees to leave burning Troy on the last night of the war, but his small grandson cannot keep up in the smoke. His son Aeneas is a strong young warrior in full armour. How does Aeneas get his father out of Troy?
answer: He hoists him onto his own shoulders
choices: He hoists him onto his own shoulders
He carries him in a litter with three servants
He puts him on a horse and leads it by the reins
He drags him on a shield across the flagstones
context: This is the founding image of Roman piety. The small son Ascanius walks beside them, holding his father's hand. Source: Wikipedia, Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius; Virgil, Aeneid Book 2.  (Legend.)

question: Gian Lorenzo Bernini, a young Italian sculptor, carved Aeneas's escape from burning Troy out of a single block of marble around 1618. Three living generations of one Trojan family stand there as one column: old grandfather, son and little grandson. In which Roman museum does that statue stand today?
context: The sculpture is titled 'Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius' and is about 220 cm tall. Anchises holds a vessel of ashes topped by two tiny Penates. Source: Wikipedia, Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius.

question: The wife of Aeneas follows a little way behind as he walks out of burning Troy on its last night with his old father and his little son. In the smoke and the dark and the panicking crowds she is separated from the family and lost forever. What is Aeneas's wife named?
context: Andromache is Hector's widow; Hecuba is Priam's queen; Cassandra is the prophetess daughter of Priam who is dragged from Athena's altar in the sack. Source: Wikipedia, Creusa of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: Aeneas gets clear of the walls of burning Troy with his old father and his small son, and he realizes his wife has been lost in the smoke behind them. Sword drawn, he rushes back alone through the flames to find her. What does he find?
answer: Her ghost, which speaks to him and then fades from his arms
choices: Her ghost, which speaks to him and then fades from his arms
Her body pinned under a burning beam in the courtyard
The Greek soldier who killed her, whom he cuts down at the well
Nothing at all -- he searches the smoke until dawn and gives up
context: She tells him a new wife and a new kingdom in a western land await him, and to care for their son; three times he tries to embrace her and three times his arms pass through her. Aeneid Book 2, from about line 650. Source: Wikipedia, Creusa of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: Aeneas gathers other Trojan survivors on Mount Ida and sails west on a long wandering that echoes the Odyssey: Delos, Crete, Sicily, and Carthage, where Queen Dido falls in love with him. He finally lands at the mouth of a river in Latium, in central Italy. At the mouth of which river does he land?
context: The river Rome will be built on, generations later, by Aeneas's distant descendant Romulus. The Rubicon is the small stream Julius Caesar later crosses; the Po and the Arno are further north. Source: Wikipedia, Aeneas.  (Legend.)

question: A young god of the Tuatha De Danann, the Irish god of love and youth, dreams of a woman standing at the head of his bed. She vanishes when he reaches for her, but comes back every night for a year. Who is he?
context: Aengus (also spelled Oengus), often called Aengus Og ('Young Aengus'), is the Tuatha De god of love and youth. Lugh is the sun-and-craft god; Nuada the Silver-Arm was king of the Tuatha De; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god. Wikipedia: Aengus; Aislinge Oenguso.  (Legend.)

question: Boann searches Ireland for a year for the woman of her son's dream and finds nothing, while Aengus grows too sick to eat or speak. At last the Dagda sends to Munster, to the king of its sidhe, the fairy mounds, who finds her after a year's search of his own. Who is this king?
context: Bodb Derg ('Bodb the Red') is king of the sidhe of Munster and later chosen king over all the Tuatha De after the Milesian conquest. Midir and Elcmar are other sidhe-lords; Manannan rules the sea-realm. Mythical Ireland: Aislinge Oengusso.  (Legend.)

question: The Irish poets say the young god Aengus can shape his own kisses into four small living creatures. In one old place-name tale he sends the four to follow a king and mock him every morning before sunrise, until the king's druid finds a way to catch them. What kind of creatures are they?
context: The Dindsenchas tells how Aengus shaped his kisses into four birds that followed a king named Cairbre and mocked him each day before sunrise, until Cairbre's druid sang a tree up so tall that it caught and held them. In later Scottish folklore, kisses become invisible birds that follow lovers home, singing. Wikipedia: Aengus.  (Legend.)

question: The king who hunts for the woman of the dream finds her at last on a lake in the west of Ireland, where a strange company of women is gathered. She stands among one hundred and fifty of them, all chained in pairs with chains of the same metal. Only she, the fairest, wears a chain of a different metal, single around her neck. What metal marks her out?
context: The hundred-and-fifty are paired by silver; the fairest, Caer, is marked out by a single gold chain. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith.  (Legend.)

question: Aengus, sick with longing, learns the name of the woman of his dreams at last. It means 'Yew-Berry', for the yew, the Irish tree of eternity, which grows in graveyards and lives for centuries. Her father is Ethal Anbuail of Connacht. What is her name?
context: Ibormeith = 'yew-berry'. Deirdre, Grainne, and Emer are other named heroines of Irish myth (Ulster Cycle and Fenian Cycle), real names, but the wrong woman here. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith.  (Legend.)

question: Aengus reaches Loch Bel Dracon to claim the woman of his dream and finds she is not simply a woman. Every other year, on one day of the calendar, she and her one hundred and fifty companions change shape. For a full year they are a company of chained birds on the water. On which day does the change come?
context: Samhain is the Irish threshold between summer and winter and the classic moment for the veil between worlds to thin -- the natural day for a shape-change. Beltane, Imbolc, and Lughnasa are the other three great Irish quarter-days. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith.  (Legend.)

question: The woman of Aengus's dreams floats among the flock on Loch Bel Dracon on the morning of the change. He calls to her from the shore, and she comes to him. To go away with her, Aengus does one thing first. What does he do?
answer: he takes the shape of a swan himself
choices: he takes the shape of a swan himself
he strikes off her silver chain with a sword
he fasts on the shore three days and nights
he gives up his home at Bru na Boinne
context: Aislinge Oenguso: when Aengus calls, Caer comes to him (in one translation only after he gives his word that she may go back to the lake), and the two sleep in the shape of swans and circle the lake three times before they fly off together. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith; Mythical Ireland: Aislinge Oengusso.  (Legend.)

question: Two lovers lift off the water together in bird shape, Aengus and the maiden he first saw only in dreams, and circle back toward his mound beside the Boyne, singing a love-song as they fly. The song is so sweet that every ear in Ireland is overcome. What does the singing do?
answer: it puts all of Ireland to sleep for three days and three nights
choices: it puts all of Ireland to sleep for three days and three nights
it heals every wound in Ireland at once
it silences every other bird in Ireland for a year
it turns every lake in Ireland to gold at sunrise
context: This is the closing image of Aislinge Oenguso: the swan-song lays the whole island under a three-day sleep. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith.  (Legend.)

question: Agatha, a young Christian woman in Sicily, would not renounce her faith during a Roman persecution of Christians around the year 251, and she was killed for it. Her city still keeps her white silk veil in a shrine. Every February, the bakers there make round white pastries in her name. In which Sicilian city did she die?
context: Catania sits on the east coast of Sicily at the foot of Mount Etna. Syracuse is Sicily's other famous martyr-city (its own martyr is Lucia); Palermo and Messina are the western and northeastern great cities and are the home cities of other saints (Rosalia of Palermo, for instance) -- but Agatha is Catania's own.

question: A Roman emperor ordered every person in his empire to burn incense before the old gods on pain of death, in the middle of the third century AD. In Sicily a young Christian noblewoman named Agatha refused, and she was arrested and killed. It was the first empire-wide persecution of Christians. Under which emperor did Agatha die?
context: The Decian persecution of 250-251 CE was the first empire-wide required sacrifice -- refusing meant death. Nero's persecution (60s CE) was earlier and confined to Rome after the great fire; Diocletian's (303 CE) was later and worse; Trajan's early-second-century policy was much milder and case-by-case (see Pliny's famous letter).

question: Agatha turned down the Roman governor of Sicily in the middle of the third century AD, though he wanted her family's wealth and hoped to marry her. She also would not renounce Christ, and he became the villain of her whole martyrdom story. What was that governor's name?
context: Quintianus is the prefect of Sicily in the Passio Agathae. Aspasius, Rusticus and Anullinus were all real Roman officials, but they judged OTHER famous early martyrs: Aspasius Paternus was the proconsul who sent Cyprian of Carthage into exile, Rusticus was the prefect of Rome who condemned Justin Martyr, and Anullinus prosecuted Felix of Thibiuca in North Africa. Real names, wrong martyr.  (Legend.)

question: The Roman governor of Sicily tried to break the young Christian Agatha before he put her on trial for her faith, the Golden Legend says. Instead of a prison, he sent her to a house of ill fame run by a woman with nine equally corrupt daughters. For a whole month they failed to bend her. What was the name of the brothel-keeper?
context: Aphrodisia -- her name openly evokes Aphrodite, the goddess of the trade -- is the madam in the Legenda Aurea's version. Herodias is the wife of Herod Antipas who calls for John the Baptist's head; Salome her daughter dances for it; Livia is the empress-wife of Augustus. Real ancient women, all wrong for a third-century Sicilian brothel.

question: Agatha lay alone in agony in her cell the night after her worst torture, the story says. Then an old man came to her, a small boy walking ahead of him carrying one thing. The old man had come to heal her wounds. What was the boy carrying?
context: The Golden Legend says that an old man came to her cell, a child going before him bearing a light, and offered to heal her wounds as a surgeon would. When she answered that Christ alone would heal her if he willed it, he named himself as Christ's apostle, and she was made whole. Retellings often make the light a lamp.  (Legend.)

question: An old man visited the prison cell of the young Christian Agatha in Sicily around the year 251, the story says, and offered to heal the wounds of her torture. Then he told her he was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus. Which apostle did he say he was?
context: In the Passio the old man reveals himself as Saint Peter the apostle and heals her wounds so completely that when the jailers open the cell in the morning she is untouched. Andrew is Peter's own brother and was crucified on the X-cross of Patras; John was exiled to Patmos and lived to old age; James son of Zebedee was the first apostle martyred, beheaded under Herod Agrippa. Real apostles all, but Peter is the visitor named in Agatha's Passio.  (Legend.)

question: A baker in Agatha's home town sets out small round pastries called minni di Sant'Agata on the morning of 5 February, her feast day. Agatha was a young Christian woman killed in the 3rd century for her faith. Each pastry is topped with white icing and a single candied cherry, and inside each is a creamy filling. What is the filling?
context: Sweetened ricotta cheese is the classic Sicilian pastry filling (the same filling used in cannoli and cassata), and the minni di Sant'Agata are stuffed with it, iced snow-white, and finished with the cherry. Custard is the French/English standard; marzipan is another Sicilian classic but is usually shaped as fruit (frutta martorana); chocolate is not the traditional filling.

question: The archbishop of Agatha's city walked out in May 1886 to meet a lava flow crawling down Etna's south flank, carrying her veil before him. The lava, by tradition, halted at the outer walls of the village it had almost reached. Which village did the veil save, by that tradition?
context: Nicolosi sits high on Etna's south slope and has been threatened by lava many times; the 1886 procession is the most famous of all the veil-against-Etna stories. Zafferana Etnea on the east flank was saved from a 1992 flow (by lava barriers and dynamite, not the veil); Mascali on the northeast coast was destroyed by the 1928 eruption; Belpasso to the southwest was destroyed by the 1669 eruption (the same flow that reached Catania itself) and rebuilt.  (Legend.)

question: Agnes, a rich and beautiful girl in Rome, only twelve or thirteen years old, refuses every young nobleman who asks to marry her at the beginning of the fourth century AD. She has vowed her life to Christ and will take no husband. One rejected suitor, angry at being turned down by a child, takes a step that puts her in mortal danger. What does he do?
answer: Denounces her to the Roman authorities as a Christian
choices: Denounces her to the Roman authorities as a Christian
Challenges her father to a duel in the Forum
Kidnaps her from her family's estate
Buys her family's estates out from under them
context: Wikipedia: 'Slighted by her resolute devotion to religious purity, they submitted her name to the authorities.' The suitors expose her faith as a way of forcing her submission; it backfires into her execution. Source: Wikipedia, Agnes of Rome.

question: The Roman prefect Sempronius has Agnes before him in the early fourth century AD, a Christian girl of twelve or thirteen brought there by a suitor she has refused. Hoping to break the girl's resolve, he orders her taken from her family and marched through the streets of Rome to a place of public shame. To what place does he send her?
context: Wikipedia: 'The Prefect Sempronius condemned Agnes to be dragged naked through the streets to a brothel.' The Passio then reports that her hair miraculously grew long enough to cover her, and any customer who tried to approach her was struck blind. Legend, preserved in the medieval Passio and the Golden Legend. Source: Wikipedia, Agnes of Rome.

question: The prefect sentences Agnes to die. In one version the soldiers try to burn her at a stake, but the wood will not catch fire or the flames part around her, so a Roman officer steps forward with a sword. The bishop Ambrose tells it another way in his book On Virgins: the girl stands calm before the executioner. What does the executioner himself do as he takes his stroke?
answer: Trembles, as if he were the one condemned
choices: Trembles, as if he were the one condemned
Weeps and begs her forgiveness before the crowd
Turns his back so as not to see her face
Kneels and asks to be baptised on the spot
context: Ambrose of Milan, De Virginibus (c. 377 CE), gives the earliest full narrative of her death and describes the executioner as trembling to strike a girl so composed. Ambrose's account is a generation after Damasus's tomb epigram. Source: Wikipedia, Agnes of Rome.

question: Agnes's grieving parents come back to keep vigil at her tomb in a catacomb on the Via Nomentana, eight days after she dies for her Christian faith in the emperor Diocletian's persecution. A legend grows from what they see there, and it gives rise to a second feast called Agnes-secundo. According to that legend, what do her parents see at the tomb?
answer: Agnes standing among a flock of white lambs
choices: Agnes standing among a flock of white lambs
A single lamb at the tomb with a wound at its throat
A dove descending onto the tomb with a crown in its beak
A hand writing her name in Latin on the tomb wall
context: The legend behind Agnes-secundo ('Agnes second') held that eight days after her death Agnes appeared to her parents at her tomb surrounded by a flock of white lambs. The second feast was kept on 28 January until Pope John XXIII revised the Roman calendar in the 1960s. Source: Wikipedia, Agnes of Rome.

question: The Roman governor of Milan, Ambrose, was halfway through his speech to the crowded church, telling both sides to keep the peace during the bishop's election, when a single voice cried out from the assembly, 'Ambrose for bishop!' The whole packed church took up the shout as one. Whose voice, in the traditional story, started it?
choices: a soldier of the governor's guard
the widow of the dead bishop
context: Paulinus's Vita Ambrosii records that a child's voice began the acclamation and the packed church took it up at once. The detail has been told the same way since Paulinus, Ambrose's own secretary, wrote the Life around 412. Source: blog.oup.com/2011/12/ambrose.  (Legend.)

question: Ambrose tried to slip out of Milan by night rather than become the bishop the crowd was shouting for. He rode for the country estate of a personal friend, hoping to be hidden there until the crowd forgot him. According to his secretary Paulinus, what did the friend do?
answer: refused to hide him and gave him back
choices: refused to hide him and gave him back
hid him for a month in a wine cellar
took him on horseback into the Alps
smuggled him aboard a ship for North Africa
context: Paulinus's Vita Ambrosii records that Ambrose fled at night to the country house of a friend, but the friend, once he learned what had happened, refused to conceal him and turned him back over. Source: blog.oup.com/2011/12/ambrose.  (Legend.)

question: The crowd in Milan's church shouted the name of Ambrose in the year 374, when the city needed a new bishop. He was a Roman lawyer serving as governor of the province, no churchman, and he had never even been baptized. He tried to run, and gave in only when word arrived from a higher authority backing the crowd's choice. Whose word finally made him accept?
context: Valentinian I was the senior emperor in the West in 374, and Ambrose served as one of his governors; the emperor approved the people's choice of his own official, and that ended Ambrose's resistance. Julian had died in Persia in 363; Damasus was the bishop of Rome but had no authority to command a Milanese governor; Valens, Valentinian's brother, ruled the East. Source: Paulinus, Life of Ambrose 8.

question: In the Gospel of John, the fisherman Andrew leaves John the Baptist on the banks of the Jordan with another disciple and spends the day with Jesus at his lodgings. What does Andrew do straight away after meeting Jesus?
answer: Goes and fetches his brother Peter
choices: Goes and fetches his brother Peter
Rushes home to tell his father
Sells his fishing boat that day
Runs to the synagogue in Capernaum
context: John 1:40-42. Andrew was already a disciple of John the Baptist; he attaches himself to Jesus, then goes to find his brother -- who will later be renamed Peter.

question: Andrew, a Galilean fisherman, goes to find his older brother Simon as soon as he has stayed a day with Jesus, in the Gospel of John. He says one short line to Simon, and John's gospel preserves it, one of the first missionary sentences in Christian history. What does he tell his brother?
context: John 1:41, King James Version. It is Andrew, not Peter, who first uses the word 'Messias' in the gospel of John.

question: Andrew goes after Jesus on the banks of the Jordan, and the Greek Orthodox churches still honour that moment. They give this brother of Simon Peter, one of the twelve disciples, a special one-word Greek title that no other apostle shares. Which Greek title belongs only to Andrew?
context: Petros is Peter's nickname ('rock'); Boanerges is the epithet Jesus gives James and John ('sons of thunder'); Didymos is Thomas's nickname ('twin'). Andrew alone is Protokletos in the Eastern churches -- a title that stuck because John's gospel has him attach himself to Jesus before any of the other Twelve.

question: Andrew, brother of Simon Peter, preaches the Christian faith through Greece, tradition says, and is finally sentenced to be crucified there, in the city of Patras. But he is not put on the upright kind of cross Jesus died on. He is bound to a cross of a very different shape, and that shape becomes known ever after by his own name. What shape is Saint Andrew's Cross?
context: The saltire tradition (Andrew asking not to die on the same shape as Jesus) is later Western hagiography, not first-century record. But the X-cross is the shape that stuck.  (Legend.)

question: A medieval legend has a monk named Regulus carry some of the apostle Andrew's bones by sea and wreck his ship on a cold northern shore. The country there takes Andrew as its patron saint, flies his cross in white on a blue field, and keeps his feast day, 30 November, as its national day. Which country?
context: Scotland's flag is a white saltire on a blue field. Medieval legend says a monk named Saint Regulus brought some of Andrew's bones -- an arm bone, three fingers, a kneecap and a tooth -- shipwrecked to Fife, founding the town later called Saint Andrews. Spain claims James, Ireland claims Patrick, Portugal claims James as well through Compostela pilgrimage tradition.

question: Perseus flew home over the coast of Ethiopia on winged sandals, with the severed head of the snake-haired monster Medusa in a bag. He looked down and saw a young princess chained to a rock at the edge of a sea-cliff, and a monstrous sea-beast swimming in to eat her. What was that princess's name?
context: Andromeda, daughter of King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia of Ethiopia. Persephone (dragged to the underworld), Ariadne (Minos's daughter with the thread), and Antigone (Oedipus's daughter) are all real Greek princesses in famous tales, but none were chained to a sea-cliff.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus asked how the princess had come to be chained on the rock. He was told that her mother, the queen, had bragged that her daughter was more beautiful than the Nereids, and the great god those nymphs served took the boast as an insult. Which god took offense?
context: The Nereids were the fifty sea-nymphs of Poseidon's court; the insult to them was an insult to him, and he sent the monster Cetus in punishment. Zeus and Hera were famously jealous of mortal beauties (Semele, Io) but the Nereids were not their attendants; Dionysus punished many boasts (Pentheus, the pirates) but the Nereids were not his either.  (Legend.)

question: King Cepheus of Ethiopia chained his daughter to a rock by the sea as an offering. The queen's boast had brought a sea-monster to devour his coast, and an oracle said that only such an offering would stop it. What was the sea-monster called?
context: Cetus was the sea-monster (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.3). Scylla and Charybdis are real Greek sea-monsters but belong to the Odyssey and threaten Odysseus. Typhon was a monstrous storm-giant Zeus battled, not a sea-monster in this story.  (Legend.)

question: In the Roman poet Ovid's Metamorphoses, Perseus was flying over the coast of Ethiopia on his winged sandals when he spotted a princess chained to a rock. A sea-monster rose from the waves to devour her. He dived at it from above and killed it by stabbing it in the side. What weapon did he stab with?
answer: The harpe, the sickle-sword from Hermes
choices: The harpe, the sickle-sword from Hermes
A spear made from Cetus's earlier victim
A trident borrowed from Poseidon's temple
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.717-740: Perseus killed Cetus by driving his sickle-shaped sword (the harpe) into the monster's side. The harpe was the same divine sword Hermes had given him for beheading Medusa. Later Roman art sometimes shows him using the Gorgon head on Cetus, but Ovid's is the standard version.  (Legend.)

question: An armed band burst into the royal hall at Perseus's wedding feast, led by a man who shouted that the bride had been promised to him first. The bride was the Ethiopian princess Perseus had just rescued from a sea-monster, and her grateful father had offered him her hand. Who was this rival fiance?
context: Phineus, Andromeda's earlier suitor, burst in with armed men to reclaim her. Acrisius was Perseus's grandfather. Cepheus was Andromeda's father (and gave her willingly). Polydectes was the king back on Serifos who had sent Perseus for the head in the first place.  (Legend.)

question: Danae, the mother of Perseus, was hiding in a temple from the king who wanted her when her son sailed back with his bride to the island where a fisherman had raised him. On which island had Perseus grown up?
context: Serifos in the Cyclades: the fisherman Dictys had found the chest with Danae and baby Perseus, and Dictys's brother King Polydectes later coveted Danae. Delos (Apollo's birthplace), Aegina (Aeacus), and Ithaca (Odysseus) are famous Greek islands but not Perseus's.  (Legend.)

question: The king of the island sat at feast in his great hall with his nobles when Perseus walked straight in, told them what he had brought, and lifted the Gorgon's head from the bag one more time. The whole court turned to stone where they sat. Which king was petrified at his own dinner?
context: Polydectes of Serifos and his court were petrified at feast (Apollodorus 2.4.3). Cepheus (Andromeda's father) was spared. Acrisius (Perseus's grandfather) died later at Larissa by a badly-thrown discus. Proetus was the twin brother of Acrisius and Perseus's great-uncle, a real Argive king but not petrified.  (Legend.)

question: King Acrisius of Argos locked his daughter Danae and her baby Perseus, a son of Zeus, inside a wooden chest and threw it into the sea. The chest drifted to a small Aegean island where two brothers lived, the island's wicked king and a man named Dictys. Long after, Perseus would make Dictys king in his brother's place. On the day mother and baby came to the island, what had Dictys done?
answer: Pulled the chest from the sea in his fishing net
choices: Pulled the chest from the sea in his fishing net
Hidden the pair in a cave from Acrisius's soldiers
Carried the pair to the temple of Athena for sanctuary
Traded the pair to King Polydectes for a share of the catch
context: Dictys the fisherman drew the sealed chest out of his nets, opened it, and raised the boy Perseus as his own; his brother Polydectes was the king who later coveted Danae. The other three options are plausible-sounding but not the story told by Apollodorus and the Perseus tradition.  (Legend.)

question: The nymphs took back the winged sandals and the cap of invisibility once Perseus had beheaded the Gorgon Medusa, whose gaze turned men to stone. He returned each gift the gods had lent him. The polished bronze shield and the Gorgon's severed head went to a single goddess who had helped him plan the deed. Which goddess got the shield and the head?
context: Athena had guided Perseus from the start; she took the Gorgoneion and set it at the centre of her aegis, the goatskin storm-shield she wears on the chest. Hera was Heracles's enemy, not Perseus's helper; Artemis (hunt) and Demeter (harvest) had no part in Perseus's story.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus took his place in the northern night sky with the Ethiopian royal family and even the sea-monster, one constellation for each of them. One of them had a harder place than the rest. Which member of the family was set into her chair upside-down for half the year as her punishment?
context: Cassiopeia sits in her starry chair; the constellation rotates so that she hangs upside-down for half of each year, a punishment for her original boast about Andromeda's beauty. Andromeda, Cepheus, Perseus, and Cetus are also constellations, all near each other; Danae has no constellation.  (Legend.)

question: Odin was walking through Midgard with two other gods, long before the hero Sigurd was born, when the three stopped to rest at a waterfall. One of them was Honir. The third threw a stone at a small animal on the bank, and all the trouble of the Volsung story followed. Who was the third god?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14 and Reginsmal prose: the three travellers are Odin, Honir, and Loki. Thor is off in Jotunheim in most of Snorri's tales; Tyr belongs to the Fenrir story; Freyr is a Vanir god who rarely walks with Odin. Loki is the one who throws the stone -- and the trouble that follows fills the rest of the Volsung cycle.  (Legend.)

question: Three gods walking together came to the foot of a waterfall: Odin the All-Father, Honir the silent one and one more. They saw a small brown animal on the bank eating its catch, and the third god threw a stone and killed it in one shot. What kind of animal was it?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: the animal is an otter. Herons, beavers, and foxes were all known creatures of Norse country, but the specific animal in this story is the otter -- because it was really a man in otter-shape, as the gods will discover that night.  (Legend.)

question: Odin, Loki and Honir brought a pelt to a farmhouse and asked for shelter for the night, in the Norse tale that opens the Volsung saga. The master of the house, a wizard, wept when he saw it. The dead animal had been his own son, who took that shape to catch salmon in the river. What was the master's name?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: the wizard is Hreidmar. His shape-shifting son is named Otr. Andvari is a different dwarf altogether, whose ring will enter the story soon. Mimir is the guardian of the well of wisdom. Volund is the smith-hero of his own Eddic poem.  (Legend.)

question: Two brothers seized the gods Odin, Loki and Honir at the door of their father's house one night, after the gods killed a third brother who had taken animal shape. They held the three prisoner until a blood-price of gold was paid for the dead brother. The two names run through the whole Volsung story ever after. What were their names?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: Hreidmar's surviving sons are Fafnir and Regin. Sindri and Brokkr are the dwarves who forged Mjolnir; Fjalar and Galar murdered Kvasir for the Mead of Poetry; Baldr and Hodr are Odin's own sons in Asgard, not Hreidmar's.  (Legend.)

question: The gods sent Loki, who had thrown the fatal stone, to find enough gold to pay a blood-price. He went to a waterfall where a dwarf lived alone in the pool below, caught him and made him give up his whole treasure. What was the name of the dwarf whose gold Loki took?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: the dwarf is Andvari, and his hoard is the treasure of the whole Volsung cycle. Alviss is the all-wise dwarf whom Thor talks to death at dawn. Alberich is the name Wagner GAVE this same dwarf in Das Rheingold seven centuries later, but Andvari is his Norse name. Sindri forged Mjolnir with his brother Brokkr.  (Legend.)

question: A dwarf hid from Loki in the pool under his own waterfall, in the shape of a swift water animal that could vanish among the rocks. He hoarded a great treasure there, and Loki had come for gold to pay the blood-price the gods owed. What form was the dwarf in when Loki finally caught him?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: Andvari was in the shape of a fish (a pike, in most tellings). Loki caught him in a net borrowed from the sea goddess Ran, the net in which she gathers drowning sailors. Frogs, water-snakes and swans do not appear in the story.  (Legend.)

question: The dwarf of the waterfall surrendered his whole hoard to Loki, but he tried to keep back a single small band of gold, hoping Loki would not notice. Loki spotted it and took it too. This one ring has its own name in the Volsung cycle. By what name is that ring known?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14 and Reginsmal prose: the ring is Andvaranaut, which means 'Andvari's gift.' Draupnir is Odin's arm-ring, which drips eight new rings every ninth night. Sviagris is the boar-ring of the Swedish king Adils in Snorri's Skaldskaparmal. Brisingamen is Freyja's necklace, forged by four dwarves. Wagner later built his Ring of the Nibelung on Andvari's ring, and readers often see its pattern in Tolkien's One Ring -- but Andvaranaut is the Norse original.  (Legend.)

question: The trickster god Loki caught a dwarf at his hidden waterfall and forced him to hand over his entire hoard of gold, down to his last ring. As the ring left his hand, the dwarf spoke aloud over it, and the Volsunga saga preserves his words. He cursed the ring and the whole hoard together. What fate did the curse promise every future holder of the ring?
answer: it would be the death of whoever owned it
choices: it would be the death of whoever owned it
it would blind whoever looked at it
it would turn whoever wore it into a slave
it would burn whoever touched it to ashes
context: Volsunga saga: the dwarf went into a hollow of the rocks and cried out that the ring, and all the gold with it, should be the bane of every man who owned it. In the Edda poem Reginsmal his curse comes in verse instead: the gold will bring death to two brothers and strife to eight princes. Readers have long set Andvari's cursed ring beside Tolkien's One Ring.  (Legend.)

question: Loki brought the treasure back to the wizard whose son the gods had killed, and helped cover the otter-pelt with gold. Odin tried to keep the last ring for himself, hidden in his fist. But the wizard walked around the pelt inspecting the payment and refused it because of one thing he could still see. What did he see on the pelt that made him demand more gold?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: a single whisker of the otter-pelt was still visible above the gold. Hreidmar refused to release the gods until it was covered. Odin was forced to give up Andvaranaut to cover the last whisker -- and so the ring, and the curse, passed to Hreidmar.  (Legend.)

question: The wizard took the gold and the ring as the blood-price for his son, and in the Edda poem Reginsmal the curse soon struck. He was stabbed to death in his sleep, and one figure took the whole hoard alone and drove the surviving kin off empty-handed. Who killed the wizard for the cursed gold?
answer: his own son Fafnir in a rage
choices: his own son Fafnir in a rage
his own son Regin in a rage
the dwarf Andvari come for revenge
the god Loki come back for the ring
context: Reginsmal prose: Fafnir ran his sword through his father as he slept and took all the gold, and when Regin asked for his share of the inheritance, Fafnir refused him. The Volsunga saga has Fafnir slay his father too. (In Snorri's Prose Edda the two brothers plot the killing together.) Regin will later plot his revenge. Andvari never leaves his waterfall. Loki does not come back for the ring -- he is out of the story once the ransom is paid. The curse claims its first life soon after the ring leaves Andvari's hand.  (Legend.)

question: Fafnir carried the entire hoard, ring included, to a lonely heath called Gnitaheid and settled down there alone. Over the years gold-greed slowly changed him. What did he gradually turn into, guarding the cursed gold on Gnitaheid?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: Fafnir became a dragon (in Old Norse ormr, sometimes translated 'serpent' or 'worm'). Wolves belong to Fenrir; stone giants to Hrungnir; the eagle is the shape the giant Thiazi wears when he carries off Loki. Regin will nurse his grudge for years and eventually foster the boy Sigurd, who will kill the dragon Fafnir with the sword Gram -- and take the cursed ring for himself, and die of it too.  (Legend.)

question: Loki the trickster slips away from his loyal wife, the goddess Sigyn, in Asgard to a secret lover in Jotunheim, the wild land of the giants. She is a giantess whose very name is a warning: in Old Norse it means 'she who brings grief'. What is her name?
context: Snorri names her Angrboda in Gylfaginning 34 of the Prose Edda. Skadi is the giantess-bride of the sea-god Njord; Gerd is the giantess Freyr wins in Skirnismal; Hyrrokkin is the giantess who later launches Baldr's funeral ship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angrboda  (Legend.)

question: A giantess in Jotunheim, the land of the giants, bears the trickster Loki three monstrous children. Two of the three are terrible beasts, a great wolf named Fenrir and a huge sea-serpent named Jormungandr. The third child is a girl. What is the girl's name?
context: Snorri lists the three siblings in Gylfaginning 34: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungandr the serpent, and Hel the girl. Gerd is the shining giantess Freyr wins as bride in Skirnismal; Skadi is the giantess who marries the sea-god Njord; Nott is the giantess of night whose son is Day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson, writing in Iceland in the 1220s, describes Loki's daughter Hel, who rules the underworld. She has a shocking body: one side of her face and body is the pink of a living woman. The other side is something very different. What is the other side of Hel like?
context: Snorri writes that Hel is 'half black and half flesh-coloured' -- the corpse-side and the living-side joined in one body. Ice belongs to the giant Ymir's origin; fire to the fire-giant Surt of Muspelheim; the raven is Odin's bird. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: The gods bring the giant wolf Fenrir up inside Asgard, right among them, to keep him under control. But the wolf grows so fast and fierce that only one god will still walk up to feed him. Which god has the nerve?
context: Snorri says only Tyr had the courage to give Fenrir food. Tyr later loses his hand when the gods trick the wolf into being bound. Thor is the thunderer; Heimdall is the watchman of the rainbow bridge; Bragi is the god of poetry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenrir  (Legend.)

question: Odin hurls Jormungandr, the serpent child of Loki and the giantess, into the great ocean that runs all the way round Midgard, the world of men, where the serpent starts to grow. He grows so long that he wraps the whole world, and he does one memorable thing with his own body. What does he do?
choices: swallows the sunken sun each night
sleeps with one eye always open
context: In Gylfaginning the serpent grew so vast in the ocean around Midgard that he encircled the entire world and grasped his tail in his mouth. Because he lies in the sea round Midgard he is called the Midgard-Serpent or World-Serpent, Jormungandr. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jormungandr  (Legend.)

question: Hel takes up her rule over the dead in the misty underworld of Niflheim. But she does not receive every dead soul. The warriors slain in battle are carried up to the hall of Valhalla instead. Which dead does Hel receive in her cold underworld?
answer: those who die of sickness or old age
choices: those who die of sickness or old age
those killed by their own kin
those who die without a name
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Odin gives Hel authority over all who die of sickness or old age. Warriors killed in battle are chosen by the valkyries for Odin's Valhalla and Freyja's Folkvangr. The drowned in later folklore belong to the sea-giantess Ran. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: Snorri gives Hel's underworld hall a full grim inventory: a dish called Hunger, a knife called Famine, a bed called Sick-Bed, and a threshold called Stumbling-Block. The hall itself has a name too, from a word meaning 'sprayed with damp'. What is Hel's hall called?
context: Snorri names the hall Eljudnir ('sprayed with damp / rain-damp'). Bilskirnir is Thor's own hall in Thrudheim; Valaskjalf is Odin's silver-roofed hall; Sessrumnir is Freyja's hall in Folkvangr. Every object in Eljudnir is a grim pun on death. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: Hel's two servants creep through her dreary underworld hall with punning names built around slowness. Snorri says the manservant's name means 'slow-mover' and the maidservant's name means 'slow-goer'. What are the two servants called?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: the servant is Ganglati and the maidservant Ganglot -- everything in Hel's hall moves as slowly as death itself. Huginn and Muninn are Odin's two ravens; Geri and Freki his two wolves; Skoll and Hati are Fenrir's OWN two wolf-sons who chase the sun and moon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: The great wolf Fenrir breaks loose at Ragnarok, the final battle at the end of the world, when the gods and their monstrous enemies destroy each other. He gets the biggest kill of all: he swallows one god whole. Which god does Fenrir swallow at Ragnarok?
context: In Gylfaginning and Voluspa, Fenrir breaks loose at Ragnarok and swallows Odin the All-Father. Odin's son Vidar avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart. Thor dies fighting Jormungandr; Frey falls to the fire-giant Surt; Heimdall and Loki kill each other. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenrir  (Legend.)

question: Anthony, an orphan in a Nile village, heard the gospel read around 270: 'sell what you have and give to the poor.' He gave his land to his neighbours, sold the rest for the poor, and later left for good. Where did he go?
context: The verse was Matthew 19:21: 'If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell what thou hast, and give to the poor.' Anthony (c. 251-356 CE) becomes the most famous of the Desert Fathers and the founding figure of Christian monasticism. Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: Anthony shut himself inside an old empty place carved into the cliffs for his first years away from his village, after he gave away his lands in third-century Egypt. In that place, the story says, the demons fell on him and beat him out cold. What kind of place had Anthony chosen?
context: Athanasius's Vita Antonii (c. 360 CE) says a friend brought bread one morning, found Anthony unconscious on the floor of the tomb, and thought he was dead. Anthony revived, insisted on being carried back, and shouted at the demons, 'Here I am, Anthony; I do not flee from your blows!' Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: Crowds of visitors kept finding the hermit Anthony, so he moved deeper into the wilderness and sealed himself inside an abandoned Roman fort by the Nile. He stayed behind a bricked-up door with only a small hole through which friends passed him bread. How long did he stay shut in there?
context: When pilgrims finally break down the door after twenty years, they expect a wraith, and find Anthony 'the same as before,' in perfect physical health. He emerges to teach and quickly becomes the most famous man in Christian Egypt. Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: Jerome tells how Anthony, as an old man, set out across the desert to visit an even older hermit, Paul of Thebes, and met a creature straight out of Greek myth along the road. It pointed out his way and then vanished into the sand. What creature did he meet?
context: Jerome, Vita Pauli 7. The creature, which Jerome calls a HIPPOCENTAUR (half-horse, half-man), makes 'a sort of guttural noise,' then extends its right hand to indicate the direction Anthony seeks. A little further on Anthony meets a satyr who asks him to pray for its kind. Legend from Jerome's romantic Life. Source: New Advent, Jerome Vita Pauli.

question: A bird came to the cave of Paul of Thebes while the old hermit sat talking with Anthony, in Jerome's telling, as it had come every day for sixty years, carrying bread for Paul. This time, because there were two of them, the bird brought a whole loaf instead of half a loaf. What bird was it?
context: Jerome, Vita Pauli 10. Paul says, 'For the last sixty years I have always received half a loaf; but now Christ has doubled his soldier's rations.' The raven-feeding-a-hermit motif echoes 1 Kings 17, where ravens feed the prophet Elijah at the brook Cherith. Legend. Source: New Advent, Jerome Vita Pauli.

question: Anthony stood over the body of the old hermit Paul of Thebes, in Jerome's Life of Paul, wanting to bury him. He had no spade, and he was too old to dig with his hands. Two animals came out of the desert, mourned beside the body, then pawed a grave into the sand. What animals were they?
context: Jerome, Vita Pauli 16. Two lions come, whimper over Paul's corpse, then dig a hole 'just large enough to hold a man.' Anthony wraps Paul in the cloak that had been given to him by the bishop Athanasius of Alexandria. Legend. Source: New Advent, Jerome Vita Pauli.

question: Anthony walked out of the desert to a great Mediterranean city around 311 to visit jailed Christians, one of only two trips to a city in his long life. Around 338 he went back to the same city to help his friend the bishop Athanasius. Which city was it?
context: Alexandria is the great see of Coptic Egypt and the seat of Athanasius. The Arian controversy (which denied the full divinity of Christ) was the theological fight of the 4th century, culminating in the Council of Nicaea (325). Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: A few disciples stood by Anthony in a cave in the Egyptian wilderness as he died, at over a hundred years old. He gave them one last instruction, one very specific request about his body. What did he ask them to do?
answer: Keep his burial place a secret
choices: Keep his burial place a secret
Send his cloak to the emperor at Constantinople
Burn his body on a pyre
Bury him with the pagan hermits he had known
context: Anthony feared the growing cult of relics and asked to disappear from the world as he had lived in it. His grave was in fact unknown for centuries; relics later claimed as his were moved to Constantinople in the 6th century and to France in the 11th. Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: A monk of the Order of Saint Anthony took in a sufferer at one of the order's hospitals in medieval Europe, the man's arms and legs rotted black by ergotism, a horrible disease that came from moldy rye bread. The order was named for the third-century Egyptian desert hermit, and because of the monks' work the disease itself took the saint's name. What name was it known by?
context: Ergot poisoning produced a burning sensation and gangrene in the limbs. The Hospitallers of Saint Anthony ran hospices for its sufferers from the 11th century onward. (Distinct from 'Saint Anthony's Bread,' a modern charitable custom of Anthony of Padua, a different, later saint.) Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty, rode in a chariot drawn by one kind of bird, in later art at least. The same bird perched on her statues and nestled in pairs at her feet. What bird was sacred to Aphrodite?
context: The dove was Aphrodite's own bird; the peacock belonged to Hera (its eyes are the eyes of Argus); the owl to Athena; the eagle to Zeus. Doves drew her chariot in later art, and pairs of doves were often shown at her feet.  (Legend.)

question: In Hesiod's Theogony, the Titan Cronus took a sharp sickle to his own father Ouranos, god of the sky, and hurled the cut part far out into the sea. Where it fell, white foam spread across the water, and out of that foam a full-grown goddess rose up onto the waves. Which Olympian was born this way?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 176-206. Hesiod explicitly derives Aphrodite's name from the Greek word 'aphros' (foam). Athena was born from Zeus's head; Artemis on Delos to Leto; Hera is Cronus's daughter. This is the oldest and strangest birth-story of any Olympian.  (Legend.)

question: In Hesiod's Theogony, the foam-born goddess drifted over the sea and reached the small island of Cythera before going on to a larger island, whose name became one of her most-used titles. On which larger island did she come ashore?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 192-200. From this landing come her epithets Cypris (Lady of Cyprus) and Cyprogenes (Cyprus-born); Cythera gave her the epithet Cytherea. In the sixth Homeric Hymn it is Zephyr, the west wind, whose breath wafts her over the waves to Cyprus. The temple of Aphrodite at Paphos on Cyprus was one of the great cult centres of the ancient world.  (Legend.)

question: Aphrodite rose full-grown from the foam of the sea and came ashore, and ancient statues and later paintings often showed her standing on the same kind of seashell. Artists made that shell her badge, and centuries later pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela took it up as theirs. What kind of shell was it?
context: The scallop shell became the signature emblem of the goddess in art from antiquity onward, though Hesiod himself mentions no shell. The same scallop shell later became the badge of Christian pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela -- an odd echo across the traditions.  (Legend.)

question: The foam-born goddess of love and beauty stepped onto the beach of her island at last, in Hesiod's telling, and something remarkable happened to the earth wherever her bare feet touched it. What happened beneath her feet?
answer: Fresh green grass sprang up out of the soil
choices: Fresh green grass sprang up out of the soil
Salt crystals hardened out of the sea-spray
Wet footprints appeared that would never fade
Springs of fresh water welled up from the sand
context: Hesiod, Theogony 194-195: 'grass grew up about her beneath her shapely feet.' The scene is the origin of the tradition, in painters from Botticelli to the modern age, of scattering roses and myrtles around her feet.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess borrowed Aphrodite's magical embroidered girdle in Book 14 of Homer's Iliad, to distract Zeus on Mount Ida from the Trojan War. The belt had the power to make anyone who saw its wearer fall helplessly into love. Who borrowed it?
context: Homer, Iliad 14.214-217. Hera wanted to draw Zeus's attention away from the battlefield so the Greeks could regain ground; she borrowed the kestos himas (embroidered girdle) from Aphrodite, and Zeus was undone: beguiled, he fell asleep in a golden cloud on the summit of Ida. Leto, Demeter, and Thetis all have their own stories with Zeus but none borrow the girdle.  (Legend.)

question: Diomedes, a mortal hero, wounded Aphrodite on the battlefield in Homer's Iliad, and she fled weeping up to Olympus, where her mother, a Titaness, comforted her. Homer's story was completely different from Hesiod's sea-foam birth. According to Homer, who was Aphrodite's mother?
context: Homer, Iliad 5.370-430. In Homer's genealogy, Aphrodite is simply the daughter of Zeus and Dione -- one of the older Titanesses, worshipped beside Zeus at his oracle of Dodona. So the ancient world had two Aphrodites side by side: Hesiod's foam-born Heavenly one (Urania), and Homer's Zeus-daughter Common one (Pandemos). Plato in the Symposium makes both of them serious.  (Legend.)

question: Sandro Botticelli, the Italian painter, finished a famous picture of Aphrodite around 1485. It now hangs in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, and the image is so well known that it shapes how Western art still shows the goddess. What is the painting called?
context: Now in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence. Primavera is another Botticelli of the same period, showing Venus in a spring grove but not her birth. Venus Anadyomene ('Venus Rising from the Sea') is the ancient Greek term for the type-scene, most famously painted in antiquity by Apelles. The Judgment of Paris is a different Aphrodite story painted by many hands. But Botticelli's Birth of Venus is THE picture.

question: The mother of Apollo and Artemis clutched a palm tree on a small floating island and gave birth to the twins. Apollo was the bright god of music and prophecy, Artemis the archer-goddess of the wild woods, and their father was Zeus, king of the gods on Mount Olympus. Who was their mother?
context: Leto was a Titaness, daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, and one of Zeus's early lovers. Maia is the mother of Hermes; Metis is the mother of Athena; Demeter is the mother of Persephone. All four are divine mothers of Olympian children -- easy to confuse.  (Legend.)

question: Hera, jealous, told every land to turn Apollo's mother away, and the pregnant goddess wandered with no shelter. In the end one small floating island took her in and anchored itself to the sea floor so she could give birth under a palm tree. What was the island called?
context: Homeric Hymn to Apollo 25-88. Delos was a bare rocky island in the Cyclades; because it had been drifting, Hera's command against 'land' had not bound it. Delphi is where Apollo will later plant his oracle, not where he is born.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo was still a young archer god when he set out to hunt a great female serpent that Hera, queen of the gods, had sent to torment his mother. The beast lived in a rocky chasm on the slopes of Mount Parnassus in central Greece. Apollo tracked her down and shot her dead with his silver bow. What was the serpent called?
context: Homeric Hymn to Apollo 300-374. The name Python comes from the Greek verb 'pytho,' 'to rot' -- for the serpent's body rotting inside the chasm after Apollo buried her there. The Hydra was killed by Heracles; the Chimaera by Bellerophon; Typhon by Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo killed a giant serpent on the slopes of Mount Parnassus and took the place as his own. It became the most famous oracle in the Greek world. Kings and cities sent messengers there to ask about war, marriage, and new colonies. What is that place called?
context: Delphi sat in a great natural amphitheatre of rock high above the Gulf of Corinth. Dodona in Epirus was the oracle of Zeus, delivered by the rustling of an oak; Olympia was the shrine of Zeus with the games; Eleusis was the sanctuary of Demeter and Persephone. Delphi was considered the omphalos, the navel of the world.  (Legend.)

question: The Pythia took her seat to give Apollo's answers at his great oracle on Mount Parnassus, and it was no normal chair. She sat on a special bronze seat set right over the crack in the ground where the sacred vapor was said to rise. Copies of that seat were set up as prizes at every big Greek sanctuary. What was the seat called?
context: Plutarch, De Pythiae oraculis; Diodorus 16.26. Tripods dedicated to Apollo were among the most prized victory-offerings a Greek city could make. The Serpent Column at Delphi -- looted from Delphi in the sixth century and now in Istanbul -- was the base of one such tripod, dedicated after the Greek victory over Persia at Plataea.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo broke off his first branches of one sacred plant in the Vale of Tempe after killing the serpent, when he went there to purify himself. Before speaking her prophecies, his priestess the Pythia chewed its leaves, and his prize-winners were crowned with a wreath of it. What was the plant?
context: In myth the nymph Daphne, fleeing Apollo's pursuit, was turned by her father into the first laurel tree -- and Apollo, unable to marry her, wore her leaves in his hair ever after. Ivy is sacred to Dionysus; olive to Athena; myrtle to Aphrodite. Roman generals in triumph wore the laurel of Apollo.  (Legend.)

question: A pilgrim climbing to Apollo's temple on Mount Parnassus, the most famous oracle in the Greek world, read two short Greek sayings carved above the entrance before he went in to hear the god. One of the two was 'Know thyself', in Greek gnothi seauton. What was the other?
context: Pausanias 10.24.1; Plato, Protagoras 343a-b. Ancient sources attributed these two maxims (and a third, 'Surety is ruin') to the legendary Seven Sages of Greece, dedicated at Delphi as the first-fruits of their wisdom. 'Know thyself' became the founding motto of Greek philosophy from Socrates onward.

question: Croesus, the enormously wealthy king of Lydia, sent envoys with gold to Apollo's oracle to ask what would happen if he attacked the growing Persian empire. The Pythia answered that if he crossed the river Halys, he would destroy a great empire. Croesus crossed the Halys. Which empire was destroyed?
context: Herodotus 1.53 and 1.86-91. Cyrus of Persia defeated Croesus in battle, took Sardis, and burned Croesus on a pyre before pardoning him at the last moment. The story became the ancient world's founding lesson about the ambiguity of oracles: the god had not lied, but the questioner had not thought to ask WHOSE empire.

question: In Apollodorus's telling, Apollo killed the Cyclopes who forged Zeus's thunderbolts, after Zeus struck down Apollo's son Asclepius. Zeus sentenced him to atone: for a term of years the god had to serve as a plain mortal servant in the household of King Admetus of Pherae. What kind of work did the god do there?
answer: He herded the king's cattle in the pastures
choices: He herded the king's cattle in the pastures
He copied scrolls in the king's library
He guarded the palace gate as a spearman
He served wine at the king's table
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.10.4; Callimachus, Hymn to Apollo 47-49. During his service Apollo became so fond of Admetus that he later intervened with the Fates to spare Admetus's life on the day he was to die -- the seed of the Alcestis story dramatised by Euripides.  (Legend.)

question: Athena sat down at her loom against the mortal weaver Arachne and wove her own famous victory over another god into the centre of her tapestry, for the naming of the city of Athens. It showed her olive tree beating what he had struck from the rock. Which god did Athena show herself defeating in that central scene?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.70-82. In the story Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident and made a salt-spring gush out; Athena struck the same rock and made an olive tree grow. The people of Athens chose the olive, and the city took her name. Around the borders Athena wove four cautionary scenes of mortals turned into mountains and birds for having challenged the gods.  (Legend.)

question: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, the mortal weaver Arachne challenged the goddess Athena to a contest at the loom and, instead of praising the gods, wove twenty-one scenes of gods disguising themselves as animals or objects to trick and abduct mortal women. One god appeared in her tapestry far more often than any other. Which god was it?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.103-128. Ovid lists nine of Arachne's twenty-one scenes as Zeus in one disguise or another -- swan, eagle, satyr, shower of gold, flame, shepherd, snake, and other shapes -- each targeting a different mortal woman. Poseidon has six, Apollo four, and Bacchus and Saturn one each.  (Legend.)

question: Arachne wove a great white bull into one of her twenty-one panels, walking up to a princess picking flowers on the shore of Sidon. He knelt so she could climb on his back, then charged into the sea and swam her all the way to Crete. Who was the bull, and who was the princess?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.833-875 (the fuller telling) and 6.103-104 (Arachne's panel). Europa was a Phoenician princess; the continent of Europe is named after her. Arachne wove other Zeus-disguise scenes into the same tapestry -- as a swan to Leda, as a golden shower to Danae -- but the bull-and-princess panel is the most famous of the twenty-one.  (Legend.)

question: A young mortal weaver named Arachne boasted, in the Roman poet Ovid's telling, that she could weave better than the goddess Athena herself, patroness of weaving. Athena appeared in her workshop and challenged her to a contest at the loom. Arachne's finished tapestry was so perfect that Athena could not find a single flaw in it. What did the angry goddess do to the tapestry?
answer: She ripped it to shreds with her own hands
choices: She ripped it to shreds with her own hands
She turned it into smoke with a wave
