context: Luke 2:9 KJV: 'and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid.' The pillar of fire belongs to Moses and the Exodus; the burning wheel to Ezekiel's vision; the star of the east to Matthew's account of the magi -- not this scene.

question: In Luke's telling, angels filled the sky above the shepherds outside Bethlehem, praising God for the newborn child. Luke wrote their song out in two halves. The first half is 'Glory to God in the highest.' What is the second half?
answer: and on earth peace, good will toward men
choices: and on earth peace, good will toward men
and blessed be the name of the Lord forever
and let all the earth keep silence before him
and holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts
context: Luke 2:14 KJV: 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.' 'Blessed be the name of the Lord forever' is from the Psalms; 'let all the earth keep silence before him' is from Habakkuk 2; 'holy, holy, holy' is the seraphs' song in Isaiah 6.

question: The shepherds ran to town after the angel's news, found Mary and Joseph and the baby, and spread abroad what the angel had told them out in the field. Luke then paused on Mary alone, in one gentle verse about her response. What did Luke say Mary did?
answer: kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart
choices: kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart
knelt beside the manger and prayed silently until dawn
closed her eyes and said nothing for a long time
sang a psalm under her breath over the sleeping child
context: Luke 2:19 KJV: 'But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.' Mary's louder song, the Magnificat ('My soul doth magnify the Lord'), came earlier in Luke 1 at her cousin Elisabeth's house -- not here at the manger.

question: In the letter of the Lyon churches, torturers worked on a young slave girl in shifts from morning to evening in 177 AD. Her Christian mistress had feared she was too weak to hold out. By the end the men said they were worn out and did not know what more to try. What was the girl's name?
context: Blandina was a slave of a Christian household of Lyon and, according to Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica V.1, held out longer than any of her fellow-martyrs. Perpetua was the young noblewoman of Carthage killed in 203, Agnes and Cecilia the famous Roman virgin-martyrs of a later century; all four are real, but the slave-girl in Gaul is Blandina.

question: Blandina, a young slave girl, stood before her torturers in the Roman city of Lyon in 177 AD, and they worked on her all day trying to break her. According to the letter Eusebius later quoted in his Church History, she gave one sentence to every question. What did she keep saying?
answer: 'I am a Christian, and we do nothing to be ashamed of.'
choices: 'I am a Christian, and we do nothing to be ashamed of.'
'Into thy hands I commend my spirit.'
'Not my will, but thine, be done.'
'The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.'
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.19. The Latin martyr formula is 'Christiana sum'. The other three are also famous sayings from the western tradition -- the last words of the psalm and of Jesus on the cross, the prayer in Gethsemane, and Tertullian's line from his Apology written a generation later. Only one belongs to the Lyon slave-girl.

question: The wild beasts sent into the arena would not touch Blandina, so the Roman officials had her taken back to prison and saved for the last day of the games. She was brought out again that day, paired with a fifteen-year-old boy. What was the boy's name?
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.53. Sanctus, Attalus and Maturus were all also martyrs of the same Lyon pogrom named in the letter -- Sanctus the deacon of Vienne, Attalus the Roman citizen, Maturus a recent convert. But the fifteen-year-old boy at the climax, whom Blandina encouraged until he died, was Ponticus.

question: Blandina urged on a fifteen-year-old boy in the amphitheatre at Lyon until he died at her side, and then it was her turn. The letter of the churches says the Romans had several torments ready, and after the whips they fastened her to a piece of red-hot metal before the crowd. What piece of metal was it?
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.56 says the iron chair was heated red-hot. The iron grid (gridiron) belongs to the third-century Roman deacon Lawrence; the copper altar to various Old Testament sacrifices; the bronze bull is the tyrant Phalaris's roasting-machine of Sicilian legend. All four are real instruments in the western imagination, but the one at Lyon in 177 was the iron chair.

question: In one of the earliest Christian martyr accounts, the guards at Lyon wrapped Blandina in a heavy net and drove her into the ring, where a horned animal charged and tossed her on its horns again and again. She would not die, and finally a gladiator was sent in to finish her with a dagger. What kind of horned animal was it?
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.56 -- a young bull, driven at her by the arena-keepers. A wild cow was the beast at Carthage that killed the noblewoman Perpetua in 203, a close and deliberate parallel arena-death for a Christian woman; boars and bears also appear in other martyr-accounts. But the animal at Lyon was the steer.

question: The Roman officials at Lyon burned the bodies of all the martyrs of the year 177 AD and threw the ashes into flowing water, for the current to carry away, so that no relics could ever be gathered. Into what river did they throw the ashes?
context: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.61-63, says the pagans deliberately scattered the ashes in the Rhone 'so that not a single relic of their bodies might be left on earth' -- which shows the pagan authorities already understood exactly what the young Christian custom of relic-veneration was going to become. The Saone joins the Rhone at Lyon; the Loire and the Garonne are the other great rivers of Gaul, running to the Atlantic. Only the Rhone carries the Lyon ashes in the letter.

question: The Roman governor at Lyon asked the city's bishop point-blank, 'Who is the god of the Christians?' The bishop was a very old man, over ninety, the surviving letter of the Lyon churches says, and he had been hauled before the tribunal in 177 AD. What did he answer?
answer: 'If you are worthy, you will know.'
choices: 'If you are worthy, you will know.'
'A god who is greater than Caesar.'
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.29-31. The old man's name was Pothinus; he was beaten so badly that day that he died in prison two days later. The other three are all real Christian answers of the martyr age (from Polycarp, Justin, and the Apostles' Creed) but only one is Pothinus's reply at Lyon in 177.

question: A goddess of the Tuatha De Danann, the divine race of old Irish myth, fled across the plain of Meath with the waters of a sacred well chasing her. She drowned, and myth says her body became the water of the River Boyne, which runs past the great mound of Newgrange to the Irish Sea. Which goddess drowned?
context: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann: Boann is the eponymous goddess of the River Boyne (Irish An Bhoinn). Brigid is the goddess of poetry, healing, and the smith-fire at Kildare; Danu is the mother-goddess of the Tuatha De Danann as a whole; Aine is a Munster sun-and-fertility goddess.  (Legend.)

question: The god Nechtan of the Tuatha De Danann guarded a hidden well at the mythic heart of Ireland, and only his three cup-bearers might come near it. It was the sacred source of all wisdom, ringed with nine trees whose nuts dropped into the water, and it was forbidden to all others. What was that well called?
context: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann and Nechtan (mythology): the Well of Segais (also called Connla's Well) was the mythic source of the Boyne. Only Nechtan and his three cup-bearers could approach it. The Well of Urd is the Norse well beneath Yggdrasil where the Norns sit; the Cauldron of Dagda is a different Tuatha De treasure; the Spring of Aengus is not a named source.  (Legend.)

question: The Salmon of Knowledge, in the Fionn mac Cumhaill story, fed on nuts that dropped into the water from a ring of magical trees. The same trees grew around the hidden well of the god Nechtan, and their nuts fell into the water and drifted downstream. What kind of trees were they?
context: The Well of Segais is ringed by hazel trees whose nuts carry wisdom -- they drop into the water, the salmon eat them, and any human who eats such a salmon gains the salmon's knowledge (Fionn burns his thumb on such a salmon and sucks it, gaining the gift). Oak, rowan, and yew are all sacred Irish trees but do not carry the wisdom-nut motif.  (Legend.)

question: Boann, a proud goddess and the wife of the god Nechtan, refused to be forbidden the sacred well at Ireland's heart, ringed by trees whose nuts held all the world's wisdom. Only Nechtan and his cup-bearers were permitted to approach it. She went straight to the well and, right at its brim, made one deliberate act of defiance. What did Boann do at the well?
answer: walked three times around it counter-sunwise
choices: walked three times around it counter-sunwise
spoke a curse into the water
cut down one of the hazel trees
washed her hair in the source
context: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann: Boann walked three times around the Well of Segais tuathal -- against the sun, counter-clockwise, which in Irish tradition is the direction of ill omen and of ritual challenge. Sun-wise (deiseal) is the direction of blessing; counter-sunwise is the direction of defiance and destruction.  (Legend.)

question: Boann defied her husband Nechtan's rule over the sacred well, and the well answered her immediately. Its waters burst up and chased her down the plain of Meath, tearing at her as they went and becoming the River Boyne. What three parts of her body did the flood strip away before drowning her?
answer: an arm, a leg, and an eye
choices: an arm, a leg, and an eye
her hair, her hands, and her tongue
her voice, her sight, and her memory
her cloak, her sword, and her name
context: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann: the risen waters tore off Boann's arm, her leg, and her eye as they pursued her -- the classic Irish triple-blemish, the same body-perfection-broken that puts a king off the throne (as Nuada's lost hand did). She drowned in the flood; the flood kept running and became the river.  (Legend.)

question: In the tale called The Wooing of Etain, the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De Danann, stopped the sun in the sky for nine months so that Boann's husband Elcmar would not see her pregnancy. The child seemed to be born in a single day. He grew up to own the great mound at Newgrange on the Boyne, one of the best-loved figures of Irish myth. Who was that son?
context: Aengus (Aengus Og, 'Aengus the Young') is the son of the Dagda and Boann. In Tochmarc Etaine the Dagda made the sun stand still for nine months so Boann's husband Elcmar would not notice the pregnancy, and Aengus was born in the space of a day; in the Dindshenchas, Boann's husband is Nechtan. Lugh is a later Tuatha De hero (grandson of Balor); Ogma is the god of eloquence and inventor of ogham writing; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god.  (Legend.)

question: An English monk named Winfrid crossed the Rhine into Germany in the early 700s, to preach to the still-pagan Hessians and Thuringians. The pope in Rome gave him a new Latin name meaning roughly 'good-doer.' What name did the pope give him?
context: Winfrid was renamed Boniface ('good deeds') by Gregory II in 719 and made a missionary bishop for Germania. Willibrord was his older colleague, the apostle of the Frisians; Columbanus was the Irish monk who evangelized Gaul and Italy a century earlier; Aidan founded Lindisfarne. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Boniface.

question: Boniface walked up to a great sacred tree at Geismar in 723 and began to chop. It belonged to Donar, the thunder-god whom the Norse called Thor. A crowd of pagans stood watching, certain the god would kill him. What kind of tree was it?
context: The tree at Geismar near Fritzlar was an oak, the species most often held sacred in Germanic paganism (Roman writers had already identified Jupiter/Thor with the oak). The yew was sacred in Celtic tradition; the ash was Yggdrasil in Norse cosmology; the linden was the classic village gathering-tree of medieval Germany. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donar%27s_Oak.  (Legend.)

question: Willibald tells in his life of Boniface how the missionary made only a few cuts in a giant tree sacred to Thor, in front of the whole tribe, before a great blast of wind rose. The huge tree crashed down and split cleanly into equal trunks. Into how many parts did it burst?
context: Willibald's account (chapter 6, c. 760) specifies four trunks of huge size and equal length lying on the ground. The crowd who had been cursing Boniface as an enemy of their gods now believed and blessed him when Donar sent no lightning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donar%27s_Oak.  (Legend.)

question: The pagans at Fritzlar in central Germany watched Boniface chop down Thor's sacred tree in 723, and no thunderbolt fell. From its wood he immediately built a small chapel on the same spot, turning the old cult-site into a Christian shrine. To which saint did he dedicate the new chapel?
context: Willibald says the oratory was dedicated to Saint Peter the apostle, tying the Hessian mission directly to Rome and to the pope who had sent Boniface. Michael and Martin were the two other patrons most common for German early-medieval churches; Paul was less commonly the sole dedicatee of missionary chapels. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donar%27s_Oak.  (Legend.)

question: Boniface went back in old age to preach in Frisia, the coastland of the modern Netherlands. On 5 June 754 he waited by the river Borne for a group of new converts he was to confirm, and an armed pagan band attacked him and about fifty companions instead. Near what Frisian town was Boniface killed?
context: The martyrdom took place near Dokkum in what is now the northern Netherlands. Utrecht was the see of his colleague Willibrord; Nijmegen and Deventer were later Carolingian centers. The attackers, expecting treasure in the missionaries' chests, broke them open and found only manuscripts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Boniface.

question: In the old tradition, Boniface held a book up over his head as the pagan band struck, and the killing sword-blow cut clean through it. A codex in the cathedral treasury at Fulda still bears the deep gashes and is venerated as that very book. What is this manuscript called?
context: The Ragyndrudis Codex is a late 7th or early 8th century collection of fourteen Latin exegetical and dogmatic texts (interestingly, not actually a gospel, though the 10th-century Utrecht vita of Boniface calls the shield-book 'a gospel'). Its original binding and pages bear cuts long identified with the martyrdom. The Codex Amiatinus was made at Bede's Wearmouth-Jarrow; the Book of Kells and Lindisfarne Gospels are Insular gospel books unrelated to Boniface. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragyndrudis_Codex.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn mac Cumhaill leads the warrior-band called the Fianna, and he roams across Ireland with a great pack of hounds. Two of them are his favorites: they can outrun any deer, and they know every word he says to them. What are the two hounds called?
context: Bran and Sceolang (Sceolan, Sgeolan) are Fionn's chief hunting hounds in the Fenian Cycle. Cerberus and Orthrus are the three-headed and two-headed guardian hounds of the Greek pillar (Hades and Geryon). Garmr is the hound at the gate of Hel and Fenrir the wolf who kills Odin in the Norse pillar. Argus is Odysseus's dog and Laelaps the Greek hound that always caught its prey.  (Legend.)

question: In the Fenian tales of Ireland, Fionn mac Cumhaill treats his two favorite hounds as kin. A woman of his own family had been turned into a hound while carrying them, so they were born as pups. What kinship do the two hounds bear to Fionn?
context: Bran and Sceolang's mother, Uirne (also called Tuiren), was the sister of Fionn's own mother Muirne, which makes the hounds his first cousins. In a variant Uirne is Fionn's sister and the hounds are his nephew and niece, but the cousin-relation is the most common version. Fionn treats them accordingly.  (Legend.)

question: A woman of Ireland is carrying twins when a spell turns her into a hound, in the Irish tale The Birth of Bran, and she gives birth to her pups in that changed shape. They grow up to be Fionn's two great hounds. What is her name?
context: Uirne / Tuiren was married to Iollan of the Fianna. She was transformed while pregnant, hence her twin children were born as hounds. Deirdre is the tragic heroine of Longes mac nUislenn in the Ulster Cycle; Grainne elopes with Diarmuid from Fionn himself; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife, also in the Ulster Cycle.  (Legend.)

question: A woman named Uchtdealb curses the pregnant wife of Iollan of the Fianna into a hound, in the Irish myth The Birth of Bran. She is a jealous rival, an old lover of the husband, come to punish his new wife. To what people does Uchtdealb belong?
context: Uchtdealb (also spelled Uct Dealv) was a woman of the Sidhe, the faery folk, and had been the lover of Iollan before he married Tuiren. The Sidhe in Irish tradition are what the Tuatha De Danann became after their defeat, retreating into the hollow hills. The Fomorians are the older sea-monsters defeated at Mag Tuired; the Milesians are the ancestors of the modern Irish; the Fir Bolg are one of the older invader-peoples.  (Legend.)

question: In The Birth of Bran, the jealous Uchtdealb comes to her rival disguised as one of Fionn's own messengers. She lures the woman out of her husband's house, alone into the woods, and strikes her on the shoulder to change her shape. With what object does she strike the blow?
context: The hazel is the Irish tree of magic and wisdom (the hazels of Segais drop their nuts into the Salmon of Knowledge's pool); the druid's rod of transformation is characteristically hazel. A sword-stroke would have killed rather than transformed. The golden apple is a Greek pillar object (Atalanta, the Judgement of Paris). Yew is the tree of death in Irish tradition, not of shape-shifting.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn finds out what the jealous Uchtdealb has done and forces her to lift the spell, and the mother is a woman again. But her two whelps stay hounds for the rest of their lives. Why can the spell on them not be undone?
answer: they were born while their mother was a hound
choices: they were born while their mother was a hound
they had drunk from a faery well after birth
they had been named by Fionn before their mother was freed
the Sidhe queen had bound them separately with a golden collar
context: Uirne was already carrying the pups when she was transformed, and she gave birth to them as a hound. When the spell on the mother was broken, James Stephens's retelling says, the enchantment on the two whelps could not be. No faery well, collar or naming plays any part in the tale.  (Legend.)

question: Sceolang runs with Fionn's pack in a great hunt called the Chase of Thrush Glen, and one Fenian tradition says she meets her death there. The strange quarry is half black and half white. What are she and the pack running down?
choices: a wild boar with iron bristles
a black horse with a red mane
context: The half-black, half-white deer of the Chase of Thrush Glen was an enchanted creature, and Sceolang died in the chase. Enchanted deer run through many Fenian tales, echoing the shape of Fionn's own wife Sadhbh. The boar of Ben Bulben kills Diarmuid, not the hounds; the black horse with red mane is a horse-of-the-Sidhe motif but not the quarry here; no giant hare runs in this chase.  (Legend.)

question: Nuada, king of the Tuatha De Danann, lost his hand in a great battle, and Irish law would not let a maimed king rule. The gods chose in his place the handsomest man of his generation, called 'the Beautiful.' What was his name?
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 14-24: Bres (Bres mac Elathan) was elected king of the Tuatha De after Nuada stepped down, chosen partly for his looks and partly for his half-Fomorian blood, which was meant to make peace with the enemy. Ogma is the god of eloquence; Dian Cecht is the god of healing (who later replaces Nuada's hand with a silver one); Manannan is the sea-god.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann crowned a beautiful young king called Bres to replace Nuada, partly to keep the peace. He had the goddess Eriu for a mother and, for a father, a prince of Ireland's oldest enemies. Which people were they?
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 14: Bres's father was Elatha, a Fomorian prince (the Fomorians were the sea-raiders and monstrous elder-race of Irish myth, ruled by Balor of the Evil Eye). The Milesians are the human ancestors of the modern Irish who arrive AFTER the Tuatha De; the Fir Bolg are an earlier people the Tuatha De defeated at the FIRST Battle of Moytura; 'the Danaans' is another name for the Tuatha De themselves.  (Legend.)

question: King Bres let his own kin squeeze the Tuatha De Danann with heavy tribute, and the load grew so bad that the gods had to work the fields like slaves. What lowly job was the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De, forced to do?
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 25: under Bres's tyranny the Dagda ('the good god,' chief of the Tuatha De and owner of the club, the harp, and the cauldron of plenty) was forced to dig ditches and trenches around forts like a common labourer -- an especial humiliation for a god of abundance. Ogma was the one made to carry firewood; grinding grain and sweeping the hall are jobs from other tales.  (Legend.)

question: Bres broke the great obligation of an Irish king, to give food, drink and gifts freely to any guest and above all to poets. When a Tuatha De poet arrived at his hall for a night's stay, what was he served for dinner?
answer: three dry cakes and no meat or ale
choices: three dry cakes and no meat or ale
a single slice of raw pork
a bowl of watered barley porridge
nothing but a cup of cold water
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 39: Bres housed the poet in a small dark room and had him served three small dry cakes on a plate -- no meat, no butter, no ale. For an Irish king of the heroic age this was a shocking insult; hospitality (Irish oigidecht) was the king's first sacred duty.  (Legend.)

question: In the old tale Cath Maige Tuired, the poet Coirpre walked out onto the hillside above King Bres's hall one morning, after a night in a dark little room and a mean supper. He did something with his voice that no bard in Ireland had ever done before. What did he compose?
answer: the first satire ever made in Ireland
choices: the first satire ever made in Ireland
the first battle-hymn ever sung in Ireland
the first curse ever cast in Ireland
the first lament ever wept in Ireland
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 39 and the medieval Irish tradition on satire: Coirpre's poem against Bres (the name is also spelled Cairpre) is said to be the first satire (Irish aer) ever composed in Ireland. Satire in old Irish law was so feared that satirists had legal protection and named damages; the story of Bres is the mythic charter for that whole power.  (Legend.)

question: King Bres gave the poet Coirpre a mean welcome, and in the morning Coirpre spoke a poem against him. In Charles Squire's 1905 retelling, something then broke out on the king's face that Irish law refused to accept in a king, the same kind of unfitness that had put Nuada off the throne when he lost his hand. What broke out on Bres?
context: Cath Maige Tuired itself says only that there was blight on Bres from that hour; the Tuatha De soon demanded that he give up the kingship, and he begged seven years' grace. The great red blotches come from Charles Squire's retelling, The Mythology of the British Islands (1905), which follows the old Irish belief that a poet's satire could raise blotches on its victim's face. Old Irish law required a king to be unblemished, which is why Nuada had to step down for his lost hand.  (Legend.)

question: Irish legend tells of a fifth-century chieftain's daughter who gave her father's food, cloaks and cattle to the poor. At last he let her take the veil. She founded a great abbey and became one of Ireland's three patron saints. What was her name?
context: Brigid (Old Irish Brigit), traditional dates c. 451 to 524/525 CE, daughter of the Leinster chieftain Dubthach and (in most Lives) a Christian slave-woman Broicsech baptized by Patrick. Hilda ruled the Northumbrian abbey of Whitby in the seventh century; Clare founded the Poor Clares at Assisi in the thirteenth; Genevieve is the patroness of Paris. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Saint Brigid founded her abbey around 480 on a spot where a great oak already stood. The place's old Irish name, Cill Dara, means 'church of the oak,' and her byname comes from it. What is the town called in English?
context: Cill Dara, the church of the oak, is Kildare, county town of County Kildare in Leinster. All four choices are real Irish places whose names begin with Cill, meaning 'church'. Killarney (Cill Airne, the church of the sloes) is a lake town in Kerry; Kilkenny (Cill Chainnigh, the church of Cainneach) is a different Leinster town; Kilcullen is a village in County Kildare but not Brigid's shrine. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Kildare'; Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Saint Brigid of Kildare lived in Ireland around the year 500, but her name is far older. She shares it with a goddess of poetry, healing, smithcraft and above all fire, said to be the daughter of a great chieftain-god of the Tuatha De Danann. Who was the goddess's father?
context: In Irish myth the goddess Brigit is a daughter of the Dagda ('the good god'), chief of the Tuatha De Danann. Lugh Lamhfhada is the spear-wielding sun-hero; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god; Nuada Silver-Arm is the earlier king of the Tuatha. The saint inherits her fire-associations, her name, and her feast-day from this goddess. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Brigid, the chieftain's daughter who grew up to be Ireland's great saint, gave things away to any beggar at the door. In the most famous kitchen miracle of her girlhood, she handed the family's whole food-crock to a poor man. Her mother came home in a rage, but when they opened the crock it was brimming again, fuller than before. What food had Brigid given away?
context: The specific food is butter, and the miracle makes Brigid the patron of dairy work, milkmaids, and the safe keeping of the family cow. All four are staples of an early-medieval Irish household kitchen. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.  (Legend.)

question: A king refused Saint Brigid the ground for her convent, so she asked for only as much as her cloak would cover. She laid it on the ground, and it spread over acres of his flat green plain. Kildare still stands there, in one of Ireland's five old provinces. Which province?
context: Kildare lies in Leinster, the province of the east, whose king in the legend grants Brigid the ground her stretched cloak covers. Munster is the south, Ulster the north, and Connacht the west; the fifth province Meath contained the High King's seat at Tara. Source: Brigidine Sisters, 'Legend of St Brigid's Cloak'; Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Gerald of Wales traveled through Ireland in the twelfth century and described a fire kept burning day and night at Kildare in honor of Brigid, a flame that was never allowed to go out. The nuns tended it in strict rotation, each keeping it for one full night in turn. How many nuns made up the rotation?
context: Gerald of Wales wrote in Topographia Hibernica (c. 1188) that nineteen nuns took turns keeping the fire, one per night; on the twentieth night, the tradition ran, Brigid herself came and tended it, and the flame never went out. He said the fire had been burning since Brigid's own lifetime, and some traditions make its first keepers priestesses of the older goddess before they were nuns. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.  (Legend.)

question: Saint Brigid founded her monastery at Kildare in the late 400s, and it was a rare thing in Christendom: a double monastery, with separate houses of nuns and monks under one abbess. Brigid was that abbess. She ruled alongside a hermit and metalworker she had invited down out of the hills to be Kildare's first bishop. What was his name?
context: Conleth (Conlaed) was a metal-worker and hermit whom Brigid invited to Kildare as its first bishop; the two are traditionally buried together in the old cathedral. Ciaran founded Clonmacnoise; Kevin founded Glendalough; Finnian founded Clonard. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Saint Brigid of Kildare is counted one of the three patron saints of Ireland. Two other early Irish saints from the fifth and sixth centuries share that honor with her -- one the missionary who first brought Christianity to Ireland, the other the abbot who later founded the great monastery on the island of Iona off Scotland. Which pair stands beside Brigid?
context: The three national patrons of Ireland are Patrick (fifth-century British-born missionary bishop who converted the island), Brigid (Kildare, fifth to sixth century), and Columba, also called Colum Cille (sixth-century abbot who left Derry and founded Iona in 563). Kevin (Glendalough), Ciaran (Clonmacnoise), and Malachy (twelfth-century reformer) are all major Irish saints but not among the three national patrons. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Irish myth tells of a daughter of the Dagda, a great goddess of the Tuatha De Danann. She watched over poetry, healing and the forge, and had a title for each: of the Poets, of the Healers, of the Smiths. What was her name?
context: Brigid is uniquely the goddess who owns all three crafts, and her name is thought to mean 'the Exalted One'. Danu is the mother-figure of the Tuatha De; Boann is the goddess of the River Boyne; the Morrigan is the war-and-crow goddess. Wikipedia: Brigid.  (Legend.)

question: An old Irish glossary from the 800s calls Brigid the goddess whom poets adored. It explains that she is really three sisters, all bearing the same name, one for each of her separate crafts. Which other Irish goddess appears in this three-in-one pattern?
context: The Morrigan is likewise a triple-goddess (Morrigan, Macha, and Badb, or in other lists Morrigan, Nemain, and Badb) -- a war-goddess made of three sisters. Danu, Boann, and Aine are single goddesses. Wikipedia: The Morrigan; Sanas Cormaic.  (Legend.)

question: Saint Brigid's feast falls on 1 February, and the date was not chosen at random. On the older Gaelic calendar the day was already a great festival, one of the four quarter-days of the turning year: the first day of spring, when the lambing began and the ewes came into milk. What was it called?
context: Imbolc (1 February) is the first of the four great quarter-days of the Gaelic year, when the ewes come into milk. The other three fire-festivals are Beltane (1 May, cattle driven between fires), Lughnasadh (1 August, the first harvest), and Samhain (1 November, the year's end when the dead walk). Brigid's feast overlays Imbolc exactly. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Imbolc'; Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.  (Legend.)

question: Irish families weave a small four-armed charm from freshly cut rushes every year on 1 February, the feast of Saint Brigid and the old Gaelic first day of spring. With a woven square at its middle, it hangs over the front door to guard the house through the coming year. What is the charm called?
context: The Brigid's cross is one of the most recognisable Irish folk-objects: rushes cut fresh on February 1, woven in a few minutes, hung above the threshold. Wikipedia: Brigid's cross.  (Legend.)

question: The Bethu Brigte, the ninth-century Old Irish Life of Saint Brigid, tells of a startling moment at her consecration. Mel read the wrong rite over her by mistake and would not withdraw it, saying the honor had come from God. No woman was supposed to hold the office he gave her. What was it?
choices: an abbot of a men's house
context: Bethu Brigte, ch. 19: Mel reads the ordinal for a bishop over Brigid and refuses to withdraw it, saying the honour has come from God. Many scholars read the episode as the priestess-authority of the goddess absorbed into the saint. Wikipedia: Bethu Brigte; Brigid of Kildare.  (Legend.)

question: The Lebor Gabala Erenn, the Book of Invasions, credits the goddess Brigid with a set of sacred animals: two named oxen, a 'king of boars' called Torc Triath and a 'king of wethers' called Cirb. All of them shared one strange power. What could they do?
answer: cry out whenever plundering happens in Ireland
choices: cry out whenever plundering happens in Ireland
speak human speech on Samhain night
context: The Lebor Gabala reports that Brigid's beasts raise a cry across Ireland the moment any theft or raid is done -- a guardianship shared across her whole animal household. Wikipedia: Brigid.  (Legend.)

question: Young Sigurd, fresh from killing the dragon Fafnir and the smith Regin, rode up a great mountain. From far off he saw a great light on its summit, as if a fire were blazing up to the sky. What was the mountain called?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 21 and the prose introduction to the Poetic Edda's Sigrdrifumal: the mountain is Hindarfjall, meaning 'Hind Mountain.' Gnitaheid is the heath where Sigurd killed Fafnir the dragon in the previous story. Bifrost is the rainbow-bridge between Midgard and Asgard. Yggdrasil is the world-tree. Hindarfjall is the specific peak of this wake-scene.  (Legend.)

question: Odin himself, in the shape of an old greybeard, helped young Sigurd choose a grey colt from a herd of horses. In a later adventure that horse alone would carry a rider through a wall of flame. What was the name of Sigurd's horse?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 13-21: Grani is Sigurd's horse, chosen for him by Odin in disguise as an old man, and descended from Odin's own eight-legged steed Sleipnir. Sleipnir belongs to Odin, not Sigurd. Gullfaxi is the golden-maned horse of the giant Hrungnir, later given to Thor's son Magni. Hofvarpnir is the goddess Gna's horse. Later, when Sigurd rides to win Brynhild for Gunnar, Gunnar's own horse balks at her wall of fire and Grani will not stir under Gunnar; only with Sigurd in the saddle does Grani leap the flames.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd reached the summit and found a hall walled with shields. Inside, a figure lay in full war-armour, helm on the head, sword at the side. He bent to unlace the helm, expecting to see a slain warrior's face. What did Sigurd find under the helm?
choices: a stone carving with no face
a wolf curled in a heap
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 21 and Sigrdrifumal prose 2-5: under the helm is a sleeping woman. The saga lingers on Sigurd's mistake -- he came expecting a dead warrior and found a living Valkyrie. There is no carving, no dwarf-corpse, and no wolf in the hall. The whole point of the scene is the shock of unlacing armour and finding a woman's face.  (Legend.)

question: The sleeper in the mail-coat lay as if she would never wake. Only when Sigurd slit the mail open with his sword, the blade biting 'as if it were cloth,' did she open her eyes and ask what thing of great might had drawn her from her sleep. What was her name?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 21: the saga calls her Brynhild. In the Eddic poem Sigrdrifumal the sleeper names herself Sigrdrifa, and the saga takes her to be Brynhild. Freyja is the Vanir goddess of love and battle who owns half of Valhalla's slain. Sigrun and Skuld are two other named Valkyries from the Norse corpus. Brynhild is the specific Valkyrie of this story.  (Legend.)

question: The Valkyrie told Sigurd how she came to be sleeping on the mountain. Odin had already promised victory in her last battle to an older king named Hjalmgunnar. She disobeyed and awarded the day to a younger king instead. What was the name of the young king she gave the victory to?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 21; Sigrdrifumal prose 4: the young king is Agnar. Hrothgar is the Danish king in Beowulf. Sigmund is Sigurd's own father, a previous Volsung. Helgi is Sigurd's half-brother, hero of the Helgi lays. Agnar is the specific name in the Brynhild-punishment story.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd meets the Valkyrie in an old poem of the Poetic Edda, and the poem breaks off in mid-sentence inside the single manuscript that carries it. Scholars have to finish his story from a later prose saga. What has happened to the manuscript at that exact spot?
answer: a whole gathering of pages is missing
choices: a whole gathering of pages is missing
a monk erased the vellum to reuse it
the ink faded in a house-fire
a page was cut out and sent abroad
context: The Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda has a physical gap at this point -- an entire gathering (a folded set of vellum sheets) is lost. Editors call it 'the great lacuna.' There was no erasure and no fire; the leaves simply went missing before the codex was rebound. Because of the lacuna, everything between Sigurd leaving Hindarfjall and arriving at the Gjukungs' court has to be reconstructed from the later prose Volsunga Saga.

question: Gudrun and Brynhild go down to the river one day to bathe, and there the two queens quarrel. Gudrun is Sigurd's wife and Brynhild is Gunnar's. What do they quarrel about?
answer: whose husband is the greater warrior
choices: whose husband is the greater warrior
which queen is the more beautiful
which brother should sit on the high seat
who owns the golden hoard of Fafnir
context: Volsunga Saga, the queens' quarrel: Brynhild wades farther out into the river than Gudrun, and when Gudrun asks why, the rivalry comes out as a contest over the husbands' honour -- whose man is greater, and who rode the flaming fire. It is the boast about husbands that starts the whole doom.  (Legend.)

question: Brynhild boasts at the river that only Gunnar crossed the fire around her mountain. Gudrun laughs and says Sigurd crossed it, wearing Gunnar's face. To prove it, she holds up a single object Sigurd took from Brynhild that night. What does Gudrun hold up as her proof?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 30: Gudrun holds up the ring Andvaranaut, which Sigurd had taken from Brynhild's finger during the shape-swap night and given to Gudrun. The lock of hair belongs to a different Norse story (Sif's hair, cut by Loki). A broken helm and a torn shift are not in this scene. The ring is the object that makes the quarrel deadly, because Brynhild recognises it at once.  (Legend.)

question: Brynhild goes straight home from the quarrel at the river and takes to her bed. She has been tricked into marrying Gunnar, while the hero she loved has married Gunnar's sister Gudrun. For seven days and seven nights she does one thing that frightens the entire household. What does she do?
context: Volsunga Saga: Brynhild takes to her bed and lies there as if dead; she answers Gunnar nothing and drinks neither mead nor wine, and Gudrun says that for seven days and seven nights no one has dared to wake her. When Sigurd at last asks why she will not speak to anyone, her fury breaks out.  (Legend.)

question: Gunnar comes in at last and asks Brynhild what is wrong, as she lies on her bed in cold fury. She has found out that Sigurd disguised himself as Gunnar to ride through a wall of flame and win her as Gunnar's bride. What does Brynhild demand of Gunnar as the price of the deception?
choices: that Sigurd be banished across the sea
that Sigurd swear a new oath in her presence
context: Volsunga Saga: Brynhild tells Gunnar that Sigurd has betrayed them both and that it shall be Sigurd's death, or Gunnar's, or her own; then she warns that she will go home to her kin unless he kills Sigurd and Sigurd's young son. She does not ask for exile, for the gold, or for a fresh oath -- only for his death. The rest of the cycle turns on Gunnar's answer.  (Legend.)

question: Gunnar and his brother Hogni cannot lift a hand against Sigurd. Years earlier at Gjuki's hall the three men swore an oath, and it now binds Gunnar and Hogni from raising a weapon against him. What oath did Gunnar, Hogni and Sigurd swear to each other?
choices: a joint quest for Andvari's gold
loyalty to King Gjuki their father
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 26-32: Sigurd, Gunnar, and Hogni had mingled blood from their arms in the earth and sworn foster-brotherhood -- Old Norse fostbraedralag. The marriage to Gudrun was a separate transaction. The quest for Andvari's gold was over long before Sigurd came to Gjuki's court. Loyalty to King Gjuki did not bar personal murder. The oath specifically forbade one of them to raise a hand against another, and that is why Gunnar must find someone else.  (Legend.)

question: A boy named Guttorm, the youngest brother of Gunnar and Hogni, will not lift a sword against the greatest hero in the north on his own. To make him wild enough for the deed, his brothers seethe the flesh of two creatures together and feed it to him. What two kinds of flesh go into the dish?
context: Volsunga Saga: the brothers take a serpent and some wolf's flesh, seethe them together and give them to Guttorm to eat, and the verse the saga quotes sets the dish in his wine. That and his mother Grimhild's urging make him wild enough to walk into the bedroom of Sigurd Fafnir-slayer with a drawn blade. Raven and goat, hare and salmon, and bear and stag are all Norse animals but not this recipe.  (Legend.)

question: The dying Sigurd hurls his sword after Guttorm, the youngest brother of King Gunnar, as the boy flees the bedchamber. The blade catches him from behind and cleaves him clean in two. The saga preserves the exact place on his body where it struck. Where does the sword strike Guttorm?
answer: across the middle of his back
choices: across the middle of his back
at the base of the skull
context: Volsunga Saga: Gram strikes Guttorm in the back and cuts him asunder in the middle, so that his feet and legs fall one way and his head and hands fall back into the room where Sigurd lies dying. It is one of the most-remembered images in the whole saga.  (Legend.)

question: Brynhild laughs once aloud on the day the hero she loved dies, when she hears his widow moan. Later she hands out her gold to anyone who will take it and turns a sword on herself. Before she dies she asks a favour of her people. What does Brynhild ask them to do with her body?
answer: to burn her on Sigurd's funeral pyre
choices: to burn her on Sigurd's funeral pyre
to bury her at the foot of Hindarfjall
to lay her in Freyja's temple at Uppsala
to place her body back inside the ring of fire
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 33 and Sigurdarkvida hin skamma stanzas 49-71: Brynhild asks to be burned on the same pyre with Sigurd, and asks that the sword Gram be laid unsheathed between their bodies -- as it had lain between them on the shape-swap night when Sigurd first slept beside her wearing Gunnar's face. She is not buried at Hindarfjall, not sent to Uppsala, and not returned to the ring of fire. The pyre-with-sword-between-them is the specific request the saga preserves.  (Legend.)

question: King Arthur, the young king who pulled the sword from the stone, set his court in one city of the old British legends. His knights feasted in its great hall and rode back there to report each finished quest. What was Arthur's capital called?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, passim; Wikipedia: Camelot. Tintagel is where Arthur was conceived by Uther Pendragon. Avalon is the enchanted island where the wounded Arthur is carried at the end. Glastonbury is a real Somerset abbey where medieval monks later claimed to have found Arthur's tomb.  (Legend.)

question: The Norman poet Wace gave a plain reason around 1155 for the shape of King Arthur's Round Table. Arthur's court suffered one ugly problem at its feasts, Wace said, and the king meant to end it. What problem was the table built to stop?
answer: barons quarrelling over who sat highest
choices: barons quarrelling over who sat highest
assassins hiding behind the hall pillars
spies overhearing counsel through open doors
poison being slipped along the high table
context: Wace, Roman de Brut (c.1155): each of Arthur's noble barons thought himself the best, and none would accept a lower seat than another, so Arthur made the Round Table, where all sat as equals. A round table has no head and no foot, so every seat is equal in dignity. Assassins, spies, and poisoners are all real medieval court-worries, but the Round Table specifically solves the seating-rank problem.  (Legend.)

question: King Arthur married Guinevere, the daughter of a lesser British king, in Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur. Her father sent the Round Table along with her as a dowry, a great table he had kept safe since Uther Pendragon's day. Which king gave the Round Table to Arthur?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book III ch.1. Leodegrance is Guinevere's father and the king of Cameliard; he had the Table from Uther Pendragon. Pellinore is the king who broke Arthur's first sword. Uriens is Morgan le Fay's husband. Bagdemagus is the king of Gorre in Chretien's Lancelot.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Thomas Malory wrote Le Morte d'Arthur, the great collected Arthurian book, while sitting in prison, and he gave King Arthur's Round Table an exact seating count. Every seat, he said, had the name of the knight worthy to sit there written in gold letters around the rim. In Malory's telling, how many knights did the table seat?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book III ch.1: Leodegrance sends the Table 'and a hundred knights' with it -- Arthur later fills the remaining seats, and Malory gives 150 as the count of the fellowship at its full strength. Twelve is the round number of Charlemagne's Twelve Peers of France, not Arthur's fellowship. Twenty-four is the number of knights' places painted on the Winchester table, not Malory's count. Three hundred is the count of Roman senators.  (Legend.)

question: One seat at King Arthur's Round Table stood empty year after year in Malory's telling, waiting for a knight who had not yet come. Merlin, who made it, warned what would happen to any other knight bold enough to sit there. What fate did he foretell for such a knight?
answer: he would be destroyed where he sat
choices: he would be destroyed where he sat
he would be struck blind for life
he would be turned to stone
he would be cast out of the fellowship
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur: the seat was the Siege Perilous, and Merlin warned that if any knight but the one destined for it dared to sit there, he would be destroyed. At Pentecost Galahad came, his name appeared in letters of gold on the seat, and he sat in it unharmed. 'Siege' is Old French for seat or throne.  (Legend.)

question: An English king ordered the bare oak Round Table at Winchester painted with Arthur and his knights, reportedly to impress the visiting emperor Charles V. The table itself, built in the 1200s, hangs on the wall of Winchester's great hall, eighteen feet across and over a ton in weight. Which king ordered the paintwork?
context: Wikipedia: Round Table. The oak table itself was built c.1250-1280 in the reign of Edward I but was left plain. It was Henry VIII who ordered the surviving paintwork -- Arthur enthroned above a Tudor-rose centre, the names of the knights around the rim -- to impress Charles V during his 1522 state visit. Richard the Lionheart lived a century before the table was built; Alfred the Great five centuries before.

question: John Leland, the Tudor antiquary, rode through Somerset in 1542 and heard the local people call one hill the true seat of Arthur's court. Leslie Alcock dug there from 1966 to 1970 and found a major refortification from Arthur's era, though no proof it was his. Which hill did Leland record?
context: Wikipedia: Camelot. John Leland recorded the Cadbury tradition in 1542; Leslie Alcock's 1966-1970 excavations at the hillfort found evidence of major refortification 'by a Brittonic ruler and his war band from c. 470' -- exactly the era of the historical Arthur, if there was one. Cadbury Castle is in Somerset. Glastonbury Tor is a nearby Somerset religious hill. Maiden Castle is a huge Iron Age hillfort in Dorset. Silbury Hill is a neolithic mound in Wiltshire.

question: Agravaine and Mordred accused Lancelot of loving Arthur's queen in the last books of Malory, and the quarrel split the Round Table into two warring parties. Lancelot killed Gareth and Gaheris when he rescued Guinevere from the stake. Which knight, after losing those two brothers, led the party demanding vengeance?
context: Malory, Books XX-XXI. Gawain leads the party demanding Lancelot's punishment after Lancelot kills Gawain's brothers Gareth and Gaheris in the rescue of Guinevere from the stake. Sir Bors is Lancelot's own kinsman and stays loyal to him. Percival died in the East after the Grail quest. Kay has faded by the end of the book. The Gawain-Lancelot feud is what ends the Round Table.  (Legend.)

question: The chief druid of Ulster gathered his young pupils one morning at King Conchobar mac Nessa's royal fort of Emain Macha, to teach them to divine what would come to pass. He also served as the king's chief adviser. What was this druid's name?
context: Cathbad is the chief druid at Emain Macha and stands beside Conchobar throughout the Ulster tales. Amergin was the great druid of the Milesian invasion who chanted the land into their possession; Mug Ruith is the huge blind wheel-riding druid of Munster; Fintan mac Bochra is the salmon-shaped survivor of the Flood in Irish tradition. All are druids, but Cathbad is the Ulster chief.  (Legend.)

question: Cathbad was teaching his pupils outside the fort of Emain Macha one morning, reading the fitness of the day. Any warrior who took up arms for the very first time on this day, he told them, would win fame everlasting through Ireland. But the day of arms carried a price. What was the price?
answer: he will live only a short life
choices: he will live only a short life
he will lose the use of one eye in his first battle
he will father no son to carry his name
he will never sleep under a roof again
context: Cathbad's day-of-arms prophecy is the Irish equivalent of Achilles's choice: fame or long life, not both. Losing an eye is Odin's price for wisdom in the Norse pillar; the son-less price echoes Cuchulainn's later grief over Connla; sleeping under no roof is a geis (taboo) on other heroes, not the day-of-arms condition.  (Legend.)

question: Cathbad learned that King Conchobar had armed the boy Setanta that very morning, and he came before the king in anger and rebuked him for it. The boy answered the druid with a single line that sealed his character for the rest of the Tain, the great cattle-raid tale. What did the boy say?
answer: that a short life with lasting fame is better than a long life without it
choices: that a short life with lasting fame is better than a long life without it
that no druid's word could bind a warrior of Ulster
that his mother had already promised the fate to him
that only the sword would tell what the day would bring
context: The boy's answer is the Ulster Cycle's version of the Achilles-choice speech from the Iliad and it seals his character for the rest of the Tain. Denying druid-authority is Ferghus's later stance, not the boy's here. His mother Deichtine is not part of this scene. The 'sword will tell' line is not attested.  (Legend.)

question: Cathbad stood over the newborn daughter of Feidlimid and foretold that she would grow into the fairest woman in Ireland and be a disaster for Ulster. His words terrified the whole court, and the warriors demanded that the child be killed at birth. Whose birth was this?
context: The tale is Longes mac nUislenn, 'The Exile of the Sons of Uisliu'. Cathbad prophesied that Deirdre would bring blood, ruin, and exile on the men of Ulster. Medb is the Connacht queen who raises the Tain against Ulster; Macha (of the twins) is the goddess-figure who curses the Ulstermen with their debility; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife, and no such prophecy is attached to her birth.  (Legend.)

question: King Conchobar mac Nessa refused to let his warriors kill a newborn girl, though their swords were already drawn. Cathbad had just prophesied over her that her beauty would one day bring disaster on the men of Ulster. What did Conchobar do with the infant instead?
answer: had her raised in isolation so he himself could marry her when she was grown
choices: had her raised in isolation so he himself could marry her when she was grown
gave her in fosterage to a smith of the border country
sent her to be reared by the druids of Emain Macha
cast her adrift in a leather bag on the western sea
context: Conchobar's plan was to keep Deirdre hidden away with tutors and never let her see any young man until she was of age for him. She saw Naoise anyway, one of the sons of Uisliu, and eloped with him -- which set off the tragedy Cathbad had foretold. The smith-fosterage recalls the Setanta / Culann story; druid-fosterage is Finn Emna's youth in a different tale; the leather bag on the sea is the birth-exposure of Taliesin in the Welsh tradition.  (Legend.)

question: Ulster's greatest warrior guaranteed the safety of the sons of Uisliu, and King Conchobar treacherously killed them. Cathbad's prophecy over a newborn girl was coming true. Shamed, the warrior left for the court of Queen Medb of Connacht, then led her army against his own people in the great cattle-raid of the Tain Bo Cuailnge. Which warrior was he?
context: Fergus mac Roich had guaranteed safe conduct to the sons of Uisliu, and Conchobar's treachery in killing them dishonoured Fergus so utterly that he left Ulster forever. In the Tain he is the great Ulster exile in Medb's army. Conall Cernach and Loegaire Buadach stayed with Ulster and fought for Conchobar. Sualtam is Cu Chulainn's mortal father, not an exile.  (Legend.)

question: The warriors of Ulster drew their swords at a newborn girl's cradle and demanded that the child be killed at once. Cathbad had just laid a prophecy over her, naming three things that her beauty would bring on the men of Ulster. Which three things did he name?
context: The prophecy of Longes mac nUislenn -- 'The Exile of the Sons of Uisliu' -- is Cathbad's most famous cradle-word. Blood: the killing of the sons of Uisliu. Ruin: the burning of the royal hall at Emain Macha in the retaliations that followed. Exile: Fergus mac Roich and his followers going over to Connacht, which set up the whole Tain Bo Cuailnge. The other three options are invented; blood, ruin, and exile are the three named in the tale.  (Legend.)

question: Lapa, wife of the wool-dyer Jacopo Benincasa, bore twin girls in Siena in 1347. One died as a baby; the other grew up to be Saint Catherine. The twins came near the tail end of a very large family. How many children did the couple have in all?
context: Catherine was the 24th of 25 children of the wool-dyer Jacopo Benincasa. Her twin sister died shortly after birth. Source: Wikipedia, Catherine of Siena.

question: Catherine of Siena's brother had to shake her to make her move. She had frozen in the street at about six years old, walking home with him, her eyes on the sky above the city's great church. According to her own later account, what had she seen?
answer: Christ dressed as a pope, blessing her
choices: Christ dressed as a pope, blessing her
A giant silver key crossed with a sword
A ladder of angels reaching to the piazza
A ring of white fire around the bell tower
context: The child Catherine reported seeing Christ in papal vestments seated above the Basilica of San Domenico, blessing her. She ran home changed. Source: Dominican Sisters (dominicansisters.co.uk); Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: The family of Catherine of Siena tried to force her to marry her older sister's widower, though she had vowed her life to God as a small girl. She went into her room and did one drastic thing to make the marriage impossible. What did the teenage Catherine do?
answer: She cut off her long hair
choices: She cut off her long hair
She burned her dowry chest on the hearth
She smashed her wedding cup at the door
She locked herself in the cellar for a week
context: Catherine cut off her hair to make herself an unfit bride. Her family finally relented and let her take a Dominican habit. Source: Wikipedia, Catherine of Siena.

question: Catherine of Siena set out in June 1376 on her boldest journey, to a walled city where seven popes in a row had lived for nearly seventy years under the shadow of the French crown. She confronted Pope Gregory XI face to face there and urged him to move his court back to Rome. In what city did she find him?
context: The Avignon Papacy (1309-1377) had kept seven popes on the Rhone. Catherine's June 1376 visit is credited with pushing Gregory XI to leave; he re-entered Rome on 17 January 1377. Source: Wikipedia, Catherine of Siena.

question: A young Roman girl of the third century, wed against her will to a pagan husband, won him over on their wedding night, the legend says. Later she was put to death slowly in her own home, which became one of the great churches of Rome. Which martyr was she?
context: Cecilia takes her name from the plebeian Caecilii, one of the great Roman families; her feast is already in the Depositio Martyrum of 354 CE. Agnes was another young Roman martyr (feast 21 January); Lucy was martyred at Syracuse in Sicily; Perpetua was martyred at Carthage in 203 with her slave Felicity. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Cecilia'.

question: Cecilia told her pagan husband on their wedding night that an angel stood guard over her virginity, and that he too would see the angel if he accepted baptism, the legend says. He went to the pope on the Via Appia, was baptised, saw the angel, and died a martyr before her. What was the husband's name?
context: Valerian is baptised by Pope Urban at the third milestone on the Via Appia and, seeing the angel on his return, converts and is later martyred before Cecilia. Turcius Almachius is the prefect who later orders her death. Sebastian is another Roman soldier-martyr, shot with arrows a generation later. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Cecilia'.  (Legend.)

question: Cecilia's husband, won over on their wedding night, brought his own brother to the same milestone on the road out of Rome for baptism, the legend says. The brother was killed for the faith along with him, before Cecilia herself was martyred. What was the brother's name?
context: Tiburtius is Valerian's brother; the two are venerated together as the martyred brothers of Cecilia's household. Cyprian was a third-century bishop of Carthage; Pancras a fourteen-year-old Roman martyr; Cornelius a mid-third-century pope. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Cecilia'.  (Legend.)

question: The executioner failed to behead Cecilia, and she did not die at once. She lay teaching the Christians who gathered around her bedside, and she asked the pope to convert her house into a church. According to her legend, how long did she linger after the sword-strokes?
context: Cecilia lives three days after the wounds, teaching from her bed, giving her property to the poor, and asking Pope Urban to make the house a church. The number three shapes the martyrdom: three strokes, three days. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Cecilia'.  (Legend.)

question: Geoffrey Chaucer gave Cecilia's story to one of the pilgrims of the Canterbury Tales in the late fourteenth century, as her contribution to the tale-telling on the road. He gave this pilgrim no name of her own, only her office in the party. Which of the pilgrims told Cecilia's story?
context: The Second Nun's Tale is Chaucer's Middle English hagiography of Cecilia, drawn largely from Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend; its prologue offers the fanciful etymology of the name Cecilia as caeli lilia, 'lily of heaven'. The Prioress tells the tale of the little clergeon; the Wife of Bath tells a knight-and-old-hag Arthurian story; the Parson closes the cycle with a long prose sermon. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Second Nun's Tale'.

question: Pope Leo III crowned the kneeling Frankish king at Christmas Mass in St. Peter's in 800 and hailed him Emperor of the Romans. Einhard, his biographer, records what Charlemagne later said about that day. What did he claim?
answer: He would not have gone in had he known
choices: He would not have gone in had he known
He had begged the pope for it for years
He had dreamed of it the night before
He had picked Christmas so Rome would see
context: Einhard, Life of Charlemagne 28: the emperor said that he would not have set foot in the church that day, great feast though it was, if he could have foreseen the pope's plan. Historians still argue over how real the surprise was. Source: Einhard, Vita Karoli Magni 28.

question: Charlemagne met an English deacon at Parma in northern Italy in 781, a man on his way home from Rome and already famous across Europe as the finest scholar of the age. The deacon had been trained at the great library of his home city, and Charlemagne asked him to come and run the palace school. Which English center trained him?
context: Alcuin (c. 735-804) was schooled at York Minster's library, one of the finest in Latin Europe. Charlemagne met him at Parma in 781. Source: Britannica, Alcuin.

question: Charlemagne built a stone chapel at Aachen and deliberately modeled it on an older church he had seen on a trip to Italy. He even had columns and marble shipped north from that Italian city to build it. Which basilica was his model?
choices: St. Paul's Outside the Walls at Rome
context: Ravenna's sixth-century octagonal Basilica of San Vitale, with its mosaics, provided the model. Charlemagne shipped marble columns north from Ravenna. Source: Wikipedia, Palatine Chapel, Aachen.

question: Alcuin went by Flaccus, after the Roman poet Horace, at Charlemagne's palace school at Aachen around the year 800, and the court poet Angilbert went by Homer. The scholars there gave each other classical or biblical nicknames for fun. Charlemagne himself took the name of a great biblical king of Israel. Which king?
context: Charlemagne = David in the court's poetry; Alcuin = Flaccus (his Latin name was Albinus); Angilbert = Homer. The comparison flattered Charlemagne as the ideal warrior-king united with his priest (Alcuin/Nathan). Source: Medievalists.net (Garrison, 'Nicknames at the Carolingian Court').

question: Einhard knew Charlemagne well and wrote his life story, and he shares a strange detail about the emperor. For all his conquests and his palace school full of scholars, Charlemagne never mastered one ordinary skill. He kept wax tablets in a particular place at night so he could practice whenever he woke. Where did he keep the tablets, and what was he trying to learn?
answer: Under his pillow, to practice forming letters
choices: Under his pillow, to practice forming letters
Under his saddle, to practice Latin verses
Under his throne, to practice Greek
Under his crown, to practice arithmetic
context: Einhard's Vita Karoli Magni reports that Charlemagne kept wax tablets and notebooks under his pillow to practice forming letters at night, but never learned to write well. He could read, and dictated fluently, but the hand of a scribe eluded him. Source: Wikipedia, Vita Karoli Magni.

question: Italian humanists came upon old books written in a clear, rounded hand with real spaces between the words, six hundred years after Alcuin's monasteries had spread it so that scribes could copy the Bible correctly. They copied the letters eagerly, and modern lowercase type descends from their copies, but they had made a mistake about what they were looking at. What did the humanists think they were copying?
choices: The lost script of the druids
The private hand of the apostles
context: Fifteenth-century humanists took the Carolingian manuscripts in monastic libraries to be ancient Roman originals and copied the script as 'lettera antica'. From their humanist minuscule descends modern Roman printed type -- the lowercase letters you are reading right now. Source: Wikipedia, Humanist minuscule; Britannica, Carolingian minuscule.

question: Otto I sat down in 936 on a plain marble throne in the upper gallery of the chapel at Aachen where Charlemagne lay buried, and German kings went on being crowned there until Ferdinand I sat on it in 1531. The throne was older than any of them, built from re-used pieces of a much earlier civilization's stonework. What civilization's stone was recycled to make it?
context: The Aachen throne is four ancient marble slabs (some reworked from Roman spolia) clamped in bronze, reached by six marble steps. About thirty German kings were crowned on it between 936 and 1531. Source: Wikipedia, Palatine Chapel, Aachen; Throne of Charlemagne.

question: Charlemagne rushed his army back over the mountain in the old song of Roncesvalles, and he came too late. Oliver, the archbishop and the twelve peers lay dead beside their young captain, the emperor's own nephew. What was the young captain's name?
context: The Song of Roland (Oxford Digby 23, c. 1100) centres on Roland, Charlemagne's nephew and leader of the rearguard. Baligant is the pagan emir who arrives later; Marsile is the Saracen king of Zaragoza who plotted the ambush; Ganelon is the Frankish traitor who sold Roland out and is judged in this closing section of the poem.  (Legend.)

question: The Franks forced the pagans into a great Iberian river and pressed them from behind until they drowned in the current, the medieval French epic of Roncesvalles tells. Charlemagne had ridden south in fury after his nephew's death, pursuing the Saracen force deep into Spain. Which river was it?
context: Song of Roland: the Saracens are driven into the Ebro, the largest river in northeast Spain, and drown. The Tagus runs through Toledo and Lisbon in the centre-west; the Duero cuts across Castile and northern Portugal; the Guadalquivir flows through Cordoba and Seville in the south -- all Iberian, but none the Ebro of the Roland pursuit.  (Legend.)

question: Ganelon stood trial at Aachen for betraying Charlemagne's rearguard, and words alone did not decide his guilt. Frankish law allowed a judicial duel, one champion for the accuser and one for the accused, with God granting victory to the just side. Pinabel, a kinsman of Ganelon, fought as his champion. Who fought for the emperor?
context: Song of Roland laisses 273-291: Thierry, Roland's kinsman, argues that Ganelon's revenge is treason and offers his body against Ganelon's champion. Naimon is Charlemagne's wise old counsellor; Ogier the Dane is another peer; Oliver is Roland's sworn brother, already dead at Roncesvalles.  (Legend.)

question: The traitor Ganelon died torn apart by horses, and Charlemagne did not stop there. On that same day the emperor had a large number of Ganelon's kin hanged, the men who had stood surety for the traitor's champion Pinabel. How many of Ganelon's kinsmen were hanged?
context: Song of Roland: 'All those thirty kindred were swiftly hung.' The number is significant -- thirty pieces of silver in the Christian pillar, but also simply a large clan-remnant, marked as forfeit for their kinsman's treason. Twelve, three, and one hundred are wrong counts.  (Legend.)

question: An angel appeared to the sleeping Charlemagne in his palace at Aachen at the very end of the great French epic, with the traitor Ganelon punished at last. The angel commanded him to ride out yet again, to aid King Vivien, besieged by pagans at Imphe. The old emperor wept and pulled his white beard, but he got up to obey. Which angel brought the summons?
context: Song of Roland (final laisses): Saint Gabriel appears to Charlemagne with the summons to Imphe. Gabriel is the messenger-angel of the Christian tradition, associated in this poem with prophetic word to the emperor. Michael is the warrior-angel who judges souls; Raphael is the healer of the Book of Tobit; Uriel appears in later apocryphal tradition.  (Legend.)

question: 'But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD,' an old warrior told the tribes he had gathered for his farewell. It is one of the most-quoted lines in the whole Old Testament. Which Israelite leader gave that speech?
context: Joshua 24:15 (KJV): 'And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye shall serve ... but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' Samson pulled down the Philistine temple; Gideon fought Midian with 300 men and a trumpet-and-pitcher trick; Elijah confronted Ahab and Baal's prophets on Mount Carmel.

question: Joshua called the elders, heads, judges and officers of every tribe of Israel to one old covenant town in the hills of Ephraim for his farewell. Abraham had first pitched his tent there, and Jacob later bought a plot of ground there for a hundred pieces of silver. Which town was it?
context: Joshua 24:1: Joshua 'gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem.' Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim is the town where Abraham built his first altar in Canaan (Genesis 12:6-7), and where Jacob bought the parcel of ground (Genesis 33:19). Bethel is where Jacob dreamed of the ladder; Hebron holds the tombs of the patriarchs; Beersheba is far to the south.

question: The Israelites laid the old warrior Joshua in his grave, and then they came to a second burial. They had carried these bones up out of Egypt more than forty years earlier and lugged them the whole way through the wilderness, and now they laid them in the plot of ground Jacob had bought. Whose bones were they?
context: Joshua 24:32: 'And the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, buried they in Shechem, in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought ... for an hundred pieces of silver.' Aaron was buried on Mount Hor (Numbers 20); Moses on a mountain in Moab, in a grave no one knows (Deuteronomy 34); Jacob himself was carried back to the cave of Machpelah at Hebron (Genesis 50:13).

question: A giant waded across a raging river with a small child on his shoulders, old Christian legend tells, and learned only afterward that the child was the young Christ himself. He was later baptized Christopher, a Greek name whose first part is Christos, meaning Christ. What does the whole name literally mean?
context: Greek Christophoros = Christos (Christ) + phero (to bear or carry). The name is a story unto itself: the man who bore Christ across the river. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'.

question: A huge Canaanite carried a small child across a dangerous river one night, the Golden Legend tells, after wandering the world looking for the greatest king to serve. Baptism gave him the name Christopher, but the book opens with the name he bore before it. What was he called before?
context: The Golden Legend opens: 'Christopher tofore his baptism was named Reprobus, but afterwards he was named Christopher, which is as much to say as bearing Christ.' The tale itself calls him Christopher throughout. Reprobus is Latin for 'rejected'. Ignatius, Marcellus and Cassian are all real early Christian martyrs. Source: Golden Legend (Caxton), sourcebooks.fordham.edu.  (Legend.)

question: Jacobus de Voragine gave a heathen giant, later baptized Christopher, a height past any real human size in his Golden Legend, the medieval collection of saints' lives. He measured it in cubits, the old unit equal to a grown man's forearm. How many cubits tall did he say the giant stood?
context: Twelve cubits (a cubit being roughly a foot and a half) works out to about eighteen feet. Later medieval retellings sometimes push him higher, but the Golden Legend's figure is twelve. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.

question: The giant who became Saint Christopher set out to serve the strongest master in the world, the legend tells, and first pledged himself to a great earthly king. Then the king flinched at a name, and the giant left in search of that master instead. Whom did the great earthly king fear?
choices: the ghost of a dead prince
context: In the Golden Legend the earthly king fears the devil, so the giant leaves to serve that stronger master; the devil in turn flinches at another name, and the giant leaves again in search of the master the devil fears. It is a giant's plain step-by-step logic about what deserves service. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.

question: The giant ferryman of the Golden Legend carried travellers across a dangerous river on his shoulders. A small child asked to be taken over one night, and as the giant waded in the boy grew heavier and heavier, until the giant nearly drowned under the weight. On the far bank he gasped that nothing could have weighed more. What did the child tell him he had borne on his shoulders?
answer: him that made all the world
choices: him that made all the world
the last of the Hebrew prophets
context: The Golden Legend has the child answer: 'Thou hast not only borne all the world upon thee, but thou hast borne him that created and made all the world upon thy shoulders.' It is the moment that gives the giant his name Christophoros. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.

question: In the Golden Legend, the child Christ told the giant Christopher, on the far bank of a dangerous river, to plant his walking staff in the ground as a sign that the story was true. By morning the dry wood had done something no dead wood does. What did the planted staff do overnight?
context: The Golden Legend has the staff put forth leaves, flowers, and dates by morning, echoing the Old Testament blossoming rod of Aaron. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.

question: Some Eastern icons give Saint Christopher the head of an animal. An older Greek tale had made him one of a whole people of such creatures, and one scholar thinks a Latin scribe later misread their name as 'Canaanite.' What animal's head do the icons give him?
context: Wikipedia, citing the historian David Woods, notes that the Greek kunokephalos, 'dog-headed', may have been rendered canineus in Latin and later misread as Cananeus, 'Canaanite', which would explain the Golden Legend's giant from Canaan. Bulls, lions and rams crown figures of other traditions (the Apis bull, the lion-headed Sekhmet, the ram-headed Khnum), but not Christopher. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Christopher.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus's men spot smoke rising from a stone house among the trees of a wooded island, in Homer's Odyssey. Inside lives an enchantress who welcomes strangers to a feast and then turns them into beasts with a wave of her wand. What is her name?
context: She is a daughter of the sun god Helios. Calypso is the nymph who keeps Odysseus seven years on Ogygia later; Medea is Circe's niece and a sorceress in her own right; Nausicaa is the princess who finds him washed up on Scheria. Source: Wikipedia, Circe.  (Legend.)

question: The witch of the wooded island welcomes Odysseus's men and gives them a warm feast of cheese, meal, honey and wine. Then she touches each of them with her wand, and they change and are driven out to a pen. Into which animal are the men transformed?
context: Circe already has tame wolves and lions in her yard from earlier visitors; the crew is turned specifically into swine and fed acorns. Source: Wikipedia, Circe.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus sends only half his men to investigate the house on the island, led by an officer who suspects the invitation. The officer hangs back at the door while the others go inside to feast. When his comrades change, he escapes and runs back to warn Odysseus. Who is he?
context: Elpenor is the crewman who later falls drunk off Circe's roof; Polites is another crewman; Antiphates was the Laestrygonian king who ate the earlier scouts. Source: Cliffs Notes, Odyssey Book 10.  (Legend.)

question: Circe strikes Odysseus's sailors with her wand on the island of Aeaea, and they turn into beasts. She shuts them in her pen. There they do something no ordinary beast does: they weep. Why do the beasts in Circe's pen weep?
answer: They still have their human minds inside
choices: They still have their human minds inside
They are hungry for the acorns Circe throws down
Circe has laid a curse of sorrow on the pen
The moon has risen and the spell weighs on them
context: This is the horror of the punishment -- the men know they are men, and remember Odysseus, but can only grunt. Source: Cliffs Notes, Odyssey Book 10.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus sets out alone from the ship to rescue his men from Circe. On the forest path a god meets him and hands him a magical plant as an antidote to her drugs, one Homer describes as 'black at the root, white as milk at the flower.' Which god gives him the plant?
context: The messenger god, patron of travelers and tricksters -- the obvious ally against a sorceress. Source: Wikipedia, Moly (herb); Odyssey 10.302-306.  (Legend.)

question: A god stops Odysseus on the path to Circe's hall and hands him a plant that will keep her magic from working. Homer says the plant has a black root and a milk-white flower, and only the gods can safely pull it from the soil. What does Homer call it?
context: Nepenthe is another Homeric drug, the sorrow-killer served at Helen's table in Odyssey 4; silphium is a real medicinal plant from Cyrene; asphodel is the flower of the meadow of the dead. Odyssey 10.302-306. Source: Wikipedia, Moly (herb).  (Legend.)

question: A god tells Odysseus on the forest path exactly how to break Circe's magic. When she strikes with her wand and orders him to the sty, he must draw the sword and rush her. She will drop the wand and invite him to her bed. What must Odysseus force Circe to do before he agrees?
answer: Swear a great oath to do him and his men no more harm
choices: Swear a great oath to do him and his men no more harm
Cut a lock of her golden hair and burn it on the hearth
Give up her wand and throw it into the sea
Kneel before him and name him her master
context: Hermes coaches him line by line; the oath by the gods is what makes the alliance safe. Source: Wikipedia, Circe.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus does exactly as he has been told. Circe strikes with the wand, the magic plant holds, and he draws the sword and rushes her. She stares at him, drops the wand, and greets him with a phrase from a warning she was given long ago. Which phrase does she use?
context: The famous Homeric epithet 'polytropos' -- of many ways, many turns, many tricks. 'Breaker of horses' is Hector's epithet; 'son of Peleus' is Achilles. Source: Cliffs Notes, Odyssey Book 10.  (Legend.)

question: Circe walks out at last to her sty of enchanted beasts on the island of Aeaea and touches each one in turn with a fresh potion. Their bodies change back into human shape. Homer describes exactly how the restored men look after the change. How does Homer say they come back?
answer: Taller, younger, and handsomer than they had been before
choices: Taller, younger, and handsomer than they had been before
Shrunken and old, their beards suddenly white
The same as they had been the moment Circe struck
Silent, and unable to speak for three days
