context: A rare gift on top of the mere reversal. Source: Cliffs Notes, Odyssey Book 10.  (Legend.)

question: Circe turns Odysseus's crew back into men and welcomes them as guests in her feast-hall on Aeaea. They stay on, eating and drinking so well that they nearly forget their home island of Ithaca, until at last the men beg Odysseus to remember it and sail on. How long do Odysseus and his crew stay on Aeaea?
context: It is Eurylochus and the crew who finally shake Odysseus and remind him of Ithaca. Seven years is what Calypso keeps him on Ogygia much later. Source: Wikipedia, Aeaea.  (Legend.)

question: Circe tells Odysseus he cannot sail straight home to Ithaca, when at last he asks her the way on the island of Aeaea. First he must make a terrible detour and consult one specific blind seer of Thebes. Which seer must Odysseus consult, and where must he go to find him?
context: The reason the next book of the Odyssey is the Nekyia -- the descent to Hades. Calchas was the seer of the Greek army at Troy; Melampus and Mopsus are other famous Greek seers. Source: Wikipedia, Circe.  (Legend.)

question: Clare listened from an upstairs window in the Italian hill town of Assisi in the early 1200s, as a strange young preacher named Francis drew big crowds in the piazza below. He was about twelve years older than she was. What kind of home had Clare grown up in?
answer: A noble palazzo near the cathedral
choices: A noble palazzo near the cathedral
A shepherd's cottage in the hills
A merchant's house on the market square
A stonemason's workshop by the church
context: Clare (b. 1194) was of the Offreduccio family, Assisi nobility. Her family lived in a palazzo near the cathedral of San Rufino. Source: Wikipedia, Clare of Assisi.

question: Francis and his brothers waited by torchlight at their own chapel at the bottom of the hill, on the night of Palm Sunday 1212. Eighteen-year-old Clare of Assisi had turned down a rich marriage, and she came running down to them through the fields. Which chapel was it?
context: The Portiuncula ('little portion') -- the tiny chapel of St. Mary of the Angels below Assisi -- was Francis's mother-house. Clare met him there on Palm Sunday night 1212. Source: Franciscan Media; Wikipedia.

question: Clare of Assisi slipped out of her father's house in the middle of the night in 1212 to join Francis, and she went out through a narrow side door built into the wall. The great houses of Assisi had these small doors, with only one everyday purpose. What was the side door normally used for?
answer: Carrying a corpse out of the house
choices: Carrying a corpse out of the house
Leading a bride out to her wedding
context: The porta dei morti -- 'door of the dead' -- was a small side-door reserved by tradition for taking a body out to burial. Clare using it to run to Francis is a beat kept by later biographers. Source: Christian History Institute.  (Legend.)

question: Francis received the vows of Clare of Assisi at the little chapel, by torchlight, and clothed her in a rough tunic like his own. She gave up her old life on the spot. What did he do with her long hair?
answer: He cut it off with shears
choices: He cut it off with shears
He wound it around a cross
He burned it in the altar lamp
He buried it in the churchyard
context: Francis cut off Clare's long hair as the visible sign of her renunciation of the world -- the same gesture Catherine of Siena would later make on herself. Clare was 18. Source: Franciscan Media; Wikipedia.

question: Clare's uncle and her armed relatives arrived at the convent where Francis had placed her for safety, and they tried to drag her home to be married. She ran to the altar, clung to the altar cloth, and did something that stopped them cold. What did she do at the altar?
answer: Threw back her veil to show her shorn head
choices: Threw back her veil to show her shorn head
Called down a curse on her uncle by name
Broke the wedding ring meant for her finger
Held up a burning coal from the altar lamp
context: Shorn hair marked a woman consecrated to God -- legally, her family could no longer marry her off. The gesture ended the argument. Her sister Agnes joined her days later. Source: Christian History Institute; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: Saracen troops in the pay of the Emperor Frederick II attacked Assisi in September 1240 and reached the walls of Clare's little house. Clare was too sick to stand. She had the sisters carry her out to the courtyard and lift a covered vessel from the chapel into her hands. When she raised it toward the soldiers, they turned back without attacking. What was she holding?
answer: The consecrated host from the altar
choices: The consecrated host from the altar
The sword Francis had once carried
A relic of the true cross
The rule of the order in a silver box
context: Clare had the pyx (or later monstrance -- the vessel is anachronistically depicted in art) containing the consecrated eucharistic bread brought out; the Saracens withdrew. Clare died three years later, on 11 August 1253. Source: Franciscan Foundation for the Holy Land.  (Legend.)

question: An Irish monk of royal blood crossed to Scotland in 563 and founded a monastery on the island of Iona, the most famous in the Atlantic west. His Irish name was Colum Cille. What does that name mean?
context: Colum Cille (later latinised as Columba) literally means 'dove of the church'. He was descended from Niall of the Nine Hostages through his father's line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba.

question: The young monk Columba stayed up nights in secret at Movilla around 560, Irish tradition tells, transcribing a beautiful psalter that belonged to his old teacher Finnian. Finnian found out and claimed the new manuscript as his own. High King Diarmait was asked to judge, and his ruling became a famous line of medieval law. What was the ruling?
answer: To every cow her calf, and to every book its copy
choices: To every cow her calf, and to every book its copy
A borrowed book is a borrowed sword
What the scribe writes, the abbey keeps
The pen has no owner but the psalm
context: In Irish: 'le gach boin a boinin, le gach leabhar a leabhran.' Later Irish tradition called this the first copyright judgment in Western history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cul_Dreimhne.  (Legend.)

question: The O Neill clans met High King Diarmait's forces near Drumcliff in 561, and later writers count some three thousand dead. Tradition blamed the slaughter at Cul Dreimhne on the scholar-monk Columba, who had transcribed his teacher's book. What penance does the tradition say he took on?
answer: An exile, to win as many souls to the faith as had died in the fighting
choices: An exile, to win as many souls to the faith as had died in the fighting
A year of silence and fasting on bread and water at Clonmacnoise
The building of a great high cross at every monastery he had known
A pilgrimage on foot to Rome and back, with only a psalter for a purse
context: A synod of clerics threatened to excommunicate Columba, but Brendan of Birr spoke for him, and on the counsel of the old hermit Molaise he chose exile; the sentence was to win as many souls to the faith as had been lost in the battle. The exile is what made Iona possible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_C%C3%BAl_Dreimhne.  (Legend.)

question: Columba pushed a small hide-covered boat off the shore of Derry in 563, after a bloody quarrel over a copied psalter, and sailed across the Irish Sea to the western coast of Scotland. A royal cousin there granted him a bare little island, later famous as Iona, for a new monastery. How many companions sailed with him on that voyage?
context: Twelve companions -- the same number as Christ's apostles -- crossed with Columba in a curragh. The island he was given, later mother-house of the northern British church, became Iona. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba.

question: Columba sent his companion Lugne swimming across the River Ness in Pictish country to fetch a boat, Adomnan's Life says, and a great beast rose from the current and rushed at the swimmer. Columba raised his hand, made the sign of the cross, and spoke one sharp command, and the beast fled as if hauled back by ropes. What did Columba say to it?
answer: Go no further, do not touch the man, go back at once
choices: Go no further, do not touch the man, go back at once
In the name of the Father, be still and drown no more
Return to the deep places, beast, and trouble none
Peace, creature, and leave this man his life
context: Adomnan, Life of Columba II.28 (Reeves): 'Thou shalt go no further, nor touch the man; go back with all speed.' Adomnan places the encounter at the River Ness itself, not the loch of the same name, and gives no year; 565 is later reckoning. Source: sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/columba-e.asp.  (Legend.)

question: Columba, the old abbot of Iona, sat copying out Psalm 33 in his hut one June day in 597. He reached the verse 'They that seek the Lord shall want no manner of thing that is good' and stopped at the foot of the page, naming the man who should write what came next. That night he died before the altar. Who took up the pen after him?
context: Adomnan, Life of Columba III.23 (Reeves): 'Here at the end of the page I must stop; and what follows let Baithene write.' Baithene, Columba's cousin, succeeded him as abbot of Iona, in writing as in teaching, Adomnan says. Aidan was the later missionary to Northumbria; Diarmait (Diormit) was Columba's attendant, who found him dying in the church; Oran was an early companion buried on the island. Source: sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/columba-e.asp.  (Legend.)

question: Iona's monks fled their island under Viking raids, carrying with them a gospel book they had begun around the year 800. It was so richly painted that later ages called it the finest surviving manuscript of the early Middle Ages. What is that book called today?
context: Kept today at Trinity College Dublin. The Book of Durrow is an earlier Iona-family manuscript, the Book of Armagh is a Patrick-tradition compendium, the Book of Deer is a small Aberdeenshire gospel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba.

question: In the Gospel of Mark, a desperate father came running through the crowd and fell at the feet of Jesus. He was a ruler of the local synagogue, and his twelve-year-old daughter was dying at home. He begged Jesus to come lay hands on her. What was this father's name?
context: Mark 5:22 KJV: 'And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name.' Zacchaeus is the tax-collector up the sycamore tree in Luke 19; Cornelius is the Roman centurion in Acts 10; Nicodemus is the Pharisee who comes to Jesus at night in John 3.

question: The hired mourners were already wailing in the courtyard when Jesus reached a synagogue ruler's house in Mark's gospel, for the man's little girl had died. Jesus told them she was only sleeping. Mark gives their reaction in one blunt phrase before Jesus put them out of the house. What did the mourners do?
context: Mark 5:40 KJV: 'And they laughed him to scorn.' The scene turns on Jesus then putting them all out of the house and taking only the parents and the inner three disciples in -- the laughing crowd sees nothing of what follows.

question: Jesus took a dead girl's hand in Mark's gospel and spoke in Aramaic, the ordinary language Galilean children spoke at home. Mark kept the actual words and then translated them for his Greek readers as 'Damsel, arise'. Which Aramaic words did Jesus speak?
context: Mark 5:41 KJV: 'And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise.' Ephphatha is what Jesus says to a deaf man in Mark 7; Eli lama sabachthani is his cry from the cross in Mark 15; Maranatha is a very early Christian greeting preserved in Aramaic at the end of Paul's first letter to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:22).

question: A dead twelve-year-old girl got up at the word of Jesus in the house of a synagogue leader, in Mark's gospel, and walked around the room, to the astonishment of her parents. Mark records one final instruction from Jesus in that room, and it was an ordinary one. What did Jesus tell her parents to do?
choices: keep her indoors for seven days
walk her three times around the house
context: Mark 5:43 KJV: '...and commanded that something should be given her to eat.' It is Mark's touch of realism -- a girl who has just crossed back has to eat like a girl. The other three instructions are invented.

question: Two sisters in the little village of Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, sent urgent word to Jesus in the eleventh chapter of John: their brother Lazarus was very ill. He died and was buried before Jesus arrived. Whom does John name as the two sisters?
context: John 11:1 KJV: 'Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany, the town of Mary and her sister Martha.' This Mary is Mary of Bethany -- not Mary Magdalene and not Mary the mother of Jesus. Rachel and Leah are Jacob's two wives; Naomi and Ruth are the mother-in-law and widow of the Book of Ruth; Priscilla and Lydia are early Christian women from Paul's letters and Acts.

question: Jesus heard that Lazarus was sick, John says, and he deliberately did not set out at once. By the time he arrived, Lazarus lay sealed in the tomb, and the dead man's sister warned Jesus at the stone that the body 'stinketh'. How many days does John say Lazarus had been in the tomb?
context: John 11:17 KJV: 'Then when Jesus came, he found that he had lain in the grave four days already.' Repeated in Martha's protest in verse 39. Forty is the wilderness number; twelve is Jairus's daughter's age; seven is the day-count for the Genesis creation week.

question: The greatest warrior of Ulster sailed away as a young man to learn to fight, in the old Irish stories. He trained with a fearsome war-woman named Scathach on an island called the Isle of Shadow. Who was this Ulster warrior?
context: Cu Chulainn ('the Hound of Culann') is the central hero of the Ulster Cycle. Conall Cernach is his foster-brother and Ulster's second-greatest warrior; Ferghus mac Roich is the exiled Ulster king; Conchobar mac Nessa is the reigning king of Ulster. All four are the great Ulstermen -- but the trip to the Isle of Shadow to learn from Scathach belongs to Cu Chulainn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connla.  (Legend.)

question: Scathach's rival, a warrior-queen whose lands lay right next to hers, met the young hero Cu Chulainn in single combat and lost, but he spared her life. Later she bore him a son. What was this warrior-queen's name?
context: Aife (also spelled Aoife) is the warrior-queen Cu Chulainn defeats and spares, and who bears him a son. Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife back in Ulster; Deirdre is the tragic heroine of a different Ulster tale; the Morrigan is the war-goddess who both loves and torments Cu Chulainn. Of these Ulster-Cycle women, only Aife is the mother of his son. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connla.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn left the warrior-queen he had defeated a small gold token before he sailed home to Ireland, meant for their unborn son. He told her that when the boy had grown enough to wear it, she should send him to Ireland. What was the token?
context: The thumb-ring is the tale's age-test: the boy may set out only when it fits him. Keating's History calls the gold token the sign by which his father should know him. A brooch, a torc and an arm-band are all real early-Irish gold ornaments, but the tale names a ring. Source: iso.ucc.ie/Aided-aife.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn laid three commandments on the son he had never seen, three unbreakable geasa meant to shape the boy into a great warrior. The boy must never turn back once he set out, and he must never refuse a challenge. What was the third commandment?
answer: he must never give his name
choices: he must never give his name
he must never draw first blood
he must never sleep on the ground
he must never eat the flesh of a hound
context: The three geasa -- never turn back, never refuse, never name yourself -- are the whole engine of the disaster: they make it impossible for father and son to recognise each other in time. 'Never eat the flesh of a hound' is a REAL geis in Irish myth, but it is Cu Chulainn's OWN geis (his name means 'Hound'), not Connla's. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connla.  (Legend.)

question: A woman threw her arm around Cu Chulainn's neck as he went down to the strand, where a boy was slaying Ulster's champions, and she pleaded with him not to go, for she had guessed that the boy was his own son. She was his wife. What was her name?
context: Emer, daughter of Forgall Manach, is Cu Chulainn's wife, famed for the six gifts of womanhood. In Aided Oenfhir Aife she tells him outright that the boy is his only son; he answers that even so he would kill him for the honour of Ulster. Deirdre is the tragic heroine of a different Ulster tale (Longes mac nUislenn); Fedelm is a prophetess in the Tain; Nes is Conchobar's mother. Source: iso.ucc.ie/Aided-aife/Aided-aife-text.html.  (Legend.)

question: The young shepherd Cuthbert was watching his flock on the Northumbrian hills one night in 651 when he saw a vision of angels carrying a soul up to heaven. In the morning he heard that an Irish missionary had died at the very same hour. Whose soul had Cuthbert seen carried up?
context: Aidan, an Irish monk from Iona, had founded Lindisfarne in 635 and was its first bishop. Cuthbert soon entered Melrose Abbey to begin his own monastic life. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert.  (Legend.)

question: Cuthbert withdrew in 676 to a tiny rocky outcrop in the North Sea, wanting greater solitude than even a tidal monastery could give him. He grew barley there for food, dug a well in the rock, and raised his cell walls until he could see only the sky. Which island did he choose?
context: Inner Farne is the largest of the Farne Islands, a cluster of low rocky islands a few miles south of Lindisfarne. Coquet Island is another Northumberland island Cuthbert is recorded visiting. He built his cell so that nothing but the sky was visible from inside. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert.

question: Cuthbert's fellow monks opened his coffin on Lindisfarne in 698, eleven years after his burial, intending to lift his bones into a shrine. What they found instead became the most famous wonder told of him for the next thousand years. What did they find inside?
context: The body was reported whole and uncorrupted, the vestments still fresh. The coffin was opened again at Durham in 1104, and once more in 1827, when it was found in fragments but with recognizable relics. Source: sites.nd.edu/manuscript-studies/2023/03/23/by-the-bones-of-saint-cuthbert.  (Legend.)

question: The monks of Lindisfarne lifted Cuthbert's coffin and carried it with them when Viking raids began smashing their island in 793. For over a hundred years they wandered northern England, hunting for a safe place to lay him. In which English city did they finally settle, where the cathedral later rose over his tomb?
context: The Community of Saint Cuthbert rested for over a century at Chester-le-Street before finally settling at Durham around 995. Durham Cathedral, begun in 1093, was built over the tomb, and Cuthbert lies there still. Source: durhamworldheritagesite.com/learn/history/st-cuthbert/body.

question: Two Greek brothers from a Byzantine port, where Slavic was heard on the streets, became missionaries and first put Slavic into writing. The older was Methodius. The younger took a monk's name late in life, and history remembers him by it. What was that name?
context: The younger brother was born Constantine and only took the name Cyril late in life in Rome. Athanasius was the 4th-c. Alexandrian bishop; Basil the great Cappadocian; Jerome the Latin translator of the Vulgate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_and_Methodius.

question: Cyril, a Greek monk and scholar, was chosen around 862 for a mission north to the Slavs of Moravia, who had no written alphabet of their own. For the mission he designed a brand new writing system to fit the sounds of Slavic speech, the first alphabet used for Slavic manuscripts. What do historians call his original design?
context: The name Glagolitic comes from the Slavic 'glagol', meaning 'word'. The alphabet later named Cyrillic was actually developed after Cyril's death by his students at the Preslav Literary School, based largely on Greek majuscule letters. Ogham was the early Irish script cut on stone edges; Uncial was a Latin manuscript hand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_and_Methodius.

question: Cyril stopped in Venice in 867 and stood up to the local clergy for his right to celebrate the liturgy in Slavic. His opponents insisted that God could only be praised in the three languages Pilate had written above the cross. Which three languages did they name?
context: John 19:20 says the inscription above the cross was in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. The Slavonic sources call the trilingualist position the 'Pilatian heresy' after this passage. Aramaic, Syriac, and Arabic are all real languages of the region, but not the three named at the cross. Source: scribd.com/Ss-Cyril-and-Methodius-and-a-Mythical-Western-Heresy-Trilingualism.

question: Daniel's enemies at court tricked King Darius the Mede into signing an edict that anyone who prayed to any god but the king would be executed. Daniel kept praying to God anyway, and he was sealed overnight in a pit of hungry wild beasts. What kind of beasts filled the pit?
context: Daniel 6:16 KJV: 'they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions.' Bears appear in the Elisha / mocking-boys story (2 Kings 2:24); serpents in the Moses / brazen serpent scene (Numbers 21); wolves are metaphorical only.

question: Daniel learned that King Darius had signed a decree: for thirty days no one might pray to any god except Darius himself. He did not hide. He went home to his upper room and knelt by the open windows, as he had always done three times a day. In what direction did those windows look?
context: Daniel 6:10 KJV: 'his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem.' Jews in exile prayed toward Jerusalem (the Temple) -- the tradition Daniel is honoring. The rising sun is a sun-worship posture the OT condemns (Ezek 8:16). Mount Sinai is where Moses received the law. 'Toward the four winds' is Ezekiel's phrase for scattering.

question: King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon captured Jerusalem and brought the smartest young Hebrew captives back to be trained in his own royal court. One of them was a boy named Daniel. The Babylonians renamed each of these boys after their own gods. What court name did they give Daniel?
context: Daniel 1:7 KJV. Belteshazzar is Daniel's Babylonian name (do not confuse with king Belshazzar, a different figure). Abednego and Meshach are the Babylonian names of Daniel's three companions (Hananiah and Mishael); the fourth companion Azariah became Shadrach.

question: King Darius, trapped by his own thirty-day decree, had the Jewish official Daniel thrown into the den for the crime of praying. A great stone was rolled over the mouth of the den. Then the stone was sealed, so that no one could dig Daniel out in the night and cheat the decree. What sealed the stone?
answer: The king's own signet, and the signets of his lords
choices: The king's own signet, and the signets of his lords
The high priest's ephod, and the seals of the Levites
A tablet of clay bearing the name of Marduk
A cord of scarlet and blue, tied by the palace guard
context: Daniel 6:17 KJV: 'a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that the purpose might not be changed concerning Daniel.' The double sealing is why not even the king himself can rescue Daniel until dawn.

question: King Darius spent the night sleepless in his palace, refusing to eat, after his own decree forced him to throw the Jewish official Daniel into the den. At the first light of dawn he ran to the mouth of the pit and cried down to him. Daniel answered up out of the darkness and explained why the beasts had not eaten him. What did Daniel say his God had done?
answer: Sent his angel, and shut the lions' mouths
choices: Sent his angel, and shut the lions' mouths
Sent a whirlwind, and driven the beasts back
Laid his hand upon them, and made them tame as sheep
Blinded their eyes, that they should not see me
context: Daniel 6:22 KJV: 'My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me.' The other options are stylistic parallels drawn from other OT rescue-vocabulary but not from Daniel's answer.

question: Daniel came out of the pit unhurt, the beasts never having touched him, and King Darius the Mede turned in fury on the palace officials who had tricked him into sending Daniel down there. Daniel 6:24 records the sentence the king passed on them. What was done to those men?
answer: Thrown into the pit with their wives and children, and torn by the lions
choices: Thrown into the pit with their wives and children, and torn by the lions
Stoned outside the city walls with their wives and children
Beheaded with their households, their heads set on the palace gate
Cast with their wives and children into a burning furnace
context: Daniel 6:24 KJV: '...the lions had the mastery of them, and brake all their bones in pieces or ever they came at the bottom of the den.' The famous 'furnace heated seven times' belongs to the Daniel 3 story of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego -- a different scene in the same book.

question: Joab, Israel's general, is off besieging Rabbah, the Ammonite capital on the far side of the Jordan, 'at the time when kings go forth to battle.' But King David is not out there fighting with his army. Where is he?
answer: in Jerusalem, at his own palace
choices: in Jerusalem, at his own palace
hiding in the cave of Adullam
keeping his father's sheep at Bethlehem
context: 2 Samuel 11:1-2 KJV. Kings normally rode out with the army in spring; David has stayed behind. The next verse puts him walking on the palace roof at evening. Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1), Gath under King Achish (1 Samuel 27) and the Bethlehem sheepfold (1 Samuel 16:11) are all places from earlier in David's story.

question: King David gets up from his bed one evening and walks on the flat roof while his army is off at war. Looking down, he sees a beautiful woman doing something, and he sends to find out who she is. What is the woman doing?
context: 2 Samuel 11:2 KJV: 'from the roof he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.' The text does not say where she was. The messenger returns with her name and her husband's: Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite.

question: King David's servants tell him the woman he has seen from the roof is Bathsheba, the wife of a soldier the king knows well. Her husband is a foreigner serving in Israel's army, one of the thirty listed later as David's own mighty men. Who is he?
context: 2 Samuel 11:3 KJV, with Uriah listed among David's thirty at 2 Samuel 23:39. Ittai the Gittite, Doeg the Edomite and Zelek the Ammonite are also real foreigners in the books of Samuel: Ittai followed David out of Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15:19-21); Doeg was Saul's chief herdsman (1 Samuel 21:7); Zelek is another of the thirty (2 Samuel 23:37).

question: The prophet Nathan comes to King David with a story, after the king has had a soldier killed and taken his wife. A rich man has vast flocks and herds; a poor man has one small animal, raised with his children. It eats from his plate, drinks from his cup and lies in his bosom: 'it was unto him as a daughter.' What one animal does the poor man have?
context: 2 Samuel 12:1-4 KJV. The rich man spares his own flock and takes the poor man's lamb for a traveller's meal. Goats, a red heifer and turtledoves all appear among the offerings of the Law of Moses, but Nathan's poor man owns a lamb.

question: Nathan finishes his story of a rich man who robbed his poor neighbour to feed a traveller, and David's anger flares up. The king swears an oath that the rich man deserves to die. Nathan answers with one short sentence that turns the story on David himself. What does Nathan say?
context: 2 Samuel 12:5-9 KJV. David has just sworn 'the man that hath done this thing shall surely die.' Nathan replies, 'Thou art the man,' and then charges him outright: 'thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and hast taken his wife to be thy wife.' It is one of the sharpest lines in the Hebrew Bible.

question: David fasts and lies on the ground for seven days, refusing food, while Bathsheba's baby is sick. The child dies, and David's servants are afraid to tell him. When he learns of it he rises, washes, changes his clothes and asks for a meal, and they ask him why. He explains himself in one line. What does David say?
answer: 'I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.'
choices: 'I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.'
'The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away.'
'Naked came I out of my mother's womb.'
'The days of my mourning shall be ended.'
context: 2 Samuel 12:20-23 KJV. David fasted while there was any hope, and stopped when there was none. Job says 'Naked came I out of my mother's womb' and 'the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away' in Job 1:21, when he hears his children are dead; Isaiah 60:20 promises 'the days of thy mourning shall be ended.'

question: The Philistine giant Goliath strides down at dawn between two armies camped on facing hills and shouts for any Israelite brave enough to fight him one-on-one. King Saul's men hold one hill and the Philistines the other, with a broad valley between them. Which valley does the Bible name as the setting?
context: 1 Samuel 17:2-3 KJV. The three wrong choices are all real named valleys in the Hebrew Bible: Hinnom outside Jerusalem (the child-sacrifice site, later Gehenna), Jezreel where Ahab's dynasty falls, and Achor where Achan is stoned in Joshua 7.

question: King Saul's men watch the Philistine champion Goliath march out in his bronze armor and dare any one of them to fight him, and once more no Israelite goes down. He does it every morning and every evening. The stand-off drags on until David arrives with food for his brothers. How many days does 1 Samuel 17 say it lasts?
context: 1 Samuel 17:16 KJV: 'And the Philistine drew near morning and evening, and presented himself forty days.' Forty is the Bible's long-wait number -- forty days of the Flood, forty years in the wilderness, forty days of Jesus fasting in the wilderness -- so the number is doing work.

question: David is not with the army. His father Jesse sends him from the sheepfold to the camp with food for his three oldest brothers and their captain. Jesse packs an ephah of parched corn, ten loaves of bread, and one more gift to be given to the captain of the thousand. What does Jesse send for the captain?
context: 1 Samuel 17:17-18 KJV. Ten cheeses for the officer is one of those specific homely details the storyteller preserves. The three wrong choices are all real OT foodstuffs in gift-lists elsewhere (Abigail's stores at 1 Samuel 25, Jonathan's honey in the wood at 1 Samuel 14).

question: David takes off the armor King Saul has dressed him in and goes down to the brook that runs through the valley. He stoops and picks something up out of the water, choosing with care, and drops it into the shepherd's bag he already carries. What does he pick up, and how many?
context: 1 Samuel 17:40 KJV: 'he chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip.' He will use only one -- the other four are the answer to why kids remember this story.

question: Goliath curses the young David, and David answers the giant back. He names the giant's own weapons, sword and spear and shield, and says in whose name he himself is coming. He finishes with why the fight is going to happen this way: 'that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.' What does David say he is coming in the name of?
answer: 'the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel'
choices: 'the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel'
'the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob'
'the LORD, the God who brought thee out of Egypt'
'the Rock of Israel, the shield of my salvation'
context: 1 Samuel 17:45-46 KJV: 'I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.' The wrong choices are all real OT divine-title formulas (Exodus 3:6, Exodus 20:2, 2 Samuel 22 in David's own song) -- but not the one he uses in the valley.

question: David walks out from the Israelite line to face Goliath with only a sling and his shepherd's bag. He runs at the giant, reaches into the bag for one stone and slings it. The stone sinks in, and the giant falls face-first to the earth. Where in Goliath's body does the stone strike?
context: 1 Samuel 17:49 KJV: 'the stone sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth.' A helmeted target with an exposed forehead is a real puzzle scholars raise -- most read Goliath's helmet as leaving the brow open, or read the giant as raising his visor to shout.

question: The priest Ahimelech feeds David and hands him Goliath's own sword, years later, when David comes to him unarmed, fleeing King Saul. For that kindness Saul orders Doeg the Edomite to kill Ahimelech and eighty-five priests of his house. At which sanctuary town does the massacre happen?
context: 1 Samuel 21:1-9 (Ahimelech gives David the giant's sword and the showbread at Nob) and 1 Samuel 22:9-19 (Doeg the Edomite butchers the eighty-five priests on Saul's order). The wrong choices are all real OT sanctuary towns: Shiloh where the ark rested under Eli, Bethel of Jacob's ladder, Gilgal where Joshua's twelve stones stood.

question: Another man of Bethlehem slays Goliath of Gath, 'the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam,' at 2 Samuel 21:19, a well-known puzzle deep in the David story. The matching verse in 1 Chronicles says he killed Goliath's brother Lahmi instead. Who is this other Bethlehemite?
context: 2 Samuel 21:19 KJV; the parallel at 1 Chronicles 20:5 smooths the puzzle by saying Elhanan killed 'Lahmi the brother of Goliath.' The wrong choices are all real named champions of David's thirty from 2 Samuel 23: Benaiah who killed a lion in a pit in the snow, Abishai who lifted his spear against three hundred, Eleazar who fought the Philistines until his hand cleaved to the sword.

question: Jonathan, King Saul's eldest son, sealed his friendship with David with a gift. He stripped off what he was wearing and handed it over, giving David the outward marks of the throne he himself stood to inherit: his royal robe, his belt, his bow, and one more thing. What was the fourth item?
context: 1 Samuel 18:4 KJV: 'And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle.' The prince is handing his heir's kit to the man Samuel has anointed to replace him, and doing it with his eyes open.

question: King Saul snatched a weapon from his side and hurled it across the room at young David's head, while David sat quietly playing his harp to calm the king's dark moods. Saul had grown jealous of David's fame with the people, and he did it twice. What weapon does the Bible say Saul threw?
context: 1 Samuel 18:10-11 and 19:9-10 KJV: 'Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it.' David slips out from under it both times. Saul carries the javelin as his royal token throughout the story -- it stands beside him when he sleeps in the camp at Hachilah.

question: Jonathan worked out a signal for David, who had fled the palace and was hiding in a field. He would come to the field pretending to practice and shoot arrows past a boy servant. If he called that the arrows were on this side, it was safe; if he called that they were beyond, David must flee. How many arrows did Jonathan say he would shoot?
context: 1 Samuel 20:20-22, 35-38 KJV. Jonathan promises: 'I will shoot three arrows on the side thereof, as though I shot at a mark.' On the day he shoots past the lad and cries 'Is not the arrow beyond thee?' and 'Make speed, haste, stay not', the warning for David hidden by the stone Ezel. The two friends then meet one last time in secret before David runs.

question: Jonathan met David in secret in the field after the arrows were shot, and the two friends kissed one another and wept together. Before they parted, Jonathan made David swear an oath. 'The LORD be between me and thee,' it ran, and then it named two more, 'for ever.' What were the other two?
context: 1 Samuel 20:41-42 KJV: 'they kissed one another, and wept one with another'; then 'The LORD be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever.' The oath about seed, descendants, is what saves Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth years later, when David is king.

question: King Saul, wounded by Philistine archers on a mountain in the north, asked his armour-bearer to run him through so he would not be captured. His sons had been cut down around him, and when the man refused, the king did it himself. On what mountain did Saul and his sons, Jonathan among them, die?
context: 1 Samuel 31:1-6 KJV. Saul falls upon his own sword after his armour-bearer refuses; the armour-bearer then does the same. Carmel is the mountain of Elijah's contest, Tabor of Deborah and Barak, and Hermon stands on Israel's northern border.

question: The Philistines fastened the bodies of Saul and his sons to the wall of Beth-shan. The valiant men of one Israelite town, once rescued by Saul from the Ammonites, marched all night, took the bodies down and carried them home, burned them, and buried what was left beneath a tamarisk, then fasted for seven days. What town's men came by night to recover Saul and Jonathan?
context: 1 Samuel 31:10-13 KJV: they 'burnt them there. And they took their bones, and buried them under a tree at Jabesh, and fasted seven days.' The Hebrew names the tree as a tamarisk. Saul had saved Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite at the start of his reign (1 Samuel 11); the town pays the debt at the end. Kiriath-jearim, Ramoth-gilead and Beersheba are other towns of the same books, and none of them does this deed.

question: David turned from Saul and the army to Jonathan alone in the lament he sang over them. He called his dead friend 'my brother' and gave one line about their friendship, saying it surpassed another kind of love. How did David finish the line 'Thy love to me was wonderful, passing'?
context: 2 Samuel 1:26 KJV: 'I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women.' The line has been read as poetic hyperbole for sworn heroic brotherhood (the Hebrew match to Achilles and Patroclus, Roland and Oliver, Fionn's Fianna) and, by other readers, as something closer; the text itself does not say.

question: The prophetess Deborah sat down under one tree in the hills of Ephraim to settle Israel's quarrels, in the days of the Judges. Israelites walked up from all over the country to see her there, and the tree came to bear her name. Under what kind of tree did Deborah sit?
context: Judges 4:5 KJV: 'And she dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim: and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment.' The oak and terebinth are real judgment-trees elsewhere in scripture (Abraham's oak at Mamre, Gideon's terebinth); the cedar of Lebanon is a real temple wood but no one sat under one for judgment.

question: Barak, Israel's war-captain, heard God's order from the prophetess Deborah: gather ten thousand men and march north against Sisera, the Canaanite general who had been terrorizing Israel. Barak agreed to go, but only on one strange condition. What did Barak ask for?
answer: that the prophetess come with him
choices: that the prophetess come with him
that a lamb be offered first
that the king of Hazor be named
that the tribes of Judah lead
context: Judges 4:8 KJV: 'If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go.' Deborah agreed to go, but told him the glory of the day would not be his: the Lord would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:9).

question: Sisera, general of the Canaanite king Jabin of Hazor, marched out to crush the tribes of Israel, mustered on Mount Tabor under the warrior Barak. He brought a force that terrified the lightly armed Israelites, one their foot soldiers could not stand against on open ground. What fearsome force did Sisera bring with him?
context: Judges 4:3 KJV: 'he had nine hundred chariots of iron; and twenty years he mightily oppressed the children of Israel.' Iron chariots were the terror-weapon of the Canaanite lowlands; Israel's foot-levy had nothing that could stand against them on open ground.

question: Barak mustered his men on Mount Tabor, and the great host of the Canaanite general Sisera rolled down into a river valley in northern Israel. A sudden storm turned the streambed to thick mud, the heavy wheels sank fast, and Sisera's whole host was routed. What river was the trap?
context: Judges 4:7 KJV: 'I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin's army, with his chariots and his multitude.' The Song later says the Kishon swept them away. The Kidron runs by Jerusalem; the Arnon and Jabbok are east-Jordan rivers of other stories.

question: The beaten general Sisera ran on foot to a nomad's tent, and a woman named Jael took him in. When he begged for water she opened a skin bottle and gave him something richer to drink instead. What did Jael give him?
context: Judges 4:19; the Song of Deborah remembers it more richly: 'He asked water, and she gave him milk; she brought forth butter in a lordly dish' (Judges 5:25 KJV). The full stomach and the warmth of the mantle she then covered him with sent him straight to sleep.

question: Jael, a Kenite woman, took the beaten Canaanite general Sisera into her tent, gave him a drink and covered him with a mantle to hide him. The prophetess Deborah had foretold that he would fall into the hand of a woman. Jael watched him sink into exhausted sleep, then crept to him. What did Jael use to kill him?
choices: a bronze dagger from his own belt
the leg-bone of a young ram
a rope drawn tight round his neck
context: Judges 4:21 KJV: 'Then Jael Heber's wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground.' Ehud killed King Eglon with a dagger and Samson killed a thousand with the jawbone of an ass; Jael's weapon was neither warrior's blade nor hero's improvisation but a peg and a mallet from her own tent.

question: Deborah sang a triumphant war-poem after the fall of the Canaanite general Sisera, and Judges chapter 5 preserves it. Her song refused to credit only human weapons, not the spears of the warrior Barak and not the hand of Jael. It insisted that heaven itself had joined the fight against the Canaanite host. What did Deborah's song claim fought against Sisera from above?
context: Judges 5:20 KJV: 'They fought from heaven; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.' Read with the next verse ('the river of Kishon swept them away'), the song turns the storm that flooded the Kishon into a cosmic army answering Deborah's call.

question: A woman at a latticed window in a Canaanite palace strained her eyes down the road and cried, 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the wheels of his chariots?' Deborah's victory song leaves the battlefield for this scene in its last verses, and the man she waited for lay dead in Jael's tent. Who was the woman at the window?
context: Judges 5:28 KJV: 'The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming?' Her wise ladies reassure her the men must be dividing the spoil ('to every man a damsel or two'); the reader knows the truth. Ending the war-hymn on a grieving enemy mother is one of the oldest and strangest moves in Hebrew poetry.

question: Zeus's older sister Demeter searched the earth for her stolen daughter, and her grief fell on the whole world. She was one of the twelve Olympian gods, each with a share of the world to rule. Which share was Demeter's?
context: Demeter is the Olympian goddess of grain, cereals, and the harvest. She and Zeus are siblings, children of the Titans Cronus and Rhea. Source: Wikipedia (Demeter).

question: Demeter lost her daughter to the underworld, a girl fathered by her brother Zeus. In her grief Demeter let no seed sprout, and ever after the fields lay bare for part of every year. What was Demeter's daughter's name?
context: Persephone (also called Kore, 'the Maiden') is the daughter of Demeter and Zeus. Source: Wikipedia (Persephone).  (Legend.)

question: Earth herself grew one especially beautiful flower in a sunny meadow, as a trap for the young daughter of Demeter. The lord of the dead had asked his brother Zeus for the girl. She was gathering flowers with her friends, and when she reached for the bloom the ground split open. Which flower was the lure?
context: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 8-14) describes a marvellous narcissus Earth made to grow at Zeus's will, with a hundred blooms from a single root, put there to lure the girl. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Demeter's daughter reached for a strange and beautiful flower in a sunlit meadow, and the earth split open beneath her feet. A dark god rushed up through the crack in a golden chariot pulled by immortal horses, seized the girl and took her below as his queen. Which god took her?
context: Hades, lord of the dead and Zeus's brother, seizes Persephone in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 15-20) with Zeus's silent consent. Poseidon rules the sea, Apollo brings prophecy and the sun's light, and Hermes conducts souls to the underworld gates but does not rule there. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Demeter searched the whole world for her daughter for nine days, refusing ambrosia and nectar, the food and drink of the gods, and no one would tell her where the girl had gone. She walked even by night, and in the Homeric Hymn she held something in her hands all the way. What did Demeter carry as she searched?
context: Homeric Hymn to Demeter lines 45-50: 'for nine days queenly Deo wandered over the earth with flaming torches in her hands.' Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Helios, the sun-god who sees everything from above the sky, heard Demeter's daughter cry out as she was dragged into the underworld, in the ancient Homeric Hymn to Demeter. Only one other god heard her: a goddess of crossroads, listening from her cave. Which goddess was the second witness?
context: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 22-27), no god or mortal heard Persephone's cry but Hecate, from her cave, and Helios the Sun. After the compromise, Hecate becomes Persephone's attendant in the underworld. Nyx (Night), Eos (Dawn) and Selene (Moon) are goddesses of the heavens too, but the Hymn names Hecate. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Queen Metaneira of Eleusis caught her baby's old nurse at her work one night. The nurse was Demeter in disguise, trying to make the prince Demophoon immortal. She anointed him with ambrosia by day and hid him at night in the heart of one dangerous thing. What was he hidden in?
context: Homeric Hymn to Demeter lines 236-248: Demeter hid Demophoon 'like a brand in the heart of the fire.' Queen Metaneira spied by night, cried out, and stopped the rite. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Demeter blighted every field on earth in her grief and fury over her stolen daughter. The oxen dragged the plows in vain, the seeds never sprouted, and humans everywhere began to starve. At last Zeus, king of the gods, sent the messenger god Hermes down to fetch the girl back. What was the one thing that finally forced Zeus to act?
answer: The gods received no sacrifices from the empty altars
choices: The gods received no sacrifices from the empty altars
The other Olympians rose up against Zeus
Hera demanded it as her price
context: Demeter's blight starved mortals, but the pressure that broke Zeus was divine: with no grain there were no offerings, and the Olympians received no sacrifices from the empty altars. Zeus then sent Hermes to Hades to negotiate Persephone's return. Source: Wikipedia (Demeter); Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus sent the swift messenger god Hermes down into the underworld to bring Demeter's daughter back to her mother. But the lord of the dead was cunning. Before he let the girl go he slyly offered her one small thing, because anyone who tasted any food in the underworld could never fully leave it. What did he give her to eat?
context: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (line 371) Hades gives Persephone a single sweet pomegranate seed; Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book 5) gives the number as seven, and later tradition settled on six seeds for six months. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2; Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus arranged a compromise. Because Demeter's daughter had tasted food in the underworld, she had to go back for part of every year as queen below, and spend the rest above with her grieving mother. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, what share of each year did she spend below?
context: Homeric Hymn to Demeter lines 395-400: Persephone spends 'a third part of the seasons every year' with Hades and two-thirds with Demeter. Ovid (Metamorphoses 5) and Hyginus give half the year. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: The royal family of one small Greek town took in an old woman and treated her kindly, and she turned out to be Demeter in disguise. In gratitude she revealed her secret rites to them. The rites were celebrated for over a thousand years, and every initiate was sworn to lifelong silence about the central secret. What were these rites called?
context: Homeric Hymn to Demeter lines 473-479: Demeter taught her rites to Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus, and Celeus at Eleusis. The Mysteries ran from the Mycenaean period to the 4th century AD; initiates were sworn to never reveal what they saw, and the secret was kept for the entire history of the cult. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Prince Triptolemus learned to grow grain from Demeter and did not keep the gift for Greece alone. She gave him a flying chariot so that he could travel the world and teach farming, and it was pulled by two of the strangest animals in Greek myth. What drew Triptolemus's chariot across the sky?
context: In the fuller Eleusinian tradition, Triptolemus flew a winged serpent-drawn chariot given by Demeter and spread grain-farming across the world -- shown often in Attic vase-painting. Source: Wikipedia (Triptolemus).  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek flood story, Zeus drowned the wicked human race, but one couple was warned in time: Deucalion, king of Phthia, and his wife. After the waters fell, they filled the world again with stones that turned into people. What was her name?
context: Pyrrha, daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, was the wife of Deucalion; in Ovid the two of them are the only people left alive after the flood. Source: Wikipedia (Pyrrha of Thessaly).  (Legend.)

question: Zeus sent a deluge to destroy a wicked human race, but Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survived by floating in a wooden chest. Deucalion's father, a Titan who could see the future, had warned him to build it, and this same Titan once took fire from the gods for people. Who was he?
context: Deucalion was the son of the Titan Prometheus, whose name means 'forethought' and who could foresee the future. Iapetus was Prometheus's own father; Menoetius and Atlas were his brothers. Source: Wikipedia (Deucalion).  (Legend.)

question: Zeus grew disgusted with humankind and sent a great flood to wipe it out. Warned in time, Deucalion built a wooden chest and rode out the storm inside it with his wife Pyrrha, drifting over the drowned world until the waters fell. In Apollodorus's telling, how many days and nights did the couple float?
context: In Apollodorus's Library (1.7.2), Deucalion and Pyrrha float in the chest for nine days and as many nights before drifting to Parnassus. Ovid tells the same flood with a small boat and gives no count of days. Forty days and nights is the length of the rain in the Noah story of Genesis. Source: Apollodorus, Library 1.7.2; Wikipedia (Deucalion).  (Legend.)

question: Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha rode out Zeus's flood in a wooden chest, drifting over a drowned world. At last the chest grounded on the peak of a great twin-topped mountain, the one that rises above the oracle at Delphi and is sacred to Apollo and the Muses. Which mountain does the standard version name?
context: In Ovid the little boat, and in Apollodorus the chest, comes to rest on Parnassus, above Delphi in central Greece. Helicon is also sacred to the Muses; Cithaeron and Pelion are other famous mountains of Greek myth. Variant traditions of the landing name Etna, Athos or Othrys, but Parnassus is the settled landing. Source: Wikipedia (Deucalion); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.316-317.  (Legend.)

question: Alone in an empty world after the flood, Deucalion and Pyrrha asked the oracle of Themis how the human race could begin again. The answer was a chilling riddle: they must throw behind them 'the bones of your great mother.' Pyrrha was horrified. Deucalion thought a while and then told her what the words really meant. What did he say the great mother was?
context: Deucalion realised the great mother was the Earth (Gaia), and the bones of the Earth were stones scattered on the ground. Pyrrha at first believed the oracle was demanding she desecrate her own mother Pandora's grave. Source: Wikipedia (Pyrrha of Thessaly); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.383-390.  (Legend.)

question: Deucalion and Pyrrha, alone after the flood, begged the oracle of the goddess Themis to tell them how to refill the empty world. The oracle answered with a riddle about the bones of their mother, and Deucalion solved it. But before they threw anything, the oracle had ordered them to do something to their own bodies. What did they do?
answer: Veiled their heads and unloosed their girdles
choices: Veiled their heads and unloosed their girdles
Removed their sandals and cut their hair
Turned their faces east and knelt
context: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.381-383, the oracle commands them to cover their heads, unbind their girdles, and throw behind them the bones of their great mother. The stones Deucalion threw became men and those Pyrrha threw became women. Source: Wikipedia (Pyrrha of Thessaly); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.395-415.  (Legend.)

question: Deucalion and Pyrrha refilled the world by throwing stones over their shoulders, but they also had a son of their own in the ordinary way. His three sons, Aeolus, Dorus and Xuthus, gave their names to the great tribes of Greece: the Aeolians, the Dorians, and through Xuthus's sons the Ionians and Achaeans. The whole Greek people took their name from this one father. Who was he?
context: Hellen is the eponymous ancestor of the Hellenes. His sons Aeolus, Dorus, and Xuthus (father of Achaeus and Ion) gave their names to the Aeolians, Dorians, Achaeans, and Ionians. Cadmus was the Phoenician founder of Thebes; Danaus was the ancestor of the Argives; Pelasgus was the mythic ancestor of the pre-Greek Pelasgians. Source: Wikipedia (Deucalion).  (Legend.)

question: The High King of Ireland, ruling from the sacred hill of Tara, promises his young daughter to Fionn mac Cumhaill, the ageing chief of the Fianna war-band. Fionn has grown older than the High King himself, in these old Irish Fenian tales. What is the princess's name?
context: Grainne (pronounced GRAWN-ya) is the girl who will not have old Fionn. Sadhbh is Fionn's earlier wife, the mother of Oisin (she is a deer under enchantment); Etain is the heroine of Tochmarc Etaine in a different cycle; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife from the Ulster Cycle. All four are famous women from Irish mythology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.  (Legend.)

question: A fairy woman sets a magical mark on the forehead of a young warrior of the Fianna, the war-band of Fionn mac Cumhaill. Any mortal woman who catches even a glimpse of this love-spot falls hopelessly in love with him. Which young warrior of the Fianna is he?
context: Diarmuid Ua Duibhne (Diarmuid of the love-spot) is one of the finest and most beloved young warriors of the Fianna. Oisin is Fionn's poet son; Caoilte mac Ronain is Fionn's runner-messenger; Goll mac Morna is Fionn's older rival within the Fianna. All four are Fenian heroes, only one carries the ball seirce. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.  (Legend.)

question: The young princess looks around the betrothal feast at Tara at old white-haired Fionn and refuses the match in her heart. She sees Diarmuid across the room, his love-spot showing under a cap, and she acts. What does she do to the rest of the hall?
answer: drugs every cup with a sleeping potion
choices: drugs every cup with a sleeping potion
sings a lullaby that puts them to sleep
throws a druidic mist over them
sets a spell of silence on the tables
context: Grainne passes the drinking-cups herself, dosing every guest EXCEPT Diarmuid. The sleeping-cup at the feast is one of the most famous images in the tale. The other three -- lullaby-sleep, druidic mist, spell of silence -- are all real motifs elsewhere in Irish myth (druidic mist is very common), but the tool here is a straightforward drugged cup. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn and his war-band chase the young warrior Diarmuid and the princess he has run away with across the length and breadth of Ireland. She has forced him to it by a binding vow at the feast at Tara, and the hunt goes on so long that five children are born to them along the way. About how many years does the pursuit last?
context: The pursuit is remembered as sixteen years -- long enough for Diarmuid and Grainne to have five children on the run. Seven is the standard folk-year (as in the seven years' service of Jacob); three years is the geasa-year; twenty-one is a marker in Fenian tales too. Only sixteen matches Toraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/pursuit-of-diarmuid-and-grainne.  (Legend.)

question: Diarmuid's foster-father shelters the lovers again and again with mist and trickery as Fionn hunts them, and eventually he mediates a peace. He is one of the Tuatha De Danann, master of the great passage-tomb on the Boyne. Who is Diarmuid's foster-father?
context: Aengus Og (Aengus 'the Young') is the god of love, master of the great passage-tomb at Newgrange (Brugh na Boinne). Lugh Lamhfhada is the many-skilled hero; the Dagda is the 'good god' with the club and the cauldron; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god. All four are Tuatha De Danann -- only Aengus is Diarmuid's foster-father. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn organises a great boar-hunt, years after the peace, on a real Irish mountain in County Sligo, a limestone table-mountain with a sudden northern cliff, still visible from Sligo town today. It is here that Diarmuid meets his death. Which mountain is it?
context: Ben Bulben (Beann Ghulbain, 'peak of Gulba') is a real 526-metre limestone mountain in County Sligo, its flat top and prow-like north face famous in Irish landscape (Yeats is buried in its shadow at Drumcliffe). Slieve Bloom is the mountain-range of central Ireland; Cnoc Aine is the fairy-hill of the goddess Aine in Limerick; Slieve Mish is a range in Kerry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.  (Legend.)

question: A druid turns the body of a child killed long ago into an enchanted boar and binds it by prophecy to kill Diarmuid. Years later the beast meets him on Fionn's great hunt. In the boy's identity lies the whole tragedy. Who was the boy?
answer: a half-brother of the doomed man
choices: a half-brother of the doomed man
a stable-boy of Cormac mac Airt
context: The half-brother -- Roc's son -- was killed as a child by Diarmuid's father Donn (crushed between his knees when Donn feared the boy was not his own); the boy's father, the druid Roc, then turned the body into a boar bound by prophecy to be Diarmuid's death. So Fionn's boar-hunt on Ben Bulben deliberately sends Diarmuid against a beast fated by druidic craft to kill him. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.  (Legend.)

question: The boar gores Diarmuid, but he mortally wounds it in return, and Fionn arrives to find him dying. Long ago Fionn gained a gift from the Salmon of Knowledge: he can heal any wound with well-water, if only he carries it back to the wounded man in one specific way. How must he carry it?
answer: cupped in his own two hands
choices: cupped in his own two hands
soaked into a folded oak leaf
wrung from a cloth on his sword
context: The healing-water in Fionn's cupped hands is the whole hinge of the death-scene: he CAN save Diarmuid, and the whole Fianna is watching. Fionn walks to the well three times -- and the first two times the water is gone before he reaches Diarmuid. Oak leaves, sword-cloths, and drinking-horns all appear as folk vessels elsewhere in Irish tradition, but the gift attached to Fionn is his own cupped hands. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn walks to the well twice for the dying Diarmuid. Both times he brings the healing water back close to him, and both times it is gone before it can touch the wound. He goes back a third time and does deliver it, but by then it is too late. How does the water get away from Fionn on the first two trips?
answer: it slips through his cupped fingers
choices: it slips through his cupped fingers
it evaporates in the noon sun
his hound-pups drink it from the bowl
a raven of the Morrigan strikes it out of his hand
context: Fionn LETS the water fall through his cupped fingers twice on purpose -- remembering Grainne, remembering the sixteen years of pursuit, remembering the humiliation. On the third trip he brings the water, but Diarmuid has already died. It is one of the darkest moments in the Fenian Cycle: the leader murdering a friend by deliberate omission, in front of witnesses. Grainne curses Fionn when she hears, and the Fianna is never the same again. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.  (Legend.)

question: Old Fionn loses a young bride to a young warrior bound to her by a love-spell, and he hunts the pair through the wild for years. Scholars see this Irish tale as an ancestor of a great Continental romance, though they still debate the direction of borrowing. Which later medieval romance do they name?
context: Tristan (nephew of old King Mark of Cornwall), the young Irish princess Iseult he escorts home to marry his uncle, the love-potion, the flight into the forest, the pursuit -- the beat-list matches Toraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne almost exactly. Most scholars now think the Irish material fed the Continental Tristan through Brittany. Lancelot and Guinevere is a different Arthurian love-triangle; Roland and Aude are the doomed betrothed of the Chanson de Roland; Aucassin and Nicolette is a 13th-c. French chantefable. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.  (Legend.)

question: Dionysus joined the twelve Olympian gods as their youngest, a Greek god of wild rites and madness whom the Romans later worshipped as Bacchus. His festivals gave the world the first theater. Which drink was Dionysus the god of?
context: Dionysus is the Greek god of wine, the grape harvest, ecstatic madness, and the theatre. His Roman name is Bacchus. Source: Wikipedia (Dionysus).  (Legend.)

question: Jealous Hera disguised herself as the old nurse of Semele, a mortal Theban princess pregnant by Zeus. She came whispering that the girl's mysterious lover might not really be a god, and that Semele should force him to prove himself in one particular way. Hera knew the demand would kill her. What was Hera's fatal suggestion?
answer: Appear to her in his true form
choices: Appear to her in his true form
Give her a cup of ambrosia
Sacrifice a bull at her altar
Take her up to Mount Olympus
context: Hera, disguised as an old nurse (in some versions Semele's old nurse Beroe), persuades Semele to make the request that will kill her. Source: Wikipedia (Semele); Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.259-315.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus had already sworn an unbreakable oath by the river Styx to grant Semele any request. He begged her not to ask this one, but he was bound, and he came to her as she demanded. One thing about him killed her instantly. What killed Semele?
answer: The lightning of his divine glory
choices: The lightning of his divine glory
A single glance from his eyes
context: Zeus appeared to Semele with thunderbolts and lightning; the divine glory burned her to death on the spot. Source: Wikipedia (Semele); Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.308-309.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus kept his oath to the mortal princess Semele of Thebes, and she burned to ashes before him. But Semele was pregnant with his son, the future god Dionysus. Moving fast, Zeus snatched the unborn baby out of her burning body and sewed the child into a part of his own body to finish growing him. Into what part of his own body did Zeus sew the baby?
context: Zeus sewed the unborn Dionysus into his own thigh and carried him there until he was ready to be born a second time. (Athena burst from Zeus's forehead -- a different birth story.) Source: Wikipedia (Dionysus).  (Legend.)

question: Dionysus wandered the world as a grown god with a wild band of female followers, in Greek myth. They wore spotted fawnskins, and each one carried a long fennel wand called a thyrsus, topped with a pine cone and wrapped in ivy. What were these ecstatic female followers of Dionysus called?
context: The maenads -- the name means 'raving women' -- are Dionysus's ecstatic female followers; the wand they carry is the thyrsus, a fennel stalk topped with a pine cone. Nereids are sea nymphs, oreads are mountain nymphs, and the graces are the three Charites. Source: Wikipedia (Dionysus).  (Legend.)

question: Dionysus came back to his mother's city of Thebes to be worshipped, in the Bacchae of Euripides, and the young king refused to accept him as a god and tried to shut down his wild rites. In revenge, the god lured the king up a tall evergreen on Mount Cithaeron to peep down at the frenzied women dancing below. What was this doomed young king's name?
context: Pentheus, king of Thebes and Dionysus's own cousin, is the tragic figure of Euripides's Bacchae. Actaeon was another Theban torn apart on Cithaeron (by his own hounds after seeing Artemis bathing); Creon and Laius are other Theban kings. Source: Wikipedia (The Bacchae).  (Legend.)

question: Agave led the frenzied women who spotted the young king of Thebes spying from his tree, pulled him down and tore him limb from limb. He was her own son. She carried his head back to Thebes on her fennel wand, believing until the madness lifted that it was the head of one particular wild animal. What did she believe she was holding?
context: Agave, Pentheus's mother, led the maenads that tore him apart and returned to Thebes carrying his bloodied head, convinced it was a mountain lion until the divine frenzy faded. Source: Wikipedia (The Bacchae).  (Legend.)

question: Dionysus stood on a seashore in the shape of a handsome young man, the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus says, and Tyrrhenian pirates seized him, sure he was a king's son worth a fortune. Out at sea, wine streamed across the ship and ivy twined about the mast, and Dionysus took the form of a great beast in the bows. What beast did he become?
context: Homeric Hymn 7 (Evelyn-White): 'the god changed into a dreadful lion there on the ship, in the bows, and roared loudly', and amidships he made a shaggy bear. In Apollodorus's telling he instead turns the mast and oars into snakes. Source: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns and Homerica (Gutenberg).  (Legend.)

question: Tyrrhenian pirates seized the young Dionysus off the seashore in the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, mistaking him for a rich prince they could ransom. Out at sea a vine ran along the top of the sail and the god took on the shape of a great beast, and the terrified pirates leapt overboard. They did not drown; they were changed. What did the Tyrrhenian pirates become?
context: In Homeric Hymn 7 the pirates leap overboard into the bright sea and are changed into dolphins; only the good helmsman, who had recognised the god and begged the crew to release him, is spared. Source: Evelyn-White translation of Homeric Hymn 7.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus sailed away from Crete with a princess, the daughter of King Minos, who had given him a ball of thread to find his way out of the twisting Labyrinth after he killed the Minotaur. He abandoned her, sleeping, on the island of Naxos, and the god Dionysus found her there and married her. Whom did Dionysus marry?
context: Dionysus wed Ariadne on Naxos and set her bridal crown among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis; he also brought his mother Semele up from the underworld to Olympus, where she was given the new name Thyone. Phaedra was Ariadne's sister, Europa her ancestress, Pasiphae her mother. Source: Wikipedia (Ariadne).  (Legend.)

question: Jane of Aza, a Spanish noblewoman, had a vivid dream while carrying the future Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican preachers. An animal ran from her womb with a burning torch in its mouth and set the whole world afire. Which animal was it?
context: The son grew up to be Dominic, and later a Latin pun read his order's name as Domini canes, 'the Lord's dogs'. Jane of Aza was herself later beatified. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic.  (Legend.)

question: Dominic de Guzman, a Spanish priest, rode with his bishop through Languedoc in southern France in 1203. Barefoot preachers of a condemned sect were walking from village to village, while Catholic officials rumbled past with loaded pack-trains. Only poor preachers, Dominic realized, could win people back. Which sect did he set out to win over?
context: The Cathars, also called Albigensians after the town of Albi, were a dualist movement particularly strong in Languedoc. The Waldensians were a poverty movement of the same period; the Bogomils were the eastern dualist parent; the Iconoclasts were an earlier Byzantine controversy over images. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic.

question: Pope Honorius III approved a small band of like-minded preachers as a new religious order in 1216. Dominic de Guzman had gathered them at the city of Toulouse, and they were soon nicknamed the Dominicans. Each brother wore the same distinctive habit, and the order still wears it today. What did the Dominican habit look like?
context: The two colors gave the Dominicans their English nickname 'Blackfriars'; the white is said to stand for purity and the black for penance. The Carmelites wore brown-and-white; the Franciscans wore all-brown with a knotted cord; the Cistercians wore all-white. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic.

question: Dominic scattered his handful of brothers across Europe as soon as he had them together, sending them to preach and to study at the two great universities of the age. Jordan of Saxony records the reason he gave for the risk: 'Hoarded seed does not bear fruit.' To which two university cities did Dominic send them?
context: Paris was the great northern university, Bologna the great southern one. Oxford and Cambridge were still young in 1217; Naples had no university until 1224; Salamanca and Coimbra rose later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic.

question: A young Florentine sculptor fled political trouble at home and came into Bologna, almost three centuries after Dominic was buried there. He was hired to finish the small marble figures still missing from Dominic's tomb, and he carved a Saint Petronius, a Saint Proculus and a candle-bearing angel. Who was that young sculptor?
context: Michelangelo was nineteen when he fled Florence in 1494 after the expulsion of the Medici; the senator Aldrovandi sheltered him in Bologna and got him the arca commission. Nicola Pisano had begun the tomb-arca two centuries earlier; Donatello worked a generation before Michelangelo; Bernini was a 17th-century Roman. These three small figures are Michelangelo's earliest signed sculptures in Bologna. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arca_di_San_Domenico.

question: Odin, the chief Norse god, wore a gold ring on his arm. Gold fell from it again and again in fresh rings, like drops off a wet blade, and its Old Norse name means 'the dripper'. What was the ring called?
context: Old Norse Draupnir literally means 'the dripper'. Gungnir is Odin's spear; Andvaranaut is the cursed ring the dwarf Andvari gives up to Loki in the Volsung cycle; Gjallarhorn is Heimdall's warning-trumpet at the rainbow bridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupnir  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson set down how the magic worked in Odin's gold arm-ring, forged for him by the dwarves. Fresh rings of exactly equal weight fell from it, over and over, forever, on a strict schedule. By Snorri's account, how many rings fell, and how often?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: 'every ninth night there fell from it eight gold rings of equal weight.' The number nine echoes through Norse myth -- the nine worlds of Yggdrasil, Odin's nine nights hung on the tree, Thor's nine paces after killing the World-Serpent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupnir  (Legend.)

question: Odin walked up to the pyre on the funeral ship Hringhorni, where his shining son Baldr lay dead, killed by his blind brother Hodr through Loki's cruel trickery. All the gods had gathered around the body in grief. Odin laid his own most precious treasure on the fire, a father's last gift. Which of his treasures was it?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: Odin lays Draupnir on Baldr's pyre as the last gift. Gungnir the spear he keeps for himself; Huginn is his living raven, not a burnable object; there is no wolf-pelt cloak in the myth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupnir  (Legend.)

question: Roland, nephew of Charlemagne, holds the pass of Roncesvalles to the death in the great French epic the Song of Roland. All through the poem he carries one named blade, which an angel bade Charlemagne give him. What is that blade called?
context: Roland's sword in the Chanson de Roland is Durandal; in laisse 172 he recalls that God sent an angel to bid Charles give it to a captain count. Joyeuse is Charlemagne's OWN sword (a separate weapon in the same poem). Tizona is one of the two swords of El Cid. Excalibur is King Arthur's sword. Source: Wikipedia, 'Durendal'; Song of Roland (Moncrieff).  (Legend.)

question: Roland, nephew of Charlemagne, carries relics of famous saints sealed in the hollow hilt of his sword Durandal, in the medieval French epic the Song of Roland. A piece of the Virgin Mary's robe lies inside, with blood from Saint Basil. Whose tooth does the poem also name?
context: Song of Roland, laisse 173: the hilt of Durandal holds a tooth of Saint PETER, the blood of Saint Basil, the hair of Saint Denis, and a scrap of the Virgin Mary's robe. Peter was the chief of the apostles for the medieval church, which is why his relic tops the collection. Source: Wikipedia, 'Durendal'.  (Legend.)

question: Charlemagne, the emperor whom Roland serves, also carries his own famous named sword in the Song of Roland, a separate blade from his nephew's. The poem says thirty fresh hues appear on it each day. What is Charlemagne's sword called?
context: Joyeuse means 'the joyful one'. The Song says of it, 'Whereon each day thirty fresh hues appear' (Moncrieff), and that the point of the holy lance is set in its golden hilt. Curtana is the sword of mercy carried at English coronations. Notung and Balmung are two names for Sigurd's sword in the Volsung / Nibelung cycle. Source: Wikipedia, 'Joyeuse'; Song of Roland (Moncrieff).  (Legend.)

question: Roland lies dying at the pass of Roncesvalles, with the rearguard of Charlemagne's army broken. His sword must not be captured by the enemy and turned against Christian knights, so he rises one last time to destroy Durandal himself. What does the dying Roland do to try to destroy the sword?
answer: smashes it against a great rock at his side
choices: smashes it against a great rock at his side
throws it into a deep gorge below the pass
buries it under a heap of the fallen
sets it in the flames of a burning cart
context: Song of Roland: with his last strength Roland brings Durandal down again and again on the rock beside him, meaning to shatter the blade so that no pagan hand can carry it home. Source: Medievalists.net, 'Roland's Sword Goes Missing'.  (Legend.)

question: Roland raises Durandal high over a huge boulder, mortally wounded and alone on the mountainside after the ambush of Charlemagne's rearguard in the Pyrenees. He means to destroy his sword so no enemy can carry it away, and he strikes it down on the stone. What does the rock itself do as the blade lands?
choices: melts to slag around the point
swallows the blade to the hilt
rings out like a struck bell
context: Song of Roland, laisse 173 (Moncrieff): 'Rollant his stroke on a dark stone repeats, / And more of it breaks off than I can speak. / The sword cries out, yet breaks not in the least.' A later legend says the blow cut Roland's Breach in the Pyrenees. Source: Song of Roland (Gutenberg); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durendal.  (Legend.)

question: Roland cannot break Durandal, so at the point of death he hides it beneath his body and turns his face in one deliberate direction. Charlemagne, he intends, will find him fallen forward and still on the attack. In which direction does the dying Roland turn his face?
context: Song of Roland: unable to break the sword, Roland hides Durandal beneath his body and lies down with his face turned toward Spain -- toward the enemy -- so that Charlemagne, returning, will find him fallen forward, still on the attack rather than in retreat. Aachen was Charlemagne's northern capital, which would have signalled flight. Source: Wikipedia, 'Song of Roland'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Italian romances that retold Roland's story centuries after the Song, Roland is not the first man to wield Durandal. Boiardo and Ariosto give the sword a past much older than the poem allows, with a hero of the ancient world as its first owner. Which ancient hero do they say wielded Durandal first?
context: Boiardo's Orlando Innamorato traces Durindana to Hector of Troy; it passes to the Amazon queen Penthesilea and on to Almonte before Orlando wins it, and Ariosto's Orlando Furioso follows him.
