Achilles carried the armour Hephaestus forged for him; Aeneas carried a shield forged by Vulcan; Alexander of Macedon belongs to history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durendal.

question: Hera cursed a talkative mountain nymph in the forests of Boeotia, who had chattered on and on to hide Zeus's tricks. The nymph could never again speak first. What was her name?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.359-401. Echo is an oread (mountain nymph). Daphne is the nymph turned into a laurel to escape Apollo; Calypso keeps Odysseus seven years on Ogygia; Arethusa is the nymph turned into a spring in Sicily to escape the river-god Alpheus. The English word 'echo' -- a repeating voice -- comes directly from her name.  (Legend.)

question: One rejected lover lifted his hands to the sky and prayed against a beautiful young hunter of Boeotia. The hunter was so proud and cold that every girl and boy who fell in love with him went away in tears. What was this cruel young hunter called?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.339-350, 3.404-406. His father was the river Cephissus, his mother the nymph Liriope. Adonis is the beautiful youth Aphrodite loved, killed by a boar; Hyacinthus is the youth Apollo killed by accident with a discus; Endymion is the shepherd the Moon loved in his sleep. The English word 'narcissism' -- love of self -- comes from Narcissus.  (Legend.)

question: Liriope carried her newborn son Narcissus to the Theban seer who would one day speak to Odysseus in the underworld, and she asked whether the boy would reach old age. The seer gave a strange, riddling answer nobody understood at the time. Who was the seer she asked?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.339-348. Tiresias is the Theban seer of the Odyssey and of Sophocles. Calchas is the Greek seer at Troy; Melampus is an earlier seer of Argos; Amphiaraus is the seer of the Seven Against Thebes. Tiresias's answer -- that the boy would live long only if he never came to know himself -- would prove exact.  (Legend.)

question: A mountain nymph followed the beautiful hunter through the trees, longing to speak but unable to begin. He called out 'Is anyone here?' and she called back 'Here!' He called 'Here, let us meet together!' and she answered 'Together!' and stepped out to throw her arms around his neck. What did he say to her?
answer: He would sooner die than give himself to her
choices: He would sooner die than give himself to her
He had vowed himself to Artemis alone
She must speak first or leave him in peace
She was a shade and must go back to the wood
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.379-392. In A. S. Kline's translation Narcissus runs from her crying 'Away with these encircling hands! May I die before what's mine is yours.' Echo answers only 'What's mine is yours!', hides her face among the leaves and wastes away until only her voice is left.  (Legend.)

question: 'So may he himself love, and so may he fail to command what he loves!' One of the youths scorned by the proud hunter Narcissus of Boeotia lifted his hands to the sky and prayed those words. Narcissus had broken the heart of every girl and boy who loved him. Which Greek goddess heard the prayer and answered it?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.402-406 (A. S. Kline's translation). Nemesis, whom Ovid calls Rhamnusia, is the goddess of righteous retribution, the punisher of pride. Hecate is the goddess of witchcraft and crossroads; Eris is strife (the golden apple at the wedding of Peleus); Ate is reckless folly. Nemesis's answer will fall on Narcissus at a clear pool in the woods.  (Legend.)

question: Narcissus knelt at a clear pool to drink, tired from the hunt on a hot day. A beautiful face rose to meet him from the water as he bent down, and there was one thing about that face he did not realise. What did Narcissus fail to realise about the face in the pool?
choices: it was a naiad of the spring
it was the ghost of a lover he scorned
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.407-436. Narcissus falls in love with his own reflection without knowing what he is looking at -- and Nemesis's answer, and Tiresias's oracle, both come true in that instant.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess had trapped Narcissus in love with the beautiful face gazing back from a still pool in the woods of Boeotia, and he knelt beside it. Again and again he leaned down to kiss the face and to embrace it, but each attempt brought something that made him weep. What happened each time Narcissus reached for the face in the pool?
answer: the water rippled and the arms in it dissolved at his touch
choices: the water rippled and the arms in it dissolved at his touch
a cold hand from the pool pushed his own hand away
the face closed its eyes and turned aside from him
a black fish rose up between them and hid the face
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.427-436. Every reach broke the surface -- so the beautiful arms in the water reached back to him and dissolved the instant he touched them. Narcissus refused to leave the pool, unable to eat, unable to sleep, weeping for a body that vanished at his fingertips.  (Legend.)

question: A mountain nymph who loved Narcissus watched from the trees as he lay dying at the pool, day and night, unable to eat or leave the face in the water. Hera's curse on her voice still held. When he finally cried out his last words to that face, what could she do?
answer: repeat his 'Alas!' and 'Farewell!' back to him
choices: repeat his 'Alas!' and 'Farewell!' back to him
step out at last and lay her hands on his face
sing his mother Liriope to the pool
call up Nemesis to break the curse
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.494-501. Echo's curse still held -- she could not speak first, could not comfort him, could only give back the last words: 'Alas!' -- 'Alas!' -- 'Farewell!' -- 'Farewell!' Two doomed lovers, each stranded from the object of longing, one at the pool and one in the trees.  (Legend.)

question: In Ovid's telling, the wood-nymphs came to burn the body of a proud young hunter on a pyre, after he wasted away by a still pool in Boeotia, unable to stop staring into the water. Where he had lain they found no body at all, only a small flower with white petals and a golden centre. What is that flower still called?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.509-510. The nymphs found only the flower we still call the narcissus. The hyacinth grew from the blood of Hyacinthus (Apollo's discus); the anemone from the blood of Adonis (the boar); the crocus from the youth Crocus who loved the nymph Smilax. Three flowers from three doomed loves; Narcissus's is the one that loved only itself.  (Legend.)

question: Rodrigo Diaz, a warrior from a village near Burgos in Castile, fought for Christian kings and Muslim emirs both. His Christian friends and his Muslim foes alike gave him one nickname of honor. What is that famous nickname today?
context: Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar (c. 1043-1099) is called El Cid ('the lord' -- see another question for the language it comes from). El Conquistador ('the conqueror') is the standard title given to the New World Spanish invaders of centuries later. El Rey means 'the king'; El Caballero means 'the knight' -- both generic titles, not his nickname. Source: Britannica, 'El Cid'.

question: Rodrigo Diaz wept at the opening of the Cantar de Mio Cid, Castile's oldest surviving epic poem, written down around 1207. His king had just unjustly ordered him into exile from all Castile, on the whispers of enemies at court. Which king of Leon and Castile pronounced the exile?
context: Alfonso VI of Leon and Castile (r. 1065-1109) exiled the historical Rodrigo Diaz twice, in 1081 and 1089; the Cantar de Mio Cid conflates the two into one dramatic opening exile. Alfonso VII was Alfonso VI's grandson. Sancho II of Castile was Alfonso VI's brother, murdered before the story starts. Ferdinand I was Alfonso VI's father. Source: Poetry in Translation, El Cantar de mio Cid Part I; Britannica, 'El Cid'.

question: Rodrigo Diaz had men to feed in his exile, so he sold his sword to anyone who would pay. For a time the real Rodrigo served the Muslim rulers of one Spanish city, fighting for them against Christians and other Muslims alike. Which Spanish city was it?
context: For years in his historical exile the Cid served the Muslim Banu Hud emirs of ZARAGOZA in the Ebro valley, campaigning for them against neighbouring Christian and Muslim powers alike. The Cantar tidies this into a purely Christian arc; the history is messier. Cordoba was by then a fading caliphate remnant, Granada and Seville were rival Taifa emirates the Cid did NOT serve. Source: Britannica, 'El Cid'.

question: Rodrigo took a sword in battle from the Count of Barcelona, in the Cantar de Mio Cid, and its name was Colada. He took his second named sword from the Moroccan king Bucar, and each blade had the honour of a proper name of its own. What was the name of that second sword?
context: The Cid's two named swords in the Cantar are COLADA (from the Count of Barcelona) and TIZONA (from king Bucar of Morocco). Durandal is Roland's sword; Joyeuse is Charlemagne's; Curtana is the English coronation sword of mercy -- all real named blades from other traditions. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tizona'.  (Legend.)

question: Rodrigo Diaz besieged one of the richest cities of Muslim al-Andalus, a great port on Spain's Mediterranean coast, and took it in 1094. He ruled it as his own princedom until his death there in 1099. Which city did he take?
context: The Cid took Valencia in 1094 after a long siege and ruled it as his own princedom until his death there in 1099. Toledo had already been taken by Alfonso VI in 1085. Cordoba fell to Ferdinand III much later, in 1236. Malaga was taken by the Catholic Monarchs at the very end of the Reconquista, in 1487. Source: Britannica, 'El Cid'.

question: The Infantes de Carrion committed a crime against Rodrigo's two daughters, their new wives, and the third and last cantar of the Poem of My Cid turns on it rather than on more battles. What did the Infantes do to the daughters?
answer: stripped, beat, and abandoned them in a forest
choices: stripped, beat, and abandoned them in a forest
poisoned them at a banquet in Carrion
sold them into slavery in Africa
shut them up in a convent at Leon
context: Cantar III: the Infantes de Carrion take Elvira and Sol into the oak-wood of Corpes, strip them, beat them mercilessly with their belts and spurs, and leave them for dead. It is a shocking scene by any age's standards. The daughters are rescued by their cousin Felez Munoz and the Cid demands justice from King Alfonso. Source: Poetry in Translation, El Cantar de mio Cid Part VI.  (Legend.)

question: Rodrigo's king arranged much better second marriages for Elvira and Sol, Rodrigo's two daughters, once the Infantes de Carrion had been shamed and defeated. The Poem of My Cid says with pride that the Christian kings of Spain descend from these marriages. To the princes of which two Iberian kingdoms did the king marry them?
context: Cantar III's closing lines re-marry Elvira and Sol to the princes of Navarre and Aragon; the poem claims this is why 'today the kings of Spain descend from Mio Cid'. The other pairs are real Iberian kingdoms of the age but not the ones the poem names. Source: Poetry in Translation, El Cantar de mio Cid Part VI.  (Legend.)

question: Rodrigo Diaz may never have carried the eleventh-century sword displayed in the Museum of Burgos, though it has long been identified as one of his two named blades. The regional government of Castile and Leon paid 1.6 million euros in 2007 to keep it in Spain. Which of his two swords is the Burgos blade venerated as?
answer: Tizona -- the one from king Bucar of Morocco
choices: Tizona -- the one from king Bucar of Morocco
Colada -- the one from the Count of Barcelona
Tizona -- the one from the Count of Barcelona
Colada -- the one from king Bucar of Morocco
context: The Burgos sword is TIZONA -- the sword won from king Bucar of Morocco. It is an eleventh-century blade the regional government bought in 2007 for 1.6 million euros. Its bill of ownership traces back through Spanish noble families but the identification with the Cid's actual sword is disputed by historians. Colada, the other of the Cid's two swords, was the one taken from the Count of Barcelona -- no surviving blade is claimed as Colada. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tizona'.

question: In 1 Kings, the prophet Elijah stood before King Ahab of Israel and swore no rain would fall except by his word. God told him to hide by a brook east of the Jordan. What creatures brought him bread and meat there, morning and evening?
context: 1 Kings 17:6 KJV: 'And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook.' The brook is called Cherith. Ravens are ritually unclean birds in the law -- part of the story's shock is that unclean birds keep God's own prophet alive.

question: King Ahab's foreign-born queen drove the hunt for Elijah's life, after the prophet swore that no rain would fall on Israel except by his word. While he hid, she hunted down the prophets of Israel's God across the land. Who was she?
context: 1 Kings 16:31; 18:4, 13. Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and she was cutting down the prophets of the LORD while Elijah was in hiding. Athaliah is her daughter, later queen of Judah; Bathsheba is Solomon's mother; Delilah belongs to the Samson story.

question: Elijah left Israel at God's command and went to stay with a poor widow in a town along the coast of Sidon. King Ahab's queen, a Sidonian princess, wanted him dead, so he was hiding in her own homeland, the last place her killers would think to look. What was the widow's town called?
context: 1 Kings 17:9. Zarephath sits between Tyre and Sidon. Tyre is the other great Phoenician city; Tishbe is Elijah's own hometown ('the Tishbite'); Shunem will appear later in Elisha's stories.

question: Elijah came to the gate of a foreign town and called to a widow gathering firewood, asking for water and a bite of bread. She swore there was nothing baked, only a scrap of flour and a little oil. She had come out, she said, to gather wood for one final cake for herself and her son before they starved. How many sticks did she say she was gathering?
choices: As many as her arms could hold
context: 1 Kings 17:12 KJV: 'behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.' The number matters -- two sticks is barely a fire, and it makes the widow's poverty concrete.

question: Elijah told a poor widow in the long drought to bake him a small cake first, and he promised that God had said her food stores would not run out until the rain returned to Israel. In the King James Bible, which two household containers did his promise name?
answer: A barrel of meal and a cruse of oil
choices: A barrel of meal and a cruse of oil
A jar of meal and a flask of oil
A sack of meal and a jug of oil
A pot of meal and a horn of oil
context: 1 Kings 17:14 KJV: 'The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth.' The 'cruse' is a small clay flask; the 'barrel' is a large storage jar. Modern translations often say 'jar of flour and jug of oil' -- the barrel/cruse pairing is the KJV's signature phrasing.

question: Elijah carried the widow's son up to the loft where he was staying, after the boy fell sick and stopped breathing. He laid the child on his own bed and stretched himself out on him, crying to God. How many times does the story say he stretched himself upon the boy?
context: 1 Kings 17:21 KJV: 'And he stretched himself upon the child three times, and cried unto the LORD.' Seven and forty are recurring biblical numbers in other stories -- seven for Naaman's dips, forty for the wilderness -- so all three feel plausible until you know the verse.

question: Elijah cried to God over the widow's dead boy in the upper room, and the child breathed again. The prophet carried him down the stairs and handed him to his mother. In the King James Bible, what did Elijah say to her as he gave back the boy?
context: 1 Kings 17:23 KJV. This is the first raising-of-the-dead scene in the Hebrew Bible; Elisha will do the same thing later for the Shunammite woman's boy. 'Rise up and walk' and 'Thy faith hath saved him' come from the New Testament (the paralytic and the woman with the issue of blood).

question: Obadiah, King Ahab's own steward, gathered a hundred prophets and hid them in caves while the queen was killing prophets across the land. He secretly feared God, and he kept them alive on bread and water while Elijah was in hiding. How did he split them between the hiding places?
context: 1 Kings 18:4 KJV: 'Obadiah took an hundred prophets, and hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water.' Two caves, fifty each. Obadiah is Ahab's governor of the household -- the parallel to Elijah is deliberate: God is feeding his prophet with ravens, and this quiet insider is feeding a hundred more with bread and water.

question: In the Gospel of Luke, Jesus reminded the crowd at Nazareth of the widows of Israel and gave Elijah's drought a specific length. The letter of James held Elijah up as a model of prayer and gave the same figure. How long did both say the drought lasted?
context: Luke 4:25 and James 5:17 KJV both give 'three years and six months.' 1 Kings itself only says 'in the third year' the word came to Elijah to return (1 Kings 18:1) -- the exact 3.5-year figure is the New Testament's gloss, which is why later Christian tradition speaks of a three-and-a-half-year drought.

question: David, a shepherd boy of Bethlehem, sat down at the court of King Saul of Israel to play for him. An evil spirit had been tormenting Saul and making him rage, and as David played the king felt well again. What instrument was David playing?
context: 1 Samuel 16:23 KJV. The Hebrew word is kinnor -- technically a small lyre rather than a modern concert harp, but the KJV chose 'harp,' and that is the word the story is remembered by (David the harpist, the Psalms as harp-songs).

question: Elijah, with his time nearly up, walked up to his chosen successor, Elisha son of Shaphat, who was plowing his father's field with twelve yoke of oxen, twenty-four beasts in all. Without a word he cast the sign of his prophet's office over the young man's shoulders. What was that object called?
context: 1 Kings 19:19 KJV: 'Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.' Elisha then slaughters his oxen, boils the flesh over the burning plow-wood, feeds the people, and follows Elijah as his servant. Elijah's own look is described later: 'an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins' (2 Kings 1:8) -- but the specific object that names the prophet's office, and that later parts the Jordan for Elisha, is the mantle.

question: A king asked his servants 'what manner of man was he?' and knew Elijah from their answer alone: a hairy man with a belt, the King James 'girdle', about his loins. John the Baptist appeared out of the wilderness centuries later in the same signature belt, with a garment of camel's hair. What was the girdle made of?
context: 2 Kings 1:8 KJV: 'He was an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins.' Matthew 3:4 says John the Baptist wore 'a leathern girdle about his loins,' the same phrase word-for-word. When the crowds thought John was Elijah come back, this outfit was the reason.

question: The tribes of Israel fell into a dispute, and to settle it a wooden rod for each tribe was placed overnight before the ark. In the morning one rod had come alive. It had put out buds and blossoms and even ripe fruit. Whose rod was it?
choices: the rod of the tribe of Judah
context: Numbers 17:8 KJV: 'the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.' Moses's rod is famous for turning into a serpent and for striking the rock; 'the rod of Jesse' is a phrase from Isaiah 11 about David's line; the tribe of Judah had a rod placed alongside the others -- but only Aaron's, for the house of Levi, budded and bore almonds, marking Levi as the priestly tribe.

question: Elisha, a young farmer just called by the prophet Elijah, kills his own oxen and gives his village a farewell feast, to show he is not going back. In the King James Bible, what does he use as firewood to boil the meat?
context: 1 Kings 19:21 KJV: 'and took a yoke of oxen, and slew them, and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen.' The 'instruments' are the plow-gear -- the wooden yokes and plow-frame. Elisha is deliberately burning the tools of his old life so he cannot return to it.

question: Elijah and Elisha cross the Jordan on dry ground, and the older prophet asks his heir what final gift he wants before being taken away. Elisha asks for no silver, long life or kingdom, but for something of Elijah's own. In the King James Bible, what exact phrase does Elisha use?
answer: A double portion of thy spirit
choices: A double portion of thy spirit
A share of thy prophetic gift
All the strength thou canst spare me
The full weight of thy anointing
context: 2 Kings 2:9 KJV: 'let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.' The 'double portion' echoes an Israelite inheritance law -- the firstborn son received a double share of the father's estate. Elisha is asking to be treated as the firstborn heir of Elijah.

question: Elisha climbs the road up to the town of Bethel in 2 Kings, and a gang of small children pours out to mock him. They shout the same jeering taunt at him twice as he walks. In the King James Version, what do they shout?
choices: 'Where is the word of the LORD?'
context: 2 Kings 2:23 KJV. They shout it twice: 'Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head.' The 'go up' is likely a jeer about Elijah having been taken up in the whirlwind -- as if to say, 'why don't you go up too and leave us alone?' Compare the taunt Amaziah's priest throws at Amos: 'Get thee hence, thou seer' (Amos 7:12).

question: Elisha turns on the children who have jeered at him on the road to Bethel, looks at them and curses them in God's name. Out of the woods come two she-bears, and they tear a specific number of the children. How many children do the bears maul?
context: 2 Kings 2:24 KJV: 'and tare forty and two children of them.' The bears are SHE-bears, and there are two of them, and the count is forty-two. The story is deliberately disturbing -- it is told here as it is, without softening.

question: A young prophet is chopping wood by the Jordan when his borrowed axe head slips off the handle, splashes into the river and sinks. He cries out to Elisha in a panic, because he cannot afford to replace the tool. Elisha cuts a stick and throws it into the water at the spot. What happens?
answer: The iron head floats up to the surface
choices: The iron head floats up to the surface
A great fish carries the head to shore in its mouth
The river dries in a circle around the sinking spot
An angel appears standing on the water holding the head
context: 2 Kings 6:6 KJV: 'And he cut down a stick, and cast it in thither; and the iron did swim.' 'The iron did swim' is one of the strangest four-word phrases in the Old Testament -- the whole miracle is that iron floated, which iron does not do.

question: Naaman, the Syrian general, flies into a rage when Elisha's messenger tells him to dip in the Jordan seven times to cure his leprosy. To him the muddy Jordan is nothing next to the great rivers back home. In the King James Bible, which two Damascus rivers does he name as better than all the waters of Israel?
context: 2 Kings 5:12 KJV: 'Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?' Naaman's servants talk him down, he wades in and dips seven times, and 'his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child.'

question: A wealthy woman of Shunem tells her husband that the prophet Elisha, who eats with them whenever he passes through, is a holy man. Together they build him a private guest-room up on the wall of their house. The King James Bible names the four pieces of furniture they put in the little chamber. Which set does the story list?
answer: A bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick
choices: A bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick
A pallet, a jug, a bench, and a hanging lamp
A cot, a chest, a footstool, and an oil-lamp
A couch, a bowl, a chair, and a brazier
context: 2 Kings 4:10 KJV: 'Let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick.' The specific four-item list is why the story is remembered -- 'the Shunammite's little chamber' becomes a proverb for hospitality to holy men.

question: Gehazi, Elisha's servant, runs after the great Syrian general when his master refuses payment for the leprosy cure. He lies that Elisha needs silver and clothes for two visiting young prophets, and he keeps the silver. When he returns, Elisha already knows and pronounces a terrible curse. What does the King James Bible say happens to Gehazi?
answer: Naaman's leprosy cleaves unto him and unto his seed for ever
choices: Naaman's leprosy cleaves unto him and unto his seed for ever
His hands turn as leprous as Miriam's when she mocked Moses
A leprosy breaks out in his brow like Uzziah's at the altar
The plague that killed the firstborn of Egypt falls upon his house
context: 2 Kings 5:27 KJV: 'The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow.' The moral is on the surface: the disease is transferable but so is the greed that draws it.

question: The Shunammite woman's promised son, out in the harvest field, cries to his father that his head hurts. He is carried home to his mother's lap and dies at noon. Elisha comes, sends everyone out and lies down upon the dead child. In the King James Bible the child comes back to life and does one thing a specific number of times before he opens his eyes. What is it?
context: 2 Kings 4:35 KJV: 'and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.' The sneezing detail is one of the most oddly specific miracle-endings in the Bible -- kids remember it because sneezes are the last thing you expect from a resurrection story.

question: Mourners at a burial in Israel spot a Moabite raiding party rushing down on the funeral, years after Elisha's death. They panic and shove the corpse into the nearest tomb, which turns out to be Elisha's own. What happens the moment that corpse touches the prophet's bones?
answer: The dead man revives and stands up on his feet
choices: The dead man revives and stands up on his feet
The bones flare with fire and consume the whole corpse
The tomb seals shut and the raiders retreat in terror
The corpse turns to salt and the stone tomb splits open
context: 2 Kings 13:21 KJV: 'when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.' Elisha's miracles keep going after his death -- the closing beat of his whole cycle, and the reason his bones were later treated as holy relics in Christian tradition.

question: Cu Chulainn came courting at Forgall's fort and found Emer at her needlework among her foster-sisters. He spoke to her in a way the girls could not follow, and she answered him the same way, every bit as sharp. How did they talk?
context: Tochmarc Emire, 'The Wooing of Emer' (Kuno Meyer's translation): Cu Chulainn tells his charioteer afterwards, 'we disguised our words lest the girls should understand that I am wooing her, for if Forgall knew it, we should not meet with his consent.' Emer matches him riddle for riddle. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T301021.html  (Legend.)

question: Emer's father disguised himself and went to King Conchobar's court, rather than refuse Cu Chulainn to his face. He hated the match and did not want any Ulster warrior for a son-in-law. He told the young hero that no warrior of his talent was ready without training abroad, with the warrior-woman Scathach on the Isle of Shadow. What was the father's real hope in sending him?
answer: that Cu Chulainn would die on the perilous journey
choices: that Cu Chulainn would die on the perilous journey
that Scathach would refuse him and shame him home
that a rival hero would seize Emer while he was away
that the sea-voyage would humble his pride
context: The father-in-disguise trick is the whole engine of Tochmarc Emire and the reason Cu Chulainn ends up trained by Scathach. The father assumed he would never return; he did. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochmarc_Emire  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn came home alive from his training with Scathach and went back for Emer, to the fort at Lusk in what is now north County Dublin. The master of that fort had set the Isle of Shadow trap for him. What was the name of the father who had tried to kill him?
context: Forgall Manach ('Forgall the Wily') was chief of Lusk. Ailill mac Mata is Queen Medb's husband at Cruachan; Daire mac Fiachna is the Ulster owner of the Brown Bull of Cooley; Sualtam mac Roich is Cu Chulainn's own mortal father. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emer  (Legend.)

question: Emer was carried off from her father's fort at Lusk, and the treasure with her, when Cu Chulainn came back from Scathach and stormed it. Twenty-four of the fort's warriors fell in the fight. But the master of the fort died in a way that had nothing to do with the hero's sword. How did he die?
answer: he fell from the ramparts of his own fort trying to escape
choices: he fell from the ramparts of his own fort trying to escape
he choked on the poisoned cup he had prepared for the raider
he drowned in the fort's own well hiding from the sack
he was crushed by his own gate as he swung it shut
context: Tochmarc Emire (Meyer): 'Forgall then made a leap on to the rampart of the rath without, in fleeing from Cuchulaind, and he fell and was without life.' The trap-setter died by his own walls. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T301021.html  (Legend.)

question: Emer came to a meeting with a troop of women armed with knives, meaning to kill her rival, in the later tale Serglige Con Culainn ('The Sickbed of Cu Chulainn'). Her husband had fallen in love with a woman of the sea-people. What did Emer do when she saw the strength of the fairy woman's love for him?
answer: she decided to give her husband up to her
choices: she decided to give her husband up to her
she stabbed the fairy woman where she stood
she cursed her husband and left the country
she asked the druids to divide his years between them
context: Emer's generosity is the turn of the tale: moved by it, the fairy woman decides not to take Cu Chulainn and goes home to her own husband. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serglige_Con_Culainn  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn took a fairy lover in Serglige Con Culainn, a woman of the sea-people and the wife of a sea god, and Emer came with her noblewomen to confront her. The fairy's name is one of the most famous in the whole Ulster Cycle. What was she called?
context: Fand is the sea-fairy of Serglige Con Culainn, wife of Manannan mac Lir. Aife is the warrior-queen who bore Cu Chulainn's son Connla; Uathach is Scathach's daughter; Sadhbh is Fionn's wife in the later Fenian Cycle (mother of Oisin). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serglige_Con_Culainn  (Legend.)

question: One god of the Tuatha De comes forward at the end of Serglige Con Culainn, once the sea-fairy has gone home. He does one specific act between Cu Chulainn and the woman the hero has just given up, so that the two will never see each other again in this world. Which god acts, and what does he do?
answer: Manannan mac Lir shakes his cloak between them
choices: Manannan mac Lir shakes his cloak between them
Lugh Lamhfhada casts his spear between them
the Dagda plays his harp until she forgets
Aengus Og calls his four swans to carry her away
context: Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god and the fairy woman's own husband; he shakes his cloak between Cu Chulainn and Fand so that the two will never meet again. Then the druids give Cu Chulainn and Emer drinks of forgetting. Lugh's spear, the Dagda's harp and Aengus's swan-maiden belong to other tales. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serglige_Con_Culainn  (Legend.)

question: A stranger fell in beside two travellers on the road to Emmaus, seven miles or so from Jerusalem, in Luke's telling. He walked and talked with them along the way, and they never realised who he was. What reason does Luke give?
answer: their eyes were holden that they should not know him
choices: their eyes were holden that they should not know him
the noonday sun stood full in front of their faces
he had wrapped a traveller's cloak over his head
a great dust rose up around him on the road
context: Luke 24:16 KJV: 'But their eyes were holden that they should not know him.' Luke names the reason directly -- not weather, not disguise. 'Holden' is an old English past-participle of 'hold', meaning 'kept'.

question: Two disciples of Jesus reached the village of Emmaus at evening and invited a stranger from the road to stay for the meal. He sat down at the table, blessed the bread and broke it. In that moment, Luke says, something happened at the table. What was it?
answer: their eyes were opened, and they knew him
choices: their eyes were opened, and they knew him
the room shook, and a voice spoke
the bread turned into flame in his hands
a white dove flew down through the doorway
context: Luke 24:31 KJV: 'And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight.' The recognition happens over broken bread, and Jesus disappears the same instant.

question: In the Gospel of Luke, the stranger who had walked with two travellers to Emmaus, opening the Hebrew scriptures, vanished from their sight at the table. The two looked at each other and spoke one memorable line about what they had felt on the road. What did they say to each other?
answer: Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way
choices: Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way
Surely the Lord was in this place, and we knew it not
Blessed be his name from generation to generation
How is it that we have not perceived until this hour
context: Luke 24:32 KJV: 'And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?' Jacob says 'Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not' at Bethel (Genesis 28:16).

question: The disciples of Jesus sat behind locked doors in a room in Jerusalem on the evening of the third day, afraid of the Jewish leaders, John says. With the doors still shut, Jesus was suddenly among them and spoke first. What were his opening words to the terrified room?
context: John 20:19 KJV: 'came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.' 'Weep not for me' is on the way to the crucifixion in Luke 23; 'Follow me' is the calling of the fishermen; 'Behold, it is I' is close to but not the wording of the walking-on-water scene.

question: Thomas refused to believe on hearsay when the other disciples told him they had seen Jesus alive. He had not been in the room that first evening. He named two things he must see and touch, the second of them not the hands, and his demand gave English the phrase 'a doubting Thomas.' What did Thomas say he must thrust his hand into?
context: John 20:25 KJV: 'Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.' The side-wound is from the Roman soldier's spear thrust in John 19:34. Feet were also nailed at crucifixion, but that is not the wound Thomas names.

question: Jesus appeared again in the same locked room in Jerusalem, in John's gospel, eight days after Thomas had refused to believe unless he could touch the wounds himself. With the doors still shut, Jesus turned straight to Thomas and offered him those wounds. Thomas answered with five quiet words. What did Thomas say?
context: John 20:28 KJV: 'And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.' The scene turns on it being a startled man's line to someone he thought was dead.

question: Peter and six other disciples fished all night on the Sea of Galilee and caught nothing, in the last chapter of John's gospel. A figure on the shore at dawn told them to cast the net on the right side of the boat, and the net filled. Peter dragged it to land, and John records the exact count. How many fish were in it?
context: John 21:11 KJV: 'and drew the net to land full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken.' 144 (thousand) is the sealed of the tribes in Revelation 7; 5,000 is the crowd fed with five loaves and two fish; 490 is seventy times seven, Jesus's forgiveness count in Matthew 18.

question: One disciple in a boat on the Sea of Galilee knew the figure standing on the beach before any of the others did, as they drew near the shore in the dawn light. John calls him the beloved disciple, and he said one blunt short line to Peter. What did he say?
context: John 21:7 KJV: 'Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved saith unto Peter, It is the Lord. Now when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girt his fisher's coat unto him, (for he was naked,) and did cast himself into the sea.' Peter cannot wait for the boat -- he jumps and swims for the shore. Traditionally the beloved disciple in the fourth gospel is identified with the apostle John.

question: Jesus turned to Peter after the breakfast he had cooked for the disciples on the shore, and he asked him one question. He asked it again, and then he asked it a third time, and the third asking grieved Peter. What was the question Jesus asked Peter three times?
answer: Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?
choices: Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?
Simon, son of Jonas, wilt thou follow me?
Simon, son of Jonas, whom sayest thou that I am?
Simon, son of Jonas, canst thou drink of my cup?
context: John 21:15-17 KJV records the question three times. The threefold asking mirrors Peter's three denials on the night of the arrest, and the shore fire in John 21:9 uses the same rare Greek word for 'charcoal fire' (anthrakia) that appears at Peter's denial fire in John 18:18; the word appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Jesus asks 'whom say ye that I am?' of all the disciples (Matthew 16:15), and 'Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of?' of James and John (Matthew 20:22).

question: Jesus questioned Peter three times beside a charcoal fire on the beach, in John's gospel, as many times as Peter had denied even knowing him on the night of the arrest. After each of Peter's answers Jesus handed back the same short commission, almost the same three words each time, with only one word varying between the rounds. What was the commission?
context: John 21:15-17 KJV. The exact three variations across the three rounds are 'Feed my lambs' (v.15), 'Feed my sheep' (v.16), and 'Feed my sheep' (v.17) -- Peter, who denied Jesus at a fire in a courtyard, is restored at a fire on a beach and told to look after the flock. 'Take my yoke upon you' is Matthew 11; 'wash one another's feet' is the Maundy Thursday scene in John 13; 'let him deny himself' is Mark 8.

question: Erasmus wrote his most famous satire in about a week, as the guest of a good friend at that friend's London house. Its Latin title has a second sense: it also reads as a joke on the host's own Latinised surname. Whose name was the pun on?
context: More's surname was Latinised as Morus, and Moriae ('of Folly') doubles as 'of More'. Erasmus wrote the book in about a week at More's house in London in 1509. Colet, Warham and Fisher were all English scholarly friends of Erasmus in this period, but the pun is on More. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Praise_of_Folly.

question: Erasmus published the Novum Instrumentum at Basel in 1516, a book Europe had never seen printed before: the New Testament in its original language, with his own fresh Latin translation next to it. In which original language did Erasmus print it?
context: The New Testament was written in Koine Greek in the first century; Erasmus's 1516 edition was the first ever put in print in the original. Hebrew is the language of most of the Old Testament; Aramaic was the everyday language of first-century Palestine but not of the New Testament writings; Coptic is a much later Egyptian translation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus.

question: Erasmus broke with Martin Luther in print in 1524, after first supporting the German reformer. He defended the traditional Catholic teaching that humans have real freedom to choose between good and evil. Luther fired back the next year with 'On the Bondage of the Will', arguing that the human will is enslaved to sin. What Latin title had Erasmus used for the book Luther was answering?
context: Erasmus's 'De Libero Arbitrio' (On Free Will, 1524) drew Luther's crushing 'De Servo Arbitrio' (On the Bondage of the Will, 1525) in reply; the exchange marked the final break between humanist reform-from-within and Protestant break-from-without. De Copia and De Ratione Studii are earlier Erasmus works on Latin style and education; De Contemptu Mundi is an early monastic-life treatise of his -- all real Erasmus titles, none the anti-Luther book. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus.

question: Erasmus, a Latinist all his working life whose Latin letters fill volumes, cried out on his deathbed at Basel on 12 July 1536. His friend Beatus Rhenanus records that he slipped out of Latin altogether and called 'Dear God' in his childhood tongue instead. In which language did he say it?
context: Beatus Rhenanus reports Erasmus's dying words as 'Lieve God' -- 'Dear God' in Dutch, the language he had grown up with in Rotterdam and largely abandoned in adult life for Latin. German was the language of his printer's city Basel; French of the great university at Paris; English of his English friends. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus.  (Legend.)

question: Ahasuerus, the Persian king the Greeks called Xerxes, threw out Queen Vashti and ordered a beauty search across his empire for a new queen. A young Jewish orphan named Hadassah, raised by her older cousin, was chosen. What royal Persian name did she take?
context: Esther 2. Hadassah (myrtle) is her Hebrew name; Esther is her Persian throne name. The other three are all real named Jewish women -- Deborah the judge, Judith of the Assyrian general, Miriam sister of Moses.

question: Queen Esther's older cousin warned her not to reveal she was a Jew. He had raised the orphan girl himself, and he sat every day at the king's gate in Susa. The Jewish festival of Purim is built around him and her. Who was he?
context: Esther 2:5-7, 2:20. Mordecai is Esther's older cousin who raised her after her parents died. The others are all real Jewish figures from adjacent books -- Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, Ezra the scribe led a return from exile, Boaz married Ruth.

question: The princes, nobles and servants of Persia and Media feasted at the winter palace in Susa as guests of King Ahasuerus, who meant to show off the staggering riches of his kingdom. The book of Esther records the exact length of the feast. How long did it last?
context: Esther 1:3-4. The 180-day feast is followed by a further seven-day feast for the people of Shushan; it is at the close of that shorter feast that Vashti refuses to appear.

question: A proud royal official at the Persian palace in Susa cast lots, called purim, to pick a day for a massacre, furious that Mordecai the Jew would not bow to him. He offered King Ahasuerus a huge pile of silver to make the order destroying every Jew across the empire stick. Who was he?
context: Esther 3:1-13. Haman is called 'the Agagite'. The others are all real named officers of Ahasuerus's court from the same book -- Hegai kept the women, Harbonah was a chamberlain who later pointed out Haman's gallows, Shaashgaz kept the concubines.

question: Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth, then sent word begging Esther to go in to the king. She sent back word to fast three days and nights on her behalf, saying she would then go in unbidden, even though it was against the law. What were her last words in that message?
choices: into thy hand I commit my spirit
context: Esther 4:16 KJV. The three-day fast is why Purim is preceded by the Fast of Esther. The other three lines are all real biblical quotations -- Psalm 23, Isaiah 6, Psalm 31.

question: Mordecai, the older cousin who had raised Esther as his own daughter, sent her a warning: she must risk her life and go before the king to plead for the Jews against the king's minister Haman. He asked her, in Esther chapter 4, 'Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom...' How did the line end?
answer: for such a time as this
choices: for such a time as this
to break the yoke of thine enemies
context: Esther 4:14 KJV. The line is Mordecai's warning that if Esther keeps silent, deliverance will come from another quarter but her house will perish -- and God may have raised her up precisely for this crisis. The others are biblical-sounding but not the verse.

question: Queen Esther stood in the king's inner court at Susa on the third day of her fast, to plead for her people against Haman's massacre order. Anyone who came in uncalled was put to death by his guards, unless the king held out one specific royal object in mercy. What did King Ahasuerus hold out to her?
context: Esther 5:1-2. The sceptre is the physical sign of the king's favor; Esther touches its tip. The signet ring is a real palace object -- it seals the edicts -- but is not what he holds out.

question: Zeresh, the wife of the proud chief minister Haman, told him to build an execution frame in his own courtyard right away, the night before he planned to ask the king for leave to hang Mordecai. Mordecai, Queen Esther's cousin, had refused to bow to him. How tall did Haman build the frame?
context: Esther 5:14 KJV. A cubit is roughly 18 inches, so about seventy-five feet -- absurdly, deliberately huge, meant as public humiliation. The others are real biblical measurements (Solomon's porch, Noah's ark, the walls of Jericho).

question: King Ahasuerus could not sleep on the night between Esther's two banquets, so he had the chronicles of his reign read aloud to him. He learned there that Mordecai had once uncovered an assassination plot by two of his own doorkeepers and had never been rewarded. What were the plotters' names?
context: Esther 2:21-23, 6:1-3. Bigthan and Teresh are two eunuchs who guarded the door and conspired against Ahasuerus; Mordecai overheard them and Esther told the king in Mordecai's name. The others are all real named officers of the same Persian court -- Hegai and Shaashgaz kept the women, Hatach carried messages to Esther and Harbonah later pointed out the gallows, Carshena and Memucan were princes of Persia and Media in Esther 1.

question: Haman arrived at dawn to request Mordecai's death, but the king asked him first what should be done for a man he wished to reward in public. Haman, thinking of himself, named royal robes, the king's own horse and a herald crying a specific line. The king then made Haman do all of it for Mordecai. What was the line the herald was to cry?
answer: Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour
choices: Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour
Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the king
Bow the knee, ye people of Shushan
Long live the king of Persia and Media
context: Esther 6:7-11 KJV. Haman himself must lead Mordecai on horseback through the city street crying the words he had designed for his own honour. He goes home mourning with his head covered.

question: Esther named Haman as the enemy at the second banquet. The king stormed into the palace garden in fury, Haman fell across Esther's couch pleading for his life, and the returning king took it for assault. A chamberlain named Harbonah pointed to Haman's own courtyard. What did the king say?
choices: Let him be cast into the pit
context: Esther 7:9-10 KJV. Harbonah's aside about the fifty-cubit gallows Haman had raised for Mordecai is the pivot; the king answers in three curt words and Haman dies on the frame he built. 'The wrath of the king was pacified.'

question: Esther and her cousin Mordecai saved their people from Haman's plot, and the Jewish festival of Purim still celebrates that rescue every spring. The book that tells their story is famous among rabbis and scholars for one specific absence in its text, a puzzling silence debated for over two thousand years. What is missing from the whole book of Esther?
answer: God is never named in it
choices: God is never named in it
Jerusalem is never named in it
no feast is ever described in it
the Persian king is never named in it
context: Esther. God is never named -- not YHWH, not Elohim, not Adonai. Traditional Judaism reads this as the point: providence works through what looks like coincidence (a sleepless night, a chronicle read aloud). The Song of Songs also omits the divine name in some counts, so this is the classic case rather than the strictly unique one.

question: The young Arthur rode out with Merlin, in Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, and met a very tall, very proud king who challenged him to single combat. They fought until the sword Arthur had drawn from the stone shattered in his hand. Which king broke it?
context: Malory, Book I ch.23-24. Pellinore is the questing knight who nearly kills the young Arthur in this duel until Merlin intervenes. Pellinore later becomes an ally and a companion of the Round Table. Uriens is Morgan le Fay's husband; Lot is Gawain's father; Rience is the king of North Wales who had trimmed his mantle with the beards of eleven kings and sent for Arthur's.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur forgot the name of the sword the Lady of the Lake had given him, Malory says, so she told him the name and what it meant. Malory took the meaning from a French romance, the Vulgate Merlin, which calls the name Hebrew. What does the name mean?
context: Malory, Book II ch.3: 'The name of it, said the lady, is Excalibur, that is as much to say as Cut-steel.' The Vulgate Merlin had called Escalibor a Hebrew name meaning, in French, 'cuts iron, steel and wood'. In Welsh the sword is Caledfwlch ('hard-cleaver'), and Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin form is Caliburnus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur; Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur (Gutenberg).  (Legend.)

question: Arthur chose the sword when Merlin asked him on the ride home which he liked better, the sword or the scabbard he had just taken from the arm in the water. Merlin sharply corrected him, for the scabbard had a magical property of its own. What did Merlin say the scabbard does?
answer: stops all bleeding from any wound
choices: stops all bleeding from any wound
makes its bearer invisible in shadow
lets its bearer ride without tiring
context: Malory, Book I ch.25 verbatim: 'the scabbard is worth ten of the swords, for whiles ye have the scabbard upon you, ye shall never lose no blood, be ye never so sore wounded.' Losing that scabbard to Morgan le Fay later costs Arthur dearly.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin told the young Arthur he was wrong to like the sword better than its scabbard, and he used a rule of thumb to show just how much more the scabbard was worth. The line is one of the most quoted in Malory's whole Excalibur scene. In Merlin's phrase, the scabbard was worth what?
context: Malory, Book I ch.25: 'the scabbard is worth ten of the swords.' A hundred horses and a king's ransom are the ordinary medieval measures of great value, but Merlin's exact rule of thumb is ten of the swords -- and that ratio is what makes losing the scabbard a catastrophe later.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur lay with a mortal wound after the final battle of Camlann, and he ordered his sword thrown back into a lake. His last surviving knight needed three tries, coming back twice with the deed undone. Which knight threw Excalibur back on the third try?
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5. Bedivere and his brother Lucan are the last knights left with Arthur, and Lucan dies of his wounds; on Bedivere's third throw an arm and a hand rise from the water, catch the sword, brandish it three times and vanish. Lancelot is far away in France after his love for Guinevere split the Round Table; Gawain has died of the old head wound Lancelot gave him; Kay has no part in the last scene.  (Legend.)

question: The Lady of the Lake came to Arthur's court, in Malory's telling, to collect the gift he had promised her for the sword, and she asked for a knight's head. Arthur refused her, but that same knight, who blamed her for his mother's death, strode up and cut off her head before the king. Which knight beheaded her?
context: Malory, Book II ch.3. She asks for the head of the knight who won the damsel's sword, or the damsel's own; Arthur refuses; Balin, who says she caused his mother to be burnt, smites off her head before the king. Arthur sends him from court, and Balin rides on toward the Dolorous Stroke that wounds King Pellam. Bedivere, Gawain and Kay play no part in this scene.  (Legend.)

question: Young Culhwch faced some forty impossible tasks before he could marry Olwen, in one of the earliest Arthurian tales. Arthur's sword in that story was not yet called Excalibur. It bore a much older name meaning 'hard-cleaver.' What was that oldest known name?
context: The Welsh tale 'Culhwch and Olwen' (c. 11th-12th century) is one of the earliest Arthurian stories; Arthur's sword there is Caledfwlch (from 'caled' hard + 'bwlch' breach/cleft). Caliburnus is Geoffrey of Monmouth's later Latin form; Escalibor is the Old French of the twelfth century, from which English 'Excalibur' comes. Durendal belongs to a different hero, Roland of the Chanson de Roland.  (Legend.)

question: Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote of King Arthur's sword around the year 1136, in his Latin 'History of the Kings of Britain', and he called it Caliburnus, the earlier form of Excalibur. His book helped establish Arthur as a legendary figure across European literature. Where did Geoffrey say the sword was forged?
choices: on the anvil of the Dagda
context: Wikipedia: Excalibur, from Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book IX. Geoffrey says the sword 'was forged in Avalon.' Annwn is the Welsh otherworld from Culhwch and Olwen. The Dagda is the Irish father-god with his own great club. Weyland the Smith is the Anglo-Saxon smith-hero -- a real English legend, but not the maker of Excalibur.

question: A young Jewish priest in exile from Jerusalem saw the heavens open by the river Chebar in Babylon. He watched a cloud of fire roll out of the north, with gleaming metal glowing in its middle. Who was this strange prophet of the Hebrew Bible?
context: Ezekiel 1:1-4. Ezekiel is a priest deported to Babylon in the first wave of exiles under Jehoiachin (597 BC). Jeremiah, Isaiah and Daniel are the other great prophets: Jeremiah stays behind in Judah, Isaiah lived a century earlier, and Daniel is a court official in the same exile.

question: Ezekiel saw four living creatures come out of a fiery cloud by the river Chebar. Each had four wings and feet like a calf, and each had four different faces on one head. Which set of four faces does the text name?
answer: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle
choices: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle
a bull, a serpent, a hawk, and a jackal
a ram, a goat, a lion, and a leopard
a lamb, a dove, a lion, and a child
context: Ezekiel 1:5-10 KJV. These four faces are later picked up by Revelation 4 and become the traditional symbols of the four Gospel-writers: Matthew (man), Mark (lion), Luke (ox), John (eagle). A lion, a leopard, a ram and a he-goat are beasts of Daniel's visions (Daniel 7-8); the bull, serpent, hawk and jackal are sacred animals of Egypt.

question: Beside each winged creature in his vision by the river Chebar, Ezekiel watched an enormous wheel within a wheel. The text says the rims of those wheels were 'so high that they were dreadful,' and one strange thing covered them all the way around. What did the rims have around them?
context: Ezekiel 1:18 KJV: 'their rings were full of eyes round about them four'. It is the eyes, not the height, that make the wheels most memorable -- the whole apparatus is a chariot-throne that sees in every direction.

question: Above the winged creatures of his great vision by the river Chebar, the exile Ezekiel saw a crystal sky. Above that stood a throne of one specific gemstone, with the appearance of a man upon it and a rainbow all around. What stone was the throne made of?
context: Ezekiel 1:26 KJV: 'the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone'. Compare Moses in Exodus 24:10 who sees under God's feet 'a paved work of a sapphire stone'.

question: A hand held out a scroll to the exile Ezekiel in his commissioning vision, covered in writing on both sides: 'lamentations, and mourning, and woe.' A voice told him to eat it, and in his mouth it tasted sweet, like one specific thing. What does the text say the scroll tasted like?
context: Ezekiel 3:1-3 KJV: 'it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness'. The prophet has to swallow the message before he can speak it. John in Revelation 10 eats a similar scroll -- sweet in the mouth, bitter in the belly.

question: Ezekiel lay down on his left side for three hundred and ninety days to carry the sins of the northern kingdom of Israel, in a strange sign God ordered him to act out against Jerusalem. Then he turned and lay on his right side for the sins of the southern kingdom of Judah. For how many days did he lie on his right side?
context: Ezekiel 4:4-6 KJV. Each day counts for a year -- 390 years for Israel, 40 for Judah. It is one of the most physically demanding sign-acts in the Old Testament: over a year on one side of his body, then more than a month on the other.

question: Ezekiel stood in a valley full of dry human bones, set down there by God in one of his strangest visions. God asked him whether the bones could live, then told him to prophesy over them. As Ezekiel spoke, a noise and a shaking ran through the valley. The King James Version catches what happened first in a four-word phrase quoted ever since. What is the phrase?
context: Ezekiel 37:7 KJV: 'the bones came together, bone to his bone'. Then sinews and flesh and skin come up, and when the breath comes in verse 10 they stand upon their feet 'an exceeding great army'. 'Flesh of my flesh' is Adam's line over Eve (Genesis 2:23), 'the breath of life' is what God breathes into Adam (Genesis 2:7), and 'after his kind' runs through the creation in Genesis 1.

question: God warned Ezekiel in advance that his wife, 'the desire of thine eyes', would be taken from him at a stroke, and that he must show no sign of grief at all: no weeping, no bare head, no bare feet. His strange silence among the exiles in Babylon was to be a public sign of one event to come. What was that silence meant to foreshadow?
answer: the coming fall of the Temple
choices: the coming fall of the Temple
the birth of a great king
context: Ezekiel 24:15-24. His wife dies at evening; the next morning he does as commanded. When the exiles ask why, he tells them that they too will lose 'the desire of your eyes' -- the Temple -- and will not be able to mourn it publicly.

question: A single young champion held off Queen Medb's whole army at the river fords of Ulster, killing her champions one after another, in the Irish epic the Tain Bo Cuailnge. A strange curse had left Ulster's grown warriors bedridden. What was his name?
context: Cu Chulainn is the great hero of the Ulster Cycle and the sole defender of Ulster in the Tain, killing champion after champion at the fords to slow Medb's army. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: Queen Medb of Connacht ran out of champions willing to face the Ulster hero Cu Chulainn at the river fords. So she sent for a man of her own army who had once trained beside Cu Chulainn under the same warrior-woman. What was his name?
context: Ferdiad, son of Daman, of the Fir Domnann, is the only warrior in Medb's whole host who trained under Scathach beside Cu Chulainn and so knows every one of his feats. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: Ferdiad refused to fight his own foster-brother Cu Chulainn at the ford, because the two had grown up together. So Queen Medb of Connacht called in people from her court whose public word could shame a warrior into fighting. Whom did she call in?
context: In early Irish culture the satire of the filid was a genuine weapon: their public verse could raise three blisters on the target's face, named Blame, Blemish and Disgrace, and to be so shamed was social death. Ferdiad said he deemed it better to fall by the shafts of valour than by the shafts of satire. Source: https://mythopedia.com/library/tain-bo-cuailnge-dunn-1914/20-the-combat-of-ferdiad-and-cuchulain/  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn and his foster-brother Ferdiad, forced to fight to the death at a river ford, hurled one class of weapon at each other again and again on the first morning, from dawn until noon. Neither could draw blood. With what did they fight on that first day?
context: The Tain lays out the four days as an escalating scale. Day one is small darts and light casting-spears from morning's early twilight till noon; each day the weapon grows heavier. Source: https://mythopedia.com/library/tain-bo-cuailnge-dunn-1914/20-the-combat-of-ferdiad-and-cuchulain/  (Legend.)

question: Ferdiad raised his high shield against Cu Chulainn's throws all morning on the fourth day at the ford. Cu Chulainn shouted down to Loeg, his charioteer, to bring the one feat-weapon their teacher had reserved for him alone and never taught to any other pupil. Which did he call for?
context: All four are feats or weapons from Scathach's warrior-school on the Isle of Shadow, so a player must actually know which one Scathach withheld from every other pupil. The Gae Bolg, the 'belly-spear', was that feat. Ferdiad had no defence against it because he had never learned it, and Loeg readied it in the river-stream for the throw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: Ferdiad lay dead in the water at the end of his four-day combat with his foster-brother Cu Chulainn, the emotional heart of the Irish epic the Tain Bo Cuailnge. The river ford where they fought is still named for the man who died there. What is the modern Irish town on that ford?
context: The ford was called Ath Fir Diad, 'the Ford of Ferdiad', and the town that grew there kept the name: Ardee (Baile Atha Fhirdhia) in County Louth. Every other choice is a real Irish site of the Ulster Cycle era: Armagh the church seat, Navan the modern town near the royal fort of Emain Macha, and Tara the seat of the High King. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: Almost every named Aesir god dies in one great final battle when the Norse world ends, as Snorri Sturluson tells it. The sky splits, and the sea rises to swallow the earth. What is the Norse name for this doom of the gods?
context: Ragnarok is prophesied in the Voluspa (the opening poem of the Poetic Edda) and retold by Snorri Sturluson in Gylfaginning chapters 51-52. Yggdrasil is the world-tree at the centre of the nine worlds. Valhalla is Odin's warrior-hall in Asgard. Midgard is the middle earth where humans live. Ragnarok is the specific name for the ending.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson says a monstrous winter arrives before the end as a warning to the world, with snow driving in from every side and no growing season to break it. What is the name of that winter?
context: Snorri Gylfaginning 51: the winter is Fimbulvetr, the 'Great Winter' (Old Norse fimbul- 'mighty' + vetr 'winter'). Skidbladnir is the folding-ship of the god Freyr. Nastrond is the shore of corpses in Hel. Muspelheim is the fire-realm of Surt in the south. Fimbulvetr is the specific name of the winter, and Snorri names it plainly.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri describes the Great Winter: snow blowing in from every direction, a sun that gives no warmth, and no growing season to feed anyone. One season never comes between the winters. How many winters does the Great Winter last in a row without summer?
context: Snorri Gylfaginning 51 and Vafthrudnismal stanzas 44-45: three winters in a row with no summer between. The number nine is Norse for cosmology (nine worlds of Yggdrasil), forty is the Biblical wilderness number, seven has no place here. Three is the specific count in the Prose Edda, and it is what makes the winter unlivable -- no growing season means no food.  (Legend.)

question: Brothers kill brothers when the food runs out in the Great Winter, and the seeress of the Voluspa sums up what people become in a famous chain of names: 'an axe-age, a sword-age, shields are cloven, a wind-age, a ___-age, before the world plunges.' Which age fills the blank in that stanza?
context: Voluspa stanza 45 (Bellows translation): 'an axe-age, a sword-age, shields are cloven, a wind-age, a wolf-age, before the world plunges.' The same stanza says brothers will murder brothers and sisters' sons will violate the kinship-bond. Fire belongs to Surt at the end; frost belongs to the giants at the beginning of the world; iron-age is a Greco-Roman scheme, not Norse. The Voluspa's specific word here is wolf-age -- the wolves Skoll and Hati are about to catch the sun and moon.  (Legend.)

question: A wolf runs behind the sun's chariot trying to catch it, and it has run there since the beginning of the world, Snorri says. In the last days, above the frozen earth, the old chase ends and the wolf runs the sun down at last. What does the sky-wolf do to the sun?
context: Gylfaginning 12 and 51: the wolf catches the sun-chariot at last and swallows the sun whole. He does not shatter, burn, or drown it. Norse eschatology is precise on this -- the sun goes DOWN a wolf's throat, and the stars go out. The image is meant to be simple and terrifying to a child listening at a hearth.  (Legend.)

question: Two wolves hunt across the sky in the Prose Edda of Snorri Sturluson. One chases the sun and the other chases the moon, and at the world's end they will catch their prey at last. The wolf who hunts the sun has a name that means 'treachery' in Old Norse. What is this sky-wolf called?
context: Gylfaginning 12: the wolf is named Skoll, meaning 'treachery.' Fenrir is a different much larger wolf -- the one who bites off Tyr's hand and eventually kills Odin himself. Garmr is the hound at the gate of Hel. Managarmr ('Moon-hound') is a variant name given by some sources. Skoll is the specific name Snorri gives the sun-chaser.  (Legend.)

question: Roosters crow at the exact same moment across separate worlds, the Voluspa says, just before the horn blast that calls the gods to battle. One crows among the giants, one down in the halls of the dead and one in Asgard. Which rooster crows in Odin's Valhalla to rouse the einherjar?
context: Voluspa stanzas 42-43: Gullinkambi ('Golden-comb') wakes the warriors in Odin's Valhalla. Fjalar is the red rooster who wakes the giants in Jotunheim. A third un-named rooster (called only 'Hel's rooster') crows in the halls of the dead. Vidofnir is a different mythical bird sitting in the branches of Mimameid. Chanticleer is the rooster of Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale, not a Norse creature. Gullinkambi is the specific Asgard rooster.  (Legend.)

question: A hunted orphan who had grown up hidden in the Irish wilds won all-knowing wisdom from a magical salmon. He grew up to become captain of the Fianna, the roving warrior-band that guarded the High King at Tara. Who was this hero?
context: Fionn mac Cumhaill, anglicised 'Finn MacCool', is the central hero of the Fenian Cycle and captain of the Fianna. Cu Chulainn belongs to the older Ulster Cycle; Conaire Mor is a High King in the Cycles of the Kings; Oisin is Fionn's son. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: In the Boyhood Deeds of Fionn, a rival clan leader killed Cumhall at the battle of Cnucha before Cumhall's son was even born, and he seized the Fianna for himself. The boy grew up hidden in the forest of Sliabh Bladhma. Who was that rival?
context: Goll mac Morna led the rival clan Morna against Cumhall's clan Baiscne at Cnucha. He took the captaincy of the Fianna and would have killed the infant heir if he could find him. Later Goll and the grown Fionn reconcile and Goll serves under him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: The mother of Cumhall's infant heir gave him to two women to hide from the men of clan Morna, and they raised him in secret in the forest for years. One was a druidess, the other a warrior-woman. What was the boy's given name in those forest years, before he ever ate the salmon?
context: The boy's birth-name was Deimne, meaning 'sureness' or 'certainty', a word that also names a young male deer. The druidess Bodhmall and the warrior-woman Liath Luachra raised him in Sliabh Bladhma. Setanta is Cu Chulainn's boyhood name from a different cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: The boy who would be called Fionn left the forest where he had been hidden, and he was sent to a hut on the banks of the River Boyne. There he was to study poetry with an old master who had been fishing the same pool for years. What was that poet's name?
context: Finnegas (Finn Eces, 'Finn the seer') lived by the Boyne teaching poetry and waiting for one particular fish. Amergin is the poet who chanted the Milesians ashore; Cathbad is the Ulster druid who foretold Deirdre's fate; Mog Ruith is a Munster wizard. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: An old poet spent years on the banks of the River Boyne trying to catch one particular fish, an unremarkable-looking salmon that would grant all the world's knowledge to whoever ate it. How had that ordinary salmon come by all the world's knowledge?
answer: By eating nuts from the nine hazels of wisdom over the Well of Segais
choices: By eating nuts from the nine hazels of wisdom over the Well of Segais
By swallowing a ring cast into the pool by the Dagda
By drinking from the Cauldron of Rebirth at Bran's court
By living a hundred years under the standing stone at Tara
context: In Irish tradition nine sacred hazels stood over the Well of Segais at the source of the Boyne; their nuts fell into the water, and the salmon that ate them gained all the knowledge in the world. The hazel is the Irish tree of wisdom, as Genesis has its tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_of_Knowledge  (Legend.)

question: An old poet waited by the River Boyne for the salmon of wisdom through a very long stretch of his life, in the Boyhood Deeds of Fionn. He fished the same pool until he finally caught it. How many years had he been fishing?
context: The Boyhood Deeds says: 'Seven years Finneces had been on the Boyne, watching the salmon of Fec's Pool.' That is why his grace in giving up the fish is so remarkable. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T303023.html  (Legend.)

question: A boy on the River Boyne took the Salmon of Knowledge from the old poet who had finally landed it. The poet gave him one strict order before walking off. The fish held everything there was to know. What was the poet's order?
answer: Cook it but do not taste even a bite of the flesh
choices: Cook it but do not taste even a bite of the flesh
Bury it under the hazel tree till nightfall
Cast the hazelnuts back into the well first
Bring it whole and uncooked to the elder-druid
context: In the Boyhood Deeds it had been foretold that Finnegas himself would eat the salmon of Fec's Pool, and then nothing would remain unknown to him, so he set the boy only to cook it and told him not to eat any of it. Source: Kuno Meyer, The Boyish Exploits of Finn, celt.ucc.ie/published/T303023.html  (Legend.)

question: The boy cooked the great salmon over the fire for the old poet, as he had been told, and he meant to keep his promise not to taste a single bite. But as he turned the fish, its hot flesh burned his thumb. What did he do next?
answer: He put the burnt thumb into his mouth
choices: He put the burnt thumb into his mouth
He shook the burnt hand in the river to cool it
He wiped the burnt thumb on the wet grass
He wrapped the burnt thumb in a strip of his tunic
context: In the Boyhood Deeds the boy tells the poet, 'I burned my thumb, and put it into my mouth afterwards.' Ever after, whenever Fionn put his thumb into his mouth, what he had not known was revealed to him. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T303023.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_of_Knowledge  (Legend.)

question: The boy brought the cooked salmon to the old poet, who asked whether he had tasted it. The boy owned up, and the poet did something remarkable rather than raging over the wasted years. What did the old poet do?
answer: Gave the whole fish to the boy and gave him a new name, Fionn
choices: Gave the whole fish to the boy and gave him a new name, Fionn
Cast the boy out and forbade him ever to return to the Boyne
Demanded the boy split all future wisdom equally with him
Kept silent and never told the boy what he had eaten
context: Finnegas told the boy that Finn was his name, that the salmon had been given to him to eat, and that he was truly the Finn of the prophecy; and the boy ate the salmon. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T303023.html  (Legend.)

question: A young hero of Norse myth sucked his finger and suddenly heard the language of the birds. Fionn's own boyhood tale has the same shape: a gift of second sight won by accident. Who was the Norse hero, and what was he doing when it happened?
answer: Sigurd, roasting Fafnir's heart for Regin
choices: Sigurd, roasting Fafnir's heart for Regin
Beowulf, cutting off Grendel's arm at Heorot
Odin, hanging nine nights on Yggdrasil
Thor, wrestling Elli in Utgard-Loki's hall
context: In the Volsunga Saga, Sigurd kills the dragon Fafnir and roasts the heart for the smith Regin. He burns his finger on the roasting heart, sucks it, and at once understands the birds warning him that Regin means to murder him for the treasure. The accidental taste that brings a gift of knowledge is often read as a motif shared by Irish and Norse tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_of_Knowledge  (Legend.)

question: In one Irish folk tradition, a great warrior-chief is said to sleep in a cave beneath an Irish hill, with his warriors around him in full armour, waiting for the day Ireland needs him most. He has no death-tale. Who is this sleeping figure?
context: Fionn mac Cumhaill leads the Fianna in the later Fenian Cycle and the folk-tradition retires him into a sleeping cave rather than a death-tale. Cu Chulainn is the Ulster Cycle hero who has a very famous death-tale (tied upright to a standing stone). Conall Cernach is Cu Chulainn's foster-brother and avenger. Lugh Lamhfhada is a Tuatha De Danann warrior of an older cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: The Fianna lie sleeping in a great circle inside the cave, weapons at their sides, in the folk tale. One thing hangs in the middle of the circle, the object that will wake them when the day comes. What is it?
context: The hunting horn of the Fianna hangs in the middle of the ring of sleepers. A silver harp belongs to the Dagda; a druid's rod is Cathbad's or Uchtdealb's; a crowned helmet belongs to no Fenian scene. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: A company of warriors lies asleep in a hidden cave somewhere in Ireland, in one famous Fenian legend, waiting for the day their country will need them again. A horn hangs among them, and every telling of the tale names it. What is the horn called?
context: Dord Fiann means 'the horn (or humming-chant) of the Fianna' in Old Irish. The Olifant is Roland's ivory war-horn at Roncesvalles in the Western-medieval pillar. Gjallarhorn is Heimdall's horn on Bifrost in the Norse pillar. The Horn of Bran is a Welsh instrument. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: Irish legend tells that the Fianna now sleep in a hidden cave until Ireland has need of them again. Their horn hangs above them, and it must be sounded a certain number of times before they will wake, rise and ride out. How many times must the horn be sounded?
context: Three blasts of the Dord Fiann fully wake Fionn and the Fianna. The tale that turns on the exact number is coming up in another question. The other three counts belong to unrelated Irish and Norse rites (nine is the Norse ritual number). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: A lone shepherd who had wandered into the cave by accident lifted down the great horn and blew it once, the folk tale says. The Fianna in the circle stirred, opened their eyes and half-rose on their elbows. The shepherd panicked. What did the shepherd then do?
answer: dropped the horn and ran out of the cave
choices: dropped the horn and ran out of the cave
blew the second blast at once and fled
prayed aloud and asked their forgiveness
cut a chip from Fionn's shield as a token
context: The horn falls, the shepherd bolts, the Fianna are left only half-awake and sink back into sleep -- and they cry out that he has left them worse than he found them. It is the shape the whole tradition preserves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: The Fianna sank back into their sleep, half-woken by a single blast on the great horn, and cried out one bitter sentence after the shepherd. The tale hangs on that sentence, and folklorists know the story by it. What did the sinking warriors cry after him?
answer: you have left us worse than you found us
choices: you have left us worse than you found us
the age of heroes has ended in shame
the horn has broken faith with us
we sleep now for a thousand years
context: In Irish the sentence is 'Is measa a dfhag na mar a fuair' -- 'worse have you left us than as you found us'. It is the folk-formula that fixes the tale in memory. The other three are invented parallels of the same shape. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: A great king of another legend is said to lie in a similar sleep on a mist-hidden island of apples, waiting to return. That sleep is one of the widest folk patterns in Europe, and the Latin words on his supposed tomb call him the once and future king. Who is this parallel sleeping king?
context: Arthur at Avalon is the parallel Malory refuses to resolve: 'yet some men say... that King Arthur is not dead, but... he shall come again' (Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI). Barbarossa is the Holy Roman Emperor asleep under the Kyffhauser mountain with his red beard growing through the stone table -- another once-and-future-king, but not the one on the apple-island. Olger Danske sleeps in the vaults of Kronborg in Denmark. Charlemagne was buried at Aachen with elaborate ceremony and does not carry the sleeping-return legend.
