Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_in_the_mountain

question: A Scottish editor published what he claimed were 3rd-century Scots-Gaelic poems by 'Ossian son of Fingal', in the 1760s. Fingal was the Scots-Gaelic form of Fionn. The poems swept Europe: Napoleon carried a copy on campaign, and Goethe cited them in Werther. Later scholarship judged the work largely a forgery drawing freely on real Fenian tradition. Who was the editor?
context: James Macpherson (1736-1796) issued Fragments of Ancient Poetry in 1760 and Fingal in 1761-2. Hugh Blair was the Edinburgh professor who championed and defended Macpherson's Ossian in print. John Home was the Scottish playwright who first put Macpherson onto the Highland poetry trail. Allan Ramsay was an earlier Scots-vernacular editor. Only Macpherson issued the Ossian publications themselves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossian

question: A German composer visited a sea cave on the uninhabited isle of Staffa, off Scotland's west coast, in 1829, and heard the ocean swells roll into its hexagonal basalt chamber. Fingal, the Scots-Gaelic form of Fionn, gave the cave its name. The composer wrote an overture built around the sound he heard there. Who was he?
context: Felix Mendelssohn visited Fingal's Cave on Staffa in August 1829 and completed The Hebrides Overture (Op. 26, sometimes called 'Fingal's Cave Overture') in 1830. Wagner wrote sea-legend music (The Flying Dutchman) but not this piece; Sibelius's Swan of Tuonela is Finnish; Berlioz's Corsair is a Byron piece. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hebrides_(overture)

question: A boy carried his own lunch in a huge crowd that had followed Jesus into a lonely, grassy place beside the Sea of Galilee. Late in the afternoon the disciples wanted to send everyone home to buy supper. Jesus started instead with what the boy had brought. How many loaves did the boy have?
context: John 6:9 (KJV): 'There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?' All four gospels agree on five loaves (Matthew 14:17, Mark 6:38, Luke 9:13, John 6:9).

question: The disciples asked Jesus to send a crowd of thousands away to buy food, as evening came on in a lonely place beside the Sea of Galilee. Jesus refused, and gave them a short instruction instead. What did he say?
choices: Let the children come to me
Sit and rest, they will not stay
context: Matthew 14:16 (KJV): 'They need not depart; give ye them to eat.' Also in Mark 6:37 and Luke 9:13. The instruction is directed at the disciples -- the miracle begins as a task laid on them.

question: Matthew counted the men who ate that day in a lonely place beside the Sea of Galilee, when a huge crowd followed Jesus out from the towns. He counted them 'beside women and children'. About how many men did he count?
context: Matthew 14:21 (KJV): 'And they that had eaten were about five thousand men, beside women and children.' The true total, women and children included, is likely much higher -- perhaps twice that.

question: Jesus turned to one disciple in John's version of the feeding by the Sea of Galilee and asked where they could buy bread for such a crowd. John says it was a test, for Jesus knew already how he would feed them. That disciple protested that even two hundred days' wages worth of bread would not be enough for each person to have a little. Which disciple was it?
context: John 6:5-7 (KJV): Jesus asks Philip, and Philip answers, 'Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little.' A 'pennyworth' here is a Roman denarius, roughly a day's wage for a laborer.

question: One of the apostles spotted a boy in the crowd by the Sea of Galilee and brought him forward to Jesus, with nothing else to eat in that lonely place. All four gospels tell of the feeding that followed, but John alone says where the loaves and fishes came from: the boy's own lunch. Which apostle brought the boy forward?
context: John 6:8-9 (KJV): 'One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, saith unto him, There is a lad here...' Andrew is Peter's brother; the boy and his picnic are unique to John's account.

question: In Mark's telling, Jesus would not feed the crowd on the Sea of Galilee shore in a chaotic press. He first had the disciples organize them, and the people sat down 'upon the green grass' in an unusual, orderly arrangement. What arrangement did Mark describe?
answer: In ranks, by hundreds and by fifties
choices: In ranks, by hundreds and by fifties
In two rings of five hundred each
In twelve companies of four hundred
In rows of ten, four hundred rows deep
context: Mark 6:39-40 (KJV): 'And he commanded them to make all sit down by companies upon the green grass. And they sat down in ranks, by hundreds, and by fifties.' The image is almost military -- easy for the disciples to count as they distribute the bread.

question: A disciple brought forward a small boy with a lunch of loaves and fish, on a hillside by the Sea of Galilee, in the Gospel of John. A hungry crowd waited. John says the loaves were made of the humblest grain of that region, the bread the poor of first-century Galilee ate when they could not afford anything better. What grain were the boy's loaves made of?
context: John 6:9 (KJV): 'five barley loaves'. Barley was cheaper than wheat and associated with poorer diets -- the detail marks the boy's lunch as ordinary and small, which sharpens the point.

question: Jesus told the disciples to gather up what was left over so that nothing would be lost, after the huge crowd beside the Sea of Galilee had eaten and was full. They walked the grass filling baskets with fragments, and all four gospels record the same striking count, more food than the boy had brought. How many baskets?
context: Mark 6:43 (KJV): 'And they took up twelve baskets full of the fragments'. Matthew 14:20, Luke 9:17, John 6:13 all agree on twelve -- one per disciple. There was more food AFTER the miracle than the boy had brought BEFORE it.

question: Jesus caught the disciples worrying on a boat trip, in Mark's telling, over the bread they had forgotten to bring. He quizzed them on his two great feedings. About the smaller of the two, he asked how many baskets of fragments they had taken up. What answer did the disciples give?
context: Mark 8:19-20 (KJV): 'When I brake the five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? They say unto him, Twelve. And when the seven among four thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? And they said, Seven.' The number of baskets mirrors the starting loaves.

question: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus went from his baptism in the River Jordan alone into the Judean desert and ate nothing there. Matthew and Luke give the same figure for the length of that fast. How long did it last?
context: Matthew 4:2 (KJV): 'And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred.' The number echoes Moses's forty days on Sinai (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah's forty days walking to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8).

question: In the Gospel of Luke, a visitor came to Jesus alone in the Judean desert, when he was starving at the end of a long fast. The visitor tested him three times, then went away. Who was the visitor?
context: Matthew 4:3 (KJV) calls him simply 'the tempter'; Matthew 4:10 has Jesus name him: 'Get thee hence, Satan'. Luke 4:2 uses 'the devil' throughout. The scene is a plain, three-round contest between two figures alone.

question: Matthew tells how Jesus refused the devil three times in the Judean desert, at the end of a long fast, until the devil left him. One last group of visitors then came to look after Jesus. Who came?
choices: The twelve disciples, come to find him
Shepherds from the nearby hills, drawn by the story
His mother and brothers, worried for him
context: Matthew 4:11 (KJV): 'Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.' The disciples have not yet been called at this point in the story; the family and shepherds appear in other Gospel scenes but not this one.

question: A Christian knelt in church as Lent began, with six weeks of prayer and penance ahead of her before Easter. The season runs forty days if the Sundays are not counted. The season's length and its readings both look back to one scene from the life of Jesus in the Gospels. Which scene?
answer: His time alone in the wilderness before his ministry
choices: His time alone in the wilderness before his ministry
The time between his resurrection and his ascension
The time he spent teaching in the Temple as a boy
The time he spent hidden in Egypt as a child
context: Lent runs the six weeks before Easter, forty days if the Sundays are not counted, and its readings recall the wilderness testing. Ash Wednesday opens the season, and Easter ends it.

question: Jesus had gone without food for so long in the Judean wilderness that he was starving when the devil came to test him. In Matthew's telling the devil pointed at the ground and dared him to prove he was the Son of God by turning the objects in front of them into bread. What objects were they?
context: Matthew 4:3 (KJV): 'If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.' The Judaean wilderness floor is littered with pale limestone rocks roughly the size and shape of small loaves.

question: In Matthew's order, the devil took Jesus to Jerusalem for the second test and set him on the highest point of one building. He dared Jesus to jump, quoting a psalm about angels catching him before he struck the ground. Which building's pinnacle was it?
context: Matthew 4:5-6 (KJV): 'Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple, And saith unto him... he shall give his angels charge concerning thee.' The psalm the devil quotes is Psalm 91:11-12.

question: The devil took Jesus up 'into an exceeding high mountain' for the third and last temptation, in Matthew's telling. There he showed Jesus something all at once and offered him the whole of it if he would fall down and worship the devil. What did the devil show him?
answer: All the kingdoms of the world
choices: All the kingdoms of the world
The twelve tribes gathered in one place
context: Matthew 4:8-9 (KJV): 'sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me.'

question: The devil made Jesus one last offer on a high mountain at the end of the fast. Everything the devil had just shown him would be his in exchange for a single act: bowing down to worship the devil. Jesus did not argue or explain. Matthew gives his answer in the King James Version as a short, sharp command. What did Jesus say?
context: Matthew 4:10 (KJV): 'Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.' Jesus then closes with a third Deuteronomy quotation (6:13). The devil leaves; the angels arrive.

question: Pietro Bernardone, a wealthy merchant of Assisi in Italy around the year 1200, gave his son the nickname Francesco, 'the little Frenchman,' because his trade tied him so closely to France. The son, Francis, would one day give the family fortune away. In what did Pietro deal?
context: Pietro dealt chiefly in fine French cloth and silks, so much so that he nicknamed his son Francesco -- 'the little Frenchman'. Francis worked in the family shop as a boy and later gave the merchandise away. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.

question: Young Francis of Assisi, riding on the road below his town, met a man he had always dreaded. He got off his horse, hugged him and pressed money into his hand, and later called it the turning point of his life. Whom did he hug?
context: Francis dictated the Testament in the last year of his life (1226) and opens it with this scene: 'What had seemed bitter to me was turned into sweetness of soul and body.' Lepers lived apart in colonies below the towns; a rider would normally throw coins from horseback and hurry past. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.

question: Francis of Assisi rode out around 1202 with the cavalry of his town against a neighboring city, and he was taken prisoner at the battle of Collestrada. He spent a full year in an enemy dungeon and came home broken by illness. Which nearby city held him?
context: Perugia sat just across the Tiber from Assisi and was the region's traditional rival. Francis's captivity and subsequent illness are marked by his biographers as the first opening of his old life. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.

question: Francis of Assisi wandered into the little chapel of San Damiano, just outside his town, and knelt before an old painted crucifix on the wall. He later told his brothers that it spoke to him, three times. In the medieval Legend of the Three Companions, what did the crucifix tell him to do?
answer: Repair my house, which as you see is falling into ruin.
choices: Repair my house, which as you see is falling into ruin.
Sell all you have and give it to the poor.
Feed my sheep and my lambs.
Leave your family and follow me into the desert.
context: The chapel was San Damiano, just outside the walls of Assisi. Francis first took the command literally and rebuilt the stones; only later did he understand it as a call to renew the whole Church. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.  (Legend.)

question: Francis of Assisi stood in the piazza before the bishop, the crowd and his furious father, and he did not argue. He peeled off every stitch he wore, even his undergarments, laid the heap at his father's feet with a purse of the coins he had taken, and stood there naked in the square. What did the astonished bishop do next?
answer: Wrapped his own cloak around Francis
choices: Wrapped his own cloak around Francis
Ordered the crowd to be silent
Called for a scribe to record the renunciation
Blessed the coins and returned them to Pietro
context: Giotto's fresco cycle in the Upper Basilica of San Francesco at Assisi, painted around 1297-1299, shows the moment: Francis naked on one side of the piazza, Bishop Guido leaning across to cover him. Sources: cac.org/daily-meditations/naked-before-god-2019-10-04/.

question: Bernard of Quintavalle sold everything to join Francis of Assisi, and Peter Catani and Giles came after him. Francis walked to Rome in 1210, when the little band numbered twelve, and won provisional approval for a new order from Pope Innocent III. What did he call his brothers?
context: Ordo Fratrum Minorum in the Latin -- the 'lesser brothers'. Dominic's Order of Preachers came a few years later; the White Monks are the Cistercians; the Hermits of Saint Augustine were formed decades on. Innocent III gave verbal approval in 1210; Honorius III confirmed the Rule in writing in 1223. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.

question: The friar Francis staged the first live nativity scene on Christmas night 1223, in a small hill village north of Rome, so the farmers could see how poor Bethlehem was. Villagers came with torches and candles. What was the village called?
context: Greccio sits about fifty miles north of Rome on a rocky hillside above the Rieti valley. Assisi was Francis's hometown; Rieti is the valley's main town; Gubbio was where the legend of Francis taming the wolf is set. The sanctuary at Greccio keeps a chapel in the rock where, by tradition, the scene was staged. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativity_scene, wantedinrome.com/news/greccio-home-of-the-worlds-first-nativity-scene.html.

question: Francis of Assisi wanted the villagers to see the stable at Bethlehem with their own eyes when he staged the first nativity scene at Christmas 1223. So he had a manger filled with hay and two live animals brought to it, the same pair that stand in every crib today. Which two animals?
context: Thomas of Celano, who wrote up the Greccio scene in his First Life (1 Celano 84-86) within a few years, has the manger filled with hay and the ox and the ass brought in. The pairing comes from Isaiah 1:3, 'The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib', read from early times as a foreshadowing of Bethlehem.

question: A Tuscan count named Orlando of Chiusi heard Francis of Assisi preach and was so deeply moved by the sermon that in May 1213 he gave the friars an entire mountain in the central Apennines. It was a wild wooded peak, well fit for prayer and penance. What is the name of that mountain?
context: La Verna (also spelled Alverna) rises on Monte Penna in the Tuscan Apennines. Monte Cassino was Benedict's monastery, Subiaco his earlier cave; both are real places from Benedictine history, but not this one. The sanctuary Francis built on La Verna still stands. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Verna.

question: Francis of Assisi climbed a wild mountain in early August 1224 with only a few companions, to keep a forty-day fast before the feast of Michael. He took with him as scribe the friar he trusted most, the one he called 'God's little sheep.' Who was that friar?
context: Leo (Frate Leone) was Francis's secretary in the last years and one of the very few witnesses left alive to describe the La Verna events. Elias later became Minister General; Giles was one of the first three companions; Masseo was famed for his simplicity. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Verna.

question: In Bonaventure's life of him, Francis was praying on the mountainside one morning about the Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross, in 1224, when a seraph with fiery wings swept down from heaven, the figure of a crucified man between its wings. The prophet Isaiah gave the seraphs a set number of wings, and this one kept to it. How many wings did it have?
context: Bonaventure, Major Legend 13.3, and Celano, First Life 94: six wings, two raised above the head, two spread for flight and two covering the body; in Isaiah 6 the seraphs cover their faces and feet and fly with the third pair. Bonaventure took the six-winged vision as the pattern for his Journey of the Mind to God, mapping the wings onto six stages of contemplation. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stigmata.  (Legend.)

question: In the Fioretti, a book of tales about him, the friar Francis of Assisi walked out alone from the hill town of Gubbio to meet a beast that was killing sheep and people outside the walls. What kind of animal was it?
context: The story is told in chapter 21 of the Fioretti (Little Flowers of Saint Francis), a Tuscan vernacular retelling of the earlier Latin Actus beati Francisci et sociorum eius. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_of_Gubbio  (Legend.)

question: Francis of Assisi stood alone outside the walls of Gubbio as a killer beast charged him with open jaws. He made the sign of the cross and called out to it as kin, and the greeting stopped it in its tracks and laid it at his feet. In the Fioretti, what did he call it?
context: In the Fioretti Francis addresses the animal 'Frate Lupo' — Brother Wolf — the same fraternal address he uses for Brother Sun and Sister Moon in the Canticle. Source: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/ugolino/flowers.iii.xxi.html  (Legend.)

question: Francis of Assisi stood before the whole town of Gubbio and brokered a peace with the killer beast that had preyed on it. The town would feed the beast every day for the rest of its life, and the beast would stop killing men and their livestock. How did the beast seal the pact in front of him?
answer: It placed its right paw in his hand
choices: It placed its right paw in his hand
It licked his open palm three times
It bowed its head to the ground
It rolled onto its back at his feet
context: In chapter 21 of the Fioretti Francis asks the wolf to shake on the promise a second time before the whole town, 'and the wolf raising his right paw, placed it in the hand of Saint Francis.' Source: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/ugolino/flowers.iii.xxi.html  (Legend.)

question: Walking with his brothers through the plain near Bevagna in Umbria, Francis of Assisi saw a huge flock sitting together in a field, doves, crows and jackdaws. He left the road, walked in among them and preached. How did he address them?
context: The sermon to the birds is Fioretti chapter 16. Francis tells them they are much beholden to God their creator for giving them 'liberty to fly everywhere' and 'clothing double and triple.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sermon_of_St._Francis  (Legend.)

question: Nearly blind from years of hard fasting, Francis of Assisi composed a long poem of praise in 1224, in a small hut beside the chapel of San Damiano. It thanked God for Sister Moon, Brother Wind, Sister Water, Brother Fire and Mother Earth, and it was the first known poem written in the Italian vernacular by a named author. What is it called?
context: Also called the Canticle of the Creatures (Cantico di frate Sole). It is the earliest surviving vernacular Italian poem with a known author, in the Umbrian dialect. The 'Peace Prayer of Saint Francis' is a much later French composition from around 1912, often misattributed to him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canticle_of_the_Sun

question: Francis of Assisi wrote a hymn near the end of his life in the everyday Italian of 13th-century Umbria. It praised God through a whole household of siblings: 'Brother Sun,' 'Sister Moon,' Brother Wind, Sister Water, Brother Fire. Each verse opened with the same Italian phrase, which means 'Praised be you, my Lord.' What was that opening phrase?
context: 'Praise be to you, my Lord.' Pope Francis (elected 2013) took his name from Francis of Assisi and titled his 2015 encyclical Laudato Si' after this opening line. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laudato_si%27_(disambiguation)

question: Francis Xavier, the Jesuit missionary, left the family castle of Xavier, high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, to study in Paris. His family came from one of the oldest peoples in Europe, with a language unlike any other tongue there. Which people were the Xaviers?
context: Xavier's mother Maria de Azpilcueta was heiress to Xavier castle in the Kingdom of Navarre. His older brothers fought against the Spanish crown in the conquest of Navarre in 1512. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: Francis Xavier shared rooms at the College Sainte-Barbe in Paris in the late 1520s with a much older former soldier who limped. Xavier dreamed of a knight's career to restore his family fortune, and over six years the roommate wore him down with one line from the Gospel of Mark. Which line did the roommate keep asking?
answer: What shall it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul?
choices: What shall it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul?
Who among you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?
How can a camel pass through the eye of a needle?
Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye and not the log in your own?
context: The roommate was Ignatius of Loyola, wounded at the siege of Pamplona and turned pilgrim. Mark 8:36. Xavier finally joined the little band of companions around 1533. Sources: jesuits.org/stories/the-feast-of-st-francis-xavier-sj/.

question: Francis Xavier packed his things in two hours. The king of Portugal had asked Rome in 1540 for missionaries for his new Asian empire, another priest had suddenly fallen ill, and Ignatius of Loyola sent Xavier at short notice. Xavier sailed from Lisbon and stepped ashore thirteen months later at the capital of Portuguese India. What port was that?
context: Goa on the Konkan coast was the seat of the Portuguese viceroy of India from 1510. Xavier used it as his base for the next decade, ranging as far as the Moluccas and Japan. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: Francis Xavier met a fugitive Japanese samurai named Anjiro in Malacca in the 1540s. Anjiro, who had fled his homeland after killing a man, learned Portuguese, was baptized as Paulo de Santa Fe and guided Xavier back to his home island. The two landed on Kyushu on August 15, 1549, and Xavier became the first Christian missionary to Japan. At which Kyushu port did he step ashore?
context: Anjiro was from Satsuma in southern Kyushu, and Kagoshima was his own home city. Nagasaki grew into the great Christian port only decades later. The Japanese converts came to be called kirishitan. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anjir%C5%8D; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: Convinced that if China were converted the rest of Asia would follow, Francis Xavier waited on a small offshore island near Canton in 1552, trying to bribe a merchant to smuggle him ashore, since Chinese law forbade any foreigner to enter. He caught a fever in a straw hut on the beach and died there on December 3, aged 46, within sight of the coast he never reached. What was the island called?
context: Shangchuan (Sancian in Portuguese sources) lies off the coast of Guangdong. Macau was not yet a Portuguese enclave; that came a few years later. A stone chapel now marks the spot on Shangchuan where Xavier is said to have died. Sources: britannica.com/biography/Saint-Francis-Xavier.

question: Francis Xavier lay in the Basilica of Bom Jesus, his body reported incorrupt, when a request came from the Vatican in 1614. A single piece of him was cut off and taken to Rome, where it is still displayed in a silver reliquary in the Gesu, the Jesuit mother church. Which body part was sent to Rome?
context: The forearm -- the arm that had baptized, by tradition, some thirty thousand converts -- is displayed in a raised silver reliquary at the Chiesa del Gesu in Rome. The rest of the body remains in Goa and is exposed for public veneration once a decade. Xavier was canonized in 1622 alongside Ignatius, Teresa of Avila, Philip Neri, and Isidore. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: Snorri tells how Freyja, the Norse goddess of love and beauty, rode across the sky in a chariot drawn by a team no one else drove. Thor's chariot ran on two goats. What pulled Freyja's chariot?
context: Snorri Sturluson gives the two cats plainly as her team in Gylfaginning 24 of the Prose Edda. Thor's chariot is pulled by goats, and Freyr owns the golden boar Gullinbursti. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: In the poem Grimnismal, Freyja picks out half of the dead each day, and Odin has the other half for his great hall Valhalla. She takes her half to a field of her own, whose name is Old Norse for 'People-Field.' What is that place called?
context: Grimnismal 14: half of the slain she chooses each day; the other half is Odin's. Folkvangr is her realm, and Sessrumnir her hall within it. Bilskirnir is Thor's hall, and Vingolf is the hall of the goddesses. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: Freyja, the Norse goddess of love and beauty, won a necklace from four dwarves, and it became the most famous of all her treasures. Snorri names it when he lists what she owns. What is the name of that necklace?
context: Brisingamen means roughly 'the necklace of the Brisings'. Draupnir is Odin's arm-ring that drips eight copies of itself every ninth night; Andvaranaut is the cursed ring of the Volsung cycle; Sviagris is a legendary Swedish king's ring. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brisingamen'.

question: Freyja bargained with each of four dwarves in turn to win her famous necklace, which the company had forged deep underground. It was not the work of the gods. The medieval Icelandic tale Sorla thattr preserves the names of all four. What were the four dwarves called?
context: The Sorla thattr (a story preserved in the 14th-century Flateyjarbok manuscript) names the four smiths as Alfrigg, Dvalin, Berling and Grerr. Sindri and Brokkr forged Mjolnir; Fjalar and Galar brewed the Mead of Poetry; Nordri, Sudri, Austri and Vestri are the four dwarves who hold up the four corners of the sky. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brisingamen'.  (Legend.)

question: Loki borrowed Freyja's magic feather cloak, the valshamr, and flew north into Jotunheim, the land of the giants. A giant had stolen away the goddess Idunn, keeper of the golden apples of youth, and whoever wore the cloak could fly. What kind of bird's feathers was Freyja's cloak made from?
context: Valshamr means literally 'falcon-skin'. Loki borrows it to fetch Idunn back from the giant Thjazi (Snorri's Skaldskaparmal) and again to spy out where the giant Thrym has hidden Mjolnir (Thrymskvida 3-5), where Freyja lends it at once, saying she would give it even were it made of gold or silver. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: Freyja searched for her husband Odr, a mysterious god who had gone away on long travels across the nine worlds, and she could not find him. What she wept for him grew so famous that the skalds, the poets of the Viking age, turned it into a kenning, a compact metaphor for a treasured thing. What did Freyja weep for Odr?
context: Snorri says in Gylfaginning 35 that Freyja's tears turn to red gold as they fall. In Norse skaldic poetry, 'Freyja's tears' became a standing kenning (poetic phrase) for gold itself (Skaldskaparmal 37). She searches for Odr under many names -- Mardoll, Horn, Gefn, Syr. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Sorla thattr, Loki turned himself into a fly one night and slipped through a tiny hole by the gable-top into Freyja's locked bower. Then he turned into a flea, bit her cheek so she rolled over, and stole her golden necklace right off her neck. Snorri tells how one of the Aesir tracked Loki down and won the necklace back. Which god was it?
answer: Heimdall, the watchman of the gods
choices: Heimdall, the watchman of the gods
Tyr, the one-handed god of oaths
Vidar, the silent son of Odin
context: Heimdall found Loki with the necklace; both took the shape of seals and fought over it at a rock called Singasteinn out at sea, and Heimdall won it back for Freyja. In the Sorla thattr itself, Odin returns the necklace only when Freyja sets two kings to fight forever. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brisingamen'; Tunstall's translation of the Sorla thattr (germanicmythology.com).  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir and the Vanir, the two families of Norse gods, fought the first war in the world, and when it ended in peace they traded hostages. In the Ynglinga saga the Vanir send the god Freyr and his wealthy father, and Freyr's sister Freyja comes to live in Asgard too. What was the father's name?
context: Ynglinga saga 4 and Snorri's Gylfaginning: the Vanir send Njord the Rich and his son Freyr as hostages, and Freyja is Njord's daughter. Aegir is a sea-giant, Ymir the first frost-giant, and Mimir the wise one whom the Aesir sent the other way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Æsir–Vanir_War.  (Legend.)

question: Freyja bore two daughters to Odr, the wandering god who went away on long travels. Both their names mean 'treasure' or 'precious jewel,' as though even her children were more gold to a grieving mother. What were Freyja's two daughters called?
context: Both names in Old Norse mean 'treasure': Hnoss is a word for a precious jewel or a treasure, and Gersemi for something exquisite and prized. Snorri names Hnoss; the Ynglinga saga gives her a sister, Gersemi. Sol and Mani are sun and moon, Nott and Dag are night and day, and Skuld and Verdandi are two of the three Norns. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: The older gods gave Freyr, a Vanir god of sunshine and good harvests, an entire realm of the nine worlds when the baby cut his very first tooth. Later stories name that bright kingdom as the home of the light elves. What is the name of Freyr's realm?
context: Grimnismal 5 in the Poetic Edda: 'Alfheim the gods to Frey gave in days of yore for a tooth-gift.' The name literally means 'Elf-Home'. Asgard is the whole home of the Aesir; Svartalfheim is the home of the dark elves / dwarves; Midgard is the human world.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr, the god of fertility and harvest, slipped into the great hall of Asgard one afternoon and climbed onto a high place meant only for the two highest gods. Anyone up there could see into every world at once. Whose forbidden place had Freyr climbed?
context: Only Odin and his wife Frigg are allowed to sit on Hlidskjalf. Freyr's trespass is what sets the whole Skirnismal story in motion. Skinfaxi is a horse, not a seat; Himinbjorg is Heimdall's hall, not a watching-seat; Fensalir is Frigg's hall.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr came down from a forbidden high seat where he had looked out across the Nine Worlds and seen a shining giantess. He went home too lovesick to eat, sleep or say a word. The worried gods finally sent his own personal servant to find out what had happened. What was the servant's name?
context: Skirnir means 'the Shining One' and he is Freyr's messenger throughout Skirnismal. Skidbladnir is Freyr's magical ship (not a person); Skadi is Njord's giantess wife; Skoll is one of the wolves that chases the sun.  (Legend.)

question: A giant-girl stepped out of her father's hall in Jotunheim and reached her arm up to open a door. The plain skin of that one arm shone so brightly that the sea and the sky lit up all the way to Asgard. Freyr saw it from the high seat and fell silent. What was her name?
context: Gerdr is the daughter of the giant Gymir. Skirnismal stanzas 4-7 describe the bare-arm-shining moment; it is one of the most sudden coup-de-foudre scenes in Norse verse. Gunnr is a valkyrie; Gefjun is an Aesir goddess; Grid is another giantess but the mother of Vidar.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr's servant rode into Jotunheim, the land of giants, to win a giantess for his lovesick master. When he reached her hall he first tried to buy her with treasure: a set of golden apples, and then a very famous named object made by the dwarves. Which dwarf-made treasure did he offer her?
context: Draupnir is Odin's ring, dwarf-made, which drips eight matching golden rings every ninth night. Skirnir offers eleven apples and then Draupnir itself -- Gerdr refuses both, saying the Vanir have gold enough (Skirnismal 19-22). Andvaranaut is the cursed dragon-treasure ring from the Sigurd cycle; Sviagris is a Swedish royal ring (Hrolf Kraki's saga); Brisingamen is Freyja's necklace -- all real dwarf-made Norse treasures, but only Draupnir is the one Skirnir offers.  (Legend.)

question: The giantess refused both gifts and drawn steel, so Freyr's servant stopped asking and started cursing. He told her exactly the kind of husband she would get if she kept refusing, a monstrous mate she could not escape. What kind of husband did he promise her?
context: Skirnir's curse in Skirnismal 27-36 is one of the darkest passages in Norse poetry: Gerdr will pine forever, be mocked by gods and men, sit weeping under the giants' gate, and be married to a three-headed frost-giant she loathes. The threat, not the treasure, is what finally breaks her.  (Legend.)

question: A terrified giantess in Jotunheim at last named a time and a place to meet the god Freyr. His servant had ridden to her hall to win her, and when gold could not tempt her he threatened her with a terrible rune-curse: she would live forever hated, hungry and alone. She chose a small, quiet wood far from the giants' halls, in nine nights' time. What is the name of that grove?
context: Skirnismal 39: Gerdr sets the meeting in the grove Barri after nine nights (nine is the sacred Norse number -- nine worlds, Odin's nine nights on the tree, Heimdall's nine mothers). Glasir is the golden-leaved tree beside Valhalla; Jarnvid ('Iron-Wood') is where the giantess-mother of wolves dwells; Myrkvid ('Mirk-Wood') is the dark border-forest between worlds.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr rode out unarmed at Ragnarok, the doom of the gods, to meet a fire-giant coming north out of Muspelheim, the burning land in the south. The giant carried a sword that shone brighter than the sun and meant to burn all nine worlds. Freyr had once given away his own sword for love. What was the fire-giant's name?
context: Surt (Surtr, 'the Swart One') leads the fire-giants of Muspelheim at Ragnarok. Fenrir is the wolf that swallows Odin; Jormungandr is the world-serpent that fights Thor; Hrym is the giant who steers the ship Naglfar. Voluspa 52-53; Gylfaginning 51.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood stumbles across a plump, jolly churchman at a riverside, a friar with a rope belt around his robe. The friar neither runs away nor preaches. He takes up a weapon and squares up to fight. What weapon does Friar Tuck swing at Robin?
context: Friar Tuck carries a sword throughout the ballad Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar (Child Ballad 123). Church law of the day officially forbade a friar from shedding blood -- clerics were supposed to fight only with bludgeoning weapons like clubs or maces -- and the joke of Tuck is that he cheerfully ignores this and fights like any yeoman with a blade. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar.  (Legend.)

question: Will Scadlock tells Robin Hood that a stout friar has beaten every man who came against him, and Robin sets out to find him. In the ballad Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar, this friar lives at a real Yorkshire monastery, still standing today as a ruin. Which abbey does the ballad name?
context: The ballad places the friar at Fountains Abbey in Yorkshire -- a Cistercian house founded in 1132, dissolved by Henry VIII, and now a UNESCO ruin. All four choices are real Yorkshire abbeys of the same era. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood meets the fighting friar at a riverside and forces him at blade's point to carry him across the water on his back. The friar carries him in silence, but halfway across he gets his revenge. What does the friar do to Robin midstream?
context: In Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar, the friar dumps Robin into the river halfway across in payment for being made to carry him. Both men then draw swords in the shallows and fight until they are exhausted. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood blows his horn to summon the Merry Men, after he and the fighting friar have fought in the shallows until both are exhausted. The friar answers by whistling up a pack of his own beasts, which had helped him guard his abbey. What kind of dogs come running out of the woods?
context: The friar whistles up his pack of mastiffs -- massive English guard-dogs bred for war and estate defence. Robin's men come with bows; the friar's mastiffs come with teeth; neither side can beat the other. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar; boldoutlaw.com, Friar Tuck.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood picks a fight with a big fighting friar by the river in the ballad Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar. A villager on the road can tell a curtal friar at a glance by one feature, the mark of a mendicant, a wandering preacher who begs for his bread, and not a monk shut up in a monastery. What is that feature?
context: A curtal friar wore a short robe -- 'curtal' is from Old French 'curt', meaning short. The short robe was the mark of a mendicant on the move, walking preaching roads instead of staying cloistered like a black-robed Benedictine monk. All four choices were real marks of medieval clergy, but only the short robe gave the 'curtal' name. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar.

question: Friar Tuck came late to Robin Hood's band. The earliest ballads and rhymes had no friar in them at all, and the jolly, fat fighter did not join the tradition until around the year 1475, more than a century after the earliest surviving Robin Hood poems. In what kind of medieval source did he first appear as a named character?
context: Friar Tuck first appears in a fragmentary text of a May Day play, Robin Hood and the Friar, dated around 1475. The Curtal Friar ballad (Child 123) was written down later. Little John, Will Scarlet, and Much the Miller's Son are in the earliest ballads; Tuck is a later arrival. Source: robinhoodlegend.com, Plays and the May Festivities.

question: King Henry V sent out royal writs twice in 1417, demanding the arrest of an outlaw who called himself 'Frere Tuk' and led a band that murdered, robbed and burned forest wardens' lodges across Surrey and Sussex. A letter of 1429 later gave his real identity. What was the man in real life?
answer: a chaplain of Lindfield in Sussex
choices: a chaplain of Lindfield in Sussex
a friar of Fountains Abbey in Yorkshire
a hermit of the Weald of Sussex
a monk of Battle Abbey in Sussex
context: The 1429 letter identifies the outlaw 'Frere Tuk' as Robert Stafford, chaplain of the village of Lindfield in Sussex. He was a real churchman who took up outlawry and borrowed a colourful nickname; the ballad-Tuck grew up on top of his memory. Source: boldoutlaw.com, The Search for a Real Robin Hood; Lindfield Life history articles.

question: In the Gospel of Luke, an angel comes to a young woman named Mary in the village of Nazareth in Galilee. He greets her as highly favoured and tells her she will conceive a son and call him Jesus. Luke gives the angel's own name. Which angel is it?
context: Luke 1:26-28 (KJV): 'the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth... And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.' Michael, Raphael and Uriel are other angels named in Jewish and Christian tradition.

question: Mary, a young woman of Nazareth, hears an angel tell her she will conceive a son called Jesus, in the Gospel of Luke. Her reply in the King James Version is polite, astonished and honest, one plain question. What does Mary ask the angel?
answer: How shall this be, seeing I know not a man
choices: How shall this be, seeing I know not a man
Why hast thou chosen me above all women
What sign wilt thou give me for a token
Where shall this thing come to pass
context: Luke 1:34 (KJV): 'Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?' 'I know not a man' is the Bible's old way of saying she was a virgin.

question: The angel who comes to Mary in Nazareth offers her a sign, in the Gospel of Luke, that nothing is impossible with God. One older woman in her family, long thought too old to bear any child at all, is already six months along in a pregnancy. Which relative is she?
context: Luke 1:36 (KJV): 'And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren.' Elizabeth's child is the future John the Baptist.

question: Mary hurries up into the hill country of Judea to visit her older cousin Elizabeth, right after the angel tells her she will conceive Jesus, in the Gospel of Luke. She enters the house and greets Elizabeth, and one thing happens that opens the whole scene of the Visitation. What happens to Elizabeth when she hears the greeting?
answer: The baby in her womb leaps
choices: The baby in her womb leaps
A dove lands on the roof
The oil in her lamp catches fire
context: Luke 1:41 (KJV): 'And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost.' Elizabeth explains at verse 44: the child 'leaped in my womb for joy'.

question: Mary bursts into a long song of praise to God in the Gospel of Luke, when her older cousin Elizabeth blesses her in the hill country of Judea. Monasteries sing it at Vespers, the evening prayer, as they have every evening for more than a thousand years. What is its traditional Latin name?
context: Luke 1:46-47 (KJV): 'And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.' The Benedictus (Zacharias's song) and the Nunc Dimittis (Simeon's) also come from Luke's first two chapters; the Te Deum is a later Latin hymn.

question: Mary sings one line in the Gospel of Luke that Christian reformers, radicals and poets have quoted for centuries as her song's political sting. In the King James wording, which line comes from Mary's song and not from somewhere else in scripture?
answer: He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree
choices: He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner
Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth
The kingdom of this world is become the kingdom of our Lord
context: Luke 1:52 (KJV). This reversal image echoes the Song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2 ('the bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girded with strength').

question: Zacharias, an old priest and Elizabeth's husband, goes into the Temple in Jerusalem in the Gospel of Luke to carry out his priestly duty, months before an angel comes to Mary. The same angel appears to him there. Where in the Temple does the angel speak to him?
context: Luke 1:9-11 (KJV): 'his lot was to burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord... And there appeared unto him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense.' The incense altar stood in the Holy Place, inside the sanctuary building, and the angel appears on its right side.

question: In Luke's telling, an angel appears to an elderly priest named Zacharias, serving in the Temple in Jerusalem, and tells him that his old wife will bear a son, the boy who will grow up to be John the Baptist. Zacharias does not believe him, and the angel punishes his doubt on the spot with a disability that lasts until the baby is born. Which one?
context: Luke 1:20 (KJV): 'And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words.' 'Dumb' in the King James English means unable to speak.

question: In Malory's telling, an old man clothed in white leads a young knight in red armor into Camelot at Pentecost. The youth takes an empty seat at the Round Table, one that has harmed every other man who sat in it. What is his name?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XIII ch.4. Galahad is the pure Grail-knight of the Vulgate Queste and Malory. Percival and Bors are his two Grail companions but only Galahad may sit in the Siege Perilous. Lancelot, his father, is the greatest fighter in the world but is barred from the Grail by his love for Guinevere.  (Legend.)

question: Dame Brusen, a great enchantress, works a spell for a king who knows his daughter is to bear Sir Lancelot a son. She gives Lancelot enchanted wine, and for one night he takes the girl for Queen Guinevere, the woman he loves. The girl bears Galahad, the future Grail knight. Who is Galahad's mother?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XI ch.2. King Pelles knew Lancelot would beget Galahad on his daughter; Dame Brusen (Brisen) sent Lancelot a ring like Queen Guinevere's as a false token, then a cup of wine that so bewitched him he took Elaine for the queen. Elaine of Astolat is a different Elaine, the lily maid who dies of love for Lancelot. Nimue is the damsel of the lake who imprisons Merlin; Morgan le Fay is Arthur's half-sister.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Gawain tries to draw a bright sword from a great stone floating on the river at Camelot at Pentecost, and he fails. Letters on the sword's pommel say only the best knight in the world shall draw it, and Sir Lancelot has refused to touch it. Which knight then draws it easily?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XIII ch.2-5. The stone of red marble floats on the river; Gawain, and then Percival, try at Arthur's command and fail, and no one else dares. Arthur drew the first sword from a stone to become king; Galahad draws this one as the knight of the Grail.  (Legend.)

question: Galahad rides out from Camelot with the fellowship of the Round Table on the great quest for the Holy Grail, the sacred vessel of the Last Supper. Out of the whole fellowship, only three knights see the Grail uncovered and complete the quest. Galahad is one. Which two complete it alongside him?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII. Percival and Bors are the two companions who ride the whole quest with Galahad and see the Grail at Corbenic. Gawain and Lancelot both attempt the quest and both fail. Kay and Bedivere are old household knights of Arthur. Tristan and Palamedes belong to a different romance-cycle -- the Tristan story of Cornwall.  (Legend.)

question: Galahad and his two companions ride at last to a mysterious castle where a maimed king lies waiting for the one knight who can heal him. It is the same castle where Galahad was conceived years before, when Lancelot was tricked. In its chapel the three knights see the Holy Grail uncovered. What is the name of the castle?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.19-21; Vulgate Queste del Saint Graal. Corbenic is King Pelles's castle, where Lancelot was tricked and Galahad conceived; there Galahad anoints the Maimed King with blood from the holy spear and heals him. Camelot is Arthur's own city, Joyous Gard is Lancelot's castle, and Tintagel is where Uther Pendragon fathered Arthur.  (Legend.)

question: Galahad, Percival and Bors kneel in the chapel of the Grail castle as the Grail is uncovered, in Malory and in the French Queste del Saint Graal. A figure steps out of the Grail vessel itself and gives each of them communion with his own hand. Who is it?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.20; Vulgate Queste del Saint Graal. A bishop borne in by angels, the first bishop of Christendom, says the Mass; then a man bearing the wounds of the Passion comes out of the holy vessel and gives the knights communion: Christ himself. Nacien is the hermit who counsels the Grail knights; the Fisher King is Corbenic's wounded lord; Michael is the warrior archangel.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Galahad and his two Grail companions carry the Holy Grail overseas from the Fisher King's castle to a mystical city said to lie somewhere in the East. There Galahad is crowned king and rules for one single year before his death. What is the name of that eastern city?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.20-22. Sarras is a mystic city of the Grail cycle, sometimes said to be in the Holy Land, sometimes further east, never pinned down on any real map. Jerusalem, Alexandria and Constantinople are the great real Christian cities of the eastern Mediterranean.  (Legend.)

question: Galahad hears Mass early one morning in the eastern city where he rules as king, and sees the Holy Grail openly at last. Malory says his mortal flesh trembles to behold such spiritual things, and he holds up his hands to heaven. What happens to Galahad there?
answer: he dies as he kneels in prayer
choices: he dies as he kneels in prayer
he goes blind for the rest of his life
he is turned to stone in the chapel
he is carried off in his sleep
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.22. Seeing the Grail openly, Galahad prays, 'Now, blessed Lord, would I not longer live, if it might please thee'; he takes communion, kisses Percival and Bors, kneels before the table, and his soul departs, borne up by a multitude of angels. Blindness belongs to Saul on the Damascus road, stone to Medusa's victims, and the sleeping abduction to fairy tale.  (Legend.)

question: Thomas Malory takes the Holy Grail out of the world at one Mass, in the eastern city where Sir Galahad is king. Something comes down from above the altar and carries the Grail off for good, and Malory says no living person ever sees it in the world again. What comes down from heaven and takes the Grail?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.22. A single HAND reaches down from above the altar, takes the Grail and the holy spear with it, and is gone. This is the very end of the Grail on earth. The white dove belongs to the Grail's arrival scenes (and to the baptism of Jesus in the gospels); Jacob's ladder belongs to Genesis; the pillar of fire is Israel's guide out of Egypt in Exodus.  (Legend.)

question: One knight rides back alone to Arthur's court when the Grail quest is finished and tells the whole tale. He is the only Grail-witness left in the world, and years later he will stand with Lancelot in the war that ends the Round Table. Which knight is this?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.23. Bors alone returns to Camelot and tells the whole tale: Galahad died at the Mass in Sarras, and Percival took the religious habit and died a hermit a year and two months later. Later Bors stands with Lancelot in the war that ends the Round Table. Gawain gave up the quest, Kay had no part in it, and Lancelot, though he came to Corbenic, was struck senseless at the door of the Grail's chamber.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory's telling, Sir Kay, Arthur's sharp-tongued steward, mocked a stranger at court who would not give his name. He named the youth for his large, handsome hands with a French nickname meaning 'Fair Hands' and sent him to the kitchen. What was the nickname?
context: Beaumains is Old French for 'fair hands' (beau + mains). Malory Book VII opens with the scene. Le Bel Inconnu ('the Fair Unknown') is a parallel French romance by Renaut de Beaujeu, not a name in Malory; La Cote Male Taile ('the badly cut coat') is another Round Table nickname, given by Kay to Sir Breunor; Perceval le Gallois ('Perceval the Welshman') is the Grail knight of Chretien de Troyes.  (Legend.)

question: An unknown young man stood before King Arthur at his Pentecost feast, in Malory's Tale of Sir Gareth, and would not give his real name. Before anything else he asked Arthur for three gifts. Which was his very first gift?
answer: food and drink for a year
choices: food and drink for a year
a place at the Round Table
the hand of a lady of the court
context: Malory Book VII ch.1: 'that ye will give me meat and drink sufficiently for this twelvemonth'. He asks the other two gifts a year later. Kay sneers that a man of gentle birth would have asked for horse and armour; a Round Table seat is not given as a gift; marriage comes only at the tale's end, to Dame Lyonesse.  (Legend.)

question: The young stranger had served a full year in King Arthur's kitchens when a damsel arrived at court, seeking a knight brave enough to rescue her besieged sister from a terrible enemy. He stepped forward and asked his second promised gift: her quest. What was the damsel's name?
context: Lynette (sometimes Lyonet) rode beside Beaumains all the way to the castle, mocking him from behind as a kitchen-boy who smelled of grease, until his deeds converted her mockery to admiration. Elaine of Astolat dies of unrequited love for Lancelot; Nimue is the Lady of the Lake figure who imprisons Merlin; Enid is the wife of Geraint in the parallel Welsh and French tales.  (Legend.)

question: A damsel rode into King Arthur's court at Caerleon with an urgent plea: her own sister, a great lady, was trapped inside her own castle, besieged by a terrible enemy knight. The whole Tale of Sir Gareth turns on a kitchen boy riding out to rescue that lady. What was the besieged sister's name?
context: Dame Lyonesse held Castle Perilous against the Red Knight of the Red Launds. Beaumains married her at the tale's end. Guinevere is Arthur's queen; Igraine is Arthur's mother; Morgause is Gareth's own mother.  (Legend.)

question: The kitchen boy met four knights on the road to Castle Perilous, each named for the color of his armor. He killed the first, the Black Knight Sir Percard, and beat the Green Knight and the Red Knight, sending them to King Arthur. Who was the fourth?
answer: the Blue Knight Sir Persaunt of Inde
choices: the Blue Knight Sir Persaunt of Inde
the White Knight Sir Balin the Savage
the Golden Knight Sir Ector de Maris
context: Malory Book VII. 'Of Inde' is the old word for indigo blue, the colour of Persaunt's arms. Sir Balin le Savage is a wholly different tragic knight (the Dolorous Stroke); Sir Ector de Maris is Lancelot's brother; Sir Palamedes is the Saracen knight of the Tristram books.  (Legend.)

question: A giant knight in blood-red armor, the Red Knight of the Red Launds, had besieged a lady in Castle Perilous and defied every rescuer when the kitchen boy rode out to fight him. Around his own pavilion outside the castle, the Red Knight had done one thing meant to terrify any challenger. What had he done?
answer: hanged nearly forty defeated knights by their necks from trees
choices: hanged nearly forty defeated knights by their necks from trees
chained a lion at each of the four corners
planted the ground with sharpened stakes and burning oil
set his slain foes' heads on pikes along the palisade
context: Malory Book VII ch.15: on great trees by the siege 'there hung nigh a forty knights shamefully with full rich arms', by the neck, with their shields and swords about them. Hanging was the shameful death of common criminals, and the Red Knight did it for a lady he loved.  (Legend.)

question: The kitchen-boy knight fought the giant Red Knight of the Red Launds at Castle Perilous and finally beat him. He let his foe live on two conditions: make amends to the lady, then beg mercy of Lancelot and Gawain. Before King Arthur, the defeated knight later named himself. What was his true name?
context: Malory Book VII ch.17-18 and 23: the Red Knight had sworn to a lady he loved, whose brother she said Lancelot or Gawain had slain, to put Arthur's knights to a villainous death; at Caerleon he tells Arthur, 'my name is the Red Knight of the Red Launds, but my name is Sir Ironside.' Sir Turquine is a different giant knight, slain by Lancelot; Sir Breunis Sans Pite is another wandering villain; Sir Marhaus is the Irish champion killed by Tristram.  (Legend.)

question: The knight who had worked in King Arthur's kitchens at last revealed his name, Gareth, and that he was the youngest son of a northern king. His older brothers Gawain, Agravain and Gaheris were already familiar at Arthur's court. What were his father's name and kingdom?
context: Malory Book VII closes with the revelation. Lot's queen was Morgause, half-sister to Arthur; this makes all four brothers Arthur's nephews. King Ban is Lancelot's father; King Pellinore is father of Perceval and Lamorak; King Uriens of Gore is husband of Morgan le Fay and father of Yvain.  (Legend.)

question: A huge stranger rides into the great hall at Camelot on New Year's Day, as King Arthur's court sits feasting. Everything about the man and his horse is one startling color: his skin, his beard, his armor, even the horse. What color is the rider?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I lines 150-220. The Green Knight -- skin, beard, armour, and horse all green -- is one of the most striking single images in medieval literature. Red is the colour of a different Arthurian arrival (Galahad in his red armour at Pentecost); the Black Knight is a common romance figure; a silver rider is not a fixed medieval type.  (Legend.)

question: A strange rider stops at King Arthur's high table at Camelot on New Year's Day. He has a heavy weapon in one hand and, in the other, a branch of an evergreen plant held out as a sign of peace. What weapon does he carry?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I lines 206-209. The Green Knight carries a huge axe in one hand and a bough of holly in the other -- the holly is the peace-sign, the axe is the game-piece. The whole story turns on which knight will use the axe on his neck. The spear, broadsword, and mace are the other standard knightly weapons of the poem's period but are not the tools of this particular game.  (Legend.)

question: The Green Knight offers Arthur's court what he calls a Christmas game. Any knight who takes up the axe may strike him one blow right now, but that knight must swear on his honour to receive one return blow at a set time later. When must the return blow be given?
answer: a year and a day later
choices: a year and a day later
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I. 'A year and a day' is the medieval formula for a full year's completion of an oath or a legal claim (used in English law of ownership, in fairy-tale, and here in the beheading game). The other three periods sound the part but do not match this poem.  (Legend.)

question: King Arthur himself starts to rise and take up the axe, as his whole court sits silent at the Green Knight's proposal. A young knight of the Round Table steps forward and asks Arthur's leave to take the game in the king's place. Which knight volunteers to strike the Green Knight?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I. Gawain -- son of King Lot of Orkney and Arthur's sister Morgause, and youngest of Arthur's chief knights -- takes the game to spare his uncle. Lancelot, Percival, and Kay are all present at the court in the wider Arthurian tradition but this poem makes Gawain its hero.  (Legend.)

question: Gawain takes the axe and strikes off the Green Knight's head with a single stroke. The headless body does not fall. It does one very deliberate thing before it mounts its horse. What does the headless Green Knight do next?
answer: picks up its own severed head
choices: picks up its own severed head
kneels and prays before the high altar
sheds its green armour on the floor
cuts off its own left hand at the wrist
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I lines 435-459. The headless body walks calmly across the hall, lifts its own severed head from the flagstones by the hair, and mounts its horse. The head then OPENS ITS EYES and speaks aloud to Gawain from the Green Knight's own hand -- telling him to meet him a year hence.  (Legend.)

question: The Green Knight's severed head opens its eyes in Arthur's hall and speaks to Gawain. It names the place where Gawain must come to receive the return blow he has sworn to take. What is the name of the meeting-place the Green Knight names?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I. The Green Chapel turns out to be no chapel at all but a low hollow mound with an opening in it in the northern wilderness -- an old barrow. The other three names sound the medieval-romance part (the Perilous Ford is a testing-place in Chretien, the Waste Land is the Grail-realm, Castle Adventurous is a Malory name) but the Green Knight names none of them.  (Legend.)

question: Gawain rides north through the winter to keep his oath and finds shelter on Christmas Eve in a fine castle in the wilds. Its lord, a big red-faced hunter, proposes a second game: he will go hunting each day while Gawain rests, and each night the two men will exchange whatever each has won that day. What is the name of this lord?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt II-III. Sir Bertilak de Hautdesert is the lord of the castle. Balin is the tragic knight of the Dolorous Stroke in Malory. Bedivere is Arthur's last steward. Sir Baudwin of Britain is one of Arthur's Table but not this lord. The exchange-of-winnings game is Bertilak's own contribution.  (Legend.)

question: The wife of Gawain's host comes to his chamber for a third day, while her husband is out hunting. Gawain has refused her so far, courteous but resolved, and each night he has given his host the kisses she pressed on him. This time she also gives him one particular gift, and Gawain, terrified of the axe waiting for him tomorrow, keeps it secret. What is the gift Gawain hides?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt III. The lady swears the green silk girdle (a woven belt) will keep its wearer from being killed. Gawain, believing he will die at the axe tomorrow, wraps it around his waist under his armour and does NOT hand it to Bertilak that night. Rings and phials and locks of hair are the ordinary courtly-love gifts but the girdle is the one the poem uses.  (Legend.)

question: Gawain kneels on New Year's Day before the Green Knight, who has been sharpening the axe by a stream, and bares his neck. The Green Knight swings three times in all. The first swing he pulls up because Gawain flinches; the second he pulls up though Gawain keeps still; only the third comes down. What does the third swing do to Gawain?
answer: nicks his neck and draws blood
choices: nicks his neck and draws blood
cuts off his ear on the left side
breaks his collarbone but not the skin
misses him entirely and on purpose
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt IV lines 2260-2330. The third swing shaves the skin of Gawain's neck and just breaks it -- one small cut, one drop of blood. That single nick is the punishment for the one day Gawain hid the girdle from Bertilak. Had he kept the exchange bargain faithfully, the axe would have missed him entirely.  (Legend.)

question: The Green Knight reveals who he really is after the three swings: he and Gawain's cheerful host of the last three days are the same man. He then names the enchantress who put him in green skin and sent him to Arthur's court to test the honour of the whole Round Table. Who sent the Green Knight to Camelot?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt IV. Morgan le Fay -- Arthur's half-sister and a great mistress of enchantments -- shaped the whole scheme; Bertilak is her servant. The old woman Gawain saw beside the lady at the castle turns out to have been Morgan herself, watching in disguise. Nimue is Merlin's apprentice. Guinevere is Arthur's queen. The Lady of the Lake gave Excalibur.  (Legend.)

question: Genevieve, a girl from a village just west of Lutetia, stopped the townsfolk as they loaded their carts to flee. Lutetia was the old Latin name of a great European capital, and she became its patron saint. Which city is it?
context: Lutetia (Lutetia Parisiorum) was the Roman name for the town on the Ile de la Cite; it became Paris in the late Empire. Genevieve was born in the outlying village of Nanterre around 419-422. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve.

question: A travelling bishop stopped at Nanterre in Gaul on his way to Britain. He picked out a grave little girl of about seven in the crowd, Genevieve, and blessed her then and there for a life given to God. What was the bishop's name?
context: Germanus of Auxerre was a well-attested Gallo-Roman bishop who did travel to Britain to argue against the Pelagian heresy; his blessing of the child Genevieve at Nanterre is one of the earliest scenes in her Vita. Athanasius was in Alexandria a century earlier; Ambrose was bishop of Milan; Boniface was an eighth-century missionary. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve.

question: The people of Paris began packing their households onto carts to flee south in the summer of 451. A huge army had crossed the Rhine and was burning cities across Gaul, and word had just reached them that its line of march would bring it straight through the city. Which warlord was leading the army?
context: Attila the Hun's western invasion of 451 is one of the best-attested events of late Roman history. Alaric was the Gothic king who sacked Rome in 410; Genseric was the Vandal king who sacked Rome in 455; Odoacer deposed the last Western emperor in 476. Source: britannica.com/biography/Saint-Genevieve.

question: Genevieve, a consecrated woman then about thirty, stepped into the panic as the people of Paris packed to flee, and she stopped it. She gathered one particular group into the churches for many days of fasts, prayers and vigils, and told them that if they held on, Paris would be spared. Whom did she gather?
choices: the Roman soldiers of the garrison
context: The Vita Genovefae is explicit that Genevieve organised the women of Paris into what modern historians call a 'prayer marathon'; her own explanation was that she was following the biblical models of Esther fasting in Persia and Judith praying before facing Holofernes. Source: britannica.com/biography/Saint-Genevieve.  (Legend.)

question: A group of men in Paris plotted to seize Genevieve and put her to death, the Vita Genovefae says, in their fury at her for halting the flight from the city. A messenger from her old protector, the bishop of Auxerre, arrived just in time to save her. How did they mean to kill her?
choices: burn her in the old arena
hang her from the city gate
starve her in a locked church
context: The Vita Genovefae records the plot to drown her; it collapsed when the archdeacon of Auxerre arrived with blessed bread sent by Germanus, a mark of the bishop's esteem for her. Alban Butler dates the plot to 449, while Germanus was away in Italy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve; ewtn.com/catholicism/saints/genevieve-582.  (Legend.)

question: The Roman general Aetius met the Huns in a great battle in the Champagne region of Gaul in 451, after their army had turned aside from Paris and wheeled south. He fought alongside a barbarian king who was killed on the field that day, and the Huns were thrown back. Which king was it?
context: The battle is known as the Catalaunian Plains (or Chalons); Theodoric I of the Visigoths was killed leading his men in the Roman-Visigothic line. Clovis was king of the Franks born decades later; Alaric was the earlier Gothic king who sacked Rome in 410; Gaiseric was the Vandal king. Parisians credited the deliverance to Genevieve's prayer marathon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve.

question: King Louis XV started a great domed church in the 1700s in honor of Genevieve, on the hill above the Left Bank of Paris where she lay buried and which still bears her name. In 1791 the Revolution rededicated the building. What is it called today?
context: The domed church of Sainte-Genevieve, designed by Jacques-Germain Soufflot 1758-1790, was rededicated by the Revolution in 1791 as the Pantheon to house the tombs of Mirabeau, Voltaire, Rousseau, Hugo and others. It still stands on the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve above the Sorbonne. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_of_Saint_Genevieve.

question: Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin were holding Paris in 885 when raiders laid siege to it and it seemed about to fall. The defenders called on Genevieve for help, and when the besiegers finally withdrew, the city gave her the credit. Which raiders were besieging Paris in 885?
context: The 885-886 Viking siege of Paris was led by the Norse jarl Sigfred with hundreds of longships; the defence by Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin, with the city calling on Genevieve, became one of the founding stories of the Capetian monarchy. Magyars raided further east; the Moors were in Spain; the Mongols came four centuries later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve.  (Legend.)

question: A Roman emperor ordered a great persecution of the Christians, and on 23 April 303 it reached a soldier named George at Lydda in Palestine. The medieval world later made George its most famous dragon-slayer. Which emperor ordered the killings?
context: Diocletian's persecution (303-311) is called the Great Persecution -- the last and worst systematic Roman effort to stamp out the church. Nero killed Peter and Paul two centuries earlier; Marcus Aurelius killed the martyrs of Lyon; Julian (the Apostate) ruled long after the persecutions had ended. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George.

question: Saint George took over his dragon from an earlier warrior-saint. The story of a knight spearing a dragon by a lake first shows up in old Cappadocian church art about a different man, and only later did it hop to George in an 11th-century Georgian text. Which earlier warrior-saint did the story first belong to?
context: Theodore Tiro ('Theodore the Recruit') is another martyred Roman soldier. Michael slays a dragon in the Book of Revelation but is an archangel, not a saint; Demetrios of Thessalonica is a lance-bearing warrior-saint but not the dragon's original owner; Mercurius is a mounted warrior-saint but again not the dragon's owner. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.  (Legend.)

question: Jacobus de Voragine put together a great book of saints' lives in the 13th century, and its George story is the version that stuck in the West: a dragon in a lake, a princess by the water, a knight with a lance and a town baptized on the spot. What is that famous book called?
context: 'Legenda Aurea', compiled around 1260 by Jacobus de Voragine, Archbishop of Genoa. The Little Flowers is a much later Franciscan collection of Francis stories; the Roman Martyrology is a Church calendar of saints' feast-days; 'Book of the Saints' is not a specific canonical title. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.

question: In Jacobus de Voragine's medieval telling, the people of Silene in Libya drew lots one day and the king's own daughter was chosen. Each day they sent the dragon in their nearby lake a young person to eat, so it would not burn the town. They dressed the princess for the sacrifice and led her out to the water's edge. In what clothing was she led out to the dragon?
context: The bride-of-the-dragon image is the same one the Greeks gave Andromeda chained to the rock as an offering to the sea-monster -- the pre-Christian ancestor of this scene. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.  (Legend.)

question: George rode by the lake, saw the weeping princess, heard her story and charged the beast; he wounded it with his lance but did not kill it. He then told the princess to fasten one thing on the wounded dragon so that she could lead it, tame, back into the city. What did he tell her to fasten on it?
answer: Her girdle around its neck as a leash
choices: Her girdle around its neck as a leash
A strand of her hair looped round its horn
A ribbon from her sleeve tied to its foreleg
Her nurse's rosary hung at its throat
context: Girdle = the belt or sash of her dress. In the Golden Legend the leashed dragon follows her meekly through the city gates so that the townspeople can see the miracle for themselves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.

question: George told the terrified people of the city he would kill the dragon in the town square if, and only if, they all agreed to be baptised. They agreed, and he killed the beast with a single sword-stroke in front of everyone. In Jacobus de Voragine's telling, how many men were baptised that day, not counting women and children?
context: 'Fifteen thousand men, without counting women and children' is the Golden Legend's own number. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.

question: Jacobus de Voragine left the princess of the dragon story without a name. English tellers gave her one from the sixteenth century onward, and it stuck in the popular version, especially in Richard Johnson's 'Seven Champions of Christendom'. What name did they give her?
context: Sabra is late medieval / early modern -- not in the Golden Legend itself. Cleodolinda and Aia appear in some regional variants; Margaret of Antioch is a different saint entirely, whose own legend also involves a dragon (she is swallowed and bursts out unharmed). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.

question: An English warrior-king placed his new order of chivalry, the Order of the Garter, under Saint George's banner in the fourteenth century, and George's red cross on white became England's flag. George had belonged mainly to the Eastern church for a thousand years. Which English king made him patron of England?
context: Edward III founded the Order of the Garter around 1348 under George's patronage. Henry V famously invoked 'God for Harry, England, and Saint George' at Agincourt, but the patronage had already been fixed a lifetime earlier. Richard I (the Lionheart) had used the red cross on crusade but had not made George patron; Alfred is centuries too early. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George.

question: In the later Passios, the legends of his martyrdom written down long after his death, George survived one outrageous torture after another, among them being broken on a wheel and boiled in molten lead. None of them killed him. Only one final punishment did. How, in these tellings, did George at last die?
choices: Buried alive in a lime pit
context: Beheading was the standard Roman military-privileged execution for a citizen soldier. Crucifixion upside down is the Peter tradition; wild horses is the death of Hippolytus of Rome in another legend; buried alive is a Vestal-Virgin punishment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George.

question: In the Book of Judges, an angel of God walked into the village of Ophrah and found the farmer Gideon hiding his harvest from the Midianite raiders in the strangest possible place. Where was Gideon beating out his wheat?
context: Judges 6:11 KJV: 'Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites.' A winepress is a sunken pit for stamping grapes; threshing normally needs an open, breezy floor to winnow chaff. Gideon was doing the job in the wrong place because doing it in the right place would get him raided.

question: Gideon crouched out of sight, secretly beating out his wheat so the Midianite raiders would not see the harvest, when an angel of God came to him. He was terrified, but the angel greeted him with a line still quoted in the King James wording. What did the angel call the frightened man?
choices: thou faithful servant of the vine
thou watchman of the high hills
context: Judges 6:12 KJV: 'The Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour.' The joke is on Gideon: he is HIDING in a winepress from camel raiders. The line is spoken as a promise, not a description, and the rest of the story is Gideon growing into it.

question: In the Book of Judges, Gideon laid a piece of sheep's wool on the threshing floor, the flat open stone where farmers beat wheat. God had told him to lead the Israelites to war against the Midianites, and he was afraid he had misheard. He asked for a sign in the morning dew. What did Gideon ask should happen overnight?
answer: the wool wet with dew and the ground dry around it
choices: the wool wet with dew and the ground dry around it
dew on the fleece and on the ground alike
the fleece frozen stiff and no dew anywhere else
dew on the wool the first night and none the second
context: Judges 6:36-38: he laid a fleece of wool on the threshingfloor and asked that dew be on the fleece only, dry on all the earth around. In the morning he pressed the fleece and wrung out a bowlful of water. The word 'fleece' comes to English from this scene by way of the KJV.

question: Gideon spread the same fleece on the same threshing floor for a second night, in the Book of Judges. The first sign had come out as he asked, but he wanted proof the fleece was not just holding water on its own. What did the second morning show?
answer: the wool dry and the ground wet with dew
choices: the wool dry and the ground wet with dew
the wool wet again and the ground wet as well
the wool doubled in weight with dew
the wool white with frost and the ground bare
context: Judges 6:39-40 KJV: 'let it now be dry only upon the fleece, and upon all the ground let there be dew.' God obliged him a second night. The double sign became the pattern behind the English phrase 'putting out a fleece' for asking a doubt-quieting proof.

question: Gideon of Israel mustered thirty-two thousand men to attack the raiding camp of the Midianites, and in the Book of Judges God called the army too large. If they won, Israel would think its own strength had saved it, not God. So Gideon called out to the ranks that any man who was frightened could turn around and go home. About how many soldiers left the camp?
