context: Judges 7:3 KJV: 'there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand.' God's reason: if Israel won with a huge army it would 'vaunt itself against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me' (Judges 7:2). Ten thousand was still too many; the second cut was coming at the water.

question: Gideon marched the men he had left down to the water, because God had told him they were still too many for the raid on the Midianites. God told him to watch how each man drank. Only three hundred passed the test and were kept. What did those three hundred chosen soldiers do at the water?
answer: they lapped with their tongues like dogs
choices: they lapped with their tongues like dogs
they knelt and drank slowly from cupped hands
they drank standing with the pool up to the knee
they took only a mouthful and spat it back out
context: Judges 7:5-6 KJV: 'Every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth, him shalt thou set by himself; likewise every one that boweth down upon his knees to drink.' Three hundred lapped, putting hand to mouth; the rest knelt. The kneelers were sent home.

question: Gideon surrounded the huge Midianite camp at night with only three hundred hand-picked men, each with a trumpet in one hand and a torch hidden inside a clay pitcher in the other. At his signal they all blew their trumpets and smashed their pitchers at once, so that torches blazed up around the camp. Then they raised a great shout, naming a weapon in their war-cry. What did they cry?
answer: The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon
choices: The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon
The bow of the Lord, and of Gideon
The shield of the Lord, and of Gideon
The fire of the Lord, and of Gideon
context: Judges 7:20 KJV. The Midianites in the sudden torchlight, hearing the shout from every side at once, panicked; 'the Lord set every man's sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host' (Judges 7:22 KJV). The three hundred did not have to fight the battle; they only had to make the noise.

question: Loki the trickster had three monstrous children by the giantess Angrboda. One was the death-goddess Hel, and another was a serpent that would one day encircle the entire world. The third, Fenrir, terrified the Aesir most of all. What kind of creature was Fenrir?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Fenrir (Old Norse Fenrisulfr, 'the Fenris-wolf') is the wolf-child of Loki and Angrboda. His siblings are Jormungand the world-serpent and Hel the death-goddess. Baldr's father Odin himself will fall to this wolf at Ragnarok.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir held a council as Fenrir grew bigger every day: they must bind him before he became too strong. They forged a first heavy fetter and put it on him as a game, and he broke free at his very first kick. What was the name of that first failed fetter?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: the first time the wolf kicked against Leyding, it burst, and he was free. Dromi is the second, stronger fetter that Fenrir also shatters. Gleipnir is the silken third fetter forged by the dwarves that finally holds him. Gelgja is the cord threaded through the stone Gjoll that anchors Gleipnir. Leyding is often anglicised as Loeding.  (Legend.)

question: The smiths of the Aesir forged a second fetter, much stronger than the first, after Fenrir, Loki's son, had snapped one of iron. They clapped it on him, and he strained once more and shattered it too, so hard its pieces flew far away across the plain. What was that second fetter called?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Dromi was made half again as strong, yet the wolf dashed it to the ground so that the pieces flew far. Gleipnir is the silken third fetter that actually holds. Gungnir is Odin's spear. Gelgja is the cord that later ties Gleipnir to a rock.  (Legend.)

question: Odin, chief of the Aesir, sent a messenger far down into the dark below the earth after Fenrir snapped two iron fetters like straw. He ordered the dwarf-smiths there to forge a fetter Fenrir could never break. In which of the Norse nine worlds did those dark dwarves live?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: the messenger Skirnir goes down to Svartalfheim, the world of the 'dark elves' or dwarves, and commissions the fetter. Muspelheim is the fire-world of Surt; Alfheim is the shining home of the light-elves; Jotunheim is the giants' country.  (Legend.)

question: The dwarf-smiths handed up a fetter for Fenrir that looked nothing like a chain at all. It was smooth and soft as a silk ribbon, and yet the strongest thing ever made. Two iron fetters had already failed. What is the name of the fetter the dwarves forged?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Gleipnir, perhaps 'the open one' or 'the ensnarer', was smooth and soft as a silken ribbon, yet strong and firm. Gelgja is the cord threaded through the stone Gjoll to anchor Gleipnir once Fenrir is bound. Dromi and Leyding are the two iron fetters Fenrir has already snapped.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson tells in his Prose Edda how the dwarves made a soft silky ribbon to bind Fenrir out of six impossible things: a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, a bird's spittle, a woman's beard, and one thing more, taken from a cat. No one can find them in the world anymore, because the dwarves used them all up. What did the dwarves take from the cat?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Gleipnir was made of six things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird. Snorri uses the list as proof: a cat's footfall makes no sound, women have no beards and mountains no roots, because the dwarves used them up.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir rowed Fenrir out to a lonely island in the middle of a black lake, to test the silk-thin ribbon on him where no one would come to help. Snorri Sturluson gives that island a name in his Prose Edda, the last place Fenrir would ever stand free. What is that island called?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: the gods take Fenrir out to the island called Lyngvi, in the lake called Amsvartnir. Hlesey is a real Danish island associated with the sea-giant Aegir in the sagas; Sokkvabekk is the hall of the goddess Saga; Idavoll is the plain where the Aesir gather in Asgard.  (Legend.)

question: The gods drove a huge stone slab called Gjoll deep into the earth with the ribbon passed through it, then anchored it with an even greater rock. They also wedged Fenrir's jaws open, with something driven in point-up so he could not bite them shut again. What did the Aesir set upright in his mouth?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: they thrust a sword into the wolf's mouth, its hilt against his lower jaw and its point against the roof of his mouth, as his gag. His slaver runs from his mouth as the river Van until Ragnarok breaks him free to swallow Odin.  (Legend.)

question: A one-eyed stranger walks into King Volsung's great hall during a wedding feast and goes to the living oak called Barnstokk, which stands in the middle of the hall. He does one shocking thing to the tree before he leaves. What does the stranger do to it?
answer: drives a sword into the trunk up to the hilt
choices: drives a sword into the trunk up to the hilt
hangs a golden ring from the highest branch
carves a runic curse into the bark
sets a torch to the roots
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 3 (Morris translation); Barnstokkr (Wikipedia). The stranger, Odin in his wanderer's guise, walks straight to Barnstokk, drives a sword into the living wood up to the hilt, speaks once to the hall and goes. The buried sword is what the saga hangs on: only the man who can pull it free will own it.  (Legend.)

question: A one-eyed stranger in a hooded cloak turns to the wedding feast in King Volsung's hall, with a sword standing in the great oak Barnstokk. He is the god Odin in disguise. He speaks to the hall once and walks out. What does he say the sword will be worth to the man who can pull it free?
answer: he shall never bear a better sword
choices: he shall never bear a better sword
he shall be king of the North
he shall never die of iron
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 3 (Morris): whoso draws the sword 'shall have the same as a gift from me, and shall find in good sooth that never bare he better sword in hand than is this.' No crown, no charm against iron and no bride is promised; Signy's wedding to Siggeir is the very feast under way.  (Legend.)

question: King Volsung gives away a bride in his great hall on the night the one-eyed stranger comes, and she is no foreign king's daughter. She is his own daughter, Sigmund's sister, and she will become one of the darkest figures in the saga. What is her name?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 2-8. Signy is Sigmund's twin sister, married against her will to Siggeir at this feast; after Siggeir massacres the Volsungs she will engineer his death and Sigmund's revenge. Sigrid is a name from other sagas. Gudrun is the woman Sigmund's son Sigurd will marry years later. Brynhild is the valkyrie Sigurd wakes on Hindarfjall.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf, hero of the Old English poem, beats a monster named Grendel and hangs a trophy of the fight in the rafters of the mead hall. That same night a second monster comes for revenge. What relation is the second monster to Grendel?
context: Beowulf lines 1251-1309 (Klaeber edition). The second attacker is Grendel's mother; the poem never names her, describing her only as 'the mother of that terror' and 'the mere-woman.' Grendel has no father in the poem, no brother, no cousin -- only his mother, herself descended from Cain according to the poem's genealogy. She is the specific attacker on the second night.  (Legend.)

question: The monster who raids Heorot for revenge takes two things away with her. She snatches Hrothgar's dearest counselor, an old warrior named Aeschere. She also takes back a trophy the Danes have hung in the rafters. What does she take from the rafters?
context: Beowulf lines 1294-1309. She takes back the arm Beowulf had torn from her son the night before, and she takes Aeschere as a hostage. Grendel's skull is not the trophy in the hall (Beowulf will bring it back himself in the next scene). Beowulf's helmet and Hrothgar's cloak do not appear in this raid. The arm is the specific trophy.  (Legend.)

question: Hrothgar warns Beowulf about the dark tarn in the moors where the monsters live. To make plain how cursed the water is, he tells of a hart, a large stag, that a pack of hounds chases to the very bank of the mere. What does the hart do at the water's edge?
answer: it turns back and lets the hounds take it
choices: it turns back and lets the hounds take it
it drinks and dies at once
it hides in the frost-bitten trees
context: Beowulf lines 1368-1372 (Heaney translation): 'Though the heather-stepper harried by the hounds takes refuge in the wood, he will lose his life on the bank sooner than plunge in.' The stag would rather die of the hunt than touch the water. Drinking and dying, swimming across, or hiding in the trees are not the story -- the stag REFUSES the water. It is one of Old English poetry's most quoted horror-images.  (Legend.)

question: One of Hrothgar's own men lends Beowulf a sword before he dives into the mere. It is the same warrior who tried earlier to shame Beowulf at the mead bench, with a story about a swimming contest with a friend named Breca. Who lends Beowulf the sword?
context: Beowulf lines 1455-1472 (Klaeber). Unferth, whose earlier taunt Beowulf had answered in full, now hands Beowulf his own sword as a peace-offering. Aeschere is Hrothgar's counsellor -- already dead in this scene, killed the previous night. Wiglaf is the young kinsman who will help Beowulf in the DRAGON fight fifty years later. Wealhtheow is Hrothgar's queen. Unferth is the sword-giver here.  (Legend.)

question: A Danish warrior who once mocked Beowulf at the feast hands him an heirloom sword to make peace, as the hero prepares to dive into a haunted mere and hunt Grendel's mother. The poem says this famous blade has never once failed the hand of any warrior who carried it. What is the sword called?
context: Beowulf lines 1455-1472; Hrunting (Wikipedia). The sword is Hrunting, an heirloom of Unferth's family. Naegling is Beowulf's OWN sword, from the dragon-fight fifty years later at the end of the poem -- a common test pitfall. Durendal is Roland's sword in the Chanson de Roland, a completely different tradition. Tyrfing is Hervor's cursed family sword in Hervarar Saga. Hrunting is the specific loaner here.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf arms himself in mail and helmet and jumps into the black water of the mere. The poem is clear about how long it takes him just to reach the bottom, and it is longer than any real dive by a man in armour could last. How long does the poem say Beowulf spends swimming down?
answer: the better part of a day
choices: the better part of a day
the length of a slow hour
context: Beowulf lines 1490-1512; CliffsNotes and LitCharts summaries. The poem gives 'the space of a day' or 'nearly a day' -- physically impossible, which is the poem's point: the mere is a supernatural descent, not an ordinary lake. A slow hour is too short for the poem's cosmic scale. Three heartbeats belongs to boasting fighter-scenes elsewhere. Seven days is Noah-scale Biblical language. Nearly a day is the specific figure.  (Legend.)

question: Grendel's mother seizes Beowulf at the bottom of the mere and drags him into her own hall, a dry, roofed chamber lit by an unearthly light. There he lifts the sword a Dane has lent him and swings it at her head. What happens to the famous blade when its edge strikes her?
choices: it sticks fast in the bone
context: Beowulf lines 1518-1528 (Heaney translation). Hrunting, which had never failed any warrior before, bounces off her neck 'and could not bite' -- Beowulf casts it aside. Snapping in half is Roland's Durendal on the rocks (a different story). Sticking in bone is the trope of a lesser sword. Burning his hand is nowhere in Beowulf. The bounce is the specific detail, and its whole point is that ordinary named weapons cannot harm this creature.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf's eye falls on the wall of the underwater hall as the monster-woman grapples him, his borrowed sword cast aside. Hanging there is a huge weapon the poem describes as 'the work of giants, from the days before the flood, that no ordinary warrior could carry.' What does Beowulf do with the giant-forged sword?
answer: strikes off her head with one blow
choices: strikes off her head with one blow
burns her body with it as a torch
throws it up through the water to Hrothgar
wedges it against the door to trap her
context: Beowulf lines 1557-1569 (Klaeber and Heaney): Beowulf seizes the giant sword two-handed and takes her head off with a single stroke. He does not use it as a torch, does not throw it away, and does not use it as a barricade. Decapitation is the specific act and matches the arm-tearing of the first fight (a Grendel-kin dies by having a body-part removed).  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf looks across the underwater hall the moment Grendel's mother falls dead, and he sees the body of Grendel himself, killed by the wound Beowulf gave him the night before. Beowulf goes over and does one more thing to the corpse before he leaves. What does he do?
answer: strikes off the head as a trophy
choices: strikes off the head as a trophy
burns the body on the hall's floor
buries it under the giant sword's blade
cuts open the chest and takes the heart
context: Beowulf lines 1584-1590. Beowulf beheads Grendel's corpse as a trophy for Hrothgar; the head will need four men to carry back to Heorot on a spear-shaft. He does not burn, bury, or open the body. The double beheading (mother alive, son dead) is the specific pattern -- Grendel-kin are ended by losing heads and arms.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf stands over the two corpses and notices something strange happening to the giant-forged sword in his hand: its blade begins to shrink, 'like an icicle when the Father lets go of the frost-fetters,' dissolving in the hot blood of the monsters. By the time he swims back to daylight, only one part of the weapon is left in his hand. Which part remains?
context: Beowulf lines 1605-1617 (Heaney translation); Hrunting (Wikipedia). The blade melts away in the monster-blood and only the hilt is left. The pommel is only the ornamented cap on top of the hilt; the scabbard is empty by the time Beowulf dives; the point melts first, not last. The hilt is what Beowulf carries back to Hrothgar and hands to him -- and it is one of Old English literature's most-quoted supernatural details.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf swims up out of the black mere into the daylight, bringing one huge trophy from the fight below. No single warrior can lift it. How many of his men are needed to carry it back to the mead hall Heorot on a spear-shaft?
context: Beowulf lines 1633-1639. Four of Beowulf's men are needed to carry Grendel's severed head back to Heorot, lashed to a spear-shaft between them. The number is precise and deliberate: it is the poet's way of driving home how monstrous the skull is. Two, seven, and twelve are common poetic numbers elsewhere but the poem is specific: four men, one head.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf crosses the sea to Hrothgar's kingdom to fight a monster, because Hrothgar once did a favour for Beowulf's father. He is no Dane. What people is Beowulf a prince of, the tribe he sails home to when the whole adventure is over?
context: Beowulf lines 194-200, 1830-1839. Beowulf is a Geat, from the south of what is now Sweden; his uncle Hygelac is king of the Geats. The Frisians are a coastal North Sea people Beowulf raids much later. The Saxons are a different Germanic group (some settled England). The Suebi are a Central European tribe from Roman-era sources. The Geats are Beowulf's specific people.  (Legend.)

question: A queen on the Rhine hands a charmed drink to a guest in the hall of King Gjuki, her husband. She is a witch of great cunning, and her drinks set the Volsunga Saga's second half on its road to ruin. What is her name?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 25-28; Morris calls her 'Grimhild the Wise-wife'. Gudrun is her daughter, the bride she wants for Sigurd; Brynhild is the warrior-woman Sigurd has already sworn to; Signy is Sigmund's sister from the earlier generation.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd, slayer of the dragon Fafnir, rides into King Gjuki's hall south of the Rhine, and the queen sees that he is the greatest hero of the age. She wants to bind him to her family through her daughter, though he is already promised to a valkyrie. What is the daughter's name?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 25-26. In the saga Gjuki's children are Gunnar, Hogni, Guttorm and Gudrun. Freyja is a Vanir goddess, not a Rhine princess; Sigrid is a name from later Norse historical sagas; Signy belongs to the earlier Volsung generation, Sigmund's sister.  (Legend.)

question: The young dragon-slayer Sigurd has lived a while in King Gjuki's hall when, one night as they sit drinking, the queen rises and hands him a horn with warm words of welcome. She wants him bound to her house. He drinks, and something inside him changes. What was in the horn?
choices: a healing draught for his wounds
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 26 (Morris): 'lo now, take this horn and drink thereof' ... 'with the drinking of that drink all memory of Brynhild departed from him.' It does not poison him, weaken him or heal him: it erases one memory, and that is where everything begins to go wrong.  (Legend.)

question: The queen of the Gjukungs hands the dragon-slayer Sigurd a magic drink one night as her hall sits drinking. She has aimed it with care: it wipes one particular person entirely out of his memory, so that he will marry her daughter. Which person does the potion erase from Sigurd's thoughts?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 26 (Morris): with that drink 'all memory of Brynhild departed from him': the ring of fire, the runes she taught him, the oath he swore, everything about her. Hjordis is Sigurd's own mother from the earlier Volsung chapters; Signy is Sigurd's father's sister, from the generation before; Gudrun is the Gjukung daughter Grimhild means him to marry. The drug erases exactly one person, the woman he had sworn to.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd and Gunnar ride to the hall where the valkyrie waits behind a wall of fire, so Gunnar can cross it and claim her as his bride. Gunnar first tries his own horse, and it refuses the flames. He climbs onto Grani, Sigurd's horse, sired from Odin's own stock, and tries again. What does Grani do?
answer: stands still and will not move
choices: stands still and will not move
bolts back down the road to Sigurd
leaps the flames but turns back halfway
rears up and throws Gunnar to the ground
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 27 (Morris): Gunnar's horse Goti shrinks from the fire; on Grani nothing will make the horse stir, nor can Gunnar ride through. Only when Sigurd, in Gunnar's likeness, spurs him does Grani leap into the flames. It is the horse's refusal that forces Grimhild's shape-changing spell into action.  (Legend.)

question: King Gunnar of the Gjukungs wants to marry the valkyrie, but her hall is ringed by a wall of fire that only Sigurd's horse Grani will cross. Gunnar's mother, the queen, has a spell ready for this very moment. Sigurd mounts Grani a second time to ride through the flames, but no longer as himself. What has the queen's spell done?
answer: Sigurd and Gunnar have swapped faces
choices: Sigurd and Gunnar have swapped faces
Sigurd has been made invisible under a cloak of shadow
Sigurd has been shape-shifted into a wolf
Sigurd has been wrapped in a mist that hides his features
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 27; Grimhild (Wikipedia). Sigurd and Gunnar change semblance 'even as Grimhild had taught them': Sigurd wears Gunnar's outward form, Gunnar wears Sigurd's. Invisibility cloaks, wolf-shifting (as in Sigmund and Sinfjotli's earlier chapters) and mist-veiling are all Norse magical shapes, but here the saga is plain: it is a face-swap. Wagner in Gotterdammerung keeps the trick but uses the Tarnhelm, a magic helmet, instead of Grimhild's spell.  (Legend.)

question: In the Volsunga Saga, on the third morning, before Sigurd rides back through the fire in Gunnar's shape, the valkyrie draws a ring from her own hand and hands it to Sigurd, who gives her another from Fafnir's hoard. The ring she gives up is the cursed gold one Sigurd had given her as a token of their love. What is it called?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 27 (Morris): 'she took from off her the ring Andvari's-loom, which he had given her aforetime, and gave it to him, but he gave her another ring out of Fafnir's hoard.' Andvaranaut, 'Andvari's gift', is the cursed dwarf-ring Loki forced from Andvari; when Brynhild learns who took it, she wants Sigurd dead. Draupnir is Odin's arm-ring that drips eight copies of itself every ninth night; Sviagris is a Swedish royal ring; the Sampo is a Finnish wonder, not a ring.  (Legend.)

question: Brynhild learns how she has been tricked and demands Sigurd's death. The two elder sons of Gjuki are bound by their oath, so they work up a younger brother, who swore no oath, into a killing rage, and he murders Sigurd in his own bed. Which brother is the killer?
context: Volsunga Saga (Morris): Gunnar says, 'let us egg on our brother Guttorm to the deed; he is young, and of little knowledge, and is clean out of all the oaths moreover.' They feed him a snake and wolf's flesh, and with Grimhild's heavy words besides he gives his word. Gunnar and Hogni are the two elder brothers, Sigurd's sworn brothers; Hjalli is a thrall from the later Atli chapters.  (Legend.)

question: King Arthur's queen at Camelot falls into a long secret love with Lancelot of the Lake, and in the end it brings the whole kingdom down. Her name comes from an old Welsh word often explained as 'white phantom.' What is the queen's name?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books III-XXI; Wikipedia: Guinevere. The Welsh original is Gwenhwyfar -- 'gwen' (white) + 'hwyfar' (phantom, spirit). Isolde is the tragic queen of the parallel Tristan story in Cornwall. Morgause is Arthur's sister, mother of Gawain and Mordred. Nimue is the sorceress-apprentice of Merlin.  (Legend.)

question: Guinevere, daughter of a neighboring king in the medieval Arthur legends, marries King Arthur and comes to his court at Camelot with one great gift as her dowry. It becomes the very heart of Arthur's court. What is Guinevere's dowry?
choices: the horn of Bran the Blessed
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book III ch.1. Guinevere's father King Leodegrance of Cameliard sends the Round Table to Arthur along with a hundred knights to sit at it. Excalibur was given to Arthur separately by the Lady of the Lake. Uther Pendragon's crown Arthur already held. The horn of Bran the Blessed is a treasure of Welsh myth (in Culhwch and Olwen) outside the Arthurian marriage story.  (Legend.)

question: In a French romance of about 1180 by Chretien de Troyes, an enemy king kidnaps Queen Guinevere. To rescue her, her knightly lover rides in a common cart of shame, the wagon used to carry prisoners and outlaws, and gives up his knightly honor to prove his devotion. Who is Guinevere's lover through most of the Arthur cycle?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Lancelot ou le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177); Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books XVIII-XX. The romance is titled Lancelot, le Chevalier de la Charrette ('Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart') -- the cart of shame Lancelot rides in to reach the queen when she is kidnapped costs him his knightly honour but proves his devotion. Sir Tristan is Isolde's lover in the parallel Cornish story; Gawain and Percival have no such affair.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Agravaine lies in wait outside the queen's chamber at Camelot in the closing books of Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, with twelve armed men and one other knight. The two mean to expose Guinevere's secret affair to King Arthur by catching Lancelot with her. Which knight has joined Agravaine in setting this trap?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.2-4. Mordred is Arthur's illegitimate son by Arthur's own half-sister Morgause -- the future usurper of Camelot. Gaheris and Gareth are two more of Gawain's brothers (Agravaine, Gaheris, Gareth, and Gawain are the four sons of King Lot and Morgause). Sir Bors is Lancelot's kinsman and stays LOYAL to him.  (Legend.)

question: Lancelot, trapped inside the queen's own chamber and given no chance to explain, arms himself, throws open the door and fights his way through the ambush in the corridor. When it ends, Sir Agravaine himself lies dead among the others. How many knights does Lancelot kill on his way out?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.4. Malory gives the exact tally: Lancelot kills thirteen knights (including Agravaine himself) fighting his way out. Three would be the fair-fight number; twenty-four is a Round-Table capacity; a hundred is the number of Round-Table seats in Malory Book III ch.1 -- all wrong for this scene.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, King Arthur has to judge his own wife. Lancelot has fought his way out of Queen Guinevere's chamber and escaped into the countryside, and she has been left behind and arrested for treason. By the law of his own kingdom Arthur must pass sentence on her, and he does so with grief. What sentence does he pass?
answer: to be burned at the stake
choices: to be burned at the stake
to be beheaded on Tower Hill
to be walled up in a nunnery
to be drowned in a sack in the river
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.7. Burning at the stake is the specific medieval punishment for a queen's adultery -- a form of high treason against the king. Beheading on Tower Hill is the Tudor-era punishment (Anne Boleyn, Catherine Howard). Being walled up alive is a late-legend punishment. The sack-and-drowning is the ancient Roman poena cullei for parricides.

question: The guards lead Queen Guinevere out to her execution in the courtyard of Carlisle castle, condemned for her love-affair with Lancelot. Sir Thomas Malory names exactly what she is wearing as she walks out: one simple garment, chosen for shame. What is Guinevere wearing?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.8. The 'smock' is a plain linen undergarment (later called a shift or chemise) -- the medieval condemned wore a smock alone as a mark of stripped honour. Wedding gown, crown, and mourning-robes would each have signalled a different scene entirely; the smock is Malory's exact word.  (Legend.)

question: Lancelot and his kinsmen ride into Carlisle at full charge, cut through the guard around the condemned queen, sweep her onto his horse and ride out again. In the melee his sword kills two of Arthur's household knights, both unarmed, both there because they had refused to bear arms against him. Their eldest brother, who had loved Lancelot best of all, becomes his mortal enemy. Which two knights does Lancelot kill by mistake?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.8. Gareth (nicknamed Beaumains, 'fair hands') and Gaheris are two of Sir Gawain's four brothers; they had been on guard at the pyre unarmed because they honoured Lancelot too much to want to fight him. Kay and Bedivere are Arthur's oldest household. Percival and Bors are Grail-knights. Ector is Lancelot's brother; Balin is a tragic loner from earlier in the book.  (Legend.)

question: Guinevere takes vows and enters a nunnery when it is all over, with Arthur dead of the wound at Camlann and Lancelot in exile. She lives out her days there in penance and dies as its abbess. Which abbey does Guinevere retire to at the end of the story?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.7. Amesbury Abbey in Wiltshire is a real Anglo-Saxon foundation (later a Benedictine nunnery); Malory places Guinevere there. Glastonbury is where Arthur's tomb was later claimed to be found. Iona is Columba's Scottish island monastery. Whitby is the great Northumbrian house of Hilda's synod.  (Legend.)

question: Lancelot hears that Guinevere has become a nun and rides once more to her abbey, at the end of Malory's tale, hoping to take her out of it and away with him at last. The queen comes to hear he is at the gate. What does Guinevere do when Lancelot arrives for her?
answer: sends him away for ever, refusing him a parting kiss
choices: sends him away for ever, refusing him a parting kiss
orders the nuns to bar the gate against him
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.9-10. Guinevere sends word from the cloister that she will not see Lancelot again in this life; she asks only that he pray for her soul. Lancelot rides away, takes his own vows at Glastonbury, and dies a hermit soon after -- the last scene of the book. The other three answers are all endings the poet might have chosen and did not.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr, the Norse harvest god, rode in a chariot behind a living beast with a coat of solid gold. Dwarf smiths had forged it for him, and its gleaming hide lit up even the darkest winter night. What animal drew Freyr's chariot?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43 and Gylfaginning 49: Freyr's mount is a golden boar. Boars were sacred to Freyr in the Viking age -- warriors wore boar-crested helmets called hildisvin, and roast boar was offered at midwinter feasts in his honour. Freyja rides a chariot pulled by cats, and also has her own separate boar Hildisvini.  (Legend.)

question: A hostage came to Asgard after the very first war of the gods: Freyr, the Norse god of harvest and sunshine. Odin's family and his own made peace by trading hostages. Which family of gods did Freyr come from?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 24: Freyr, his sister Freyja, and their father Njord are the three Vanir gods who came to live in Asgard after the Aesir-Vanir war. The Aesir are Odin's family. The Jotnar are the giants. The Alfar are the light-elves of Alfheim, which Freyr was given as a tooth-gift when he cut his first tooth.  (Legend.)

question: Two dwarf brothers forged Freyr's golden boar, one at the anvil and the other at the bellows. Loki turned himself into a biting fly and stung the bellows-brother's hand, but the dwarf kept pumping. Which dwarves made the boar?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri (also called Eitri) at the anvil, Brokkr at the bellows. The Sons of Ivaldi were a rival dwarf-team who made Odin's spear and Sif's golden hair. Fjalar and Galar are the two dwarves who murdered Kvasir to brew the Mead of Poetry. Nordri and Sudri are the two dwarves holding up the sky.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson gave two names in his Prose Edda to the golden boar that lit Freyr's road through the darkest night. The famous one, Gullinbursti, means 'Gold-Bristle.' The other boasts of the beast's dangerous tusks and means 'cutting-tusk.' What was that second name?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the boar is called both Gullinbursti ('gold-bristled') and Slidrugtanni ('cutting-tusk'). Hildisvini ('battle-swine') is Freyja's separate boar. Saehrimnir is the boar cooked and eaten every night in Valhalla and reborn every morning. Freki is one of Odin's two wolves.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr rode his golden boar Gullinbursti faster than any horse alive, and not only across the land. Snorri Sturluson wrote in his Prose Edda that the beast could run through two other elements as well, at full speed. Which pair of elements could Freyr's boar cross?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Freyr's boar 'runs through the air and over the sea better than any horse.' The boar is one of the Norse cosmos's few land-sea-sky mounts, alongside Odin's eight-legged horse Sleipnir and Freyr's own folding ship Skidbladnir.  (Legend.)

question: Odin, the one-eyed lord of the slain in Valhalla, took his last ride at Ragnarok with the same weapon he had carried into every battle, a treasure forged by the dwarves. What weapon did Odin carry?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal and Gylfaginning 51: Odin's weapon is a spear (Gungnir), forged by the sons of Ivaldi. The hammer Mjolnir belongs to Thor; axes belong to warriors like the berserkers but to no named god; the bow is Ullr's weapon.  (Legend.)

question: Odin went to war against a rival family of Norse gods in the first war of all. His own side counted Thor the thunderer and Baldr the shining. The other counted Freyr and his sister Freyja. Which family did Odin belong to?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 20: Odin, Thor, Baldr, Tyr, and Frigg belong to the Aesir. The Vanir include Freyr, Freyja, and Njord. The Jotnar are the giants of Jotunheim. The einherjar are not a family at all but the chosen dead warriors who feast in Valhalla.  (Legend.)

question: The one-eyed king of the gods rode to war with a great spear that bore a name of its own, as all the gods' treasures did. The name may mean 'the swaying one' or 'the trembler.' What was Odin's spear called?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: 'Odin has the spear called Gungnir.' The name is thought to mean 'the swaying one' or 'the trembler'. Mjolnir is Thor's returning hammer. Draupnir is Odin's dripping gold arm-ring. Skidbladnir is Freyr's folding ship that can hold every Aesir and still fit in a pocket.  (Legend.)

question: Loki cut off all the goddess Sif's hair for mischief, and to save his bones from Thor he got a team of dwarf brothers to make her a new head of hair from gold. The same brothers forged Odin's great spear. Which dwarf team forged it?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal: Loki goes to the dwarves called Ivaldi's sons, who make Sif's golden hair, Freyr's ship Skidbladnir and Odin's spear Gungnir. Brokk and his brother (Sindri in some manuscripts) then forge the boar Gullinbursti, the ring Draupnir and the hammer Mjolnir. Fjalar and Galar are the killers of Kvasir; Nidavellir is the dark field where Voluspa puts the hall of Sindri's kin.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson gives Odin's great spear one line that is quoted more than any other. He says it does one thing in flight that no other spear in all of Norse myth is said to do. In Snorri's line, what does the spear do once it has been thrown?
answer: it never stops in its thrust
choices: it never stops in its thrust
it returns to Odin's hand each time
it splits into three points in flight
it drinks the blood of the slain
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal: Loki says of Gungnir that it would never stop in its thrust; other translators put it that the spear never misses its mark. The returning weapon is Thor's hammer Mjolnir. Three-pointed spears and blood-drinking weapons belong to other myths.  (Legend.)

question: Odin opened the very first war between the two families of gods with one act aimed at the whole army of the Vanir, the seeress-poem Voluspa says. Later tales show kings doing the same in their own battles. What did Odin do to open the war?
answer: hurled his spear across the enemy host
choices: hurled his spear across the enemy host
sent his ravens Huginn and Muninn to circle above them
context: Voluspa 24 (Bellows): 'On the host his spear did Othin hurl'; that was the first war in the world. Whether the spear was Gungnir the poem does not say. Gjallarhorn is the horn Heimdall blows at Ragnarok; Huginn and Muninn are Odin's scout-ravens.  (Legend.)

question: King Eric of Sweden threw a reed over Styrbjorn's army on the third day of the battle of Fyrisvellir, the tale of Styrbjorn says, and in flight it became a spear. The gesture echoed Odin's throw in the first war of the gods. What did Eric declare every man beneath it to be?
choices: a war-band already claimed by the valkyries
a host consecrated to Freyr for the harvest
context: Styrbjarnar thattr (Flateyjarbok): Eric, who has vowed himself to Odin, throws a reed given him by Odin; it flies as a spear over Styrbjorn's host, and he gives them all to Odin. Eyrbyggja saga tells of a spear shot over the enemy band after the old custom. The valkyries choose the slain in battle, not before it; Freyr is a peace-and-harvest god; and no saga records a dedication to Loki. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fýrisvellir.  (Legend.)

question: The valkyrie Sigrdrifa woke on her mountain and taught the young hero Sigurd a whole lesson in runes. She named the places where such runes are carved: the paws of a bear, the tongue of Bragi, the beak of an eagle, and one place on Odin's own spear. Where on the spear did she say the runes are carved?
context: Sigrdrifumal 15-17 (Poetic Edda): the valkyrie lists the places where runes were cut, among them the bear's paw, Bragi's tongue, the wolf's claws, the eagle's beak, a Norn's nail and the point of Gungnir. The poem does not say what the runes on the point do.  (Legend.)

question: In a dark Robin Hood ballad, a fearsome bounty hunter stalks through the greenwood to kill Robin for the reward on his head. He wears a whole animal's hide as a cloak, head and tail still attached. What animal is his cloak made from?
context: Stanza 7 of Child Ballad 118 'Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne': 'A sword and a dagger he wore by his side / Had beene many a mans bane / And he was cladd in his capull-hyde / Topp, and tayle, and mayne.' 'Capull-hyde' is Middle English for horse-hide. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: A bounty hunter comes through the greenwood in a whole animal's hide, head and tail still on. Sir Guy of Gisborne has come for Robin Hood, and an enemy of Robin's stands ready to reward the kill. Who is waiting to pay the hunter?
context: In the ballad, when Guy's horn sounds, the Sheriff of Nottingham cries that Guy has slain Robin Hood and bids him ask whatever reward he will; he should have had a knight's fee, the Sheriff says. The Bishop of Hereford, the Abbot of St Mary's and the Prioress of Kirklees are enemies of Robin in other ballads. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Robin and Little John quarrel and go their separate ways in the wood. Alone, Robin meets the hunter in the hide cloak, not knowing who he is, and the two men fight for two hours of a summer's day, the ballad says. With what weapons do they fight?
context: Stanzas 36-37 of the ballad: 'To see how together these yeomen went, / With blades both browne and bright', fighting 'Two howers of a summers day.' The fight is with blades: swords. The bow-shot in this ballad is only an earlier contest at a target. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Guy of Gisborne falls to 'an awkwarde stroke' when Robin Hood, stumbling in their duel, recovers and strikes. Then Robin turns to the corpse, and the ballad gives the deed in two lines: 'He tooke Sir Guys head by the hayre / And sticked itt on his...' On what does Robin fix the severed head?
context: 'He tooke Sir Guys head by the hayre / And sticked itt on his bowes end.' Robin walks with the head raised on his own longbow like a standard. It is one of the grimmest single images in any Robin Hood ballad. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood has beheaded the bounty hunter Sir Guy of Gisborne, and he is not done with him. He draws a knife and slashes the dead man's face until 'hee was neuer on a woman borne / Cold tell who Sir Guy was.' What kind of knife does the ballad say Robin draws?
context: Stanza 42: 'Robin pulled forth an Irish kniffe, / And nicked Sir Guy in the face.' The same Irish knife later cuts Little John free. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: An outlaw strips the hide from the dead hunter in the greenwood and means to pull it on over his own body, so that he can walk out dressed as the man he has killed. But first Robin Hood has to take off his outlaw's gown of Lincoln green. What does Robin do with the green gown after removing it?
answer: throws it over the hunter's corpse
choices: throws it over the hunter's corpse
hangs it on the branch of an oak
buries it under a heap of leaves
carries it rolled up under his arm
context: Stanza 44: 'Robin did off his gowne of greene / Sir Guye hee did it throwe / And hee put on that capull-hyde / That cladd him topp to toe.' The disguise-swap is total: Robin becomes the horse-hide hunter and the hunter is dressed as Robin. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: The Sheriff takes the figure walking out of the trees for Sir Guy, come to report the kill, but it is Robin Hood in the dead man's hide. Robin fools him with a signal the Sheriff has been waiting for. What signal does the disguised Robin give?
answer: he blows the hunter's hunting horn
choices: he blows the hunter's hunting horn
he waves the hunter's Lincoln bow
he holds up a green rag on a stick
context: Stanza 46: 'Robin sett Guyes horne to his mouth / A lowd blast in it he did blow.' The Sheriff hears Guy's own horn and rides toward it thinking Guy has won -- and Robin is waiting. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: The Sheriff's men catch Little John in the woods, away from Robin Hood, and they hold him there while they wait for word of the hunter's kill. The ballad runs: 'they haue tane Litle Iohn / And bound him fast to a...' What do they bind him to?
context: Stanza 19 of Child 118: 'And they haue tane Litle Iohn, / And bound him fast to a tree.' The Sheriff swears he shall be drawn by dale and down and hanged high on a hill, and Little John answers that the Sheriff may fail, if it be Christ's own will. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Little John is still a captive when Robin Hood stands over him as though to finish him, but Robin cuts his ropes with a knife instead and hands him a bow. The Sheriff flees, and Little John looses one broad arrow at him that 'did cleaue his heart in twinn.' In the ballad's poetic justice, whose bow launches that killing arrow?
choices: a bow snatched from a Sheriff's man
context: The point of the ballad's poetic justice: the hunter's own bow finishes the man who would have paid him. Robin hands Little John Guy's bow, and stanza 58 reads: 'But Litle Iohn, with an arrow broade, / Did cleaue his heart in twinn.' The Sheriff dies by Sir Guy's own bow. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: In Greek myth, a newly dead soul reached a black river and found a grim old boatman waiting in a long flat boat. He would pole it across to the land of the dead for one small bronze coin, placed under the tongue at burial. What was the boatman's name?
context: The coin is called an 'obol', and archaeologists have found real bronze coins in the mouths of Greek burials. Those who could not pay had to wander the near shore for a hundred years. Source: Wikipedia, 'Charon'.  (Legend.)

question: Cerberus, the monstrous dog at the gate of Hades, fawned on every dead soul coming in, but he raged at any soul trying to slip back out. Hesiod gave him fifty heads and Pindar a hundred. How many heads did artists and storytellers nearly always give him?
context: In Hesiod's Theogony (line 311) the dog actually has FIFTY heads, and Pindar gives him a hundred, but later art and story almost universally settle on three. His name is Cerberus. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cerberus'.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus borrowed a magic cap from the underworld god Hades to behead the gorgon Medusa, and it made whoever wore it invisible. Athena wore the same cap in Homer's Iliad to slip past the war-god Ares on the plain of Troy. Hades had not made the cap himself. Who forged it for him?
context: The Greek name of the cap is 'kynee' -- literally 'dog-skin cap', because the earliest such caps were made from dog-hide. The one-eyed Cyclopes also forged Zeus's thunderbolt and Poseidon's trident. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cap of invisibility'.  (Legend.)

question: A dead soul crossed one dark river to reach the land ruled by Hades, but that land was threaded with others. There was Acheron, the river of woe, and Cocytus, the river of wailing, and each of the rest carried its own meaning for the dead. How many rivers does the classical count give for the Greek underworld?
context: Styx (hatred / oath), Acheron (woe), Cocytus (wailing), Phlegethon (fire), and Lethe (forgetfulness). Source: Wikipedia, 'Greek underworld'.  (Legend.)

question: An Olympian god swore his most solemn oath on the black waters of one river of the underworld. If he broke it, he was struck mute for a full year and cut off from the halls of Olympus for nine more. That river winds around the underworld nine times. Which river was it?
context: The Styx's name means 'hatred'. The Acheron is the river of woe (the one Charon actually ferries across in most Greek sources), the Cocytus of wailing, the Phlegethon of fire. Source: Wikipedia, 'Styx'.  (Legend.)

question: Minos, once king of Crete, sat in judgment over the newly dead with his brother Rhadamanthys and one other. They sent some souls to punishment in Tartarus, some to bliss in Elysium and most to the drifting fields of asphodel. Who was the third judge, a former king of Aegina and the grandfather of the hero Achilles?
context: Aeacus was king of Aegina and Achilles's grandfather on his father Peleus's side. Tantalus and Sisyphus are among the punished IN the underworld, not judges. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greek underworld'.  (Legend.)

question: A crafty king of Corinth tricked Death itself, twice, into letting him escape, and the gods sent him to Tartarus, the deepest pit of the underworld, where they punished the worst offenders forever. There he pushed a huge boulder up a steep hill, only to watch it roll back down every time he neared the top. What was his name?
context: Tantalus stands in Tartarus under fruit he can never reach; Ixion is bound to a spinning wheel; Prometheus was chained to a mountain in the Caucasus (outside Tartarus proper) where an eagle ate his liver each day. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greek underworld'.  (Legend.)

question: Hades drew the land of the dead when Zeus and his brothers cast lots for the world, and all the gold and gems beneath the earth lay in his realm. The Greeks were so afraid to say his real name aloud that they called him by a name meaning 'the Rich One.' The Romans kept it as his Roman name. What was that name?
context: 'Plouton' becomes the Roman 'Pluto' -- same word, same wealth-meaning. 'Chthonios' just means 'of the earth' and is an epithet of many underworld gods. 'Aidoneus' is another byname of Hades. Nyx is the primordial goddess Night, not an underworld euphemism. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hades'.  (Legend.)

question: In Genesis, Sarah, who could not bear a child of her own, handed her Egyptian handmaid Hagar to Abraham so that he might have a son. Hagar bore the boy, and Abraham named him. What was the name of that first son?
context: Genesis 16:15 KJV: 'And Hagar bare Abram a son: and Abram called his son's name, which Hagar bare, Ishmael.' Isaac is the LATER son Sarah herself bears; Esau and Jacob are the grandsons of Isaac, two generations later.

question: Sarah bore a son of her own in her old age and demanded that Abraham cast out the Egyptian handmaid Hagar and her boy. Early in the morning he laid two things on her shoulder and sent her out into the wilderness with the child. What two things did he give her?
answer: bread and a bottle of water
choices: bread and a bottle of water
a sack of grain and a lamb
a mantle and a walking staff
context: Genesis 21:14 KJV: 'And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away.' The narrator is deliberately spare: nothing else -- no gold, no beast to carry them, no escort.

question: Hagar wandered lost with her young son in one wilderness of the dry south, after Abraham sent them out of his camp at Sarah's insistence. The water in her skin ran out, and she was sure the boy would die of thirst. Genesis names the wilderness. Which one was it?
context: Genesis 21:14 KJV: 'she departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.' Paran comes LATER in the story, after Ishmael grows up and settles there as an archer (Genesis 21:21). Sinai is where Moses receives the tablets, a generation later. Moab lies east of the Jordan, out of the picture.

question: Hagar had no water left and could not watch the boy die of thirst. She laid him under a shrub and walked a certain distance away before she sat down to weep. Genesis measures that distance in an ordinary unit of the ancient world. How far off did she sit?
context: Genesis 21:16 KJV: 'she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child.' A bowshot -- roughly two hundred yards -- is far enough that she cannot hear him, close enough that she is still with him. The stone's-throw measure belongs to Luke's Gethsemane scene; a day's journey belongs to Elijah under the juniper tree.

question: God opened Hagar's eyes, Genesis says, as she sat far off from her son in the wilderness with the water gone, weeping, 'Let me not see the death of the child.' She saw something she had not seen before, one object that saved the boy's life. What did she see?
choices: a stream running from a rock
a stag standing in the thicket
context: Genesis 21:19 KJV: 'And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink.' The raven bringing bread belongs to Elijah at the brook Cherith; the stream from the rock belongs to Moses at Horeb -- both real other wilderness-miracles, both wrong for this scene.

question: An angel met Hagar by a spring on the way to Shur, years before she was sent away for good, when she was pregnant and running from Sarah's harshness. There she did something no other human being in the whole book of Genesis does. What did Hagar do at that spring?
context: Genesis 16:13 KJV: 'And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me.' In Hebrew: El-Roi -- 'God who sees me'. The well itself became known as Beer-lahai-roi, 'the well of the Living One who sees me'. Wrestling God for a blessing is Jacob at Peniel, a later Genesis story (Genesis 32). No one in Genesis writes God a letter, and refusing God a sacrifice does not fit the scene.

question: Heimdallr, the shining watchman of the Aesir, stands guard on a rainbow span that reaches from Midgard, the world of humans, up to Asgard. It is a burning arch of three colors, and any giant who set foot on it would be burned. What is this bridge called?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 13 and 27. Bifrost is the burning rainbow span to Asgard. Gjallarbru is the gold-roofed bridge over the river Gjoll on the road to Hel. Naglfar is the corpse-nail ship that sails at Ragnarok. Gleipnir is the silky-thin ribbon that binds Fenrir. Bifrost is the specific rainbow.  (Legend.)

question: Odin leaves the council of the gods on the plain of Idavoll when Heimdallr's horn-blast fades from the worlds. He rides off alone, one more time, to a certain well beneath a root of Yggdrasil, to ask counsel of a severed head. Whose head does Odin ride to consult?
context: Voluspa stanza 46; Snorri, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Mimir's severed head, preserved by Odin with herbs and spells, sits beside the well of wisdom under Yggdrasil's root and speaks counsel to Odin. Kvasir is the wise man from whose blood the Mead of Poetry was brewed. Ymir is the primordial giant from whose body the world was made. Vafthrudnir is a giant Odin once out-riddled. Mimir is the specific counsellor.  (Legend.)

question: Heimdallr walks Midgard among humans in one Poetic Edda poem, under a different name. He sleeps three nights apiece in three different farmhouses, and he fathers the ancestors of the three classes of Norse society: thrall, farmer and jarl. Under what alias does Heimdallr wander?
context: Rigsthula (Poetic Edda), whose title literally means 'the lay of Rig.' Heimdallr calls himself Rig ('king') as he walks among humans. Grim is one of Odin's many wandering names (from Grimnismal, 'the masked one'). Bolverk ('evil-worker') is another Odin alias, from the theft of the Mead of Poetry. Ganglati is a servant in the hall of Hel, not a wandering god. Rig is the specific alias Heimdallr uses.  (Legend.)

question: A great fire-giant rides up from Muspelheim with a flaming sword as Heimdallr's horn calls the muster of the last battle. The giant is the first to try the rainbow bridge that Heimdallr guards, and the bridge cannot bear him. Who is this fire-giant, whose crossing shatters the rainbow?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Surtr the fire-giant leads the host of Muspelheim, and Bifrost breaks beneath him into pieces as he crosses. Hrym captains the ship Naglfar in the flood; he does not ride the bridge. Thrym is the giant who stole Mjolnir long before Ragnarok. Fenrir is the great wolf who breaks his chain and swallows Odin -- but he comes at the muster on the plain, not by the bridge. Surtr is the specific bridge-breaker.  (Legend.)

question: A watchman-god, one of Odin's own sons, stands guard at the upper end of the rainbow bridge Bifrost and lets no giant across it. Snorri Sturluson names him the white god, with teeth of gold. What is this watchman's name?
context: Heimdallr (also spelled Heimdall) is described in Gylfaginning 27 as 'the whitest of the gods'; his gold teeth give him the alternate name Gullintanni ('gold-tooth'). Bragi is the god of poetry; Tyr is the one-handed war god; Forseti is a god of justice -- none of them stand watch.  (Legend.)

question: Sisters on the edge of the world bear Heimdallr together beside the sea, Snorri Sturluson says, quoting a lost poem. Every other god has one mother, but he has a whole set of them. How many mothers does Heimdallr have?
context: Gylfaginning 27 quotes the lost poem Heimdalargaldr: Heimdallr was born of nine sisters. Nine is the sacred Norse number and it appears again in Heimdallr's own story -- Odin's throne can see everything but Heimdallr's ears can catch things the throne cannot, and the number nine belongs to him personally.  (Legend.)

question: Heimdallr stands watch on the rainbow bridge Bifrost with the sharpest senses in all the worlds, Snorri Sturluson says. He sleeps less than a bird, and his ears catch two nearly silent living things growing at the very same time. Which pair of soft growing-sounds does he hear?
answer: grass on the earth and wool on sheep
choices: grass on the earth and wool on sheep
grain in the ear and hair on horses
roots in the soil and hair on goats
moss on stones and hooves on cattle
context: Gylfaginning 27, word-for-word: 'he hears grass as it grows on the earth, wool as it grows on sheep, and all things that make more noise.' This is the detail every Norse kid remembers about Heimdallr -- his ears are that fine.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson fills a whole chapter of the Prose Edda with the wonders of Heimdallr, watchman of the rainbow bridge Bifrost. First Snorri praises the god's uncanny hearing. Then he adds a second wonder right after it. What is that second wonder?
answer: he sees a hundred leagues off as clearly by night as by day
choices: he sees a hundred leagues off as clearly by night as by day
he needs no sleep at all, ever
he can taste poison in any drink
he can smell a giant a league off
context: Gylfaginning 27: Heimdallr 'sees a hundred leagues off just as clearly by night as by day.' Snorri also says he needs less sleep than a bird -- less sleep, not none -- and Snorri never gives him poison-tasting or giant-scenting powers.  (Legend.)

question: Heimdallr will sound one great war-horn only once in the whole story of the world. Until then, Snorri Sturluson says, it lies hidden under one of the roots of the world-tree Yggdrasil, beside Mimir's well of wisdom. What is this horn called?
context: Gjallarhorn means 'Yelling Horn' or 'Hollering Horn'. Voluspa 27 and Gylfaginning 15 place it beside Mimir's well under Yggdrasil. Odhroerir is one of the vessels of the Mead of Poetry; the horn of Bragi is a drinking-horn of the god of poetry; Mimir's head is also kept by the well but it is a severed head, not a horn.  (Legend.)

question: The giants march on Asgard at Ragnarok, and Heimdallr lifts his great horn to his lips and blows the alarm. Snorri Sturluson says the blast carries through every one of the Norse worlds. Across how many worlds is the blast heard?
context: The Norse cosmos has nine worlds (Asgard, Midgard, Jotunheim, Alfheim, Svartalfheim, Vanaheim, Muspelheim, Niflheim, Helheim). Voluspa 46 says the horn's blast fills them all. Nine again -- the number that keeps returning around Heimdallr.  (Legend.)

question: The warriors of Odin's hall Valhalla and every Aesir god hear Heimdallr sound the alarm at the very start of Ragnarok, the doom of the gods. Snorri Sturluson says they do one specific thing together at that blast. What do they do?
answer: take up their weapons and go out to fight
choices: take up their weapons and go out to fight
kneel and swear a new oath to Odin
run to bar the gates of Asgard shut
sail out from Asgard on Skidbladnir
context: Voluspa 46 and Gylfaginning 51: at the first sight of the giants coming for Asgard, Heimdallr raises Gjallarhorn and blows. Every Aesir hears it, every warrior in Valhalla hears it, and gods and warriors alike arm themselves and march out onto the field. There is no oath-scene and no shutting of Asgard's gates -- the point is to go out and meet the end.  (Legend.)

question: A traveller climbing the rainbow bridge Bifrost from the mortal world comes to the hall of the watchman Heimdallr, right at the top, on the very edge of the gods' country. Snorri Sturluson says the name of the hall means 'Sky-Cliff.' What is the hall called?
context: Himinbjorg is listed in Grimnismal 13 and Gylfaginning 27. Valhalla is Odin's hall of slain warriors; Bilskirnir is Thor's; Sessrumnir is Freyja's. His horse there is called Gulltoppr ('Golden-Top').  (Legend.)

question: Menelaus, king of Sparta, comes home from a trip to the island of Crete and finds his wife gone, and much of his palace treasure with her. She has crossed the Aegean Sea with a young prince of Troy. What is the name of Menelaus's wife?
context: Andromache is the wife of the Trojan Hector; Hecuba is queen of Troy; Iphigenia is Agamemnon's daughter. Source: Wikipedia, Helen of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: A prince of Troy, King Priam's son, carries the wife of the king of Sparta east across the Aegean Sea. As a shepherd boy on Mount Ida he was made to judge a beauty contest among three goddesses, and he picked Aphrodite because she promised him the most beautiful woman in the world. Who is he?
context: He chose Aphrodite, who promised him the most beautiful woman in the world -- Helen. Hector is Paris's older brother, Troy's greatest warrior; Aeneas is a cousin of the Trojan royal house; Deiphobus is another brother, who will marry Helen after Paris is killed. Source: Wikipedia, Helen of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: Helen's stepfather looks out at the Greek kings and princes who have come to court her and fears the losers will go to war over her. Young Odysseus proposes a clever answer: every suitor should swear an oath to defend the winner. Who is the stepfather?
context: Tyndareus was king of Sparta; Icarius was his brother and Penelope's father; Peleus is the father of Achilles; Priam is king of Troy. Source: mythologystories.net, The Oath of Tyndareus.  (Legend.)

question: The clever young Odysseus gives Helen's stepfather a piece of advice at Sparta: make every suitor swear an oath to defend whichever man wins her. In return, Odysseus asks a favor, help winning the hand of another young woman, the girl he has actually come to Sparta to court. Whom does Odysseus want as his wife?
context: Penelope was the daughter of Icarius, Tyndareus's brother, so Tyndareus had the family standing to arrange the match. Clytemnestra is Helen's sister and Agamemnon's wife; Cassandra is Priam's prophetic daughter; Briseis is Achilles's captive. Source: mythologystories.net, The Oath of Tyndareus.  (Legend.)

question: Menelaus calls in the old suitors' oath after a Trojan prince carries his wife off, and every former suitor is sworn to sail east and get her back. He goes first to his own older brother, the overlord of the Achaeans, to lead the whole expedition. Who is Menelaus's brother?
context: Agamemnon becomes commander of the entire Greek force. Nestor, Diomedes, and Idomeneus are real Achaean chieftains, all wrong for 'Menelaus's brother.' Source: Wikipedia, Catalogue of Ships.  (Legend.)

question: One of the sworn suitors tries hardest to dodge the summons. An oracle has warned him he will be gone for many years if he sails to Troy. When the envoys arrive he pretends to be mad, ploughing his own field with an ox and a donkey yoked together and sowing the furrows with salt. Which Greek king does this?
context: It is the same young Odysseus who first invented the oath years before. Source: Wikipedia, Palamedes (mythology).  (Legend.)

question: Palamedes, a Greek chief, comes to fetch the clever king of Ithaca for the Trojan War and finds him faking madness, ploughing with an ox and a donkey yoked together and sowing salt in his fields. Palamedes sees through the ruse. He sets the king's small son down right in the path of the plough, and the king swerves to save the child. What is the child's name?
context: The exposer is Palamedes; the father's grudge against him lasts the whole war. Neoptolemus is Achilles's son; Astyanax is Hector's baby; Eurysaces is Ajax's son. Source: Wikipedia, Palamedes (mythology).  (Legend.)

question: Christopher Marlowe gives Helen 'the face that launched a thousand ships,' the most famous English line about her, and a thousand is a poet's round figure. Homer keeps his own count of the fleet in the Catalogue of Ships, in the second book of the Iliad. About how many Greek ships does Homer name?
context: Twenty-nine contingents under 46 captains. Agamemnon brings the largest single contingent, 100 ships. Marlowe wrote his line in Doctor Faustus (1604), roughly 2,300 years after Homer. Source: Wikipedia, Catalogue of Ships.  (Legend.)

question: The poet Stesichorus sends only a phantom Helen to Troy, and the playwright Euripides does the same, so that the ten-year war is fought over a shape. The historian Herodotus keeps the real Helen away from Troy as well. Where does Herodotus say she spends the war?
context: Herodotus (2.113-115) says Paris's ship was blown to Egypt, King Proteus took Helen for safekeeping, and Menelaus recovered her there after Troy fell. Source: Wikipedia, Helen of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: Helen stands with old King Priam on the great walls of Troy, in the third book of Homer's Iliad, while the Greek army moves across the plain below them preparing for battle. The scene's Greek name, Teichoscopia, means a view from the walls. What does Helen do for the old king there?
answer: Names each Achaean chieftain for him one by one
choices: Names each Achaean chieftain for him one by one
Weaves the great tapestry Priam later burns
Sings a lament in Trojan for the coming siege
Draws a map of the Greek camp in the dust
context: One of the great catalogue scenes of Greek literature; Homer's way of introducing the Greek commanders through Helen's eyes. Source: Wikipedia, Helen of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: A young warrior sails across the sea to Denmark to help the Danes kill a hall-monster. Years later, as an old king of his own people, he dies fighting a dragon. The greatest surviving poem in Old English tells his story. What is the name of this poem?
context: Klaeber's Beowulf, 4th edition (University of Toronto Press). Beowulf is 3,182 alliterative lines long and is named for its hero. The Wanderer and The Seafarer are shorter Old English elegies about exile at sea. The Dream of the Rood is an Old English dream-vision in which the cross of the crucifixion speaks. All four are real Anglo-Saxon poems; Beowulf is the one with the hall-monster and the dragon.

question: An old Danish king of a people called the Scyldings raises the greatest mead-hall in the north and hands out arm-rings and treasure to his warriors after his feasts. The Old English poem Beowulf opens at his court. What is this Danish king's name?
context: Beowulf lines 78-83; Klaeber's Beowulf. Hrothgar is the king of the Danes at the story's start. Hygelac is Beowulf's own king back in Geatland. Scyld Scefing is the legendary founder of Hrothgar's dynasty, whose ship-burial opens the poem. Wiglaf is the young Geatish warrior who stands with Beowulf against the dragon at the end. Hrothgar is the specific host of the great hall.

question: The king of the Danes mounts a huge pair of stag's antlers on the gables of his mead-hall, a vast timber palace where his warriors drink and hear songs at night. He gives the whole building a name that means 'the hart,' the male deer. What is the name of the mead-hall?
context: Beowulf lines 78-83; Klaeber's Beowulf. Heorot ('the hart') is Hrothgar's antler-gabled hall. Valhalla is Odin's hall of slain warriors in Norse myth. Camelot is King Arthur's court in the Arthurian legends. Barnstokk is the tree that stands in the middle of King Volsung's hall in the Volsunga Saga. All four are famous halls, but only Heorot is Hrothgar's.

question: Beowulf and Grendel nearly burned in London in 1731, when flames swept through Ashburnham House and scorched the edges of the one book that holds their story. The pages held. Under what name is that book catalogued today?
context: British Library manuscript description; Kiernan, Beowulf and the Beowulf Manuscript. Cotton Vitellius A.xv (also called the Nowell Codex) is the sole Beowulf manuscript. Codex Sinaiticus is a 4th-century Greek Bible in Saint Catherine's Monastery. The Book of Kells is an illuminated Latin gospel-book in Trinity College Dublin. The Exeter Book is another Old English poetry manuscript in Exeter Cathedral (it holds The Wanderer and The Seafarer, but NOT Beowulf). Cotton Vitellius A.xv is the specific Beowulf codex.

question: The Beowulf poet, a Christian in an Anglo-Saxon world, roots his fen-monster's family tree in the book of Genesis rather than in Norse giant lore. Which figure from Genesis does the poet make Grendel's ancestor?
context: Beowulf lines 102-114; Klaeber's Beowulf. The poet traces Grendel to Cain, the first murderer -- the killing of Abel put a curse on Cain's line, and the poet imagines Grendel as a distant, monstrous descendant of that curse. Nimrod is the mighty hunter and would-be builder of Babel. Esau is Jacob's cheated elder brother. Ham is Noah's son whose descendants were cursed for the tent-vision. All four are real Genesis figures around whom cursed lineages were built in medieval commentary; Cain is the specific one the Beowulf poet chose.  (Legend.)

question: Grendel comes up out of the marshes one night to eat the warriors in the king's mead-hall, as he has for twelve years, and the Danes cannot stop him. The poet says more than once that they do not lack courage; the reason lies elsewhere. What happens when the king's warriors strike Grendel with an ordinary blade?
answer: no sword can wound him at all
choices: no sword can wound him at all
his skin turns to iron in the fight
he vanishes in mist before the blow
he catches every blade in his teeth
context: Beowulf lines 801-805; Klaeber's Beowulf. The poet writes that Grendel had laid a charm on the edges of all weapons -- 'no sword could bite the sinner' in translation. He does not turn to iron, does not vanish, does not disarm his attackers by mouth. The point is that ordinary weapon-craft, however brave, is useless against this enemy; only bare-handed strength will do.  (Legend.)

question: King Hygelac hears the news of the Danish king's long grief from across the sea, after Grendel has raided that king's mead-hall for twelve winters. One of Hygelac's young warriors, Beowulf, decides to sail south and fight Grendel himself. To which people, ruled by King Hygelac, does Beowulf belong?
context: Beowulf lines 194-228; Klaeber's Beowulf. The Geats were a people of what is now southern Sweden. The Danes are Hrothgar's people, the ones being saved. The Franks are the Germanic people of continental Europe from whom France takes its name. The Angles are one of the two peoples (with the Saxons) who gave England its name and its language. The Geats are the specific nation of Beowulf and his fourteen thanes.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf chooses the best fighters he can find, boards a ship and sails to Denmark to help the old Danish king. The poet gives an exact count of the war-band that lands at the king's door. How many thanes does Beowulf bring with him besides himself?
context: Beowulf lines 194-228; Klaeber's Beowulf. The poem names 'the sturdiest thane he could find' and gives a total of fifteen sea-crafty warriors -- Beowulf plus fourteen others. Seven, twelve, and thirty are round Germanic and biblical numbers (the seven sleepers, the twelve apostles, the thirty pieces of silver) but not the number Beowulf brings to Denmark. Fourteen is the specific count.  (Legend.)

question: Grendel comes at dark, tears open the door of the great hall and eats one of Beowulf's sleeping men. Then he reaches for Beowulf, who is only pretending to sleep, and finds a grip stronger than any he has ever felt. What does Beowulf do to Grendel in the fight that leaves the monster mortally wounded?
answer: tears his arm from its socket
choices: tears his arm from its socket
breaks his neck against a pillar
chokes him with a chain from the wall
context: Beowulf lines 710-836; Klaeber's Beowulf. In the wrestling in the dark, Beowulf holds Grendel's arm so hard that when the monster tries to pull free the arm rips from the shoulder; Grendel flees back to the fen to die. He is not broken against a pillar, not thrown into fire, not chained. The severed arm is hung as a trophy above Heorot's door the next morning.  (Legend.)

question: Saxo Grammaticus, the medieval Danish chronicler, sets the great hall of the Beowulf story in a village on the Danish island of Zealand, and that hall may have been real. Archaeologists digging there have found huge long-hall foundations from the Viking age and before. In what village did they find these hall-foundations?
context: Tom Christensen, Lejre beyond the Legend (Roskilde Museum, 2015). At Lejre on Zealand, Danish archaeologists have excavated a series of massive 6th-11th century long-hall foundations that Danish tradition (from the medieval chronicler Saxo Grammaticus onward) identifies with the seat of the Scyldings. Uppsala is the ancient royal-cult centre of Sweden. Jelling is the site of Harald Bluetooth's rune-stones in Jutland. Ribe is Denmark's oldest surviving trading town. Lejre is the specific place where the hall-foundations were found.

question: One of the twelve Olympian gods limped to his forge on braces of his own devising, the only god on Olympus not perfect in body. There he hammered out the thunderbolts of Zeus, the armor of heroes like Achilles and every impossible metal thing the other gods needed. Which god was he?
context: In Hesiod's Theogony Hera bore him alone, in jealous revenge after Zeus produced Athena from his own head without a mother. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: Hephaestus tells the story himself in Book 1 of the Iliad: he took his mother's part in a quarrel and made his father Zeus so angry that Zeus grabbed him by the foot and flung him off Olympus. He fell for an entire day. On what island did he finally land?
context: Iliad 1.590-594. The people of Lemnos were the first to find him and worshipped him ever after. Delos is Apollo's birth island, Crete is Zeus's own, Ithaca is Odysseus's home. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: Hera hurled her newborn son Hephaestus out of Olympus for being ugly, in one of the two stories of his fall in Homer's Iliad, and he fell into the sea. Which two sea-goddesses caught him and raised him for nine years in a cave under the waves?
context: Iliad 18.394-405. Thetis is later the mother of Achilles -- which is why she can walk into Hephaestus's forge and ask him to make her son a shield. That's the debt he owes her. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: Hephaestus plotted a quiet revenge on his mother Hera, who had hurled him off Mount Olympus as a baby because she thought him ugly. He sent her a beautiful golden throne as a peace-gift. She sat down proudly to admire it and could not get up. What sprang from the throne to hold her?
context: No other god can undo them; only their maker can. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus' and 'Return of Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: The bard Demodocus, in Homer's Odyssey, sings of the day Hephaestus caught his wife with the war-god Ares, her lover, in his own bed. The smith forged a metal snare finer than any spider's web and let it fall over the two of them. Which goddess did he trap in the net with Ares?
context: Odyssey 8.266-366 -- the blind bard Demodocus sings this story at the court of the Phaeacians. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: Hephaestus called the gods to look at his wife and Ares tangled in his net, and they burst into laughter. Poseidon negotiated the couple's release, and the war-god slunk off to Thrace. Where did the shamed goddess flee?
context: Odyssey 8.362-363: 'And laughter-loving Aphrodite went to Cyprus, to Paphos'. Cyprus and Paphos are her sacred island and city -- she was born from the sea-foam off Cyprus. Cythera is also a birth-story island for her but the Odyssey text names Cyprus. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: A crew of monstrous, ancient giants swung the hammers beside Hephaestus, deep under a volcano in later tellings. They were the same beings who long ago hammered out Zeus's thunderbolts and Poseidon's trident. What race of giants were his forge-assistants?
context: Not the same as Polyphemus the Odyssey cyclops (a wild son of Poseidon) -- these are the elder, craftsman Cyclopes. The Hecatoncheires had a hundred hands, the Gigantes were snake-legged rebels, the Titans were the older generation of gods. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cyclopes'.  (Legend.)

question: Golden handmaidens waited on Hephaestus inside his own house, and in Homer's telling they were his own work. Unlike normal statues, these golden women could do something specific that no other statue could do. What could they do?
context: Iliad 18.417-421 -- Homer's own words: 'in whom is understanding in their hearts, and in whom is speech and strength'. The oldest robot story in Western literature. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: Vulcan, the smith-god Hephaestus by his Roman name, hammered at a forge deep beneath a still-active volcano, and his fire was what made the mountain smoke. Under which mountain did the Roman forge lie?
context: Etna sits in Sicily; Vesuvius is the volcano that buried Pompeii; Stromboli is a smaller volcanic island north of Sicily; Santorini (ancient Thera) is the Greek volcano whose Bronze Age eruption may have inspired the Atlantis legend. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vulcan (mythology)'.

question: Zeus, king of the twelve Olympian gods, took his own sister as his wife and seated her beside him as queen of the gods. She was the divine patron of marriage, the guardian of wives and homes, and the mother of the war-god Ares. Which goddess was Zeus's queen?
context: Hera is one of the six children of Cronus and Rhea; her brothers include Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades, and her sisters include Demeter and Hestia. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hera'.  (Legend.)

question: Hera, queen of the Olympian gods, claimed one corner of the Peloponnese as her own sacred country, and the Heraion, her greatest temple, rose on the plain outside its city. Which Greek city held the Heraion?
context: The Argive Heraion is one of the oldest large stone temples in the Greek world. It is why Homer calls Hera 'Argive Hera' throughout the Iliad. Source: Wikipedia, 'Heraion of Argos'.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus fell for a young mortal priestess named Io, who served in the temple of his own wife Hera. Desperate to hide the girl from Hera's eyes, he turned her into an animal so that his wife would not know her. What kind of animal did Zeus turn Io into?
context: The transformation does not fool Hera at all. Source: Wikipedia, 'Io (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: Hera saw through Zeus's trick when he hid his mortal lover Io in an animal's shape, and she asked for the creature as a gift. To make sure he could never rescue the girl, she set a monstrous watchman over her, a giant whose whole body was covered in eyes, so that some could stay open while others rested. What was this hundred-eyed giant's name?
context: 'Panoptes' means 'all-seeing' -- the same root as the modern word 'panopticon'. Talos was the bronze guardian of Crete; Antaeus was a giant who drew strength from the earth; Tityos was chained in the underworld and had his liver eaten. Source: Wikipedia, 'Argus Panoptes'.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus sent one god down in a shepherd's disguise to Io's many-eyed watchman.
