question: Joan's captors took her to the cemetery of Saint-Ouen on 24 May 1431 and showed her the stake that had been built for her burning. She collapsed there, and in exchange for her life she agreed to a document giving up her men's clothing and submitting to the authority of the church. She could not write. What did she use in place of a signature?
choices: Her banner's motto, drawn by another and touched by her thumb
A drop of her own blood
A ring pressed into hot wax
context: Joan was unlettered and could not write her name; contemporary accounts differ on whether the mark was a cross or a circle. Within a few days she was back in men's clothes in her cell, and Pierre Cauchon declared her a relapsed heretic on 28 May 1431. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joan_of_Arc.

question: The crowd in a public square of Rouen watched Joan of Arc arrive in a cart on Wednesday morning, 30 May 1431. A tall plaster stake had been built high enough for all of them to watch her burn. Above it a wooden placard listed the four crimes for which she was being executed. Which four words were written on the placard?
context: The placard's four charges were formal church-court categories; 'relapsed' meant she had returned to a condemned position after abjuring it - the trigger for the death sentence. The square was the Place du Vieux-Marche, the Old Market. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joan_of_Arc.

question: Joan of Arc, tied to the stake and weeping, asked for a cross to hold as the fire was lit. An English soldier in the crowd tied two small sticks together and passed her the improvised cross. Then a Dominican friar ran to the nearby church of Saint-Sauveur for the great processional crucifix and held it up for her to see through the flames. Which friar was it?
context: Isambard de la Pierre and Martin Ladvenu were both Dominicans with Joan at the end - Isambard is the one the 1456 witnesses named as running for the church cross. Jean Massieu was the trial usher; Jean Beaupere was one of the interrogators. Source: maidofheaven.com/joanofarc_nullification_rouen_testimony2.asp.

question: The Rouen executioner Geoffroy Therage burned Joan of Arc at the stake in the market square of the city on 30 May 1431. When the flames died, he was ordered to gather every scrap left of her, so that her supporters could keep no relic. Where did he dispose of her ashes?
choices: Into a common lime-pit outside the walls
Into an unmarked grave at the cathedral
Into an iron chest stored at the Tower of London
context: The point of scattering the ashes in the river was to prevent a cult of relics; Therage is later reported to have said he feared he was damned for burning a saint. Twenty-five years later Charles VII ordered a retrial - the Nullification of 1455-1456 - and 115 witnesses testified; the 1431 sentence was overturned. Joan was canonized in 1920 by Pope Benedict XV. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joan_of_Arc.

question: Jan Hus, a priest in Prague, filled a chapel with about three thousand townsfolk around the year 1400 by preaching in the plain speech of the streets. Almost every other pulpit in Europe used one set church tongue for sermons. Which tongue was it?
context: The priest was Jan Hus, and the chapel was the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, founded in 1391 with the explicit rule that all preaching there be done in Czech. Latin was the ordinary church language of the medieval West; German was a spoken vernacular but not the pulpit standard; Church Slavonic was the liturgical language of Orthodox Slavs, not the Bohemian Latin-rite; Greek belonged to the Eastern church. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem_Chapel, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hus.

question: The churchmen at Constance stripped Jan Hus of his priesthood in July 1415. They cut his tonsure with scissors, pulled off his liturgical robes and set on his head a tall paper cap painted with three demons, the sign of a condemned heretic bound for the fire. Hus looked at that cap and made one comparison out loud. Whose crown did he say had been much heavier than his own?
context: His full recorded words: 'My Lord Jesus Christ for my sake wore a much heavier and more painful crown of thorns.' The three other choices are all real famous crowns in Christian tradition, so the parallel is genuine, but only the crown of thorns is the one Hus named. Source: christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/hus-reformation-connection.

question: A Carmelite friar barely five feet tall had decided at Medina del Campo in 1567 to leave his order for the stricter Carthusians. A firm Carmelite nun of fifty-two, already famous across Spain for reforming her own convents, talked him into staying to help her fix the friars instead. Which nun changed his mind?
context: Teresa had begun her Carmelite reform among women and wanted parallel houses for the friars. Ana de San Bartolome was Teresa's own nurse and secretary; Maria de San Jose Salazar was a leading discalced prioress at Seville; Anne of Jesus led the reform into France -- all sixteenth-century Discalced Carmelite nuns, but Teresa was the founder who recruited John at Medina del Campo.

question: John of the Cross set up the very first reformed men's Carmelite house in November of 1568, inside a broken-down farmhouse deep in the Spanish countryside, so poor that the friars slept on straw. In what tiny Castilian village did he set it up?
context: The Duruelo foundation, with Antonio de Jesus de Heredia, launched the male Discalced Carmelites. Mancera and Pastrana were later small Discalced houses of that first generation; Fontiveros was John's own birthplace in Old Castile, not a foundation site.

question: The unreformed friars raided the house of John of the Cross in Avila one December night in 1577. They seized him and took him under guard to their own monastery, where they locked him in a windowless closet barely six feet wide. In which Castilian city did they imprison him?
context: The Toledo Carmelite monastery held him from December 1577 to August 1578 in a room described as a converted latrine off a friar's cell. Salamanca, Segovia, and Granada were all real Discalced houses John later worked in, but the imprisonment was Toledo.

question: The friars holding John of the Cross brought him to their refectory and whipped him across the shoulders before the community. They did it three times a week, and the scars stayed visible until his death. His food was bread, water and scraps of salt fish on the floor of his cell. How long did they keep him there?
context: From December 3, 1577, to the night of his escape in August 1578 -- nine months of the tiny cell, the vermin in his clothing, the summer bake and winter cold of Toledo, and the beatings.

question: John of the Cross broke out of his cell on a night in August 1578, after spending weeks loosening the door hinges. He lowered himself from a high window on a rope made by tearing up and knotting together strips of an ordinary object in the cell. What did he tear up to make the rope?
context: Testimony from the jailer Fray Juan de Santa Maria describes John tying blanket strips together and fastening an old tunic at the bottom; even so the rope ran short and he had to drop the last ten feet or so onto a wall.

question: By Christian tradition, a Roman emperor banished the aged apostle John to a rocky island off Asia Minor late in the first century. There John saw the visions of the Book of Revelation, and its opening verses name the island. What is the island called?
context: 'I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation... was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ' (Revelation 1:9 KJV). Patmos is a small volcanic island in the Dodecanese, off the coast of Asia Minor.

question: The exiled apostle John was praying on his island when he heard a great voice like a trumpet behind him. It told him to write down what he saw and send letters to a set of Christian churches in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey. How many churches received letters?
context: The seven are Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea (Revelation 1:11). Smyrna's letter is where 'be thou faithful unto death' is spoken; Laodicea's is the 'neither cold nor hot' rebuke.

question: The apostle John turned to see who was speaking behind him, and he saw a shining figure like a son of man, clothed to the foot in a long robe, with hair white as wool and eyes like a flame of fire. Out of the figure's mouth came something strange. What came from the mouth?
context: 'And out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength' (Revelation 1:16 KJV).

question: In the Book of Revelation, John saw a great scroll sealed shut, and as each of its first seals broke, one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse rode out. When the first seal broke, a rider came out on a white horse, wearing a crown given to him. What weapon did that first rider carry?
context: 'And I saw, and behold a white horse: and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him: and he went forth conquering, and to conquer' (Revelation 6:2 KJV).

question: Four horsemen rode out as John watched the first seals of a great scroll break open. Later tellers gave labels to the first three, while the text gives a personal name only to the last, a single terrible word. That fourth horseman rode a pale horse. What was his name?
context: 'His name that sat on him was Death' (Revelation 6:8 KJV). The names War, Famine, and Plague are popular labels invented later for the first three riders; the text names only the fourth.

question: A woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, appeared in heaven as a great sign in John's vision in the Book of Revelation. She was pregnant and cried out in the pain of labor. Around her head was a crown of stars. How many stars were in the crown?
context: 'And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars' (Revelation 12:1 KJV).

question: A great dragon appeared in the sky in John's vision, seven-headed and ten-horned, and crouched before a woman clothed with the sun who was crying out in labor. It waited to devour her child the very moment the child was born. What color was this dragon?
context: 'And there appeared another wonder in heaven; and behold a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and seven crowns upon his heads' (Revelation 12:3 KJV). The child is caught up to God, and the woman flees into the wilderness.

question: The old serpent, a great dragon, tried to devour a newborn child in John's vision in the Book of Revelation, and war broke out in heaven itself. One archangel led the armies of heaven against the dragon, defeated him and cast him down to the earth. Which archangel was it?
context: 'And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels' (Revelation 12:7 KJV). Michael is the warrior-archangel; Gabriel is the announcer; Raphael and Uriel appear in earlier Jewish tradition and in the deuterocanonical books.

question: John saw a New Jerusalem come down out of heaven at the very end of his vision, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. The holy city had walls of jasper, set with gates, one for each tribe of Israel, and each gate was made out of one enormous piece of one precious thing. What was each gate made of?
context: 'And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass' (Revelation 21:21 KJV). The wall itself is jasper, and 'there shall be no night there' (Revelation 22:5).

question: Out in the desert land east of Jerusalem, a wild preacher stood by the river and called the crowds to turn their lives around. He dressed like the old prophets, in a rough coat of animal hair with a leather belt. What animal's hair was his coat made of?
context: Matthew 3:4 KJV: 'And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins.' The outfit was a deliberate echo of the prophet Elijah, who wore 'a garment of hair' and a leather girdle (2 Kings 1:8). Camel-hair cloth was coarse and cheap -- the opposite of the fine wool a rich man would wear.

question: John the Baptist scraped wild honey from the rocks of the wilderness of Judea, where he called the crowds to repent. He lived off whatever the desert gave him. The gospel of Matthew names just two foods: the honey and one other. What did he eat with the honey?
context: Matthew 3:4 KJV: 'his meat was locusts and wild honey.' The Greek word akrides means the insect, not carob pods -- a later medieval reading tried to soften it. Leviticus 11:22 lists locusts as clean food. Locusts are still eaten today across the Arabian peninsula. So: real insects, roasted or dried, chased by honey scraped out of rocks. That was dinner.

question: John stood in a river in the wilderness and dunked the people who had walked out from Jerusalem to hear him, to show they were washing away their old lives. That dunking gave him the title 'the Baptist,' Greek for 'the dipper.' Which river was it?
context: Matthew 3:5-6 KJV: 'Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan, And were baptized of him in Jordan.' The Greek word baptizein means to dip or immerse -- so 'the Baptist' is literally 'the Dipper.' The Jordan is the river Joshua crossed to enter the promised land, so John dunking penitents in it carried a strong echo of a fresh start.

question: A delegation of Pharisees and Sadducees walked down to the river to be baptized, and John the Baptist greeted them with a stinging insult. Jesus himself would later reuse it on the same crowd. John demanded to know who had warned them to flee from the wrath to come. What did he call them?
context: Matthew 3:7 KJV. 'Generation of vipers' -- a brood of snakes. Jesus would later use the same insult on the same crowd (Matthew 23:33). 'Whitewashed tombs' and 'blind guides' are also real -- but both are Jesus's lines from Matthew 23, not John's. 'Sons of Belial' is Old Testament language for lawless men.

question: John the Baptist stood knee-deep in the river, baptizing the crowds who came out from Jerusalem to confess their sins. Someone far greater was coming after him, he told them, someone whose humblest servant he himself was not fit to be. In Mark's gospel, what did John say he was not worthy to stoop down and do to that man's sandals?
context: Mark 1:7 KJV: 'the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose.' The 'latchet' is the leather thong that tied the sandal on -- untying it was the household slave's job. Washing feet (John 13) comes later, when Jesus does it for his disciples -- a different scene entirely.

question: Jesus walked down from Galilee to the river where John the Baptist was baptizing the crowds, and he stepped into the water in front of John, asking to be baptized like everyone else. John was appalled. The gospel of Matthew records his exact protest. What did he say?
answer: I have need to be baptized of thee
choices: I have need to be baptized of thee
Depart from me, for I am a sinful man
Who am I, that I should come?
Let this cup pass from me
context: Matthew 3:14 KJV in full: 'I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?' Jesus insists -- 'Suffer it to be so now' -- and John gives in. The other lines are also real but come from very different scenes: 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man' is Peter after the great catch of fish (Luke 5:8); 'Who am I, that I should come?' is David (2 Samuel 7:18); 'Let this cup pass' is Jesus in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39).

question: Jesus came up out of the water at his baptism, and Matthew says the sky opened and he saw the Spirit of God coming down and settling on him. All four gospels agree on the exact bird it was like. Which bird was it?
context: Matthew 3:16 KJV: 'the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him.' All four gospels use the dove image -- one of the very few details all four agree on word-for-word. Ravens carry a very different mythology (Elijah in 1 Kings 17, Noah's raven in Genesis 8, Odin's Huginn and Muninn); eagles belong to Roman legionary standards, not this scene.

question: John the Baptist baptized his kinsman Jesus in the river, and the sky opened as Jesus came up out of the water. Then a voice came out of the open heavens. It was short, one sentence, and it named who Jesus was and how the speaker felt about him. Matthew gives the exact words. What did the voice say?
answer: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased
choices: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased
Behold my servant, whom I uphold, mine elect in whom my soul delighteth
I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine
Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee
context: Matthew 3:17 KJV. The voice returns nearly word for word at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:5), where it adds 'hear ye him.' The other choices are real prophetic 'voice from God' lines from elsewhere in scripture: Isaiah 42:1 (a servant song sometimes read as messianic), Isaiah 43:1 (to Israel), and Jeremiah 1:5 (to the young prophet Jeremiah).

question: Herod Antipas threw John the Baptist in prison for calling him out over his marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife. At Herod's birthday feast Herodias's daughter danced, and Herod swore to give her anything. Prompted by her mother, she asked for John's head, carried in on one specific item that Mark names. What was it?
context: Mark 6:25 KJV: 'I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist.' A 'charger' is a large flat serving platter -- the King James word for a big dish. Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.2) locates the imprisonment and execution at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Notice the gospels never actually name the dancing daughter -- the name 'Salome' comes only from Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.4).

question: John the Baptist's disciples came to their teacher upset, because Jesus was now drawing bigger crowds than John was, and their master was being overshadowed by the man he had baptized. John cut them off with one line about himself and Jesus. It closes his last recorded speech in the fourth gospel. What did John say?
answer: He must increase, but I must decrease
choices: He must increase, but I must decrease
The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away
I am not worthy to be called an apostle
Not I, but Christ liveth in me
context: John 3:30 KJV -- the closing line of John's last recorded speech in the fourth gospel. The other choices are Job (Job 1:21), Paul on his unworthiness (1 Corinthians 15:9), and Paul again on the changed self (Galatians 2:20) -- all real, none John's.

question: God told a prophet, son of Amittai, to go east and cry out against a great enemy city. Instead the prophet went down to the port of Joppa, paid his fare and boarded a ship that sailed the other way, off toward Tarshish. Who was this runaway prophet?
context: Jonah 1:1-3 KJV. Jonah son of Amittai is a real prophet mentioned at 2 Kings 14:25. The other three are also 8th-century northern-kingdom prophets whose books stand next to Jonah in the Bible -- easy to confuse.

question: God sent a mighty tempest after Jonah's ship as it sailed away from the port of Joppa. The sailors threw the cargo overboard, and each man cried to his own god. Meanwhile what was Jonah, whose flight had caused the storm, doing, and where on the ship?
answer: fast asleep down in the sides of the ship
choices: fast asleep down in the sides of the ship
up on the mast pleading with God to spare the crew
at the helm shouting orders at the terrified sailors
kneeling in the prow tearing his robes in repentance
context: Jonah 1:5 KJV: 'Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.' The KJV 'sides of the ship' means the inner hold. The captain has to wake him and ask him to pray.

question: The terrified sailors on Jonah's storm-tossed ship did one specific thing to find out for whose sake this disaster was hunting them. When the answer pointed at the stranger aboard, they still tried to row to shore before they finally threw him overboard. What did they do to name the guilty man?
choices: they questioned each man under oath
context: Jonah 1:7 KJV: 'Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.' Casting lots was the standard biblical way of asking heaven a yes/no question -- the priests used them, the apostles used them to replace Judas.

question: The sailors flung Jonah overboard from a ship bound away from the great city of Nineveh, where God had commanded him to preach. As soon as he hit the water the sea grew calm, and God prepared a great fish to swallow him up alive. Jonah stayed inside it for a very specific stretch of time. How long was he inside?
choices: one full day from dawn to dawn
context: Jonah 1:17 KJV: 'the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.' Note the KJV says GREAT FISH, not whale -- the whale image is later tradition. The other choices are all real biblical durations -- Noah's rain, Job's mourning silence, a fast.

question: Jonah prayed a psalm to God from inside the belly of the great fish, and at the end of it God spoke to the fish and gave it a single order. The fish obeyed. According to the book of Jonah, how did the prophet finally get free?
answer: it vomited him out upon the land
choices: it vomited him out upon the land
it swam onto a beach and died open-mouthed
it split down its own belly to release him
it carried him three days more toward the east
context: Jonah 2:10 KJV: 'And the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.' The unglamorous ending is the point -- the prophet is spat out where he should have started. Only after this does he finally go to Nineveh.

question: Jonah finally reached the enormous Assyrian capital, so vast the text calls it a three days' journey across, and he walked in one day's journey preaching a single blunt line. That line named an exact number of days until Nineveh's destruction. How many days did he give the city?
context: Jonah 3:4 KJV: 'Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.' Forty is a recurring biblical span -- Noah's rain, Moses on Sinai, Israel in the wilderness, Elijah walking to Horeb, Jesus fasting in the wilderness. The other choices are also all real biblical countdowns.

question: Jonah sat in his booth under a shade plant God had made grow over him. At dawn God prepared one small living thing that killed the whole plant, and the sun and a hot east wind beat on Jonah's bare head until he fainted and asked to die. God's whole final lesson turned on this tiny creature. What was it?
context: Jonah 4:7 KJV: 'But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered.' The book ends with God's rebuke: Jonah pitied the plant he did not labour for -- should God not pity Nineveh, wherein are 'more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also much cattle?'

question: Pharaoh dreams a strange dream one night. Seven fat and sleek beasts come up out of the river Nile and feed in the meadow. Then seven lean beasts of the same kind climb out after them and eat the fat ones. Pharaoh wakes shaking. What kind of animal is in his dream?
context: Seven fatfleshed kine and seven leanfleshed kine, Genesis 41:1-4 KJV. The Nile setting is exact; cattle grazing in the river-meadows would have been the everyday sight along its banks in Egypt.

question: Pharaoh falls back asleep and dreams a second time. He sees seven ears of grain, full and good, growing on a single stalk. Then seven thin ears sprout after them, blasted with the east wind, and the thin ears swallow the seven full ones. When morning comes, whom does he first send for to read the dreams?
answer: The magicians and wise men of Egypt
choices: The magicians and wise men of Egypt
The high priest at the temple of Ra
The desert oracle at the oasis of Siwa
His own mother the queen dowager
context: Genesis 41:5-8 KJV. Pharaoh calls for all the magicians of Egypt and all the wise men, and none of them can interpret the two dreams. Only then does the chief butler remember the young Hebrew in the prison.

question: The chief butler, still cupbearer to Pharaoh, suddenly remembers a young Hebrew he met in prison who read his own dream true. Pharaoh sends for the man at once, and he is brought hastily out of the dungeon. Before the prisoner can stand in front of Pharaoh, what two things does he do first?
answer: He shaves himself and changes his raiment
choices: He shaves himself and changes his raiment
He fasts three days and drinks only water
He bows to the four corners and casts lots
He binds his forehead and washes his feet
context: Genesis 41:14 KJV: 'Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.' Clean-shaven faces were Egyptian court style; a bearded Hebrew prisoner had to be made presentable.

question: Joseph listens to both dreams and tells Pharaoh they are one and the same warning. Seven years of great plenty are coming across all Egypt, he says, and after them seven years of famine so terrible the plenty will be forgotten in the land. What does he advise Pharaoh to do during the plenty?
answer: Appoint a wise man to store up a fifth of the harvest in the cities
choices: Appoint a wise man to store up a fifth of the harvest in the cities
Send the army east to conquer the granaries of Canaan
Build a great temple to the sun to turn the famine aside
Ration the people at once so they learn to live on little
context: Genesis 41:33-36 KJV. Joseph advises setting officers over the land and taking up the fifth part of the harvest during the seven plentiful years to lay up food against the seven years of famine.

question: Joseph stands before Pharaoh at thirty years old, and Pharaoh marries him to Asenath, the daughter of Poti-pherah, priest of the sun-city of On. To finish making Joseph an Egyptian, Pharaoh gives him a new Egyptian name as well. What is the name?
context: Genesis 41:45-46 KJV. Jewish interpreters (Targum Onkelos, Rashi) read the name as 'revealer of hidden things', fitting the dream-reader. He was thirty when he went out from before Pharaoh and went throughout all the land of Egypt.

question: A rich man went in to see the Roman governor Pontius Pilate on the afternoon Jesus died in Jerusalem, and boldly asked for the body. The Gospel of Mark says he was a respected councillor of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, who had also been hoping for the kingdom of God. What was his name?
context: Mark 15:43 KJV. The 'counsellor' in Mark's phrasing means a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish supreme court. Luke 23:51 KJV specifies that Joseph 'had not consented to the counsel and deed of them' -- he had voted against condemning Jesus. Not the same as Joseph the father of Jesus. Simon of Cyrene carried the cross (Mark 15:21); Lazarus was the man Jesus raised in Bethany (John 11); Cleopas walks the road to Emmaus (Luke 24).

question: Joseph, a wealthy secret disciple, went boldly to the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, asked for the body of Jesus, and was granted it. Mark says he first went and bought fine cloth to wrap the body in, before taking Jesus down from the cross. What kind of cloth did he buy?
context: Mark 15:46 KJV: 'And he bought fine linen, and took him down, and wrapped him in the linen.' Linen was the traditional Jewish burial cloth -- plain, white, and undyed; the Shroud of Turin, whether it belongs to this scene or not, is a linen cloth. Sackcloth is the coarse mourning material worn BY the grieving, not wrapped around the dead.

question: The Roman governor Pontius Pilate was startled by one thing when Joseph, a wealthy Jewish councillor, walked in and asked for the body of Jesus. Pilate sent for the centurion in charge of the execution to check on it before he would release the body. What surprised Pilate?
choices: That Joseph was on the council
That the sky had gone dark
context: Mark 15:44 KJV: 'Pilate marvelled if he were already dead: and calling unto him the centurion, he asked him whether he had been any while dead.' Crucifixion typically killed slowly over days by exhaustion and asphyxiation; Jesus was on the cross roughly six hours. Pilate only released the body once the centurion confirmed the death. The darkness (Matthew 27:45) and Joseph's Sanhedrin membership were real but not the marvel Mark records here.

question: Joseph the councillor did not carry the body of Jesus to a common grave. Matthew says he laid it in a new tomb of his own, one he had just had cut for himself out of solid rock, and then set something heavy across the entrance to seal it. What did he put at the door?
context: Matthew 27:60 KJV: 'And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed.' Rock-cut tombs sealed by a disc-shaped rolling stone are archaeologically documented in first-century Judea -- the stone sat in a channel and had to be pushed. The Sunday-morning women worry aloud on the way there about who can roll it back for them (Mark 16:3).

question: A small group of women set out for Jesus's tomb before dawn on the Sunday after the crucifixion, carrying spices to finish anointing his body properly. The Friday burial had been rushed, and no one had been allowed to work on the body during the sabbath. Mark names three of the women. Which group is it?
answer: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome
choices: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome
Mary the mother of Jesus, Martha, and Joanna
Mary of Bethany, Susanna, and Elizabeth
Mary the wife of Cleopas, Anna, and Rhoda
context: Mark 16:1 KJV. The four gospels give slightly different lists: Matthew has Mary Magdalene and 'the other Mary'; Luke adds Joanna; John names only Mary Magdalene. Mark's Salome here is a different woman from Herodias's daughter -- 'Salome' was a common name. Mary of Bethany (Martha and Lazarus's sister) is a different Mary; the 'daughters of Jerusalem' are the women Jesus addressed on the way to the cross (Luke 23:28).

question: Several women walked toward the tomb of Jesus before sunrise, carrying spices to anoint his body. As they went in the half-dark, they kept discussing one practical worry aloud among themselves, about the door of the tomb. Mark records their exact question. What did they keep asking each other?
answer: Who shall roll us away the stone
choices: Who shall roll us away the stone
Who will lend us fresh oil
Who will open the outer gate
Who will speak for us to the guards
context: Mark 16:3 KJV: 'And they said among themselves, Who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulchre?' The three women were carrying spices alone, with no man to help them, and the great stone Joseph had rolled across the door was far too heavy for them to shift. The next verse resolves it in the driest way possible -- 'And when they looked, they saw that the stone was rolled away: for it was very great.' It is one of the small human touches Mark is famous for.

question: In Matthew alone, an angel of God came down, rolled back the stone at the tomb and sat on top of it, as if to make a point. Matthew described him in two vivid images. His raiment was white as snow. What was his face like?
context: Matthew 28:2-3 KJV: 'the angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled back the stone from the door, and sat upon it. His countenance was like lightning, and his raiment white as snow.' Note the almost cheeky detail -- he SITS on the very stone that had sealed the tomb. The other images are real biblical descriptions of divine or angelic beings elsewhere: 'his feet like unto fine brass' (Revelation 1:15), 'the morning star' (Revelation 22:16), the sun-face of the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:2).

question: In the Gospel of John, Mary Magdalene stayed behind at the tomb weeping after the others had left. She turned and saw a man she took for the gardener, and she asked where the body had been carried. He answered with a single word, her own name, and she knew him. She cried out one Aramaic word back. What word did she say?
context: John 20:16 KJV: 'Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.' Rabboni is a heightened form of 'rabbi' -- 'my teacher.' The other choices are all real Aramaic words the New Testament preserves untranslated: Maranatha ('Our Lord, come,' 1 Corinthians 16:22), Hosanna ('save us,' from Palm Sunday), and Abba ('Father,' Mark 14:36). Jesus then tells her not to hold on to him but to go tell the others.

question: Jacob sends ten of his sons down to Egypt to buy grain when famine reaches Canaan, and they bow with their faces to the earth before the vizier. He knows them at once, but they have not seen him for more than twenty years and do not know him. Who is the vizier?
context: Genesis 42:6-8 KJV. Joseph was seventeen when the brothers sold him to the Ishmeelites; he is now about thirty-seven, second only to Pharaoh in Egypt. He recognises them; they do not recognise him.

question: The governor makes himself a stranger to the ten brothers and speaks roughly to them through an interpreter. He accuses them of a crime that would carry a death sentence in Pharaoh's court and demand a search of their story from top to bottom. What does he accuse them of being?
context: Genesis 42:9 KJV: 'Ye are spies; to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.' Border-crossing foreigners in a time of famine were the classic suspects; the charge lets Joseph hold them without seeming cruel.

question: Joseph tells the brothers he will hold one of them in prison in Egypt while the others fetch their youngest brother Benjamin down from Canaan. He binds one man before their eyes and keeps him behind. Which brother does he choose to hold as the hostage?
context: Genesis 42:24 KJV. Simeon is the second son of Leah. Some Jewish commentators (Rashi) note Reuben tried to save Joseph at the pit, so Joseph passed over him and chose the next brother in line.

question: The brothers murmur among themselves in Hebrew before the vizier of Egypt, not knowing he understands every word. He sits behind a table and speaks to them only through an interpreter, to hide who he is, and he has just accused them and demanded that their youngest brother be brought down. What are they saying to each other?
answer: That God has finally punished them for selling their brother into slavery
choices: That God has finally punished them for selling their brother into slavery
That the governor's harshness is a sign Simeon will die in prison
That Reuben was right to warn them not to harm the boy at the pit
That their father Jacob's grief has followed them all the way to Egypt
context: Genesis 42:21-23 KJV: 'We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear.' Joseph turns aside and weeps when he hears it.

question: The brothers come back with Benjamin, and Joseph invites all eleven of them to a feast at his own house. As they sit down, they look at one another and marvel: without a word spoken to any Egyptian, the seating has been arranged in a way that no Egyptian steward could have guessed. What order are they seated in?
answer: The exact order of their birth, from oldest to youngest
choices: The exact order of their birth, from oldest to youngest
The order of their mothers, Leah's sons first
By height, tallest at the head of the table
Alphabetical by name in the Egyptian tongue
context: Genesis 43:33 KJV: 'And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth: and the men marvelled one at another.' The seating is a private signal: only a brother could know it.

question: Joseph sends portions of food from his own table to each of his brothers at a feast in his house, still hiding who he is. To one of them he sends a portion far larger than the others, so large that no one at the table can miss the favour. Which brother, and how much more?
context: Genesis 43:34 KJV. Benjamin is Joseph's only full brother, Rachel's other son. Joseph is watching the ten half-brothers to see if the old jealousy over a father's favourite will flare up again.

question: Judah has stepped forward and begged to be made a slave in Benjamin's place, telling the vizier of an old father whose life is bound up in the lad's life. The vizier can hold in no longer. He orders every Egyptian sent out of the room, weeps aloud so the whole house hears him, and speaks. What are the first words he says to his brothers?
answer: I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?
choices: I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?
Come near to me, I pray you.
God did send me before you to preserve life.
Fear not: for am I in the place of God?
context: Genesis 45:1-3 KJV. His brothers cannot answer him, for they were troubled at his presence. The other three choices are real lines Joseph speaks moments later (Gen 45:4, 45:5) or after Jacob's death (Gen 50:19), but this is the first sentence out of his mouth. Later he tells them, 'Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good' (Genesis 50:20).

question: Jacob gives his son Joseph a gift to mark him as the favorite, the son of his old age, born to his wife Rachel. The gift is so striking that Joseph's ten older brothers cannot speak kindly to him. What does Jacob give him?
context: Genesis 37:3-4 KJV. The Hebrew is disputed (some read 'a long coat with sleeves'), but the KJV 'coat of many colours' is the phrase that stuck in Western imagination. It is the visible token of the favoured son.

question: Joseph tells his brothers a dream. They are all binding sheaves of grain in the field when suddenly his sheaf stands upright, and their sheaves gather round about it and bow down to it. He tells them a second dream in which the sun and moon and eleven stars also bow to him. When they see him coming, what do the brothers mutter to one another?
choices: Behold, the boy of the fine coat
context: Genesis 37:19 KJV. Immediately after they say it, they plan to kill him and cast him into a pit and say some evil beast has devoured him, and then, they say, 'we shall see what will become of his dreams.'

question: The brothers reach Dothan, strip Joseph of his coat, and throw him into a pit with no water in it. As they sit down to eat bread, a caravan comes along the road below, its camels loaded with spicery, balm, and myrrh going down into Egypt. To whom does the caravan belong?
context: Genesis 37:25 KJV. The Ishmeelites are descended from Ishmael, Abraham's other son; their spice-trade route runs from Gilead down through Canaan into Egypt. The detail is almost cinematic: the smell of balm and myrrh drifting past a pit.

question: Judah speaks up as the spice-caravan passes by on the road down to Egypt. Killing their brother, he says, will not profit them; concealing his blood will only weigh on them. He proposes selling Joseph to the traders instead. For how many pieces of silver do they sell him?
context: Genesis 37:28 KJV. The wrong choice 'thirty' is the Judas price for Jesus in Matthew 26:15; different sale, different number. Twenty shekels was roughly the going market price for a young male slave in that era, according to Levitical valuation tables.

question: The brothers kill a kid of the goats and dip Joseph's coat in its blood, now that they must explain the missing boy to their father. They send the bloodied coat to Jacob with a short, cold message that will not even name his son. What do they tell him?
answer: Know now whether it be thy son's coat or no
choices: Know now whether it be thy son's coat or no
See now if this be the coat of the son thou lovedst
Come and see the beast that hath devoured thy son
Take up thy staff and search the hills for his body
context: Genesis 37:32 KJV. It is a cold sentence: they will not even name Joseph. Jacob knows the coat at once, rends his clothes, puts sackcloth on his loins, and mourns for his son many days. It is the first false evidence in the Hebrew Bible.

question: Potiphar, the captain of Pharaoh's palace guard, buys the young Hebrew Joseph in Egypt and sets him over the whole household. Then Potiphar's wife tries to seize Joseph, and he flees from her. She keeps one thing in her hand to use as false evidence against him with her husband. What does she keep in her hand?
context: Genesis 39:11-18 KJV. Once again a garment of Joseph's is used as false proof against him: the coat to his father, now the garment to Potiphar. He is thrown into the prison where the king's prisoners are bound, and there Pharaoh's officers will one day be sent.

question: In the prison Joseph interprets the dreams of two of Pharaoh's officers who have offended their king. To one he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up thy head and restore thee to thy office. To the other he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up thy head and hang thee on a tree. Which two officers are they?
answer: The chief butler and the chief baker
choices: The chief butler and the chief baker
The chief steward and the chief herald
The chief scribe and the chief physician
The chief cupbearer and the chief taster
context: Genesis 40:9-22 KJV. The butler is restored on Pharaoh's birthday and forgets Joseph for two full years, until Pharaoh dreams of the cows and the corn and needs a dream-reader. The baker's hanging is the tell that Joseph reads dreams true.

question: Moses climbed Mount Nebo after forty years of leading Israel, looked out at the promised land he was not allowed to enter, and died there. One of his lieutenants took his place, led Israel across the Jordan River on dry ground, and prepared to attack the walled city of Jericho. Who was he?
context: Joshua son of Nun succeeded Moses and led the crossing at the Jordan and the siege of Jericho (Joshua 1-6, KJV).

question: Rahab, a Canaanite woman of Jericho, hid Joshua's two spies on her flat mud roof, in a house built into the city wall itself. She had already spread a certain crop up there in orderly rows to dry in the hot sun, and she laid the two men down beneath it. What crop covered them?
context: Joshua 2:6 (KJV): 'she had brought them up to the roof of the house, and hid them with the stalks of flax, which she had laid in order upon the roof.'

question: Joshua's two Israelite spies went down a rope from Rahab's window, her house being built right into the wall of Jericho. Before they left, they gave her a promise: tie one visible mark in that same window, and when Israel took the city only her house would be spared. What was the mark?
context: Joshua 2:18 (KJV): 'thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by.' Blue, purple, and scarlet are all real Tabernacle colors -- only scarlet is the sparing-mark.

question: Joshua looked up near the walls of Jericho, just before the great battle, and saw a man standing before him with a drawn sword in his hand. He walked right up to the stranger and asked, 'Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?' The stranger refused both sides, for he had not come to belong to either army. Who did the stranger say he was?
answer: captain of the host of the Lord
choices: captain of the host of the Lord
prince of the tribe of Judah
watchman of the walls of Jericho
elder of the men of Gibeon
context: Joshua 5:14 (KJV): 'Nay; but as captain of the host of the Lord am I now come.' Joshua fell on his face; the captain told him to loose his shoe from off his foot.

question: Joshua marched the army of Israel around the walled city of Jericho in silence, on a strange plan God had given him. Seven priests went ahead of the ark of the covenant, each one blowing a trumpet. What were those trumpets made of?
context: Joshua 6:4 (KJV): 'seven priests shall bear before the ark seven trumpets of rams' horns.' Numbers 10:2 describes a different pair of trumpets, of solid silver, for calling the assembly -- not these.

question: The army of Israel besieged the walled Canaanite city of Jericho under Joshua's command, in a way no army had ever tried. For six straight days it marched once around the city, priests in front carrying the ark. On the last day the men rose early and circled the city many more times before the trumpets blew and the walls came down. How many times around did they go that day?
context: Joshua 6:15-16 (KJV): 'on the seventh day... they compassed the city after the same manner seven times.' Then the priests blew, the people shouted, and the wall fell down flat (6:20). Three days marks Jonah in the fish and the resurrection; twelve is the tribes and the apostles; forty is the wilderness years and Jesus's fast.

question: Jesus of Nazareth chose twelve close followers to walk with him through Galilee and Judea, and one of them was Judas Iscariot. The gospels remember Judas above all for betraying Jesus for silver, but before that he had one everyday job for the little travelling band. What did he carry for them on the road?
context: John 12:6 and 13:29 say Judas 'had the bag' -- he kept the disciples' shared purse. John's gospel then adds a sharp aside: 'this he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag'.

question: A woman named Mary poured a jar of costly perfume over Jesus's feet and wiped them with her hair, at a dinner in the village of Bethany. One of the twelve disciples spoke up loudly at the table and said the perfume should have been sold and the money given to the poor. Which disciple was it?
context: John 12:3-6. John's narrator adds that Judas said this 'not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag'.

question: Judas Iscariot went in secret to the chief priests, soon after Mary had poured her costly perfume on Jesus's feet at Bethany. He offered to hand Jesus over at a quiet moment when no crowd would be watching. Matthew's gospel names the exact price the priests weighed out to him. How much silver did they agree on?
context: Matthew 26:14-15. Thirty pieces of silver was also the compensation set in Exodus 21:32 for a slave killed by an ox -- a bitterly pointed sum.

question: Judas Iscariot walked into the olive grove of Gethsemane late one night, leading a mob with torches and swords, while Jesus was praying with his disciples. He had given the guards a pre-arranged signal so that in the flickering torchlight they would know which man to seize. What sign did Judas use to point Jesus out?
context: Matthew 26:48-49: 'Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast. And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him.' Jesus answered, 'Friend, wherefore art thou come?'

question: Matthew echoed an older Jewish law when he wrote down the silver paid to Judas Iscariot for betraying Jesus. Exodus, in the covenant given at Mount Sinai, set the same sum as the exact compensation for one very particular kind of loss. What did Exodus value at that sum?
answer: A slave killed by an ox
choices: A slave killed by an ox
A field of barley in harvest
context: Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels of silver as the payment an ox's owner must give if the ox gores a slave to death. Matthew echoes the price to underline what Jesus was being sold for.

question: In Matthew's gospel, Judas Iscariot rushed back into the Temple once he saw that Jesus had been condemned to die, seized with remorse. He flung the silver down on the floor, went out and killed himself. How did Judas take his own life in Matthew's account?
choices: He fell on his own sword
He threw himself from the Temple wall
He drank poison in the courtyard
context: Matthew 27:3-5: 'and cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.' Matthew's ending is one of two very different accounts of the death of Judas in the New Testament.

question: In the book of Acts, Judas Iscariot bought a field with the reward of his treachery, and there something gruesome happened to his body. Acts tells his end in a very different way from Matthew. According to Acts, what happened to Judas in that field?
answer: He fell headlong and his body burst open
choices: He fell headlong and his body burst open
He was struck dead by lightning at the gate
He was stoned by a crowd of pilgrims
He wandered into the desert and starved
context: Acts 1:18 (KJV): 'and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.' Both accounts sit in the New Testament side by side -- Matthew has the hanging in the Temple, Acts has the falling in the field; the church has never smoothed them into a single story without inventing extra detail.

question: The chief priests picked up the coins after Judas hurled the silver back at them and ran out, in Matthew's account, and they at once faced a problem. Their own Temple law said the silver was blood money that could not be returned to the treasury chests. What did they decide to do with it instead?
answer: They bought a potter's field as a graveyard for foreigners
choices: They bought a potter's field as a graveyard for foreigners
They sent it as tribute to the Roman governor
They gave it to the widows of the city
They melted it into a lampstand for the sanctuary
context: Matthew 27:6-8: 'It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in.'

question: Judas Iscariot took silver for handing Jesus over, and that silver bought a plot of ground just outside Jerusalem. Matthew and Acts disagree on who bought it, but the ground picked up the same grim Aramaic nickname among the people of Jerusalem in both. By what name did it become known?
context: Acts 1:19: 'insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood.' Golgotha was the place of Jesus's execution; Gehenna was the burning refuse valley south of the city; Bethesda was the pool of the healing at the sheep gate.

question: Matthew paused over the priests' purchase with the silver to say it echoed the words of a prophet, and he quoted a line about silver coins cast to the potter. He named Jeremiah at the head of the quotation. Which prophet's book actually holds that line about the coins and the potter?
context: The line is Zechariah 11:12-13 -- 'And they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter... and I cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD.' Matthew's gospel names Jeremiah at the head of the quotation, a wording puzzle scholars still argue about.

question: A priest held up a wooden cross before the failing eyes of a woman about thirty, dying of a strange illness in an English city on the east coast in May 1373. She began to see visions that made her a famous writer. In which English city was she?
context: Norwich was then a plague-stricken port on the eastern coast, one of the largest towns in England. Canterbury, York, and Ely are all real English cathedral cities, but the visionary of May 1373 was in Norwich -- and she takes her name from a church there.

question: An Englishwoman saw vivid visions of Jesus on the cross while close to death, recovered, and went to live as an anchoress, walled into a small cell for prayer. Her birth name has been lost. Readers call her Julian, but that was not her name at birth. Where does the name come from?
answer: the parish church her later cell was built against
choices: the parish church her later cell was built against
the ship her father sailed on out of Norwich harbour
the older nun who taught her at a Norwich priory
the pen name she signed at the end of her book
context: The parish church of St Julian, Conisford, in Norwich gave her the name Julian; her birth name is genuinely lost. She never gave herself a pen name; no father-and-ship story is recorded; no priory teacher is named in her Long Text.

question: Julian looked at the palm of her hand in one of her visions and saw a small round object lying there. It was so tiny she marvelled why it did not fall to nothing, and she understood that it was 'all that is made.' What did she say the little round thing was the size of?
context: 'A little thing, the quantity of an hazelnut, lying in the palm of my hand, as it seemed, and it was as round as any ball' (Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 5). The mustard seed and the pearl of great price come from Jesus's parables in the Gospels; the poppy pod is not a scripture image.

question: Julian saw a whole sequence of visions between about four and nine one morning in May 1373, she says: Christ's suffering in vivid physical detail, the mother of Jesus and more. She called each one a 'shewing.' Exactly how many shewings does her Long Text say she received that morning?
context: Sixteen shewings between roughly four and nine in the morning, according to the opening of Julian's Long Text; she spent the next twenty years working out what she thought they meant. The other numbers are famous elsewhere (seven sacraments, twelve apostles, forty days in the wilderness).

question: The anchoress Julian finished the longer version of her book about twenty years after her visions of Christ, working out at last what she had seen. It is known as the Long Text, or Revelations of Divine Love. What distinction does that book hold in the history of English writing?
answer: the earliest surviving book in English by a woman
choices: the earliest surviving book in English by a woman
the earliest English translation of the Bible
the earliest printed book in England
the earliest hymnal used in an English cathedral
context: Julian's Long Text (c. 1393) is the earliest book in the English language whose named woman author is known. The first printed book in England was William Caxton's, more than eighty years later; the earliest full English Bible translation was Wycliffe's, at about the same time as Julian; hymnal history goes back centuries earlier.

question: Julian asked about sin and suffering, and she records Christ's reply in chapter 27 of her Long Text. It was a promise stated three times in a single breath, not once, and it would become perhaps the most quoted line in all English mysticism. What was the exact threefold form?
answer: All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well
choices: All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well
Blessed be the name, and blessed be the name, and blessed be his holy name
Peace, peace be with you, peace be with you always, peace be with you now
Fear not, and fear not still, and fear no more the doom that comes
context: The threefold repetition is the whole point -- kids often shorten it to one 'all shall be well' and miss the drumbeat. The other threefold forms are pastiche; Julian's line comes from Revelations of Divine Love ch. 27, given as Christ's answer about sin.

question: A much louder, tearful, wandering visionary sat down at Julian's window around 1413 and asked whether her own noisy sobbing fits were really from God. Julian told her they were. The visitor went home and wrote the days at the window into what is now considered the first autobiography of its kind. Who was the visitor?
context: The Book of Margery Kempe records the days Margery of Bishop's Lynn sat with Julian at the anchorage window in Norwich; it is the first surviving autobiography in English. Bridget of Sweden died in 1373, the year of Julian's visions; Catherine of Siena died in 1380; Hildegard of Bingen died in 1179 -- all real medieval visionaries but far too early for a 1413 visit.

question: T. S. Eliot was finishing his greatest sequence of poems, the Four Quartets, in 1942, as German bombs were falling on England. He closed the fourth and last of them by quoting Julian's threefold promise, ending with an image of a rose and a flame folded together. Which of the Four Quartets is that poem?
context: 'And all shall be well and / All manner of thing shall be well / When the tongues of flame are in-folded / Into the crowned knot of fire / And the fire and the rose are one.' Little Gidding, published September 1942, closes the sequence; the other three Quartets are titled after other English and American places Eliot cared about.

question: Merlin gave the baby Arthur to a country knight to raise in secret, and one of the knight's own sons grew up alongside him. The two boys believed they were true brothers, and Arthur did not know he was the son of King Uther Pendragon. What was the foster-brother's name?
context: Sir Kay (Welsh Cei, French Ke) is the son of Sir Ector, in whose house Merlin had hidden the infant Arthur. Lancelot is fostered by the Lady of the Lake, not Arthur; Gawain is Arthur's blood nephew, not foster-brother; Bedivere is another Round Table knight but not the foster-brother.  (Legend.)

question: Young Arthur rode with Sir Kay to a New Year's tournament near London, on the day the sword was pulled from the stone in Malory's telling. Kay's father rode with them, the knight who had raised Arthur in secret since he was a baby. What was the father's name?
context: Merlin gave the infant Arthur to Sir Ector to raise, so no one would know he was Uther's son. Sir Bors is one of the Grail knights; Sir Uwain is Morgan le Fay's son; Sir Kynon is a companion of Owain in the Welsh tradition.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Kay realised on the road to a New Year tournament outside London that he had left a crucial piece of tournament gear back at the inn, in Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur. He sent his squire, young Arthur, back to fetch it. What had Kay left behind?
context: Arthur rode back, found the inn locked, saw a blade standing in the stone in a nearby churchyard, and pulled it out to bring to Kay. A knight might arrive at a tournament without a spare shield or helm and borrow; a blade was harder to borrow at short notice.  (Legend.)

question: Kay saw what young Arthur had carried back to the tournament: the sword from the stone in the churchyard. He understood what it meant, and for a moment he said he had drawn it himself. Then one man put him on his oath over a holy book, asked how the sword came into his hands, and heard him confess. Who forced the truth out of Kay?
context: Malory Book I. Ector had Kay lay hand on holy relics and swear how he had come by the sword; Kay confessed, and Ector then had Arthur put the sword back in the stone and pull it out again in front of him. Merlin arranged the sword-test but was not present at this exact moment; the Archbishop presided at the churchyard trials that followed; the Lady of the Lake gives Excalibur later, a different sword.  (Legend.)

question: A mysterious young man came to Arthur's court in Malory's Round Table stories, asking only to be fed and lodged for a year and refusing to give his name. Sir Kay mocked him with the scornful nickname Beaumains, 'Fair Hands,' and put him to work in the kitchen for a whole year. Then the young man rode out on quest and proved himself. Who was he?
context: Malory Book VII. Kay named the disguised Gareth 'Beaumains' ('Fair-Hands') and set him scrubbing pots for a year. In Chretien de Troyes Kay also mocks the young Perceval when he first arrives at court, but Percival is not the knight Kay puts in the kitchen for a year in Malory; Bors and Tristan arrive at court fully known as noble.  (Legend.)

question: In the old Welsh tale Culhwch and Olwen, written down around 1100, Cei could hold his breath underwater for a striking stretch of time. Cei was Sir Kay under his earlier Welsh name, not yet Malory's sharp-tongued seneschal but a magical warrior with strange powers. How long could he hold it?
context: Culhwch and Olwen names several magical powers Cei has: nine days without breath, nine days without sleep, and the ability to grow as tall as the tallest tree in the forest. Nine is a number of mythic completion in the Welsh tradition (as in the Nine Witches of Gloucester).  (Legend.)

question: King Arthur stood with two chief companions in the earliest Welsh tales, old poems and stories like Culhwch and Olwen, written down long before Chretien de Troyes and the French romances. Lancelot did not yet exist in this older Welsh layer. Cei, the earlier Sir Kay, was one of the two. Who was the other?
context: Bedwyr (later Bedivere in French and English) is Kay's constant companion in Culhwch and Olwen and other early Welsh tales; the pair are Arthur's inner circle. Owain (later Yvain), Peredur (later Perceval), and Geraint all belong to the Welsh corpus of Arthurian heroes but are protagonists of their own separate tales, not Arthur's paired inner companions.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri tells how the Aesir, Odin's warrior clan, and the Vanir, the fertility gods, ended a long war around one great vat. Every one of the gods, Aesir and Vanir alike, did one shared thing into it to seal the truce. What did every god do into that vat?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: the Aesir and Vanir sealed their peace by all spitting together into a vat. From that spittle grew the wise-man Kvasir. The oath-ring belongs to Icelandic Thing-law, not to this scene; blood-oaths and wine belong to other traditions.  (Legend.)

question: A full-grown man stood up out of the vat where the Aesir and Vanir had sealed their peace. He was said to be the wisest being that had ever lived, and no question could be put to him that he could not answer. What was his name?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: from the peace-vat spittle grew Kvasir, wisest of all beings. Mimir is the guardian of the well of wisdom whose severed head Odin keeps to counsel him. Bragi is the god of poetry. Heimdall is the watchman of Bifrost.  (Legend.)

question: Two dwarves welcomed a wandering wise man into their hall as a guest, after he had walked the nine worlds answering every question put to him. There they killed him. What were the names of the two dwarves who murdered him?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: Fjalar and Galar invited Kvasir to their hall and killed him. Sindri and Brokkr are the dwarf-brothers who forged Mjolnir. Nordri and Sudri (with Austri and Vestri) hold up the four corners of the sky. Alviss is the all-wise dwarf trapped by Thor at daybreak; Andvari owns the cursed ring of the Volsung cycle.  (Legend.)

question: The two dwarves who murdered the wise man drained his blood into two vats and a kettle, in Snorri's Prose Edda. Then they mixed it with one common hall ingredient and brewed a drink so strong that one taste made a man a poet and a sage. What did the dwarves mix the blood with?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: the dwarves drained the blood into two vats (Son and Bodn) and a kettle (Odrerir), mixed it with honey, and brewed a mead. Mead is the honey-fermented drink of the Norse hall; ale was made from grain. The dwarves later told the Aesir that Kvasir had 'choked on his own wisdom' because no one was clever enough to ask him a question.  (Legend.)

question: Suttung, a giant's son, seized the two dwarves who had drowned his father and stranded them on a rock in the tide, where the rising water would drown them in turn. The dwarves bought their lives by handing him one thing. What did they give him in ransom for their lives?
answer: the Mead brewed from Kvasir's blood
choices: the Mead brewed from Kvasir's blood
the millstone they had killed his mother with
a chest of gold rings from the workshop
the drill they used to bore into stone
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: the giant Suttung stranded Fjalar and Galar on a tidal skerry, and they bought back their lives with the Mead. He took it home to his mountain and set his own daughter to guard it -- and that is how the drink passed from dwarves into the hands of the giants.  (Legend.)

question: The giant Suttung carried the Mead of Poetry home from the dwarves who had brewed it, a drink that gave wisdom and the gift of verse to anyone who tasted it. He hid it deep inside his mountain, Hnitbjorg, and set one guardian to watch it in an inner chamber. Who did Suttung set to guard the Mead?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: Suttung hid the Mead in the mountain Hnitbjorg and set his daughter Gunnlod to guard it. Baugi is Suttung's brother, whom Odin will use as his way in. Angrboda is Loki's giantess-lover (mother of Fenrir, Jormungand, and Hel) -- not Suttung's wife. Gilling is Suttung's own already-dead father.  (Legend.)

question: Odin set out to steal the Mead disguised as a farm-labourer. He came to the fields of Suttung's brother and made himself so useful that nine slaves working there died in a quarrel over a single thing he had brought with him. What did Odin bring that made the nine slaves kill each other in a scramble for it?
choices: a silver ring he had promised
a helmet he had worn in war
a spear he had brought from Asgard
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: Odin, calling himself Bolverk, arrived at Baugi's farm and outworked nine slaves, then offered to sharpen their scythes with a whetstone. When they saw how well it worked they all lunged for the stone at once; Odin threw it in the air and the nine cut each other's throats. This is how he manoeuvred Baugi into needing him.  (Legend.)

question: Baugi, the brother of the giant Suttung, bored a hole through the rock with a drill called Rati, because the mountain that held the Mead had no door in it. Odin then had to slip through the drilled hole himself. What shape did Odin take to pass into the mountain?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: Odin turned himself into a snake and slithered through the hole Baugi had bored with the drill Rati. Baugi stabbed after him with the drill but missed. Inside the mountain Odin found Gunnlod alone.  (Legend.)

question: Odin slipped into the giant Suttung's mountain, Hnitbjorg, to steal the Mead of Poetry, and he courted the guard who kept three vessels of it inside. He spent three nights with her, and each night she granted him one sip from the vessels. In three sips what exactly did he drink?
answer: all three vessels dry to the bottom
choices: all three vessels dry to the bottom
one third of the smallest kettle
the surface layer of each vessel
half of the largest vat only
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: Gunnlod gave Odin one sip each of the three nights; in three sips he drained all three vessels (Son, Bodn, and Odrerir) to the last drop. Havamal 104-110 tells the same theft from Odin's own voice, and calls the sips the greatest bargain a woman ever gave.  (Legend.)

question: Odin fled the mountain and raced for Asgard with every drop of the Mead swallowed and held inside him. Suttung woke, saw him going, and pursued in the same shape Odin himself had taken for the escape. What shape did both Odin and Suttung take for the chase across the sky?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: both took eagle-shape for the pursuit. The Aesir on the walls saw Odin coming and put out great vats; he spat the Mead into them as he crossed. Suttung the eagle arrived just after, and the Aesir lit a fire on the wall that burned him to death. The story is carved on the Stora Hammars III picture-stone on Gotland from around 700 CE.  (Legend.)

question: Odin raced for the gods' waiting vats with the Mead of Poetry held inside him and the giant Suttung on his tail. He lost a small portion of it the wrong way, not from his beak into the vats but out of his back end across the middle world. The Norse gave that spilled portion a name. What was the spilled Mead said to be?
answer: the share of the bad poets
choices: the share of the bad poets
the drink of the fallen valkyries
the tears of the giant's daughter
the wine of the buried kings
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: what Odin lost out his rear end is called 'the share of the bad poets' and belongs to any hack-versifier who can pick it up. The good stuff Odin spat into the vats belongs to Asgard and to the true skalds. That is why 'Kvasir's blood' remains the standard kenning for poetry itself.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus of Mycenae sent Heracles, the hero the Romans called Hercules, to the valley around Nemea, where a dangerous beast was killing farmers and their flocks. It was the first of his twelve labors. What kind of animal was the beast of Nemea?
context: The Nemean Lion was the first of the twelve labors (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.1). The Erymanthian Boar, the Ceryneian Hind (golden-horned stag), and the Lernaean Hydra are later labors, all real Heracles monsters.  (Legend.)

question: A monstrous beast near the town of Nemea turned back every hunter in Greece before he ever saw it. Its coat shone like polished bronze in the sun, and it was known for one scary trait. What was that trait?
answer: No mortal weapon could pierce it
choices: No mortal weapon could pierce it
It shed its skin like a snake each dawn
It caught fire when touched by iron
context: The lion's golden pelt turned aside bronze, iron and stone; even arrows glanced off. Its own claws were sharper than any mortal sword. This is what made the labor an execution, not a hunt.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles tracked the beast of Nemea through the hills to a rocky den, and he found that the den opened at two ends. Before he crawled in after it, he stopped to do one thing. What did he do?
answer: He blocked up one of the den's mouths with heavy boulders
choices: He blocked up one of the den's mouths with heavy boulders
He wedged burning brands in a ring around the mouth
He drove a javelin up under its foreleg
He waited three days for the beast to starve out
context: The den had two openings; with one sealed, the lion could not slip out the back while Heracles came in the front. He then went in unarmed to face it up close.  (Legend.)

question: The golden-coated beast turned to fight Heracles deep in a two-mouthed cave in the hills above Nemea. His bronze arrows bounced off its hide, and his sword-edge slid across the fur as if off polished stone. He laid both aside and killed it a very different way. How did he kill it?
answer: He wrestled it and choked it to death with his bare arms
choices: He wrestled it and choked it to death with his bare arms
He rolled a heavy boulder down onto its skull
He drove a javelin up under its foreleg
He blinded it with a torch and let it starve
context: Heracles wrestled the lion in the dark of its own den and strangled it to death by main strength (Apollodorus 2.5.1). This is why his cult image shows him always with a lion-skin and empty hands.  (Legend.)

question: Athena, his patron goddess, watched Heracles struggle over the dead beast of Nemea. No blade of his would cut the hide he needed to carry back to King Eurystheus. She gave him one piece of advice that solved it. What did she tell him to use?
answer: One of the lion's own claws
choices: One of the lion's own claws
A shard of stone from the cave wall
A tooth from the lion's jaw
A shaft of sunlight through the cave mouth
context: The claws were the only things sharp enough to slice the invulnerable pelt. Athena is Heracles's constant patron; she appears again in the twelfth labor guiding him into Hades.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles cut the hide free at last and kept it. Through the rest of the twelve labors, every vase-painter and marble-carver who showed him gave him that pelt, always in one particular way. How did they show him carrying it?
answer: As a cloak, with the head pulled up over his own as a hood
choices: As a cloak, with the head pulled up over his own as a hood
As a shield strapped across his left arm at the elbow
As a banner tied to the shaft of his olive-wood club
As a wide belt bound around his waist with a knot
context: The lion-head hood is Heracles's signature; combined with his olive-wood club, it is how the ancient world recognized him in art. The pelt was arrow-proof and sword-proof and served as his armor through every later labor.  (Legend.)

question: Hera drove Heracles mad before any of the labors began, and in that madness he killed the people of his own household. He sought cleansing at Delphi, and the Pythia ordered him to serve King Eurystheus for ten years. Whom had he killed?
answer: His wife Megara and their children
choices: His wife Megara and their children
His teacher Linus and his father Amphitryon
context: After the killing, Heracles went to the Pythia at Delphi for cleansing. The oracle told him to serve Eurystheus of Mycenae for ten years and perform whatever labors the king set. Linus (his music tutor) he had killed years earlier in a separate incident, not in the madness.  (Legend.)

question: One strange tradition, preserved in scattered fragments, says Hera arranged for a certain goddess to hurl the great beast of Nemea down out of her own realm onto Greek soil. Hesiod and Apollodorus gave the beast other parents entirely. Which goddess did Hera ask?
context: In this variant, Selene the moon-goddess threw the lion from the moon at Hera's request. Other traditions (Hesiod) make the lion a child of the two-headed hound Orthrus; Apollodorus makes it a child of Typhon. Iris is Hera's rainbow messenger; Hebe is her cupbearer; Nyx is Night herself.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles hauled the carcass of the beast of Nemea into Mycenae and dumped it in the courtyard, and King Eurystheus, terrified, hid inside a great bronze storage jar. He refused ever to face the hero in person again and set up a go-between to shout each new labor down from the palace walls. Ancient sources name this herald. Who was he?
context: Copreus, a son of Pelops in exile at Eurystheus's court, delivered the labors from labor two onward. Iolaus is Heracles's nephew and chariot-driver; Hylas is his young companion on the Argo; Telamon is his comrade at Troy's first sack. All three fight alongside him, but the shouted-messages herald is Copreus.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus ordered Heracles past the western ocean for his tenth labor, out to an island called Erytheia, to drive home a famous herd of cattle. Who owned that herd at the world's western edge?
context: Geryon, king of the red island of Erytheia -- a giant with three bodies joined at the waist, three shields, and three spears. Antaeus is the giant Heracles wrestles in Libya on a later trip; Cacus is the Italian cattle-thief we meet at the end of this same labor. (Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles found a herd unlike any in Greece on the western island of Erytheia. Herds at home were dun or brown, but every ox here was one striking color, and the island's own name comes from it: 'the ___ land.' What color was the herd?
context: The setting sun over the western ocean, the storytellers said, dyed the cattle's coats red -- and the island's name Erytheia comes from the same root as the Greek word for red. (Apollodorus 2.5.10; Hesiod, Theogony 287-294.)  (Legend.)

question: The hero of the twelve labors walked west along North Africa to the strait between Africa and Spain, on his way to the edge of the world. One peak in Morocco and one in Spain still bear a matching name from Greek myth. What are the two peaks called?
context: The northern pillar is the Rock of Gibraltar; the southern is Jebel Musa in Morocco. In some versions the hero split a single mountain in two to open the strait, letting the Atlantic into the Mediterranean. (Apollodorus 2.5.10; Britannica, 'Pillars of Heracles'.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles stopped in the North African desert on his way west, with the sun beating down so cruelly that he could not walk another step. He drew his bow and pointed the arrow straight at the sun-god himself. The god, more amused than angry, made him a loan. What did he lend Heracles for the last leg of the trip?
answer: A golden cup to sail in
choices: A golden cup to sail in
A chariot pulled by winged horses
A cloak that turned aside heat
A crown that lit its own path
context: The golden cup of Helios is the vessel the sun himself sails from west to east every night while he sleeps. Heracles sailed it out to Erytheia, then loaded the cattle into it and sailed home. (Athenaeus 11.469; Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles swung his olive-wood club on the island of Erytheia and dropped Orthrus, the two-headed guard dog of the herd. The same club dropped the herdsman who had watched those cattle day and night, himself a giant and the son of the Greek war-god Ares. What was the herdsman's name?
context: Eurytion the herdsman, son of Ares. (There is a separate Eurytion who is a centaur in a different story -- Greek myth is not shy about reusing names.) The olive-wood club is Heracles's signature weapon. (Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: A fire-breathing giant came out of his cave and stole some of the cattle as Heracles drove the herd back through Italy. The cave lay on one of the seven hills that would one day belong to Rome. Heracles hunted the thief down and killed him in it. What was this cattle-thief's name?
context: Cacus lived in a cave on what would become the Aventine Hill. Virgil's Aeneid Book 8 has old Evander tell the whole story to Aeneas at that very spot. (Virgil, Aeneid 8.185-275; Livy 1.7.)  (Legend.)

question: Livy wrote that the killing of a fire-breathing cattle-thief on the Aventine hill, on the future site of Rome, explains why Rome's oldest altar was said to be dedicated to Heracles. The giant had dragged some of the herd backwards by the tails into his cave, and the altar stood in the cattle-market of the Forum Boarium. What is the name of that ancient altar?
context: The Ara Maxima ('greatest altar') stood in the Forum Boarium and was in continuous use for centuries. Livy 1.7 traces its founding straight back to Heracles thanking the site of his fight with Cacus. (Livy 1.7; Virgil, Aeneid 8.)  (Legend.)

question: Hera sent a creature after the herd on the last stage of the drive back to Mycenae. It panicked the cattle and scattered them across the length of Thrace. She had once used the same creature to torment the wandering princess Io. What did Hera send?
context: The gadfly is a small biting fly whose sting sends cattle mad -- exactly the insect Hera used to torment Io as a wandering cow. A Hera-signature weapon. (Apollodorus 2.5.10; Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 566ff.)  (Legend.)

question: In Virgil's telling, a giant in a cave on the future site of Rome drove part of Heracles's herd in backwards, so the tracks led away from his lair, not toward it. Heracles had won those cattle in the far west and was driving them home. How did he find the cave anyway?
answer: A stolen cow inside the cave lowed and gave the hiding place away
choices: A stolen cow inside the cave lowed and gave the hiding place away
A river running through the cave carried out a scrap of hide
Cacus's own footprint faced the wrong way in the mud
A raven flew straight to the cave's mouth
