context: The lowing cow is the whole point of Virgil's telling in Aeneid 8: even the cleverest theft cannot silence a living animal. The rest of the herd, walking past outside, called back and forth with the ones inside. (Virgil, Aeneid 8.212-218.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles reached Mycenae at last with the herd, after his long drive from the western edge of the world. King Eurystheus, the cousin who had set him all these deadly tasks, did not keep the cattle for himself or for the city. What did Eurystheus do with the cattle?
choices: He set them free on the plain
He gave them to Heracles as reward
He drove them into the sea
context: Eurystheus was Hera's client-king throughout the whole labor cycle -- Hera made the labors happen through him. Sacrificing Geryon's cattle to Hera closes the loop: her enemy Heracles has done all the work, and her altar gets the prize. (Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles set out for the garden of the Hesperides, the 'daughters of Evening,' at the western edge of the world, on his eleventh labor. He was to steal a fruit from a tree that had been a wedding gift to a goddess. What kind of fruit was it?
context: The golden apples of the Hesperides -- a wedding gift from Gaia (the earth) to Hera when Hera married Zeus. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; Hesiod, Theogony 215-216.)  (Legend.)

question: Gaia, the earth-goddess, gave a bride a magical tree on her wedding day on Mount Olympus. It grew at the western edge of the world, and Heracles was sent for its fruit. Which goddess did the tree belong to?
context: Gaia gave the tree to Hera when Hera married Zeus. That is why the fruit can never be kept by a mortal thief -- it is Hera's, and Athena eventually returns it to the garden. (Apollodorus 2.5.11.)  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod gave the tree at the world's edge a truly terrible guard: a dragon that never slept and that had one hundred heads. Heracles would have to reach that tree for his eleventh labor. What was this dragon's name?
context: Ladon coiled around the tree and never let his eyes shut. Python was Apollo's dragon at Delphi; the Hydra was Heracles's second labor; Typhon was the world-monster Zeus fought in a much older war. (Hesiod, Theogony 333-336.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles caught an old sea-god on his way west, because he did not know how to reach the garden and the old god knew every path in the world. The prisoner turned into water, then fire, then a serpent, but Heracles held on until the old god answered. Who was this shape-shifting old man of the sea?
context: Nereus, the 'old man of the sea' and father of the sea-nymph Nereids, has the gift of prophecy and the gift of shape-changing. Proteus is a similar shape-shifter but belongs to Menelaus's story in the Odyssey, not to Heracles. (Apollodorus 2.5.11.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles came to the world's edge to bargain with a lone Titan, bent under a punishment-burden since the Titans' war, thousands of years before. This Titan was the only one nearby who could walk into the garden and pick the fruit. Which Titan was this?
context: Atlas, condemned since the Titanomachy to stand at the world's edge with the sky on his shoulders. He would prove eager to set the burden down, even briefly -- which is exactly what Heracles was counting on. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; Hesiod, Theogony 517-520.)  (Legend.)

question: The Titan at the world's edge heard a strange offer from Heracles. The hero would do the Titan's punishment-work for him, and in the meantime the Titan would go and fetch three of the fruit from the garden. What punishment-work did Heracles offer to take on?
choices: Rolling a boulder up a hill
context: Atlas jumped at the chance to be free of the sky for even a little while, gave the burden to Heracles, and walked off to the garden. That opened the trap the whole labor turns on. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; Hesiod, Theogony 517-520.)  (Legend.)

question: A goddess set the coiled stars of Draco around the north pole, Hyginus wrote in his Astronomica, as a memorial to the slain guardian of her tree at the western edge of the world. Which guardian did he say those stars commemorate?
context: Hyginus, Astronomica 2.3, identifies Draco at the pole as Ladon, put up by Hera in memory of her lost hundred-headed guardian. Python was Apollo's dragon at Delphi; Typhon was the world-monster Zeus fought; Cetus is the sea-beast Perseus killed. (Hyginus, Astronomica 2.3.)  (Legend.)

question: Back from the garden came the Titan, with the fruit in his hand and an idea of his own. He would carry it to Mycenae himself, and Heracles could just keep the punishment-burden forever. Heracles agreed cheerfully, but he asked one small favor first. What was the favor?
answer: Take the sky back while he padded his shoulders with his lion-skin
choices: Take the sky back while he padded his shoulders with his lion-skin
Take the sky back while he stretched his cramped arms a moment
Take the sky back while he shifted his footing on the stones
Take the sky back while he tied a knot in the burden's edge
context: The moment Atlas took the sky back to let Heracles adjust his lion-skin as a shoulder-pad, Heracles snatched up the apples and walked away. The whole trick works because Atlas asked for it. This is the single cleverest moment in the twelve labors. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; https://www.greekmyths-greekmythology.com/apples-of-hesperides/)  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus of Mycenae, the coward king who had set Heracles his labors, saved the worst for last. He ordered the hero down into Hades, the land of the dead, to bring back the great hound that guarded its gates. What was the hound's name?
context: The twelfth and final labor set by Eurystheus (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.12). Orthrus is Geryon's two-headed dog (also a Heracles labor); Argus is the hundred-eyed watchman of Hera; Laelaps is the hound that always caught its prey.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles walked straight into the throne-room of Hades, king of the underworld, and asked leave to take the huge three-headed hound that guarded its gates. It was his twelfth and final labor. Hades answered with a single condition. What did Hades demand?
answer: That Heracles subdue the dog using no weapons
choices: That Heracles subdue the dog using no weapons
That Heracles give up his lion-skin cloak
That Heracles first free a mortal from a chair
That Heracles swear never to return
context: Hades granted the request on the sole condition that Heracles overpower the beast with brute strength alone (Apollodorus 2.5.12). Heracles wrapped himself in his invulnerable Nemean-lion cloak for armor but kept his hands empty.  (Legend.)

question: The priest Eumolpus, near Athens, initiated Heracles into a famous secret cult before the hero went down to fetch the three-headed hound. Its rites were said to promise safe passage through the land of the dead. Which cult was it?
context: Heracles went to Eumolpus at Eleusis to be initiated before descending. The Orphic mysteries are a separate secret cult; Dodona and Delphi are oracle sites, not initiation cults for the underworld.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus and his best friend Pirithous went down into Hades with the mad idea of carrying off its queen, Persephone. Hades welcomed them politely and invited them to sit, and the moment they sat, the stone seat fused fast to their thighs. Years later Heracles came down on his own labor and wrenched at the trapped pair by main force. Who came away from the stone?
choices: Both -- Heracles took them out together
context: Pirithous was the main offender (he had wanted to abduct Persephone as his bride) and could not be moved; he stayed in Hades forever. Heracles tore Theseus free but had to leave pieces of his thighs stuck to the chair.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles walked through the dark of the underworld on his twelfth labor with two divine guides at his side, or so the Greek vase-painters showed him. In almost every painting the same pair flanked him. Which pair of Olympians walked with him?
context: Hermes Psychopompos escorts souls; Athena is Heracles's lifelong patron and had already advised him at the very first labor. The other pairs are real god-pairs but not tied to Heracles's descent.  (Legend.)

question: The three-headed hound at the gates of Hades closed its teeth on the pelt of the Nemean lion, the trophy of Heracles's very first labor. Heracles had walked up to the dog wearing only that pelt as armor. How did he take the three-headed dog?
answer: He wrapped his arms around the necks and squeezed until the beast went limp
choices: He wrapped his arms around the necks and squeezed until the beast went limp
He fed it a drugged honey-cake and put it to sleep at the third head
He blinded all three heads with the light of a burning torch
He tied all three heads together with a strong braided rope
context: Apollodorus 2.5.12: Heracles used the Nemean lion-skin as armor against Cerberus's bite and choked the dog. The drugged honey-cake belongs to the Sibyl in Virgil's Aeneid VI, a different underworld story.  (Legend.)

question: Ovid tells that as Heracles dragged the great hound up into the daylight, the beast was blinded by the sun, twisted against the grip and slavered white foam onto the Greek soil. Wherever a fleck of the drool fell, a poisonous plant is said to have sprung up. Which plant was it?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.408-419. Aconite (wolfsbane) is a real and deadly Greek mountain plant that Ovid traces to Cerberus's foam. Hemlock was famously used to execute Socrates; mandrake and nightshade have their own separate poison traditions.  (Legend.)

question: One heavily armed ghost stood his ground down in Hades when every other shade fled from Heracles. The hero recognized an old comrade. Weeping, the ghost asked one thing: that Heracles marry Deianira, the ghost's own unwed sister, on his return to the living. Who was the ghost?
context: The scene is preserved in Bacchylides, Ode 5. Meleager's request bound Heracles to marry Deianira, whose jealousy years later sent him the shirt of Nessus, poisoned with Hydra-blood, that finally killed him. Achilles and Patroclus die at Troy long after; Ajax kills himself at Troy.  (Legend.)

question: A monster in a swamp in the Argolid, near the town of Lerna, had been burning crops with its breath and eating the local cattle when King Eurystheus sent Heracles against it for his second labor. What kind of creature was it?
choices: A giant boar with iron tusks
context: The Lernaean Hydra, born of Typhon and Echidna, lived in the marsh at Lerna (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.2). The other choices are all real Heracles-cycle monsters (the Erymanthian Boar, Cerberus, the Stymphalian Birds), from different labors.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles waded into the swamp at Lerna and landed his first solid blow on the Hydra, chopping one head clean off with his sword. What happened next showed him that the fight could not be won this way at all. What did the wound do?
answer: Two new heads grew back from the stump
choices: Two new heads grew back from the stump
The severed head kept biting on its own
The stump spat venom that blinded him
The body split into two full serpents
context: This regeneration is the wonder of the story: cutting a head off doubled the problem. It is why Heracles needed a second-order idea and a helper to win.  (Legend.)

question: A young man watched from the bank at Lerna as his uncle Heracles fought the Hydra and lost ground. He had ridden in as the hero's charioteer, and he was the one who figured out the trick that broke the deadlock. Who was he?
context: Iolaus, son of Heracles's twin Iphicles, is Heracles's regular chariot-driver and nephew. Telamon and Hylas fight with him elsewhere; Philoctetes is the friend who lights his funeral pyre years later, taking his bow as thanks.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles's nephew ran up beside him at Lerna as each head of the Hydra fell to the sword. The young man's answer was to stop the stumps from healing, so he pressed something against each raw wound to keep fresh heads from sprouting. What did he press against the stumps?
answer: A burning firebrand from a torched grove
choices: A burning firebrand from a torched grove
A cold blade pulled from a bucket of well-water
A handful of clay from the swamp-bank
A bronze cup filled with wine from the road
context: In some versions Iolaus set fire to a nearby grove to keep a supply of burning branches. Cauterizing the wound with the flame is what finally cleared head after head. Cold, clay, and wine are all plausible-sounding but only heat sealed the stumps.  (Legend.)

question: The Hydra lost its last head to Heracles at Lerna, the one that no fire could touch. He had cut it off, but it could never truly die and he could not destroy it. What did he do with it?
answer: He buried it under a huge rock beside the road
choices: He buried it under a huge rock beside the road
He hurled it into the sea from the cliffs at Malea
He gave it to Iolaus to guard for life
He fed it to Cerberus at the gates of Hades
context: The immortal head was pinned under a boulder on the road from Lerna to Elaeus. It could not be killed, only trapped. Ancient travellers pointed out the very rock.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles stood over the poisonous body of the Hydra of Lerna once the fight was done, and he took from it something that made him more dangerous for the rest of his career. A three-bodied giant at the western edge of the world and a man-eating flock in Arcadia would later find out what it was. What did he do?
answer: He dipped his arrows in the blood
choices: He dipped his arrows in the blood
He cut a bowstring from the sinew
He forged a helmet from the scales
He wove a cloak from the shed skin
context: The serpent's blood was so venomous that from then on every one of Heracles's arrows carried an incurable poison. This one act sets up several of the later stories, including the death of the centaur Nessus and, in the end, Heracles's own death.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles loosed a stray arrow from his poisoned bow years after Lerna, and it grazed one of his old teachers, an immortal being who had trained Jason, Asclepius and Achilles up on Mount Pelion. The wound could not be cured, and the teacher gave up his immortality just to be released into death. Which teacher did Heracles kill by mistake?
context: Chiron the immortal centaur, tutor of heroes on Mount Pelion, was grazed by a stray Hydra-poisoned arrow during a brawl among centaurs and gave up his immortality to end the pain. Nessus is the ferryman-centaur killed by Heracles at the river Evenus; Pholus is another centaur friend who died examining one of the same arrows; Silenus is the drunken old satyr-tutor of Dionysus.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus refused to count the labor when Heracles brought the Hydra's corpse home to Mycenae, expecting credit. The king, the cousin who had set him the labors, later added an extra task to bring the total up to twelve. Why did he refuse?
answer: A nephew had helped, so it was not a solo victory
choices: A nephew had helped, so it was not a solo victory
Heracles had used a weapon Hades had forbidden
Heracles had brought back only pieces, not the whole body
A nephew had killed the immortal head, not Heracles himself
context: The rule was ten labors done alone; because Iolaus had cauterized the stumps, Eurystheus struck this one off, and later did the same for the cleansing of the Augean stables, adding two more labors to make twelve.  (Legend.)

question: One monstrous pair bred a whole family of beasts, and Heracles spent a good part of his labors killing or capturing it. The Hydra in the swamp at Lerna was one of them. So were the Nemean Lion he strangled and Cerberus, the hound he dragged up from Hades. Who were the parents of all these monsters?
context: Typhon (the storm-giant Zeus buried under Etna) and Echidna (half-woman, half-serpent) produced the Nemean Lion, the Chimera, Cerberus, Orthrus, and the Lernaean serpent. Uranus and Gaia are Sky and Earth; Cronus and Rhea are the Olympians' parents; Nereus and Doris are sea-parents to the fifty Nereids.  (Legend.)

question: Deianira, the second wife of Heracles, soaked a tunic in blood and sent her husband the love-gift. A dying enemy had tricked her, telling her that his blood would keep Heracles faithful. When the hero put it on, the Hydra's venom burned into his flesh and could not be pulled off. Under what name is that garment remembered?
context: The dying enemy was the centaur Nessus, killed by one of the Hydra-poisoned arrows after trying to carry Deianira across the river Evenus. Heracles climbed Mount Oeta, built his own pyre, and asked Philoctetes to light it. The robe of Medea is the poisoned wedding-gift she sent Jason's new bride; the gown of Glauce is that same bride's burning dress; 'the cloak of Iason' is an invented wrong choice tied to Jason's name.  (Legend.)

question: A sacred deer on Mount Ceryneia slipped away from every hunter until King Eurystheus sent Heracles to fetch her alive for his third labor. Two things set this hind apart from any ordinary deer. Her horns were made of gold. What were her hooves made of?
context: Gold horns and bronze hooves are the standard details for the Ceryneian Hind in Apollodorus and Callimachus; the striking metal-pairing is what marks her as a sacred beast. Iron is too late a metal for Bronze-Age myth; silver is Artemis's bow-metal; flint belongs to arrow-heads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Apollodorus 2.5.3.  (Legend.)

question: An Olympian goddess caught the gold-horned deer of Mount Ceryneia long before Heracles hunted her, and yoked her magic sisters to a chariot-team. This deer alone slipped her harness and got away. Which goddess did the deer belong to?
context: Callimachus's Hymn to Artemis names her as the owner of the golden-horned chariot-hinds; the escaped fifth became the labor of Heracles. Aphrodite's chariot is drawn by doves or sparrows; Athena's beast is the owl; Demeter's is the harvest-serpent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Callimachus, Hymn to Artemis 100-112.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles kept walking after the hind, because he could not use his club or his poisoned arrows on her and she could outrun even an arrow. The chase went on and on, across Greece, north through Thrace, into the far north and back. How long did the pursuit last in Apollodorus's telling?
context: Apollodorus says the pursuit lasted a full year, ending at the river Ladon in Arcadia (or on Mount Artemisius, or as far as the Hyperboreans in the far north, depending on the source). Three years is Odysseus's stretch with Circe; seven is the epic long-service span; nine days is how long Hephaestus fell from Olympus when Zeus hurled him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Apollodorus 2.5.3; Pindar, Olympian 3.  (Legend.)

question: The golden-antlered hind led Heracles clear off the edge of the Greek map, and he had orders to catch her alive. He ran north into the land where Apollo went each winter and the sun never quite set. What did the Greeks call the blessed people who lived there?
context: Hyperborea meant 'the land beyond Boreas', the north wind; Apollo wintered there each year, and Heracles is said to have chased the hind to its edge. The Scythians and Thracians were real northern peoples the Greeks traded and fought with; the Cimmerians lived in perpetual fog and gloom in Odyssey 11. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperborea.  (Legend.)

question: Two angry Olympians stopped Heracles on the road through Arcadia as he carried the hind home in his arms. They demanded to know why he was carrying off a creature sacred to their family. One was the goddess who owned her. Who was with that goddess?
context: Artemis and her twin brother Apollo confronted Heracles on the road; he explained that Eurystheus had set the labor and promised to return the hind alive, and the twins let him pass. Leto is their mother but does not travel with her adult children in the stories; Zeus is above such quarrels; Hera loathed Heracles and would not have helped Artemis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Apollodorus 2.5.3.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles carried the hind alive into the courtyard at Mycenae and set her before King Eurystheus, who meant to keep her for himself. Heracles had promised the goddess to return the beast, so he pulled a trick to keep both promises at once. What did he do?
answer: let her bolt free the instant Eurystheus had seen her
choices: let her bolt free the instant Eurystheus had seen her
handed her to a huntsman who let her escape overnight
asked Eurystheus to fetch her himself and dropped the rope
carried her back to Ceryneia during the king's afternoon meal
context: Heracles kept the letter of both promises: Eurystheus had 'received' the deer with his own eyes, and Artemis had her beast back alive and free. The other options are all thin variants of the same trick -- the classic version is the sudden release the moment the king's eyes were on her. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind.  (Legend.)

question: Callimachus told in his hymn how the goddess who owned the hind, as a girl, ran down a whole set of golden-horned deer. She yoked most of them to her chariot-team, all but one, who escaped to Mount Ceryneia to wait for Heracles. How many did she catch in that hunt?
context: Callimachus says Artemis caught five golden-horned hinds as a girl, yoked four to her chariot, and the fifth got away to Mount Ceryneia in the northern Peloponnese -- setting up Heracles's labor generations later. Three, seven, and twelve are the standard mythic small-numbers (three Graces, seven Pleiades, twelve Olympians), but the hinds are five. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Callimachus, Hymn to Artemis 100-112.  (Legend.)

question: A wise centaur, a creature half man, half horse, welcomed Heracles to his cave on the road to catch the huge wild Erymanthian Boar. He set roasted meat before his guest but held back a jar of wine, saying it belonged to all the centaurs. What was the friendly centaur's name?
context: Pholus, the son of Silenus in Apollodorus, was one of the two civilised centaurs of Greek myth (Chiron the other). Nessus is the centaur Heracles kills later at the river-crossing with Deianira, whose poisoned shirt kills Heracles himself. Eurytion and Rhoecus are lesser centaurs of the wilder sort. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pholus_(mythology); Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles opened a wine-jar in the cave of his centaur host, against the host's warning, though it belonged to all the centaurs of the mountain. The fragrant smell drew the others to the cave, armed with rocks and pine-trunks. What weapon did Heracles use to drive the enraged centaurs back?
answer: arrows dipped in the blood of the Hydra
choices: arrows dipped in the blood of the Hydra
the jawbone of the Nemean Lion
a torch snatched from Pholus's fire
the club of olive-wood he cut on Helicon
context: The venom Heracles had drawn from the Hydra in his second labor becomes the poison on every arrow he shoots for the rest of his life -- and eventually the poison Nessus's shirt uses to kill him. The club, the lion-hide and the torch are all real Heracles gear but the centaur-rout is arrow-work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pholus_(mythology); Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: A fleeing centaur took refuge at the cave of the wise elder Chiron, tutor of Jason and Achilles, and Heracles fired one shot too many in the confusion. The poisoned arrow struck Chiron himself. Chiron was immortal, but the poison meant he could not heal, only suffer. How did the story end his agony?
answer: Prometheus traded his own immortality with Chiron so Chiron could die
choices: Prometheus traded his own immortality with Chiron so Chiron could die
Zeus struck Chiron with a thunderbolt as a mercy
Apollo drew the poison out with a hymn of healing
Chiron leapt from the cliffs of Pelion into the sea
context: In one of the great cross-linked twists of Greek myth, Chiron's agony from the accidental arrow-wound is what frees Prometheus from the eagle -- Prometheus inherits Chiron's immortality and Chiron is allowed at last to die. Zeus later sets Chiron among the stars as the constellation Centaurus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiron.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles's centaur host picked through the aftermath of the brawl at his own cave, where many centaurs lay dead. He had warned his guest off the wine-jar that began it all. Now he died there too, in his own doorway. How did the host die?
answer: he dropped one of the poisoned arrows on his own foot
choices: he dropped one of the poisoned arrows on his own foot
the last centaur to flee turned and speared him
he choked on the wine he had been forbidden to serve
Heracles killed him by mistake in the twilight
context: In Apollodorus, Pholus draws an arrow from a dead centaur to examine it, wondering how so small a thing could kill so large a creature; it slips, falls point-first on his foot, and the Hydra-poison kills him almost at once. Heracles buries him where he lies. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pholus_(mythology); Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles went on alone to hunt the boar, and the labor demanded it alive. One swing of the club and he would have a dead beast, not a live one. He chased it with shouts up the mountain until it was exhausted. What terrain finished the capture for him?
choices: a pit trap the shepherds had dug
context: Apollodorus has the boar driven uphill into deep snow, where it sinks belly-deep and can no longer move; Heracles then binds it in chains. The bog, the gorge and the pit trap are the shapes of other capture-stories in Greek myth (Bellerophon's traps, the Calydonian Boar hunt), not this one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erymanthian_Boar; Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus looked out at Mycenae and saw his cousin Heracles coming into the courtyard with a live, chained monster over his head. The king had lost his nerve once already, when the hero dragged the huge corpse of the Nemean lion up to the palace gates. Now he lost it completely. Where did Eurystheus hide?
answer: inside a great bronze jar sunk in the ground
choices: inside a great bronze jar sunk in the ground
under his own throne with a cloak drawn over him
in the treasury vault behind the double doors
up in the watchtower with the archers
context: The bronze pithos sunk into the palace floor became the king's favourite refuge whenever Heracles turned up with a live monster; he had first used it after the Nemean Lion. Eurystheus gave the rest of his orders through a herald called down through the jar's mouth. The scene is one of the most-painted Heracles moments on Greek vases. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erymanthian_Boar; Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus sent Heracles to clean the enormous stables of one of the greatest cattle-kings in Greece for his fifth labor. They had gone uncleaned through the king's long reign. Which king of Elis owned them?
context: Augeas ruled Elis in the western Peloponnese and was famous for the size of his herds. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.5.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles arrived at the palace of the rich king of Elis with an order from King Eurystheus of Mycenae, who meant it as a shame as much as a physical task. What one-day chore had Heracles been told to finish there?
answer: Muck out thirty years of dung from his cattle-yards
choices: Muck out thirty years of dung from his cattle-yards
Wrestle every one of his bulls to the ground
Count every animal in his herds
context: The stables had not been cleaned in three decades, and the surrounding fields had gone uncultivable. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.5.  (Legend.)

question: A god gave his son thousands of cattle, old tellers said, and that is how the king of Elis came to own the largest herd in all Greece. The herd filled his stables year after year, and no one ever cleaned them. Which god was the king's father?
context: Theocritus's Idyll 25 says the enormous herd was given by the Sun to his son. Augeas was one of several 'children of Helios' in Greek myth.  (Legend.)

question: The king of Elis laughed at the bargain Heracles offered him before starting the job. The hero would clean the filthy stables in a single day, and in payment the king would give him a share of the herd. What share did Heracles ask for?
context: Augeas laughed and agreed, thinking the job impossible. Heracles brought a member of the king's own household in as witness to the deal.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles stood before the cattle-yard of the king of Elis, packed with dung from the largest cattle herd in Greece, with a single day to clear it. He did not lift a shovel or a pitchfork. What did he do to the cattle-yard instead?
answer: Broke open the walls and ran two rivers through it
choices: Broke open the walls and ran two rivers through it
Burned the whole yard down with a torch
Called down a thunderstorm from Zeus
Set his bull-team to trample the yard flat
context: He knocked a gap in the upstream wall and another downstream, ran the water through, then closed the gaps so the rivers returned to their beds. Apollodorus 2.5.5.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles let two nearby rivers do the work at the stables of Elis, and he never touched a shovel. The rushing water carried the dung out of the cattle-yard with it. The job was the fifth of his labors, and he finished it in a single day. Which pair of rivers did he use?
context: Both are real rivers of the western Peloponnese and still flow today. The Eurotas runs by Sparta, the Achelous through Aetolia; the Scamander and Simois are the rivers of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles walked back up to the palace at Elis to collect his pay. He had made his bargain with the king, cleaned the vast stables inside the single day, and come for the share of the herd he was owed. How did the king answer him at the gate?
answer: Refused to hand over anything he had promised
choices: Refused to hand over anything he had promised
Ordered his household to sing Heracles's praises
Handed over twice the agreed share
Named Heracles his heir on the spot
context: Augeas even denied ever making the deal, once he learned the labor had been imposed on Heracles by Eurystheus.  (Legend.)

question: A witness from inside the king's own household stood up at a public hearing in Elis and testified that the bargain with Heracles had indeed been struck. The king had refused to pay, and the witness was driven out of Elis for it. Who spoke against the king?
context: Phyleus was banished from Elis for testifying against his father, and settled on the island of Dulichium. Apollodorus 2.5.5.  (Legend.)

question: The king of Elis came out at the head of his own men to meet Heracles, years after he had cheated the hero of his pay for the stables. Heracles had brought an army to Elis to settle accounts. How did that reckoning end?
answer: Heracles killed Augeas and set the banished son on the throne
choices: Heracles killed Augeas and set the banished son on the throne
Heracles spared Augeas and took the promised cattle at last
Heracles was defeated and driven back to Tiryns
Heracles married Augeas's daughter and inherited Elis
context: Phyleus, who had testified against his father and been exiled for it, came back as the rightful king of Elis after Augeas fell.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus of Mycenae refused to count the cleaning of the stables of Elis toward the twelve labors. He ruled that Heracles had broken a condition of the labors, though the stables were clean. What did Eurystheus say Heracles had done?
answer: Contracted to be paid for the job
choices: Contracted to be paid for the job
Killed one of the sacred bulls
Left the job unfinished by nightfall
Called on Iolaus for help again
context: The bargain with Augeas disqualified the labor. Combined with the Hydra (where Iolaus's help was ruled out), Heracles now owed two extra labors to reach twelve.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles is said, by later tradition, to have founded a great festival of games after his victory over the king of Elis, at a sanctuary on the banks of one of the very rivers that had washed the king's stables clean. Which festival did he found?
context: The sanctuary at Olympia sat on the banks of the Alpheus, one of the very rivers that had washed the stables clean. The Pythian, Isthmian, and Nemean Games are the other three Panhellenic festivals, each with its own founding story.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus sent Heracles against something new for the sixth of his twelve labors: no single beast to grapple, but a whole man-eating flock that had terrorized the countryside around Lake Stymphalia in Arcadia. What kind of animal made up this flock?
context: The sixth labor targets the Stymphalian birds -- a whole flock of man-eating birds nesting in the marshes of Lake Stymphalia in Arcadia. Wild pigs recall the Erymanthian boar (a single beast, labor 4); wolves belong to no labor; goats to the Ceryneian hind's forest (a single deer, labor 3, not a flock).  (Legend.)

question: Pausanias wrote of the flock Heracles was sent to drive off from a swamp in Arcadia, and these were no ordinary creatures. Their beaks and feathers were made of one metal, so hard that they could shoot the feathers out like arrows, and their droppings were poison. What metal were the beaks and feathers?
context: Pausanias 8.22 and later mythographers describe the Stymphalian birds' beaks and feathers as bronze; the birds can loose the feathers like arrows, and their droppings poison crops. Iron is later than the mythic Bronze-Age setting; silver and obsidian belong to other traditions (obsidian is Aztec/Meso-American, out of lane).  (Legend.)

question: Heracles reached the lake with his bow and could not get at the flock. It refused to fly, reeds hid it, and the boggy ground would not carry his weight. He needed a way to send the whole flock into the air at once. Which Olympian goddess handed him a rattle to do it?
context: Athena, the patron of most Greek heroes (Perseus, Odysseus, Bellerophon, Heracles himself), appears in the Stymphalian labor. Hera is Heracles's lifelong enemy who set the labors in motion by driving him mad; Aphrodite is the goddess of love (her interventions are Trojan-War romances); Demeter is grain and the seasons.  (Legend.)

question: Jason's Argonauts clashed spears against their shields on a lonely island in the Black Sea, warned by the seer Phineus, and drove off what was left of the flock Heracles had shot at. They were copying his noise-trick, generations after him. Whose island had the survivors fled to, in Apollonius Rhodius?
context: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2.1030-1089: the surviving Stymphalian birds settle on the island of Ares (Aretias) in the Black Sea, where the birds are already sacred to the war-god; the Argonauts clash spears against shields to raise a wall of noise -- exactly Heracles's krotala trick reapplied. Hades has an underworld realm, no island; Dionysus's islands are Naxos and Chios (wine, not war); Hermes has no cult island of this kind.  (Legend.)

question: A great white bull went wild on a certain Greek island, and King Eurystheus sent Heracles across the sea to bring it back alive for his seventh labor. It was trampling through the fields and orchards. On which island was it loose?
context: Apollodorus places the seventh labor on Crete, where the bull was uprooting crops and knocking down orchard walls. Rhodes is Helios's island; Naxos is where Theseus abandons Ariadne after Crete; Cyprus is Aphrodite's home. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 2.5.7.  (Legend.)

question: A god sent a great white bull to King Minos as a sign that his rule was rightful. That was long before the beast went wild and Heracles was sent to capture it. Which god sent the bull?
context: Poseidon, god of the sea and of bulls and horses, sent the bull walking out of the surf as the sign that Minos held Crete by divine right. In return Minos had sworn to sacrifice the bull straight back to Poseidon. Zeus's own bull-form is the one that carried off Europa; Apollo's animals are the swan and the deer; Hephaestus is the smith of the gods. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 3.1.3.  (Legend.)

question: King Minos saw the white bull walk out of the surf, and he could not bring himself to burn it. He had sworn to offer it up to the god who sent it, in thanks for the sign, but the animal was too magnificent. What did Minos do instead?
answer: substituted an ordinary bull from his own herd for the sacrifice
choices: substituted an ordinary bull from his own herd for the sacrifice
sacrificed a hundred lesser bulls together in its place
sent it in secret to be hidden in the mountain caves
carved a wooden image of the bull and burned that
context: Minos kept the sea-bull for himself and sent up a common bull from his own herd to the altar. Everything that follows -- Pasiphae's curse, the Minotaur, Heracles's labor, the Marathonian Bull, Theseus's early fame -- runs out of that one broken promise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 3.1.3-4.  (Legend.)

question: Aphrodite cursed the wife of King Minos, on an angry god's order, to fall in love with a white bull. Minos had promised that bull in sacrifice to the god who sent it and had kept it for his own herd. The god's anger did not fall on the king himself. Who was the queen?
context: Pasiphae was daughter of the sun-god Helios and wife of Minos; Aphrodite laid the curse. Europa is the earlier bull-carried queen -- Zeus took her to Crete as a bull and she became Minos's mother. Ariadne and Phaedra are Pasiphae's own daughters, both later tied to Theseus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 3.1.4.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles landed on the island after the mad white bull, the same beast that had fathered the Minotaur on the queen, and he asked King Minos to help him hunt it. Minos set one condition before the hunt could begin. What did Minos require?
answer: Heracles could take the bull if he could capture it alone
choices: Heracles could take the bull if he could capture it alone
Heracles must return the bull unharmed to Crete after the labor
Heracles must first swear an oath at the palace altar
Heracles must pay a tribute of a hundred cattle for the beast
context: Minos gave permission and no help. Heracles did the capture single-handed, wrestling the bull to the ground bare-handed -- exactly the pose on the black-figure vases, arm hooked over the horn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 2.5.7.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles carried the captured bull back across the sea and dumped it in front of Eurystheus at Mycenae. Eurystheus tried to dedicate it, as he had tried before with Heracles's other live catches. To which goddess did he try to dedicate the bull, only to have her refuse the gift?
context: Hera hated Heracles from the day he was born -- he was Zeus's son by another woman, and his very name means 'glory of Hera' as a taunt at her. She refused every gift that came from him, and this bull was no exception; it was set loose. Athena is Heracles's usual patron among the gods; Artemis owns the Ceryneian Hind; Demeter has no quarrel with him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus sent Heracles north for his eighth labor, to fetch four wild mares owned by King Diomedes, a cruel son of the war-god Ares. No rope could hold them. What made these mares so feared across Greece?
answer: they had been fed on human flesh
choices: they had been fed on human flesh
they breathed fire like the bulls of Colchis
no bit or bridle could touch them
context: Diomedes had trained them on the flesh of travellers and shipwrecked strangers, an outrage against every rule of Greek hospitality; that outrage is what makes the labor a punishment as well as a task. Fire-breathing belongs to Aeetes's bulls in Colchis; winged horses to Pegasus and to the horses of the Sun; the bit-and-bridle line is wrong -- the mares WERE controllable, they just had to be tamed the hard way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Apollodorus 2.5.8.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles sailed north for the eighth of his twelve labors, to the land of King Diomedes. It was a wild coast famous for its horses and its warlike tribes. In which country did Diomedes rule?
context: Diomedes was king of the Bistonian people on the Thracian coast. This is NOT the Diomedes who fights at Troy in the Iliad -- that Diomedes is a Greek prince from Argos, on the other side of the Aegean. Colchis is where the Golden Fleece hangs; Thessaly is Achilles's country; Lydia is where Heracles later serves Queen Omphale. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Apollodorus 2.5.8.  (Legend.)

question: Hyginus, a Roman writer, preserved the names of all four mares that Heracles came to steal from King Diomedes. Three of them were Podargos, Lampon and Xanthos. What was the fourth?
context: The four names in Hyginus's Fabulae are Podargos ('swift-foot'), Lampon ('shining'), Xanthos ('yellow'), and Deinos ('terrible'). Aithon ('blazing') is one of the sun-horses; Balios is one of Achilles's own horses at Troy (his brother is a different Xanthos); Phlegon is another sun-horse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Hyginus, Fabulae 30.  (Legend.)

question: King Diomedes kept his four mares chained fast in a stable at the palace, because they snapped every ordinary rope and ate the grooms. In the traditional telling, what material were the chains and mangers made of?
context: Bronze chains to bronze mangers -- the hero-age metal, the same material as Talos and as Eurystheus's own hiding-jar. Iron is a later metal that mostly stays out of Bronze-Age myth. Silver has no strength in it. Doubled hemp is a wrong choice too -- the whole point of the mares is that NO rope held them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles left a young friend in charge of the captured horses on his eighth labor and went back to fight the king. The young man had come along with the small band of companions Heracles brought on the voyage, and the hero trusted him. What was the young man's name?
context: Abderus is the friend Heracles brings on this labor. Hylas was the boy who drowned when Heracles took him on the Argo (the nymphs pulled him into a spring). Iolaus is the nephew who helped with the Hydra and stays with Heracles for most of the labors -- so he is often confused with Abderus, but he SURVIVES this one. Philoctetes is much later, the boy who lights Heracles's funeral pyre. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Apollodorus 2.5.8.  (Legend.)

question: The people of King Diomedes came after Heracles in force to take the horses back. He had surprised the four mares in the stable, broken their chains and driven them down to the shore. What was the king's tribe called?
context: The Bistones were Diomedes's Thracian people. The Myrmidons are Achilles's men from Phthia. The Amazons will be Heracles's ninth labor, for Hippolyta's belt. The Lapiths fought their own famous battle -- with the centaurs, at Pirithous's wedding. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Apollodorus 2.5.8.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles came back to the horses from the battle on the shore with King Diomedes dead, and the news was awful. His young friend was dead, torn apart and eaten by the very mares left in his charge. In grief, Heracles founded a city on that coast in the friend's name. What city rose there?
context: The real Greek colony of Abdera on the Thracian coast traced its founding-legend to this labor and to Heracles's grief for his friend. Abdera was later famous as the birthplace of the philosophers Democritus and Protagoras. Byzantium is the Bosphorus city (later Constantinople); Miletus and Ephesus are Ionian cities in Asia Minor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdera,_Thrace.

question: Heracles killed King Diomedes in the fight with the king's own tribe on the shore, and he still had to deal with the four mares themselves, as wild as ever. What did Heracles do that finally calmed them?
answer: fed the king's body to them
choices: fed the king's body to them
made them drink from the river Nestos
yoked them to a plow for a full day
sang to them with Orpheus's lyre
context: In Diodorus and Apollodorus, Heracles throws Diomedes's body to the horses. Once they had tasted their own master, the beasts became calm and controllable -- the horror ended the horror. It is the same shape as Perillos the bronze-smith roasted in his own hollow bull, or Haman hung on his own gallows in the Book of Esther: the tyrant destroyed by his own instrument. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Diodorus Siculus 4.15.  (Legend.)

question: King Eurystheus of Mycenae sent his cousin Heracles far from Greece for the ninth of his twelve labors, to the land of the Amazons, a tribe of warrior women beyond the Black Sea. What did the king order him to bring back from their queen?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Eurystheus set Heracles to fetch the girdle -- Greek 'zoster', a warrior's war-belt -- of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons. Older English translations call it a 'girdle', which is why the labor keeps that name.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles sailed to the Amazons, a tribe of warrior women who lived by a river on the south coast of the Black Sea, to fetch a treasure from their queen. What was the name of the Amazon queen?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: the queen was Hippolyta. Andromache is the Trojan wife of Hector; Cassandra the Trojan seer-daughter of Priam; Iphigenia the daughter of Agamemnon sacrificed at Aulis -- all real names from adjacent Greek stories.  (Legend.)

question: A great god of Olympus gave his daughter, queen of the Amazons, a belt that was more than armor. It was the token that she ruled the Amazon warriors, and Heracles came to fetch it for his ninth labor. Which Olympian was her father?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Ares, god of war, fathered Hippolyta and gave her the belt in token of her supremacy over the Amazons. In myth the whole Amazon tribe descend from Ares.  (Legend.)

question: A priestess in the household of King Eurystheus asked for the Amazon queen's belt to keep in her temple. So the king sent Heracles to fetch it, and the king did not want it for himself. Who was the priestess?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: the labor was set at the request of Admete, Eurystheus's daughter and a priestess of Hera. She wanted the Amazon queen's war-belt as a temple treasure.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles sailed with a small band of companions to Themiscyra, the capital of the Amazons on the shore of the Black Sea, expecting a fight. He had come for the belt of their queen, and she came out herself to meet him at the shore. What did the queen do?
answer: agreed to give him the war-belt willingly
choices: agreed to give him the war-belt willingly
sent him to consult the Amazon oracle
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Hippolyta was impressed by Heracles and agreed to hand the belt over peacefully. For one moment the ninth labor was a friendly diplomatic errand -- which is what makes what happens next so bitter.  (Legend.)

question: A disguised figure ran through the ranks of the warrior women crying that Heracles was carrying off their queen by force. In the panic they armed and rushed the Greek ships, and a peaceful errand turned into a battle. Who was the disguised troublemaker?
answer: Hera in the shape of an Amazon
choices: Hera in the shape of an Amazon
Athena in the shape of an old woman
Aphrodite in the shape of a priestess
Artemis in the shape of a huntress
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Hera hated Heracles as the son of Zeus by a mortal, and she went down to the Amazons herself in Amazon-shape to spread the rumor that turned the peace into a slaughter. The scene is a mirror of Loki in disguise or the Morrigan in disguise -- a goddess as a story-mover.  (Legend.)

question: The Amazon queen came down to the water at her capital to meet Heracles, where a river ran out to the south coast of the Black Sea. He had sailed there for his ninth labor. What was the name of the river the Amazon capital stood on?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9; Herodotus 4.110: the Amazon capital Themiscyra stood on the Thermodon on the south coast of the Black Sea. The Styx is an underworld river; the Scamander runs at Troy; the Eurotas runs at Sparta.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles saw the Amazon warriors charging the shore in arms, and he believed the queen had betrayed him, that her welcome had been a trap. He had not come to kill anybody, only to fetch a belt. What did Heracles do to the queen who had welcomed him?
answer: killed her and took the belt from her body
choices: killed her and took the belt from her body
took her prisoner and dragged her aboard
wounded her and left her on the shore
spared her and fled without the belt
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: believing Hippolyta had betrayed him, Heracles killed her, stripped the belt from her body, and fought his way back to the ships. Hera's disguise-and-rumor trick had turned a peaceful labor into the death of a queen who had done him no harm.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles put in at Troy on the voyage home from the Amazons and discovered the king's daughter chained to a rock at the water's edge. She had been offered as a sacrifice to a sea-monster sent by an angry Poseidon. Who was the Trojan princess?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Hesione was the daughter of King Laomedon of Troy. Andromeda is the Ethiopian princess Perseus rescued (a very similar scene, different heroine). Iphigenia was sacrificed by her father Agamemnon at Aulis. Chryseis was Agamemnon's captive in the Iliad.  (Legend.)

question: The king of Troy refused Heracles the promised divine horses, after the hero killed the sea-monster and freed the king's daughter. The king had already cheated Poseidon over the building of the city's walls. Heracles came back later with an army. What did Heracles do to Troy?
answer: sacked the city and killed Laomedon
choices: sacked the city and killed Laomedon
besieged the city and made a treaty
burned the walls but spared the king
carried off the temple treasures only
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.6.4: Heracles returned with an army, breached the walls, killed Laomedon and all his sons except young Podarces (who was ransomed and renamed Priam -- the same Priam who would rule Troy in Homer's war). This is the FIRST sack of Troy, a generation before Achilles.  (Legend.)

question: A Greek friend of Heracles was first over the walls when the hero came back to Troy with an army. Heracles gave him the princess he had rescued from the sea-monster as a bride, and their son Teucer became an archer famed in the Trojan War. To which of his companions did Heracles give her?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.6.4 and 3.12.7: Telamon of Salamis was first over the wall in the sack and received Hesione as his war-bride. Their son was Teucer the great archer of the Trojan War; Telamon's other son Ajax the Great was born to his wife Periboea. Peleus of Phthia (father of Achilles) was on the same expedition. Nestor and Iolaus are other companions of Heracles from the wider cycle.  (Legend.)

question: A fairy took a baby boy from his mother's arms on the day his father, a king, died fleeing a burning castle. She raised him as her own in her enchanted realm under the water, and he grew up to serve King Arthur. Who was this fostered boy?
context: Vulgate Cycle, Lancelot en prose (c.1215-30); Wikipedia: Lancelot. Ban of Benwick's castle Trebes falls to King Claudas of Gaul; Ban dies fleeing, and the Lady of the Lake abducts the infant. Gawain is King Lot's eldest son. Tristan is the tragic hero of the parallel Cornish story. Percival is the innocent Grail-knight of the forest.  (Legend.)

question: A boy rode into Camelot with a plain white shield, announced only as the White Knight and still not knowing his own true name. His fairy foster-mother had taught him arms and letters and sent him out to serve Arthur. What title is she known by?
context: Vulgate Cycle; Wikipedia: Lady of the Lake. The Lady (called Viviane in French tradition, Nimue in Malory) raises him in her otherworld realm and sends him out as a nameless White Knight. Morgan le Fay is Arthur's half-sister and often his enemy. Igraine is Arthur's mother, not a foster. Ragnell is the loathly lady of Gawain's marriage tale.  (Legend.)

question: Meleagant carried off Queen Guinevere, in the earliest surviving romance to make Lancelot her lover, and Lancelot took on a public disgrace to follow her trail. The French poet Chretien de Troyes named him for that humiliation in the poem's title. What did Chretien call him the Knight of?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Lancelot ou le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177-1181); Wikipedia: Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart. The cart is a criminal's tumbrel -- a shame-cart used to haul the condemned to the gallows; riding in it is a knight's disgrace, and Lancelot does it because it is the only way to follow the trail of the kidnapped queen. 'Knight of the Green Chapel' is Gawain's poem; 'Knight of the Two Swords' is Balin's tale in Malory; 'Knight of the Fountain' is Yvain's -- three real Arthurian titles.  (Legend.)

question: In Chretien's romance, Lancelot pulled off his gauntlets at the border river of Gorre, the otherworldly realm where Meleagant had carried the queen. He gripped a razor-edged span with his bare hands and crawled across, bloodied to the elbows. What weapon was the crossing shaped from?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Lancelot le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177-1181); Wikipedia: Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart. The 'Pont de l'Espee' is a single giant sword laid edge-up as a bridge, one of the two entrances into Gorre. A spear-bridge, axe-bridge, or arrow-bridge would each be a plausible medieval-romance ordeal but is not the one Chretien invents.  (Legend.)

question: The sorceress Brisen gave Lancelot drugged wine at Corbenic, in the pay of a daughter of King Pelles who desperately wanted a child by him. Brisen passed the young lady one of Guinevere's rings to fool him in the darkness. He woke to find the wrong woman beside him, and a son had already been conceived. What was the child's name?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XI; Wikipedia: Galahad, Elaine of Corbenic. Elaine of Corbenic is the mother; Galahad grows up to be the one pure knight who alone sees the Grail uncovered -- the purity Lancelot himself could not attain. Bors is Lancelot's cousin, also a Grail knight. Perceval finds the Grail castle first but does not achieve it. Mordred is Arthur's incest-son and the future usurper of Camelot.  (Legend.)

question: Guinevere found Lancelot with the daughter of King Pelles at Camelot, tricked a second time by the same lady, and drove him from court in a rage. He threw himself from a window and vanished into the forest, forgotten. In Malory, how long did Lancelot wander mad in the wild before he was found again?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books XI-XII; Wikipedia: Lancelot. Malory gives the interval as two years (some earlier French versions say five); Lancelot is fed by hermits and shepherds and does not know his own name. Forty days is the biblical wilderness. Seven weeks and twelve summers sound like the period, but Malory does not use them.  (Legend.)

question: Lancelot's companions found him dead at Glastonbury in the morning, laid out with a smile on his face, in the last chapter of Malory. One of the hermits with him, a former bishop of Canterbury, woke laughing and told them at once what he had dreamed. What had the bishop dreamed?
choices: the Grail carried up the aisle
the Lady of the Lake returning Excalibur
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.13; Wikisource. The bishop tells them: 'here was Sir Launcelot with me with more angels than ever I saw men in one day, and I saw the angels heave up Sir Launcelot unto heaven, and the gates of heaven opened against him.' The other three answers are all Arthurian endings this scene is NOT -- the Grail is Galahad's ending; the Round Table breaks and is not remade; Bedivere returns Excalibur at Arthur's death, not Lancelot's.  (Legend.)

question: Lancelot slept at Corbenic while the covered Grail passed over him and healed his madness, but for all his greatness he never saw it uncovered. Malory carried the vision on to the far city of Sarras, where one knight alone of all Arthur's court knelt before the Grail unveiled and died in that same hour. Who was that knight?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII; Wikipedia: Galahad, Sarras. Galahad -- Lancelot's own son by Elaine of Corbenic -- is the virgin knight who alone achieves the uncovered vision at Sarras and dies at that moment. Bors is the third companion who survives and returns to Camelot to tell the tale. Perceval reaches Sarras with Galahad and dies soon after as a hermit. Lancelot is shut out by the adultery with Guinevere -- the one flaw the Grail tests -- and his son achieves what he could not.  (Legend.)

question: A Roman officer ordered Lawrence to produce the church's treasure in the year 258, and Lawrence held it all: the silver plate, the charity to the city's widows and the written list of every gift. Only the bishop of Rome ranked above him. What was Lawrence's title?
context: The archdeacon was the chief of all the deacons of a city church, in charge of its property and its charity. Deacon, subdeacon, and acolyte are the ranks beneath him. Above the archdeacon stood only the bishop. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: Lawrence came back to the Roman officer with a line of people behind him. The officer had ordered him to hand over the riches of the church at Rome. Lawrence pointed at the line and said, 'These are the treasures of the Church.' Who were the people?
answer: The poor and crippled of Rome
choices: The poor and crippled of Rome
The bishops of Italy in exile
The other deacons of the city
The virgins who served the altar
context: Ambrose of Milan reports this scene about a century after the event. Lawrence had spent his three days' grace selling every gold vessel the church owned and distributing the money to the widows, sick, and poor of the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.  (Legend.)

question: An old soldier-emperor sent a sharp order against the church across the empire in 258. In weeks it struck Lawrence in Rome, the bishop of Rome and Bishop Cyprian of Carthage. Two years later the Persian king took this same emperor alive. Which emperor was it?
context: Valerian's edict of 258 fell heaviest on the church's leadership: Pope Sixtus II was beheaded on 6 August, Lawrence roasted on 10 August, Cyprian of Carthage beheaded on 14 September of the same year. Valerian himself was captured by Shapur I two years later in 260 and died in Persian hands. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: The guards led the old bishop of Rome past Lawrence in the street, on the way to his beheading, and the bishop turned back to the weeping young man. He told Lawrence he would soon follow him. Who was the bishop of Rome executed just before Lawrence?
context: Sixtus II was beheaded on 6 August 258; Lawrence followed on 10 August, four days later. The scene of Sixtus's farewell on the road to execution is one of the earliest reported details of the story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.  (Legend.)

question: Lawrence sold off every vessel in secret and gave the money to the widows of Rome. He had not refused the Roman officer who demanded the church's silver and gold. He had only asked for a short window to gather it. How many days did Lawrence ask the officer for?
context: The three-day grace period is the hinge of the story: it is exactly enough time for Lawrence to convert every gold vessel in the Roman church into food, coin, and medicine for the poor, so that when the prefect arrived to collect gold he was shown a crowd of beggars instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.  (Legend.)

question: The Roman officer, humiliated by Lawrence's answer about the treasures of the Church, refused him the quick beheading the bishop of Rome had received. He ordered a slow, showy death instead, on the Esquiline Hill in view of the whole city. What did the officer use to kill him?
context: The site of the martyrdom on the Esquiline Hill is now occupied by the church of San Lorenzo in Panisperna. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.  (Legend.)

question: The Roman officer had Lawrence stretched over the coals on one of the sharpest dates in the Roman calendar. Later Italian folklore tied it to a natural event in the summer night sky, which comes every year within a day or two of it, and to the harvest of certain golden pears named after him. On what date did Lawrence die?
context: The Perseid meteor shower peaks on 12-13 August, right after Lawrence's 10 August feast. Sixtus II fell on 6 Aug; Cyprian of Carthage was beheaded on 14 September of the same year; 29 June is Peter and Paul. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: Lawrence went into the fire at Rome just before the Perseid meteor shower reached its peak. Italian folk-tradition renamed the streaks of light in that shower, in poetic reference to the fire that killed him. What did the tradition call them?
context: In Italian: 'le lacrime di San Lorenzo.' The peak of the Perseids falls on 12-13 August, right after his 10 August feast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: King Philip II of Spain built a massive grey monastery, palace and tomb in one, north of Madrid, to give thanks for a victory on Lawrence's feast day. It was one of the largest Renaissance buildings anywhere, and he had its rectangular floor plan deliberately shaped like a Roman cooking grill. What was the palace called?
context: Full name San Lorenzo de El Escorial. Philip started it in 1563 in thanks for his victory at St Quentin on 10 August 1557 -- Lawrence's feast day. Construction ran 1563-1584 under Juan Bautista de Toledo and Juan de Herrera. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Escorial.

question: Patrick J. Healy, a historian of the last century, argued that the grill may not have been the real instrument at all. He suggested the tradition may rest on a single copying mistake in Latin: 'passus est' (he suffered), misread by a scribe as 'assus est' (he was roasted), one letter different. If Healy is right, how would Lawrence actually have been killed?
answer: Beheaded, like Pope Sixtus II days before
choices: Beheaded, like Pope Sixtus II days before
Thrown to lions in the Colosseum
context: Healy's minority argument is that the standard Roman execution of a clergyman in 258 was the sword, and that the whole cooking-grill drama grew from that one-letter scribal slip. The gridiron is nonetheless what Ambrose and Prudentius already report within a century, so the tradition is deeply rooted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: Jesus told a parable in Luke's Gospel about two men who died on the same day. One was a wealthy man dressed in purple linen who feasted every day. The other was a poor beggar covered in sores, who lay outside the gate hoping for scraps. What was the beggar's name?
context: Luke 16:20 (KJV): 'a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores.' This is the parable-Lazarus -- NOT the historical Lazarus of Bethany whom Jesus raises from the tomb in John 11. Bartimaeus was the blind beggar of Jericho; Nicodemus came to Jesus by night; Zacchaeus climbed the sycamore tree. Source: Luke 16:19-21 (KJV).

question: A poor beggar lay at the gate of a rich man's mansion, in one of Jesus's parables in Luke's Gospel, hungry and covered in open sores. Only the unclean street animals came right up to him and licked his wounds. What kind of animals did Luke say came to him?
context: Luke 16:21 (KJV): 'moreover the dogs came and licked his sores.' The image doubles the horror of the rich man's neglect -- even street dogs pay Lazarus more mind than the master of the house. Source: Luke 16:19-21 (KJV).

question: The rich man cried out to Abraham from his torment with one small, desperate request, in the parable Jesus told in Luke's Gospel. He did not ask to be freed or brought over. He asked only that the beggar be sent to do one specific thing, to give him a moment's ease. What did the rich man ask the beggar to do?
answer: Dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue
choices: Dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue
Say a single prayer to Abraham on his behalf
Fetch a length of cloth to cover his burning eyes
Lead him quietly across the gulf to the other side
context: Luke 16:24 (KJV): 'send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.' The horror of the image is the smallness of the request against the size of the refusal. Source: Luke 16:19-31 (KJV).

question: Abraham refused the rich man's plea in Luke's Gospel. Something had been established between the two sides of the dead, he told him, and no one at all could pass it from either direction. What image did Abraham use for this barrier?
context: Luke 16:26 (KJV): 'between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.' Source: Luke 16:19-31 (KJV).

question: A king welcomed the sheep on his right with a great blessing, in the parable Jesus told in Matthew's Gospel, because they had fed him when he was hungry and visited him when he was sick. They protested that they had never seen him in any such state. He answered: 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of ______ of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.' Which words fill the gap?
context: Matthew 25:40 (KJV): 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.' From this scene the medieval church drew the Seven Corporal Works of Mercy -- feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the stranger, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned, and (added later from the Book of Tobit) bury the dead -- which shaped hospitals, hospices, and prison-visiting orders across centuries. Source: Matthew 25:31-46 (KJV); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_works_of_mercy.

question: A giant of a stranger joins Robin Hood's outlaws in Sherwood Forest, and the band laughs and calls him Little John, since he is anything but little. What is his actual birth-name?
context: His true name in the seventeenth-century broadside 'Robin Hood and Little John' (Child 125) is JOHN LITTLE; the outlaws swap his first name and surname to make 'Little John' as an ironic nickname. 'Nailer' or 'Naylor' is given as his surname in some late versions -- adjacent but not the joke-inversion form. Miller and Scarlet belong to other Merry Men (Much the Miller's Son and Will Scarlet). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood meets a stranger in the forest, and the old English ballads make a great point of the man's enormous size. He is the outlaw the band will call Little John. How tall do the ballads say he stands?
context: The seventeenth-century broadside describes him as 'seven feet high, large-limbed, and fearsome to behold'; medieval Englishmen averaged about five foot seven, so a seven-foot man was a walking marvel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood sets out alone across a stream in an old English broadside ballad, and a stranger approaches from the far side. The crossing has room for one man only, and neither will yield it. What kind of crossing are they standing on?
context: Child Ballad 125 'Robin Hood and Little John': 'They happened to meet on a long narrow bridge / And neither of them would give way.' The bridge duel becomes iconic -- every later film and pantomime uses it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: The stranger steps up to fight Robin Hood with the poor man's weapon of the English commons, cheap and two-handed, needing no gentry training or royal license. Robin lays his bow aside and arms himself to match, so the fight will be fair. Which commoner's weapon is the duel fought with?
context: The quarterstaff was the standard peasant and yeoman weapon of medieval and early-modern England -- a two-handed wooden stave about six to nine feet long. Robin's own bow is put aside so the stranger is not disadvantaged. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: A huge stranger and Robin Hood trade blows above a brook in the old English ballads of Sherwood Forest, neither man willing to step aside. The blows come thick and fast, until one great stroke settles it. How does the duel end?
answer: the stranger knocks Robin into the brook
choices: the stranger knocks Robin into the brook
Robin knocks the stranger into the brook
the two men yield at the same moment
the stranger yields and swims away
context: Child 125: 'The blow it so bent his bones, / That he tumbled him into the brook.' The whole point of the story is that Robin -- the greatest outlaw in England -- is dunked in a stream by a total newcomer; that is why the man earns a place in the band. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal125.html.  (Legend.)

question: The Merry Men come running through Sherwood Forest at one loud signal from Robin Hood, the outlaw who robs the rich to help the poor. He wants them to meet the stranger he has just fought over a brook. What instrument does he sound to call them?
context: The ballad: 'He blowd a loud blast on his fine bugle-horn.' The bugle-horn -- a curved cattle-horn with a mouthpiece -- is the standard summoning-signal of the Sherwood band. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: One of the Merry Men stands godfather to the giant stranger in a mock baptism, to give him a new name in the band. He pours brook-water over the man's head and announces the name, turning the man's first and last names around. Which Merry Man performs the christening?
context: Child 125: 'William Stutely then said, this jocular blade / Shall be Godfather to him.' Stutely (also spelled Stukely or Stutley) is a Merry Man from several ballads. Much the Miller's Son, Will Scarlet, and Alan-a-Dale are all real named companions -- but the christening job in this ballad is Stutely's alone. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal125.html.  (Legend.)

question: Little John hires himself into the household of the Sheriff of Nottingham as a disguised servant, in the fifteenth-century poem 'A Gest of Robyn Hode.' Robin Hood's giant lieutenant is there to spy on the Sheriff. What false name does he give at the hiring?
context: A Gest of Robyn Hode, Fytte 3: 'Reynolde Grenelefe' is Little John's alias in the Sheriff's kitchens -- an in-joke, since 'green leaf' hints at the greenwood he has come from. Holderness is a real district of the East Riding of Yorkshire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Gest_of_Robyn_Hode.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood lends a ruined knight four hundred pounds in silver, in 'A Gest of Robyn Hode,' the earliest long Robin Hood ballad. The knight has fallen deeply into debt to the greedy Abbot of St Mary's Abbey and is about to lose his lands, so Little John rides out from Sherwood Forest to save him. What is the knight's name?
context: Fyttes 1-4 of the Gest turn on Robin's rescue of the poor knight Sir Richard at the Lee, who repays every penny with interest a year later. Sir Guy of Warwick is the hero of a different English romance; Sir Kay is Arthur's foster-brother; Aymer de Valence was a real Earl of Pembroke, unconnected. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Gest_of_Robyn_Hode.  (Legend.)

question: Little John goes to his grave far from Sherwood, English legend says, up north in the Peak District of Derbyshire. A churchyard there has kept an unusually long grave-mound for centuries, and a modern tombstone marks it, though nothing proves it is his. In which English village is the traditional grave shown?
context: St Michael's churchyard in the village of HATHERSAGE, Derbyshire, has for centuries been shown to visitors as Little John's grave -- an over-long mound with a modern tombstone. There is no historical proof, but the tradition is old. Barnsdale is Robin's Yorkshire haunt; Loxley is the village some legends give as Robin's birthplace; Kirklees is where Robin died. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_John.

question: The charioteer Loeg went out as usual to yoke the chariot on the morning of Cu Chulainn's last fight, in the Aided Con Culainn, and the Grey of Macha would not let him. The horse turned his left side against Loeg three times and would not be harnessed until Cu Chulainn came out. What did the Grey do as the harness went on?
answer: he wept tears of blood onto Cu Chulainn's feet
choices: he wept tears of blood onto Cu Chulainn's feet
he tore his own bridle-rein in his teeth
he cast his own shoe into the fire
he stamped a print into the flagstones
context: The tears-of-blood omen is one of the darkest images in the whole cycle; the Grey knows what the day will bring. Loeg had never been refused before that morning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liath_Macha_and_Dub_Sainglend  (Legend.)

question: Lugaid mac Con Roi held three magical spears at Cu Chulainn's last fight, and each was prophesied to kill a king. The killings came in a very deliberate order. His first spear did not take Cu Chulainn. Whom did it take instead?
answer: Loeg the charioteer -- 'the king of chariot-drivers'
choices: Loeg the charioteer -- 'the king of chariot-drivers'
the Grey of Macha -- 'the king of horses'
the Black of Saingliu -- 'the king of dark runners'
context: The three-spear order in the Aided Con Culainn: first spear takes Loeg (king of charioteers); second spear takes the Grey of Macha (king of horses); third spear takes Cu Chulainn himself. The prophecy attached to each spear is that it will fell a king, and each does. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1eg  (Legend.)

question: Loeg the charioteer set out alone into the fairy country while his lord lay ill for love of a woman of the Otherworld, in the tale called 'The Sickbed of Cu Chulainn.' He went to bring back a report on her, and a strange guide led him on the road. Who guided Loeg into the Otherworld?
answer: Li Ban, sister of the fairy Fand
choices: Li Ban, sister of the fairy Fand
Manannan mac Lir, sea-god of the wave
Cathbad the druid of Emain Macha
context: Li Ban is Fand's sister; she comes as messenger and takes Loeg into the Otherworld so he can describe Fand's country back to the bedridden Cu Chulainn. Manannan is Fand's own husband and closes the tale. The Morrigan and Cathbad are figures of a different cycle-strand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1eg  (Legend.)

question: Medb's warriors were holding off at a distance from the dead Cu Chulainn when the wounded Grey of Macha turned back from the water and charged into them. The horse was defending his master's body from being looted. The tradition counts the kill in specific numbers. What tally did the horse take?
answer: fifty men with his teeth and thirty with each hoof
choices: fifty men with his teeth and thirty with each hoof
twelve men with his teeth and twelve with each hoof
ninety men in total, evenly split among his four feet
a hundred and one -- one for each of the Fianna
context: The horse-tally is one of the most cited numbers in all of Irish heroic corpus: fifty by tooth, thirty by each of four hooves. It is the horse, not any man, that defends the corpse. The other three counts belong to no source. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liath_Macha_and_Dub_Sainglend  (Legend.)

question: The wounded Grey of Macha finished defending the corpse of Cu Chulainn and did not just run off to die. He went across the country to his master's foster-brother, Ulster's second warrior, the man who owed the vengeance, and led him back to the standing stone. Which foster-brother did the Grey lead there?
context: Conall Cernach is Cu Chulainn's foster-brother and the vengeance-taker of the Ulster Cycle; the Grey's guiding him to the body is what sets Conall on Lugaid mac Con Roi. Ferdiad was killed by Cu Chulainn himself at the Ford; Fergus was in Connacht exile; Loegaire had fled the beheading-bargain long before. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liath_Macha_and_Dub_Sainglend  (Legend.)

question: A mysterious host beneath the ocean brews ale in an enormous cauldron and invites the whole company of Norse gods, Aesir and Vanir alike, down to feast in his undersea hall. Which Norse figure is this undersea host?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna prose introduction (and Hymiskvida): Aegir (also called Hler or Gymir) is the sea-giant who hosts the gods in his undersea hall. Njord is the Vanir god of the coast (father of Freyr and Freyja). Jormungand is the Midgard serpent Thor will fight at Ragnarok. Utgarda-Loki is the giant-king who tricks Thor in the eastern lands.  (Legend.)

question: The gods at an undersea feast praise one serving-man for his skill with cup and platter: he serves so smoothly that he can barely be seen moving. Two named servants wait on the tables that night. Jealousy rises in one uninvited guest. What is the name of the servant whose praise sets off the trouble?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna prose introduction: Aegir's two serving-men are Fimafeng and Eldir. The gods praise Fimafeng, and Loki kills him on the spot. Eldir is the second servant, who later meets Loki at the door when he tries to come back in. Skirnir is Freyr's messenger. Byggvir is Freyr's own servant, present at the feast and mocked by Loki later.  (Legend.)

question: Loki, the trickster god, comes uninvited to an undersea feast and cannot bear to hear the gods praising a serving-man for pouring their ale so smoothly. In a fit of jealousy he does something terrible in the middle of the hall, and they drive him out at once. What does Loki do to the servant?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna prose introduction: Loki, in jealousy at the praise the servant gets, kills Fimafeng on the spot. The gods shake their shields, howl at him, and drive him out into the forest before returning to their drinking. Loki will not stay outside for long.  (Legend.)

question: Unferth trades barbs with the hero at Heorot in Beowulf, and the same old Germanic form returns in the undersea hall of the Norse gods. There Loki works his way down the benches, one god at a time and one shame at a time, in matched verse. What is the name of the form?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna: the poem is the great mythic exemplar of a flyting -- a formal verse-duel of insults. The same form appears in Beowulf when Unferth trades barbs with Beowulf at Heorot (lines 499-606), and later in Scots poetry. A saga is a prose narrative; a rune-cast is a divination; a nithing-pole is a real cursing-post erected against an enemy.  (Legend.)
