question: Odin hardly denies the charge when Loki rounds on him in the undersea hall of the poem Lokasenna and throws the island of Samsey in his face. The trickster has forced his way back to the table and is shaming each god in turn. What does Loki say Odin did on Samsey?
answer: dressed as a woman to work seidr magic
choices: dressed as a woman to work seidr magic
raised nine dead men to fight for him
sold his other eye for a second sip
murdered a sleeping king in his bed
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna 24: Loki throws in Odin's face that on Samsey he beat a drum like a seeress and dressed as a woman to work seidr, a magic considered unmanly for a warrior. Odin does not really deny it -- he answers with an accusation about Loki's own strange forms (Loki once became a mare and bore Odin's own horse Sleipnir).  (Legend.)

question: Frigg, Odin's wife, takes her turn as the argument in the undersea hall grows uglier. Loki accuses her to her face of having gone to bed with two of Odin's own kin while Odin was long away from Asgard. Which two brothers of Odin does Loki name?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna 26: Loki accuses Frigg of having slept with Vili and Ve, Odin's brothers, while Odin was away. Snorri's Ynglinga saga 3 echoes the same charge. Hoenir and Lodur are Odin's companions in creation-stories; Baldr and Hodr are Frigg's own sons; Bragi and Njord are guests at the same feast, insulted separately.  (Legend.)

question: Freyja sits on the benches of the undersea hall when Loki reaches her, and he does not spare her either. He accuses her of the widest shame he can invent, and the sharpest point of it is that among her lovers she has taken one member of her own family. Which relative does Loki name?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna 30, 32: Loki accuses Freyja of having slept with every one of the Aesir and specifically with her own brother Freyr. Sibling-marriage was normal among the Vanir before their peace with the Aesir (Njord had married his own sister in Vanaheim, per Ynglinga saga 4). Njord is her father; Hnoss is her daughter by Od, her own missing husband.  (Legend.)

question: Loki storms out of the undersea hall at last, with every god insulted, and throws one parting curse back at his host. It promises that the hall itself will not survive Ragnarok, the end of the world. What does Loki promise the hall?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna 65: Loki curses Aegir's hall that fire shall take it -- a curse fulfilled at Ragnarok when Surt's flames burn the nine worlds. The prose ending of the poem then names Loki's own coming doom: he will be bound with his own son's guts under a serpent whose venom drips on his face until the world ends.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson, setting down the Norse myths around the year 1220, tells his readers that the trickster Loki lives with the Aesir gods in Asgard but is not truly an Aesir by blood. In the Prose Edda, what race are Loki's mother and father?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 33: Loki's father is the giant Farbauti ('cruel-striker', a poetic name for lightning) and his mother is the giantess Laufey (also called Nal, 'needle'). This giant-blood plus Asgard-oath split is why the gods keep having to punish and forgive him rather than execute him outright. The Vanir are the other tribe of gods (Njord, Freyr, Freyja); the elves and dwarves are separate races again.  (Legend.)

question: Loki walks uninvited into the sea-giant Aegir's undersea feast in the poem Lokasenna, and the other Aesir want him thrown out at once. Odin tells them to fetch him a cup and reminds them of an old bond. What bond does Odin invoke?
answer: Odin and Loki are sworn brothers
choices: Odin and Loki are sworn brothers
Loki once saved Odin's life at sea
Loki is married to Odin's daughter
context: Lokasenna 9: Odin says he will not drink at the feast unless a cup is brought for Loki as well, because he and Loki once mingled their blood as sworn brothers. This oath -- an Aesir king and a giant-born trickster bound as brothers -- is the crack in Asgard through which everything Loki does gets in.  (Legend.)

question: A woman stands bowl in hand over the bound Loki, in the single great scene Snorri gives her. She is his Asgard wife and the mother of Narfi and Vali, and that scene makes her one of the tenderest figures in Norse myth. What is her name?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 33 (household), Gylfaginning 50 (the bowl-scene): Sigyn is Loki's Asgard wife and mother of Narfi and Vali. Angrboda is Loki's giantess-lover in Jotunheim, mother of Fenrir, Jormungandr, and Hel. Skadi is the giantess-goddess who fastens the snake over Loki's face. Idunn is the keeper of the golden apples.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr and Sindri took on the dwarves called the Sons of Ivaldi in the smithing contest Snorri tells of. The gods judged which of the six treasures was finest, and the winner would go with its god into every battle afterward. Which treasure won?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the gods judge Mjolnir the greatest of the six treasures because it will defend Asgard from the giants. Gungnir (Odin's spear, never misses) and Skidbladnir (Freyr's ship, folds into a pocket) were the Sons of Ivaldi's treasures. Draupnir (Odin's gold ring that drips eight copies of itself every ninth night) was Sindri and Brokkr's, alongside Mjolnir and the golden boar Gullinbursti.  (Legend.)

question: Loki stood cornered with his head forfeit, and he tried to buy off Brokkr with a rich payment in its place. The dwarf refused, so Loki bolted. Only one god was fast enough to run him down. Which god caught Loki and brought him back to Brokkr?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Thor catches Loki and drags him back for the dwarf. Heimdall is the watchman at Bifrost. Tyr is the one-handed god of oaths. Vidar is Odin's silent avenger-son who will one day rip Fenrir's jaws apart. Note how ready Thor is to see Loki punished; he owes Brokkr a debt because the very reason Mjolnir's haft is too short is that Loki (as a fly) bit Brokkr during the forging.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr came at Loki with the knife to collect the head he had won in the contest of treasures. Loki pointed to the exact words of the bet and played a lawyer's trick: the dwarf could have the head, but one rule made it impossible to cut the head off at all. What rule did Loki name?
answer: Brokkr may not touch Loki's neck
choices: Brokkr may not touch Loki's neck
Brokkr must take the head without spilling a drop of blood
Brokkr must first speak Loki's true name backwards
Brokkr must take the head with his bare hand and no tool
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki tells Brokkr he may have the head but may not touch the neck -- because the wager named the head only. Brokkr cannot cut off a head without cutting a neck, and the exact wording of the bet gives Loki the wriggle. The move is one of the earliest surviving Indo-European trickster escape-clauses; it echoes into medieval legal riddles (compare Shylock's pound of flesh but no blood in Merchant of Venice).  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr pressed his own tool against Loki's lip and it would not go through the skin, however hard he pushed. Snorri says the dwarf then wished aloud for a very specific replacement, and the wish was granted at once. What did Brokkr wish for that finally punched through the lip?
choices: a spark from the forge of Muspelheim
the point of a giant's tooth
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Brokkr wishes for his brother Sindri's awl, which is sharper, and it appears at once and punches straight through. Sindri is the master-smith of the two brothers; Brokkr is his bellows-worker and hands. Even in this dark comic scene the older-brother-and-younger-brother rhythm of the dwarf pair is preserved.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr threaded a length of leather thong through the holes he had punched in Loki's lips and stitched up the trickster's mouth, so that Loki could make no mischief with words for a while. Snorri names that thong, the one piece of cord in Norse literature with a name of its own. What is the thong called?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the thong is called Vartari. Gleipnir is the ribbon-thin fetter that binds Fenrir the wolf (made from six impossible things -- a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, and so on). Vidofnir is the rooster on Yggdrasil's crown. Sviagris is the gold ring of the Yngling king Adils.  (Legend.)

question: Loki went back to Asgard with his mouth sewn up by the dwarf Brokkr, so that the trickster could boast no more. Snorri Sturluson closes the scene with one grim note about what Loki's face carried from that day on. What did Snorri say remained?
answer: the scars where he tore the thong out of his own lips
choices: the scars where he tore the thong out of his own lips
a thin silver line where each stitch had been
a thong knotted at each corner of his mouth
a set of iron pins where the thong had been
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki rips the leather thong Vartari out of his own lips and the scars remain. The image of a trickster whose face carries the record of every lie he has been silenced for is one of the sharpest character-details in Snorri -- one of the very few places the Prose Edda lingers on a physical mark left by punishment.  (Legend.)

question: Loki cut off a goddess's beautiful long hair while she slept, and the smithing contest that ended with his stitched mouth grew out of that one prank. He then had to find dwarves who could replace it, or die. Whose hair had Loki cut off?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki cut off Sif's golden hair as a prank; Thor (Sif's husband) threatened to break every bone in Loki's body unless he brought her back real hair. Loki went to the Sons of Ivaldi, who spun the new hair from gold, and also produced Gungnir and Skidbladnir on the same visit. That is why Loki then goaded Brokkr and Sindri into a rival contest -- and how the whole six-treasures wager (and Loki's own head) came to be at stake.  (Legend.)

question: Loki flees Asgard after bringing about the death of the god Baldr, with the other gods sworn to vengeance. He hides in the mountains of the middle world and builds a strange little house on a lonely peak. What is odd about the house?
answer: it has one door on each of its four sides
choices: it has one door on each of its four sides
it is a tower with a single narrow door he can defend
it stands on high stilts with a ladder he can pull up
it is dug entirely into the earth with no windows
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50: Loki's house has four doors, one on each of the four sides, so he can watch the approach from every direction at once. The other three are inventions -- plausible watchtower shapes, but Snorri names only the four-door design.  (Legend.)

question: Loki leaves his house on the peak by day, takes the shape of a fish and slips into a waterfall, catching food and watching for pursuers. Snorri names both the fish and the waterfall. What shape does Loki take, and in what waterfall does he hide?
answer: a salmon in the waterfall of Franang
choices: a salmon in the waterfall of Franang
a pike in the waterfall of Andlang
an eel in the waterfall of Elivagar
a trout in the waterfall of Vimur
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50: Loki becomes a salmon and hides in the waterfall of Franang ('the glistening'). The other three pair real Norse cosmological rivers/streams (Elivagar the primordial ice-rivers of Ginnungagap; Vimur the river Thor wades) with wrong fish -- the point is that only the salmon is named in the source, and salmon are the traditional wise-fish of Northern myth (compare Fionn's Salmon of Knowledge in Irish story).  (Legend.)

question: Loki sits by his fire one evening in a mountain hut beside a waterfall, on the run from the other gods. He twists linen thread into a shape no one in the nine worlds has ever made before. What has Loki invented?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50: Loki weaves the world's first fishing-net from linen thread. When he sees the gods coming he throws the half-made net into the fire -- but the ashes preserve the pattern, and the gods copy it and use that first net to catch him at his own waterfall. It is a classic 'trickster caught by his own new tool' motif. The other three are real Northern catching-devices, but Snorri names only the net.  (Legend.)

question: The gods drag Loki to a cave to punish him, and they start with his two sons by his Asgard wife Sigyn, Narfi and Vali. They do not kill the boys with their own hands. They turn Vali into an animal, and in that shape he kills his brother. What animal do the gods turn Vali into?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50 and the prose epilogue to Lokasenna: the gods turn Vali into a wolf, and he tears his brother Narfi (Nari) to pieces. The Loki-son called Vali here must not be confused with Odin's avenger-son Vali, who kills the blind god Hodr to avenge Baldr -- two different figures with the same name in Norse myth. The wolf is Norse myth's own recurring image of a family-killer (Fenrir will kill Odin at Ragnarok).  (Legend.)

question: The gods stretch Loki over three flat stones in the cave, one under his shoulders, one under his loins and one under his knees. Snorri says they lash him there with a cord that then hardens into iron. What cord do the gods use?
choices: a rope braided from his son Narfi's bones
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50 and the prose epilogue to Lokasenna: the gods use Narfi's entrails, which then harden into iron -- an unusually cruel detail even by Norse standards, and one Snorri does not soften. The other three are body-derived bonds Snorri does NOT name; the horror in the source is specifically the entrails, laid on the father by his own son.  (Legend.)

question: One goddess steps forward when Loki lies bound to the three stones, ready to add a cruelty of her own to the punishment. She fastens a snake above his face so that its venom will drip on him day after day. Who fastens the snake?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50: Skadi ('shadow') fastens a serpent above Loki's face so its venom will drip on him. Her father was the giant Thjazi, whom the gods had killed after Loki lured him into their fire-trap; Skadi had marched armed on Asgard for weregild and been made a goddess by marriage instead. The snake above Loki is her private revenge, at last, on the man behind her father's death. Frigg is Odin's wife; Freyja is the leader of the Vanir goddesses; Idunn keeps the golden apples.  (Legend.)

question: Sigyn refuses to abandon Loki in the cave, faithful even to a bound and shameful husband. She takes her place beside him under the dripping serpent and holds one small thing above his face, day and night, until the world ends. What does Sigyn hold above him to protect him?
answer: a wooden bowl to catch the venom
choices: a wooden bowl to catch the venom
a mirror to reflect the venom back
a shroud to smother the snake
her own cupped hands to gather the venom
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50 and the prose epilogue to Lokasenna: Sigyn holds a wooden bowl above her husband's face and catches the venom as it drips. The image of a wife standing over her criminal husband's centuries of torment is one of the tenderest in Norse myth -- and one of the earliest depictions of it survives in stone on the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria from around 900 CE, carved by a Christian mason who put it beside a Crucifixion scene.  (Legend.)

question: A young warrior in a gold crown led a band of men to the gate of Tara during King Nuada's feast. Tara was the hall of the Tuatha De Danann, the fair god-people said to have ruled Ireland before humans. Who was the stranger?
context: Lugh Lamhfhada, grandson of the Fomorian tyrant Balor through his mother Ethniu, arrived at Tara during King Nuada's feast wearing a diadem and leading a company of warriors. Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired), CELT edition, sec. 53-55.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh reached the gate of the royal hall at Tara during King Nuada's feast, and the doorkeeper challenged him with the one question asked of every man who came. What was that question?
choices: How many battles have you won?
context: 'What art do you practice? For no one without an art enters Tara.' The rule turned the doorkeeper's post into a filter: Tara admitted skill, not birth. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 53.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh came through the gate of Tara at last, and what he had done at the door to get in won the young god a famous title. He is still remembered by it: Samildanach. What does Samildanach mean?
answer: Equally skilled in all the arts
choices: Equally skilled in all the arts
context: Samildanach is the honor Lugh earned at the gate by claiming every craft at once. His other epithet, Lamhfhada ('Long-Arm'), belongs to his skill with the spear. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55; Wikipedia, Lugh.  (Legend.)

question: 'I am a wright,' the young warrior-god Lugh said to the doorkeeper at the royal hall of Tara, naming his skill as a builder in wood. The doorkeeper answered that Tara already had a wright among the Tuatha De Danann gods, the maker of the shafts for their spears, and he named him. Who was Tara's wright?
context: Luchta was the wright (carpenter) of the Tuatha De who made the shafts for their spears. Goibniu was the smith, Credne the brazier, Dian Cecht the physician. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: The doorkeeper at Tara heard the young hero Lugh say, 'I am a smith,' and he had his answer. Tara already had a smith of that trade among the Tuatha De Danann, the one who would forge the weapons that armed them at the coming Second Battle of Moytura. Who was Tara's smith?
context: Goibniu forged the spearheads and blades of the Tuatha De and lent his name to the eternal Feast of Goibniu whose ale kept the gods young. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh stood at the gate of the royal hall of Tara naming craft after craft, hoping to be let into the king's service, and he said, 'I am a physician.' The doorkeeper answered that Tara already had a physician, the healer who would restore the fallen warriors of the Tuatha De Danann at the Second Battle of Moytura. Who was Tara's physician?
context: Dian Cecht was the healer-god of the Tuatha De and would tend the Well of Slaine to revive the wounded at Moytura. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh named craft after craft at the gate of the royal hall at Tara: smith, physician, warrior, harper, poet, historian, brazier. Each time the doorkeeper answered that the Tuatha De Danann already had a master for that work. Then Lugh saw the game and asked one last question. What did he ask that opened the gate?
answer: 'But have you one man who is ALL of these at once?'
choices: 'But have you one man who is ALL of these at once?'
'But which of your craftsmen can also swing a sword in the shield-wall?'
'But which of your smiths is also a poet of the court?'
'But which of your masters can beat the king at fidchell?'
context: 'Ask the king whether he has one man who possesses all these arts.' No craftsman inside could claim every trade Lugh had claimed; the doorkeeper ran to Nuada, who ordered the gate opened. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh claimed at last to be a brazier, a worker in brass and the softer metals, after naming craft after craft at the gate of Tara. The doorkeeper answered that the Tuatha De Danann already had a brazier, and he named their master craftsman in that softer metal. What was the name he gave?
context: Credne Cerd was the brass-worker (cerd) of the Tuatha De, distinct from Goibniu the iron-smith. He would later forge the silver hand for Nuada. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: Tailtiu cleared Ireland's plains for planting, and Irish legend says the labor killed her. Her foster-son, a young hero-god, founded a harvest festival in her name on the first of August, one of the four great festivals that divide the medieval Irish year. What is this harvest festival called?
context: Lughnasadh ('Lugh's assembly') is the harvest festival Lugh founded in honor of his foster-mother Tailtiu. It survives as the August bank-holiday Lughnasa. Wikipedia, Lugh.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood rode into the three oldest surviving ballads about him, all written down in medieval England: A Gest of Robyn Hode, Robin Hood and the Monk, and Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne. The movies set a sweetheart named Maid Marian at his side. How often did her name show up in those three?
context: Maid Marian is never mentioned in any of the earliest extant Robin Hood ballads. The only woman in the Gest is the villainous Prioress of Kirklees, who eventually causes Robin's death. Marian is a much later addition to the legend.

question: A woman bled Robin Hood to death when he came to her for healing, in A Gest of Robyn Hode, printed in England around the year 1500 and the oldest full-length story of him. She was no sweetheart, and no other woman had a real part in the plot. Who was she?
context: In the Gest, the Prioress of Kirklees is the one woman with a role: she bleeds Robin to death under the pretence of a medicinal blood-letting. Marian does not appear at all in the Gest. The May-Queen belongs to the folk games. The Sheriff has no named wife in the ballads.  (Legend.)

question: Adam de la Halle, a poet in Arras, took a French pastourelle, one of the songs about a knight meeting a shepherdess, and turned it into a musical play around 1283. In his play a knight rides up to the shepherdess Marion and tries to carry her off. Whom does Marion choose over the knight?
choices: no one -- she runs into the woods alone
context: In Adam de la Halle's Le Jeu de Robin et Marion (c. 1283), the shepherdess Marion resists the knight and stays with her shepherd-lover Robin. The play is considered the first musical drama on a non-religious subject written in French; it is the seed from which the English May-games pair of Robin and Marian later grew.

question: An English village crowned a girl its queen, named her Marian and set a boy beside her as Robin. The pair had crossed the Channel from France, out of a musical play by Adam de la Halle, and got mixed into one of the great village festivals. Which festival was it?
context: In the English May-Day games a village girl was crowned May Queen and called Marian, paired with a village boy playing Robin. Twelfth Night and Plough Monday had their own customs (the Lord of Misrule; the plough-blessing). Michaelmas was a rent day, not a Marian festival.

question: Anthony Munday paired the festival Marian and the outlaw Robin in a play of 1598, after the two had long been separate figures. His Marian was really a noblewoman under a different name, and she became Marian only on fleeing to join Robin in the woods. What was her real name in the play?
context: In Anthony Munday's plays The Downfall of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1598) and The Death of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1601), the noblewoman Matilda takes the name Marian on joining Robin in the greenwood. Munday's two plays fixed Marian as Robin's wife and a full member of the outlaw band, the shape we know today.  (Legend.)

question: Manannan mac Lir set the point of a sword at a man's chest, and that man could not tell a single lie. No armor or shield could turn the blade aside, and no wound it dealt could be healed. It was the third of the sea-god's great treasures. What was the sword called?
choices: Excalibur, the sword of the stone
context: Fragarach ('the Answerer') sliced through any armor and compelled its target to answer any question truthfully. Manannan later gave it to Lugh, and it walked through the whole later mythology. Wikipedia, Manannan mac Lir.  (Legend.)

question: Manannan mac Lir fostered a young hero as his own son and armed him with three great treasures: the boat Wave-Sweeper that sailed itself, the horse Enbarr that ran over land and wave alike, and a truth-sword. Who was Manannan's foster-son?
context: Manannan fostered Lugh in the otherworldly islands and armed him for the coming war with the Fomorians. Wikipedia, Enbarr; Wikipedia, Manannan mac Lir.  (Legend.)

question: A dead hero sat down to an endless banquet in the paradise islands of Manannan mac Lir, far out in the western sea, where nobody grew old. The first and most famous of these otherworld islands was called Emain Ablach, a place of swans and yew trees. What does its name mean?
context: Emain Ablach ('Emhain of the Apples') is the paradise island of Manannan, filled with swans and yews and apple trees always in fruit. Wikipedia, Emain Ablach.  (Legend.)

question: The wounded king of the Arthurian romances was carried to a paradise island to be healed, centuries after the stories of Manannan mac Lir's Emain Ablach. The island's name carries the same meaning as Emain Ablach's, and scholars trace it directly back to Manannan's realm. What was the Arthurian island called?
context: Avalon (Insula Avallonis in Geoffrey of Monmouth) shares its name and its whole picture with Emain Ablach: apple-orchard paradise where the wounded king is taken to be healed. Wikipedia, Emain Ablach.  (Legend.)

question: Manannan mac Lir took charge of the Tuatha De Danann when the Milesians defeated them and drove them underground. He allotted each of the surviving gods a sidhe mound and fed them all at an eternal banquet whose ale kept them young forever. What was that feast called?
context: The Feast of Goibniu (Fled Goibnenn) was the eternal banquet whose ale conferred everlasting youth on the Tuatha De after their retreat into the sidhe mounds. Wikipedia, Manannan mac Lir.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess of Mount Olympus took her new invention, a double-reed pipe called the aulos, to a forest pool to practice. She saw her own cheeks puff out in the water like two ugly balloons and flung the pipe away forever. Which goddess was she?
context: Athena, patron of arts and crafts, invented the double-flute but cast it away when she saw how it disfigured her face; her curse falls on the satyr Marsyas, who picks it up. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'; Ovid, Fasti 6.697-710.  (Legend.)

question: Marsyas, a Phrygian satyr, found a discarded double-flute called the aulos and grew so proud of his playing that he challenged the god Apollo to a music contest. When the day came he brought his aulos, the loud reed-flute of country music. Which instrument did Apollo bring?
context: The contest is famously flute-against-lyre: Marsyas's wild reed-piping against Apollo's ordered stringed music. The syrinx (pan-pipes) belongs to Pan; the sistrum is an Egyptian temple rattle; the tambourine is the frame-drum of the ecstatic cults. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.383-400.  (Legend.)

question: Marsyas agreed to terms with the god Apollo before a single note was played in their music contest, sure of his skill on the aulos flute. It was a bargain no mortal should ever make with a god. What did the loser of the contest have to submit to?
answer: whatever the winner wished to do to him
choices: whatever the winner wished to do to him
a year of silent exile from Phrygia
context: The terms were open: the winner could inflict any penalty at all on the loser. It is a bargain made by trickster-figures and by fools; Marsyas is here the fool. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.383-400.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo and the satyr Marsyas played the first round of their music contest to a tie, both of them beautifully. To break the tie Apollo produced a new challenge, one he could meet on his own instrument but Marsyas could never match on his flute. What was Apollo's trick?
answer: he played his instrument upside-down and dared Marsyas to do the same
choices: he played his instrument upside-down and dared Marsyas to do the same
he sang along with his instrument in the god's own voice
he played with his eyes shut behind a thick cloth
he handed his instrument to a Muse to play in his stead
context: Apollo inverted his lyre and played it just as sweetly upside-down, then challenged Marsyas to do the same with the aulos -- a physical impossibility for a flute-player whose breath drives the reeds. The Muses ruled for Apollo. Source: Theoi Project, 'Marsyas'; Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo carried out his punishment of the satyr Marsyas in the Phrygian countryside, not up on Mount Olympus. Marsyas had lost a music contest to the god, and the winner's prize was to do anything he wished to the loser. Apollo chose one kind of tree from which to hang him upside down. What tree was it?
context: Ancient tradition (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.391-393) places the flaying on a pine near Celaenae in Phrygia; the pine was already sacred to Pan and the satyrs. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.391-393; Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'.  (Legend.)

question: Ovid tells in his Metamorphoses how Apollo began to peel the skin from the satyr Marsyas, who hung from a tree in the Phrygian countryside after losing a music contest to the god. Marsyas cried out to Apollo in a single line, one of the most quoted in all of Latin poetry. What did Marsyas cry?
answer: Why do you tear me from myself?
choices: Why do you tear me from myself?
Give me back my breath, Apollo!
context: The Latin is 'quid me mihi detrahis?' -- Metamorphoses 6.385. The line has been read for two millennia as the cry of every artist stripped of his art. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.385.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo faced a second flute-player long after the death of Marsyas: the goat-god Pan. A single mortal sat as judge, a king who happened to be listening in the hills, and he gave his verdict for Pan and against Apollo. Who was the mortal judge?
context: Midas of Phrygia -- the same king with the golden touch -- happened by while Pan and Apollo played, and alone judged for Pan. Priam ruled Troy; Croesus ruled Lydia; Tantalus is famous for his crime and eternal thirst. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.146-179; Wikipedia, 'Midas'.  (Legend.)

question: A king pulled a tall Phrygian cap over his shameful new ears, reshaped on the spot by the god Apollo for a verdict that insulted him. Only one servant, his barber, saw them. Unable to hold the secret in, the barber dug a hole, whispered the truth into it and covered it over. What later grew from the hole and betrayed the secret to the wind?
context: Reeds grew from the covered hole, and every time the wind blew through them they whispered aloud 'King Midas has ass's ears'. The story is Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.180-193. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.180-193; Wikipedia, 'Midas'.  (Legend.)

question: Martin, a young Roman soldier, rode up to a city gate on a bitter winter night and met a beggar. He had no coins on him, so he drew his sword and cut one piece of his own gear in half. What did he cut?
context: The scene comes from Sulpicius Severus's Life of Saint Martin, chapter 3, written from Sulpicius's own conversations with Martin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.  (Legend.)

question: The young Roman soldier Martin drew his sword for a nearly naked beggar at a city gate in northern Gaul on a freezing night. Centuries later that city became famous across Europe for the enormous Gothic cathedral built at its heart. What city was it?
context: Roman-era Amiens was called Samarobriva. Martin was posted there with the Gallic cavalry around age 18. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.

question: Martin rode with the Gallic cavalry, a tribune's son pressed into service in his mid-teens, but he was no Gaul by birth. His birthplace of Savaria sat far to the east, in a province of the middle Danube, one of four the empire cut out of that frontier. Which province was it?
context: Martin was born around 316 in Savaria (modern Szombathely in western Hungary), inside the Roman province of Pannonia. Roman law required soldiers' sons to enter the army; Martin was pressed into cavalry service in his mid-teens. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.

question: Martin lay asleep the night after he met the beggar, not yet baptised, and Sulpicius Severus tells what he dreamed. The beggar stood before him again in a crowd of angels, wrapped in Martin's gift and saying Martin's name. Who did Martin see the beggar as?
context: Sulpicius Severus reports the words of the dream in Vita Martini 3: 'Martin, still only a catechumen, has clothed me with this cloak.' Martin was baptised at the following Easter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.  (Legend.)

question: Martin's commander heard him say he could no longer serve as a soldier, just as his unit was about to fight the Alemanni at Worms. The commander called it cowardice, so Martin made a startling offer to prove he was not afraid of the enemy. What did he offer to do?
answer: Stand unarmed in the front line of the army
choices: Stand unarmed in the front line of the army
Fight three of the enemy champions at once
Ride alone into the enemy camp with a message
Take his commander's place at the very front rank
context: Martin declared 'I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight,' and volunteered to stand at the front of the army without weapon or shield. The battle never happened -- the enemy sued for peace, and Martin was released. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.  (Legend.)

question: The townspeople of Tours tricked the hermit Martin out of the woods in 371 and into their city to make him bishop. He had protested strongly against the choice and would never have come willingly. How did they get him through the gates?
answer: They said a sick woman needed him to bless her
choices: They said a sick woman needed him to bless her
They said the city was under attack and needed prayers
They said his mother had arrived and was asking for him
They said a hunting bear was loose in the marketplace
context: Once Martin was inside the walls the townspeople of Tours acclaimed him bishop on the spot, and the neighbouring bishops confirmed the acclamation despite his protests. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.  (Legend.)

question: Martin, bishop of Tours, turned his back on the bishop's palace and made his own cell in a soft rock cliff above the Loire. The monastery he founded there stood just outside the city on the riverbank, and its name is still remembered today. What was it called?
context: The cliff-cells are still visible in the tufa above the Loire. Cluny, Fontevraud, and Fecamp are all famous French monasteries -- but they are all founded many centuries after Martin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.

question: Martin kept one half of his famous garment when he gave the beggar the other, and after his death the Frankish kings held that half as a relic in their treasury. The relic had a specific Latin name, which became one of the most productive words in the whole of medieval Europe. What is that Latin word?
context: The other three -- toga, sagum, palla -- are all real Roman garments, but the Frankish relic of Martin's half-cloak is specifically called the cappa. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.

question: One of the twelve men Jesus chose to travel with him sat at a customs booth on the trade road by the Sea of Galilee, collecting tolls for Rome. Tax collectors like him were hated by their fellow Jews. Which of the Twelve was he?
context: Matthew 9:9. In first-century Judea, publicans -- men who bought the right to collect Roman customs and taxes and skimmed a living off the top -- were treated as collaborators with the occupying power. Matthew's fellow Jews grouped them in a single scornful phrase with sinners.

question: Jesus walked along the lakeshore at Capernaum and stopped at a customs booth, where Matthew sat taking tolls for Rome. Jesus spoke only two words. Matthew stood up at once, left his money on the table and never went back. What did Jesus say?
context: Matthew 9:9: 'and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.' Mark and Luke tell the same scene, using Matthew's other name -- Levi.

question: Jesus called a tax collector away from his customs booth by the Sea of Galilee, and the Gospel of Matthew named the man Matthew. Mark and Luke told the same scene but gave him a completely different name. What name did they use?
context: Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 name him Levi (Mark adds that he was 'the son of Alphaeus'). Christian tradition identifies Levi and Matthew as the same man -- he seems to have gone by both.

question: Matthew threw open his own house right after he was called and put on a great banquet for Jesus. The Pharisees, watching from outside, were scandalised by the guest list. The gospels of Matthew and Luke summed up the crowd at the tables in one blunt phrase. What phrase was it?
context: Luke 5:29 says Levi 'made him a great feast in his own house', and Matthew 9:10 notes the guests were 'many publicans and sinners' -- fellow tax collectors and the outcasts who kept them company.

question: A bishop named Papias wrote a note about Matthew around the year 130, and the church historian Eusebius later saved it in his Church History. Papias said Matthew first collected Jesus's sayings in one language before they reached the Greek world. Which language did Papias name?
context: Papias, quoted in Eusebius Church History 3.39: 'Matthew collected the oracles [logia] in the Hebrew language, and each one interpreted them as best he could.' The gospel we now read is in Greek; what Papias meant by the Hebrew original is one of the oldest puzzles in New Testament study.

question: Caravaggio painted his Calling of Saint Matthew for the Contarelli Chapel in Rome, one of three canvases of the same apostle for that one small room. All three have been on those chapel walls since around 1600. In which Rome church is that chapel?
context: The Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi holds all three Caravaggio Matthew paintings: The Calling on the left wall, The Martyrdom on the right, and The Inspiration over the altar between them.

question: Caravaggio set a third canvas above the altar of the Contarelli Chapel in Rome, between two other scenes from the apostle Matthew's life. The Calling hung on one wall and the Martyrdom on the wall opposite, all three in the same small room. What did the third painting show?
answer: Matthew being dictated to by an angel
choices: Matthew being dictated to by an angel
Matthew washing the feet of a beggar
Matthew preaching to a crowd in Ethiopia
Matthew asleep during a storm at sea
context: The altarpiece is Caravaggio's The Inspiration of Saint Matthew (1602). Matthew sits at a writing desk while an angel leans in from above, counting off points on its fingers -- the moment of the gospel's composition.

question: Jason sailed the Argo to Colchis on the Black Sea to win the Golden Fleece from its king. The king's daughter, a sorceress, fell in love with Jason at first sight and helped him survive every deadly test her father set. What was her name?
context: Medea, priestess of the witch-goddess Hecate, was a princess of Colchis. Hera and Athena arranged the love through Aphrodite. Apollonius, Argonautica 3.  (Legend.)

question: Medea, a sorceress and princess of Colchis on the Black Sea, fell in love with the Greek hero Jason. She helped him steal the Golden Fleece from her father's sacred grove, betraying father and country for love. Which king of Colchis was her father?
context: Aeetes ruled Colchis at the far end of the Black Sea and was Medea's father. Pelias sent Jason for the Fleece; Creon ruled Corinth; Polydectes is from the Perseus story.  (Legend.)

question: Medea, daughter of King Aeetes of Colchis, slipped Jason an ointment made from a mountain herb before his first trial: yoking her father's fire-breathing bulls and ploughing a field with them. He smeared it on his skin, shield and sword. For one day it made him proof against two things. What were they?
context: The ointment guarded him against the bulls' fire and any weapon's blade for one day. Apollonius, Argonautica 3.828-878.  (Legend.)

question: The Khalkotauroi were a pair of fire-breathing bulls, forged by the smith-god Hephaestus and given to King Aeetes of Colchis as a gift. Before Jason could try for the Golden Fleece, Aeetes ordered him to yoke them and plough a field. Their hooves were made of one metal. Which metal?
context: The Khalkotauroi had bronze hooves and breathed fire from their nostrils. Medea's ointment guarded Jason as he wrestled each bull down to the yoke.  (Legend.)

question: Jason faced three impossible tasks in Colchis before King Aeetes would hand over the Golden Fleece. The second was to plough a great field behind a pair of fire-breathing bulls, then seed the furrows with a bag of serpent's teeth. As Jason walked along scattering the teeth, something rose out of the ground behind him. What sprang up?
context: They were called the Spartoi, 'sown men' -- the same seed-crop Cadmus once sowed at Thebes.  (Legend.)

question: Jason was sowing a ploughed field with a serpent's teeth at King Aeetes's command. As he scattered them, men with drawn spears sprang out of the furrows behind him, ready to cut him down. But Medea, the king's own daughter and a sorceress, had whispered a trick to Jason the night before. What did he do?
answer: Threw a rock into their middle so they killed each other
choices: Threw a rock into their middle so they killed each other
Blew a horn that sent them back into the earth
Sang a lullaby that put them to sleep
Held up a bronze mirror so they turned to stone
context: Not knowing who had thrown it, the sown men turned on one another and cut each other down until none was left. Apollonius, Argonautica 3.1354-1407.  (Legend.)

question: The Golden Fleece, the shining hide of a magical ram, hung on an oak tree in the sacred grove of the war-god Ares, far away in Colchis. King Aeetes had set an enormous serpent coiled around the tree to keep any thief from taking it. What was uncanny about this serpent that made it such a perfect guard?
choices: It could not be wounded by iron
context: Ladon at the Hesperides had a hundred heads; Argus Panoptes had a hundred eyes; the Colchian serpent's uncanny mark was sleeplessness.  (Legend.)

question: Jason had yoked the bulls and beaten the earth-born warriors of Colchis, but King Aeetes still refused to hand over the Golden Fleece. So Medea led Jason by night into the sacred grove of Ares, where an enormous serpent lay coiled around the oak that held the Fleece. She did one thing to the beast so that Jason could climb the tree and take the prize. What did she do?
answer: Sang a charm and sprinkled its eyes with the juice of magic herbs
choices: Sang a charm and sprinkled its eyes with the juice of magic herbs
Cut off all its heads with the harpe sword
Traded her own life to it for the Fleece
context: For the first time in its life the serpent slept. The harpe belongs to the Perseus story; there was no lamb offering here.  (Legend.)

question: King Pelias of Iolcus refused to give up his nephew Jason's rightful throne. So Medea gave the king's grown daughters a demonstration: she chopped up an old ram, dropped it into her cauldron with her secret herbs, and out sprang a young lamb. Most of the daughters then cut their aging father to pieces and dropped him into the cauldron. What went wrong?
answer: Medea did not add the herbs, and Pelias stayed dead
choices: Medea did not add the herbs, and Pelias stayed dead
The cauldron cracked from the heat, and Pelias was scalded
The ghost of Jason's father struck Medea down mid-spell
Pelias came out young but blind for the rest of his days
context: Alcestis alone of the daughters refused to lay a hand on her father. The trick was Medea's revenge for Pelias's usurpation of Iolcus.  (Legend.)

question: Medea used her sorcery to help Jason win the Golden Fleece from her father, then fled her homeland to marry him. Years later in Corinth, Jason abandoned her to marry Glauce, the young daughter of King Creon. Medea sent the bride a wedding gift wrapped as a peace-offering but soaked in a poison she had brewed herself. What was the gift?
answer: A poisoned wedding dress that burned her alive
choices: A poisoned wedding dress that burned her alive
A cup of wine that turned her hair white
A gold ring that struck her mute
A basket of serpents in flowers
context: Euripides put the whole Corinth story on the stage in his Medea, first performed at Athens in 431 BCE. Medea also killed her own children by Jason before fleeing.  (Legend.)

question: The three Fates, who spin, measure and cut every human life, stood beside the newborn prince Meleager's cradle at Calydon. They told his mother his whole life was tied to one plain thing burning right there in the room. What was it?
answer: a burning log on the hearth
choices: a burning log on the hearth
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.451-458; Apollodorus 1.8.2: the Fates declared that Meleager would live only as long as a particular firebrand -- a log then burning in the hearth -- was unburnt. A common Greek word for the log-brand is 'dalos'.  (Legend.)

question: Althaea leapt up the moment the three Fates finished speaking her newborn son's destiny and vanished. She had heard exactly how long he would live, and she did one quick thing to save him. What did she do?
answer: snatched the log from the fire and hid it in a chest
choices: snatched the log from the fire and hid it in a chest
carried the baby out of the room and up the mountain
sent a servant to the oracle at Delphi for counsel
sacrificed a black lamb on the household altar
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.457-461; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Althaea seized the burning log, doused the flames, and locked it away in a chest, where it stayed safe for years while Meleager grew into a man.  (Legend.)

question: King Oeneus of Calydon burned harvest offerings to the Olympian gods in thanks for a good year, but he forgot one goddess. Furious at the slight, she sent an enormous wild boar down onto Calydon to wreck the farms and kill the farmers. Which goddess had he forgotten?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.270-283; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Artemis, huntress and mistress of wild beasts, was passed over in the harvest sacrifice and in fury sent the giant boar. Athena is the war-goddess of Athens; Hera the queen of Olympus; Demeter the grain-mother -- none matches the Calydon story.  (Legend.)

question: Prince Meleager gathered the greatest heroes of Greece to hunt the monstrous Calydonian Boar, men like Theseus, Jason, Peleus and Nestor. But he also invited one hunter who made every man in the party furious just by showing up: a woman who could out-run and out-shoot them all. Who was she?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.317-328; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Atalanta, the huntress raised by a she-bear and trained as an archer, was the only woman on the hunt. Meleager was in love with her. Antigone is the daughter of Oedipus; Andromache the wife of Hector; Iphigenia the daughter of Agamemnon.  (Legend.)

question: Toxeus and Plexippus watched their nephew Meleager, leader of the hunt, award the boar's hide and tusks to a huntress, passing over himself and them. She had drawn first blood, he said, and had earned the prize. What did the two uncles do when they saw the trophy go to a woman?
answer: tried to take the hide from Atalanta by force
choices: tried to take the hide from Atalanta by force
demanded a share of the tusks for themselves
walked out of the hunt-feast in silence
called on Artemis to judge between them
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.435-444; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Toxeus and Plexippus, enraged at seeing the greatest hunt-prize in Greek memory given to a woman, tried to snatch the hide from Atalanta by force. What happened next set the tragedy in motion.  (Legend.)

question: Meleager stepped in to defend the huntress he had just given the boar's hide, when his uncles Toxeus and Plexippus, his mother's two brothers, turned on her over the prize. What did he do to his two uncles in that moment?
answer: killed both of them on the spot
choices: killed both of them on the spot
wounded them and drove them out of the hall
cursed them and left the feast
swore an oath never to speak to them again
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.435-444; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Meleager killed Toxeus and Plexippus defending Atalanta. His mother Althaea now had to choose between vengeance for her brothers and love for her son -- the choice that ends the story.  (Legend.)

question: Althaea heard what her son Meleager had done to her two brothers over the huntress's prize. She went to the chest she had guarded for years and took out the firebrand the Fates had spoken of at his cradle. Ovid gave her a long, tormented speech, and then she made her choice. What did she do with the firebrand?
answer: threw it back onto the fire
choices: threw it back onto the fire
carried it to a temple altar
broke it in half over her knee
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.460-525; Apollodorus 1.8.3: Althaea, torn between mother-love and blood-vengeance for her brothers, threw the firebrand back into the hearth. Ovid gives her a long anguished speech before she casts the log in.  (Legend.)

question: Meleager's sisters wept over him so long that the gods turned them into birds. He had been in perfect health, far from home, when he felt his body catching alight from the inside as a firebrand crumbled to ash. The scientific genus of those birds, Meleagris, is still named for him today. What kind of birds did his sisters become?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.533-546: Meleager's weeping sisters were turned into guineafowl, called meleagrides in Greek. The bird's Latin scientific genus is still Meleagris today (which is also the genus of the wild turkey, named by Linnaeus by confusion with the true meleagris). Swans belong to Cygnus; nightingales to the Philomela story; ravens to Apollo.  (Legend.)

question: A white-bearded old man in a long robe carried the baby Arthur out of the palace and hid him with a country knight. Years later the same man set the famous test that showed who should be king of Britain. Who was he?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1136); Malory Books I-IV. The Latin name Merlinus comes from the Welsh Myrddin. Blaise is Merlin's own confessor and chronicler. Bedivere is Arthur's steward-knight who returns Excalibur. Bagdemagus is the king of Gorre in Chretien's Lancelot.  (Legend.)

question: The wizard set a test for the barons of Britain when old King Uther died and left no known heir. Whoever passed it would be the true king, and the boy who passed it was Arthur. What is this test called?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.5-6. Arthur draws the blade as squire to his foster-brother Kay at a tournament. The horn on the hearth is a chastity-test in Arthurian romance. The bridge of glass is an invented wrong choice. The burning bush is Moses at Sinai (Christian tradition).  (Legend.)

question: A council of demons plotted in Robert de Boron's poem Merlin to sire their own antichrist on a sleeping virtuous woman. The plot failed at the very moment of the birth: one act performed on the newborn stripped their claim on his soul, though he kept their gift of perfect memory. What act saved him?
context: Robert de Boron, Merlin (c.1195-1210); Wikipedia: Merlin (Robert de Boron poem). The mother tells her confessor of the demonic pregnancy, and the child is baptised at birth, freeing him from the devil's power. Exorcism is the ritual expulsion of a demon already in possession. Circumcision is the Jewish covenant rite of the eighth day. Anointing with oil is a separate sacrament used at confirmation and last rites.  (Legend.)

question: The Saxon Hengist killed hundreds of British nobles at Amesbury, Geoffrey of Monmouth tells, and the king wanted a great stone memorial for the dead. The wizard told him to send men across the sea for a ring of old stones, which the wizard's magic would raise. Which king did the wizard build it for?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae Book VIII (c.1136); Wikipedia: Giant's Dance. Aurelius Ambrosius is Uther's older brother and king before him; the monument becomes Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain. Uther Pendragon leads the men who ship the stones but is not yet king. Vortigern is the earlier king who let the Saxons into Britain in the first place. Cadwallader is the last British king in Geoffrey's chronicle, centuries later.  (Legend.)

question: Giants set a ring of old stones down at Mount Killaraus after carrying them from Africa, Geoffrey of Monmouth says. Merlin came for that ring long after, and his magic would raise it again as Stonehenge. Which country did Merlin bring the stones from?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Book VIII; Wikipedia: Giant's Dance. Geoffrey names Mount Killaraus in Ireland; Waun Mawn in Pembrokeshire (Wales) is one modern candidate for a real dismantled circle behind the legend. Iceland has no Arthurian role. Norway is Beowulf's neighbour. Brittany is where Lancelot's father Ban is from.

question: Arthur broke his first sword in single combat, and Merlin led the young king to a lake in the wilderness. In Malory's telling a woman's arm clothed in white samite rose from the water holding a great blade above the surface, and Merlin told Arthur to row out in a small barge and take it. What was the second sword called?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.25 (the second sword; the first was the sword-in-the-stone). The arm in white samite is the Lady of the Lake's. Durendal is Roland's sword (Chanson de Roland). Tizona is El Cid's sword. Gungnir is Odin's spear (Norse pillar).  (Legend.)

question: Merlin, the great wizard of Arthur's court, fell in love in his old age with a young damsel of the Lady of the Lake's kin, and he followed her everywhere like a lovesick fool. Sir Thomas Malory gives her a name. What is she called?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV ch.1 (Caxton 1485). Malory's spelling is Nimue (with variants Nenive, Niviene); the French Vulgate calls her Viviane. Igraine is Arthur's mother. Enide is the heroine of Chretien's Erec et Enide. Iseult is the queen of the parallel Tristan story.  (Legend.)

question: The damsel refused to love Merlin back, and Malory makes it plain that she feared him. An old rumor about his birth frightened her, one that Robert de Boron had already put in writing a century before. What did the damsel think Merlin was?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV ch.1; Robert de Boron, Merlin (c.1200). Nimue's fear is rooted in de Boron's antichrist-plot origin story for Merlin. Fairy child, Saxon spy, and Roman priest are the sort of thing a distrusted stranger might be called in Arthur's Britain but not what Malory writes.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin gave up one secret after another to the damsel he loved, for she promised to love him more each time. Afraid of him as she was, she made that promise whenever she wanted him gone. What did she coax out of him bit by bit, in Malory's telling?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV ch.1. Merlin hands over his spells one by one, and Nimue collects the whole arsenal -- which she will shortly use against him. The language of birds is Solomon's; naming saints is a monk's work; teaching Britain's geography is the sort of thing Merlin ALREADY tells Arthur (from prophecy). Only the magic is the fatal gift.  (Legend.)

question: The damsel shut Merlin up alive under a rock, but the tellers of the tale disagree about where. The French Vulgate Cycle moved the trap out of Cornwall and into a real forest in Brittany, still visited today for its Arthurian associations: the Forest of Paimpont, on the road out of Rennes. What is that forest's legendary name?
context: French Vulgate Cycle; Wikipedia: Broceliande; the Forest of Paimpont in Brittany is the real forest identified with Broceliande. Argonne is a French forest famous from WWI. Sherwood is Robin Hood's forest in Nottinghamshire. Ardennes is the Belgian-French forest of Chretien's Cliges and later of many wars.  (Legend.)

question: Tennyson's Vivien waved her arms over the sleeping Merlin and wove her spell, and the hollow trunk of one great tree closed over him. Alfred Tennyson published that new trap in 1859, as part of his long Arthurian cycle Idylls of the King, with no stone, no tower of air and no hawthorn. Which tree closed over Merlin?
context: Alfred Tennyson, Idylls of the King, 'Merlin and Vivien' (1859). Tennyson's Vivien puts the sleeping Merlin inside a hollow oak; Tennyson favours the oak because it is the great sacred tree of British antiquity, the tree of the druids. Apple, rowan, and walnut are other significant British trees but not this poem's.

question: A god of the Tuatha De Danann, the old gods of Ireland, heard of the most beautiful woman ever born on the island, then courted and married her. He ruled the glowing fairy mound of Bri Leith in the Irish midlands. Who was this god?
context: Midir, son of the Dagda, lived in the sidhe mound of Bri Leith (Ardagh Hill in modern County Longford). Tochmarc Etaine ('The Wooing of Etain'), Yellow Book of Lecan; Wikipedia, Midir.  (Legend.)

question: Midir of the Tuatha De Danann, the old gods of Ireland, fell in love with the most beautiful woman ever born there and brought her home to his sidhe mound at Bri Leith in the midlands. What was her name?
context: Etain was said to be the most beautiful woman ever born in Ireland. Tochmarc Etaine ('The Wooing of Etain') part I; Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: Midir brought the young beauty Etain home to his hall at Bri Leith as his new bride, but he was already married. His first wife, a powerful druidess of the Tuatha De Danann, blazed with jealousy the moment she saw the girl. Who was Midir's first wife?
context: Fuamnach had been trained by the druid Bresal Etarlam and is described in the tale as 'intelligent, cunning, and versed in the knowledge and power of the Tuatha De Danann'. Wikipedia, Fuamnach.  (Legend.)

question: Midir's jealous first wife struck the young Etain with her wand and turned her, one form after another, first into a pool of water, then into a worm, and finally into the creature she would live as for centuries. What was the last form?
context: The Old Irish text calls her cuil corcrai, a scarlet or purple fly. Even as a fly Etain was so beautiful that her wing-buzz was sweet music and her scent healed the sick. Wikipedia, Fuamnach.  (Legend.)

question: Etain flew high over Ireland in her small new shape, swept along by a great wind that Midir's jealous first wife had raised. She could settle on no leaf or branch in all the island. How long did the wind blow her around?
context: Fuamnach's storm blew Etain the fly for seven years without rest. In one version Etain then reached Aengus's protective bower before a second storm drove her onward. Wikipedia, Fuamnach.  (Legend.)

question: Etain dropped out of the wind at last, in her small new shape, into a mortal hall and straight into a golden cup sitting on a woman's table. The magic wind of Midir's jealous first wife had carried her across Ireland for years. What happened next?
answer: The woman drank her down and later gave birth to Etain reborn
choices: The woman drank her down and later gave birth to Etain reborn
A hound leapt to the table and swallowed her whole
A druid caught her in a jar of honey
A crow snatched her out and dropped her at Bri Leith
context: The fly fell into the cup of the wife of a warrior named Etar; the woman drank without noticing, and nine months later gave birth to a girl who was Etain reborn, with no memory of her earlier life. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: Etain grew up a second time as the mortal daughter of the warrior Etar, with no memory of the life before. The Irish tale called Tochmarc Etaine, The Wooing of Etain, counts exactly how long it had been since her first marriage. How long had it been, according to the tale?
context: Tochmarc Etaine sets the reborn Etain 1,012 years after her original marriage to Midir. This makes her one of the earliest recorded reincarnation stories in Western literature. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: A High King ruling from the great royal hill of Tara took the reborn Etain to wife, the most beautiful girl of her time, in the second half of her tale. He had no idea that a god had married her first, long before. Which High King took her to wife?
context: Eochaid Airem sat at Tara when the reborn Etain grew up and did not know that his queen had once been the wife of a Tuatha De god. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: The High King at Tara faced a stranger across a board of silver with pieces of gold: Midir in disguise, come to win back Etain, now the king's queen. Midir challenged him to a series of games at an Irish board game of thought and strategy. What was the board game called?
context: Fidchell (Old Irish for 'wood-sense') was the great Irish chess-like game of kings. Midir's board was silver, its playing pieces gold, its corners jeweled. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: Midir deliberately lost the early games to the High King at Tara and paid every prize the king demanded: mounds of horses, chariots and treasure. Then he asked for one last game with his own choice of prize, and this time he won. What did Midir claim as his prize?
answer: An embrace and a kiss from Etain
choices: An embrace and a kiss from Etain
The sword of the high king
context: Midir named a modest-sounding prize: one embrace, one kiss. Eochaid agreed, thinking to guard against it, and set the day a month later. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: The High King barred every door and window of the great hall at Tara with armed guards on the day Midir was to collect his prize from Queen Etain, determined that the disguised god would not steal her away. Midir simply appeared inside the hall anyway and took Etain in his arms, and the pair vanished out of Tara. How did they leave?
answer: Flying up through the skylight as two swans
choices: Flying up through the skylight as two swans
Melting into the flames of the great hearth
Riding out on Enbarr the sea-horse
Sinking through the floor into the sidhe below
context: 'The pair fly away through the skylight, turning into swans as they do so.' Eochaid dug up every sidhe mound in Ireland after them and never found her again. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: Etain changed shape in the arms of Midir, a lord of the fairy folk under the green hills of Ireland, who had slipped into the High King's hall at Tara to win back his true love. The two of them rose out of the hall as birds, and one striking detail bound the birds together as they flew. What linked them?
context: A chain of gold linked the two swans as they flew, a scene the Middle English romance Sir Orfeo (c. 1330) would later borrow and transfer to a British setting. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: A red-bearded god of Asgard drives across the clouds in a chariot behind two goats, their hooves striking sparks. He swings a short-handled hammer at the giants, and people down on earth see the flash and call it lightning. Which god is he?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 21: Thor is the son of Odin and Jord (Earth), god of thunder, defender of Asgard and Midgard against the giants. Freyr is the harvest and fertility god; Tyr is the god of law and single combat (the one who lost a hand to Fenrir); Baldr is the shining god slain by mistletoe.  (Legend.)

question: Sindri lays a pig-skin in the forge while Brokkr leans on the bellows, and one of the Aesir badly wants that fire to go out. He has wagered his own head that the sons of Ivaldi can out-craft the two brothers. Which of the Aesir has made the bet?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki set up the whole contest by boasting that the sons of Ivaldi were the finest smiths in the nine worlds, then wagered his own head that Sindri and Brokkr could not beat them. Thor is the customer for the hammer, not the gambler; Odin and Heimdallr are not in the wager.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr works the bellows over a pig-skin fire while his brother Sindri hammers out three named gifts for the gods, with Loki's head riding on the outcome. One is Thor's great hammer, Mjolnir. The other two have to stand up to the treasures of the sons of Ivaldi. What are the other two treasures?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri and Brokkr produce Draupnir (Odin's gold ring that drips eight matching rings every ninth night) and Gullinbursti (Freyr's golden boar whose bristles light the dark and who outruns any horse) in the same session as Mjolnir -- three of the six treasures at the wager. Gungnir (Odin's spear) and Skidbladnir (Freyr's folding ship) are the OTHER three treasures, made by the rival dwarf-team, the sons of Ivaldi; Andvaranaut is Andvari's cursed ring from the Volsung cycle and Gram the sword Sigurd swings there; Sif's hair (also from the sons of Ivaldi) and Brisingamen (Freyja's necklace, made by four different dwarves) are unrelated forgings.  (Legend.)

question: Baldr's grieving family lays him on his own great longship, Hringhorni, to burn on the sea. His brother Hodr has killed him, tricked into it by Loki. Before the fire is lit, Thor steps up to the ship's side with Mjolnir in his hand. What does Thor do with the hammer?
answer: raises it to consecrate the pyre
choices: raises it to consecrate the pyre
throws it at a passing giant
smashes the mast of the ship
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: at Baldr's funeral aboard the ship Hringhorni, Thor stands and raises Mjolnir to hallow the pyre. The scene shows Mjolnir as a sacred object -- it is used the same way over births, marriages, and funerals in the sagas, not just in battle. The giant Litr is kicked into the flames at the same funeral, but by Thor's foot, not the hammer.  (Legend.)

question: An archaeologist lifts a little silver hammer out of a Viking-age grave, a copy of Thor's own, made to hang on a cord round the neck. Graves and hoards across northern Europe have given up many kinds of Viking-age pendant. Where does the silver Mjolnir rank among all those surviving types?
answer: the most-collected single pendant type from the Viking age
choices: the most-collected single pendant type from the Viking age
about as common as silver cross-pendants of the same era
the second-most-collected pendant type after cross-pendants
context: British Museum and Nationalmuseet Copenhagen catalogues: silver Mjolnir-pendants are the most abundant single amulet type recovered from Viking-age burials and hoards (roughly 9th-11th centuries), found from Iceland to the Danelaw to Kievan Rus. Many were worn alongside crosses in the transition to Christianity -- direct evidence of the hallowing role Snorri describes.

question: Thor the thunder-god charges out to meet the frost-giants of Jotunheim when they come down from their icy mountains to fight the gods. He carries his one signature weapon, and the gods count on it above all others. What weapon does Thor carry?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 21 and Skaldskaparmal 43: Thor's weapon is Mjolnir, a war-hammer. Odin's weapon is the spear Gungnir; the god Ullr is the bowman of Asgard; Tyr carries a sword. The hammer is unique to Thor and is the single most famous weapon in Norse myth.  (Legend.)

question: The thunder-god Thor swings a great hammer that has a name of its own in the old Norse stories. Vikings carved that same name onto the little hammer-shaped amulets they wore on cords around their necks to keep them safe. What is the name of Thor's hammer?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the hammer is called Mjolnir. Gungnir is Odin's spear; Draupnir is Odin's self-multiplying gold arm-ring; Gram is the sword Sigurd uses to kill the dragon Fafnir. Around a thousand hammer-shaped amulets have been dug up across Viking-age Scandinavia.  (Legend.)

question: Two dwarf brothers agree to make Thor's hammer as a wager against Loki, the trickster, who bets his own head on the outcome. The medieval Icelandic writer Snorri Sturluson names one brother standing at the anvil and the other working the great bellows. What are the names of the two smith-brothers?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri (also called Eitri) stands at the anvil and his brother Brokkr works the bellows. Fjalar and Galar are the dwarves who murder the wise Kvasir. Baugi and Suttung are the giant brothers in the Mead of Poetry story. Nordri and Sudri are two of the four dwarves who hold up the sky. It is a common wrong answer to say the Sons of Ivaldi made Mjolnir -- the Sons of Ivaldi make Gungnir and Skidbladnir in the SAME wager, but not the hammer.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson lists three marvellous properties of Thor's hammer as the god uses it in battle. Two of them are that it will never miss its mark when thrown, and that it can shrink small enough to hide inside Thor's shirt. What is the third property Snorri names?
answer: it always returns to Thor's hand
choices: it always returns to Thor's hand
it grows red-hot when giants are near
it splits the earth wherever it lands
it can be lifted by no one but Thor
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Thor's hammer will never miss the mark, will always fly back to his hand, and can be shrunk small enough to hide inside his shirt. The choice 'can be lifted by no one but Thor' is a modern comic-book addition, not from Snorri; the belt Megingjord is what lets Thor lift it at full strength.  (Legend.)

question: The giant Thrym steals Thor's hammer out of Asgard one evening and hides it eight leagues underground. He sends word to the Aesir that he will give it back only if one of their goddesses is brought to his hall to marry him. Which goddess does Thrym demand as the price of its return?
context: Poetic Edda, Thrymskvida: Thrym names Freyja specifically, and the gods must plan a trick because Freyja refuses to be handed over -- her rage shakes Asgard, and Brisingamen bursts from her neck. Heimdall then proposes that Thor go to Thrym's hall himself dressed in Freyja's bridal veil, with Loki as bridesmaid; when the hammer is finally laid in the 'bride's' lap Thor throws off the veil and kills Thrym and every giant present.  (Legend.)

question: The poet of Thrymskvida hides a true custom of the Viking age in his comic story of the stolen hammer. Someone raises a small hammer, or the sign of one, above the participants while sacred words are spoken to bless the moment. At what ceremony is the hammer-sign used?
choices: a naming of a newborn child
context: Poetic Edda, Thrymskvida stanza 30 and Snorri after it: the hammer is brought forth and laid in the woman's lap to sanctify the union -- the story-detail preserves the real Viking-age custom. Naming ceremonies for newborns used water-sprinkling (ausa vatni) rather than the hammer; ship-launchings used sacrifice; there was no single Norse coronation-rite. The hammer-role at weddings is also why so many small Mjolnir-pendants have been dug up in Viking graves across Scandinavia -- around a thousand of them.  (Legend.)

question: The young King Arthur spends one night with a queen visiting his court, in Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, not knowing she is his own half-sister. She conceives a son by him. Who is the queen whose son will one day bring the kingdom down?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.19-20 (Caxton 1485). Morgause is Igraine's daughter by her first husband Gorlois of Cornwall and thus Arthur's half-sister; she is married to King Lot of Orkney. In the older French Vulgate tradition Mordred's mother is Arthur's half-sister the wife of King Lot, left unnamed there -- also Arthur's half-sister -- and Malory's switch to Morgause is idiosyncratic. Guinevere is Arthur's queen, not his sister. Elaine of Astolat dies of unrequited love for Lancelot.  (Legend.)

question: A boy grows up in secret, Arthur's own son by his half-sister. Years later he arrives at court as a young knight, half-brother to Gawain, and takes his seat with the fellowship of the Round Table. What is the boy's name in Malory?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.27 and passim. Galahad is Lancelot's pure son by Elaine of Corbenic, the Grail-achiever. Bors is Lancelot's cousin, a Grail knight. Kay is Arthur's foster-brother and seneschal. Mordred is Arthur's own son by incest and the ruin of his reign.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin warns Arthur that his own child, born on May Day, will destroy his kingdom, so Arthur orders all the noble children born that day gathered up. He puts them into a single ship and sends them out to sea to drown. In Malory, what happens to the infant Mordred aboard that ship?
answer: he is cast up alive on shore
choices: he is cast up alive on shore
he is nursed to safety by a passing dolphin
Merlin himself lifts him from the wreck
Morgause hides him ashore before the ship sails
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.27. The ship wrecks and every other child drowns; the infant Mordred is thrown up alive on shore, is found by a good man, and is raised until age fourteen before being brought to court. Malory adapts the episode from the Post-Vulgate Suite du Merlin. Many of Arthur's lords are furious over the drowned children -- some blame Arthur, some blame Merlin.  (Legend.)

question: Lancelot flees to France when his love for Guinevere comes out at court, and Arthur takes an army across the sea to besiege him. Britain cannot be left kingless while the king is gone. Who does Arthur put in charge of the kingdom, in Malory's telling?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.1. Arthur trusts the regency to his own acknowledged son. Gawain is with Arthur on the campaign, driving him to press Lancelot for having killed Gawain's brothers Gareth and Gaheris. Kay and Bedivere are Arthur's oldest household knights but neither is the regent. Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI (c.1136) is the first to make Mordred the treacherous regent -- an invention that becomes central to the whole later legend.

question: Mordred forges letters saying Arthur has been killed at Benwick, has himself crowned king in his father's place, and moves to take Guinevere as his own wife by force. She pretends to agree and asks leave to fetch her wedding clothes. Where does Guinevere shut herself up to escape him, in Malory's telling?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.1. Guinevere pretends to consent, asks Mordred's leave to go to London for her wedding-clothes, and instead shuts herself up in the Tower of London stocked with provisions and men-at-arms. Amesbury is the nunnery she retires to at the very end of the story after Arthur's death. Avalon is where Arthur is carried on the barge. Camelot is Arthur's own court and would be Mordred's stronghold, not her refuge.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur breaks off the siege of Lancelot at Benwick and races back across the Channel with his army to face his usurping son. The two armies meet on a plain in the west of Britain, placed in Cornwall in most later traditions and entered under the year 537 by the earliest Welsh source. What is the name of the plain?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.3-4. Camlann is the name in Malory and in the earlier Welsh Annals under 537. Badon (Mons Badonicus) is Arthur's earlier victory in the Historia Brittonum, not his last battle. Roncesvalles is the pass where Roland's rearguard is destroyed in the Song of Roland (Western-medieval pillar) -- a parallel of a great order's last stand, but a different story. Bosworth is 1485, Richard III's death, real history not legend.

question: Arthur and Mordred meet in a tent on the morning of the battle to sign a truce, with the two armies drawn up facing each other in the heather. Each side is ordered to charge if a single sword is seen drawn. Then a knight in the ranks is stung on the foot and draws his sword to kill what stung him. What stings the knight, in Malory's account?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.4. The adder in the heather is Malory's own vivid detail. Both armies see the drawn blade, take it for the signal of treachery, and charge. In one instant a truce is broken by a snake and the whole day is set on fire. Hornets and scorpions belong to warmer traditions; the marsh viper is a real snake but not what Malory names.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur looks across the field at evening and sees Mordred alone, leaning on his sword among heaps of the dead. Only Sir Bedivere and Sir Lucan still stand beside the king. Arthur takes his spear and runs at his son. What does Mordred do as the spear goes clean through his body?
answer: pulls himself up the spear shaft
choices: pulls himself up the spear shaft
hurls his sword to break Arthur's helm
kneels and calls for Morgause his mother
context: Malory Book XXI ch.4. Arthur's spear goes clean through Mordred's body, but the dying Mordred grips the shaft with both hands and drags himself up it until he can reach his father, then strikes Arthur through the helm and the skull with his sword. Both men fall together. Malory gives this act the whole weight of the ending: the son will not let the father live, even at the cost of his own last moment.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Bedivere carries the dying Arthur from the field where father and son have struck each other down, and he lays the king on a barge. Three queens wait aboard it to heal the wound. In Malory's telling, where do they say the barge is bound?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.5. The three queens on the black barge tell Bedivere they are taking Arthur to the vale of Avalon to heal him of his grievous wound. Glastonbury is the site LATER identified with Avalon by the monks of Glastonbury Abbey (who claimed in 1191 to have found Arthur's tomb), but Malory's own text names Avalon. Camelot is Arthur's court, empty now. Cornwall is where Camlann is placed.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur and Medraut, the Welsh form of Mordred, fall together in a single bare line of a Latin chronicle, compiled at St David's in Wales in the mid-10th century and listed under the year 537. No older mention of their last battle survives, and the line says nothing more. What is the name of that chronicle?
context: Annales Cambriae (Welsh Annals), entry for the year 537: 'Gueith Camlann in qua Arthur et Medraut corruerunt' -- the strife of Camlann in which Arthur and Medraut fell. Medraut is the Welsh name for Mordred. The Historia Brittonum (c.828, attributed to Nennius) gives Arthur's twelve battles but not Camlann. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is the English royal chronicle and does not mention Arthur. Bede's Historia Ecclesiastica (731) mentions Badon but not Camlann.

question: Medraut falls beside Arthur in the oldest Welsh record with no word that he is a nephew or a son, no word that the two stand on opposite sides, and no word of why either is there. Forging the letter, seizing the crown and taking Guinevere all come later. Which writer is the first to turn Mordred into Arthur's treacherous regent?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI (c.1136). Geoffrey invents the treacherous-regent story a full six centuries after the annals' bare line; every later Arthurian writer builds on his invention. Chretien de Troyes (c.1170-90) writes the great courtly Arthurian romances but not the Camlann story. Wolfram von Eschenbach (c.1210) writes Parzival, the German Grail poem. Malory (Caxton 1485) is 350 years after Geoffrey and gathers the whole tradition into English prose.
