question: A woman slips into the strong-room and takes the scabbard of Excalibur. Later she sends a burning cloak to Camelot. She is a sorceress, one of King Arthur's three older half-sisters, and she grows into his lifelong enemy. What is her name?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_le_Fay. Her name in Old French is Morgain la Fee -- 'Morgan the Fairy'. Her sisters are Morgause (mother of Gawain and, in Malory, of Mordred) and Elaine of Garlot -- a DIFFERENT Elaine from Elaine of Astolat, who dies of love for Lancelot. Nimue is the chief Lady of the Lake, Morgan's opposite -- she saves Arthur repeatedly from Morgan's plots. Iseult belongs to the parallel Tristan cycle.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur marries Morgan le Fay off to a northern king against her will, and she hates the match. She takes lovers at court and eventually plots to kill both her husband and Arthur himself. That husband is the father of Sir Ywain of the Round Table. Which king does Arthur force on her, in Malory?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV. Uriens of Gore is the father of Sir Ywain (Yvain), one of Arthur's Round Table knights. King Lot of Orkney is Morgan's SISTER Morgause's husband and the father of Gawain -- easily confused with Uriens because both are northern kings married to Igraine's daughters. Pellinore is the hunter of the Questing Beast. Bagdemagus is another northern king and Morgan does keep him at her court, but he is not her husband.  (Legend.)

question: Morgan le Fay goes secretly to the strong-room and takes Excalibur's scabbard, the one gift that keeps Arthur alive in battle. He pursues her hard across the country. When she sees she cannot outrun him she rides to the edge of a lake and hurls it far out into the deep water. What does Malory say she cries out as she throws it?
answer: whatever happens, her brother shall not have it
choices: whatever happens, her brother shall not have it
let the lake keep what the king has lost
so passes the pride of Camelot
may Merlin himself never find it
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV; https://sacred-texts.com/neu/trt/trt09.htm. Morgan rides to the edge of a lake on the plain at the forest's edge and, crying out that whatever happens her brother shall not have the scabbard again, throws it far into the deep water where it sinks -- gone forever. From that day forward Arthur can bleed and die, and eventually will.  (Legend.)

question: Morgan le Fay sends Arthur what looks like a peace-offering, a magnificent mantle covered in jewels, and one of her damsels brings it to Camelot. Arthur is about to put it on when a lady who watches over him whispers to make the messenger try it first. In Malory, what happens to the damsel the moment the cloak touches her?
choices: she falls into a bewitched sleep
she turns to stone standing there
her tongue is struck dumb forever
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV ch.16. The cloak has been enchanted to consume its wearer in fire; Nimue, who watches over Arthur, saves him at the last instant. The messenger burns to a cinder in front of the whole court. Sleep-curses, stone-curses, and dumbing-curses are the classic witch-gifts of a fairy-tale but not Morgan's here.  (Legend.)

question: The Green Knight reveals himself as Sir Bertilak of Hautdesert at the end of the great poem of Sir Gawain, and he says the whole beheading game was Morgan le Fay's doing. He had ridden into Camelot at the New Year's feast with an axe, daring any knight to strike off his head. What did Morgan send him there to do?
choices: shame Gawain out of the Round Table
test whether Arthur himself would take the blow
steal back the scabbard from Camelot
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt IV; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gawain_and_the_Green_Knight. Bertilak reveals that the old woman Gawain has ignored at his host's castle is Morgan le Fay in disguise, and that she sent the Green Knight to Camelot in the hope that the sight of a man picking up his own head would frighten Guinevere to death. Gawain survives the return-blow with only a nick on the neck.  (Legend.)

question: Morgan le Fay swaps the real Excalibur and its scabbard for cheap copies at court and slips the true sword to her lover, Sir Accolon. He challenges Arthur to a duel, expecting to face the king while Arthur holds the fake. Who steps in at the last moment and knocks the real blade back into Arthur's hand, in Malory?
context: Malory Book IV; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accolon. Nimue the Lady of the Lake attends the duel invisibly and, at the moment Accolon's blade is about to fall, uses her magic to jolt Excalibur out of his hand -- Arthur grabs it and wins. Bedivere and Gawain are Arthur's household knights, present at court but not sorcerers. Merlin is by this point already sealed under the stone by Nimue herself (Malory Book IV ch.1) and cannot help.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Bedivere carries the dying Arthur down to the edge of a lake at nightfall, at the very end of Malory. A dark barge waits on the water with three queens veiled in black hoods, and they receive the king aboard with great weeping. Morgan le Fay, at the head of the barge, takes his head into her lap. What does she say to him?
answer: Ah, dear brother, why have ye tarried so long from me?
choices: Ah, dear brother, why have ye tarried so long from me?
Sleep now, king, the wound is healed already.
The scabbard is returned, and the debt is paid.
Avalon has waited long for its rightful lord.
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.5; https://kingarthur.fandom.com/wiki/Morgan_le_Fay. Morgan is the queen at the head of the barge; she takes his head in her lap and says only 'Ah, dear brother, why have ye tarried so long from me?' Guinevere is at the same moment shutting herself into the nunnery at Amesbury -- she and Arthur do not meet again in this life. The barge carries Arthur to Avalon.  (Legend.)

question: Geoffrey of Monmouth sets Morgan le Fay on the enchanted Isle of Avalon in his Latin poem Vita Merlini, about 1150, the earliest text about her. She is no villain there but a healer-queen, the most beautiful and wisest of a company of magical sisters, able to heal any wound. How many sisters does Geoffrey say rule Avalon, Morgan among them?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (c.1150). The Vita Merlini gives the benign healer-Morgan at the head of nine magical sisters on the Isle of Avalon; the malevolent Morgan is the invention of the later French Vulgate Cycle and of Malory, which blends both -- hostile in life, restorative at death. Three, seven, and twelve are the other classic magical numbers in medieval story (the three Fates, the seven sages, the twelve peers) but Geoffrey's Avalon-sisters are nine.  (Legend.)

question: In the book of Exodus, a new Pharaoh who had never even heard of Joseph enslaved all the Hebrews in Egypt. Afraid their numbers were growing, he gave a new order about every newborn Hebrew boy. What did he command be done to them?
choices: shut in the temple of Ra
context: Exodus 1:22 (KJV): 'Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive.' The river is the Nile.

question: A Levite woman hid her newborn son in her own house, out of reach of Pharaoh's order, the book of Exodus says. She kept him silent as long as she dared, hoping no soldier would come looking. How long did she keep him hidden?
context: Exodus 2:2 (KJV): 'when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.' Later tradition names her Jochebed.

question: The Levite mother wove a small basket-boat, called an ark, out of river reeds, so that she could set her baby son afloat on the Nile. To keep the water from soaking through she smeared it thickly inside and out with two waterproof materials. What does Exodus say she daubed it with?
context: Exodus 2:3 (KJV): 'she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein.'

question: The baby's mother hid a small reed ark among the tall flags at the water's edge, in the book of Exodus, then forced herself to walk away. One member of the baby's family stayed hidden nearby, watching quietly to see what would happen to the child. Who kept the watch?
context: Exodus 2:4 (KJV): 'And his sister stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him.' Miriam is named at Exodus 15:20. Aaron, Amram, and Korah are all real Levite men from Moses's family.

question: A royal woman bathing in the river that morning spotted a small basket among the tall flags and had her maid bring it to her. She opened the lid, found a Hebrew baby inside and took pity on him. Who found the baby Moses?
context: Exodus 2:5 (KJV): 'the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river... and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it.'

question: A maid carried a small reed ark up from the river Nile to a royal woman, who opened it and found a Hebrew baby boy inside, one of the very boys Pharaoh had ordered killed. In that moment the baby did one small thing that moved her to pity and made her decide, right there, to keep him. What did the babe do?
context: Exodus 2:6 (KJV): 'when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him.'

question: A Hebrew mother weaned her son in the book of Exodus, and once he reached the palace the royal woman who had kept him gave him the name Moses. She gave a reason with the name. What was her reason?
answer: because I drew him out of the water
choices: because I drew him out of the water
because he shall lead a people
because his cry moved my heart
because he was hidden three months
context: Exodus 2:10 (KJV): 'she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water.' Hebrew mashah = to draw out.

question: King Ahab of Israel blamed one man for a three-year drought. It was the fierce prophet who had stood before the whole court and declared that no rain would fall on the kingdom until he gave the word. What was that prophet's name?
context: 1 Kings 17:1 KJV -- Elijah the Tishbite tells Ahab there shall not be dew nor rain 'but according to my word.' The drought sets up the Mount Carmel duel in 1 Kings 18. Elisha is his student and successor; Isaiah and Jeremiah are prophets of later centuries.

question: Queen Jezebel's prophets came up Mount Carmel when Elijah called the whole nation there for a contest, his God against her gods. One group served Asherah of the sacred grove, and the other served the storm-god Baal. How many prophets of Baal stood against Elijah?
context: 1 Kings 18:19 KJV -- 'the prophets of Baal four hundred and fifty, and the prophets of the groves four hundred.' The Asherah prophets are 400; the Baal prophets are 450. Total 850 against Elijah alone.

question: Elijah set the rules for his contest on Mount Carmel: two altars, one for Baal and one for Israel's God, the wood laid, the bullocks placed, with no human hand to touch them further. The god who answered by one element, he said, would be God. What element decided it?
context: 1 Kings 18:24 KJV -- 'call ye on the name of your gods, and I will call on the name of the LORD: and the God that answereth by fire, let him be God.' The drought made rain the obvious sign -- but Elijah names fire, and gets rain as the aftershock.

question: The prophets of Baal cried aloud from morning to noon and cut themselves with knives, and no answer came. Elijah stepped forward mocking their silent god: 'Cry aloud: for he is a god; either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, or ______.' How did Elijah finish the taunt?
context: 1 Kings 18:27 KJV verbatim. 'Peradventure' is old English for 'perhaps.' The mockery is savage -- Elijah is saying maybe your storm-god is off in a bathroom, on a trip, or napping. The prophets of Baal then cut themselves with lancets 'till the blood gushed out upon them' (v.28) and still nothing.

question: The crowd on Mount Carmel watched Elijah rebuild the ruined altar of Israel's God before the sacrifice, laying twelve stones side by side. He chose that count on purpose, and every stone meant something. What did each of the twelve stones stand for?
context: 1 Kings 18:31 KJV -- 'Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob.' Every altar-stone rebuilds the covenant with the whole nation. Apostles-of-Jesus is a New Testament twelve; months and prophets are real twelves-of-something, but the wrong twelve here.

question: Elijah's helpers on Mount Carmel poured barrels of water over the bullock, the wood and the stones of his altar, on his orders, to rule out any hidden ember under the pile. They did it again and again, until the water filled the trench cut around the altar. How many rounds of water-pouring did Elijah order before he prayed?
context: 1 Kings 18:34 KJV -- four barrels each round, 'do it the second time... do it the third time.' Four barrels times three rounds equals twelve barrels of water soaking the wood before Elijah's short prayer in v.36.

question: Elijah soaked his bullock, his wood and his altar at evening until the trench around them filled, and then he prayed a short prayer to the God of Israel. The answer fell straight down from heaven, the King James Bible says, burning the bullock and the wood, and it did not stop there. What else did it consume?
answer: the stones, the dust, and the water in the trench
choices: the stones, the dust, and the water in the trench
the ropes, the bones, and the oil of the sacrifice
the priests, the altar cloth, and the seven jars
the bulls of Baal, the wooden idols, and the grove
context: 1 Kings 18:38 KJV -- 'the fire of the LORD fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.' Twelve barrels of water and the fire still ate it.

question: Elijah marched the defeated prophets of Baal down from Mount Carmel while the people lay face down, crying that his God alone was God. He slew the prophets beside a single small watercourse in the valley just below. What was the name of that brook?
context: 1 Kings 18:40 KJV -- 'Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon, and slew them there.' Kidron runs by Jerusalem; Cherith is where ravens fed Elijah earlier (1 Kings 17); Jabbok is where Jacob wrestled the angel. All four are real Old Testament brooks.

question: Elijah climbed back up Mount Carmel after the killing at the brook, cast himself down with his face between his knees, then sent his servant to look toward the sea for a sign that the drought would break. How many times did he send the servant to look before the sign came?
context: 1 Kings 18:43 KJV -- 'Go again seven times.' The first six times the servant reports nothing; the seventh brings the cloud from the sea.

question: King Ahab climbed into his chariot to race home before the roads washed out, as the three-year drought broke in a deluge over Mount Carmel. The prophet Elijah tucked his robe into his belt and ran on foot ahead of the chariot, all the way to the entrance of the royal city where Ahab and Queen Jezebel had their palace. To which city did Elijah run?
context: 1 Kings 18:46 KJV -- 'he girded up his loins, and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.' Jezreel was Ahab and Jezebel's royal residence in the valley below Carmel. Samaria was Ahab's other capital; Jericho and Bethel are other real Old Testament cities of the northern kingdom.

question: The wolf Fenrir breaks loose at Ragnarok and the sea rises over Midgard. Then a great ship crosses the flooded world, carrying an army of giants and monsters to the last battle. What is the name of this ship?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapters 43 and 51; Voluspa stanza 50. Naglfar is the ship of the dead. Skidbladnir is Freyr's magical folding ship that always has a fair wind and can be folded into a pocket. Ringhorn is Balder's funeral-ship, which the giantess Hyrrokkin launches into the sea with a single push. Mannigfual is a giant ghost-ship of German North Sea sailor-legend, not Norse myth. Naglfar is the specific Ragnarok-ship.

question: Giants and monsters sail to the last battle of Ragnarok on a ship built of no oak or pine or any tree, Snorri Sturluson says. Its planks come from something harvested off dead people, one small piece at a time. What is Naglfar built from?
answer: the fingernails and toenails of the dead
choices: the fingernails and toenails of the dead
the swords of every fallen warrior
the golden coins of every buried king
the black stones of the underworld
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Every corpse in the nine worlds contributes its clippings; the ship has been slowly assembling itself out of the leavings of the world's funerals for as long as there have been funerals. Norse myth is full of dark images -- this is arguably the darkest.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson turns aside from the story of Naglfar, the doom-ship of Ragnarok, to speak straight to the people of his own day in the 1200s. He gives them one plain funerary instruction, meant to slow the building of that ship. What does he tell them to do?
answer: clip the nails of every corpse before burial
choices: clip the nails of every corpse before burial
cover every corpse's mouth with a coin
burn every corpse instead of burying it
lay every corpse with its head toward the east
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51 (Brodeur translation): 'And there is this also to say concerning it, that any man who dies with untrimmed nails contributes materially to this ship's building -- both gods and men would fain the ship's completion be far off.' The other choices are real funerary practices from various cultures (Charon's obol, cremation, cardinal-direction burials), but none is Snorri's instruction. Cutting the dead's nails is the specific Norse practice.  (Legend.)

question: A frost-giant steps to the helm of Naglfar when the ship breaks loose from its moorings on the flood at Ragnarok, Snorri says, and he steers it against the gods. Snorri gives this captain a name. Who steers Naglfar?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51; Voluspa stanza 50 ('Hrym steers from the east, the serpent writhes'). Hrym is the frost-giant helmsman. Thrym is the giant who once stole Mjolnir. Skrymir is the giant who tricked Thor with the illusion-glove in Utgard. Suttung is the giant who kept the Mead of Poetry in the mountain until Odin stole it. All four are real Norse giants -- Hrym is the specific captain of Naglfar.  (Legend.)

question: The poet of the Voluspa fixes the direction of Naglfar's last voyage in a line that Snorri Sturluson quotes. The ship sails to the final battle at Ragnarok with a frost-giant at the helm: '... steers from the ___, the serpent writhes.' From which direction does Naglfar sail?
context: Voluspa stanzas 50-51; Snorri, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Naglfar sails from the east; the fire-giants under Surtr come from the south (from Muspelheim). North and west are not directions given for either muster. The east-origin is the specific Voluspa detail.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus sits on the shore of a far island, stuck there for seven years, and weeps for Ithaca. A woman there wants him for her husband, and she offers him a life that never ends if he will forget his home. What is her name?
context: Calypso keeps Odysseus on the island of Ogygia; every morning he sits on the shore weeping for Ithaca. Circe is the earlier witch who turned his men to pigs; Athena is his patron goddess; Penelope is the wife he is trying to get home to. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calypso.  (Legend.)

question: A god who has hated Odysseus ever since Odysseus blinded a Cyclops sends a great storm against the raft the hero has built himself, and it smashes the raft to splinters. Which god breaks the raft?
context: Poseidon is the father of the blinded Cyclops Polyphemus and has hunted Odysseus across the sea for the injury. Zeus rules Olympus but does not smash the raft; Hades rules the underworld; Hermes is the messenger who ordered Calypso to let him go in the first place. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus crawls ashore on the island of the Phaeacians after two days swimming through a storm, half-drowned, salt-caked and naked, and drags himself up into a thicket of scrub. To survive the cold night he scrapes something up around himself and falls asleep. What does Odysseus cover himself with?
context: The detail is Homeric and homely: no cloak, no hero-blanket, just leaves scraped up under an olive scrub. It matters because when he wakes up moments later he is still naked and covered in salt, and a princess is about to meet him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess slips into the dream of the young princess Nausicaa, asleep in the royal palace, wearing the face of one of her girl friends. She tells the princess it is time to take the family's fine clothes to the river-mouth and wash them, for her wedding-day is near. Which goddess sends the dream?
context: Athena has been steering Odysseus's rescue at every step, and she chooses the princess Nausicaa's dream as her tool: a friendly-friend visit, a marriageable-girl errand, a wash-day that puts a wagon and a party of young women on the exact beach where Odysseus is sleeping. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: Nausicaa hears Odysseus make his speech from a distance. He has stopped rather than clutch her knees as a suppliant would, since touching a young woman would give offence, and he compares her to a young tree he once saw shooting up beside Apollo's altar at Delos. What kind of tree does he compare her to?
context: The palm at Apollo's altar on Delos was a real cult-object in Odysseus's world, and the compliment lands: a tall, slender, sacred, well-nurtured shoot beside a god's altar. Cypress and laurel are also Apollonian trees, but the shoot Odysseus actually names is the Delian palm. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: Nausicaa gives Odysseus clothes and oil, lets him bathe, and then thinks like the royal she is. If a princess is seen walking a strange man into the city, the whole town will gossip that she has picked him for a husband. So she gives him a very practical order about how he is to travel. What does she tell him to do?
answer: walk behind her chariot into the city
choices: walk behind her chariot into the city
wait outside the city walls until dark
come dressed as one of her handmaids
swear an oath he is not seeking her hand
context: The line is one of the shrewdest things any young character says in Homer: a princess who has just met a hero already knows the difference between a rescue and a scandal. She goes ahead in the chariot; he follows on foot at a distance. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus hears a piece of court advice from Nausicaa before he reaches her father's great hall. He is not to stop at the throne of King Alcinous, she says, but to go past the king and clasp the knees of someone else in the room as a suppliant. Whose knees does she tell him to clasp?
choices: the old bard beside the fire
context: Nausicaa tells the stranger plainly: in Phaeacia any stranger my mother accepts is safe, because it is she who really rules. Odysseus does exactly that; the queen accepts him; the whole rescue turns on it. Homer is quietly saying who runs the palace. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaeacians.  (Legend.)

question: The court bard Demodocus takes up his lyre in the great hall that night and sings songs of Troy. The stranger at the table of King Alcinous hears them, hides his face in his cloak and weeps into it. The king watches, and then asks him one thing that will unlock the whole poem. What does the king ask him?
choices: whether he was at the sack
context: Alcinous's simple question is the hinge of the whole Odyssey: it is what unlocks Odysseus's own after-dinner storytelling, and the entire flashback of books 9 through 12 (Cyclops, Lotus-eaters, Circe, Sirens, the underworld, Scylla and Charybdis) is his answer, told at Alcinous's table. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey.  (Legend.)

question: King Nebuchadnezzar marched on the small kingdom of Judah, the Old Testament tells, took Jerusalem and carried off the temple treasure. Then he hauled the smartest young Hebrews east across the desert to serve at his own court. What was the name of his empire?
context: Daniel 1:1-6 KJV. Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 BC) sacks Jerusalem and carries the temple treasures and the royal youth home to Babylon. Assyria had already fallen; Persia will rise later and end the exile under Cyrus.

question: A young Judean captive prayed through the night in King Nebuchadnezzar's palace, after every wise man there had failed the king's impossible order: say what his dream was, and only then explain it. The captive came back with both. Who was he?
context: Daniel 2:14-19 KJV -- 'Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a night vision.' Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dream in Egypt; Ezekiel is a prophet of the exile; Ezra returns generations later to rebuild Jerusalem. All are honest OT dream-or-exile figures.

question: A young Hebrew captive described King Nebuchadnezzar's own dream back to him: a towering statue built of five different materials, one for each part of its body, from the top of its head down to its feet. What metal made up the statue's head?
context: Daniel 2:32-33 KJV -- 'This image's head was of fine gold, his breast and his arms of silver, his belly and his thighs of brass, his legs of iron.' All three other choices ARE in the statue -- just lower down.

question: King Nebuchadnezzar heard the end of his dream of the giant metal statue from a young Judean captive. As the colossus stood complete, one thing hit it at the feet and shattered it to pieces, and that thing was no hammer, sword or battering-ram. What smashed the statue?
answer: a stone cut out without hands
choices: a stone cut out without hands
context: Daniel 2:34 KJV -- 'a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet.' 'Without hands' means no human made it. The stone then becomes a great mountain that fills the whole earth (v.35).

question: Nebuchadnezzar raised a huge golden image of his own on a wide flat plain, some time after his dream of the metal statue. He commanded every subject in his kingdom to fall down before it whenever the music sounded. On what plain did the image stand?
context: Daniel 3:1 KJV -- 'he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.' Shinar is where Babel was built; Jezreel is Ahab's Israelite plain; Moab lies east of the Jordan. All real OT plains.

question: A herald cried out that when the music sounded, every people and language must fall down and worship King Nebuchadnezzar's golden image. His list of instruments ran cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and then one more whose name sat oddly in that court. What was the last instrument the herald named?
context: Daniel 3:5 KJV -- 'the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick.' The KJV translators chose 'dulcimer' for a stringed instrument that in Aramaic reads 'symphonia' -- probably a kind of bagpipe or drum, but the KJV word 'dulcimer' is the one every English reader remembers.

question: King Nebuchadnezzar's chief officer gave three young Judean captives new names for the royal court, in place of Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. Those court names are the ones history remembers, because the three friends later refused to bow to the king's golden image and were thrown into a fiery furnace. What were their three court names?
context: Daniel 1:6-7 KJV -- the chief of the eunuchs renames Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah as Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. The other choices are all real Babylonian / Neo-Assyrian court names and titles that appear in the OT: Nebuzaradan is Nebuchadnezzar's captain of the guard, Ashpenaz is his master of eunuchs, Arioch is his captain who fetches Daniel; Rabsaris / Rabmag / Rabshakeh are court titles used as names in 2 Kings and Jeremiah; Belteshazzar is Daniel's own Babylonian name, Nergal and Sin are Babylonian gods appearing in courtier-names like Nergal-sharezer.

question: Three young Hebrew captives refused to bow to King Nebuchadnezzar's golden idol, and in his fury he ordered the great furnace stoked hotter than it had ever been. He named the multiple himself, and it was so extreme that the heat killed the strong soldiers carrying the three young men up to it. How much hotter than usual did he order it heated?
context: Daniel 3:19 KJV -- 'he commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated.' Verse 22: 'the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.'

question: Standing before King Nebuchadnezzar with the fiery furnace roaring behind them, three young Judeans told him that their God could deliver them from the flames. Then they added three short words that made the refusal unbreakable, and they would not bow. What were the three words?
context: Daniel 3:17-18 KJV -- 'our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods.' Three of the boldest words in the Bible.

question: Four figures walked in the flames when King Nebuchadnezzar peered into the furnace, though he had thrown in only three men. About the fourth walker he said, 'the form of the fourth is like _____.' What did the king say the fourth figure looked like?
context: Daniel 3:25 KJV verbatim -- Nebuchadnezzar's own words. This question reports what the king says; Christian tradition later reads this fourth figure as a pre-incarnation appearance of Christ, Jewish tradition as a delivering angel. The line is the king's, not the question's.

question: Stone Age farmers raised a great round mound of white quartz and dark stone on a bend of a river in County Meath. In Irish myth it was the palace of the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De Danann. What is the mound called today?
context: Bru na Boinne (the palace of the Boyne) is the ancient Irish name for the mound known today as Newgrange, in the bend of the River Boyne in County Meath. Knowth and Dowth are its two great sister passage-tombs on the same bend of the Boyne. Loughcrew is another Irish megalithic complex, further west in Meath.

question: A farming people of the Stone Age raised a great passage-tomb on a bend of the River Boyne, before anyone set the first stone at Stonehenge or cut the first block for the Great Pyramid. Roughly how many years ago was that?
context: Newgrange was constructed around 3200 BC, roughly 5,200 years ago -- older than the Great Pyramids of Giza by about six centuries and older than Stonehenge by more than a thousand years. Stone Age farmers, not Celts or Vikings, raised the mound; the Tuatha De story was attached to the site much later.

question: The Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De Danann, wanted the goddess Boann, but she was married to another god of the Tuatha De, named Elcmar. To hide the affair the Dagda sent Elcmar off on an errand and cast a spell on the day. What did the spell do to time while Elcmar was away?
answer: made a single day last nine months
choices: made a single day last nine months
reversed the sun's course across the sky
froze the moon at its full for a year
sank the sun beneath the sea for a winter
context: In the Old Irish tale Tochmarc Etaine and the fragment De Gabail in tSida, the Dagda enchanted the sun to stand still so that Elcmar would not notice time passing, and a single day lasted nine months. In that endless day Boann conceived their son Aengus and gave birth before Elcmar returned. Reversing the sun and freezing the moon are common in Greek myth (Atreus, Zeus with Alcmene) but are not the shape of this story.  (Legend.)

question: Aengus learned at last whose son he was, and he went to the Dagda and asked for a portion of the earth, like all the other gods of the Tuatha De. The Dagda's reply set up the whole trick to come. What did the Dagda tell his son about the land of Ireland?
answer: all of it had already been divided; nothing was left
choices: all of it had already been divided; nothing was left
he would inherit only after the Dagda's death
he must fight another god to win his share
context: In De Gabail in tSida ('The Taking of the Fairy Mound'), the Dagda tells Aengus that all the sidhe mounds and lands of Ireland have already been distributed among the Tuatha De. There is no share left for the latecomer. That answer is what forces Aengus into wordplay to get any place of his own -- and the place he chooses is his father's own palace on the Boyne.  (Legend.)

question: Manannan mac Lir sent Aengus back to the Dagda with a small-sounding request, in some tellings; in others the adviser was his foster-father Midir. Aengus asked to stay in his father's palace for one set length of time, and the Dagda agreed to it as a small favour. How long did Aengus ask to keep the palace?
answer: for a day and a night
choices: for a day and a night
for the length of a single feast
from one harvest to the next
context: In the Old Irish text, Aengus asks for the Bru 'la ocus aidche' -- literally 'a day and a night'. The Dagda, thinking his son wants only a brief visit, agrees. The whole trick will turn on the fact that this exact Old Irish phrase can be read two different ways.  (Legend.)

question: Aengus met the Dagda with a point of grammar when the agreed time ran out and his father came back to the palace. The Old Irish phrase in his request, 'la ocus aidche', could also be read another way, and once the Dagda had granted it in those exact words, that second reading stood. Which second meaning did Aengus claim?
answer: 'day and night' -- meaning all days and all nights, always
choices: 'day and night' -- meaning all days and all nights, always
'a day into a night' -- meaning until the next dusk
'the day and its night' -- meaning until the following dawn
'day and night together' -- meaning a single full cycle of the sun
context: Old Irish 'la ocus aidche' with the definite article dropped can mean either 'a day and a night' (one span) or 'day and night' (all of them, always). Under early Irish law of the spoken word, once the Dagda had granted the request in those exact terms, the wider reading stood. The Dagda was tricked out of his own palace by his son's grammar. This is one of the earliest Irish stories of the clever-son-outwitting-the-old-father motif.  (Legend.)

question: The Stone Age people who raised the Dagda's great mound raised two other giant passage-tombs of similar age within a few hundred metres of it, on that same bend of the River Boyne. What are the names of those two sister mounds?
context: Knowth (the largest by area, ringed with more carved stones than any monument in Western Europe) and Dowth (whose passages face the winter solstice sunset, not sunrise) are the two sister mounds of Newgrange on the Boyne bend. Tara and Uisneach are inland royal seats. Emain Macha and Cruachan are the royal centres of Ulster and Connacht. Loughcrew and Carrowmore are other Irish megalithic complexes elsewhere in the country.

question: Bishop Nicholas of Myra, the story goes, carried secret gold to a ruined merchant's house after dark. On the night before his feast, 6 December, Dutch children still leave one thing out by the fireplace or the front door, and by morning, if they have been good, it is full of treats. What do they leave out?
context: Dutch children leave a shoe by the fireplace on the eve of 6 December. The tradition crossed the Atlantic to the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam (later New York) and mixed with English Father Christmas customs to produce the modern Christmas stocking -- the shoe is the direct ancestor of the stocking. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: A merchant in Myra watched his business collapse and could no longer feed his three daughters, the famous story of Bishop Nicholas begins. In that time and place a father in his spot had one desperate way to survive, and the poorest really did resort to it. What was he close to doing with his daughters?
context: In the Roman world a girl without a dowry could not marry and, in a truly destitute family, was often sold into brothels. The threat to the three daughters is what triggers the Nicholas gift story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.  (Legend.)

question: Bishop Nicholas came to the ruined merchant's house night after night with a heavy purse of gold, one purse for each of the three daughters. He did not knock and did not want the father to see him. The way he delivered them has fixed the scene in Christian art ever since. How did he get the purses to the family?
context: The window version is the earliest and most widespread; in some later medieval retellings the purse is dropped down the chimney instead, which is why Santa Claus still comes down chimneys. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.  (Legend.)

question: Painters took the three purses of gold that Bishop Nicholas gave a ruined merchant's daughters and simplified them into three golden balls, at his feet or in his hand. One trade in medieval Europe adopted those balls as its shop sign and took Nicholas as its patron saint. The sign still hangs over the doors of its old shops. Which trade was it?
context: Nicholas is the patron saint of pawnbrokers because the three purses of gold in the dowry story became the three golden balls of the pawnshop sign. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: A great storm caught a ship bound for the Holy Land with Nicholas aboard as a pilgrim, the legend says, and the men on it were giving themselves up for lost. Nicholas stood, rebuked the wind and the waves as though they were disobedient servants, and the storm died away. Because of that one scene he became the patron of one working group in medieval Europe. Which group?
context: Nicholas's image was carried on Mediterranean vessels for over a thousand years. Fishermen usually take Peter as patron (a fisher of Galilee); shipwrights take Joseph the carpenter; divers have no ancient patron. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.  (Legend.)

question: In a grim medieval legend, three young travellers stopped one night at a wayside inn and were never seen again. Bishop Nicholas came by, went straight to the innkeeper's back room, revealed the bodies, and named exactly what the wicked innkeeper had done with them. What had the innkeeper done with the bodies?
answer: Salted them into brine to sell as ham
choices: Salted them into brine to sell as ham
Buried them under the cellar floor
Fed them to the pigs in the sty
Baked them into loaves in the oven
context: This 13th-century legend, told in Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend, has Nicholas find the three boys pickled in a barrel in the innkeeper's back room -- and raise them back to life out of it. It is why Nicholas is also patron saint of children. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: The priest Arius argued at the Council of Nicaea in 325 that Jesus was not fully divine. A tale written down about a thousand years after Nicholas died put the bishop there, one of 318, and had him grow so angry that he attacked Arius in front of the whole council. What did Nicholas do to Arius in that tale?
choices: Threw a cup of wine at him
Kicked him out of his chair
context: The slap is a late (14th-century) tradition with no historical support -- there is no evidence Nicholas was even at Nicaea. It has become one of the most beloved Nicholas legends anyway. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: Dutch settlers carried a name across the Atlantic to New Amsterdam, later New York, and American mouths wore it down into Santa Claus. It was the name Dutch children shouted on the night of 5 December as they waited at their fireplaces for gifts. Which Dutch name is Santa Claus a corruption of?
context: Sinterklaas is the Dutch contraction of 'Sint Nikolaas' (Saint Nicholas). Sint-Maarten is Martin of Tours (11 November); Kerstman is modern Dutch for 'Christmas Man'; Zwarte Piet is Sinterklaas's controversial helper. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: In the book of Genesis, God saw the world grown full of violence, and Noah rode out the great flood in a huge wooden ark with his family and a pair of every kind of animal. Genesis names an exact span for the rain. How long did it fall?
context: Genesis 7:12 (KJV): 'And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights.'

question: Noah's three grown sons worked beside him on the enormous wooden ark, in the book of Genesis, and then rode out the world-drowning flood in it with their wives. What were the names of the three sons?
context: Genesis 7:13 (KJV): 'In the selfsame day entered Noah, and Shem, and Ham, and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and Noah's three wives with them.' The other trios are real Genesis families -- not Noah's sons.

question: God sent the great flood on Noah's world from two directions at once, in Genesis chapter 7. Rain poured from the sky, and on the same day water came up from underneath the earth, as if a hidden ocean had burst its lid. What did Genesis say burst open from beneath?
answer: the fountains of the great deep
choices: the fountains of the great deep
context: Genesis 7:11 (KJV): 'the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.'

question: Noah sent out a raven and then a dove, once the ark had come to rest on the mountains of Ararat and the flood was drying up. The dove came back empty-clawed the first time. On her second flight, at evening, she returned with a freshly plucked leaf in her beak, the sign that living plants stood above the water again. What kind of leaf did she bring?
context: Genesis 8:11 (KJV): 'the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated.' The olive branch as a peace-sign traces from here.

question: A king led the Tuatha De Danann, the god-people of Irish myth, from four northern cities to Ireland with a burning blade in his hand. Once it was drawn from its sheath, no enemy could escape it. He was the first of them to rule the island. What was his name?
context: Nuada was the first king of the Tuatha De Danann in Ireland. He carried Claiomh Solais, the Sword of Light, one of the Four Treasures brought from the city of Findias. Lugh and Bres come later in the story (Lugh becomes king after Nuada dies; Bres is the tyrant who rules while Nuada heals). Ogma is the great champion of the Tuatha De who invented the ogham alphabet, but he was never king.  (Legend.)

question: King Nuada of the Tuatha De Danann, the god-people of Irish myth, went into battle with one of their Four Treasures in his hand, and no enemy who felt its bite could ever get away from it. What was this treasure called?
context: The Claiomh Solais, or Sword of Light, is Nuada's weapon from the city of Findias. It is one of the Four Treasures alongside the Dagda's Cauldron, the Spear of Lugh, and the Lia Fail (the Stone of Destiny). Gae Bolg is Cuchulainn's belly-spear from a later Ulster-cycle story. The Spear of Lugh is a different Treasure. Excalibur is Arthurian, not Irish.  (Legend.)

question: Sreng, champion of the Fir Bolg, stepped out at the first battle of Moytura, when his people still held Ireland. With a single stroke of his sword he shore clean through King Nuada's guard. Which limb did Sreng take from Nuada with that stroke?
answer: Nuada's right arm at the shoulder
choices: Nuada's right arm at the shoulder
Nuada's sword hand at the wrist
context: In Cath Maige Tuired Cunga (the First Battle of Moytura) Sreng, the Fir Bolg champion, cut off Nuada's right arm at the shoulder with one blow. Nuada survived, but the wound would cost him his throne. Sreng was later offered Connacht as the Fir Bolg's share of Ireland after peace was made.  (Legend.)

question: King Nuada lost his throne after the first battle of Moytura, for by the old law of the god-people no man could rule them if he was not whole in body. Two Tuatha De craftsmen then built him a new limb out of pure silver, so cleverly hinged that every single finger moved like real flesh. Which pair made it?
answer: Dian Cecht the healer and Creidhne the wright
choices: Dian Cecht the healer and Creidhne the wright
Goibniu the smith and Luchta the carpenter
Ogma the champion and Bres the Beautiful
Manannan mac Lir and Aengus Og
context: Dian Cecht the physician-god crafted the arm itself, and Creidhne the wright helped with the jointing so that every finger moved as freely as flesh. From that day Nuada is called Nuada Airgetlam, Nuada of the Silver Hand. Goibniu and Luchta are the smith and carpenter of the Tuatha De -- makers of weapons, not this arm. Ogma and Bres are champion and king. Manannan and Aengus are sea-god and love-god, not craftsmen.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland out of four hidden northern cities, and they carried one Treasure from each. Falias sent the Stone of Fal, and Gorias sent Lugh's fiery Spear. A third sent the Dagda's bottomless Cauldron. Which city sent King Nuada's sword?
context: The Four Cities and their Treasures: Findias gave the Sword of Light (Nuada's blade); Falias gave the Lia Fail, the Stone of Destiny that cried out under a rightful king at Tara; Gorias gave the Spear of Lugh; Murias gave the Dagda's Cauldron of plenty. All four are named in the Lebor Gabala Erenn.  (Legend.)

question: A son of the healer Dian Cecht chanted over King Nuada for nine days, 'joint against joint of it, sinew against sinew'. He took the silver limb off the king and grew a living limb of flesh in its place. What was the name of this son of Dian Cecht?
context: Cath Maige Tuired section 33 records the healing: Miach son of Dian Cecht set the arm to Nuada's shoulder and, over nine days of chant ('bone to bone, sinew to sinew'), grew back living flesh. Ogma is the champion who invented the ogham alphabet. Goibniu is the smith of the Tuatha De. Aengus is the young god of Newgrange -- a different son of a different father (the Dagda).  (Legend.)

question: Dian Cecht, healer of the Tuatha De Danann, watched his own son grow King Nuada a real hand of flesh and bone back onto the arm, and he saw that the young man was the greater physician. Jealousy flared, and he turned on him. What did Dian Cecht do to his son next?
answer: struck him dead with four sword-blows to the head
choices: struck him dead with four sword-blows to the head
banished him beyond the western sea forever
cursed him into the shape of a running wolf
shut him alive in a hollow standing stone
context: Cath Maige Tuired records the killing in awful detail: the first stroke cut only skin, the second reached bone, the third pierced the brain-membrane, and the fourth killed Miach outright. It is one of the darker set-pieces in early Irish myth. The lupine curse is a Norse or Anglo-Saxon shape; hollow-stone imprisonment belongs to the Bres and Aoife stories.  (Legend.)

question: Airmed carefully laid out the herbs from her dead brother's grave in order on her cloak, so that no healer would ever be without the knowledge of them. One had grown for every joint and sinew in the human body. What exact number of herbs, in the Cath Maige Tuired reckoning, grew from the grave?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: 365 herbs grew from Miach's grave, 'as many as his joints and fibres'. Airmed the sister spread her cloak on the ground and laid each herb in its right place so that later healers could know which one cured which joint. The number matches the days of the year and is one of the oldest 'herbal correspondence' images in Western myth.  (Legend.)

question: Dian Cecht came upon a cloak of healing herbs beside his dead son's grave, and jealousy took him a third time. His daughter Airmed had spread the herbs out on it in perfect order, a living map that could cure any wound. What did Dian Cecht do to the cloak of herbs?
answer: overturned it so the herbs mixed beyond sorting
choices: overturned it so the herbs mixed beyond sorting
burned it and scattered the ashes to the sea
sold it to the Fomorians for a boat
buried it in the same grave as Miach
context: Dian Cecht, still enraged that his son Miach and his daughter Airmed had surpassed him, overturned the cloak and mixed the 365 herbs past any hope of sorting. Cath Maige Tuired ends the episode with the line that no human physician after that knew the powers of every herb -- 'only Airmed remembers'. The mixing-of-the-herbs is Irish myth's folk-etiology for the limits of the healing craft.  (Legend.)

question: King Nuada Silverhand stepped off his own throne just before the Tuatha De Danann fought the Fomorian giants, an odd thing for any king to do. He put a younger champion in his seat for the days leading up to the fight. Who took Nuada's seat as war-leader?
context: Cath Maige Tuired (Elizabeth Gray trans.): Nuada rose up before Lugh Samildanach ('many-skilled') at the king's seat because a champion was needed to lead the preparations. Ogma is the god of eloquence; the Dagda is the club-and-cauldron chief; Manannan is the sea-god.  (Legend.)

question: A young champion took King Nuada's throne before the great battle with the Fomorian giants, but only for a set number of days. Nuada said it was easier for a king to fill in for a champion than a champion to fill in for a king. How many days did he yield the throne?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: 'the king rose up before him till thirteen days had ended.' Seven, forty, and one hundred are all sacred numbers in other traditions (seven in Hebrew scripture, forty in the wilderness, one hundred in the Odyssey's suitors) but the Irish figure here is thirteen.  (Legend.)

question: The Fomorian giants met the Tuatha De Danann in battle on a plain in what is now County Sligo, where the Tuatha De had once fought an earlier people of Ireland, the Fir Bolg. Its name in Irish means 'the plain of pillars,' after the ancient standing stones that dotted it. What was that plain called?
context: Cath Maige Tuired ('the battle of Moytura'): Mag Tuired in County Sligo. Tara is the seat of the High King in Meath; Tailtiu is where the Tuatha De later lose to the Milesians and where the Lughnasadh games are held; Emain Macha is the Ulster capital of Conchobar mac Nessa.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann posted a guard of warriors behind the ranks in the war with the Fomorian giants, to keep their young champion away from the front line. They judged him too valuable to lose in the fighting. He slipped the guard and ran to the battle anyway. How many warriors had been set over him?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: 'his nine comrades keeping Lugh... then when the battle follows, Lugh escaped from the keeping in which he was.' Nine is a repeating Irish sacred number (the Nine Hazels of Segais, the nine worlds of Yggdrasil in Norse). Three, twelve, and twenty-one are the wrong counts.  (Legend.)

question: The victors of the battle found Bres alive and captive. He was half Fomorian and had once been their king, until they deposed him. They spared him, but only on condition that he teach them a set of skills the Fomorians had guarded from them until then. What did Bres have to teach them?
answer: how to plough, sow, and reap
choices: how to plough, sow, and reap
how to smelt iron and forge weapons
how to read the stars for war-omens
how to sail the western ocean
context: Cath Maige Tuired: Bres bought his life by teaching the Tuatha De the agricultural cycle -- ploughing, sowing, and reaping. The tale is a mythic charter for the Tuatha De's transition from a warrior-god people to farmers. Iron-smelting, star-reading, and ocean-sailing are staples of other myth-cycles.  (Legend.)

question: The young champion who had led the Tuatha De Danann to victory over the Fomorian giants took King Nuada's throne for good, for Nuada had fallen in the fighting. Irish tradition remembers the young champion's reign as the golden age of his people. How long did that tradition say he ruled?
context: Irish tradition (Lebor Gabala Erenn and later synchronisms): Lugh reigned forty years over the Tuatha De after Moytura. Forty is the number of the wilderness in the Christian pillar (Moses, Elijah, Jesus) -- an interesting cross-pillar echo. Seven, one hundred, and three hundred are other sacred spans.  (Legend.)

question: A monstrous wolf snaps his fetters at Ragnarok, the last battle of the Norse gods, and races across the world with his jaws stretched wide from earth to sky. He is hunting one target: the All-Father Odin himself. What is the name of this wolf?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51; Voluspa stanza 53. Fenrir is the great wolf who kills Odin at Ragnarok. Garm is a different Ragnarok-hound who guards the gate of Hel and kills Tyr. Skoll and Hati are Fenrir's OWN sons -- the two wolves who chase the sun and the moon across the sky and swallow them at Ragnarok. Fenrir is the specific killer of Odin.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson, the Icelander who collected the Norse myths in the 1200s, picks out one son of Odin as one of the strangest of the Aesir. He almost never speaks a word, yet Snorri names him the second-strongest god of all, after Thor, and at Ragnarok he will avenge his father. What is his name?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapters 29 and 51. Vidarr is the silent god, second-strongest of the Aesir after Thor. Vali is a different son of Odin -- born and grown in one day for the sole purpose of avenging Baldr, not Odin. Bragi is the god of poetry and eloquence (the opposite of silent). Forseti is the just-judging son of Baldr. Vidarr is the specific avenger of Odin.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri has the great wolf burst loose at Ragnarok, his jaws opening so far that one touches heaven and the other drags on the ground. Something bursts from his eyes and nostrils as he runs out onto the plain. What comes from the wolf's eyes and nose as he charges?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51: 'flames burst from his eyes and nostrils' as Fenrir runs. Poison is what the Midgard-serpent Jormungandr breathes over Thor a few lines later in the same passage, and what kills Thor nine steps after the serpent dies. Smoke and ice belong to other Ragnarok forces (Surtr's fire-smoke; the fimbulwinter). Fire is the specific detail Snorri gives Fenrir at the last battle.  (Legend.)

question: The All-Father Odin goes out to meet the loose wolf at Ragnarok and falls, the single greatest loss the Aesir suffer that day. The wolf does not merely bite him or gore him. The Norse poem Voluspa and Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda use the same shocking phrase. What does the wolf do to Odin?
context: Voluspa stanza 53; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Fenrir swallows Odin whole -- the All-Father, wisdom-god of a hundred and seventy names, the hanged god of the runes, goes down the wolf's throat. Odin's missing eye was long ago pledged to Mimir's well for wisdom. Sleipnir the eight-legged horse carries him to and from the battle. The wolf's specific killing of Odin is the swallowing.  (Legend.)

question: Odin's silent son steps forward at Ragnarok to avenge his father on the wolf, wearing one very special piece of armour on one foot. It is the thick-soled shoe he will need when he plants that foot inside the wolf's mouth. What is the shoe made of?
answer: leather scraps trimmed from every boot
choices: leather scraps trimmed from every boot
iron bands worked by the sons of Ivaldi
the scales of a fallen dragon
the tanned hide of Fenrir's father
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. The shoe is made of the strips of leather trimmed from the toes and heels of every boot ever made in the human world. It has been growing since the beginning of time and it must be thick enough to protect the foot that will one day step inside a wolf's mouth.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson stops the story at the shoe of Odin's silent son and gives his Norse readers a plain rule. If they want to help the Aesir at Ragnarok, they must do a certain thing whenever they cut a shoe. What does Snorri tell every cobbler to do?
answer: throw away the trimmings from his own workbench
choices: throw away the trimmings from his own workbench
keep the trimmings and place them in his grave
burn the trimmings on a bonfire at midwinter
hand the trimmings to his lord as tribute
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51: 'That shoe has been being made since the beginning of time. Any man who wishes to help the Aesir must throw away the strips of leather he cuts off the ends of his own boot when making it.' Discarded scraps drift somehow to Vidarr's foot -- the myth turns every cobbler in the medieval North into a small contributor to the vengeance of a god. The other three choices are plausible medieval practices, but only discarding the scraps is what Snorri asks.  (Legend.)

question: A silent son of Odin meets the great wolf on the plain of Vigrid at Ragnarok, after the wolf has already killed his father. He plants one strange, thick-soled shoe on the wolf's lower jaw. In Snorri Sturluson's account, how does he kill the wolf from there?
answer: rips the wolf's mouth apart with his hands
choices: rips the wolf's mouth apart with his hands
drives Gungnir through the wolf's heart
hurls the wolf into the sea
beheads the wolf with a great axe
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Vidarr plants his shod foot on Fenrir's lower jaw, grips the upper jaw with both hands, and tears the wolf's mouth apart, killing him. Odin's spear Gungnir is already lost inside the wolf; there is no beheading, no drowning. The specific act is a two-handed jaw-rending.  (Legend.)

question: The All-Father, chief of the Norse gods, paid dearly for a single drink of water. He ruled Asgard as master of poetry, war and death itself, with Thor the thunder-god for a son and Frigg for a wife. What was the All-Father's name?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 20: Odin (Old Norse Odinn, English Woden) is the All-Father, chief of the Aesir. Baldr is his shining son slain by mistletoe; Heimdallr is the watchman at Bifrost; Njord is a Vanir god, father of Freyr and Freyja.  (Legend.)

question: Odin traded away one part of his body at the well of a wise giant, in exchange for a single drink of its magic water, and it never grew back. Every carving the Vikings left of him shows the same wound. What part of his body was Odin missing?
context: Odin is famously ONE-EYED, the eye left as a pledge in Mimir's well. Tyr is the god who lost a hand (bitten off by the wolf Fenrir); Fionn mac Cumhaill lost a fingertip on the Salmon of Knowledge in the Irish tradition; no major Norse god loses an ear.  (Legend.)

question: Odin came to a well beneath one root of the world-tree Yggdrasil, the giant ash that holds up the nine worlds. Its water granted wisdom to whoever drank it, and an old and knowing giant watched over it day and night. Well and giant shared one name. What was the well called?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 15: under one of Yggdrasil's three roots (the one running toward the frost-giants) lies Mimir's well, whose water gives wisdom. Urd's well is under a DIFFERENT root and is where the three Norns shape fate. Hvergelmir is the roaring spring under the third root, in Niflheim. Byrgir is a well from a different myth (Bil and Hjuki).  (Legend.)

question: In a poem of the Poetic Edda, Odin told his own story from inside a fire-torture, under one of the hidden names he had gathered as he walked Midgard in disguise. The poem takes its title from that name, which means 'the Masked One.' Which name was it?
context: Grimnismal (Poetic Edda) takes its title from Grimnir, 'the Masked One' or 'the Hooded One' -- one of Odin's many aliases when he goes among mortals in disguise. Bolverk (the Ill-Worker) is the name he uses stealing the Mead of Poetry from the giant Suttung; Hangatyr (God of the Hanged) comes from his self-hanging on Yggdrasil; Har (the High) is his throne-name in the Havamal.  (Legend.)

question: A seeress in the Voluspa told Odin she knew exactly where he had hidden the pledge he paid for his drink of wisdom. The giant who guarded the well, she said, still drank from that pledge every single morning, and not plain water. She named the drink. What did the giant drink each morning?
context: Voluspa 28-29: 'Well I know, Odin, where you hid your eye -- in Mimir's famous well; Mimir drinks mead every morning from the Father of the Slain's pledge.' Mead (fermented honey drink) is the sacred liquor of the Norse gods generally -- see also the Mead of Poetry that Odin later steals from the giant Suttung, and the mead that the goat Heidrun's udder pours in Valhalla for the einherjar.  (Legend.)

question: Odin sets out after deeper knowledge, with one eye already paid for his first taste of it. He wants the magic marks that shape fate itself, the ones gods and men still carve on stone and wood for spells. What is the Norse name for those marks?
context: The RUNES are the Old Norse writing system (Elder Futhark, Younger Futhark), and in the myths they are also the raw shapes of fate that gods, elves, dwarves, and men learn from Odin. The sagas are the long Icelandic prose stories written down centuries later; the Eddas are the two main mythological compilations (Poetic and Prose); the galdr are the spoken magic-songs (Odin learns nine of THOSE at the same time as the runes, but they are different from the runes themselves).  (Legend.)

question: The All-Father Odin climbs the great ash tree at the middle of the nine worlds and uses it as no god has used it before, as his own gallows. He wants a secret that no book holds and no friend will hand over. What is the name of that great ash?
context: Yggdrasil is the great ash tree at the center of Norse cosmology, with three roots and nine worlds strung through its branches. Laeradr is the tree that stands over the roof of Valhalla, browsed by the goat Heidrun and the stag Eikthyrnir; Mimameidr ('Mimi's tree') is a tree named in Fjolsvinnsmal, often identified with Yggdrasil but named separately; Hoddmimir's holt is the wood where the two human survivors of Ragnarok, Lif and Lifthrasir, hide out the end of the world.  (Legend.)

question: With no hand but his own, Odin ties a rope around his neck and hangs himself from a branch of the world-tree. To make the sacrifice complete he also wounds himself in the side with a weapon of his own, forged by dwarves. What weapon does Odin use to wound himself?
context: Havamal 138: Odin is 'wounded with a spear' -- his own spear Gungnir (made by the sons of Ivaldi, the same dwarf-team who lost the wager to Sindri and Brokkr in the Mjolnir story). Odin is not a swordsman in the myths; his weapon is always the spear.  (Legend.)

question: In the Havamal, Odin hangs nine nights on the world-tree without bread or drink, offering himself to himself. On the ninth night the ordeal breaks: he looks down, seizes what he came for and falls back off the tree. The poem gives him one loud, physical act at the very moment he grabs it. What does Odin do?
context: Havamal 139: on the ninth night Odin looked down, screamed out, and took up the runes -- then fell back from the tree. The scream is the release: the pain of nine nights and a spear-wound crashing at once into knowledge. There is no laughter, no prayer, no hymn in the passage.  (Legend.)

question: Odin hangs himself on the world-tree, and the tree keeps the story in its name. A gallows in Old Norse is a 'horse of the hanged,' and the tree's name means 'the horse of' one of Odin's many names, the one that points straight at his nine long nights on it. Whose horse is the world-tree?
context: Ygg is one of Odin's names -- it means 'the Terrible' or 'the Awesome'. 'Horse of the hanged' is an Old Norse kenning for GALLOWS, and because Odin hangs himself from this tree, the tree becomes 'Ygg's horse' -- Ygg's gallows. So the very NAME of the world-tree carries this story inside it. Grimnir ('the Masked One'), Bolverk ('the Evil-Doer', the alias he uses in the Mead of Poetry theft), and Har ('the High One', the name that titles the Havamal itself) are all real Odin-names -- but the tree's name specifically embeds Ygg.  (Legend.)

question: Odin himself speaks much of the Havamal, the long Old Norse poem that holds the whole passage about the tree. Its title means 'Sayings of the ___', and the blank is one of his plainest names. What does 'Havamal' mean?
context: Havamal = 'Sayings of Har', and Har ('the High') is Odin's throne-name. Gangleri ('the Wanderer') is another Odin-name he uses when he travels in disguise (see the Grimnismal frame). Hangatyr ('God of the Hanged') and various wolf-related names are also his, but the poem's title takes the 'High One' name specifically.  (Legend.)

question: Odin falls back off the world-tree with what he came for, and he does not keep it to himself. In the part of the Havamal known as the Runatal, he names four different kinds of being who each receive the fate-shaping marks from him and use them ever after. Which four groups get them?
answer: the Aesir, the elves, the dwarves, and mortal men
choices: the Aesir, the elves, the dwarves, and mortal men
the Aesir, the Vanir, the giants, and mortal men
the einherjar, the Valkyries, the Norns, and the trolls
the light-elves, the dark-elves, the frost-giants, and the fire-giants
context: Havamal 143 lists the four groups who receive the runes: the Aesir (Odin among them), the elves (through Dain the elf), the dwarves (through Dvalin the dwarf), and mortal men (through Odin himself, called Odroerir here). The Vanir and giants are notably NOT named as recipients -- the giants especially have their own separate wisdom-lore, and the runes come to gods and mortals through Odin's ordeal alone.  (Legend.)

question: An old stranger walked the roads of Midgard, the human world, with a broad hat pulled down low over his face, a grey-blue cloak and a staff. He had traded one eye for a drink at a well of wisdom beneath the world-tree. Which Norse god was he in disguise?
context: The one-eyed wanderer in the broad hat is Odin, All-Father of the Aesir. Thor is red-bearded and rides a goat-cart, never disguises himself as an old man. Freyr is the Vanir god of harvests. Heimdall is the golden guardian of the Bifrost bridge -- he stays at his post.  (Legend.)

question: King Geirroth of the Goths took a stranger in a broad hat and dark cloak for a spy or a wizard, in the Grimnismal, and he demanded the man's name. The stranger refused. Geirroth ordered him seized and tortured to force him to speak. What form of torture did Geirroth use on the captive?
answer: seated between two roaring fires for eight nights
choices: seated between two roaring fires for eight nights
hung upside-down from a rafter for a day
tied to a stake and lashed at dawn
sealed alive in a barrel of brine
context: Geirroth sets the captive on a bench between two fires and leaves him there for eight nights, hoping thirst and heat will loosen his tongue. This is the setup for the entire Grimnismal -- the captive stays silent for eight days and then, on the ninth, begins to speak. In some translations the count is 'eight nights and into the ninth day'.  (Legend.)

question: A ghost ride of the dead crossed the winter sky over the Norwegian villages, and the villagers had an older name for it than the Wild Hunt, even a thousand years after they became Christian. Their word meant 'the Terrifying Ride.' What was that Norse name?
context: Oskoreia (also spelled Oskorei, Oskorreid) means 'the Terrifying Ride' or 'the Thundering Host'. Another Norwegian name is Odensjakt, 'Odin's Hunt'. In German it is Das Wutende Heer, 'the Furious Army' (from Wodan, Odin's German name), and Die Wilde Jagd, 'the Wild Hunt', which the English name translates. The wrong choices are real Norse terms but different things: the Einherjar are Odin's chosen warriors in Valhalla waiting for Ragnarok, the Ragnarok is the doom of the gods itself, and the Landvaettir are the land-spirits who guard the ground.  (Legend.)

question: A fairy-woman rode up on a white horse and carried Oisin, the warrior-poet son of Fionn mac Cumhaill, away over the sea to a faraway island of joy. Nobody grew old there, and few mortals ever came back from it. What was the Irish name of that island?
context: Tir na nOg means 'the Land of the Young': no one there grows old, the trees are always in flower and fruit at once, and no sickness comes. Emain Ablach, Mag Mell ('the plain of delight'), and Ynys Wydryn ('the isle of glass') are three other real Celtic Otherworld names, all cognate with Avalon in Arthurian legend. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/

question: The Fianna were out hunting on the shore of a lake in Kerry one morning when a woman rode up out of the water on a white horse whose hooves never broke the surface. She named herself as the daughter of the sea-god Manannan mac Lir. What was her name?
context: Niamh Chinn Oir means 'Niamh of the Golden Head' (her hair fell to the horse's flank). Sadhbh is Oisin's own mother; Grainne is the woman Diarmuid runs away with; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife (Ulster Cycle). Source: https://godsandmonsters.info/oisin/  (Legend.)

question: Oisin, the poet son of Fionn mac Cumhaill, rode off the sand at Loch Lein behind a fairy-woman on a white horse, out over the sea itself, bound for the Land of the Young. In which direction did they ride to reach it?
context: In Irish tradition the Otherworld is always west, across the sea: the same direction where the ancient Irish believed the sun went to die each night. This is why later medieval Irish voyage-tales, the immrama, always sail west toward the islands of the blessed. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: The sea-god Manannan mac Lir's daughter borrowed a magical white horse to carry Oisin away, one that could gallop across ocean waves as easily as across grass. It had been her father's own, and the tale gives it a name. What was that horse's name?
choices: Liath Macha of the Grey Battle
context: Embarr (sometimes spelled Enbarr, meaning 'water-foam') belonged to the sea-god Manannan mac Lir before being lent to his daughter Niamh. Sleipnir is Odin's horse (Norse pillar); Pegasus is Bellerophon's (Greek pillar); Liath Macha is Cu Chulainn's chariot-horse from the Ulster Cycle. Source: https://godsandmonsters.info/oisin/  (Legend.)

question: Oisin married the fairy-woman who had carried him over the sea and had children with her in the Land of the Young, where nobody grew old. It felt to him like only a short stretch of years. How many years did he count there before the homesickness for Ireland grew unbearable?
context: In the Otherworld the time seemed to be only three years to Oisin. The bitter joke of the tale is that three years in Tir na nOg were three hundred years in Ireland: the whole Fianna had been dead for centuries while he lived what he thought was a short married idyll. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: The fairy-woman let Oisin take her white horse when he grew homesick at last and asked leave to ride back to Ireland, to visit his father Fionn mac Cumhaill and the old warband, the Fianna. She gave him one strict warning about a thing that must never happen while he was there. What did she warn him?
answer: That his feet must never touch Irish soil
choices: That his feet must never touch Irish soil
That he must never look back over his shoulder
That he must never speak his own name aloud
That he must never eat any food grown on land
context: The warning is a fatal condition: as long as he stayed on horseback the Otherworld's timelessness would hold him, but the moment he touched Irish ground the three hundred years he had missed would fall on him. Compare Orpheus's warning not to look back at Eurydice, a Greek-pillar tale of the same shape. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: Riding through Ireland on the white horse, Oisin found the country changed beyond recognition, Fionn centuries dead and the Fianna a legend not living men. Then he saw a group of men by the roadside working at something that was too heavy for them, and stopped to help. What were the men trying to do?
choices: Push a cart out of the mud
context: The detail is one of the sharpest in the tale: three hundred years on, the men of Ireland are so much smaller and weaker than the Fianna were that a group of them together cannot budge a boulder Oisin can lean down from the saddle and move with one hand. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: Some men were struggling by an Irish road when Oisin leaned down from the white horse to help them. His fatal moment came not from a spear or an enemy. One small piece of horse-tack snapped under him and sent him to the ground. What broke?
context: The saddle-girth is the strap that runs under the horse's belly and holds the saddle on. When it broke, saddle and rider both slid sideways to the ground. The whole three hundred years poured into him the instant his foot touched the soil. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: A wandering Christian saint found old Oisin by the road, at the opening of the Acallam na Senorach, 'The Colloquy of the Ancients.' The saint questioned him for months about the old pagan days of the Fianna. Which saint heard the old stories from Oisin?
context: The Acallam na Senorach (c. 1200) uses Patrick as the sympathetic Christian listener to whom the last surviving pagan Fenian dictates the old warrior-tales before dying. Every other saint listed is a real early Irish saint. The device gave medieval Christian Ireland a way of preserving the pagan legends. Source: https://godsandmonsters.info/oisin/

question: A white horse, lent by the fairy princess, carried Oisin home to Ireland from the Land of Youth. It did not stay by his side when he crashed to the ground beside the road and the lost centuries fell on him at once. What did the horse do?
answer: Galloped riderless back over the waves to Tir na nOg
choices: Galloped riderless back over the waves to Tir na nOg
Reared up and vanished into a sea-mist
Was struck to stone where it stood beside him
Threw itself into the nearest river and drowned
context: Embarr of the Flowing Mane, Manannan mac Lir's own sea-horse, turned back the way it had come and ran west across the water to the Land of the Young, leaving Oisin ancient and blind by the Irish road. W. B. Yeats later reshaped the whole tale into his long poem The Wanderings of Oisin (1889), drawing on Michael Comyn's Laoi Oisin ar Thir na nOg (c. 1750). Source: https://godsandmonsters.info/oisin/  (Legend.)

question: Jesus of Nazareth stopped just outside Jerusalem on the Sunday before he was killed, and sent two of his disciples ahead into the next town. They were to bring back one animal tied up by a doorway, and it was not the warhorse a conquering king would ride. Which animal did he send for?
context: Mark 11:2 KJV: 'Go your way into the village over against you: and as soon as ye be entered into it, ye shall find a colt tied, whereon never man sat; loose him, and bring him.' The choice of a donkey rather than a horse is the whole point of the scene -- a king coming in peace, not conquest. If any owner challenged them, the disciples were told to say 'The Lord hath need of him' (Mark 11:3).

question: Two disciples went ahead of Jesus to a nearby village, in the Gospel of Mark, to fetch the animal he would ride into Jerusalem for the last week of his life. Mark added one small detail about it, spelled out in six words. What did Mark note about the animal?
answer: No one had ever ridden it
choices: No one had ever ridden it
It had been born that spring
context: Mark 11:2 KJV: 'a colt tied, whereon never man sat.' The Old Testament required a similar untouched-ness for animals used in rites (see the red heifer in Numbers 19:2, or the cart for the Ark in 1 Samuel 6:7 -- 'a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke'). Nothing about colour, age, or tack is emphasised.

question: The crowds threw branches and cloaks in the road ahead of Jesus as he rode into Jerusalem, and they shouted one Hebrew word over and over. The Gospel of Matthew gives the whole cry, 'Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord,' but the single shout before it is the one everyone remembers. What was it?
context: Matthew 21:9 KJV: 'Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.' Hosanna comes from Psalm 118:25 KJV, 'Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD' -- literally 'save, please.' By New Testament times it had drifted from prayer into acclamation. Hallelujah means 'praise the Lord'; Selah is an untranslated musical direction from the Psalms; Amen means 'so be it.' All four are real preserved-Hebrew words in scripture -- only Hosanna belongs to this scene.

question: The prophet Zechariah wrote of a coming king centuries before Jesus rode into Jerusalem, and the scene on that road matched his line. The king would arrive not on a warhorse. Zechariah 9:9 reads, in the King James words, 'Behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; ______, and riding upon an ass.' What word fills the blank?
context: Zechariah 9:9 KJV in full. 'Lowly' means humble, close to the ground -- the opposite of a general on a war-horse. Zechariah wrote in the sixth or fifth century BC; by Jesus's time this verse was one of the standard messianic passages. Note the parallelism: JUST, HAVING SALVATION, LOWLY. Riding an ass rather than a horse was the deliberate sign of a king coming in peace rather than conquest.

question: Jesus walked into the outer courts of the Temple and found a marketplace: money-changers making a profit on the temple-tax exchange rate, dealers selling animals for sacrifice. One gospel says he did not just yell at them. He made a specific object and used it to drive them out. What object did he make?
context: John 2:15 KJV: 'And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overturned the tables.' A scourge is a whip -- knotted together from small cords. This is the single most physically confrontational act of the ministry -- Jesus took the time to braid a whip before starting. Only John's gospel records the whip; the synoptics have the same scene without the cord detail.

question: The money-changers in the Temple heard Jesus shout as he overturned their tables. His accusation was stitched together from two Old Testament lines, one from Isaiah about what the Temple was supposed to be, one from Jeremiah about what it had become.
