The Gospel of Matthew gives it in the King James words: 'My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a ______.' What words fill the blank?
context: Matthew 21:13 KJV in full. The 'den of thieves' is the exact phrase from Jeremiah 7:11: 'Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?' A den is a robbers' hideout -- Jesus is not just calling them cheats, he is calling the temple a hideout for cheats. Mark 11:18 says the chief priests heard about the scene and 'sought how they might destroy him.'

question: Jesus drove the merchants out of the Temple in all four gospels, but the gospels do not agree on when. Three of them place the scene in the very last week of his life, just after his entry into Jerusalem. The fourth places the same scene at the opening of his ministry, three years earlier. Which gospel is the odd one out?
context: John 2:13-17 places the cleansing at the start of the ministry -- the same chapter as the wedding at Cana; the synoptic gospels (Matthew 21, Mark 11, Luke 19) place it in Holy Week. Some readers reconcile the difference by proposing Jesus did it twice; others treat the timing as an artistic choice by John, who arranges his gospel by theme more than chronology. The question states the divergence honestly rather than picking a side.

question: Prometheus steals fire from Olympus, gives it to people, and warns his younger brother never to accept any gift sent down by Zeus. He knows every such gift carries a hidden curse. When Zeus sends down the first woman, Pandora, as a bride, the younger brother takes her anyway. What is that brother's name?
context: Epimetheus ('Afterthought' in Greek) accepts Pandora and remembers his brother's warning only afterwards. All four choices are Titans of the same family: Menoetius was a brother of Prometheus struck down by Zeus in the Titanomachy, Iapetus was their father, Atlas was another brother, condemned to hold up the sky. Source: Hesiod, Works and Days 83-89; Wikipedia, 'Epimetheus'.  (Legend.)

question: Pandora, the first woman, comes down from the gods as a bride with a sealed vessel, a wedding gift under strict orders never to be opened. Zeus has sent her as payback for the stolen fire. Alone in the house of her new husband, she is overcome by curiosity and lifts the lid. What happens the moment the lid comes off?
answer: every evil swarms out and scatters over the world
choices: every evil swarms out and scatters over the world
the vessel bursts into an unquenchable flame
the vessel sinks silently into the earth
she is turned into stone where she stands
context: In Works and Days 94-99 the evils -- sickness, old age, hard labour, envy, war, hunger -- fly out of the jar as a swarm and can never be gathered back in. From that day on, mortals live with them. Source: Hesiod, Works and Days 94-99.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod leaves one thing inside Pandora's jar after the lid has come off, and he never explains which way the reader should take it. Readers have argued over his line since antiquity, and two readings still stand against each other. What is the great dispute over what remained inside the jar?
answer: whether it is trapped away from mortals or saved for them
choices: whether it is trapped away from mortals or saved for them
whether the Greek word means Hope or Fear
whether it is a goddess or an abstract quality
whether Zeus put it there or Pandora did
context: One reading: Hope is imprisoned in the jar, so mortals go through life with only the evils that flew out. The other reading: Hope is safe in the jar, kept for mortals to draw on. Hesiod does not say. Both readings have serious defenders. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pandora'; 'Pandora's box'.

question: Patrick, whose feast fills the streets of Dublin, Boston and New York every 17 March, gave his birthplace in his own writing: an estate called Bannavem Taburniae. His father was a deacon and his grandfather a priest, in a Roman-Christian family. In which land did that family live?
context: Patrick calls his childhood home Bannavem Taburniae, a Romano-British estate whose exact location is unknown; most scholars place it in western Britain, perhaps modern Cumbria or Wales. The point matters: Ireland's patron saint was a foreigner, taken there as a slave. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Irish pirates raided the coast and seized Patrick, still a boy, at his father's villa, then shipped him across the sea to be sold as a slave. He told the story himself, and he even gave his age. How old was he when the pirates took him?
context: Patrick's own Confessio names the age. He is one of the very few Christian saints for whom we have such a precise personal biography in his own hand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick stood praying among his master's flock on a bare hill in Ireland, a slave and a changed man. He had been a careless Roman-British teen who barely cared about God. By his own count he now prayed a hundred times a day. How many years was Patrick a slave in Ireland before he escaped?
context: The Confessio is explicit on the count of six years. The prayer habit he formed in those years -- 'a hundred prayers by day and nearly as many at night' (Confessio 16) -- is what he credits with his conversion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: A voice came to Patrick in a dream one night on the Irish hillside. It told him his fasting had been well done and that he would soon go home to his own country. Then a second voice, later that night, spoke a single short line that sent him walking straight out of slavery. What was the second voice's line?
choices: 'The angels of God go with you.'
context: Both dream-lines are recorded in the Confessio. Patrick took them literally, left his master's flock, and walked to the sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: A ship's captain took Patrick aboard at an Irish port, after the runaway slave had walked about two hundred miles across the country to reach it and talked his way on. The ship was bound for the Continent, and it was carrying one famous Irish export. What was on board with Patrick?
context: The great Irish hounds were sought after in Rome and Gaul as war-dogs and hunting-dogs; a shipload of them was a serious cargo. The Confessio does not say the captain believed Patrick's story -- only that he took him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Jocelyn of Furness wrote that Patrick drove the snakes out of Ireland with his crozier, in a medieval Life of the saint, the first time anyone set the story down. Patrick never mentions any snakes in his own writings, and Ireland has had none since the last ice age. In which century did Jocelyn write?
context: The story first appears in Jocelyn of Furness's Life of Patrick, written around 1185 -- about 700 years after Patrick himself. Patrick's own writings never mention snakes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.  (Legend.)

question: The escaped slave got home to Britain and did not settle down. He crossed to Gaul and trained in theology, perhaps at Auxerre or the island monastery of Lerins. Patrick made a decision in the 430s or 440s that shaped every year of the rest of his life. What did he decide to do?
answer: Go back to Ireland as a missionary bishop
choices: Go back to Ireland as a missionary bishop
Stay in Gaul as a teacher at Auxerre
Retire to a hermit cave on the Loire
context: This is the moral centre of Patrick's story: he VOLUNTARILY RETURNED to the country of his enslavement, was ordained bishop, and spent decades preaching among the pagan Irish kings and druids -- never leaving again. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick set down two writings in his own Latin, the oldest personal writings from all of Ireland's history. One was a fierce open letter against a Christian British warlord who had sold Patrick's new converts as slaves. The other was the story of his own life. What was that autobiography called?
context: 'Confessio' is Latin for 'declaration' or 'testimony' (not 'confession' in the modern sense). Vita Patricii is the title of the LATER Lives written by others; Peregrinatio means 'pilgrimage'; Lorica means 'breastplate' -- the name of a famous later prayer wrongly attributed to Patrick. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick introduced himself to those who would come after in the first line of his autobiography, the oldest personal book from Ireland's history. He had founded a whole Christian church by then, and this was the way he chose. How did he open the book?
answer: 'I am Patrick, a sinner, most unlearned, the least of all the faithful.'
choices: 'I am Patrick, a sinner, most unlearned, the least of all the faithful.'
'I, Patrick, bishop and apostle to the Irish, greet you.'
'Blessed are you who read these words in the peace of the Lord.'
'By the grace of God I have brought the Gospel to the ends of the earth.'
context: The full opening: 'I am Patrick, a sinner, most unlearned, the least of all the faithful, and utterly despised by many.' The self-deprecation is not false modesty -- Patrick genuinely believed his shepherd-slave years had made him a rustic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessio_of_Saint_Patrick.

question: The men of Coroticus, a Christian British warlord, raided an Irish village of Patrick's new converts and shipped the captives away to be sold as slaves in Britain. Patrick answered with a letter that did something a bishop had no clear right to do to a warlord in another country. What does the letter do to Coroticus and his soldiers?
choices: It petitions the Pope in Rome to try them
It curses their descendants to the third generation
It offers them absolution if they will free the slaves
context: The Letter to Coroticus is one of the earliest surviving Christian denunciations of slave-trading by Christians. Patrick declares Coroticus's soldiers cut off from the Christian community until they repent and free the Irish captives -- an astonishing use of episcopal authority across a national border in the fifth century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: A slave girl began to follow Paul and his companion Silas through the streets of Philippi, shouting again and again that these men were servants of the Most High God. Her owners made a lot of money off her strange power. What kind of spirit ruled her, in the book of Acts?
context: Acts 16:16 -- the girl 'brought her masters much gain by soothsaying'. Divination meant she was used as a fortune-teller. When Paul finally turned and commanded the spirit out of her, her owners lost their income and dragged Paul and Silas before the magistrates.

question: The judges of Philippi had Paul and Silas stripped, beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison. The jailer then fastened their feet in one device to hold them still through the night. What was the device?
context: Acts 16:24 -- the jailer 'thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks'. Roman stocks pinned the ankles wide apart in a beam, an agonizing position after a public flogging.

question: Paul and Silas lay bruised in the innermost cell of the prison at Philippi, beaten with rods for preaching about Jesus. At midnight they did something that the other prisoners stopped to listen to. What were the two men doing in the middle of the night?
context: Acts 16:25 (KJV): 'And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.' The other captives listened from their own cells while the two beaten men sang.

question: An earthquake threw open every door of the prison at Philippi and woke the Roman jailer. He saw the ruined doorway and stood with his sword drawn, ready to fall on it, for if his prisoners had escaped he would be executed anyway. A voice from the darkened cell stopped his hand, as Paul shouted a single sentence out of the black. What did Paul cry out?
answer: Do thyself no harm: for we are all here
choices: Do thyself no harm: for we are all here
Peace be with thee: the LORD is at hand
Fear not: the angels have delivered us
Stay thy hand: we come out unbound
context: Acts 16:28 (KJV): 'But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here.' Not one prisoner had used the open doors to bolt.

question: The shaken jailer of Philippi called for a light, ran into the inner prison and fell trembling at the feet of Paul and Silas. Then he took them out to his own house. Before daylight ever reached the city he did two things: he cleaned the beating-wounds on his prisoners, and he brought his whole family through the same ritual he had just accepted. What was that ritual?
context: Acts 16:33 -- 'And he took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes; and was baptized, he and all his, straightway.'

question: Paul preached on a riverbank outside Philippi to a group of women who had gathered there to pray, earlier in the chapter of Acts that holds the slave girl and the earthquake. One of them was a wealthy merchant from Thyatira, and she became the first convert on European soil that Acts records. What did she sell for a living?
context: Acts 16:14 -- 'a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira'. Thyatira was famous for its purple-dye trade; Lydia's baptism and hospitality at Philippi came just before the events of the jail.

question: Paul walked the streets of Athens alone about AD 50, waiting for his friends Silas and Timothy to catch up. One sight above all others stirred him up. What did he see everywhere in the city that troubled him?
answer: Statues and altars to countless gods on every corner
choices: Statues and altars to countless gods on every corner
Roman soldiers dragging Jewish believers to prison
Beggars starving outside the marble temples
Slaves being sold in the marketplace
context: Acts 17:16 KJV: 'his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry.' Athens was the philosophical and religious capital of the Greek world, thick with shrines. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Philosophers from two of the city's most famous schools took Paul up in the Athenian marketplace and dismissed him as a 'babbler' and a 'setter forth of strange gods.' Which two schools did Acts name as the ones that confronted him?
context: Acts 17:18: 'Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him.' Epicureans followed Epicurus (pleasure as absence of pain); Stoics followed Zeno (virtue and reason). https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Paul stood on Mars' Hill and opened with a compliment. Walking through the city, he told the Athenian philosophers, he had seen many altars, and one had caught his eye for the strange inscription cut into it. What did Paul say the altar was inscribed to?
choices: To the god of the earth
To the god of the sea
context: Acts 17:23: 'I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.' Athenians built such altars as insurance against overlooking any deity. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Aratus, a famous poet from Cilicia, wrote a line of Greek verse that Paul, a Jew from Tarsus in the same province, quoted back at the Athenian philosophers on Mars' Hill. Paul treated it as a bridge to his own message. Which line of Aratus did he quote?
answer: For we are also his offspring
choices: For we are also his offspring
No man steps in the same river twice
Great is Diana of the Ephesians
context: Acts 17:28: 'as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.' The line comes from the Phenomena of Aratus of Soli, a Stoic-flavored poem about the heavens - and Aratus, like Paul, was from Cilicia. The other choices: Heraclitus's river fragment, Homer's Odyssey dawn-formula, and Acts 19's Ephesus riot cry - all real quotes, wrong scenes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areopagus_sermon

question: Paul quoted not one but two Greek poets in a single sentence on Mars' Hill. Alongside the line from Aratus he offered another verse, 'in him we live, and move, and have our being,' a line traditionally credited to a poet-sage of six hundred years earlier. Who was that poet-sage, by tradition?
context: Acts 17:28: 'For in him we live, and move, and have our being.' The line is traditionally attributed to Epimenides, the same Cretan sage credited with the plague-story behind the very altar 'to the unknown god' that Paul had quoted moments before. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areopagus_sermon

question: The Athenian court on Mars' Hill listened politely to Paul for most of his sermon, until he reached one claim that Greek philosophy could not swallow. The audience broke apart, some mocking, some saying 'we will hear thee again of this matter.' Which claim of Paul's split the Areopagus in two?
answer: That the dead would rise again in bodily form
choices: That the dead would rise again in bodily form
That the temples of Athens must all be torn down
That the emperor in Rome was a false god
That the Jewish Law bound Greeks as well as Jews
context: Acts 17:32: 'when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.' For an Athenian philosopher, the soul might survive - but a body coming back was absurd. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Paul preached on Mars' Hill in Athens, and most of his hearers mocked him; only a small handful believed. The book of Acts names just two of these converts, a rare specificity for such a thin missionary haul: one man, and one woman named alongside him. Which pair did Acts record?
answer: Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris
choices: Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris
Aquila the tentmaker and his wife Priscilla
Crispus the ruler and a woman named Lydia
Justus the god-fearer and a woman named Phoebe
context: Acts 17:34: 'certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris.' Dionysius sat as a member of the Areopagus council itself; later church tradition made him first bishop of Athens. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Paul left Athens for the next Greek city down the isthmus, after one of his thinnest missionary results anywhere in Acts. It was a boisterous port where his mission finally took deep root, and he remained there for a year and a half. To which city did Paul go next?
context: Acts 18:1-11: after Athens Paul went to Corinth, met the tentmaker couple Aquila and Priscilla, and 'continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.' Athens was the philosophical showpiece; Corinth was the churn where the mission took hold. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areopagus_sermon

question: An angry mob seized Paul at the Temple in Jerusalem, and Roman soldiers rescued him. For two full years the Romans held him in the city where the Roman governor of Judea kept his headquarters, and there he was tried. In which city was Paul held?
context: Acts 23:33-35, 25:1-6. Caesarea Maritima was Herod the Great's showpiece harbor city and the seat of the Roman procurator in Judea. Paul had been sent there under armed escort after a plot against him in Jerusalem. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herod_Agrippa_II

question: The governor Felix answered a recall to Rome at last, leaving Paul still under Roman guard. He had put off the case for two years, hoping for a bribe. A new governor arrived to take his place. What was the new man's name?
context: Acts 24:27-25:1: Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judea around AD 59. Pilate had been governor a generation earlier under Tiberius; Sergius Paulus was proconsul of Cyprus in Acts 13; Claudius Lysias was the tribune who arrested Paul in Jerusalem. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herod_Agrippa_II

question: Paul stood in chains before King Herod Agrippa the Second and retold the story of his own conversion, years after a blinding light stopped him on the road to Damascus. In this retelling the voice from the light added one extra line, a farmer's saying that the other tellings leave out. Which King James line did Paul say the voice added?
answer: 'it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks'
choices: 'it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks'
'my yoke is easy and my burden is light'
'the harvest is plenteous, but the labourers are few'
'thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder'
context: Acts 26:14 (KJV): 'And when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking unto me, and saying in the Hebrew tongue, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.' 'Pricks' translates the Greek kentra, the sharp goads a farmer used to prod an ox; a stubborn ox that kicked back only drove the iron in deeper. The image was already a Greek proverb (Euripides uses it), and the extra line only appears in the Agrippa retelling. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: The Roman governor sat on the judgement seat and listened to Paul tell the visiting King Agrippa of Jesus's death and resurrection and of his own vision on the Damascus road. He could not take any more, and he broke in on Paul with a shout. What did the governor shout at Paul?
answer: Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad
choices: Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad
If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend
Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth
Away with such a fellow from the earth: he is not fit to live
context: Acts 26:24 KJV. The other choices are real KJV lines shouted at other men: John 19:12 (the Jerusalem crowd against Pilate over Jesus); Acts 19:25 (Demetrius the silversmith rousing Ephesus against Paul); Acts 22:22 (the Jerusalem mob against Paul from the barracks steps). https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: Paul answered the Roman governor's shout calmly, called his own speech 'the words of truth and soberness,' and then swung past the governor to press King Agrippa directly. The king already knew about these events, Paul said, for 'this thing was not done ___.' What phrase finishes the line?
context: Acts 26:26 KJV: 'for this thing was not done in a corner.' The phrase became proverbial in English for a public deed no one can pretend not to have heard about. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: Paul turned toward King Agrippa in the audience-hall and pressed him harder: 'King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest.' Agrippa answered with one line that has echoed in English ever since. What did Agrippa say to Paul?
answer: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian
choices: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian
Behold the man, I find no fault in him
What I have written, I have written
Great is thy faith, be it unto thee even as thou wilt
context: Acts 26:28 KJV. The other three are famous Pilate lines and one from Jesus - none are Agrippa. The 'almost' is the point: kept in the room by the King James version and by every English speaker who has ever used the phrase since. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: King Agrippa had spoken, and Paul answered him gracefully in front of the whole audience-hall. He wished that not only the king but everyone hearing him were as he was, 'altogether such as I am, except these ___.' What single word closed Paul's reply?
context: Acts 26:29 KJV: 'I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.' Paul is standing before the king in literal chains and calls attention to them as he closes. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: The king, the Roman governor and Bernice withdrew when the hearing ended, and Agrippa turned to the governor with a rueful verdict: 'This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not ___.' What legal move had Paul already made?
context: Acts 26:32 KJV: 'This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar.' A Roman citizen's appeal (provocatio ad Caesarem) transferred the case out of provincial jurisdiction; Festus was now legally obliged to send Paul to Rome. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herod_Agrippa_II

question: Paul sat at Rome in his own rented house, a prisoner under a light form of house arrest, and preached freely to every visitor. The book of Acts stops there and never describes his death. How long did this arrangement last, according to its very last verse?
answer: Two whole years in his own hired house
choices: Two whole years in his own hired house
Six months in his own hired house
Five whole years in his own hired house
Through one winter in his own hired house
context: Acts 28:30-31 KJV: 'And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him, preaching the kingdom of God.' Acts ends here abruptly, without recording his death. https://seanmcdowell.org/blog/was-paul-beheaded-in-rome

question: A Roman emperor blamed the great fire of his city on the Christians, and the persecution that followed killed the apostle Peter. Christian tradition puts Paul's beheading outside the walls of Rome in the same wave, sometime between the years 64 and 67. Which emperor was it?
context: Traditional dates for Paul's death fall between AD 64 and AD 67, within Nero's reign (AD 54-68). Domitian's persecution came a generation later; Diocletian's was in AD 303-311; Trajan wrote to Pliny about Christians around AD 112. https://seanmcdowell.org/blog/was-paul-beheaded-in-rome

question: Soldiers stretched Paul out for the whip in Jerusalem, on their commander's order to flog a confession out of him. Paul asked the centurion if the law let him scourge a man not yet condemned. Then he named a status of his own that stopped the flogging at once. What did Paul tell the centurion he was?
choices: A Pharisee of the tribe of Benjamin
context: Paul's Roman citizenship (Acts 22:25-29) entitled him to trial in Rome and to decapitation (a citizen's death) rather than crucifixion (reserved for slaves and non-citizens). Paul was also a Pharisee of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5), a disciple of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) -- but none of those statuses stopped a Roman flogging. https://seanmcdowell.org/blog/was-paul-beheaded-in-rome

question: A church father paired the deaths of the two apostles in a single sentence about the year 200, in his work Prescription Against Heretics. He compared Peter's execution to the death of Jesus, and Paul's death to the beheading of John the Baptist. Which church father wrote that line?
context: Tertullian of Carthage, Prescription Against Heretics 36, c. AD 200: 'Rome, where Peter endures a passion like his Lord's, where Paul is crowned by the death of John' -- John meaning John the Baptist, who was also beheaded (by Herod Antipas). https://seanmcdowell.org/blog/was-paul-beheaded-in-rome

question: Paul met the sword outside Rome along the Via Ostiensis, tradition says, at a spring later called Tre Fontane, the three fountains. An abbey stands there today, held and cared for by one particular contemplative monastic order. Which order of monks holds Tre Fontane?
context: The Tre Fontane abbey is held today by the Trappists -- formally the Cistercian Order of the Strict Observance, a reformed branch of the Benedictines known for silence and manual labor. Benedictines of Monte Cassino, Franciscans of Assisi, and Dominicans of Bologna are all real orders with famous mother-houses elsewhere. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tre_Fontane_Abbey

question: Peter and Paul fell in the same wave of killing at Rome, tradition holds, and each was laid in his own great church, Peter under St. Peter's at the Vatican and Paul under St. Paul Outside the Walls on the Via Ostiensis. The Roman church keeps a single feast day for the two of them together, as the founding apostles of the city. On which date is it kept?
context: The Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul falls on 29 June, remembering the two founding apostles of the Roman church. 25 December is Christmas; 15 August is the feast of the Assumption of Mary; 1 November is All Saints' Day. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tre_Fontane_Abbey

question: The suitors lay dead in the hall at Ithaca when Penelope came down, and she would not so much as speak to Odysseus. She sat opposite him at the fire and just stared. She had waited for him longer than most people wait for anything. How long had she been waiting?
context: Ten years of Trojan War, ten years of Odysseus's wandering home. Penelope has held Ithaca and Telemachus and the household together the whole time, and has been fooled by beggars claiming news of her husband more times than she can count. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: A grown son lost patience with his mother Penelope, in Homer's Odyssey, as she sat by the fire at Ithaca and would not speak to the stranger in her hall. He rebuked her for a heart harder than the beggar's. What was the son's name?
context: Telemachus is the son Odysseus left in the cradle twenty years earlier and has just fought beside in the hall to kill the suitors. Orestes is Agamemnon's son (wrong family); Antinous was the leader of the dead suitors; Eumaeus is the loyal swineherd, not a son. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Penelope answered her son's scolding calmly as she sat by the fire at Ithaca, across from the stranger she would not welcome. Then she turned to one member of the household and gave an order that silenced the room. Whom did she turn to?
context: Eurycleia is Odysseus's own childhood nurse and the senior woman of the palace; she is the natural person to give a bed-making order to. Actoris was Penelope's dowry-attendant (Od. 23.228), Melantho a disloyal serving-girl, Eumaeus the loyal swineherd. The rest of the room is about to hear something very strange. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Penelope gave a senior woman of the household one order, and it silenced the room. A heavy piece of furniture was to be carried out of its chamber and set up somewhere else in the house. Which piece of furniture had she just publicly ordered moved?
context: The order is a deliberate trap. A household can move any loom or throne or table. But there is exactly one object in the palace that no living person could move without cutting it apart, and Penelope has just publicly ordered it moved, with fleeces on top so the stranger can sleep alone (Odyssey 23.177-180). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus flared up when Penelope ordered their bed carried out of the bridal chamber. 'What man has moved it? No mortal could do it, not the strongest man alive, unless a god came down and shifted it.' Then he explained why. A living thing had been growing on the spot when he built that room, and he had put the walls up around it. What was growing on the spot?
context: Homer is very specific (Odyssey 23.183-204): a shoot of olive, still living, that Odysseus made the center of the chamber. The choice of tree matters because the olive is sacred to Athena, the goddess who has helped Odysseus through the whole poem. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: A tree stood growing on the spot when Odysseus raised the walls of the bridal chamber and roofed the room over, he told Penelope. That was why no one could have moved the bed. What did he do to the tree so it could serve as the pedestal of the bed?
answer: cut it off at bedpost height and used the still-rooted stump
choices: cut it off at bedpost height and used the still-rooted stump
felled it, hollowed the trunk, and stood it back on the same spot as a post
uprooted it, seasoned the wood, and reset it as a corner post
left the tree whole and hung the bed from its living branches
context: The whole point of the bed is that its main pedestal is not a piece of furniture standing on the floor: it is a living tree, still rooted in the ground under the bedroom, its trunk cut to bedpost height and smoothed. The bed is literally rooted to the ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus told the secret of the bed at last: no one could have moved it to another chamber without cutting a living trunk apart. No one in the world knew that private detail except Odysseus himself and one other person. Who was the other?
context: This is exactly why Penelope's move-the-bed order was a trap. Only her real husband, who built the bed, could know the secret; a false beggar with a good tongue could not. She has just used the one detail no impostor could possibly know to be sure of him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Penelope broke the moment Odysseus named the secret of their bed, in Book 23 of Homer's Odyssey. She ran to him and threw her arms around his neck. What did she confess in the same breath about why she had been so cold to him at the fire?
answer: she feared a man would come to her with a lying story and take her
choices: she feared a man would come to her with a lying story and take her
she feared the gods would punish her for a hasty welcome
she feared her son would call her weak for believing quickly
she feared the suitors' kin would return before dawn
context: It is the single most human line in the whole recognition scene: twenty years of impostors and beggars have taught her not to trust a good story. Only the private construction of the bed is a fact no impostor could possibly have. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Homer gave the reunion of Penelope and Odysseus on Ithaca the single most beautiful simile in the Odyssey, and it turned his own plot inside out. He compared her joy at seeing Odysseus again to the joy of one group of people at seeing one thing. What was the comparison?
choices: long-lost soldiers seeing their city walls
bound captives seeing the door swing open
starving traders seeing a granary opened
context: The simile inverts everything: Homer has spent a whole poem shipwrecking Odysseus, and now uses the swimmer-sighting-land image to describe how the wife feels seeing her husband. 'She could not let go of him.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess held back the morning on Ithaca so that Odysseus and Penelope could lie in their bed and talk through the whole night. Homer says she bent the natural order for them and stretched out the darkness itself. Which goddess did Homer credit?
context: Athena delays the dawn so Odysseus and Penelope can talk all night. It is a small quiet miracle, and it fits: the tree that holds up their bed is sacred to Athena too, so this whole reunion happens inside the goddess's care. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey.  (Legend.)

question: An old woman of the house gasped as she washed the stranger's feet on Ithaca: she had recognized him by a boyhood scar, left by a boar's tusk on a hunt on Mount Parnassus. The scar was one of the tokens that made Odysseus known, along with the secret of the bed. Where on his body was it?
choices: on the sole of his foot
context: The scar on Odysseus's thigh was cut by a boar's tusk when he was a boy hunting with his grandfather Autolycus on Mount Parnassus. Eurycleia had nursed him then; her hands know the scar the moment she touches it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey.  (Legend.)

question: One of the twelve apostles of Jesus stood up in Jerusalem on the Jewish feast of Pentecost, fifty days after Passover, and preached the first Christian sermon to the pilgrim crowds in the street. About 120 followers of Jesus had poured out of one house that morning. Which apostle was he?
context: Peter stood up with the eleven and became the voice of the group (Acts 2:14). The other three are all real apostles, but the sermon on the day of Pentecost is Peter's.

question: Jesus's followers, about a hundred and twenty of them, gathered in Jerusalem to pray and wait, as Jesus had told them to. The book of Acts names the part of a house they used as their meeting place. Which part was it?
context: Acts 1:13 places the eleven and Jesus's family in an upper room in Jerusalem, and Acts 2:1-2 puts the whole company 'in one place' when the sound filled 'all the house where they were sitting'. The other three are plausible domestic spaces but not the one Acts names.

question: The followers of Jesus sat waiting in one room of a house in Jerusalem on the Jewish feast of Pentecost, about 120 of them. Suddenly a great noise came from heaven and filled the whole house. According to the Book of Acts, what did that noise sound like?
context: 'And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting' (Acts 2:2). The other three are all sounds from other scripture scenes (Sinai, Elijah's chariot, the ram's horn), real, but from other scenes.

question: Jesus's followers, some 120 of them, looked at one another in one room in Jerusalem on the morning of the feast of Pentecost. A great sound had just filled the whole house. Then something had settled on every person there, one to each. What did each of them see resting on the head of every other?
answer: a small flame like a tongue of fire
choices: a small flame like a tongue of fire
a white dove with olive branch
a bright cloud like at Sinai
context: 'And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them' (Acts 2:3). The dove is Jesus's baptism, the cloud is Sinai and Tabor, the laurel crown is Roman -- all wrong for this scene.

question: The whole company of Jesus's followers, 120 strong, poured out into the streets of Jerusalem at Pentecost, speaking in languages they had never learned. Foreign pilgrims in town for the feast were amazed to hear their own home tongues. But some in the crowd mocked the speakers and had a ready insulting explanation for the strange behaviour. What accusation did the mockers throw at them?
answer: These men are full of new wine
choices: These men are full of new wine
These men are possessed by demons
These men are prophets of Baal
These men are drunk on strong myrrh
context: 'Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine' (Acts 2:13). Peter would answer this exact charge in the next verse.

question: One apostle stood up with the eleven others in Jerusalem to answer the mockers in the street at Pentecost. He began with a very specific point about the time of day, and he told the crowd that their accusation made no sense at that hour. What hour did he say it actually was?
answer: The third hour of the day, about nine in the morning
choices: The third hour of the day, about nine in the morning
The sixth hour of the day, about noon
The ninth hour of the day, about three in the afternoon
The eleventh hour of the day, near sunset
context: 'For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day' (Acts 2:15). The Jewish daytime hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour was about nine in the morning -- much too early for the accusation to make sense.

question: The apostle who preached at Pentecost stood up 'with the eleven': eleven, not twelve, because Judas Iscariot was dead. Before the feast came, the group had put forward two men to fill the empty seat and cast lots between them. Who was chosen to make the number twelve again?
context: 'And the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles' (Acts 1:26). The two candidates were 'Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias'; they prayed and cast lots (Acts 1:23-26). Barnabas, Stephen, and Silas all become prominent later in Acts, but none was chosen to replace Judas.

question: A widow in the wilds of Wales keeps her young son from ever hearing what knights are. Knighthood has killed her husband and her older sons, and she cannot bear to lose him too. The boy will grow up to be the hero of the earliest surviving Grail story. What is his name?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceval,_the_Story_of_the_Grail. Perceval (Welsh Peredur, German Parzival) is the country-bred fool who grows into the Grail knight. Lancelot is Arthur's greatest knight, raised by the Lady of the Lake. Gawain is Arthur's nephew. Tristan is the hero of the Cornish love-story parallel to Arthur.  (Legend.)

question: Five men ride through the Welsh forest past a boy who has never seen the like, clad head to foot in shining metal on great warhorses. He has no word for what he is looking at, and he falls to his knees. What does the boy believe the five men to be?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceval,_the_Story_of_the_Grail. Perceval kneels because his mother has taught him only two things: pray to God when you see God's servants, and never harm a stranger. The shining armour convinces him he is looking at heavenly beings. Kings, giants, and demons are the other kinds of stranger a Welsh boy might imagine but he chooses angels.  (Legend.)

question: Gornemant of Gorhaut, an older knight, takes in the young Perceval, who has ridden out from King Arthur's court, and trains him in courtesy. He also gives Perceval one piece of advice that will one day cost him the Grail, in Chretien de Troyes's romance. What does Gornemant teach him never to do?
choices: speak of his mother in company
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://mcgoodwin.net/pages/otherbooks/ct_perceval.html. Gornemant tells Perceval that a proper knight does not chatter or pry -- silence at a stranger's table is a courtesy. The lesson is well-meant. When Perceval sees the great procession at the Fisher King's castle, he remembers Gornemant and holds his tongue. The rule Gornemant gave him is what ruins the world.  (Legend.)

question: A maiden walks behind the two candelabra, holding a jeweled object that gives off so much light the candles pale beside it. Chretien de Troyes calls it a graal in his Old French, and later Grail writers will turn it into the chalice of the Last Supper. In his own tongue the word means something quite different and everyday. What kind of vessel is a graal?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Grail. In Chretien the graal is a jewelled platter that gives out a great light -- it is not yet a cup and not yet identified with the Last Supper. The identification of the Grail with the chalice used at the Last Supper is the addition of Robert de Boron in his Joseph d'Arimathie (c.1200) about twenty years later. The whole 'Holy Grail as cup' idea is a second-generation invention.

question: Perceval watches the whole silent procession pass the wounded king's table, and he is astonished. He wants to ask his host what any of it means. But he remembers his old teacher's rule, holds his tongue and eats in silence. What is the specific question about the graal that Perceval fails to ask?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://urthona.com/literature/the-unanswered-question-chretien-de-troyes-and-the-first-story-of-the-grail/. The unasked question is 'whom does the Grail serve?' -- and had he asked it, the wounded Fisher King (whom the Grail was in fact serving) would have been healed. The question is one of compassion, not curiosity; that is why it heals. When Perceval swallows the question to be polite, he swallows the whole cure.  (Legend.)

question: Perceval wakes in the morning to find the great castle utterly empty, no servants, no host, no maidens, no wounded king. He puts on his armour alone, mounts his horse and rides out over the drawbridge. Then he rides on into the forest, where a weeping woman tells him what he has done. What does the drawbridge do the moment Perceval crosses it?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://mcgoodwin.net/pages/otherbooks/ct_perceval.html. The drawbridge slaps up so sharply behind him that his horse just clears it. In the forest a maiden tells Perceval that had he asked the question, the wounded king would have been healed and his kingdom (the Waste Land) restored; his silence has doomed both to remain as they are. The chance has been given once and refused.  (Legend.)

question: Peredur son of Efrawg, the country boy of an older Welsh telling, reaches the mystery hall and finds no graal in the procession at all. The telling seems to preserve a version from before Chretien wrote his French verse. The young women there carry something from an older vengeance tale. What do they carry through the hall?
answer: a severed head on a platter
choices: a severed head on a platter
a golden chalice full of wine
an ivory horn of a unicorn
context: Peredur son of Efrawg, in the Mabinogion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peredur_son_of_Efrawg. The Welsh Peredur has NO Grail question -- Peredur sees the head of a murdered kinsman on the platter and is meant later to avenge him. The Welsh version is probably a survival of an older Celtic vengeance-tale that Chretien Christianises into the Grail question. The Grail cycle grows out of the Welsh severed-head bowl.  (Legend.)

question: Guards came for Vibia Perpetua, a young noblewoman of Carthage, around the year 203, for being a new Christian. Her own prison diary opens on the ordinary task she was doing at that moment, one any young mother would know. What was she doing with her baby?
answer: Nursing her infant son at her breast
choices: Nursing her infant son at her breast
Bathing the baby in a copper basin
Wrapping the baby in swaddling cloths
context: Perpetua's baby son was still nursing when she was arrested; her family were pagan and her father brought the baby to the prison to try to break her will. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetua_and_Felicity.

question: Felicity went into the same cell at Carthage as the young noblewoman Perpetua in the year 203, and the church still names both women together on the same day of the calendar. Who was Felicity?
answer: An enslaved woman, eight months pregnant
choices: An enslaved woman, eight months pregnant
A young Roman matron in early pregnancy
A slave girl of the household, mute from birth
context: Felicitas (Felicity) is a slave; Perpetua is a noblewoman. The Passion carefully insists on their equality as Christians and their equal courage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetua_and_Felicity.

question: Perpetua's old father came back to the prison weeping, kissed her hands and held out her baby to her. He was a pagan, and he begged her to do one thing that would end the trial and let her go home. What was he begging her to do?
choices: Deny that she was ever baptised
Escape with him out of the prison
Curse the name of Jesus in public
context: Roman law allowed accused Christians to go free if they would offer even a pinch of incense to the emperor's statue or the state gods. Perpetua refused three times, in front of her father and finally in front of the governor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetua_and_Felicity.

question: Perpetua wrote of a vision in which she climbed a golden ladder, with a creature crouched at its foot to frighten climbers off. Her teacher Saturus went up first and called down, 'take care that it does not bite you.' In the name of Jesus, she answered, it would not, and she stepped onto its head as her first rung. What creature did she say was at the foot of the ladder?
choices: A lion with a bloody mane
context: Perpetua explicitly echoes Genesis 3 -- the woman stepping on the serpent's head. Some manuscripts call the creature a dragon. Passion 4. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.  (Legend.)

question: A jailer mocked Felicity as she gave birth in prison, two days ahead of time, asking what she would do in front of the beasts if she cried out like this in childbirth. She had dreaded being spared the arena, and the whole prison had prayed with her. What did Felicity answer him?
answer: 'Now it is I who suffer; but there another will suffer in me, because I too shall suffer for him.'
choices: 'Now it is I who suffer; but there another will suffer in me, because I too shall suffer for him.'
'What you see now is nothing; wait until you see me stand alone against the beasts of the arena.'
'Take my child away from me at once, so that I may enter the sand as light as any of the men.'
'Save your mockery for the day when you yourself stand before the God whose people you strike.'
context: Passion 15. Under Roman law a pregnant woman could not be executed; Felicity was afraid of being reprieved on that ground and separated from the group. Her newborn daughter was smuggled out to a Christian family in the city. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.

question: The arena managers picked one animal for the two women so that its sex would match theirs, at the games for the birthday of the emperor's son Geta. The men of the group had been sent against a boar, a bear and a leopard. Perpetua and Felicity were stripped, hung in nets and sent in. What animal did the managers send against them?
context: A young cow deliberately maddened for the arena. The crowd was so disgusted by the sight of the two half-naked women (one just having given birth) being tossed by a cow that they demanded the women be dressed and brought back in tunics before the fight went on. Passion 20. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.

question: Perpetua stood up in the sand after the animal had tossed her and torn her tunic open, and she calmly fixed her clothing to cover her legs. Then she asked for a pin and pinned her loose hair back up, in the middle of the arena, in front of the whole crowd. She did it for one very specific reason of Roman public custom. Why did Perpetua pin her hair back up?
answer: Because loose hair was the sign of mourning, and this was not a day for mourning
choices: Because loose hair was the sign of mourning, and this was not a day for mourning
Because loose hair was forbidden to freeborn Roman women in public
Because loose hair would be grabbed by the beast on the next charge
Because loose hair was the badge of a slave in Carthage
context: Passion 20. In the Roman world a woman with loose, unbound hair was in mourning. Perpetua deliberately would not let the crowd see her mourning her own death; she was going to it as to a wedding. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.

question: Perpetua saw herself in the arena in her final vision, on the eve of the games, and she wrote it down carefully. She was no longer a young mother but stripped and turned into a man, made to wrestle a formidable adversary. She threw him and trod on his head, and she understood only afterward that her real fight was with the devil and not with beasts. Whom did Perpetua say she wrestled in that vision?
choices: A veiled woman all in white
context: Passion 10. Egyptian wrestlers were famous champions in the Roman world; the vision-figure represents the devil in the shape of the toughest opponent Perpetua could imagine. Her victory over him becomes her spiritual reading of the martyrdom to come. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.  (Legend.)

question: King Acrisius of Argos heard a prophecy that his own grandson would one day kill him, so he locked his daughter Danae inside a tower of solid bronze with only a small opening in the roof. Zeus looked down from Mount Olympus and desired her. What form did Zeus take to reach her through the roof?
context: The child born from that visit was Perseus. Zeus took the form of a swan for Leda and a bull for Europa; the tower story specifically has the shower of gold. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.1.  (Legend.)

question: Danae's father, King Acrisius of Argos, faced a baby grandson fathered by the god Zeus himself. An oracle had warned him that this grandson would one day kill him, but he could not risk killing mother and child outright without angering Zeus. What did he do with them instead?
answer: Sealed them in a wooden chest and cast them out to sea
choices: Sealed them in a wooden chest and cast them out to sea
Sold them as slaves to a foreign merchant
Sent them into exile by mule caravan
Handed them over to the priestesses of Hera
context: The chest washed up on the small Aegean island of Seriphos, where a kind fisherman drew it from the surf and took Danae and her baby in.  (Legend.)

question: Danae came ashore with her baby son Perseus on a little island in the Aegean. A kind fisherman there took the two of them in and raised the boy as his own son. What was the fisherman's name?
context: Dictys raised Perseus as if he were his own. His brother Polydectes was the local king, and later became Perseus's enemy.  (Legend.)

question: King Polydectes announced a pretend wedding to another woman, because he wanted the beautiful Danae for himself and her grown son Perseus out of the way. He asked every guest to bring one specific gift, knowing that poor Perseus would have no way to give the same. What did he demand from each guest?
context: The king was Polydectes, brother of Dictys. Perseus had no horse to give, and Polydectes used that shortfall to trap him.  (Legend.)

question: Young Perseus stood cornered and shamed in front of King Polydectes's whole court at the pretend wedding-feast, penniless and without the gift every guest was expected to bring. He made a wild boast about what he would bring the king instead. What did he promise to bring?
context: Polydectes leaped on the promise and held Perseus to it, expecting the boy to die trying. The other three are the quests of Jason and Heracles.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus took a mirror-bright shield from the goddess Athena, so that he could look safely at a monster whose gaze turned any living man to stone. Another god equipped him with a curved sickle-shaped sword called the harpe, sharp enough to cut through the monster's neck. Which god did the harpe come from?
context: The same Greek word 'harpe' names the sickle Cronus used to unman Ouranos in Hesiod's Theogony.  (Legend.)

question: Athena took pity on young Perseus, sent on what looked like a suicide mission, and told him who knew the road to the Gorgons: three strange grey witches called the Graeae, daughters of an ancient sea-god. The three sisters shared a very small set of things between them, handing them back and forth. What did the three Graeae share?
answer: A single eye and a single tooth
choices: A single eye and a single tooth
A single wing and a single claw
A single mirror and a single comb
A single flame and a single ember
context: Perseus snatched the eye mid-pass and refused to give it back until the sisters told him where to find the nymphs who guarded his equipment.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus set out for the edge of the world to bring back the head of one of three sisters. Snakes writhed on their heads for hair, boar-tusks jutted from their mouths, and one look at their faces turned a traveller to stone. What was the family name of these three sisters?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 270-283, names them Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa, daughters of the sea-god Phorcys and the sea-monster Ceto. The Harpies are winged snatchers, the Erinyes (Furies) are avengers, and the Graeae are the three grey-sisters who share a single eye.  (Legend.)

question: Athena turned on a mortal priestess in her own temple on the Acropolis of Athens, in Ovid's Metamorphoses, after the sea-god Poseidon attacked the woman there. The goddess punished not the god but the priestess: her beautiful hair turned to hissing snakes, and her face turned any watcher to stone. Who was the priestess?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.794-803. Arachne is turned into a spider for boasting at weaving; Callisto is turned into a bear by a jealous Hera; Andromeda is Perseus's later bride, chained to a rock for her mother's boast.  (Legend.)

question: The nymphs gave Perseus a special bag made for exactly one job: to hold Medusa's severed head without letting its stone-turning power leak out on him or on innocent bystanders during the long flight home. What was this bag called?
context: The kibisis is named in Hesiod's Shield of Heracles and in Apollodorus 2.4 as Perseus's Gorgon-head bag. The harpe is his curved sword; the aegis is Athena's shield-cloak; the labarum is the much later Christian standard of Constantine.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus struck off Medusa's head in her cave with a single blow of his curved sword, and in that instant something impossible happened at the wound. Two beings leapt out from the open neck, both fathered earlier by Poseidon. Which pair sprang out?
choices: the Chimera and the Nemean Lion
context: Hesiod, Theogony 280-283. Pegasus is the winged horse later ridden by Bellerophon against the Chimera; Chrysaor is a warrior born already fully armed, whose name means 'he who has a golden sword'.  (Legend.)

question: A warrior sprang from Medusa's severed neck, born already grasping a golden sword, and he grew up to father one of the great three-bodied monsters. The hero Heracles had to fight that monster during his famous twelve labors. Which of the twelve labors put Heracles face to face with the warrior's son?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 287-294. Chrysaor's son is Geryon, the three-bodied giant of Erytheia whose cattle Heracles is sent to steal for his tenth labor. The twelfth labor is Cerberus, the ninth is Hippolyta's girdle, and the sixth is driving off the Stymphalian birds.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus gave the severed head away at the end of the story, as a trophy for the goddess who had first lent him the polished shield. For the rest of Greek art and myth it stared out from the middle of one specific piece of her gear. Which piece?
context: Apollodorus 2.4. The Gorgoneion at the heart of Athena's aegis is how the goddess is depicted for the rest of Greek art and myth; Zeus's aegis carries the same face. The Palladium is the wooden Athena-statue guarded at Troy; her helmet-crest and spear-shaft carry no Gorgoneion in the tradition.  (Legend.)

question: Peter, the fisherman from Galilee who had denied Jesus three times and been forgiven, walked up to the Temple in Jerusalem for the afternoon prayer. Another of the twelve apostles went up with him every day. Which apostle walked at Peter's side?
context: 'Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer' (Acts 3:1). John, the son of Zebedee, is Peter's constant companion in the opening chapters of Acts. Andrew (Peter's brother), Philip, and Matthew are real apostles but not the one at the Temple that day.

question: Peter and John came up to the Temple in Jerusalem for the afternoon prayer and found a lame beggar at one of its entrances, asking the pilgrims for coins. He had never walked. What name did the Book of Acts give that entrance?
context: 'A certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful' (Acts 3:2). Tradition identifies it with the Nicanor Gate of the Second Temple, said to be made of Corinthian bronze that shone like gold.

question: Two apostles, Peter and John, went up together to the Temple in Jerusalem at the hour of the second daily incense offering, which the Book of Acts calls 'the ninth hour'. The Jews counted their daytime hours from sunrise, not from midnight. What time was that on a modern clock?
context: 'Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour' (Acts 3:1). The ninth hour was roughly three in the afternoon -- the time of the second daily Temple sacrifice and its accompanying incense offering.

question: A man lame from birth sat begging at a Temple gate in Jerusalem as the pilgrims passed. In the Book of Acts, the apostles Peter and John came up to pray, and he begged from them too. Peter looked straight at the beggar and answered with a line the Church has quoted ever since. What did Peter say to him?
answer: Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: rise up and walk
choices: Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: rise up and walk
Take up thy bed and thy purse: rise, walk out from this gate of the Temple
Be it unto thee according to thy faith: rise up, take thy bed and go home
Thy sins are forgiven thee: rise up, take thy bed and walk into the Temple
context: Full line: 'Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk' (Acts 3:6). The other three are woven from real gospel healing lines (Mark 2:9, Matt 9:29, Mark 2:5) -- all plausible commands, none of them Peter's at the Beautiful Gate.

question: Peter answered the lame beggar at the Temple gate in Jerusalem and did not wait for a reply. He reached out, took hold of the man to raise him, and at once strength came into the beggar's feet and ankles. Acts chapter 3 records exactly how he held him. What did Peter grip?
context: 'And he took him by the right hand, and lifted him up: and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength' (Acts 3:7). In the ancient world the right hand carried the sense of power and covenant, and Acts records the detail specifically.

question: A man over forty years old sat lame at a Temple gate in Jerusalem, begging for coins, when Peter and John came up to pray. In the Book of Acts, Peter raised him up and his ankles received strength at once. He had never stood in his life. What was the healed man doing, in the words of Acts, as he went into the Temple with them?
answer: walking, and leaping, and praising God
choices: walking, and leaping, and praising God
kneeling, and weeping, and blessing God
shouting, and running, and calling on God
singing, and dancing, and glorifying God
context: 'And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God' (Acts 3:8). The Acts writer piles the three participles on purpose -- a grown man who has never walked, jumping.

question: A crowd came running to Peter and John in the Temple courts. They knew the beggar by sight, and now he was on his feet. Peter took the moment to preach a second time about Jesus. Where in the Temple courts did Peter stand to preach?
context: 'And as the lame man which was healed held Peter and John, all the people ran together unto them in the porch that is called Solomon's, greatly wondering' (Acts 3:11). Solomon's Porch was a covered colonnade along the east side of the Temple's outer court.

question: Peter stood in the Temple courts in Jerusalem preaching to a large crowd that Jesus of Nazareth had risen from the dead, after a lame man had been healed at the gate. The priests, the captain of the Temple guard and the Sadducees, who denied any resurrection, were enraged. They broke in on Peter and John. According to Acts chapter 4, what did they do with the two apostles?
answer: held them in custody until the next day
choices: held them in custody until the next day
drove them out of the city before sundown
brought them at once before Herod the king
beat them with rods and released them
context: 'And they laid hands on them, and put them in hold unto the next day: for it was now eventide' (Acts 4:3). The priests, the captain of the Temple, and the Sadducees interrupted the sermon (Acts 4:1) and held the apostles overnight before hauling them before the council the next morning.

question: Jesus called the fisherman Peter away from the Sea of Galilee. Tradition sets Peter's last years far from that shore. The early writers Clement, Ignatius and Irenaeus put him at the head of the young church in one great city. Which city was it?
context: Early Church tradition (Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Irenaeus) places Peter's final ministry at Rome. Antioch, Alexandria, and Corinth were the other great early-Church cities but the tradition of Peter's death is tied specifically to Rome.  (Legend.)

question: Peter closed a letter to believers scattered across the Roman empire with a greeting from 'the church that is at' a certain place. He used a coded Old Testament name, which his ancient readers took to mean the imperial capital. Which name did he use?
context: 'The church that is at Babylon, elected together with you, saluteth you' (1 Peter 5:13). Most ancient interpreters read 'Babylon' here as a code word for Rome -- the great persecuting capital, like the Babylon of the Old Testament.

question: Tacitus told how a great fire ran six days, died down, and flared up for three more. It had started among the wooden shops beside the Circus Maximus on the evening of the 18th of July in the year 64, and it took most of the imperial capital. Which emperor sat on the throne?
context: The Great Fire of Rome began 18-19 July AD 64, under Nero. Tacitus (Annals 15.38-44) records that it burned for six days, was quenched, then broke out again for three more. Claudius, Domitian, and Trajan are all real first-century emperors but none was on the throne in AD 64.

question: The emperor turned the mob's fury away from himself after the great fire of July in the year 64. People said he had ordered the fire himself, to clear ground for a grand new palace. So he pinned the blame on a small and unpopular group in the city. Which group did he blame?
context: Tacitus, Annals 15.44 -- a hostile pagan source -- records that Nero blamed the fire on 'a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace' and had them arrested in large numbers.

question: Tacitus wrote with disgust of the killings that followed the great fire, though he was no friend of the condemned. Some of them were driven out into the arena in the skins of beasts, before a crowd hungry for a beast-hunt. What did Tacitus record was done to them there?
answer: They were torn to pieces by hunting dogs
choices: They were torn to pieces by hunting dogs
They were mauled by African bears
They were gored by wild bulls
They were hunted down by leopards
context: 'Besides being put to death they were made to serve as objects of amusement; they were clothed in the hides of beasts and torn to pieces by dogs' (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Others in the same passage were nailed to crosses or set on fire as living torches to light the imperial gardens -- an extraordinarily hostile witness confirming the cruelty of the persecution. Bears, bulls, and leopards were all real arena beasts elsewhere, but Tacitus names dogs.

question: The church father Origen told how Peter died, and the historian Eusebius later quoted him in his Church History. In that telling, the apostle did not die on an ordinary cross, because he himself asked the soldiers for something else. In what position was Peter crucified, according to that tradition?
answer: nailed head downward, feet in the air
choices: nailed head downward, feet in the air
arms wrapped around a T-shaped cross
back to the wood, feet nailed apart
tied by the wrists to an X-shaped cross
context: Origen (early third century), preserved in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.1: Peter 'was crucified with his head downwards, as he himself had desired to suffer'. The X-shaped cross is the tradition of Peter's brother Andrew; the T-cross and the standard Latin cross are other real forms.  (Legend.)

question: Peter went to his cross, ancient tradition holds, in the persecution that followed the great fire, and not in the main forum. The place it names is the emperor's own private racecourse, a stadium at the foot of a hill outside the old city. Which hill was it?
context: Nero's private circus stood at the base of the Vatican Hill, well outside the sacred pomerium. The Palatine (imperial palaces), Capitoline (Jupiter's temple), and Aventine are all real hills of Rome, but the circus of Nero was at the Vatican -- which is why the basilica of Peter would later rise on that same slope.  (Legend.)

question: A pope announced on the 26th of June in 1968 that bones dug from under the high altar of Saint Peter's Basilica, in a first-century burial chamber, were in the Vatican's view very likely those of the apostle. They were the bones of a strongly built man aged sixty to seventy, wrapped in purple and gold thread. Which pope made that announcement?
context: Pope Paul VI announced on 26 June 1968 that the bones (of a strongly built man aged sixty to seventy, first century, wrapped in imperial purple with gold thread) were in the Vatican's view 'identified in a way that we consider convincing' as Peter's. Pius XII had begun the excavations; Paul VI reported the result.

question: Herod Agrippa had the apostle James killed and saw that it pleased the crowds. He seized Peter next, at the feast of Unleavened Bread, and held him in prison until the feast should end. Where was Peter sleeping on the night before his trial?
choices: Hanging by his wrists in a stone pit
Locked in a wooden cage on the roof
context: Acts 12:6 -- Peter was 'sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains,' with keepers before the door as well. He was guarded by four squads of four soldiers each -- sixteen men in total.

question: The apostle Peter had already escaped custody once, so Herod Agrippa took no chances with him. He set squads of soldiers called quaternions over his prisoner in Jerusalem, with a new squad coming on at every watch of the night. How many soldiers made up one quaternion?
context: Acts 12:4 -- Herod 'delivered him to four quaternions of soldiers to keep him.' A quaternion is a squad of four; four quaternions across the four watches of the night makes sixteen men guarding a single prisoner.

question: An angel appeared beside Peter as he slept in King Herod Agrippa's prison, on the night before his trial, and a bright light shone in the cell. The angel had to strike him on the side to wake him, and then said, 'Arise up quickly.' In Acts chapter 12, what happened next inside the cell?
answer: His chains fell off his hands
choices: His chains fell off his hands
The two guards turned to stone
The ceiling split open above him
A white dove landed on his shoulder
context: Acts 12:7 -- 'And his chains fell off from his hands.' The guards on either side stay asleep through the whole escape; the ceiling and the dove details are not in the text.

question: Peter got up and followed an angel out of Herod Agrippa's prison in Jerusalem. The two walked past the first guard, then the second guard, until they came to the last barrier between Peter and the city, a heavy iron gate. According to Acts chapter 12, what happened at that gate?
choices: The angel struck it with a rod
Peter spoke a psalm and it split in half
context: Acts 12:10 -- the iron gate 'opened to them of his own accord.' They walked out, went down one street, and then the angel departed and Peter realized he was not seeing a vision.

question: Peter went straight from Herod's prison to a house where disciples were up late praying for him. An angel had led him out in the middle of the night. Acts says the house belonged to a woman called Mary, and it names her not by her husband but by her son. Whose mother was she?
context: Acts 12:12 -- 'the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark.' This is the same John Mark traditionally credited with writing the Gospel of Mark and who later traveled with Barnabas and Paul.

question: A young servant girl came to answer Peter's knock at the gate. She recognized his voice through the door but was so overjoyed she ran back inside without letting him in, leaving Peter standing out in the street knocking. What was the servant girl's name?
context: Acts 12:13-14 -- 'a damsel came to hearken, named Rhoda.' Dorcas is the seamstress raised by Peter in Acts 9; Priscilla is the tentmaker with Aquila; Lydia is the seller of purple in Acts 16.

question: A servant girl burst back into the house of Mary in Jerusalem and swore that Peter was standing at the gate. The disciples inside had been praying for exactly this, and they did not believe her. First they said she was out of her mind. When she kept insisting, what did they conclude instead?
choices: It must be a Roman trick
context: Acts 12:15 -- 'Then said they, It is his angel.' The scene is the great comic beat of Acts: the church prays all night for Peter's release, gets exactly what it asked for, and refuses to open the door. All the while Peter is still outside knocking.

question: Soldiers could not find Peter in his cell when morning came in Jerusalem, and King Herod Agrippa flew into a rage. He questioned the sixteen men who had guarded the prisoner through the night, and then handed down a sentence in the harsh Roman military way. What did Herod order done to Peter's guards?
choices: Sent them to the arena to face lions
context: Acts 12:19 -- Herod 'examined the keepers, and commanded that they should be put to death.' Under Roman practice a soldier who lost a prisoner suffered the prisoner's sentence, so execution was the standard answer; slavery, the arena, and exile belonged to other punishments in other stories.

question: Herod Agrippa sat on his royal throne at Caesarea, not long after Peter's escape, and made a speech to the crowd. Josephus adds that he wore a silver robe that flashed in the morning sun. The people shouted flattery at him, and Herod did not correct them. What did they shout?
answer: It is the voice of a god and not of a man
choices: It is the voice of a god and not of a man
Long live the son of David
Blessed is he who rides the eagle
context: Acts 12:22 -- 'And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.' Because Herod did not give God the glory, verse 23 says the angel of the Lord struck him and 'he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.'

question: One of Jesus's closest disciples follows from afar on the night Jesus is taken to the high priest, and slips into the courtyard. Servants and guards have lit a fire against the cold, and he warms his hands there. Which of the twelve is he?
context: John 18:15-18 (KJV). Peter follows the arresting party into the high priest Caiaphas's courtyard. Andrew was Peter's brother; Thomas is the doubter of the Upper Room; Philip is the disciple who asks 'shew us the Father'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denial_of_Peter.

question: Jesus turns to Simon Peter at the Last Supper in Jerusalem, on the night before he is crucified, with a specific warning. Before a certain farmyard sound is heard a set number of times that night, Peter will deny even knowing him, three times over. What sound does Jesus name?
context: Mark 14:30 (KJV): 'Verily I say unto thee, that this day, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice.' Peter had answered, 'though I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise.' Source: Mark 14:30-31 (KJV).

question: Peter warms his hands in the cold courtyard of the high priest's house, on the night Jesus is arrested, at a fire the servants and officers have kindled. John alone among the gospel writers says what kind of fire it is, in a word he uses just twice. What kind of fire is it?
context: John 18:18 (KJV): 'the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves.' The Greek word anthrakia -- 'charcoal fire' -- appears only twice in the whole New Testament, both times in John. Source: John 18:18 (KJV).

question: Someone stares hard at Peter across the firelight in Caiaphas's courtyard, on the night Jesus is arrested in Gethsemane, and says, 'Thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth.' In Mark's gospel this is the first challenge Peter faces that night. Who is this first accuser?
answer: A servant-girl of the high priest
choices: A servant-girl of the high priest
A soldier of the Temple guard
context: Mark 14:66-67 (KJV): 'there cometh one of the maids of the high priest: And when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked upon him, and said, And thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth.' The gospel underlines the humiliation -- the great disciple is broken by the challenge of a serving-maid. Source: Mark 14:66-67 (KJV).

question: Peter stands at the courtyard fire and faces a third accusation, after denying Jesus twice already. This time the bystanders name what has been betraying him in the firelight all along, a mark on him that a Jerusalem crowd can pick out at once. What is it?
context: Matthew 26:73 (KJV): 'and after a while came unto him they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee.' Mark 14:70: 'thou art a Galilaean, and thy speech agreeth thereto.' Galilean speech to a Judean ear was as distinctive as a country twang in a capital city. Source: Matthew 26:73; Mark 14:70 (KJV).

question: The bystanders press Peter a third time, and he is frantic to convince them he has nothing to do with the man on trial inside. Matthew gives what comes next in one sharp phrase, which ends with the words 'I know not the man'. What does Matthew say Peter did?
answer: Began to curse and to swear
choices: Began to curse and to swear
context: Matthew 26:74 (KJV): 'Then began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew.' The cursing here is not obscenity -- it is Peter calling down oaths on himself to prove he does not know Jesus. Source: Matthew 26:74 (KJV).

question: Peter finishes his third denial in the courtyard, and at once the sound Jesus warned him of rings out. One gospel adds a single line here that is not in the others, the moment that breaks Peter open. In Luke's gospel alone, what does Jesus do at that instant?
answer: Turns and looks upon Peter across the courtyard
choices: Turns and looks upon Peter across the courtyard
Cries out Peter's name from the hall
Sends John out to find Peter
Falls silent in front of his accusers
context: Luke 22:61 (KJV): 'And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord... And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.' Only Luke gives us the crossed gaze. Source: Luke 22:61-62 (KJV).

question: John picks one small word for the fire Peter warms himself at on the night of the denials, a word no other gospel uses. He uses it only twice in the whole New Testament, and the other time comes later in his own gospel. Where in John's gospel is the second appearance?
answer: On the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, where the risen Jesus cooks fish for the disciples
choices: On the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, where the risen Jesus cooks fish for the disciples
By the tomb where Mary Magdalene mistakes the risen Jesus for the gardener
In the locked upper room where the risen Jesus shows Thomas his hands
At the pool of Bethesda where Jesus heals the man who cannot walk
context: John 21:9 (KJV): 'they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread.' At this second charcoal fire the risen Jesus asks Peter three times -- one for each denial -- 'lovest thou me?', and each time Peter answers 'yea, Lord'. Two charcoal fires, three denials answered by three affirmations: John's writer built the parallel on purpose. Source: John 21:9-17 (KJV).

question: Jesus set out for Galilee the day after John the Baptist pointed him out at the Jordan. On the road he met a young man from Bethsaida, the fishing village of Peter and Andrew, and called him in two words: 'Follow me.' In John's gospel, which of the Twelve was this?
