context: John 1:43-44 KJV: 'The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me. Now Philip was of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.'

question: Philip ran off to find a close friend as soon as Jesus had called him, and he shared the news: 'We have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.' In John's gospel, what was the name of that friend, who later became one of the Twelve?
context: John 1:45 KJV. John's gospel alone gives this recruiting scene, and John is the only gospel that uses the name Nathanael.

question: In John's gospel, Philip told a friend that they had found the promised Messiah, Jesus of the little town of Nazareth, and the friend sneered back, 'Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?' Philip did not argue with the jibe. He gave a three-word invitation that became one of the most-quoted lines in the whole gospel. What did Philip say?
context: John 1:46 KJV. The phrase is often preached as a model of quiet witness -- no dispute, no proof, just an invitation to look.

question: Jesus greeted Philip's sceptical friend from across the way with a compliment, just after the friend had sneered at the town of Nazareth: 'Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no...' What word finished the line in the Gospel of John?
context: John 1:47 KJV. 'Guile' means deceit or cunning -- Jesus is calling him a straightforward, honest man. Given his blunt Nazareth remark a moment before, the reader has just seen the trait firsthand.

question: Philip brought his suspicious friend to meet Jesus. As the friend walked up, Jesus greeted him with a compliment. Startled that this stranger seemed to know him already, the friend asked, 'Whence knowest thou me?' Jesus answered that he had seen him in a particular spot before Philip ever fetched him. In John's gospel, where did Jesus say he saw the man?
context: John 1:48 KJV: 'Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee.' The fig tree in Jewish tradition was a place of study and prayer -- 'every man under his vine and under his fig tree' (Micah 4:4).

question: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, faced Jesus at dawn and cut straight to the political charge: 'Art thou the King of the Jews?' Jesus did not deny it. Mark's gospel gives his answer in three words. What did Jesus say?
context: Mark 15:2 KJV: 'And Pilate asked him, Art thou the King of the Jews? And he answering said unto him, Thou sayest it.' The phrase throws the assertion back on the questioner -- neither a full yes nor a denial. Matthew 27:11 and Luke 23:3 have almost the same exchange. 'I am he' is Jesus's line at the arrest in the garden (John 18:5-6). 'So it is written' and 'Blessed art thou' are other gospel phrases.

question: In the Gospel of John, Jesus told the Roman governor Pontius Pilate what his purpose in the world was. Pilate threw back a three-word question and walked straight out of the room without waiting for an answer. What did Pilate ask?
context: John 18:38 KJV: 'Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews.' A Roman governor tossing off a philosophy-final question at the accused and then leaving before the answer has kept commentators busy for two thousand years -- some hear a sneer, some hear a genuine question. Only John records it.

question: The Roman governor walked back out of his hall after questioning Jesus and faced the crowd. He could not see any crime the man had committed. John's gospel keeps Pilate's public verdict in the King James Bible: 'I find in him no ______ at all.' Which word fills the gap?
context: John 18:38 KJV: 'And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them, I find in him no fault at all.' Luke 23:4 has the same phrase. The remarkable thing about the Passion narrative is that Rome, the executing power, records itself as having found no case -- and killed him anyway. 'Sin' would be a religious rather than legal category; 'guilt' and 'wrong' are near-synonyms the KJV does not use here.

question: The crowd in Jerusalem heard Pontius Pilate offer them a choice at the trial of Jesus, under a Passover custom that released one prisoner. The other man on offer, Mark says, had done murder in an uprising against Rome. Which prisoner did the crowd shout for?
context: Matthew 27:20-21 and John 18:40 KJV. Barabbas is called 'a robber' in John and one who 'had committed murder in the insurrection' in Mark 15:7. The Passover-release custom is otherwise unattested outside the gospels. Judas Iscariot is the disciple who betrayed Jesus; Simon Magus is a magician in Acts 8; Ananias is a name that turns up in Acts 5 and Acts 9 -- none of them belong in this scene.

question: The soldiers led Jesus out to the courtyard and stripped him, then threw a coloured robe on him. They put a reed in his right hand as a mock sceptre and knelt before him, shouting 'Hail, King of the Jews.' They also wove something and jammed it onto his brow. What was it?
context: Matthew 27:29 and John 19:2 KJV. The specific plant is not named in the gospels -- Middle Eastern candidates include Ziziphus spina-christi (jujube). A laurel wreath was the Roman victor's crown, so the mockery is precise: a real king would get laurel, this 'king' gets thorns. Matthew's soldiers use a scarlet robe (27:28); Mark 15:17 and John 19:2 have purple. Both were royal colours in the ancient world -- the gospels do not blend the two, so quote one at a time.

question: Italian archaeologists digging the Roman theatre at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 uncovered a battered limestone slab. Its Latin inscription named Pontius Pilate and gave him a specific title. Some scholars had doubted he ever held any real Roman office. What Latin title did the stone give him?
context: The Pilate Stone reads, in its damaged Latin: '[...]S TIBERIEUM / [...]PONTIUS PILATUS / [...]PRAEFECTUS IUDAEAE' -- Pilate as prefect of Judea, dedicating a building (a Tiberieum) to the emperor Tiberius. Later Roman writers sometimes called him 'procurator', but that title only came into use for such officials after AD 41 -- so the stone quietly corrects the ancient historians. Consuls headed the Roman state; a legatus was a senatorial commander; a quaestor was a junior finance official.

question: Roman soldiers dragged an aged bishop from a farmhouse outside Smyrna, in Asia Minor, and took him back to the city to face the proconsul in the stadium. He had been a disciple of the apostle John. What was this bishop's name?
context: Polycarp is the elderly bishop of Smyrna (modern Izmir). Irenaeus, who knew him personally as a boy, says Polycarp had been a disciple of the apostle John. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycarp.

question: The aged bishop Polycarp faced the proconsul in the packed stadium at Smyrna and was offered a way to save his life. He had only to burn a pinch of incense to the emperor and say 'Caesar is Lord.' What comes next in the story?
choices: He does it and repents later
He says he needs a night to think
context: Polycarp refuses the incense-test and gives his famous answer about serving Christ for eighty-six years (Martyrdom of Polycarp 9). Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.

question: Polycarp answered the Roman proconsul in the arena at Smyrna, around the year 155, by counting up the years he had served Jesus. The old bishop had been offered an easy way out: burn one pinch of incense to the emperor and go free. What number of years did he give?
context: 'Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury; how then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 9). The traditional reading is that Polycarp is counting from his baptism as a baby -- the last living link to the apostles. Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.

question: Polycarp stood calm in the stadium at Smyrna when the Roman proconsul tried one last time to frighten him. Offer incense to Caesar, the proconsul warned, or burn alive on a pyre. The old bishop answered that a fire like that burned for an hour and went out. Which other fire did he name?
answer: The fire of the judgment to come
choices: The fire of the judgment to come
The fire that will end the wicked age
The fire that already burns in his heart
The fire that fell on Sodom and Gomorrah
context: 'Thou threatenest me with fire which burneth for an hour, and after a little is extinguished' -- and he warns of the fire of judgment to come (Martyrdom of Polycarp 11). Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.

question: The crowd in the stadium at Smyrna voted for fire, around the year 155, and Jews and pagans alike ran out into the streets to gather wood for the pyre that would burn the old bishop Polycarp. His own church wrote an eyewitness letter after that day, and it names the exact places they ran to. Where, according to the letter, did they find the wood?
choices: The gates of the pagan temples
The docks and the fishing boats
context: The letter says the crowd fetched wood 'out of the workshops and the baths' -- the trades and public buildings of the city -- to build the fire. Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.

question: The executioners moved to nail the old bishop Polycarp's arms and feet to the stake in the stadium at Smyrna, so that he could not writhe free of the flames. Polycarp made them a strange request. What did he ask them to do?
answer: Leave him unbound at the stake
choices: Leave him unbound at the stake
Leave him kneeling instead of standing
Leave him with his outer cloak on
context: 'Leave me as I am; for He that giveth me strength to endure the fire, will also enable me to remain in the pyre unmoved without the security of your nails' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 13). Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.  (Legend.)

question: Eyewitnesses in the church at Smyrna sent out a letter after the burning of their old bishop Polycarp in the stadium. They said the flames did something strange when the pyre was lit: they refused to touch him. What shape did the letter say the fire took around him?
answer: An arch, like a ship's sail full of wind
choices: An arch, like a ship's sail full of wind
A tall column reaching to the clouds
A crown of flame above his head
A circle around him like a wall
context: 'The fire, shaping itself into the form of an arch, like the sail of a ship when filled with the wind, made a wall round about the body of the martyr' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 15). Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.  (Legend.)

question: The Roman proconsul at Smyrna lost patience with the fire. The ancient account says it would not consume the old bishop Polycarp, who glowed in it like bread baking in an oven. The proconsul ordered a man up onto the burning pyre to finish him by hand. Who was sent up, and with what weapon?
choices: A young archer with a bow
The chief priest with a knife
context: 'They commanded an executioner to go near and pierce him through with a dagger' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 16). The Greek word is 'confector', the arena finisher. Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.  (Legend.)

question: A man climbed the burning pyre at Smyrna on the proconsul's order and struck the old bishop Polycarp the death-blow. The letter from Polycarp's own church says a marvel happened the moment the blow landed, along with a great quantity of blood. What did the letter say came out of him with the blood?
context: 'And on his doing this, there came forth a dove, and a great quantity of blood, so that the fire was extinguished' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 16). This detail is the earliest surviving example of the dove-at-martyrdom motif in Christian literature. Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.  (Legend.)

question: One of the twelve Olympians laid out in Homer how the three brothers split the world: Zeus took the sky, Hades the underworld, and he took the sea. Horses and earthquakes were his too, and the sea-nymph Amphitrite was his wife. Which Olympian was he?
context: Homer, Iliad 15.187-193, has Poseidon himself explain the three-way division of the world with his brothers Zeus (sky) and Hades (underworld). Apollo is the god of light and prophecy; Hermes the messenger; Ares the god of war. None of them holds the sea.  (Legend.)

question: The one-eyed Cyclopes made three great weapons for the three brother gods during the war with the Titans. Zeus took the thunderbolt. Poseidon took a weapon named after the plain tool of Greek fishermen. What was Poseidon's weapon called?
context: The Cyclopes forged the trident during the war against the Titans, at the same time as Zeus's thunderbolt and Hades's helm. The caduceus is Hermes's herald staff; the aegis is Athena's goatskin shield with the Gorgon face; the labrys is the Cretan double-axe. The Hellenistic poet Leonidas of Tarentum wrote of a real fisherman dedicating 'his sharp trident weapon of Poseidon' among his gear.  (Legend.)

question: Two Olympians laid claim to a new city going up on the rock of the Acropolis, which had no patron god yet. One was Poseidon of the sea. The other was the grey-eyed goddess of wisdom and the loom, born fully armoured from Zeus's own forehead. Which goddess was Poseidon's rival?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1. Athena won the contest and the city took her name -- Athens. Artemis is the huntress; Hera is Zeus's queen (patron of Argos); Demeter is the grain-goddess (patron of Eleusis).  (Legend.)

question: Poseidon strode up onto the rock of the Acropolis and struck it hard, his gift in the contest for the new city. Something gushed up out of the wound in the stone. Centuries later the traveller Pausanias was shown the spot inside the Erechtheion. What did he say the strike had left in the rock?
choices: a well of clear fresh water
a print of a horse's hoof
a print of a giant hand
context: Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.26.5, and Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1. Pausanias also notes a trident-mark shown in the rock beside the well. Some alternate versions of the myth do have a horse spring from the strike (Poseidon's sacred animal), but the artefact still shown to travellers on the Acropolis was the sea-water well.  (Legend.)

question: Athena answered Poseidon's strike in the contest for the new city by planting something living on the Acropolis rock, right beside the mark he had left. Pausanias was shown it centuries later as the first of its kind in Attica, and the whole country's trade came to rest on it. What did Athena plant?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1; Pausanias 1.27. The laurel belongs to Apollo (Daphne turning into one to escape him); the pomegranate belongs to Persephone in the Hades story; the fig is sacred to Dionysus. Athena's tree defined Attica's industry -- olive oil filled the amphoras awarded to victors in the Panathenaic games.  (Legend.)

question: Poseidon and Athena had each offered the young city a gift, and somebody had to pick the winner. In the version the mythographer Pseudo-Apollodorus tells, the judge was neither the other Olympians nor the townsfolk but the city's earliest king, a man with a snake's legs, born from the soil. Which king did Pseudo-Apollodorus name?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1. Kekrops was the earliest of the Athenian kings -- a snake-legged autochthon (born from the soil). Erechtheus is the king the Erechtheion is named for. Aegeus is the father of Theseus (his name gave the Aegean Sea). Theseus is the hero-king of the Minotaur story.  (Legend.)

question: The traveller Pausanias walked through the Erechtheion on the Acropolis in the 2nd century AD and was shown the well that Poseidon's strike had left in the rock. The local guides told him one strange thing about it: when a particular wind blew, the well made a sound. What sound did it make in the south wind?
context: Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.26.5. Pausanias also notes that the outline of a trident was shown in the rock beside the well as further evidence of Poseidon's strike. The horse's-cry is a red herring -- the horse was Poseidon's sacred creature, but the sound reported at the well was of waves.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus stepped in as judge when Poseidon and Athena fell out a second time, long after their famous quarrel over Athens. The new fight was over the seaside town of Troezen, across the bay in the Peloponnese. Zeus would not pick one god over the other. What did he rule about Troezen?
answer: that Poseidon and Athena would share the city jointly
choices: that Poseidon and Athena would share the city jointly
that neither god would ever be worshipped there
that Athena must give her olive to Poseidon
that the town must be renamed for a mortal king
context: Pausanias 2.30.6. The Troezenians afterwards worshipped both -- Athena as Polias and Sthenias, Poseidon as King -- and the ancient coins of Troezen show a trident and Athena's head together on the same coin.  (Legend.)

question: The Persian army of Xerxes sacked the Acropolis in 480 BCE and burned every temple on it, with Athena's sacred tree among them. The historian Herodotus told what the Athenians said happened at the burnt stump on the very next day. What did he report?
answer: a fresh shoot a cubit long had sprouted from it
choices: a fresh shoot a cubit long had sprouted from it
a spring of clear water had burst out beneath it
an owl had come and perched on it at dawn
a laurel wreath had been laid on it in the night
context: Herodotus, Histories 8.55. The Athenians read the overnight sprout as a sign from Athena that the city herself would rise again -- and shortly afterwards the Greek fleet won at Salamis. Herodotus reports it plainly as fact, not as legend.

question: An old king watches from the walls of Troy, in Homer's Iliad, as the greatest of the Greeks kills his son Hector in single combat. He is left with a son he cannot even bury. Who is that aged king of Troy?
context: Priam, king of Troy, watches from the walls as Achilles kills Hector in single combat and then drags the body behind his chariot around the city. The whole Iliad turns on this loss. (Iliad Book 24; ageofheroes.org, litcharts.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Hector, the greatest son of Troy's old king, fights a duel outside the gates after ten years of Greek siege, in Homer's Iliad. His father watches in horror from the wall. Which Greek warrior kills Hector in single combat?
context: Achilles kills Hector before the walls of Troy in Iliad Book 22, and then drags the body behind his chariot in sight of Hector's parents. Twelve days later Hector still lies un-buried in the Greek camp. (Iliad Book 22-24.)  (Legend.)

question: Zeus decides that King Priam's wait has gone on long enough. For twelve days he has watched the enemy camp from the walls of Troy, unable to bury his son Hector. Zeus sends a goddess to order him to go there alone at night and beg for the body. Which goddess does he send?
context: Zeus sends Iris, the rainbow messenger of the gods, down to Priam with orders to go alone at night with ransom to Achilles's tent. Iris is his usual messenger between Olympus and mortals in the Iliad. (Iliad 24; litcharts.com.)  (Legend.)

question: The aged King Priam sets out at night in a wagon loaded with treasure to cross the plain into the Greek camp. He does not go alone -- a god, disguised as a young Myrmidon warrior, walks beside him and guides him past the sentries into Achilles's tent. Which god escorts him in that disguise?
context: Hermes, guide of souls and messenger, appears to Priam in the shape of a young Myrmidon warrior and leads him past the Greek sentries. It is the only time in the Iliad a god guides a mortal in body-shape rather than only in voice. (Iliad 24; pressbooks.pub/iliad.)  (Legend.)

question: Priam enters Achilles's tent unannounced at midnight, an old man alone before the young warrior who killed his son. He kneels, and before he says a word he does the thing that has made this scene famous. What does Priam do with his lips?
answer: He puts them to the hands of Achilles
choices: He puts them to the hands of Achilles
He puts them to the sword of Achilles
He puts them to the altar in the tent
He puts them to the forehead of Achilles
context: Priam clasps Achilles's knees in the ritual gesture of the suppliant and puts his lips to 'the terrible, man-slaughtering hands' -- the hands of the man who killed Hector. He tells Achilles he has endured what no man on earth has ever endured. (Iliad 24.503-506; litcharts.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Priam's speech breaks Achilles. The young warrior does not answer at first: he weeps, and the two enemies sit together in the tent and cry, each for his own dead. Priam weeps for Hector. Achilles weeps for his own father Peleus and for one other person he has lost. For whom else does Achilles weep?
context: Achilles weeps for Peleus, whom he will never see again, and for Patroclus, the friend whose death drove him back into the war and made him kill Hector. Then he raises the old king up from his knees. (Iliad 24.507-516.)  (Legend.)

question: Achilles has given back the body of Hector when Priam asks for one more thing: a truce, so that no Greek will attack Troy while the funeral is held. Achilles grants it. In Homer's Iliad, how many days of truce does he give?
context: The truce is eleven days total -- nine to gather wood for the pyre, one to burn the body, and one for the burial mound. It is one of the very few pauses in the whole war. (Iliad 24; americanliterature.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Homer opens the Iliad on the word 'wrath' and carries it through roughly 15,000 lines of Greeks killing Trojans and Trojans killing Greeks. But he does not close on the battlefield. King Priam comes in secret to Achilles's tent and buys back his son's body, and the poem ends at Hector's funeral. What is the very last line of the Iliad?
answer: 'And so the Trojans buried Hector, breaker of horses.'
choices: 'And so the Trojans buried Hector, breaker of horses.'
'And so Achilles laid his friend upon the pyre.'
'And they raised a mound above the son of Priam.'
'And the ships of the Greeks lay silent on the shore.'
context: The Iliad ends not on Achilles, not on victory, not on Troy falling -- but on the burial of the enemy prince Achilles killed. It is one of the most famous endings in Western literature. (Iliad 24.804.)  (Legend.)

question: Priam sets out for Achilles's tent with a wagon of ransom worthy of a king's son, as Zeus has ordered. Homer names the contents in detail: robes, cloaks, tunics, cauldrons, tripods, a great cup from the Thracians, and a weight of the most precious metal. How many talents of gold does Priam bring?
context: The ransom is twelve robes, twelve cloaks, twelve blankets, twelve tunics, ten talents of gold, two shining tripods, four cauldrons, and a great cup given to Priam by the Thracians. (Iliad 24.229-235.)  (Legend.)

question: Achilles takes pity on the old king who has crossed enemy lines alone by night to beg for the body of Hector, and he shares a meal with him inside his tent. After they have eaten, Achilles gazes across at Priam and speaks of how the old man appears to him. What does Achilles say Priam looks like?
choices: He looks like a king of old
He looks like the shade of a hero
He looks like his son Hector
context: Achilles marvels at how god-like Priam still appears even in his grief; Priam in turn marvels at how god-like Achilles is. They share a meal and sleep, enemies for one night at peace. (Iliad 24.629-634.)  (Legend.)

question: Prometheus kept his freedom when the great war of the Titans ended and most of his own family were hurled down into Tartarus for ever. He owed that to the side he chose in the war. Where did Prometheus stand in that war?
answer: the side of Zeus and the Olympians
choices: the side of Zeus and the Olympians
the side of Cronus and the older Titans
he stayed neutral and fought for neither side
he fought first for one side and then the other
context: Hesiod, Theogony (and later mythographers). Prometheus's foresight told him the Olympians would win, so he broke with his own kind. That original alliance is what makes his LATER punishment by Zeus so sharp -- Zeus is punishing a former friend, not an old enemy.  (Legend.)

question: Prometheus stood over a great sacrificial ox at Mecone in Sikyon and divided it into two piles, so that Zeus could choose which the gods would keep. In the pile he wanted Zeus to pick, he hid the bones beneath a beautiful covering. What did he cover the bones with?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 535-560. The other pile hid the meat and offal inside the ugly ox-stomach. Zeus, offered the choice, picked the fat-covered pile -- and from that day mortals kept the meat at every sacrifice while the gods received only the burnt fat and bones as smoke on the altar.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod told how the Titan Prometheus fooled Zeus at Mecone, hiding the good ox meat under an ugly stomach lining. Furious, Zeus punished mortals by taking away one gift. Prometheus slipped back up to Olympus and stole it for humans, and he was chained to a rock for the theft. What did he steal?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 561-569. Wine belongs to a different god's story (Dionysus, who brings the vine to mortals later). Sleep and speech were never withdrawn -- they were never gifts anyone could grant or take away.  (Legend.)

question: Prometheus had to smuggle live embers down from the gods' mountain without Zeus noticing. He hid them inside a hollow plant-stem, and Greek villagers used the same plant to carry embers between their hearths into modern times. In Hesiod's Theogony, what stem did Prometheus use?
context: The Greek word is 'narthex' -- the giant fennel, Ferula communis. Its dry white pith really does smoulder invisibly for hours, and Greek villagers used a fennel-stalk to carry embers from hearth to hearth well into modern times. The story matches an actual practice.  (Legend.)

question: Hephaestus shaped the first woman, Pandora, on Zeus's orders, as a further punishment for the theft from Olympus. Zeus sent her to Prometheus's foolish brother Epimetheus, who took her in against Prometheus's warning. She brought one object with her that would loose all the evils on the world. What did Pandora bring?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 90-105. The Greek word is 'pithos' -- a large storage jar. It became 'Pandora's BOX' in English only when the 16th-century humanist Erasmus mistranslated pithos as pyxis ('box'). The spindle belongs to Klotho of the Fates; the mirror to Aphrodite; the horn (the cornucopia) belongs to the Amalthea nursing-goat story.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus had Prometheus chained for the theft from Olympus to a bare, wind-battered crag at the edge of the world, to hang there alone in the cold for generations. An eagle came at his liver every day. Where did Zeus chain him?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 521-525, and Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound. The Caucasus stood at the far eastern edge of the Greek-known world, where the sun was said to come up. Mount Ida is where Zeus was hidden as a baby (Cretan Ida) and where the Judgment of Paris took place (Trojan Ida). Mount Etna is where the giant Typhon was buried under the volcano. Mount Parnassus is Apollo's mountain, above Delphi.  (Legend.)

question: A passing hero came to Prometheus's crag generations after Zeus chained him there. He saw the eagle at its work, drew his bow and shot the bird dead with an arrow. Then he persuaded Zeus to leave the prisoner free. Which hero shot the eagle?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 526-534. Perseus was the killer of Medusa (with Hades's helm). Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Cretan labyrinth. Bellerophon killed the Chimera from the back of Pegasus. Heracles was the arrow-shooter -- the same one who later killed the Nemean lion, the Hydra, and Geryon.  (Legend.)

question: Prometheus hung on his rock in Aeschylus's play Prometheus Bound with a secret Zeus badly wanted: the name of the woman by whom Zeus was fated to father a son greater than himself. He refused to give it up until Zeus agreed to free him. Which woman was the secret name?
context: Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound (with the lost sequel Prometheus Unbound). Warned by the secret, Zeus stopped pursuing Thetis and had her married off to the mortal Peleus instead -- and their son was Achilles, the greatest of the Greeks at Troy. Danae was the mother of Perseus by Zeus. Rhea was Zeus's own mother. Leto was mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: In the Volsunga Saga, King Sigmund swings his sword at a one-eyed stranger who is really the god Odin. The blade breaks apart and Sigmund falls. Dying, he tells his pregnant wife to save the pieces for their unborn son. What is the sword called?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 11-12; 15. Gram is the great sword of the Volsung line -- pulled out of the tree Barnstokk by King Sigmund, shattered against Odin's spear, and reforged for Sigurd. Tyrfing is the cursed dwarf-sword of the Hervarar saga. Skofnung is the sword of the legendary Danish king Hrolf Kraki. Hrunting is the sword Unferth lends to Beowulf for the fight with Grendel's mother. All four are named hero-swords of the Germanic legend-cycle -- Gram is the specific reforged one.

question: A pregnant widow saves the pieces of King Sigmund's shattered sword for her unborn son, in the Volsunga Saga. That son will become the greatest hero of Norse legend, a dragon-slayer whom the German poets call Siegfried. What is the hero's Norse name?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 13-15. Sigurd (Old Norse) is Siegfried (German). Sigmund is Sigurd's father, the shattered-sword king. Sinfjotli is Sigmund's son by his own sister Signy, and Signy is Sigmund's twin sister. All four are Volsungs -- the specific dragon-slayer of the next generation is Sigurd.  (Legend.)

question: King Sigmund is winning his last great battle easily when an old one-eyed man in a hooded cloak steps out from the enemy line. It is the god Odin. He meets Sigmund's next stroke, and the king's sword shatters against what he holds up. What weapon does the old god carry?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 11. The old man in the hooded cloak with a broad-brimmed hat is Odin himself in his wanderer's disguise, and the spear he carries is Gungnir -- the same spear he will one day take to Ragnarok. Sigmund's sword shatters against it. Sigmund has been Odin's favourite for a lifetime; the moment Odin turns up on the battlefield with the spear is the moment Sigmund knows the god's favour is spent.  (Legend.)

question: An old and cunning smith fosters the boy Sigurd at King Hjalprek's court, with a secret purpose. The smith's own brother has transformed into a dragon and guards a cursed hoard, and the smith wants Sigurd to kill it. What is Sigurd's foster-father called?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 14; Reginsmal prose introduction. Regin is the smith-brother of the dragon Fafnir and the foster-father of Sigurd. Andvari is the dwarf whose gold-hoard Regin and Fafnir stole in the first place (the cursed treasure). Alberich is the Nibelung dwarf of Wagner's opera -- an adjacent figure in the German retellings, but the Norse foster-father is Regin. Wayland is the great smith of another Germanic saga (Volundarkvida).  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd stands at the anvil in his foster-father's smithy, in the Volsung saga, with a brand-new sword in his hand. The cunning old smith wants him strong enough to slay the dragon Fafnir, and he has forged the boy two blades, one after the other. Sigurd swings each one down on the anvil to test its worth. What happens each time?
answer: the sword shatters at the first blow
choices: the sword shatters at the first blow
the blade sticks fast in the iron
the blade bends into a curve
the sword rings out with a clear note
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 15. Regin makes Sigurd two brand-new swords in turn; each shatters against the anvil on the first swing. Only after those two failures does Sigurd go to his mother Hjordis and ask for the pieces of Gram.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd walks home to his mother in the Volsung saga and asks for the old fragments she has saved since the battlefield. They are the pieces of the sword his father, King Sigmund, was holding when he fell, and they have gone with her through a second marriage. What is the name of Sigurd's mother?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 12 and 15. Hjordis is Sigmund's young wife, who caught the shards on the battlefield and carried them with her when she remarried. Signy is Sigmund's sister and mother of Sinfjotli. Grimhild is the queen of the Nibelungs who later gives Sigurd a drink of forgetfulness. Brynhild is the valkyrie he will one day awaken -- his fated love. Hjordis is the specific keeper of the shards.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd brings the shards of his dead father's famous sword to his foster-father in the Volsung saga. The old smith melts them down and hammers the metal back out into one reforged blade. Sigurd carries the new sword to the smithy's anvil and swings it down with all his strength. What happens to the anvil?
answer: it is cloven in two down to its foundations
choices: it is cloven in two down to its foundations
it rings with a note heard for a league
it glows red without being heated
it splits into three equal pieces
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 15. The reforged Gram cleaves the anvil clean in two, down to the foundations -- exactly the reverse of the two brand-new swords that shattered against the same anvil earlier. The anvil-cleaving is a Germanic story-motif for 'this sword is not like the others'; Beowulf's sword Naegling gets a similar test in its own poem.  (Legend.)

question: Richard Wagner puts the reforging of the shattered sword on the opera stage, in the first act of Siegfried, one of the four operas of his Ring cycle. He takes the scene from the old Norse story, but he gives the blade a completely different name. What does Wagner call the reforged sword?
context: Richard Wagner, Siegfried, Act I (Der Ring des Nibelungen). Wagner renamed Gram as Nothung ('need-sword') and made the reforging-scene one of the most famous moments in the whole Ring cycle -- Siegfried hammers the shards on the anvil while singing 'Nothung! Nothung!' Balmung is what Siegfried's sword is called in the earlier Middle High German Nibelungenlied. Grimming and Wittestein are named swords in still-other German heroic poems. Wagner's name for it is Nothung.  (Legend.)

question: The elves of Rivendell reforge the shards of Narsil for Aragorn on the eve of the final war, in J.R.R. Tolkien's Lord of the Rings. The sword of the ancient King Elendil has lain broken for thousands of years, and Tolkien openly borrows the scene from the reforging of the Volsungs' sword. What new name does he give Aragorn's blade?
context: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Return of the King; Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-Earth. Tolkien was a professor of Anglo-Saxon and read the Volsunga Saga in the original. Narsil is the earlier name of the same blade -- the sword of Elendil that broke under him at the fall of Sauron and lay in shards for three thousand years; when it is remade for Aragorn it is renamed Anduril, 'Flame of the West.' Glamdring is the elf-sword Gandalf carries. Sting is the short-sword Bilbo (and later Frodo) carries. Anduril is Tolkien's deliberate homage to Gram reforged.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood and his band robbed a rich traveller on the king's highway, in the old English ballads, and slipped away from the Sheriff of Nottingham's men into one great royal hunting wood in Nottinghamshire. In which forest did the band hide?
context: Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire is the ballad-home of the Merry Men (with an alternate northern haunt at Barnsdale in Yorkshire). The New Forest was William the Conqueror's Hampshire hunting reserve; the Forest of Arden is Shakespeare's setting in As You Like It; Epping Forest lies east of London. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.  (Legend.)

question: The Sheriff and the king's foresters hunted Robin Hood's outlaws among the oaks and the bracken. The whole band dressed alike, in a woollen cloth named for the English city famous for dyeing it. What did the outlaws wear?
context: 'Lincoln green' was a woollen cloth dyed with woad and weld in the city of Lincoln -- famous enough that Chaucer and the ballads name it. Kendal green (a duller cloth) also existed but is a different tradition. One member of the band is the exception -- he stands out in bright cloth of a different color, which is why he has the nickname he does. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood; Wikipedia, Will Scarlet.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood slung one weapon across his back in the medieval English ballads, the same weapon that won two famous English battles, Crecy in 1346 and Agincourt in 1415. English soldiers cut down mounted French knights with it by the thousand. What was the weapon?
context: The English longbow -- yew, six feet long, drawn with a 100-pound pull -- was the folk-hero weapon of Robin's own generation of readers. At Crecy and Agincourt English longbowmen shattered the French armoured cavalry; every English yeoman by law had to practice at the butts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.

question: Robin Hood rode with a far smaller band in the fifteenth-century ballads than in the modern films: only three named men. Two of them were Much the Miller's Son and Little John. Who was the third companion?
context: The three named early Merry Men are Little John, Much the Miller's Son, and Will Scarlet (spelled 'Scathelock' or 'Scarlok' in the fifteenth-century texts). Friar Tuck, Alan-a-Dale, and Maid Marian all join the tradition later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood picked up two companions the fifteenth-century ballads never mention, one from May Day pageants and one from Tudor stage plays. Only afterwards did the pair work their way into the printed tradition, and now almost everyone takes them for part of his core company. Which two joined the band later?
context: Maid Marian entered the tradition through the May Day games (originally as the queen of the May with a separate character called Robin), and Friar Tuck entered through Tudor stage plays; neither appears in the fifteenth-century ballads. Little John, Will Scarlet, Alan-a-Dale and Much the Miller ARE in the ballads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.

question: Howard Pyle spread a phrase about Robin Hood in his children's retelling of 1883, and Joseph Ritson's collection of 1795 had done the same before him. No medieval ballad says it. The old poems show Robin lending money to a knight in ruin and helping impoverished yeomen. Which slogan is the later invention?
answer: robs from the rich and gives to the poor
choices: robs from the rich and gives to the poor
steals from Norman and shares with Saxon
takes from the king and gives to the church
spoils the tax-man and clothes the widow
context: The 'rich-to-poor' formula is a Ritson / Howard Pyle nineteenth-century summary; the medieval ballads themselves show Robin lending money to distressed knights (Sir Richard at the Lee) and helping impoverished yeomen -- charity WITHIN his own class, not modern redistribution. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.

question: Sir Walter Scott grafted Richard the Lionheart and an evil Prince John onto the Robin Hood story in a novel of 1819. The medieval poem A Gest of Robyn Hode names only a king called Edward, whom some scholars take for Edward III. Almost every film since has followed Scott. Which of his novels did it?
context: Sir Walter Scott's 1819 novel IVANHOE placed the Robin Hood story in the reign of Richard I (returning from crusade) with Prince John as villain; every twentieth-century film uses that Scott frame. Waverley (1814), Kenilworth (1821), and The Talisman (1825) are other Scott novels, all real, none of them the Robin one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.

question: The poet of A Gest of Robyn Hode cut his fifteenth-century poem, over 1,800 lines of ballad verse, into long sections, each covering a different adventure. It is not one continuous story. What name does the Gest give to each of these sections?
context: The Gest is divided into EIGHT FYTTES (an old English word for a division of a long poem, related to 'fit' as in 'fitting together'). 'Canto' is Italian, from Dante and Ariosto; 'geste' is the whole-poem genre-name (as in 'chanson de geste'); 'chanson' is French for song. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Gest_of_Robyn_Hode.

question: Robin Hood, old and worn out, falls ill with a raging fever and rides north to a Yorkshire nunnery for the standard cure that monks and barber-surgeons have used on fever patients for centuries. What is the treatment they perform on him?
context: Bleeding, or phlebotomy, was the routine medieval remedy for fevers and many other ailments -- practiced in monasteries and by barber-surgeons for centuries. Purging (forced vomiting or laxatives) and leeching (using leeches, a related bleeding-method) also existed. Trepanning is drilling a hole in the skull -- a real but different medieval surgery. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: The treacherous prioress of a Yorkshire nunnery lets Robin Hood die in her house, when he rides north to be treated for a bad fever. The real house stood near Brighouse, dedicated to the Virgin Mary and Saint James. What is the priory called?
context: Kirklees Priory was a small Cistercian nunnery in West Yorkshire near Brighouse. Nostell, Bolton, and Monk Bretton are all real, well-known Yorkshire priories of the same medieval era -- but only Kirklees carries the Robin Hood tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirklees_Priory.  (Legend.)

question: Robin can no longer shout for his second-in-command, who waits outside the priory walls. He reaches for an old signal and sounds it three times, each blast fainter than the last. What does the dying Robin use to bring his lieutenant running?
context: In the B-text of Child Ballad 120 the failing horn-blasts -- three of them, each weaker -- carry from the upper window of the priory to Little John waiting outside; John hears the weakness in the call, knows something is wrong, and forces his way in. A boar-horn, a shepherd's pipe, and a shawm are all real medieval blown signals close to the real thing, but wrong here. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Robin's second-in-command hears the failing signal, breaks the locks and finds Robin dying on the bed. This lieutenant is his oldest companion, a huge man who first met him on a narrow bridge over a forest stream and fought him to a draw with quarterstaves. Who is this lieutenant?
context: The quarterstaff-bridge meeting is one of the most famous scenes in the ballads: Little John (called 'Little' in ironic contrast to his size) knocks Robin off the bridge, they laugh, and John joins the band. He is the one who forces the priory door at the death-scene. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Standing over his dying master, the lieutenant begs one furious favour: leave to take Robin's men, ride back to the priory, and put its buildings to the torch in revenge. Robin refuses, giving one clear reason. What reason does he give for forbidding the revenge?
answer: he has never harmed a woman in all his life
choices: he has never harmed a woman in all his life
the church would set a curse on any who burned it
the nuns had done nothing wrong, only their head
the fire would spread to the poor cottages nearby
context: In the ballad Robin says, in effect, that he has never harmed a woman in all his life 'nor man in woman's company' -- and forbids Little John to burn the priory even in revenge for his own murder. The moral point is heavy: even at the moment of his killing, Robin holds to his own rule. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Refusing revenge, Robin instead makes his lieutenant a strange last request. He asks for his bow and a single arrow, has himself lifted to the priory window, and looses one final shot out into the park. What does Robin ask his lieutenant to do with that arrow after it falls?
answer: dig his grave wherever the arrow lands
choices: dig his grave wherever the arrow lands
carry the arrow back to Sherwood as a token
return it point-first to the prioress
hang it above the altar of the priory chapel
context: This is the great ballad-image of Robin's death: the last arrow shot from the sickbed marks the outlaw's own grave. Little John finds it in Kirklees Park and buries Robin there, as Robin had asked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Robin lies dying at the priory and gives his lieutenant one last order. He has already said where the grave is to be, and now he asks that his gear go into it with his body, each piece in a particular place. Which arrangement does the ballad prescribe?
answer: his sword at his head, his arrows at his feet, his bow at his side
choices: his sword at his head, his arrows at his feet, his bow at his side
his cap on his chest, his horn on his shoulder, his knife in his hand
his cloak spread over him and his belt around his waist
his boots at the foot of the grave and his gloves under his head
context: The ballad specifies the burial-arrangement almost as a warrior-code: sword at his head, arrows (with the bow at his side) at his feet, and (in some versions) a green sod under his head. It reads like the burial of a yeoman-hero out of Old English tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Sightseers in West Yorkshire peer at a flat stone slab in the park beside the ruined priory, shown to them as Robin's grave. The inscription on it is now almost impossible to read. Why can they hardly make it out?
answer: souvenir hunters have chipped away pieces over the generations
choices: souvenir hunters have chipped away pieces over the generations
the priory monks scoured it clean at the Dissolution
Victorian railway-builders resurfaced it as a paving-stone
a fire in the eighteenth century blackened and cracked the face
context: The alleged grave in Kirklees Park has been pointed out as Robin's since at least the seventeenth century; visitors and pilgrims have chipped fragments from it for so many generations that the inscription is now almost gone. The slab itself is protected today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirklees_Priory.

question: Charlemagne marches his army home from Spain in the Song of Roland, and has to cross the Pyrenees by a narrow gorge that only a small unit can hold at a time. That pass gives its name to the whole disaster. What is it called?
context: Roncesvalles (French Roncevaux) is a real pass through the western Pyrenees between Spain and France. The Brenner is in the Alps; the Khyber is between Afghanistan and Pakistan; Thermopylae is in Greece -- all famous narrow passes of history, all wrong for this story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.

question: Charlemagne's most trusted knights ride at his side against the Saracen armies in Spain, in the medieval French epic the Song of Roland. They are called paladins, and Roland, the emperor's own nephew, is one of them. How does the poem count these closest men?
context: The chanson gives Charlemagne twelve peers (douze pairs) -- Roland, Oliver, Turpin the Archbishop, Ganelon before his fall, and eight others. The number twelve echoes Christ's twelve apostles and the twelve knights of Arthur's later Round Table tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: One of Charlemagne's own barons sells the rearguard's position and marching-time to the enemy, so the ambush at the pass is no bad luck. He is Roland's own stepfather, and he takes it as a public insult when he is named as envoy to King Marsile. What is the traitor's name?
context: Ganelon is Roland's stepfather in the chanson. Nominated by Roland himself as messenger to King Marsile of Zaragoza, Ganelon takes it as a mortal insult and sells the rearguard's location for revenge. Pinabel is Ganelon's champion at the trial after the disaster; Baligant is a later Saracen emir; Blancandrin is Marsile's own envoy -- all real chanson figures, all wrong here. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: Roland stands trapped in the mountain pass with his men, facing a Saracen army that outnumbers them a hundred to one. His best friend and fellow peer counts the enemy from a hilltop and pleads with him three times to sound the great horn while the emperor can still come back. Who is the friend at Roland's shoulder?
context: Oliver, Roland's sworn brother-in-arms, is the voice of prudence in the chanson: he sees the odds, counts the Saracens from a hilltop, and begs Roland three times to blow the horn while there is still time. Turpin the Archbishop is a third peer on the field; Ogier the Dane and Naimon are other paladins of Charlemagne -- all real, wrong here. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: Roland commands Charlemagne's rearguard in the mountain pass, in the Song of Roland, and he is too proud at first to blow his great ivory horn, the Olifant. Only when almost all his knights lie dead around him does he lift it to his lips. He blows with such fury that his own body gives way. What happens to him from the sheer effort?
answer: the veins in his temples burst
choices: the veins in his temples burst
his throat tears open and bleeds
the sword-cut in his side reopens
his eyes fill with blood and he goes blind
context: The chanson makes the horn-blast a physical martyrdom: Roland winds Olifant so hard that the veins in his temples burst and blood runs down his face -- but Charlemagne, thirty leagues away, hears it and turns his army back. The dying king's nephew has broken his own body to bring the news, and it is still too late. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: An archbishop rides among Charlemagne's knights in the mountain pass, in the medieval French epic Song of Roland, when the Saracen army swarms the rearguard. This fighting bishop cuts down dozens of the enemy with his own hand before falling at Roland's side. What is the fighting archbishop's name?
context: Archbishop Turpin is one of the twelve peers, a warrior-bishop who fights and dies beside Roland; both are found on the field by Charlemagne after the pass. Anselm of Canterbury, Adalhard of Corbie, and Alcuin of York are all real medieval churchmen, but not the fighting archbishop of the chanson. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: Elimelech of Bethlehem gathered up his wife Naomi and their two sons when the grain failed, in the days when judges ruled Israel, and left home to wait out the famine in a country across the Dead Sea. Which country did they go to?
context: Ruth 1:1-2 KJV. Elimelech, Naomi, Mahlon, and Chilion cross the Dead Sea into Moab. Egypt, Edom, and Philistia are all real neighbors of Israel that a starving family could have fled to, but the text names Moab.

question: Orpah kissed her mother-in-law Naomi goodbye and turned back toward her own mother's house. Naomi had lost her husband and both her sons, and she had told her two widowed daughters-in-law to go home. The other one, Ruth, clung to her and would not be sent away. What famous pledge did Ruth swear to Naomi?
answer: 'Whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.'
choices: 'Whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.'
'Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.'
'Entreat me not to weep, for the Lord hath given, and the Lord hath taken away.'
'The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want, though I walk in the shadow.'
context: Ruth 1:16 KJV, spoken by Ruth to Naomi. The other three are real famous verses -- Mary's answer to Gabriel (Luke 1:38), a mash of Job 1:21, and Psalm 23 -- but none is Ruth's pledge.

question: The women of Bethlehem crowded around Naomi and cried, 'Is this Naomi?' She had come home a widow after ten years abroad, and both her sons were dead. She told them not to use her old name any more, because Naomi means 'pleasant' and the Almighty, she said, had dealt bitterly with her. What new name did she ask them to call her?
context: Ruth 1:20 KJV: 'Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.' Mara is Hebrew for 'bitter.' Hagar, Rahab, and Zilpah are all real Old Testament women, but none is the name Naomi chose.

question: Ruth went out to glean in the fields of Bethlehem as soon as she and Naomi came home, at the very beginning of the year's first grain harvest. She worked the corners of the ground that the law of Moses left for the poor and the stranger. Which grain was ripening in the fields she went to?
context: Ruth 1:22 and 2:23 KJV. Barley ripens in Israel in April, weeks before wheat -- so it is the first harvest a hungry widow can glean. Rye and millet were not the staple grains of ancient Israel.

question: Boaz, a wealthy kinsman of Ruth's dead father-in-law, saw the poor widow gleaning stray grain from the corners of his field in Bethlehem and took pity on her. He called his young harvesters aside and gave them a secret order, so that she could gather far more grain than a stranger ordinarily could. What did he tell them to do?
answer: Let handfuls fall on purpose for her out of the sheaves
choices: Let handfuls fall on purpose for her out of the sheaves
Deliver a full sack of grain to Naomi's door each evening
Bar the other gleaners from the field until she had finished
Weigh her grain double at the threshing floor scale
context: Ruth 2:16 KJV. Boaz's instruction disguises open charity as ordinary carelessness so Ruth is not shamed. The other options are the kinds of favors a rich landowner could grant, but only the dropped handfuls are in the text.

question: Ruth washed and anointed herself on Naomi's advice and went by night to the threshing-floor in Bethlehem, where the landowner Boaz lay sleeping by his heap of corn. She lay down at his feet. He woke and promised to settle the matter. What did Boaz send her home carrying in her veil at dawn?
choices: A silver ring set with carnelian
A written pledge sealed with his signet
A lamb from his own flock
context: Ruth 3:15 KJV. The six measures are both a betrothal gift and a public sign to Naomi that Boaz means to act. Signets, silver, and livestock are all real Iron Age wedding tokens, but the text specifies barley.

question: Boaz gathered the elders at the city gate of Bethlehem to buy the field of the dead Elimelech in public and marry his widowed daughter-in-law Ruth. A nearer kinsman had the first right to redeem the field, but he refused, so the sale to Boaz went through. What did one man give the other to seal the deal before the elders?
answer: His sandal, plucked off his foot
choices: His sandal, plucked off his foot
A cut lock of his own hair
A red cord tied around the wrist
A cup of wine poured on the ground
context: Ruth 4:7-8 KJV: 'a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel.' Boaz then buys the field and marries Ruth; their son Obed becomes the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:17).

question: An angel came to the childless wife of Manoah of Zorah, in the Book of Judges. The angel told her that her son, the future strongman Samson, must be a Nazarite from birth. What one thing was forbidden ever to touch his head?
context: Judges 13:5 KJV: 'no razor shall come upon his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb.' The son is Samson; his strength lies in his uncut hair. Anointing oil and crowns did later touch the heads of Israel's kings and priests, but never Samson's.

question: Walking down to Timnath to see the Philistine woman he wanted to marry, Samson was attacked in the vineyards by a young roaring lion. He killed it with nothing in his hands, and later, going back to the carcass, he found something unlikely inside it. What did he find?
answer: A swarm of bees and honey
choices: A swarm of bees and honey
context: Judges 14:5-9 KJV. Samson eats the honey and gives some to his parents without telling them where it came from. The hidden find becomes the seed of his wedding riddle in another question.

question: The men of Judah handed Samson over to a Philistine army, wanting to end the trouble he brought on them. The moment the Philistines seized him, he snapped the new ropes on his arms 'as flax burnt with fire' and picked up the first weapon he could find on the ground. Using what did he then slay a thousand men?
choices: The broken axle of a chariot
context: Judges 15:15-17 KJV. Samson cries, 'With the jawbone of an ass, heaps upon heaps ... have I slain a thousand men,' and names the place Ramath-lehi ('Jawbone Hill'). The stone from a brook is David's weapon against Goliath (1 Samuel 17); the others are plausible battlefield finds.

question: The five lords of the Philistine cities came secretly with silver to a woman in the Valley of Sorek, offering her a fortune to tease out the secret of Samson's strength. The Israelite strongman had fallen in love with her. What was the name of the woman they paid?
context: Judges 16:4-5 KJV. Each of the five Philistine lords promised her eleven hundred pieces of silver. Jezebel, Bathsheba, and Michal are all real biblical women who married powerful men, but none is Samson's betrayer.

question: Samson lied a third time to the woman begging him for the secret of his strength. The Philistine lords had paid her to find it out, and she had already tried his first two answers on him, to no effect. This third answer was the strangest of the three. What did he tell her?
answer: That she must weave his seven locks into the web of her loom
choices: That she must weave his seven locks into the web of her loom
That she must bind him with seven fresh green withs
That she must bind him with new ropes never used before
That she must pour wine upon his hair as he slept
context: Judges 16:13-14 KJV. Delilah wove his hair into the loom and fastened it with the pin; Samson woke and 'went away with the pin of the beam, and with the web.' The first two lies -- seven green withs and new ropes -- were his earlier answers (Judges 16:7, 16:11); the wine detail is invented. Only after this third lie did he finally tell her about the razor.

question: The Philistine lords brought the blinded Samson up from his mill in Gaza on a great feast day and made him stand as entertainment inside their great temple. They had gathered to sacrifice to their chief god, and the temple would soon come down on them all. Whose temple was it?
context: Judges 16:23 KJV: 'the lords of the Philistines gathered them together for to offer a great sacrifice unto Dagon their god.' Baal, Moloch, and Chemosh are real gods of Israel's other neighbors (Canaanites, Ammonites, Moabites), not the Philistines.

question: A childless woman wept and prayed silently at the shrine at Shiloh until the old priest Eli, watching her lips move, took her for a drunk. She promised God any son she bore, and that son was Samuel. What was the woman's name?
context: 1 Samuel 1:9-20 KJV. Hannah vows that if given a son she will give him to the LORD; Samuel is that son. Sarah was Abraham's wife (barren till Isaac); Rebekah was Isaac's wife (barren till the twins); Ruth was David's great-grandmother. All four are honest OT women.

question: Saul, a tall young Benjaminite, was out on a long errand for his father Kish when he stumbled on the prophet Samuel, the man who would secretly pick him as Israel's first king. Saul was hunting for something valuable that had wandered off. What was Saul looking for?
context: 1 Samuel 9:3-19 KJV -- 'the asses of Kish Saul's father were lost.' Saul and his servant search for days; they end up in Samuel's town asking the seer where the donkeys have gone, and instead Saul is anointed king.

question: Samuel took the tall young Saul quietly aside where nobody else could see, poured something on his head, then kissed him. It was the secret sign that Saul had been chosen as Israel's first king. What did Samuel pour on Saul's head?
context: 1 Samuel 10:1 KJV -- 'Then Samuel took a vial of oil, and poured it upon his head, and kissed him.' The kiss and the oil together are the private anointing before the public choice at Mizpah.

question: The tribes of Israel gathered at Mizpah, at Samuel's call, to choose a king by casting lots. Tribe by tribe, then family by family, the lot narrowed until it fell on a very tall young man named Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin. But when the people called him forward to be crowned, he was nowhere to be found. Where had he hidden himself?
context: 1 Samuel 10:22-23 KJV -- 'Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff.' They fetch him out and he stands head and shoulders above every man there. The reluctant giant king.

question: Samuel slipped out of King Saul's court in secret, sent by God to anoint the next king of Israel. He travelled to the small town of Bethlehem, south of Jerusalem, and the house of a shepherd-farmer with eight sons, one of them the boy David. Whose house did Samuel enter?
context: 1 Samuel 16:1-5 KJV -- 'fill thine horn with oil, and go, I will send thee to Jesse the Bethlehemite.' Boaz is David's great-grandfather (from Ruth); Obed is David's grandfather; Eli is the priest who raised Samuel. Real names from David's family story, but not the right house.

question: Jesse's oldest son Eliab came before Samuel, tall and handsome, the kind of man who looks like a king, and the prophet thought he had found God's pick. Then the word came to him, in the King James Bible: 'man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the...' What is the missing word?
context: 1 Samuel 16:7 KJV verbatim -- 'the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.' Perhaps the most quoted line in the whole Old Testament about how God chooses.

question: Seven of Jesse's sons passed before Samuel at Bethlehem, and God chose none of them. Samuel asked if there was another. There was: the youngest, out of the house entirely, doing a job the family did not think worth calling him in from. What was David doing when they finally sent for him?
answer: keeping the sheep in the pasture
choices: hunting a lion in the hills
keeping the sheep in the pasture
context: 1 Samuel 16:11 KJV -- 'There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep.' When David is brought in he is 'ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to' (v.12).

question: Young Cu Chulainn crossed the sea from Ulster to learn from the greatest teacher of arms in the world, in Irish myth. She was a warrior-woman with a school on a stormy island off the coast of Alba. What was her name?
context: Scathach's name comes from Old Irish scath, meaning 'shadow' or 'phantom' -- 'the Shadowy One'. Medb is the warrior-queen of Connacht (Ulster Cycle, but an opponent, not a teacher); Deirdre 'of the Sorrows' is a tragic beauty of the same cycle; the Morrigan is the war-goddess who watches over battle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: The warrior-woman Scathach trained her pupils at Dun Scaith, 'the Fortress of Shadows,' and later tradition set it on one particular island off the west coast of Scotland. Ruins there still bear her name, and they say the island takes its own name from hers. On which island?
context: The ruins called Dun Sgathaich near Tarskavaig on the Sleat peninsula of Skye mark the mythological site. The folk-etymology holds that the Isle of Skye (an t-Eilean Sgitheanach in Scots Gaelic) takes its own name from Scathach. Iona is the monastery-island of Columba; Man is the sea-god Manannan's island; Anglesey (Ynys Mon) is a druid-heartland in Welsh tradition. Source: https://spookyscotland.net/scathach/  (Legend.)

question: A girl's father set Cu Chulainn an impossible bride-price: no man could marry his daughter until he had learned the war-arts of the warrior-woman Scathach. So the hero crossed the sea to Alba, old Ireland's name for Scotland, to study at her Fortress of Shadows. Which girl did Cu Chulainn want to marry?
context: The story is told in Tochmarc Emire ('The Wooing of Emer'), one of the great foretales to the Tain. Grainne is the Fianna beauty who runs off with Diarmuid; Niamh carries Oisin to Tir na nOg; Deirdre is a doomed Ulster-Cycle heroine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochmarc_Emire  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn came to the bridge before Scathach's Fortress of Shadows, a magic bridge that only her rightful students could pass. One step on the end, and the middle rose up and pitched the walker off. What feat carried him over it in one bound?
context: The salmon-leap (leim in bratain) is Scathach's signature technique: a running vault long enough to clear a bridge or a warrior's raised shield. Cu Chulainn will use it again years later at the Ford against Ferdiad. The chariot-wheel feat (roth-cles), the pole-vault for siege warfare, and the apple-feat (ubhall-cleas) are also real cles-feats Scathach teaches at her school -- but the bridge is crossed by the salmon-leap. Source: https://spookyscotland.net/scathach/  (Legend.)

question: Aife, the warrior-queen and rival of Scathach, met Cu Chulainn in single combat in Alba, and neither could beat the other. So he won by shouting a lie: the one thing she prized most in all the world had just fallen off a cliff behind her. What did he shout had fallen?
context: In the moment her head whips round to look, Cu Chulainn seizes her by the throat and pins her. He spares her life on the condition that she call off her enmity with Scathach and bear him a son. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: A boy sailed alone to Ireland at seven years old and stood on the shore challenging Ulster's champions. He was the son Cu Chulainn had fathered on Aife, raised in Alba without ever meeting his father. Cu Chulainn was sent to face him and killed him in single combat, knowing him for his son only when it was too late. What was the boy's name?
context: Connla comes to Ireland at age seven under a geis (a magical taboo) that forbids him to name himself. The tale of Aided Oenfhir Aife ('The Death of Aife's Only Son') is one of the most heartbreaking in the Ulster Cycle -- a Sohrab-and-Rustum tale a thousand years before Firdausi. Cormac, Lugaid, and Amergin are all real Ulster-Cycle names, none of them Aife's son. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: Scathach's daughter opened the gate of the fortress in Alba when the young hero Cu Chulainn first came to it, and she took him as her lover. Later, when she brought him a cup, he gripped it so hard that he broke her fingers by accident. What was the daughter's name?
context: Uathach ('the Spectral One' -- her name echoes her mother's Shadow-name) hands Cu Chulainn the welcoming cup on his first day; his warrior's grip crushes her fingers. Emer is his betrothed back in Ireland; Sadhbh is Fionn's doe-wife in the later Fenian Cycle; Blathnat is a queen of a different Ulster tale. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: Circe warns Odysseus, in Homer's Odyssey, about a narrow sea passage where two monsters wait on facing cliffs, so close together that a ship cannot dodge both. One lurks in a cave and the other is a churning whirlpool. What is the famous pair called?
choices: The Sirens and the Wandering Rocks
context: Circe warns Odysseus about the twin cliff-monsters Scylla and Charybdis, guarding a narrow strait where no ship can avoid both. (Odyssey 12; mythweb.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus must sail through a narrow strait between two cliffs in Homer's Odyssey. On one, sunk in a cave, crouches a monster, a woman above and writhing necks below, each ending in a dog's head, who snatches sailors off passing ships. What is her name?
context: Scylla lives on one cliff of the strait. From her cave she reaches down with her many necks to snatch sailors off passing ships. (Odyssey 12; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: Homer sets a very different horror on the cliff facing Scylla's, 'within a bowshot' of her: a great whirlpool-monster that swallows the sea three times each day and vomits it back up. No ship caught in her draw comes back. What is her name?
context: Charybdis is a monstrous whirlpool on the cliff opposite Scylla. Three times a day she swallows the sea and three times spits it up; no ship caught in her draw survives. (Odyssey 12; poetryintranslation.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Homer gives the cliff-monster Scylla twelve flailing feet and three rows of teeth in each mouth, and he sets a fixed number of long serpent-necks on her, each ending in a savage head. Odysseus must sail past her. How many heads does she have?
context: Scylla has six long necks each with a dog-fanged head, three rows of teeth per mouth, and twelve legs. (Odyssey 12; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: Circe puts the choice to Odysseus honestly: he cannot avoid both monsters, so he must pick which cliff to hug. She tells him to steer closer to Scylla, because the whirlpool would swallow the whole ship, but Scylla will only take a fixed toll. How many of his crewmen will Scylla take as they pass?
context: Circe tells Odysseus to sail close to Scylla and lose six men -- one per head -- because Charybdis would take the whole ship. She explicitly forbids him to fight, because fighting will only cost him six more. (Odyssey 12; sparknotes.com/lit/odyssey.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus watches Scylla's heads dart down from her cliff and snatch his crewmen off the deck one after another. He later says that of everything he saw in ten years of wandering, the Cyclops and the Sirens and the land of the dead among them, this was the most pitiful sight of all. What do the dying men do as they are lifted up out of reach?
context: Odysseus: 'They called on my name, and I saw them lifted, and lifted still -- this was the most pitiful thing my eyes have seen of all my wanderings.' (Odyssey 12.245-259, Lattimore.)  (Legend.)

question: Circe tells Odysseus one more strange thing about Scylla before he sails for the strait. For all the monster's size and the three rows of teeth in each of her mouths, Circe says, her voice is not what anyone would expect. What does Circe say Scylla's voice sounds like?
context: Circe warns that Scylla's voice is 'no bigger than a newborn puppy's yelp' -- a tiny yipping sound coming from a giant monster. It is one of Homer's most unsettling details. (Odyssey 12; poetryintranslation.com.)  (Legend.)

question: His men row toward the cliff in the strait, and Odysseus knows what waits there: Circe has told him Scylla will snatch men from his deck whatever he does. He makes a hard captain's decision and does not tell the crew what is coming. What is his reason?
answer: He fears they will drop the oars and hide
choices: He fears they will drop the oars and hide
He fears they will mutiny and turn back
He fears they will attack Scylla with spears
He fears they will pray for the wrong god
context: Odysseus says plainly that he kept Scylla secret because if the men knew, they would drop the oars and huddle in the hold -- and then the ship, unrowed, would drift straight into Charybdis instead. (Odyssey 12; cliffsnotes.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus clings alone to a piece of wreckage, his last ship and last crewmen gone, as the current sweeps him back into the same strait. He saves himself by grabbing a tree that grows out of the cliff over the whirlpool, and he hangs there like a bat, waiting for it to vomit his raft back up. What kind of tree does he cling to?
context: After the disaster on Thrinacia and the loss of his last ship, Odysseus is swept back through the strait alone and clings to a wild fig tree over Charybdis, hanging 'like a bat' until she spits his raft back up so he can drop onto it. One of the most vivid single images in the poem. (Odyssey 12.431-446.)  (Legend.)

question: Thucydides tries to put Homer's two monsters on a real map, and the poet Virgil and the naturalist Pliny after him name the same place: a narrow passage of water between mainland Italy and Sicily. A town on the Italian side still carries Scylla's name. Which real strait do they name?
context: Later tradition places Scylla on the Italian cliff and Charybdis on the Sicilian side of the Strait of Messina; the modern Italian town of Scilla in Calabria takes its name from the monster. (westportlibrary.libguides.com/scylla.)

question: In the old account, a young officer of the Praetorian Guard went down to the cells in Rome to cheer Christian prisoners. He was secretly a Christian, and someone reported him. The emperor Diocletian ordered him killed, around the year 288. What was his name?
context: Sebastian was captain of the Praetorian Guard under Diocletian; traditional dates are c. 286-288 CE. Ambrose already knows his name by the end of the 4th century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.

question: Sebastian's fellow archers of the imperial guard tied him to a wooden post and used him as a target, on the emperor Diocletian's order. The fifth-century account of his death has a famous line for the way they left him. He was left as full of arrows as what?
answer: An urchin is full of pricks
choices: An urchin is full of pricks
A grove is full of leaves
A quiver is full of shafts
A shield is full of dents
context: 'Sagittis obsitum ut ericium' in the 5th-century Passio -- 'as full of arrows as an urchin (hedgehog) is full of pricks'. The image became a stock phrase in medieval hagiography. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: In the old account, Irene, a Christian widow, went out to a post in Rome in the dark with a small oil lamp, once the archers had gone, planning to carry off the body of the officer Sebastian. He had been shot full of arrows there on the emperor Diocletian's orders. What did she find?
context: The Passio says the widow Irene, whom it calls the widow of the martyr Castulus, came at night to bury Sebastian and found him still breathing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: Sebastian did something no one in Rome expected, the legend says, as soon as he could walk again, after a Christian widow had nursed him in secret. He went back and ambushed the emperor Diocletian in broad daylight, denouncing him to his face for persecuting Christians. Where did he confront the emperor?
answer: On the steps of the imperial palace
choices: On the steps of the imperial palace
In the middle of a chariot race
At a banquet with the senate
context: The Passio has Sebastian post himself on the palace stairs to ambush the emperor with a public speech accusing him of cruelty to the Christians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: The emperor Diocletian had been told, the old account says, that the officer Sebastian was dead, shot full of arrows at a post by his own guardsmen. Then he saw Sebastian standing before him, giving speeches against his cruelty. He ordered the man killed a second time, with no archers now. How was Sebastian put to death?
context: The second sentence is death by cudgels in the Hippodrome. Sebastian's whole story turns on the reveal that the arrows are NOT what killed him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: Diocletian gave one last order, the legend says, once the Christian soldier Sebastian was dead at the second attempt. The emperor wanted the body dumped somewhere Christians would never be able to bury it or keep it as a relic. Where was the corpse thrown?
choices: Into the Tiber under the bridges
Onto the pyre of a criminal
Down a mineshaft outside the walls
context: The Cloaca Maxima was Rome's great main sewer, running under the Forum out to the Tiber -- meant as a final indignity, and to keep the body from becoming a relic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: A Roman Christian woman dreamed, the legend says, where to find the body of Sebastian on the night it was thrown away. She retrieved it and buried it in a catacomb on the Appian Way, at the spot where the Basilica of San Sebastiano now stands. What was her name?
context: The Passio names Lucina as the woman who recovered the body from the Cloaca Maxima after seeing Sebastian in a dream. All four choices are named early Roman Christian women martyrs or matrons. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: The young soldier Sebastian stood tied to his post, full of arrows, in the many paintings of him, and medieval Christians called on him against one mass-killing disaster above all others. He had not died of those wounds, for a Christian widow had nursed him back to health. Which disaster did they ask him to stop, and why him?
answer: Plague, because he survived arrows and plague-strike was pictured as arrows
choices: Plague, because he survived arrows and plague-strike was pictured as arrows
Shipwreck, because the sewer washed him to the Tiber and the sea
Famine, because his body was thrown away like refuse
House fires, because his executioners burned the post
context: Ancient and medieval thought pictured pestilence as 'the arrows of the gods' or 'the arrows of God'. A saint who had famously survived a hail of arrows was the natural intercessor when plague hit a town. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.

question: A young nephew of King Conchobar of Ulster earns his hero's name in one evening at a rich man's gate, in the old Irish Ulster Cycle. Until that night the boy from Dun Dealgan, today's Dundalk, goes by another name. What is his boyhood name?
context: The boy Setanta will earn a new name later in a single afternoon at a smith's gate. Fionn, Oisin, and Diarmuid are the great heroes of the LATER Fenian Cycle, a different tradition; Setanta belongs to the earlier Ulster Cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%BA_Chulainn  (Legend.)

question: The boy Setanta walks alone down a country road one evening, late for a great feast, in the old Irish tales of Ulster. The feast is at the house of a rich and honoured craftsman named Culann. What is Culann's trade?
context: Culann the smith is one of the great craftsmen of Ulster; his forge would have made the weapons of the king's warband. His name lives in Cu Chulainn's own -- 'the Hound of Culann' -- for what happens at his gate that night. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culann  (Legend.)

question: King Conchobar of Ulster arrives at Culann's feast and forgets to say that one more guest, the boy Setanta, is still on the road. Culann has already let his guard beast off its chains for the night, a creature so huge that three chains are needed to hold it. What kind of animal is it?
