context: Culann's dog was an enormous chained war-hound, bred to kill wolves and men; it took three chains to hold him and it was said no other dog in Ireland could match him. Boars belong to the tale of Diarmuid; the bulls belong to the Cattle Raid; the black horse is Cu Chulainn's later chariot-horse, the Liath Macha. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culann  (Legend.)

question: The great guard beast charges down on the boy Setanta with open jaws as he reaches Culann's gate at dusk. It has been loosed for the night. Setanta has no sword, no spear and no shield, only what he carries from the afternoon's play at Emain Macha, the royal fort. What is in his hands?
context: The boy had been playing iomain -- hurling, the old Irish stick-and-ball game, still played today. His hurley (camán) and small hard leather ball (sliotar) are all he has when the hound comes. David has the sling in the Bible (Christian pillar). Source: https://www.irelandsmythsandlegends.com/the-story-of-setanta

question: Setanta stands alone at Culann's gate as the huge guard beast springs at him out of the shadows. He is a small boy with no weapon, only his stick and one small hard leather ball. He swings the stick with the whole of his strength and sends the ball at the beast. What does the ball do to it?
answer: Kills it, driven down its throat
choices: Kills it, driven down its throat
Puts out both its yellow eyes
Turns it aside from his gate
context: In the tale the ball goes down the throat with such force that in some versions it passes right through the dog. In others he then seizes the beast by the hind legs and dashes its head against a standing stone. Either way the hound is dead at his feet before the men at the feast come running out. Source: https://www.irelandsmythsandlegends.com/the-story-of-setanta

question: Culann steps out of his house, sees the dead beast, and grieves aloud: the hound was his living defence, and no pup of the same stock can be trained to replace it in less than a year. The boy, still standing at the gate, makes him a serious offer. What does Setanta offer to do?
answer: Guard the smith's house himself in the hound's place
choices: Guard the smith's house himself in the hound's place
Pay the smith the price of the hound in cattle
Fight a champion in single combat to earn the smith's forgiveness
Bring the smith the head of a wolf as recompense
context: The boy kneels and offers to sit at the smith's gate every night in the hound's place until a new pup of the same line can be reared. This offer -- a boy taking on a war-dog's watch -- is what changes his name forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culann  (Legend.)

question: Fergus mac Roich and his fellow exiles from Ulster tell the tale of the boy and the guard beast in the enemy queen's camp. They are trying to explain to her exactly who this one boy is who keeps stopping her army single-handed. Inside which saga is the Boyhood Deeds of Cu Chulainn nested?
choices: The Cattle Raid of Fraech (Tain Bo Fraich)
The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel (Togail Bruidne Da Derga)
context: The Macgnimrada Con Culaind ('The Boyhood Deeds of Cu Chulainn') is a set of inset tales that Fergus mac Roich, exiled from Ulster, narrates to Medb of Connacht inside the Tain Bo Cuailnge -- the great cattle-raid epic. The other three are all real Ulster-Cycle tales, but the Boyhood Deeds sit specifically inside the Tain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%BA_Chulainn  (Legend.)

question: A god walks onto the battlefield of the great cattle-raid and fights beside Cu Chulainn, because the hero is his son. Cu Chulainn has a mortal father too, Sualtaim mac Roich, husband of Deichtine, and the Irish repeat that pattern of two fathers for their great heroes. Which of the gods is named as his divine father?
context: Lugh 'Long-Arm' (Lamhfhada) is the master-of-all-arts of the Tuatha De Danann and later comes down onto the battlefield to fight beside Cu Chulainn in the Tain. The Dagda is Lugh's father-in-law and lord of the cauldron; Manannan is the sea-god (father of Niamh); Nuada is the earlier king of the Tuatha with the silver arm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%BA_Chulainn  (Legend.)

question: Paul warned the centurion Julius not to sail any further that season, as their ship lay at Fair Havens on the south coast of Crete. Paul was a prisoner bound for Rome. Two men on board argued the other way, and the centurion took their word. Which two men were they?
answer: The master and owner of the ship
choices: The master and owner of the ship
The sailing master and the ship's scribe
The two senior sailors of the crew
context: Acts 27:11 -- 'the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship, more than those things which were spoken by Paul.' It is a working-sailor argument about the season, not a religious dispute; the master and owner win, and the storm proves Paul right within days.

question: The sailors on Paul's storm-driven ship dropped a plumb-line at midnight and got twenty fathoms, then a little further fifteen. Terrified the ship would strike rocks in the dark, they let down four heavy anchors and prayed for the day. From which part of the ship did they let the anchors down?
context: Acts 27:29 -- 'they cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for the day.' Anchoring from the stern (the back) is unusual -- most ships anchor by the bow -- but it kept the ship pointed toward the beach so they could run her ashore when day came.

question: The writer of Acts stopped his story of Paul's shipwreck on the night the anchors held, with the ship pitching in the dark, to count everyone aboard: prisoners, crew and passengers together. The storm had driven them for two weeks, the sails were torn away and the cargo was overboard. How many souls were on the ship?
context: Acts 27:37 -- 'we were in all in the ship two hundred threescore and sixteen souls.' Verse 44 adds that every one of the 276 made it to shore alive, some by swimming, some clinging to broken planks.

question: Paul and the other survivors of the wreck came ashore in the rain on a small Mediterranean island, after a fortnight of storm. The islanders lit a bonfire on the beach for them and showed the shivering strangers unusual kindness. Which island was it?
context: Acts 28:1 -- 'they knew that the island was called Melita,' which is the ancient name for Malta. Crete is where the storm began; Cyprus and Rhodes lie further east along the earlier part of Paul's journey.

question: Paul gathered an armful of driftwood for the islanders' fire on the beach, cold and wet from the shipwreck, and a snake driven out by the heat lunged from the sticks and fastened onto him. The islanders stood back to see him swell up and drop. Where on his body did the viper strike?
context: Acts 28:3 -- 'there came a viper out of the heat, and fastened on his hand.' The islanders stood watching, waiting for him to swell up or drop dead; when Paul shook the snake off into the fire and felt nothing, they changed their minds and said he was a god.

question: The island's chief man took in the shipwrecked party for three days and lodged them courteously on his lands near the beach. His elderly father lay sick with fever and dysentery, and Paul went in, prayed and laid hands on him. What was the chief man's name?
context: Acts 28:7-8 -- 'the chief man of the island, whose name was Publius.' Sergius Paulus is the proconsul of Cyprus in Acts 13; Gallio is the proconsul of Achaia in Acts 18; Cornelius is the centurion of Caesarea in Acts 10.

question: Paul boarded a second grain ship from Alexandria after the wreck, one with the twin gods Castor and Pollux as its figurehead. It put in first at a great harbour on the eastern coast of Sicily. The party spent three days there and then sailed on to Rhegium and Puteoli. Which port was it?
context: Acts 28:12-13 -- 'And landing at Syracuse, we tarried there three days. And from thence we fetched a compass, and came to Rhegium... and the next day to Puteoli.' Messina, Catania, and Panormus (modern Palermo) are all real Sicilian ports of the ancient world, but Acts names Syracuse.

question: Thor the thunder-god comes home to a wife famous in Asgard for one beauty. The poets say no woman in the nine worlds has hair like hers, long and thick and falling all the way to the ground. What is the name of Thor's wife?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 31 and Skaldskaparmal 43: Sif is Thor's wife and is named for her extraordinary golden hair. Frigg is Odin's wife and queen of Asgard. Freyja is the Vanir goddess of love. Idunn is the goddess who keeps the golden apples of youth. Sif is also the mother of the god Ullr, the archer and skier of Asgard.  (Legend.)

question: Loki the trickster comes upon Thor's wife one afternoon, fast asleep in her chamber, and takes out a knife. Snorri gives him no reason but mischief, and the deed starts a chain of trouble in Asgard. What does Loki do to her while she sleeps?
answer: shears her golden hair to the scalp
choices: shears her golden hair to the scalp
steals a ring off her finger
cuts the strap of her golden girdle
carves a rune on her forehead
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki simply cuts off all Sif's famous hair, leaving her scalp bare. Snorri gives no motive beyond mischief -- this is one of the purest examples of Loki being cruel because he can. The other three options are inventions built out of other Norse objects (golden rings, girdles, runes) that have nothing to do with this scene.  (Legend.)

question: Thor seizes Loki by the throat on the day he comes home to find his wife in tears over the cruel joke the trickster has played on her. Unless Loki makes it right, the thunder-god promises him one specific violence. What does Thor threaten to do to Loki?
answer: break every bone in his body
choices: break every bone in his body
hang him from the branches of Yggdrasil
throw him into the sea for Jormungandr
sew his lips shut with an awl
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Thor threatens to break every bone in Loki's body unless Loki makes it right. The other three options are not what Thor threatens in this scene.  (Legend.)

question: A Norse court-poet, a skald, wants to name something in his verse and says 'the hair of Sif' instead, and every listener understands him. The phrase is a kenning, a poet's fixed substitute-name, and it rests on the replacement hair Loki brought home from the dwarf-smiths for Thor's wife. What does the kenning mean?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 39: the standard list of kennings for gold includes 'Sif's hair', because Sif's replacement hair was spun of real gold that grew on her head. 'Wheat at harvest' is the older grain-goddess reading some modern scholars give of Sif herself, but the kenning is for gold. Norse poets loved this kind of story-derived name -- 'Kvasir's blood' for poetry, 'the sea-king's ride' for a ship, 'Odin's storm' for a battle.  (Legend.)

question: In the Volsunga Saga, the smith Regin sent his foster-son Sigurd out onto the moor of Gnitaheid with a sword remade from its broken pieces. A dragon lay there, coiled around a pile of gold. What was the dragon's name?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 14 and 18; Fafnismal prose introduction. Fafnir is the dragon on Gnitaheid, once a man and the brother of the smith Regin. Nidhoggr is the dragon that gnaws the root of Yggdrasil in the underworld. Jormungandr is the Midgard-serpent that circles the world. Grendel is the man-shaped monster of Beowulf, not a dragon. Fafnir is the specific dragon Sigurd kills.  (Legend.)

question: Fafnir murdered his own father for a hoard of gold and kept all of it for himself. Then greed drove him to use a Helm of Awe and change his shape, to keep watch over it alone as a dragon. What had Fafnir been before that?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 14 and 18. Fafnir was a man -- specifically the son of Hreidmar and the brother of Regin the smith and Otr the otter-shaped shape-shifter. When the family got the cursed hoard of Andvari's gold as compensation for Otr's killing, Fafnir killed his father, took all of the gold, and used a magic Helm of Awe to transform himself into a dragon so he could guard it alone. He is one of a small handful of dragons in world mythology who used to be human.  (Legend.)

question: Regin the smith told young Sigurd one thing about the dragon Fafnir before sending him out to Gnitaheid. The hide was so hard that no blade could pierce the back or the flanks, and only one part of the beast was soft enough for a sword. Which part of Fafnir could be pierced?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18; Fafnismal prose introduction. Only the underside of Fafnir's belly is unarmoured -- everywhere else his hide turns the blade. This is why the strategy has to be a strike from BELOW as the dragon passes overhead. Smaug in Tolkien -- whose weak underbelly is famously exposed by a single missing scale -- was directly borrowed from Fafnir.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd listened while his foster-father, the smith Regin, laid out exactly how to kill the dragon Fafnir on the moor of Gnitaheid. Each morning the dragon crawled down a worn path to drink from the river. Sigurd was to go to that path before dawn and set one specific ambush. What was Regin's plan?
answer: dig a pit in the trail and stab upward as the dragon passes over
choices: dig a pit in the trail and stab upward as the dragon passes over
drop a great stone from a cliff onto the dragon's spine
loose a burning arrow between the dragon's eyes at dawn
pour boiling oil down the mouth of the dragon's lair overnight
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18; Fafnismal prose introduction. The Norse dragon-killing method is the pit-and-upward-thrust -- Regin's plan is that Sigurd hide in a trench cut into the game-trail and drive the blade UP as the dragon's soft belly passes over his head. It has entered European folklore as the standard way to kill any large monster from below.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd was still preparing his ambush on the moor of Gnitaheid, following his foster-father Regin's plan, when a stranger came across to him. The man was old and one-eyed, in a wide-brimmed wanderer's cloak, and he gave Sigurd a critical piece of advice that Regin had left out. What did the old wanderer tell Sigurd to add to the plan?
answer: dig extra pits alongside to catch the blood
choices: dig extra pits alongside to catch the blood
smear the sword with poison before the strike
wait for the second dawn instead of the first
call the dragon by his mortal name to freeze him
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18. The one-eyed stranger is Odin himself. He warns Sigurd that a single pit will fill with the dragon's blood as Fafnir bleeds out overhead, and Sigurd would drown before he could climb out. The side-channels drain the flood away. This is one of a whole series of moments in the Volsunga Saga where Odin quietly intervenes in the Volsung line -- putting Gram in the tree at Signy's wedding, shattering it against Sigmund at the end, and now this.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd waited beside the water-trail at dawn as the dragon Fafnir crawled out of his lair toward the water, and the earth trembled under the beast. Before those teeth or that armoured hide ever reached the young hero, one weapon of the dragon's rolled out ahead along the trail. What moved down the trail in front of Fafnir?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18; Fafnismal 1. Fafnir's breath is described as poisonous -- rolling before him along the trail like a mist. The Norse do not always draw a hard line between snake-poison and dragon-fire; Fafnir is one of the venom-breathing dragons. Jormungandr the world-serpent kills Thor with the same kind of venom nine steps after Thor kills him.  (Legend.)

question: The dragon Sigurd had run through on the moor of Gnitaheid began to talk, spending his last breath on the man who had killed him. The Poetic Edda sets that dying talk in a poem of its own, and most of its verses are the beast speaking. Which poem was it?
context: Poetic Edda (Codex Regius); Carolyne Larrington translation. Fafnismal ('the sayings of Fafnir') is a dialogue-poem in which most of the verses are the dragon's dying words to Sigurd. Reginsmal ('the sayings of Regin') comes just before it in the manuscript and covers the smith's back-story. Sigrdrifumal is the awakening of the valkyrie Sigrdrifa. Vafthrudnismal is Odin's wisdom-contest with a different giant. The specific dying-speech poem is Fafnismal.  (Legend.)

question: Fafnir lay dying on the moor of Gnitaheid, run through by Sigurd's sword, and he spent his last strength on a very concrete warning about the pile of gold the young hero had just won. The rest of the Volsunga Saga proves it exactly right. What did Fafnir warn Sigurd about the gold?
answer: the cursed hoard will destroy him too
choices: the cursed hoard will destroy him too
the gold must be thrown back into the river
the ring in the hoard commands nine armies
the hoard belongs by right to the giants
context: Fafnismal stanzas 8-10 and 20-22. Fafnir tells Sigurd that Andvari's gold has destroyed everyone who has held it, and it will destroy him too. Every remaining chapter of the Volsunga Saga proves him right -- from Regin's plot to Brynhild's suicide to Sigurd's own murder in bed to the final destruction of the Nibelungs. The other three choices are plausible dragon-warnings from adjacent stories, but the specific Fafnismal warning is the curse-on-all-who-hold-it.  (Legend.)

question: Fafnir gave Sigurd a second warning as his eyes glazed over, this one not about the treasure but about the man who had sent the young hero out to the moor. That man was Sigurd's foster-father, the smith Regin, who had reforged his sword and shown him the plan. Sigurd would act on the warning within the hour. What did Fafnir warn him about Regin?
answer: his own brother will betray him for the gold
choices: his own brother will betray him for the gold
his old master has poisoned the sword-hilt
his foster-father is really a giant in disguise
his true father was killed by Regin long ago
context: Fafnismal stanzas 22 and 31; Volsunga Saga chapter 19. Fafnir tells Sigurd that Regin -- Fafnir's own brother -- means to kill him for the hoard. In the very next chapter Sigurd tastes the dragon's blood, understands the speech of birds, and hears two nuthatches confirm exactly the same warning; he then beheads Regin with Gram before Regin can strike first. This is the moment the young hero shifts from foster-son to independent man.  (Legend.)

question: Regin the smith comes over to the dragon Sigurd has just killed, drinks some of its blood and cuts one organ out of the beast. He gives it to the young hero to roast, then lies down to sleep. Which organ does Regin hand him?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal prose after stanza 31. Regin drinks the dragon's blood himself, cuts out Fafnir's heart, and tells Sigurd to cook it on a spit for him -- claiming he wants to eat it for the wisdom that comes with it. Then Regin lies down in the grass, exhausted, and falls asleep. In Norse dragon-lore the heart is the seat of the dragon's knowledge; the other organs carry no such magic.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd tends a spit on the moor of Gnitaheid, roasting meat from the dragon he has just killed. He pokes it to see if it is done, and the blood inside is boiling hot. The Volsunga Saga is exact about what gets scalded. What does Sigurd burn?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal prose after stanza 31. The scalded THUMB is a fixed detail of the story -- it is the thumb Sigurd tests with, and the thumb he then sticks in his mouth to cool it. The exact detail matters because the direct Celtic cousin of this story is Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Salmon of Knowledge, where Fionn burns his THUMB on the roasting salmon-skin and sucks it and gains all wisdom -- the same anatomical detail in a completely independent tradition.  (Legend.)

question: Without thinking, Sigurd sticks a scalded finger in his mouth to cool it, as anyone does after a burn, and the boiling blood of the dragon Fafnir is on it. The instant that blood touches his tongue, a new power comes over him. What does Sigurd suddenly discover he can do?
choices: grow to twice a man's height
call fire from an open hand
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal prose after stanza 31. Dragon-blood confers the language of birds -- one of the oldest Germanic story-shapes, appearing in folktale all across northern Europe. Sigurd hears the chirping in the trees above his head resolve into voices talking about him. This is the folkloric-magic center of the whole saga, and the pivot to everything that follows.  (Legend.)

question: Birds chatter in the branches above Sigurd's fire while Regin sleeps. The first bird looks down at the young man turning the dragon's flesh on the spit, and it says he would be a wiser lord if he did one thing with it, instead of handing it over. What does the bird tell him to do?
choices: throw the heart into the river
bury the heart in the hoard
context: Fafnismal stanza 32. The whole point of the dragon-heart in Norse dragon-lore is that whoever eats it gains its wisdom. Regin claimed the heart for himself and Sigurd is dutifully cooking it for his foster-father, but the birds see the danger: the wisdom is going to the wrong man. Their first counsel is the simple one -- eat it yourself.  (Legend.)

question: The birds over Sigurd's head turn from advice to warning. They are talking now about the man sleeping in the grass beside him, his foster-father, the smith who reforged his sword and taught him the plan that killed the dragon. What do the birds tell Sigurd that Regin is planning?
answer: to kill Sigurd for the treasure
choices: to kill Sigurd for the treasure
to lie to Sigurd about the sword
to marry Sigurd's mother by force
to sell Sigurd to the giants
context: Fafnismal stanzas 33-37; Volsunga Saga chapter 19. This is the piece of news that turns the whole saga. Regin has been a father-figure to Sigurd since childhood -- reforged Gram out of the shards of Sigmund's sword, sent him out to Gnitaheid, taught him the pit-plan. He is also the dragon's brother, and now that Fafnir is dead the whole cursed hoard passes by rights to Regin -- if Sigurd is out of the way. The dying Fafnir had already warned Sigurd of exactly this; the birds are the second warning, and the one Sigurd finally acts on.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd leaves the fire on the moor of Gnitaheid and walks over to his foster-father Regin, who lies asleep in the grass a few paces away. The birds overhead have just told him what the cunning smith means to do, and Sigurd does not wait for the sleeper to wake. What does Sigurd do to Regin?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal stanzas 39-40. Sigurd beheads Regin with a single stroke of Gram before Regin can wake up and strike first. The moment marks the young hero's shift from foster-son to independent man -- from taking orders from a tutor to acting on his own judgment. It is also the first killing Sigurd does without a tutor's plan, and the first killing that is unambiguously HIS choice.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd hears one more piece of news from the chattering birds. Someone lies asleep on a mountain called Hindarfjall, the birds tell him, ringed by a wall of flame, waiting for a hero brave enough to ride through the fire and wake her. What kind of woman is the sleeper on Hindarfjall?
context: Fafnismal stanzas 42-44. The sleeping figure is the Valkyrie who will be named Brynhild -- the birds send Sigurd toward her and the next act of the saga opens with him riding through the ring of fire. Valkyries in Norse myth are the choosers of the slain who serve Odin. A Norn is one of the three fates at the well of Urd. Giantesses and elf-queens are separate categories. The birds specifically name a Valkyrie.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd hears small birds chattering in the branches above his fire about Regin's plot, and the old books try to say exactly what they are. The Poetic Edda has the word igda for them, which translators have never settled. The Volsunga Saga's prose names one small woodland bird that creeps head-down along tree trunks. What kind of bird does the saga name?
context: Fafnismal stanzas 32-38; Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Bellows and Larrington translations. The Old Norse word igda in Fafnismal is one of the puzzles of the Poetic Edda -- Henry Adams Bellows translated it as nuthatches, Carolyne Larrington as tits, and some scholars simply as chattering birds. The Volsunga Saga's prose paraphrase of the scene commits to nuthatches, the small blue-and-buff woodland bird famous for creeping down tree-trunks head-first. Wrens, finches, and thrushes are all real woodland birds of northern Europe, but they are not the ones named in Sigurd's dragon-slaying scene.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd stands on Gnitaheid with the dragon dead and his treacherous foster-father dead beside it. The skalds, the Norse poets, give him a battle-name from that day, and it stays with him through centuries of Germanic legend. Which byname has he earned by the dragon's death?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal title tradition. Fafnisbani means Fafnir's-Bane, slayer of Fafnir -- the standard skaldic epithet for Sigurd from this day on. Fenrisbani (Fenrir's-Bane) is a possible kenning for Vidar, who kills Fenrir at Ragnarok, not for Sigurd. Volsungr just means son of the Volsung line -- his family name, not his earned byname. Gramgjafi (giver of Gram) is not a standard epithet. Fafnisbani is the specific dragon-slaying byname.  (Legend.)

question: A Syrian shepherd's son walks out of a monastery near Antioch in the fifth century, asked to leave by monks who have grown afraid of him. He refuses food for days and wears a rough rope until it cuts his skin. What is his name?
context: Simeon (c. 390-459 CE) was born in Sis in Cilicia in northern Syria, the son of a shepherd. His fellow monks near Antioch found his austerities beyond bearing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: Simeon shuts himself in a stone hut in the Syrian wilderness to live alone in prayer, but crowds of pilgrims find him anyway and press in for blessings and cures. So he does something no Christian ascetic has ever tried before and moves his home right off the ground. Where does he move it to?
answer: The top of a stone pillar
choices: The top of a stone pillar
A cave in the cliff face
The dead branches of a huge tree
A raft moored in the middle of a lake
context: The Greek word for pillar is 'stylos', from which comes 'stylite'. Simeon is the first Christian stylite. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: Pilgrims crowd the foot of Simeon's high platform near Antioch to hear him preach. He has gone up alone to pray under the open sky, and he refuses to come down. How does he get his food?
answer: Bread and water are hauled up in a basket on a rope
choices: Bread and water are hauled up in a basket on a rope
A servant climbs up each morning with a hot meal
He grows herbs in a wooden trough beside him
He is fed by ravens sent by an angel
context: Simeon's disciples tied bread and water to a rope and his followers hauled the basket up to the platform. From the top he preached twice a day to the crowd below. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: Simeon climbs to his last perch in the Syrian countryside, more than fifty feet above the ground, and he will never come down from it. The platform on top measures about one square metre, with a low balustrade around the edge. Given that space, how does he sleep at night?
choices: Curled tight in a hollow bowl
In a hammock strung across the pillar
Wrapped to the base of a wooden cross
context: There was not enough room on the platform to lie down. He slept standing, tied to a post fixed to the pillar so he would not fall while asleep. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: Simeon preaches to pilgrims from a little platform outside Antioch, where he has gone to live apart from the world in prayer. Villagers send food up to him, and he refuses to come down. He is still up there when he dies in 459. About how many years does tradition say he spends up there?
context: The traditional figure from Theodoret and later sources is thirty-seven years on the pillar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: A nearby bishop visits Simeon in person, among the crowds of pilgrims from across the empire, and writes the life story of the saint while the man is still alive up on his platform. That is rare for a saint's Life, since most are written long after the funeral. Who is this bishop?
context: Theodoret devoted a chapter of his 'Religious History' to Simeon while the ascetic was still on the pillar. He had visited him in person. The other choices are all real Greek-Christian bishops of the 4th-5th centuries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: The Byzantine emperor Zeno orders an enormous cross-shaped pilgrimage church built around the shrunken stump of Simeon's pillar, after the saint dies on top of it in 459. Four huge basilicas radiate from a central octagon. For centuries the church ranks among the largest in the Christian world. What is that church called?
context: 'Qalat Simaan' means 'the fortress of Simeon' in Arabic. Built by Zeno in the 470s-490s around the shrunken stump of Simeon's pillar in northern Syria, it was for centuries one of the largest churches in Christendom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: Roman soldiers seized a passer-by on the way out of Jerusalem and forced him to shoulder the crossbeam, because Jesus could no longer carry it alone. Mark named the man in one phrase. Who was pulled from the crowd?
context: Mark 15:21 KJV: 'they compel one Simon a Cyrenian, who passed by, coming out of the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to bear his cross.' Joseph of Arimathea is the rich man who later gives Jesus his tomb (Matthew 27:57). Nicodemus is the Pharisee who visits Jesus by night (John 3:1). Cleopas is one of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:18). All four are real named figures from the Passion week -- only one gets grabbed to carry the cross.

question: Mark alone among the gospel writers stopped his account of the road to the cross to name the two sons of the man forced to carry it, as if his first Roman readers would recognise them. One was Alexander. What was the other son's name?
context: Mark 15:21 KJV: 'the father of Alexander and Rufus.' Paul greets a 'Rufus, chosen in the Lord' in Romans 16:13, and church tradition has long guessed it is the same Rufus. Titus was a Greek convert Paul mentored; Silas was Paul's travelling companion after Barnabas; Barnabas was Paul's first missionary partner, and 'son of encouragement' in Acts 4:36. All four are real early-church names -- only one is the son of the man from Cyrene.

question: Jesus reached a low bare hill outside the walls of Jerusalem, a rise that people said was shaped like a skull. Mark gave the place its Aramaic name in his gospel. What was that name?
context: Mark 15:22 KJV: 'And they bring him unto the place Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, The place of a skull.' The Latin for skull is 'calvaria' -- the source of the English name Calvary. Gethsemane is the olive grove where Jesus was arrested (Mark 14:32). Gabbatha is the pavement where Pilate sat to judge (John 19:13). Gehenna is a valley south of Jerusalem used as a byword for hell. All four sound alike, only one is the skull-place.

question: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, had a Latin sentence nailed to the cross above Jesus at his crucifixion. Crucifixes in churches all across Europe still carry the initials of that sentence on a small plaque above the carved figure's head. What are those letters?
context: The Latin sentence was 'Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum' -- 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.' Latin uses I where English uses J, so IESUS begins with I. IHS is a different Christian monogram, from the Greek spelling of Jesus (I-H-S = IHSOUS). XPS is another Greek Christogram, from CHRIST (X-P from Greek chi-rho). SPQR is the Roman civic motto, Senatus Populusque Romanus. All four are real historic acronyms -- only one is the cross-sign.

question: Matthew and Mark each wrote down the same words of Jesus from the cross, and each kept them in the original Aramaic. Of the seven sayings scattered across the four gospels, with no single gospel holding all seven, this was the only one found in two books. Which saying did Matthew and Mark share?
answer: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
choices: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Into thy hands I commend my spirit
context: Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 KJV: 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?' (Matthew) / 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?' (Mark). It is the opening line of Psalm 22 -- an entire psalm the crucified man is quoting by its first words, the ancient way of naming a text. 'It is finished' is John 19:30; 'Father, forgive them' is Luke 23:34; 'Into thy hands I commend my spirit' is Luke 23:46. All real cross-sayings, only one is preserved in Aramaic and shared by two evangelists.

question: Jesus spoke his last saying from the cross in the Gospel of John, the three English words 'It is finished.' In John's Greek it was a single word, a form of the verb 'to finish' or 'to fulfil'. Merchants used it to mean 'paid in full'. What was that one word?
context: John 19:30 in Greek: 'tetelestai'. Papyrus tax receipts from the same century use the word to mean 'paid off, account closed'. Maranatha is Aramaic 'Our Lord, come' (1 Corinthians 16:22). Kyrios is Greek for 'Lord'. Sabaoth is Hebrew 'armies/hosts', as in the Sanctus. All four are famous preserved-in-original-language words from scripture -- only one is the last word from the cross.

question: Jesus cried out from the cross in Matthew's gospel, 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?' He did not invent that cry in the moment of dying. It was the opening line, quoted almost word for word, of a much older Hebrew poem from the Jewish scriptures, which Christians call the Old Testament. Which text was he quoting?
context: Psalm 22:1 KJV: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' In ancient Jewish practice, quoting the opening of a text was a way of pointing to the whole -- Psalm 22 goes on to describe hands and feet pierced and garments divided by lot, which is why the gospels weave the psalm's language through the crucifixion scene. Psalm 23 is 'The Lord is my shepherd'; Psalm 51 is David's confession after Bathsheba; Psalm 137 is 'By the rivers of Babylon'.

question: A Roman officer stood close to the cross watching how Jesus died, commanding the execution detail and no follower of his. Then, in the Gospel of Mark, the officer said: 'Truly this man was the Son of God.' Mark gave the man's rank. What was it?
context: Mark 15:39 KJV. A centurion commanded roughly a hundred men -- the standard Roman infantry officer, and the man who would have run this kind of detail. The gospels never name him, but medieval Christian tradition later called him Longinus (apparently from Greek longche, 'spear', because of a separate legend that he was the soldier who pierced Jesus's side in John 19:34). A tribune outranked him; a legate commanded a whole legion; a decurion commanded cavalry. Only the centurion belongs at this cross.

question: The gospel writers listed the twelve apostles, and each list ended on the same name: Judas Iscariot, the traitor. Just before him stood a second Simon, not Simon Peter but a man with a one-word tag. Which Simon came second from the end?
context: Matthew 10:4, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15, and Acts 1:13 all name him Simon the Zealot (Greek Zelotes, from the Aramaic qanai, 'zealous'). Simon Magus is the sorcerer of Acts 8; Simon of Cyrene was the man pressed into carrying Jesus's cross; 'Simon Bar-Jonah' is Peter's given name (Jesus renames him Cephas / Peter, 'the Rock').

question: Matthew and Mark gave one of the twelve apostles a second name, so that no one would mix him up with the traitor. He was Judas son of James. In Latin the second name became 'Jude', the form the Western church kept. What was the second name?
context: Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18 list him as Thaddaeus (also Lebbaeus in some manuscripts); later Latin usage flattens Thaddaeus to Jude (as in Saint Jude). Barnabas was Paul's traveling companion; Barabbas was the criminal released at Passover; Bartimaeus was the blind beggar Jesus healed at Jericho.

question: Jesus chose a man named Simon as one of his twelve disciples, and the tag on the man was 'Zealot'. It matched a real militant Jewish party of Simon's own day, whose whole plan was armed revolt against the power then ruling the Holy Land. Who were the Zealots trying to drive out of Judea?
context: The Zealots were a militant Jewish party who wanted armed rebellion against Roman rule; Josephus (Jewish War) tracks them through the great revolt of AD 66-70 that ended with the destruction of the Temple. Whether Simon actually belonged to the party or was just personally zealous, the tag placed a former militant among former fishermen. The Seleucids were the earlier Greek overlords beaten back by the Maccabees; the Hasmonean priest-kings ruled between Seleucids and Rome; Herod's dynasty were Roman client-kings, not the occupying power itself.

question: Eusebius, the ancient historian, reported a tale he said came out of a royal archive. A local king had heard of Jesus's healings and written him a letter, and had been promised that a disciple would come after Jesus's death to cure him of his disease. Which king was the disciple sent to?
context: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica 1.13, preserves the correspondence between Jesus and King Abgar V of Edessa (a small kingdom in what is now southeastern Turkey); Thaddaeus (called Addai in Syriac tradition) is sent after the resurrection and heals him. Herod Agrippa I ruled in Judea in the same century; Antiochus IV of Commagene was a Roman client-king on the Euphrates; Tigranes ruled Armenia -- all real small-kingdom rulers of the era, none tied to the Abgar legend.

question: In Western medieval legend, the apostles Simon and Jude went out as missionaries together after the crucifixion and preached far outside the Roman Empire. The legend has them die on the same day in one country, put to death for their preaching by the local pagan priests. In which country does the legend set their deaths?
context: The 'Passion of Simon and Jude', a Western medieval Passion narrative, sends them together into Persia (some sources say Suanir) where both are killed. Britain is traditionally linked to Joseph of Arimathea; Ethiopia to Matthew (Matthew the Evangelist's traditional field); Spain to James the Greater, whose shrine is at Santiago de Compostela.  (Legend.)

question: Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus, and the other apostle named Judas, the one called Jude, paid for it. For centuries almost no one prayed to Jude at all, because his name sat too close to the traitor's and people worried they were addressing the wrong Judas. Tradition then turned that neglect into a speciality of its own. What is Saint Jude now the patron of?
context: Because 'Jude' (Judas son of James) was so easily confused with Judas Iscariot the betrayer, few Christians for centuries invoked him -- so tradition made him especially glad to help anyone who did. He became the patron of lost causes. Safe sea travel is Christopher (or Nicholas); students traditionally invoke Joseph of Cupertino or Thomas Aquinas; finding a spouse is Anthony of Padua (also lost objects).

question: Moses led the Hebrews for three months across the wilderness after their escape from Egypt, and they pitched camp before a great mountain in the desert. He would climb it alone to receive the law. What was the mountain's name?
context: Exodus 19:1-2 KJV. Ararat is where Noah's ark landed, Carmel is where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal, and Nebo is where Moses would later die looking into Canaan -- all real mountains in the Bible, but the giving of the Law was at Sinai.

question: In the Book of Exodus, the Hebrews stood in their camp on the third morning and watched the mountain quake, wrapped in a thick dark cloud shot through with thunders and lightnings. Above all the crashing noise one sound grew louder and louder, until Moses spoke and God answered him. What was that sound?
answer: The voice of a trumpet exceeding loud
choices: The voice of a trumpet exceeding loud
The roaring of a great fire
The crashing of stone upon stone
context: Exodus 19:16, 19 KJV: 'and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud ... And when the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice.'

question: God spoke ten commandments to Moses in the book of Exodus, after Moses climbed alone into a cloud of thunder on the mountain. They were for the people to live by, and Moses came back down carrying two stone tablets. Which of the ten came first?
answer: 'Thou shalt have no other gods before me.'
choices: 'Thou shalt have no other gods before me.'
'Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.'
context: Exodus 20:3 KJV. The other three commandments are all real and part of the same Ten (Exodus 20:8, 12, 13), but the command against other gods stands at the head of the list.

question: Moses went up the mountain alone into the cloud of thunder, and Exodus has him stay at the top with God without bread or water. When he finally came down he was carrying two stone tablets with the ten commandments written on them. How long was Moses up there before he came down?
context: Exodus 34:28 KJV. The same 'forty days' shape returns with Noah's flood, Elijah's flight to Horeb, and Jesus in the wilderness. Three days and nights is Jonah in the fish; seven days is the flood-wait to send out the raven.

question: God handed Moses two tables of stone at the end of his long stay on the mountain, hidden in cloud and fire, and the Ten Commandments were on them. The book of Exodus says no human craftsman had carved that writing. How had the words come to be on the stone?
answer: Written with the finger of God
choices: Written with the finger of God
Burned in by lightning from heaven
Etched by the tip of a serpent's tooth
Cut by an angel with a diamond stylus
context: Exodus 31:18 KJV: 'two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God.' The other options fit the awe of the scene but the specific phrase in the text is the finger of God itself.

question: The Hebrews in the camp below grew tired of waiting for Moses to come down from the mountain, and they pressed his brother Aaron, the high priest, to make them gods to go before them into the wilderness. Aaron agreed and prepared to cast an idol in the shape of a calf. What did he ask the people to bring him for the metal?
answer: The golden earrings out of their ears
choices: The golden earrings out of their ears
The bronze mirrors of their women
The silver chains from their firstborn sons
The iron rings from their tent poles
context: Exodus 32:2-4 KJV. Aaron collects the earrings, melts them, and shapes a molten calf; the bronze mirrors of the women are a real biblical donation but for the tabernacle laver later (Exodus 38:8), not the calf.

question: Moses came down the mountain carrying the two stone tables of the law, and as he neared the Hebrew camp he saw the calf his brother Aaron had cast, with the people dancing before it. His anger burned hot at the sight. What did he do to the tablets at the foot of the mountain?
answer: Cast them out of his hands and broke them
choices: Cast them out of his hands and broke them
Buried them beneath a heap of stones
Hurled them into the fire of the calf
Carried them back up to the mountaintop
context: Exodus 32:19 KJV: 'and he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount.' God will later command Moses to hew two new tables 'like unto the first' (Exodus 34:1) and rewrite them.

question: Moses took the golden calf the Israelites had made while he was gone, burned it in the fire and ground the softened metal to a fine powder. His fury did not end with the stone tablets. He scattered the powder on the water of the camp. What did he then make the children of Israel do with that water?
choices: Pour it over the altar as an offering
Carry it to the far side of the camp
context: Exodus 32:20 KJV: 'and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it.' A punishment few readers remember -- the idol they had bowed to went down their own throats.

question: Homer paused over Sisyphus, king of Corinth, in Book 6 of his Iliad, and gave him a flat character reference. He said Sisyphus was this one thing above all other mortals, and every episode of the story bears it out. What did Homer call him?
context: Homer, Iliad 6.153. Swift-footed is Achilles's epithet; strongest is Heracles's; fairest suits a Ganymede or a Paris. Sisyphus's specific gift is cunning -- and every episode in his story (tricking Zeus, tricking Death, tricking Persephone) is a demonstration of it.  (Legend.)

question: Sisyphus, king of Corinth, went and told the secret of one of Zeus's love affairs. Zeus was furious that a mere mortal had dared inform on him, and he sent one god in person to fetch the king to the underworld in chains. This god's whole office was fetching mortals below. Which god did Zeus send?
context: Thanatos is 'Death' personified in Greek myth -- his job is to fetch mortals down to Hades. Hermes was the guide of souls once they were already in transit. Hypnos is 'Sleep', Thanatos's brother, a different figure. Charon is the ferryman on the river Styx, not a god who came to fetch anyone.  (Legend.)

question: Death came to Corinth with his chains to fetch King Sisyphus, and the king asked a small favour first: would the god demonstrate how they worked? Death put them on to show him, and Sisyphus locked them. Where did the king then stash the bound god of death?
context: The myth is remembered for the sheer domesticity of it -- Death himself, chained up in an ordinary Corinthian cupboard. It is that ridiculous image (a household piece of furniture holding the god of death) that made the story famous.  (Legend.)

question: Sisyphus kept Death locked away in Corinth, and no mortal anywhere could die. The sick lay dying forever and the mortally wounded could not pass on. The crisis grew until one Olympian god came storming down to Corinth in a fury, broke the bound god out and gave the king up. Which Olympian marched down and released Death?
context: Ares is the god of war -- and with no soldier dying in his battles any more, his whole business had been ruined. Apollo is the god of prophecy and archery; Hephaestus the smith; Dionysus the god of wine. None of them had a personal grievance, but Ares had every reason.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus sent for Sisyphus one last time, after the king of Corinth had talked his way back up to the living and reached a very old age. Zeus did not send Death again. He sent a different Olympian, one of the twelve, to bring the old king down by force. Which god finally brought Sisyphus in?
context: Hermes is 'psychopompos' -- the guide of the dead down into Hades, part of his broader role as the messenger of the gods. It took him personally, not Thanatos, to bring the old trickster in at last. Poseidon is lord of the sea; Apollo is Hermes's older half-brother; Ares had already been down once to release Death.  (Legend.)

question: Sisyphus shoved a great boulder up a hill in the underworld, only to see it turn at the crest and roll back down again. In Book 11 of the Odyssey, Homer gave the stone a single unforgettable adjective as it rolled back to the plain. What did Homer call the boulder?
context: Homer, Odyssey 11.593-600: 'planting his feet, straining hard, with hands and feet he pressed the huge stone toward the crest; but just as he was about to heave it over the top, the boulder's weight would turn it back, and down again to the plain the shameless thing would roll.' The stone carries the moral weight of Sisyphus's tricks -- Homer calls it shameless, as if the rock itself were in on the punishment.  (Legend.)

question: Albert Camus, the French writer, took Sisyphus's endless task as an image of the human condition in a famous essay of 1942. He closed 'The Myth of Sisyphus' on a single startling sentence about how to see the man on the hill. What was that last line?
choices: the stone is heavier than any man knows
the gods forget nothing and forgive nothing
the hill will one day end and the stone will rest
context: Camus, 'Le Mythe de Sisyphe' (1942). Camus argues that the struggle itself, if faced honestly, fills a human heart -- and so we should picture Sisyphus content at the bottom of the hill, walking back down to his stone. The other three lines are invented.

question: A god of the Vanir comes to live in Asgard after the war between the gods. He rules harvest, sunshine and good weather, and the farmers of Sweden and Norway pray to him for a peaceful year and a good crop. He owns a golden boar and a magic ship. What is his name?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 24: Freyr is the god of harvest, sunshine and peaceful weather, and the most-worshipped of the Vanir in Viking-age Sweden. Njord is Freyr's father, the sea-god who governs the winds and the tides. Tyr is the one-handed war-god. Bragi is the god of skaldic poetry. Freyr's father Njord came to Asgard as a hostage after the Aesir-Vanir war and Freyr came with him.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson, the 13th-century Icelander, calls one vessel 'the best of all ships and the most skillfully made.' It belongs to Freyr, the Norse god of harvest and sunshine, and the dwarves crafted it for him as a gift. What is the name of Freyr's ship?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43: Skidbladnir is Freyr's ship, praised by Snorri as 'the best of ships'. Naglfar is the dark counterpart -- the ship of dead men's nails that will carry the giants to Ragnarok. Ringhorn is the funeral ship of Baldr, launched with his body on it. Sessrumnir is Freyja's great hall in Folkvangr, whose name ('seat-roomer') is also listed in the Norse ship-catalogues among the named vessels of the gods.  (Legend.)

question: Dwarf smiths in Svartalfheim, the underground realm of the dwarves, have forged Freyr's ship, and Snorri Sturluson names them. They are the same family who, on an earlier errand from Loki, spun real gold thread to replace the hair of the goddess Sif after he cut it off her head. Which dwarf-family forged the ship?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 35 and 43: the Sons of Ivaldi are the three dwarf-brothers who made three treasures in one workshop session -- Sif's golden hair, Freyr's ship, and Odin's spear Gungnir. Brokkr and Sindri are the OTHER dwarf-smiths who make Mjolnir, Draupnir, and Gullinbursti in the second wager. Fjalar and Galar are the dwarves who murder Kvasir. Nordri and Sudri are two of the four sky-holding dwarves.  (Legend.)

question: The harvest god Freyr can seat one particular company on the decks of his ship, Snorri Sturluson says, in full war-gear with their weapons at their sides. The dwarves made it for him as a gift. Who is the ship large enough to carry?
answer: all the gods of Asgard together
choices: all the gods of Asgard together
all the einherjar of Valhalla in full number
all the giants of Jotunheim in one host
all the dwarves of Svartalfheim in full number
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43: Skidbladnir is big enough to carry all the Aesir at once, in full war-gear with their weapons. Valhalla's einherjar (Odin's dead heroes) number in the hundreds of thousands and no ship in the nine worlds carries them. There is no Norse story of a giant-army or a full dwarf-host sailing in Skidbladnir. The wonder of Skidbladnir is that it fits every god in Asgard AND folds into a pocket afterwards.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr steps ashore at the end of a voyage with his great ship behind him. It has one property no other ship in the Norse stories has, a property that lets him carry the whole vessel around with him even when he is not sailing. Once the voyage is over, what can Freyr do with the ship?
answer: fold it up like a cloth and put it in a pouch
choices: fold it up like a cloth and put it in a pouch
shrink it down to the size of a walnut and swallow it
leave it to sail itself home to Asgard
turn it into a wooden staff that never breaks
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43 and Skaldskaparmal 35: because it is 'assembled from thin pieces of wood' (which is what the name Skidbladnir means), the ship can be folded flat like a cloth and slipped into a pouch small enough to carry in a pocket. Mjolnir is the item that shrinks small enough to fit inside a shirt, not Skidbladnir. The other two options are inventions.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr raises the sail of his ship with no oars aboard and not one rower at the benches. A marvel comes in that very instant, one that saves Freyr any need to row. What happens the moment the sail is raised?
answer: a fair wind blows straight to Freyr's destination
choices: a fair wind blows straight to Freyr's destination
the sun rises to guide it by day and stars by night
the sea rises beneath the hull and carries it forward
the ship moves faster than any horse in Asgard
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43: as soon as the sail is raised Skidbladnir catches a fair wind blowing straight to wherever Freyr wants to go. There is no need to row, and the ship cannot be becalmed. This is the property that makes Skidbladnir most enviable to seafaring Norse audiences -- a wind on demand.  (Legend.)

question: The people of the fire-giant Surt will launch a ship of their own at the end of the world, a ship held by no god and growing steadily larger year by year. The Poetic Edda's Grimnismal sets it in one stanza with Freyr's ship, as the dark opposite of the best vessel ever made. What is the doom-ship of the giants built from?
answer: the untrimmed nails of the dead
choices: the untrimmed nails of the dead
the timbers of Yggdrasil the world-tree
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43 and 51 and Poetic Edda, Voluspa 50: the doom-ship is Naglfar, built from the untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead. Snorri says that is why the old Norse custom was to trim a corpse's nails before burial -- so as not to hand any more wood to the ship that will bring the giants to Ragnarok. In the Grimnismal stanza the two ships stand together: 'Skidbladnir the best of ships is built for shining Freyr; but of ships Naglfar is the greatest, which Muspell's people own.'  (Legend.)

question: Odin the All-Father rode a great grey horse down into the land of the dead. Snorri says this horse was stranger than any horse ever born, because of one feature of its body. What did Odin's horse have that no other horse had?
context: Gylfaginning 15: Snorri calls Odin's grey stallion the best of all horses, and says he has eight legs. Wings on horses belong to Greek myth (Pegasus). A single horn belongs to the medieval unicorn tradition. A mane of fire is a modern invention.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson praised one horse above all others in his Prose Edda, the 13th-century Icelandic book of Norse myth. It was a grey stallion, faster than any other steed, and its rider was Odin, the one-eyed chief of the gods. What was the horse's name?
context: Gylfaginning 15: the horse is Sleipnir. Grani is the horse of the hero Sigurd (and, in the Volsunga saga, said to come from Sleipnir's own line). Gullfaxi is the golden-maned stallion Thor takes from the giant Hrungnir. Hrimfaxi is the horse of Night, whose bit-foam becomes the morning dew.  (Legend.)

question: A god of Asgard shape-shifted for a night into a beautiful mare, to lure a builder's great stallion away from his master. The foal of that night became the fastest steed in all the nine worlds, and Odin's own mount. His father was the stallion. Which Norse god was the foal's mother?
context: Gylfaginning 42: Loki turned himself into a mare during the affair of the Master Builder of Asgard, and later gave birth to Sleipnir. Odin becomes Sleipnir's rider, not his parent. Heimdall was born of nine mothers (waves of the sea). Freyr owns Skidbladnir and the boar Gullinbursti but is not linked to this birth.  (Legend.)

question: A giant craftsman came to build the rampart of the gods in one winter, and he insisted on using his own stallion to haul the stones. Snorri says the horse hauled twice as much stone as his master, and the wall was nearly finished on time until a mare lured him off into the woods. What was the stone-hauling stallion's name?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder's stallion is Svadilfari, and Snorri says the horse hauled twice as much stone as the builder himself. Grani is Sigurd's horse. Blodughofi (Bloody-Hoof) belongs to Freyr. Falhofnir is one of the horses of the Aesir listed in Grimnismal.  (Legend.)

question: The god Hermod rode nine nights down dark valleys on Odin's borrowed horse, after Baldr the Shining was killed, to beg the queen of the dead for Baldr's return. At last he reached the iron gate of Hel's hall. What did the horse do at the gate?
choices: kicked it down with his hooves
refused to go a step further
context: Gylfaginning 49: Hermod rode Sleipnir nine nights down through dark valleys to Hel, and at the gate Sleipnir leapt so hard and high that he came nowhere near it -- clearing it in a single bound. Kicking down Hel's gate, passing through as mist, and refusing to go further are not part of the story.  (Legend.)

question: The valkyrie Sigrdrifa listed the great places where magic runes had been cut, in the Poetic Edda poem Sigrdrifumal. They were cut on the tongue of Bragi, on the paw of a bear, on the straps of a sledge, and on one particular part of Odin's horse. On what part of the horse did she say they were cut?
context: Sigrdrifumal 15 (Poetic Edda): runes were carved on Sleipnir's teeth, on the bear's paw, on Bragi's tongue, on the wolf's claws, on the eagle's beak, and on the sledge's strap-bands, so that magic would be borne into the world in all these places.  (Legend.)

question: A carver on Gotland, an island in the Baltic, cut a picture-stone in the eighth century, and every surviving manuscript of the Eddas came later. In its upper panel a rider reached a hall and a woman greeted him, holding up a drinking horn. That horse is the oldest picture of Odin's mount to survive. Which Gotland stone was it?
context: The Tjangvide picture-stone (Gotland, c. 700-800 CE) is read as showing Odin arriving at Valhalla on Sleipnir -- the earliest surviving image of the eight-legged horse. Ramsund and Hylestad carry the Sigurd-and-Fafnir cycle. Altuna carries Thor fishing for Jormungand.

question: The young king Solomon, son of David, went up to the high place at Gibeon to offer a sacrifice. That night God came to him in a dream and made him a startling offer: 'Ask what I shall give thee.' Instead of long life or riches, what one thing did Solomon ask for?
context: KJV 1 Kings 3:9: 'Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad.' The reply pleased God, who then granted wisdom, and long life and riches on top.

question: Two women came before King Solomon fighting over one living baby. Each swore she was the mother; the other's own child had died in the night. To settle the case, Solomon called out for one particular object to be brought in. What did he order brought in?
context: KJV 1 Kings 3:24-25: 'And the king said, Bring me a sword. And they brought a sword before the king. And the king said, Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.' Scales and elders and seals were the ordinary tools of justice, but Solomon needed something sharper.

question: King Solomon ordered his soldier to cut a newborn baby in two and give half to each woman who claimed him, to reveal the true mother. One of the two women broke down at once and cried out to the king. What exactly did she cry out?
answer: O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it
choices: O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it
O my lord, take him and raise him as thine own son
O my lord, take my life instead of the child's
O my lord, spare us and send the other away
context: KJV 1 Kings 3:26: 'Then spake the woman whose the living child was unto the king ... and she said, O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it.' Solomon then reversed the order and gave the child back to her, knowing she was the true mother.

question: King Solomon began the great Temple in Jerusalem in the fourth year of his reign, on the sacred summit of Mount Moriah. The project used thousands of stonecutters, yet one common sound of a building site was never heard there. Which line describes that silence?
answer: no iron tool struck the stone
choices: no iron tool struck the stone
no cry of a foreign labourer
no chariot wheel on the stones
no trumpet of the morning watch
context: KJV 1 Kings 6:7: 'neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.' The stones were dressed at the quarry and lifted into place already finished, so the site itself was silent.

question: Solomon set up two enormous pillars of cast bronze at the porch of his Temple in Jerusalem, one on the right hand and one on the left as a worshipper walked in. He gave each its own proper name: the right-hand name means 'he shall establish' and the left-hand name 'in him is strength.' What names did Solomon give the two pillars?
context: KJV 1 Kings 7:21: 'And he set up the right pillar, and called the name thereof Jachin: and he set up the left pillar, and called the name thereof Boaz.' Jachin means 'he shall establish'; Boaz means 'in him is strength.' Urim and Thummim were the two lots on the high priest's breastplate; Nadab and Abihu were the sons of Aaron; Zadok and Abiathar were the two high priests in David's court.

question: Solomon built the great First Temple in Jerusalem with a huge round basin of cast bronze in its courtyard, the one the Bible calls 'the molten sea.' The priests washed in its water. Ten cubits from brim to brim and five cubits high, it was far too large and heavy to rest flat on the pavement. What supported it off the ground?
choices: four bronze lions crouching at the corners
a single bronze pillar rising from the pavement
the shoulders of two carved bronze cherubim
context: KJV 1 Kings 7:25: 'It stood upon twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east.' The molten sea held water for the priests' washing.

question: The Queen of Sheba, ruler of a wealthy trading kingdom in Arabia, travelled to Jerusalem to test the wisdom of King Solomon in person. She saw his palace, the food on his table, the stair to the house of God, the seating of his servants and his cupbearers in their livery. According to 1 Kings 10 in the King James Bible, what happened to her at that whole sight?
answer: there was no more spirit in her
choices: there was no more spirit in her
she fell prostrate on the marble floor
she tore her royal garment in wonder
she wept and offered him her crown
context: KJV 1 Kings 10:4-5. The phrase captures a breath-taken astonishment -- the queen goes silent. Then she finds her words again.

question: Breathless at the sight of Solomon's court, the Queen of Sheba found her voice again and spoke her most famous line. Back home she had heard great things about his wisdom and his riches, and now she had seen them for herself. What did she say about the report she had heard?
answer: the half was not told me
choices: the half was not told me
not one word of it was true
the king's fame is greater than his house
such wisdom belongs only to the LORD
context: KJV 1 Kings 10:7: 'Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard.'

question: In 1 Kings 11, the foreign women of Solomon's household turned his heart from the God of Israel in his old age, and he raised shrines in Jerusalem to Milcom of the Ammonites and Ashtoreth of the Sidonians. How many wives and how many concubines does the King James Bible give him?
context: KJV 1 Kings 11:3: 'And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart.' He built shrines to Ashtoreth of the Sidonians and Milcom of the Ammonites in his old age -- the moral of the arc for the biblical author.

question: King Solomon set a tall lampstand of pure hammered gold in the holy place of his Temple in Jerusalem, before the inner sanctuary. Its central shaft carried six curved arms, three on each side, and held seven oil lamps in all. What was that lampstand called?
context: KJV Exodus 25:31-32: 'And thou shalt make a candlestick of pure gold ... six branches shall come out of the sides of it; three branches of the candlestick out of the one side, and three branches of the candlestick out of the other side.' The whole was to be beaten from one talent of pure gold (Ex 25:39). A thurible is a censer, a labarum was Constantine's battle standard, a monstrance is a vessel for the consecrated host.

question: King Solomon's priests laid twelve loaves on a golden table in the Temple, in two rows of six, one loaf for each of the twelve tribes of Israel. They replaced them fresh every sabbath, kept always before God. What was this weekly offering called?
context: KJV Leviticus 24:5-6: 'thou shalt take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes ... thou shalt set them in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the LORD.' The paschal lamb was the Passover meat; a wave offering was a portion lifted and waved; a drink offering was poured wine.

question: The priests came to the golden table in the Temple on the sabbath, lifted off the twelve old loaves and set out fresh ones, one loaf for each tribe. The bread had stood before God all week. What became of the loaves they took away?
answer: Aaron's sons ate them in the holy place
choices: Aaron's sons ate them in the holy place
they were burned whole on the bronze altar
they were buried outside the camp
they were sent home to the twelve tribes
context: KJV Leviticus 24:9: 'it shall be Aaron's and his sons; and they shall eat it in the holy place: for it is most holy unto him of the offerings of the LORD made by fire by a perpetual statute.' The bread was too holy to burn or bury and was reserved for the priesthood alone.

question: Moses crafted a great golden lampstand for the wilderness Tabernacle after Sinai, with seven branches to hold seven lamps. Each of the six side-branches carried cups shaped like the blossoms of one flowering tree, with a knop, a small round bud, and a flower between them. Which tree's blossom did those cups copy?
context: KJV Exodus 25:33: 'Three bowls made like unto almonds, with a knop and a flower in one branch; and three bowls made like almonds in the other branch, with a knop and a flower.' Almond blossoms are the first to open each spring in the hills of Judea. Olive and fig and cedar are all sacred trees in the Old Testament but the menorah's cups copy the almond.

question: Solomon filled the windowless inner sanctuary of his Temple in Jerusalem, the Holy of Holies where the Ark of the Covenant was kept, with two giant winged figures called cherubim. Each stood about ten cubits tall, roughly fifteen feet, with wingtips wide enough to touch the two side walls of the room. From what kind of wood were they carved?
context: KJV 1 Kings 6:23: 'And within the oracle he made two cherubims of olive tree, each ten cubits high.' 1 Kings 6:27 has their wings touching the walls on either side. The ark itself and the wilderness tabernacle furniture were of acacia (shittim) wood; the Temple's paneling and roof were cedar; cypress boards its floors.

question: Solomon added extra golden lampstands along the front of the inner shrine of his Temple, the shrine that housed the Ark of the Covenant, beyond the single seven-lamped lampstand that Moses had first crafted for the wilderness Tabernacle. First Kings records exactly how they stood before the shrine's doorway. How were they arranged?
answer: five on the right side and five on the left
choices: five on the right side and five on the left
seven on the right side and seven on the left
three on the right side and three on the left
twelve in a single row across the front
context: KJV 1 Kings 7:49: 'And the candlesticks of pure gold, five on the right side, and five on the left, before the oracle.' Beyond the single seven-lamped menorah of Moses's pattern, Solomon added ten more lampstands framing the entrance to the Holy of Holies. Seven is the menorah's own lamp-count; twelve matches the tribes and the showbread loaves; three matches the branches per side of the menorah -- all near-misses, but 1 Kings names five and five.

question: The priests carried the ark of the covenant into the inner sanctuary of King Solomon's new Temple and set it down for good. It was the wooden, gold-plated chest the Israelites had carried through the wilderness since the time of Moses. When the priests opened it in Solomon's day, what did they find inside?
answer: the two tables of stone from Horeb
choices: the two tables of stone from Horeb
the golden pot of manna from the wilderness
the rod of Aaron that had budded
the brazen serpent of Moses on its pole
context: KJV 1 Kings 8:9: 'There was nothing in the ark save the two tables of stone, which Moses put there at Horeb, when the LORD made a covenant with the children of Israel.' A golden pot of manna and Aaron's budding rod are named in Hebrews 9:4 as tabernacle relics but 1 Kings makes a point of saying they were not in the ark by Solomon's day; the brazen serpent Nehushtan was set up on a pole in the wilderness (Numbers 21).

question: In the book of Exodus, God gave Moses exact instructions in the wilderness of Sinai for the Ark of the Covenant, a wooden chest overlaid with gold. The ark had its own lid, called the mercy seat, made all of pure gold. Two smaller cherubim of hammered gold rose from that lid, of one piece with the seat itself. How were those two cherubim positioned toward one another?
answer: facing each other with wings spread over the seat
choices: facing each other with wings spread over the seat
back to back with wings folded down at their sides
kneeling with faces turned down to the floor
standing side by side facing out from the ark
context: KJV Exodus 25:20: 'And the cherubims shall stretch forth their wings on high, covering the mercy seat with their wings, and their faces shall look one to another; toward the mercy seat shall the faces of the cherubims be.' The great olive-wood pair inside the oracle stood tall over the whole ark; the two small golden ones were part of the mercy seat itself.

question: Solomon spoke at the dedication of his finished Temple, just after the priests had brought the ark to its place and come out, and a cloud had filled the house so that they could not stand to minister. His words were about the house he had built. What did he say the house was for?
answer: a settled place for thee to abide in for ever
choices: a settled place for thee to abide in for ever
a shelter for the poor and the widow
a schoolhouse for the sons of the prophets
a memorial of the wars of David my father
context: KJV 1 Kings 8:13: 'I have surely built thee an house to dwell in, a settled place for thee to abide in for ever.' The Temple was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's captain Nebuzaradan in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8-9); Solomon's 'for ever' became one of the great questions of Jewish tradition ever after.

question: The early Jerusalem apostles, overwhelmed, chose seven men to hand out the daily food to the widows, so that the twelve could keep preaching. Acts names the very first of the seven, a man 'full of faith and of the Holy Ghost.' Who was he?
context: Acts 6:5 lists the seven, and Stephen is named first. Barnabas is the encourager who later travels with Paul; Timothy and Silas are Paul's later companions; none of them are among the original seven servants of the tables.

question: Seven trusted men took on the daily meals for the widows of the Jerusalem church, so that the twelve apostles could get back to prayer and preaching. That job of waiting on tables grew into a permanent office of the church. Which office grew out of this scene?
context: Acts 6:1-6 is traditionally read as the founding of the diaconate. Bishops (overseers) and elders are named later in Acts; the office of pope develops much later as the bishop of Rome; prophet is a spiritual gift, not an ordained office.

question: Stephen preached that Jesus was the Messiah, and the religious authorities in Jerusalem dragged him before the same council that had condemned Jesus a few years earlier. It had seventy-one priests and elders, judging religious cases under the high priest. Which council tried Stephen?
choices: The council of the seventy elders
context: Acts 6:12 -- they 'brought him to the council,' the Sanhedrin, the same body that had tried Jesus. The Great Assembly (Knesset HaGedolah) was an earlier post-exilic body that had ceased centuries before; 'the council of the seventy elders' echoes Moses's seventy in Numbers 11 but is not the trial court of Acts; the high priest had no separate private tribunal apart from the Sanhedrin he presided over.

question: The whole high council in Jerusalem stared at Stephen, arrested for preaching Jesus, as he stood waiting to answer the charges against him. Acts records what they saw when they looked at him, one of the strangest single lines in the book, and gives no explanation. What did Stephen's face look like?
choices: The face of a small child
context: Acts 6:15 -- 'all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.' The verse gives no interpretation; it just reports what the council saw.

question: Stephen stood before the Jerusalem council on charges of blaspheming against Moses and the Temple, and he answered with the longest sermon in the Book of Acts. It was a swift retelling of the whole story of Israel, running down to Jesus. Where in the biblical story did Stephen begin?
context: Acts 7:2 -- 'The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran.' Stephen begins with Abraham and marches through Joseph, Moses, Joshua, David, and Solomon before turning on the council.

question: Stephen turned on the council at the end of his speech and charged its members with the same crime as their fathers, always resisting the Holy Ghost. He called them two things. One was stiffnecked. The other was the sharpest insult he could throw at Jerusalem's religious court. What was the second word?
context: Acts 7:51 -- 'Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost.' For a Jewish council whose very identity rested on the covenant of circumcision, calling them 'uncircumcised' was the most cutting reversal possible. The other three are all real biblical rebukes used elsewhere by the prophets and by Jesus, but none is what Stephen said here.

question: The council's fury boiled over as Stephen looked steadfastly up into heaven and told them the vision he saw. He had told the story of Israel and accused them of killing God's prophets. Acts records his exact words. Who did Stephen say he saw standing at the right hand of God?
context: Acts 7:56 -- 'Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God.' 'Son of man' is Jesus's own favorite title for himself in the gospels; it is the claim that pushed the council past rage into action.

question: Every man on the Jerusalem council cried out when Stephen told them he saw the heavens open. Before they ran at him with one accord to drag him out of the city, Acts records one physical thing they all did with their hands. What did they do?
context: Acts 7:57 -- 'Then they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and ran upon him with one accord.' Tearing robes is what the high priest did at Jesus's trial; the other two gestures are not in this scene.

question: The witnesses against Stephen stripped off their outer cloaks before the stoning, because the law of Moses made them throw the first stones. They piled the cloaks at the feet of a young man who stood watching. Acts names that young man for the very first time here. Who was he?
context: Acts 7:58 -- 'and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul.' This is Saul of Tarsus -- the future apostle Paul -- on stage for the first time in the New Testament, guarding the coats at the killing of the first Christian martyr.

question: Stephen's killers dragged him outside the walls of Jerusalem and stoned him to death, after the longest sermon in the Book of Acts. The witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young Pharisee, who guarded them. Acts turned at once to that young man and made one observation about him. What did it say?
answer: He was consenting to Stephen's death
choices: He was consenting to Stephen's death
He wept and asked for baptism
He was cursed with sudden blindness
context: Acts 8:1 -- 'And Saul was consenting unto his death.' Blindness comes later, on the road to Damascus in Acts 9. The same verse also reports a great persecution that scattered the church out of Jerusalem into Judea and Samaria -- which becomes the engine of the whole missionary spread of Acts.

question: Surt the fire-giant stood guard with his flaming sword at the far southern edge of the Norse cosmos, on a world older than Asgard and older than the gods. It was one of the two primal worlds that existed before creation. Which world was it?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 4 and 8. Muspelheim (also written Muspell) is the fiery southern world. Niflheim is its opposite -- the world of ice in the north -- the OTHER primal world. Jotunheim is the land of the giants. Svartalfheim is the underground realm of the dwarves. The two primal worlds are Muspelheim in the south and Niflheim in the north; the meeting of their fire and ice in the great void Ginnungagap is where creation begins.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr charged Surt on the plain of Vigrid, but he had to fight the fire-giant without his own famous weapon. Long before Ragnarok he had given his magic sword, a sword that fought all by itself against giants, to his servant Skirnir. Why did Freyr give the sword away?
answer: as bride-price for the giantess Gerdr
choices: as bride-price for the giantess Gerdr
as a fee to the dwarves who forged Mjolnir
as ransom for his sister Freyja
as payment for the horse Blodughofi
context: Skirnismal; Snorri, Gylfaginning 37 and 51. Freyr saw the beautiful giantess Gerdr from Odin's high seat Hlidskjalf, fell instantly in love, and sent his servant Skirnir to woo her. Skirnir named his fee -- Freyr's magic self-swinging sword and his horse -- and Freyr paid without hesitation. The whole point of the story is that Freyr dies at Ragnarok BECAUSE HE WAS IN LOVE. The moral of the Norse: never give away your sword, even for a wife.  (Legend.)
