question: Flaming sword in hand, Surt met Freyr on the plain of Vigrid at Ragnarok, the doom of the gods. Freyr, the Norse god of harvest and peace, had come swordless, with only a much humbler weapon in his hand, the same one he had once used to kill the giant Beli. What did Freyr fight Surt with?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 37 and 51. Freyr's antler-weapon is one of the great melancholy details of Ragnarok -- the fertility-god of the sunshine going to meet the fire-giant with nothing more than a piece of a deer's horn. Snorri notes that Freyr had earlier killed the giant Beli with the antler alone, so it is not a joke weapon; but against Surtr's flaming sword it is not enough, and Freyr falls.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr, brother of the goddess Freyja and a shining Vanir god of harvest and sunshine, went out to the last great battle at the end of the world. The giants and monsters marched on Asgard and every god had to fight. Of all the great Aesir and Vanir, the two families of Norse gods, who died that day, Freyr held one distinction. What was it?
answer: the first great god to fall
choices: the first great god to fall
the last great god to fall
the only god who leaves no body
the only god slain by his own weapon
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 51; Voluspa 53. Freyr falls first at Ragnarok -- before Odin is swallowed by Fenrir, before Thor kills Jormungandr and staggers nine steps and dies, before Tyr and Garmr end each other. The love-story that dropped his sword makes him also the first casualty of the last battle. But the fourth choice -- Freyr slain by his own weapon -- is a real motif from later tradition too: Surtr uses Freyr's own sword against him in some versions, so the fourth choice is a live-and-plausible alternative.  (Legend.)

question: The fire-giant of the far south rode out at Ragnarok, the twilight of the gods, to set the whole world alight with a sword brighter than the sun. Icelanders living on top of active volcanoes never quite let him go, and they carried his memory in the names of their mountains. What have Iceland's lava-lit peaks sometimes been called?
context: Icelandic folk-tradition; the lava-cave Surtshellir on Iceland is a documented site named for Surtr, and the 1963 eruption that created the new Icelandic island Surtsey was named for the same fire-giant. Icelanders living on top of active volcanoes never entirely forgot the being at the southern edge of the world with the burning sword.  (Legend.)

question: Tantalus, a mortal king in Anatolia and a favorite of the gods, sets a stew before them at their own table on Olympus. He has killed one of his sons and cooked him into it, to test whether they will notice. Which son has he cooked?
context: Named in Apollodorus and dramatised across the Greek tragedians. Wikipedia: Tantalus, Pelops.  (Legend.)

question: Ixion, king of the Lapiths in Thessaly, asks his own father-in-law to a feast and then shoves him into a hidden pit of red-hot coals. Greek poets call it the first mortal kin-murder ever done. Which father-in-law does Ixion push in?
context: Pindar and Apollodorus name Deioneus (father of Ixion's wife Dia) as the victim; Ixion is remembered as the founding kin-slayer of Greek myth. Wikipedia: Ixion.  (Legend.)

question: Tantalus stands in a pool of water up to his chin in Homer's Odyssey, with a branch of ripe fruit hanging just above his head. The English verb 'tantalise' comes straight from his punishment. What happens whenever he stoops down to drink from the pool?
answer: the water drains from the pool
choices: the water drains from the pool
the fruit falls into his mouth
a stone rolls onto his back
context: Odyssey 11.582-592: whenever Tantalus stoops the water drains away, and whenever he reaches the branch lifts out of reach. The verb 'tantalise' means to torment with the sight of something desired but kept out of reach. Wikipedia: Tantalus.  (Legend.)

question: Most of King Tantalus's guests on Olympus refuse the stew he sets before them, because they can tell it is his own son, cooked to test whether they truly know everything. But one goddess is absent-minded that day and eats a piece before she realizes what it is. Which goddess?
context: Demeter was mourning her daughter Persephone at the time and ate absent-mindedly; her share was a piece of the boy's shoulder. Wikipedia: Pelops.  (Legend.)

question: A king of Argos puts a dagger into the hand of each of his fifty daughters on her wedding night and orders her to kill her new husband in bed. He has forced all fifty to marry the fifty sons of his brother Aegyptus. Which king hands out the fifty daggers?
context: The daughters were called the Danaids after their father Danaus. Apollodorus 2.1.4; Wikipedia: Danaids.  (Legend.)

question: The gods piece Tantalus's cooked son back together and bring him to life, but a piece of his shoulder has already been swallowed and is gone. They give him a replacement shoulder-blade made of a special material, and Greek tradition claims it was carried to Troy centuries later. What is it made of?
context: The ivory shoulder-blade of Pelops was said to have been carried by the Greeks to Troy centuries later. Hephaestus was credited with the craftsmanship. Wikipedia: Pelops.  (Legend.)

question: King Danaus's brides of Argos, forty-nine of them, obey their father on the wedding night and kill the husbands he has forced on them, the sons of his own brother Aegyptus. One daughter refuses his command and lets her husband Lynceus live, and the line that produces Perseus survives because of her alone. What is her name?
context: Hypermnestra and Lynceus survived; their descendants included Perseus and thence Heracles. Aeschylus dramatised her in the lost Danaid trilogy. Wikipedia: Danaids.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus takes Ixion up to Olympus as a guest, after no mortal king will purify him of his father-in-law's blood. Ixion repays the hospitality by reaching for Hera. Zeus moulds a phantom in his wife's shape out of cloud as a trap, Ixion embraces the cloud, and from that coupling comes the ancestor of a whole monstrous race. Which race?
context: Pindar, Pythian 2.21-48, gives the cloud-Hera (later named Nephele) and the birth of Centauros, ancestor of the Centaur race by the Magnesian mares. Wikipedia: Ixion.  (Legend.)

question: Ixion reaches for Hera at Zeus's own table and earns a sentence that answers the crime, as every punishment in Tartarus does. Tantalus, who abused the gods at their table, gets food forever out of reach. The Danaid brides, who spilled blood in bed, get water to carry forever. Ixion is bound to a single object that becomes his emblem in Greek art. What is that object?
context: The burning wheel of Ixion, sometimes turning through the sky and sometimes deep in Tartarus, is his fixed emblem in ancient and later art. Wikipedia: Ixion.  (Legend.)

question: Teresa of Avila, a merchant's daughter from Spain, rewrote the rules of a whole religious order to make its nuns pray longer and live more simply. She became the first woman ever named a Doctor of the Catholic Church. Which order did she reform?
context: Teresa entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation in Avila at age 20 and, forty-seven years later, had founded a whole new reformed wing of the order -- the Discalced Carmelites. The Franciscans trace back to Francis of Assisi, the Dominicans to Dominic de Guzman, the Benedictines to Benedict of Nursia -- all real medieval orders, none of them Teresa's.

question: Teresa was twenty when she entered a convent in Avila where the nuns kept their own servants, received visitors freely in the parlour and traveled to family estates. She lived there in comfort for twenty-five years. The convent was named for one of the great Christian feasts. What was its name?
context: The Carmelite convent of the Incarnation still stands in Avila. Ascension, Visitation, and Annunciation are all real convent-naming feasts (the Visitation is even a whole female religious order founded by Francis de Sales), but Teresa's first house was the Incarnation.

question: A statue in a corner of the convent stopped Teresa of Avila cold as she walked past it at about forty. It showed Christ during the flogging before Pilate, wounded and bound. She wept at her lukewarm last twenty-five years, and from that day her prayer life quickly deepened into mystical visions. What did she call that turning point in her Autobiography?
context: 'Second' because she had already been a professed nun for twenty-five years; the moment in front of the wounded-Christ statue is described in her Autobiography ch. 9. 'Final vows' happened decades earlier; 'jubilee year' is a Roman canonical term for a fifty-year celebration; 'golden hour' is a modern trauma-medicine phrase, not Teresian vocabulary.

question: Teresa of Avila wrote, in chapter twenty-nine of her Autobiography, of an angel standing over her with a fire-tipped golden spear and thrusting it several times through her heart. Her ecstasies had grown so intense that other nuns sometimes had to hold her body down. What name did Teresa give this experience?
context: From Latin 'trans' + 'verberare', to strike through -- the name for the piercing itself. The other three are real spiritual-writing terms (illumination for divine light, consolation for felt sweetness, conflagration for the fire of love in later mystics), but Teresa's own word for the spear-through-the-heart vision is Transverberation.

question: Teresa's confessors pressed her to write down her experiences, and her masterwork followed in 1577. She described the soul as a crystal castle of many rooms, journeying through them in stages of prayer until it reaches the innermost one, where union with God happens. How many rooms, which she called mansions, did the castle contain?
context: Seven mansions (moradas) in the Castillo Interior (Interior Castle), each a deeper stage of prayer. The other numbers are famous elsewhere (three persons of the Trinity, twelve apostles, forty days in the wilderness); they are not Teresa's schema.

question: The Sheriff of Nottingham announced a great archery contest in the town square in A Gest of Robyn Hode, hoping Robin Hood would not be able to resist trying to win it. The prize was a single object every yeoman coveted. What was the prize?
context: The prize in the Sheriff's contest is a silver arrow. Silver-arrow archery contests were a real English town tradition and continued in some towns down to the eighteenth century -- the ballad is drawing on a genuine sporting custom. Source: World Archery, Legend of Robin Hood; A Gest of Robyn Hode.

question: Robin Hood came to the Sheriff's contest in disguise in the medieval ballad A Gest of Robyn Hode, and he won by shooting nearest the mark. His arrow split no rival's arrow there, or in any medieval ballad. Sir Walter Scott wrote that shot into a nineteenth-century novel. In which novel did it first appear?
context: Sir Walter Scott wrote the arrow-splitting shot into Ivanhoe, published December 1819 (dated 1820), chapter 13. All four choices are real Scott novels, but only Ivanhoe carries the Robin Hood arrow scene. Source: Wikipedia, Ivanhoe.

question: Sir Walter Scott sent a mystery yeoman dressed in Lincoln green to a great English tournament in his 1819 Robin Hood novel. The stranger out-shot the finest bowmen in the field, and only slowly did the reader realize he was Robin Hood in disguise. What name did the yeoman give?
context: Scott calls the disguised Robin 'Locksley' at the Ashby tournament, borrowing an older tradition (a c.1600 prose Life of Robin Hood names Locksley as Robin's birthplace). Wilfred, Athelstane, and Cedric are other main characters in Ivanhoe. Source: Wikipedia, Ivanhoe.

question: Sir Walter Scott's disguised Robin Hood stepped up at the tournament to face a rival archer, the reigning champion of the field, a proud bowman whose grandfather was said to have shot at the Battle of Hastings. Robin split this man's arrow down the shaft, and that only drew the contest level. What was the rival's name?
context: In Ivanhoe chapter 13, Locksley splits the arrow of Hubert, whose grandfather shot at Hastings. Splitting the arrow only ties the contest; Locksley then wins the tiebreaker with a second, harder shot at a still slenderer target. Source: Wikipedia, Ivanhoe.

question: Thomas Ohlgren, who studies the Robin Hood ballads, argued that the whole arrow-splitting tradition grew from a simple misreading. In A Gest of Robyn Hode, Robin's most impressive contest shot split no arrow at all. It split a slender target set up in front of the butts. What was that target?
context: In the medieval ballads Robin split a 'wand' -- a slim willow stick planted upright in front of the target. As colored targets came into fashion and readers forgot what a 'wand' was, later retellers substituted an opponent's arrow. All four choices are plausible slender targets, but the ballads specify willow. Source: Slate, Can you really split an arrow with an arrow?; A Gest of Robyn Hode.

question: A modern archer at a competition sees a second arrow lodge inside the hollow shaft of the first, already in the target. The front arrow is ruined, and the shot is so rare that most clubs would fine him a small sum to celebrate it. What do archers call this shot?
context: Archers universally call the trick shot 'a Robin Hood', in tribute to Scott's Ivanhoe scene. Genuine Robin Hoods happen every so often at modern indoor competitions and ruin the front arrow -- most clubs charge a fee to celebrate them. Source: TV Tropes, Splitting the Arrow; Slate on Merida and the Robin Hood shot.

question: Prince John presided over a great tournament in the English Midlands in Sir Walter Scott's Robin Hood novel, while King Richard was away on crusade. The disguised outlaw split his rival's arrow there. The tournament ground is a real place, and its castle still stands in ruin today. Where did the tournament take place?
context: Scott sets the tournament at Ashby-de-la-Zouche in Leicestershire, whose castle keep still stands in ruin. Kenilworth, Warwick, and Nottingham are all real English tournament-era castles Scott might have chosen; he picked Ashby. Source: Wikipedia, Ivanhoe.

question: A leading man stepped before a major Hollywood studio's cameras in 1938 to film The Adventures of Robin Hood, and his became the face every later Robin Hood answers to. Sir Walter Scott's novel, one of the most-read books of the nineteenth century, had already made the split arrow the iconic moment. Who was that leading man?
context: Errol Flynn's The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938) became the template every later Robin Hood movie followed. Douglas Fairbanks had played Robin Hood in a silent 1922 film; Costner (1991) and Elwes (1993) came much later. Source: Slate, Can you really split an arrow with an arrow?; TV Tropes, Splitting the Arrow.

question: King Arthur lay dying after his last battle against his enemy Mordred at Camlann, and he gave his most trusted surviving knight one last order: take the sword Excalibur down to the water and throw it in. Which knight did Arthur send with the sword?
context: Sir Bedivere is Arthur's cupbearer and, by Malory Book XXI, the last living knight at his side. In the older Welsh tradition he is 'Bedwyr' and one of Arthur's earliest companions. Gawain has died earlier of a head-wound. Kay, Arthur's foster-brother, is long gone. Lucan the Butler is present at the last battle but dies of his wounds before Excalibur is returned.  (Legend.)

question: Three queens and their attendants waited in a barge at the shore for the mortally wounded King Arthur, after his last battle at Camlann, to bear him away to the isle of Avalon. All of them wept, and all wore hoods of one particular colour. What colour did the ladies wear?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.6: 'a little barge with many fair ladies in it, and among them all was a queen, and all they had black hoods, and all they wept and shrieked when they saw King Arthur'. Black is the mourning colour of the whole scene. White is the colour of the Grail knights; scarlet of the martyr; green of the fairy Otherworld -- all wrong for this cortege.  (Legend.)

question: The queens on the dark barge lifted the mortally wounded King Arthur aboard at the shore, after the last terrible battle at Camlann. They were bearing him away to the isle of Avalon, and they laid him down in a very particular way. How was Arthur laid?
answer: with his head in a queen's lap
choices: with his head in a queen's lap
seated upon a throne of oak
chained to a mast of iron
context: Malory Book XXI ch.6: 'they set them down, and in one of their laps King Arthur laid his head'. It's a pieta-like image, deliberately gentle. A throne would be a coronation; a cloak-wrapping a battle-death; a chained mast a captive's death -- none fit this scene.  (Legend.)

question: Geoffrey of Monmouth traced the name of Avalon, the mist-wrapped otherworld island where a barge carried the wounded King Arthur at the end of his story, back to an older Welsh word, afal. In modern English, what does afal mean?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI (c.1136) explains 'Insula Avallonis' from Welsh 'afal' (apple) -- hence Ynys Afallon, the Isle of Apples. Apples are the fruit of the Otherworld across Celtic mythology, also seen in the Irish Emain Ablach ('Emain of Apples'). Mist, mound, and swan all suit Otherworld islands in other traditions, but Avalon's name is specifically the apple-word.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur's last knight wandered inland, weeping, on the morning after the barge left, and came upon a hermit in a valley. The hermit told him that a company of hooded ladies had knocked at midnight, bringing a body and paying him a hundred bezants. He had just finished a solemn task for them. What had the hermit just done?
choices: burned the body on a pyre
dressed the body in mail for a war-grave
context: Malory Book XXI ch.7. The hermit does not know whose body it is -- the ladies came at midnight, gave him the body, and paid him with a hundred bezants to bury it. Embalming with spices belongs to Egyptian and biblical burials (Joseph, Jesus); a pyre would be pagan Norse or Greek, not Christian British; a war-grave in mail belongs to a battlefield death like Beowulf's. The whole point of the scene is that Arthur's death is uncertain -- a grave is dug, but no name is given.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Thomas Malory finished Le Morte d'Arthur, the great English retelling of the whole Arthurian legend, in an English prison around 1470. Near the end he refused to say plainly whose body had gone into the ground. He wrote: 'yet some men say... that King Arthur is not dead, but'. How did the sentence go on?
choices: he walks with the Round Table
context: Malory Book XXI ch.7, near-verbatim: 'yet some men say in many parts of England that King Arthur is not dead, but had by the will of our Lord Jesu into another place; and men say that he shall come again, and he shall win the holy cross'. Malory refuses to give a verdict. The three wrong choices are made-up flourishes; Malory's line is specifically about RETURN, not undersea sleep or star-fire.  (Legend.)

question: Malory told of a Latin epitaph carved on Arthur's supposed tomb, after the barge had carried the king away and nobody would say whose body lay in the ground. It read 'Hic iacet Arthurus, rex quondam rexque futurus.' T.H. White named his 1958 novel after the last four words. What do those Latin words mean in English?
choices: the king who died at Camlann
the king who healed the wound
the king of the round table
context: Malory Book XXI ch.7. 'Rex quondam' = 'king in time past'; 'rexque futurus' = 'and king to come'. The line closes the whole Morte d'Arthur and gave T.H. White the title of his 1958 novel 'The Once and Future King'. The three wrong choices describe Arthur but do not translate the Latin.  (Legend.)

question: The monks of Glastonbury Abbey announced to the world in 1191 that they had discovered a famous grave in their cemetery, seven years after fire had gutted their great abbey. They were desperate to raise money to rebuild. A lead cross with a Latin inscription marked the grave, with a giant oak coffin below, and pilgrim donations poured in for centuries. Whose grave did the monks claim to have found?
context: The Glastonbury monks' 1191 discovery of a lead cross reading 'Here lies buried the famous King Arthur on the Isle of Avalon' is regarded by modern historians as a pious forgery -- perfectly timed to bring pilgrims and coin after the 1184 fire. The same abbey also promoted the legend that Joseph of Arimathea had come to Glastonbury with the Grail -- two miracles, both marketable. Patrick's burial is claimed at Downpatrick in Ireland. Merlin's grave has no such tourist site.

question: God gave Abraham a terrible command in the book of Genesis, after most of a lifetime spent waiting for a promised son. Abraham was to take that son up a mountain and offer him as a burnt offering. Which son did God name?
context: Genesis 22:2. Isaac is the son of Abraham and Sarah, the child of the covenant. Ishmael is Abraham's older son by Hagar. Jacob and Esau are Isaac's own twin sons, born a generation later.

question: Abraham rose early the morning after God ordered him to offer up his son on a distant mountain, saddled his donkey and took two young men with him. He prepared one thing above all else and loaded it on the animal. What was it?
context: Genesis 22:3. Abraham himself cleaves the wood for the fire before setting out on the three-day journey to the land of Moriah.

question: Abraham saw the place afar off on the third day of the journey, left the two young men below with the donkey and went on alone with the boy. As father and son started up the slope, what did Abraham lay on his son to carry?
answer: The wood for the burnt offering
choices: The wood for the burnt offering
The fire in a clay pot
A skin of water for the altar
context: Genesis 22:6. Abraham himself keeps the fire and the knife in his own hands; the wood he lays on Isaac's shoulders. Christian readers later heard an echo of another son carrying his own wood up a hill.

question: Abraham's son climbed the mountain in Moriah beside his father, and partway up he noticed something missing from their gear. He turned to the old man and said: 'Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the...?' How did his question end?
choices: Goat for the altar of incense
context: Genesis 22:7. Abraham answers, 'My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering.' Doves, bullocks, and goats are all real offerings elsewhere in the Torah, but the lamb is the answer Isaac's question demands.

question: Abraham built an altar of stones on the top of the mountain and bound his own son hand and foot. He laid the boy on the altar, ready to offer him as a burnt sacrifice. Then he stretched out his hand. What did he take up in that hand?
context: Genesis 22:10. The KJV word is 'knife.' It is what the angel, calling from heaven at the last instant, tells Abraham to 'lay not thine hand upon the lad.'

question: In Genesis, an angel called from heaven at the last instant and stopped the killing, with Abraham's son bound on the altar and his father's hand stretched out. Abraham lifted his eyes and saw an animal caught behind him in a thicket by its horns. What animal took his son's place on the altar?
context: Genesis 22:13. Not a lamb (the very word Isaac had asked for), not a goat, not a bullock. A ram, an adult male sheep, caught by its curled horns in the thicket. The horns are what let it be found.

question: Abraham offered up the animal from the thicket in place of his son on a mountain in the land of Moriah, after an angel had stopped his hand at the last moment. Then he named the mountaintop so the rescue would be remembered. He called it Jehovah-Jireh. What does that Hebrew name mean in English?
context: Genesis 22:14. Jehovah-jireh literally means 'the LORD will see' or 'the LORD will provide.' Jehovah-nissi (banner) is what Moses names an altar after defeating Amalek; Jehovah-shalom (peace) is Gideon's altar; 'the LORD is my shepherd' is David's psalm.

question: The boy Jesus set out from Nazareth with Mary and Joseph on the long walk south to Jerusalem, as the family did every year for one great pilgrim feast. Luke alone gives any scene of his childhood after the Nativity. Which feast was it?
context: Luke 2:41 KJV: 'Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover.' Passover was one of the three pilgrim feasts Jewish families travelled to Jerusalem to keep.

question: Luke told one story from the boyhood of Jesus, the only scene between the manger and his adult ministry. Mary and Joseph, going home from a great feast in Jerusalem, realized their son was missing and hurried back. How old was the boy?
context: Luke 2:42 KJV: 'And when he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem after the custom of the feast.' Between this scene and Jesus's baptism as an adult, the gospels record nothing else -- the so-called 'hidden years.'

question: The parents of Jesus left Jerusalem after the feast with the great caravan of pilgrims going home to Galilee. They did not notice their son was gone, since they supposed he was walking with kinsmen somewhere in the crowd. How long did they travel before they realized he was missing?
context: Luke 2:44 KJV: 'they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance.' Pilgrim caravans travelled as extended clans, so a twelve-year-old walking with cousins would not have been noticed.

question: Mary and Joseph hurried back to the crowded city of Jerusalem to look for the son they had lost on the road home. They searched the whole city before they found him at last in the Temple, sitting among the teachers and asking them questions. According to Luke, how long did the search take?
context: Luke 2:46 KJV: 'And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions.' The 'three days' echo has been noted by commentators alongside the later three days in the tomb.

question: Mary found her son in the Temple at last, sitting among the teachers of the Law, after a search that had frightened her badly. She spoke first, a mother's half-scolding line to her child. Luke's gospel records her opening words exactly. How did Mary begin?
answer: Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us?
choices: Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us?
Child, thou art weary; come home with us now
Rejoice, for that which was lost is found again
How camest thou hither, when we bade thee stay?
context: Luke 2:48 KJV: 'Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing.' It is the only line the gospels give Mary in the whole scene -- direct, wounded, a mother's voice.

question: Jesus faced his mother in the Temple after she asked why he had done this to them, and he gave the first line of speech any gospel records from him. He began 'How is it that ye sought me?' and then finished the thought in one line. How did the sentence end?
answer: wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?
choices: wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?
know ye not that a prophet is without honour, save in his own country?
hath not the Lord chosen the weak things of the world?
have ye not read what David did, when he was hungered?
context: Luke 2:49 KJV. 'Wist' is old English for 'knew.' These are the first recorded words of Jesus in any of the four gospels -- a twelve-year-old's answer to his frightened mother, setting up in one line the tension between his household and his mission; the reply also tells them where they should have looked for him.

question: Moses leads a flock to the far side of the desert in Midian, years after fleeing Egypt. The sheep are not his. They belong to his father-in-law, a priest of Midian who took him in. What is his father-in-law's name?
context: Exodus 3:1. Jethro is the priest of Midian who took Moses in after Moses killed the Egyptian and fled. Laban is Jacob's uncle in Haran; Bethuel is Rebekah's father in Genesis; Potiphar is Joseph's Egyptian master, from an earlier generation.

question: Moses, the exiled Hebrew, sees a scraggly desert bush catch fire near the mountain of God as he tends the flock in Midian. He stops and looks longer, and he sees something impossible about the fire. What is impossible about it?
answer: The bush is not being burned up
choices: The bush is not being burned up
The flames give off no heat at all
The bush is dripping honey from its branches
context: Exodus 3:2-3. The bush 'burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.' Moses says, 'I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.' That impossibility is what draws him close enough for God to speak.

question: In the book of Exodus, God calls to Moses from inside the flames, twice by name: 'Moses, Moses.' God's first command tells him that the place he has walked into is holy ground. What must Moses do at once?
answer: Take his sandals off his feet
choices: Take his sandals off his feet
Cover his face with his cloak
Bow down flat on the ground
context: Exodus 3:5. 'Put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.' Moses also hides his face, but that comes after the shoes and is not a command.

question: God orders Moses back to Egypt to lead the Hebrews out, and Moses answers with a nervous question. When the Hebrews demand to know who sent him, what name should he give? God gives him a strange name for himself. What is it?
context: Exodus 3:14. 'Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.' 'Ancient of Days' is from Daniel's vision; 'Alpha and Omega' is from Revelation; 'Lord of Hosts' is a later prophetic title. Only 'I AM THAT I AM' comes from the bush.

question: Moses casts the staff in his hand down onto the ground at God's order, a sign to prove himself to Hebrews who may not believe him. The staff changes at once into a living creature so frightening that Moses runs from it. What does the staff become?
context: Exodus 4:2-4. When Moses takes it back by the tail it becomes a rod again in his hand. Aaron later performs the same trick before Pharaoh, and the Egyptian magicians match it, but Aaron's rod swallows theirs. Frogs, locusts, and Nile crocodiles all belong to the Egypt frame Moses is being sent into, but the staff becomes a serpent.

question: Moses tries once more to talk his way out of the mission, even after both signs. He tells God the honest reason he cannot lead: he cannot speak well. In his own words he is 'not eloquent ... but slow of speech, and of a slow...' What is the last word of his excuse?
context: Exodus 4:10. 'I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.' Jewish tradition later reads this as a stutter Moses had from childhood; that stutter is why what comes next matters so much.

question: God's patience runs out at Moses's last excuse, but instead of replacing him God appoints a spokesman: an older brother who can speak well and is already on his way from Egypt to meet him. Jewish tradition later reads Moses's trouble as a stutter from childhood. Who is this brother, the mouthpiece?
context: Exodus 4:14-16. Aaron is Moses's older brother; God says Aaron 'can speak well' and 'shall be thy spokesman unto the people.' Caleb, Hur, and Joshua are all real Exodus-era men (Hur helps hold up Moses's arms at Rephidim; Joshua is Moses's captain in battle; Caleb is one of the twelve spies), but none of them is Moses's brother.

question: Odysseus sailed toward the island of Thrinacia with the warnings of two prophets behind him: the animals grazing there must never be touched. Seven herds and seven flocks lived on it, and they never bred and never died, because they belonged to one god. Which god?
context: In Homer's Odyssey (Book 12), Thrinacia is the island of Helios, the sun who sees everything from his chariot in the sky. Both Circe on Aeaea and the shade of Tiresias in Hades had warned Odysseus: do not touch a single beast on that island. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.127-141.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus wanted to sail past the island of Thrinacia entirely, for no man was allowed to touch the deathless herds there. His exhausted crew begged to beach for the night, and his stubborn second-in-command overruled him and insisted they land. Who was this second-in-command?
context: Eurylochus is Odysseus's lieutenant throughout the Odyssey and repeatedly the crew's mouthpiece against his captain -- earlier he refused to enter Circe's palace, and here he overrules Odysseus about beaching on Thrinacia. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.279-294.  (Legend.)

question: Every man of the crew swore a solemn oath before he could step ashore on the island of Thrinacia. The seer Tiresias had warned Odysseus never to touch the sacred herds there, and his men were hungry. What did they swear to do?
answer: Eat only the ship's own stores and touch nothing on the island
choices: Eat only the ship's own stores and touch nothing on the island
Sail again at first light no matter the weather
Never again drink wine on the voyage
Kill no living creature until they reached Ithaca
context: Odysseus knew the danger and made his men swear on it. But when the winds pinned them for a month and the stores ran out, the oath fell apart. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.298-304.  (Legend.)

question: Two divine sisters tended the fat cattle on the island of Thrinacia when Odysseus and his weary crew made landfall there. The herds never bred and never died, the same beasts walking the same fields, and the sisters were daughters of the god who owned them. What were the two sisters' names?
context: Phaethusa and Lampetie -- their names mean 'the shining' and 'the radiant' -- were the daughters of Helios by the nymph Neaera, and they lived on Thrinacia caring for the deathless herds. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.131-133.  (Legend.)

question: The crew of Odysseus sat pinned on the beach of Thrinacia by foul winds, every man under oath not to touch a single beast of the sacred herds. The ship's stores of food finally gave out. For how long were the crew trapped and starving before they broke the oath?
context: A full month of contrary winds -- long enough for the stores to run out and for the crew's fish-and-bird foraging to fail. Odysseus went off alone to pray for deliverance, and while he was asleep Eurylochus led the slaughter. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.325-330.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus's second-in-command told the starving crew that any death was better than starving, while his captain slept in a sheltered spot after praying to the gods for a way home. Contrary winds held them on the island of Thrinacia, and their food stores had run out. What did the crew then do?
answer: Slaughtered the deathless cattle of the god
choices: Slaughtered the deathless cattle of the god
Set fire to their own ship for warmth
Ate their captain's share of the last stores
Sacrificed the youngest crewman to the sea
context: Eurylochus argued they could build the god a great temple back on Ithaca and be forgiven. They killed the best of the herd and roasted the meat -- and Odysseus woke to the smell of it. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.339-365.  (Legend.)

question: One of the two sisters who tended the herds on Thrinacia ran straight to her father, the god who owned them, and told him what Odysseus's crew had done. Enraged, he demanded justice from Zeus and threatened an extraordinary punishment against the whole world if the killers were not repaid. What did her father threaten to do?
answer: Leave the sky and go down and shine among the dead
choices: Leave the sky and go down and shine among the dead
Burn every crop on the whole earth to ash
Never again let a wind blow across the sea
Drag the moon down out of the night sky
context: One of the most striking single lines in Homer -- Helios threatens to abandon the world of the living and shine for the dead in Hades if his cattle are not avenged. Zeus, alarmed, promises the thunderbolt. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.382-383.  (Legend.)

question: The guilty crew of Odysseus put out to sea from the island of Thrinacia when the wind at last turned fair, and once they were well clear, the storm hit. First came a black cloud, then a great gust that broke the mast, and the falling mast killed the pilot at the tiller. What came next?
answer: A thunderbolt split the ship in two
choices: A thunderbolt split the ship in two
A whirlwind lifted the ship and dashed it back down
A hailstone the size of a boulder broke the hull
The sky turned black and a rain of fire fell on the deck
context: Zeus's promised thunderbolt strikes as soon as the ship clears the island. Every man of the crew drowns; Odysseus, who ate none of the cattle, is the only survivor. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.403-417.  (Legend.)

question: The queen and king of Connacht quarrel over which of them owns more wealth, and the whole great Irish epic of the Cattle Raid of Cooley follows from it. It starts on no battlefield and in no throne-room. Where are the two of them when it begins?
answer: In their royal bed at Cruachan
choices: In their royal bed at Cruachan
On the walls of Emain Macha
By the ford at Ath Fhirdiad
context: The opening scene is famous in world literature as the Pillow-Talk -- an entire war epic launched from a marital argument in bed. Cruachan (modern Rathcroghan in Co. Roscommon) was the royal seat of the kingdom of Connacht. Source: https://mythopedia.com/library/tain-bo-cuailnge-dunn-1914/1-the-pillow-talk/  (Legend.)

question: The queen of Connacht drives her own chariot to the war against Ulster. She is no wife to fight from behind a curtain: she kills in single combat and runs the raid herself, while her husband largely keeps to her shadow. What is her name?
context: Medb (anglicised Maeve) of Connacht is one of the great warrior-queens of world myth -- her name is glossed 'she who intoxicates' and is cognate with the English word 'mead'. Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife (Ulster side); Deirdre is a tragic beauty; Grainne belongs to the later Fenian Cycle. Source: https://irishmyths.com/myths/cattle-raid-cooley-tain-bo-cuailnge/  (Legend.)

question: The king of Connacht quarrels with his queen at the fortress of Cruachan, in the great Irish saga the Tain Bo Cuailnge, over which of them owns more wealth. He rules that same western province beside her. What is his name?
context: Ailill mac Mata is Medb's husband and consort-king; the Tain repeatedly makes clear that in this marriage Medb is the driving will. Conchobar mac Nessa is the king of ULSTER, the enemy in this war; Fergus mac Roich is an exiled Ulsterman who fights on Medb's side; Cormac is a later high-king of Ireland. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A1in_B%C3%B3_C%C3%BAailnge  (Legend.)

question: Husband and wife in the fortress of Cruachan go through everything they own, item by item: gold, servants, weapons, jewellery, flocks, herds. It is a strange thing to do, and a whole war hangs on it. The count comes out exactly equal on every line except one particular kind of possession. What is the one thing on which they are not equal?
context: Ailill has one bull in his herds so magnificent that Medb has no equal to it -- and this is the fact she cannot bear. The whole war of the Tain will be a woman's determination to match a single animal her husband owns. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A1in_B%C3%B3_C%C3%BAailnge  (Legend.)

question: Finnbennach, the great White-Horned, crossed the pasture on his own, out of the queen of Connacht's herd, where he had been born a calf, and into her husband's cattle. Now she is furious to find herself one prize short of the king. Why, according to the tale, did he leave her herd?
answer: He refused to be owned by a woman
choices: He refused to be owned by a woman
He was traded away in a game of fidchell
He was stolen by raiders from Munster
He was frightened off by a druid's curse
context: The bull's own defection is the sharpest twist of the pillow-talk: the animal himself judged that a queen was not a fit owner, and walked into the king's pasture. For Medb, sovereignty over Connacht was inseparable from being able to match her husband's wealth exactly. Fidchell is a real early-Irish board game. Source: https://loraobrien.ie/tain-bo-cuailgne-cattle-raid-of-cooley-a-beginners-guide/  (Legend.)

question: Daire mac Fiachna, an Ulster lord, agrees to lease the Donn Cuailnge, the Brown of Cooley, to the queen of Connacht for a year for a fair price, and he welcomes her men into his hall for a feast. Then a single moment during that feast ruins the whole deal. What do her messengers do?
answer: Her messengers boast, drunk, that they would take the bull by force if refused
choices: Her messengers boast, drunk, that they would take the bull by force if refused
Her messengers demand the bull outright as a tribute rather than a lease
Her messengers insult Daire's wife at the feast-table
Her messengers offer Daire half the going price and no more
context: Daire overhears the drunken boast, understands that Medb was never going to leave without the bull one way or another, and formally withdraws his consent. In doing so he gives Medb the pretext for war she needed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A1in_B%C3%B3_C%C3%BAailnge  (Legend.)

question: Refused the Brown of Cooley, the queen of Connacht sends no second embassy. She raises an army instead, drawn from all the great territorial divisions of Ireland, exiled Ulstermen among them, and welds it together against Ulster alone. From how many of the provinces of Ireland does she raise it?
context: Medb raises the army of the four provinces -- Connacht, Munster, Leinster, and even a body of exiled Ulstermen -- against Ulster itself. Ireland was traditionally divided into four kingdoms with a symbolic fifth (Meath) at the centre. Twelve is the Round Table number (Arthurian pillar); seven is the number of Ulster kings-in-training at Emain Macha. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A1in_B%C3%B3_C%C3%BAailnge  (Legend.)

question: The Brown of Cooley and the White-Horned meet at last on the field of Cruachan, the two prize bulls of the great Irish epic, along the same route the raid has taken. The war ends not with the death of the queen, not with the fall of Ulster, but with these two. How does their final duel end?
answer: The Donn Cuailnge kills the Finnbennach
choices: The Donn Cuailnge kills the Finnbennach
The Finnbennach kills the Donn Cuailnge
Both bulls die at the same instant
Both bulls turn and refuse to fight
context: The Brown of Cooley gores the White-Horned to death and scatters pieces of him across the map of Ireland -- and then, exhausted, drops dead himself. The epic ends with both prize bulls dead in the mud and Medb no richer than the night of the pillow-talk. Source: https://irishmyths.com/myths/cattle-raid-cooley-tain-bo-cuailnge/  (Legend.)

question: A sharp-tongued poet of Ulster throws a great feast, and the warriors will come only if he sits alone in a raised gallery above the hall, where his poison verses cannot set them at each other's throats. Who is this host?
context: Bricriu mac Carbada is the hospitaller (briugu) and troublemaker of Ulster, known for a satirist's tongue so vicious that his mere presence at the hearth started fights. The tale of the feast is called Fled Bricrenn ('Bricriu's Feast'). Sencha mac Ailella is Ulster's chief judge and peacemaker; Amairgen mac Ecit is Conall Cernach's father, another Ulster poet; Ferghus mac Roich is the exiled king. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bricriu.  (Legend.)

question: A mischievous host at an Ulster feast goes to three champions, one at a time, and whispers to each that the Champion's Portion is his, the choicest cut of the roast, kept for the greatest fighter in the hall. Cu Chulainn is one of the three, and Conall Cernach another. Who is the third?
context: Loegaire Buadach ('Loegaire the Victorious') is the third of the top-rank Ulster champions and the first to take up the beheading challenge later in the tale. Cet mac Magach is a Connacht champion; Fer Diad is Cu Chulainn's foster-brother from Connacht; Laeg mac Riangabra is Cu Chulainn's charioteer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: Three champions of Ulster quarrel on over the Champion's Portion. Contests of arms settle nothing, and the kings asked to judge keep naming one man the winner, but the other two refuse the verdict. Then one night a stranger enters the hall of Emain Macha and offers the champions a strange bargain. What appearance does he take?
answer: a huge rough herdsman (bachlach) with an axe
choices: a huge rough herdsman (bachlach) with an axe
an armoured Fomorian captain from the sea
a druid of the Dagda in white robes
a giant of the Fir Bolg in bronze mail
context: The Irish word bachlach means 'churl' or 'lout'; in the tale the shape-shifter chooses the form of a rough herdsman with a great axe -- the most unassuming shape possible, which makes the beheading trick land harder. The Fomorians are a race of old sea-enemies of the Tuatha De; the Fir Bolg are the pre-Tuatha rulers of Ireland; a druid would judge, not challenge with an axe. Source: oxfordreference.com Bachlach entry; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: A stranger walks into the Ulster king's hall in the Irish tale Fled Bricrenn and offers the champions a bargain: any one of them may cut off his head tonight, if that man will come back and kneel for the return blow. The first to accept strikes and takes the head clean off. The next moment gives the story-motif its name, the beheading game. What does the beheaded stranger do?
answer: picks up his own head, tucks it under his arm, and walks out of the hall
choices: picks up his own head, tucks it under his arm, and walks out of the hall
grows a new head from the stump on the spot
vanishes into a mist and leaves the axe standing upright in the floor
turns into a raven and flies out through the smoke-hole
context: The picked-up-head is the visual signature of what medievalists call the 'beheading game': proof that the challenger is otherworldly and the bargain will fall due. He returns the next morning, head restored, to collect the return blow. Six centuries later Sir Gawain and the Green Knight uses exactly the same beat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beheading_game; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: The beheaded stranger returns to Emain Macha the next morning, head on shoulders again, to collect the return blow. The champion who struck him the night before, and swore to offer his own neck in his turn, refuses the bargain and slips away. Which of the three champions is the first to flee?
context: Loegaire is the first to try the challenge and the first to break his word; Conall takes the same bargain on the second night and likewise flees when the giant comes back with the axe. Only Cu Chulainn will keep faith. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: One champion takes up the axe on the third night at Emain Macha, after two others have struck and run. He beheads the stranger as they did. Next morning he alone keeps the bargain: he kneels, bares his neck and waits for the blow without flinching. Which champion is he?
context: The whole tale points at this moment: Cu Chulainn alone honours the exchange. Conall and Loegaire had both fled at first light. Fer Diad is not one of the three great Ulster champions -- he is Cu Chulainn's Connacht foster-brother, who will later fight him at the ford in the Tain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: The stranger stands over the champion kneeling at the block, lifts the axe and swings three times. For the third stroke he has turned it in his hand, and the blow lands and does no wound. What part of the axe strikes the neck?
answer: the flat or blunt back of the blade
choices: the flat or blunt back of the blade
the wooden handle just above the head
the leather thong lashing the head to the shaft
the pommel-stone at the butt of the shaft
context: The turned axe is the mercy that pays out the bargain: Cu Chulainn keeps his word, the giant keeps his (a blow, not a killing), and honour is preserved on both sides. The 14th-century Sir Gawain and the Green Knight uses the same three-swing structure at the Green Chapel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gawain_and_the_Green_Knight; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: A huge stranger rides into Arthur's hall at Camelot on Christmas Day with a holly branch and a great axe, and he offers the knights a blow for a blow. It is the old Irish bargain, six centuries on, and it has probably crossed to England through French romance. What is this English poem called?
answer: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
choices: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (late 14th century, by the anonymous 'Gawain-poet') opens with exactly the green-knight-with-holly scene: the same beheading bargain, the same year-and-a-day delay, and at the end the same three-swing axe-blow that Cu Roi gave Cu Chulainn. Pearl and Patience are two other alliterative poems in the same manuscript by the same anonymous poet; the Alliterative Morte Arthure is a separate 14th-century Arthurian poem, but has no beheading-game. Fled Bricrenn is the ancestor, likely transmitted through Chretien de Troyes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beheading_game.  (Legend.)

question: The poison-tongued host who set the champions quarrelling comes out at Cruachan in the closing hour of the great cattle-raid of Cooley. The fighting is over, and he has come to watch the sport he was so fond of stirring up in others. How does he die?
answer: trampled to death between the two great bulls of the Tain
choices: trampled to death between the two great bulls of the Tain
poisoned by his own wife at the feasting-table
beheaded by Cu Roi mac Daire in a return match
starved after being locked into his own raised gallery
context: The Brown Bull of Cooley and the White-Horned Bull of Ai fight to the death at Cruachan at the end of the Tain, and Bricriu is caught between them and trampled. The Ulster tradition treats it as poetic justice for a life of stirring fights. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bricriu.  (Legend.)

question: Lir married his first wife's sister, in Irish myth, so his four children would have a mother. She grew jealous of how much he loved them, took them to a lake and struck them with a druid's rod. What did she turn them into?
context: This is the opening of Oidheadh Chlainne Lir ('The Fate of the Children of Lir'), one of the great tragic tales of medieval Ireland. Aoife, the second wife, transforms the four children at Loch Dairbhreach (Lake Derravaragh) in modern County Westmeath. Swans in Irish myth are almost always a shape of the enchanted or the mourning; this story is why the Irish will not shoot a swan to this day.  (Legend.)

question: Oisin Kelly cast the children of Lir in bronze for Dublin's Garden of Remembrance, the eldest, a daughter, rising with her three brothers behind her. In the tale she guarded them through the long centuries of the curse. What was her name?
context: Fionnuala is the eldest child of Lir and Aoibh, sister to Aodh, Fiacra, and Conn. Deirdre is the sorrow-figure of the Ulster cycle (the Children of Uisneach). Etain is the swan-maiden of Tochmarc Etaine, a different tale. Grainne is the woman who elopes with Diarmuid in the Fionn cycle.  (Legend.)

question: Lir's second wife took his four children out to a lonely lake one day with a druid's rod in her hand. She was the sister of his dead first wife and had started out kind, until jealousy of the children's place in his heart grew inside her. What was the stepmother's name?
context: Aoife (EE-fa) is the sister of Lir's dead first wife Aoibh. Boann is the goddess of the River Boyne, mother of Aengus. Medb is the queen of Connacht in the Ulster cycle Tain. Sadhbh is Fionn mac Cumhaill's deer-wife, mother of Oisin -- also a shape-shifting story, but a different one.  (Legend.)

question: Lir came on his four children out on the water, changed in body by their stepmother's druid rod, and still he knew them. Two very human gifts had stayed inside them for the whole of the curse. Which two gifts did they keep?
context: In every telling of Oidheadh Chlainne Lir the four kept human speech and human reason inside the swan-shape -- Fionnuala could still tell her father Lir what Aoife had done, and the four could still sing plaintive songs that were said to be the sweetest in Ireland. Only the bodies were changed.  (Legend.)

question: A jealous stepmother cursed Lir's four small children, and the curse trapped them on cold lakes and stormy seas around Ireland, unable to return to human form. Everyone who had known them as children was long dead before it ended. How long in all did the curse last?
context: The curse lasted nine hundred years in total, divided into three periods of three hundred: first on the peaceful Lake Derravaragh in Westmeath; then on the cold Sea of Moyle between Ireland and Scotland; then on the wild Atlantic off the Isle of Inishglora in the west. Only after all nine centuries would the conditions of the curse's ending come together.  (Legend.)

question: The four children of Lir left the calm lake in Westmeath and beat their wings out over a narrow northern channel notorious for its storms and freezing spray. It was the hardest of their three exiles, and the tale lingers there longest. What does the tale call that water?
context: Sruth na Maoile, the Sea of Moyle, is the narrow strait between the north-east coast of Antrim and the Mull of Kintyre in Scotland -- notorious for hard weather, and the specific water the tale names for the second exile. The North Channel is a broader modern name for waters overlapping that area. The Minch is off the Scottish Hebrides. The Irish Sea is the wider basin south of it. The middle exile is always specifically the Moyle.  (Legend.)

question: The eldest child of Lir came through the black freezing nights of the northern sea with her three younger brothers beside her. One thing she did for them there made her the emblem of Irish sisterhood. What did she do for her brothers?
answer: sheltered them beneath her wings against the spray
choices: sheltered them beneath her wings against the spray
sang the psalms she remembered from Lir's hall
led them south each night to warmer water
wove a nest of driftwood to hold them together
context: In every version of the tale Fionnuala, the eldest, wraps her three brothers under her outstretched wings on the black nights of the Moyle, warming them against the freezing sea-spray. That single image -- the sister sheltering her brothers -- is the emotional heart of the tale and the reason the Oisin Kelly sculpture stands in the Garden of Remembrance in Dublin as an emblem of Irish sisterly and national protection.  (Legend.)

question: The stepmother who struck Lir's children did not leave the curse open-ended. She named two conditions, and both had to come true in the same hour before the feathers would fall away. Which pair of conditions did she lay down?
answer: a woman of the south marries a man of the north, and Christian bells ring over Ireland
choices: a woman of the south marries a man of the north, and Christian bells ring over Ireland
the moon is full over the sea three nights running, and a swan is killed by an eagle
a druid drinks from the well of Segais, and a stag is seen at dawn beside it
the High King is crowned on the Tara stone, and a raven speaks aloud in his hall
context: The two conditions in the Aoife-curse: a woman of the south (Munster) must marry a man of the north (Connacht), and the bells of Christianity must sound across Ireland. Both come true at once when the hermit Mochaomhog rings his monastery-bells on the western island of Inishglora and news comes of the Munster-Connacht royal marriage. The curse breaks in the same hour.  (Legend.)

question: All four of Lir's children changed back into human shape on the shore of Inishglora, the western island, in the hour the curse broke at last. The feathers fell away and the long sentence was over. What kind of human bodies stood there in that moment?
answer: ancient shrunken bodies, lean and bony
choices: ancient shrunken bodies, lean and bony
young adults just as Lir had first known them
little children the same age Aoife had cursed
shining figures of light without weight
context: The transformation back into human shape ages them all nine centuries in an instant: the swans' feathers fall off to reveal three lean, bony old men and one old woman. Mochaomhog baptises them in that last hour, and they die and are buried together, Fionnuala in the middle with her three brothers under her arms as she had sheltered them on the Sea of Moyle.  (Legend.)

question: A medieval Irish tale-teller finished the fate of the children of Lir and reached for its two companions, the fate of the children of Uisneach (Deirdre's tale) and the fate of the children of Tuireann. Every Irish schoolchild for a century has learned the set by one name. What did the medieval Irish call it?
choices: the Three Laments of the Bards
context: Tri Truaighe na Scealaigheachta -- the Three Sorrows of Storytelling -- is the medieval Irish grouping of the three great tragic tales: Lir, Uisneach (Deirdre), and Tuireann. The other three choices are plausible-sounding invented Irish groupings of the same emotional register; the real fixed traditional name is 'the Three Sorrows of Storytelling'.

question: El Cid, the exiled Castilian knight of the Cantar de Mio Cid, ringed a city with his war-band and starved it out rather than storm it. The poem gives the length of the blockade plainly. How many months did the poet count?
context: The poem: 'Know that for nine months he penned them there. When the tenth arrived, they were forced to yield.' (Historically the siege lasted longer, from October 1092 to June 1094; the poem compresses it to nine.) Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Part III (poetryintranslation.com).  (Legend.)

question: Dona Jimena and her two young daughters stayed behind when King Alfonso VI sent the Cid into exile, in the medieval Spanish epic Cantar de Mio Cid. The poem says he left them safe at a Castilian monastery just outside Burgos, where they waited out the war. Which monastery kept the Cid's family?
context: San Pedro de Cardena, a Benedictine monastery just outside Burgos, sheltered Jimena and the daughters through the exile. The Cid himself was originally buried there before his tomb was moved to Burgos Cathedral. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Parts I and III; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.  (Legend.)

question: Two girls stood on the highest battlement of the alcazar of Valencia, staring out at the roofs of the city and the sea beyond. The Cid had brought his wife and their two daughters up there once the city had fallen, the poem's most tender image. In the Cantar de Mio Cid, what were the girls called?
context: The poem names them Dona Elvira and Dona Sol -- though the historical Cid's real daughters were called Cristina and Maria. The poet changed the names, and the poem's names are the ones that survived in Spanish story. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Part IV; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.  (Legend.)

question: The Cid broke the Moroccan relief army on the plain outside Valencia. The captured horses and gold from its camp would make every one of his men rich for life. He chose the finest horses of his own share and sent them across Castile as a gift to King Alfonso VI, the king who had once exiled him. How many did the poem have him send?
context: The poem: 'And lead a full two hundred to King Alfonso.' This gift is the pivot of the poem's second cantar -- the beginning of the Cid's reconciliation with the king who banished him. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Part IV.  (Legend.)

question: King Alfonso VI, softened by the Cid's gift and his growing fame, arranged a match for the Cid's two daughters: two young men of a great house he favoured. The Cid himself was uneasy about it, but the king insisted. The feasting at the church of Santa Maria in Valencia lasted fifteen days. Whom did the poem have the daughters marry?
context: The Infantes (princes) of Carrion, Fernando and Diego, are the villains of the third cantar -- the marriage ends in the outrage at the oak-wood of Corpes, where they beat the daughters and abandon them, and the Cid takes his vengeance in the king's court. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Parts III-IV.  (Legend.)

question: Rodrigo Diaz won the respect of even his Muslim foes with his skill in battle, fighting for Castile against the rulers of the south. They gave him a short Arabic title meaning 'lord' or 'master.' By what name do Spanish songs and chronicles call him?
context: 'Cid' comes from Arabic 'sayyid' meaning lord -- a title of respect his Muslim opponents used, which stuck to him permanently in the Castilian tradition. Caudillo (leader), alcalde (mayor), and adelantado (frontier governor) are all real Spanish titles, but not his. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: A huge Muslim army from Morocco sat outside the walls of Valencia when the Cid died in his palace there on 10 July 1099. It was ready to take back the great east-coast city he had captured in 1094, once his death was known. Which North African Berber empire was besieging the city?
context: The Almoravids -- a Berber dynasty from what is now Morocco and Mauritania -- had crossed into Spain in 1086 and were the great new threat to Christian and independent principalities alike. The Almohads came a generation later; the Umayyads were the earlier caliphs of Cordoba; the Nasrids were the last Muslim dynasty of Granada. All real, only the Almoravids fit 1099. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: The Cid's widow took charge of the deception inside Valencia: nobody outside must learn that he was dead, or morale would collapse. She was a noblewoman who had stayed beside him through his years of exile. What was her name?
context: Dona Jimena Diaz, a noblewoman of Asturias, was the Cid's wife; she took over the defence of Valencia in the days after his death. Urraca, Berenguela, and Constanza are all real names of medieval Castilian and Leonese queens or noblewomen -- adjacent, wrong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: Later chroniclers tell how the Cid's widow had his corpse strapped into the saddle to lead his warband, and how the besiegers broke and ran. The saddle sat on the same warhorse he had ridden into battle for years, the one the Cantar de Mio Cid praises as without equal in the world. What was the horse called?
context: Babieca is the Cid's warhorse in the Cantar and every later chronicle. Bucephalus was Alexander the Great's warhorse; Sleipnir was Odin's eight-legged horse in Norse myth; Veillantif was Roland's horse in the Song of Roland -- all real named steeds of Western legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babieca.

question: The Cid's widow held Valencia for about three years after his death in 1099, with North African armies pressing at the walls. He had captured the great city from its Moorish rulers and governed it as its own lord. What did she do in 1102?
answer: she abandoned the city and carried her husband's body west to Castile
choices: she abandoned the city and carried her husband's body west to Castile
she was killed on the walls in a final Almoravid assault on the palace
she surrendered the city to King Alfonso the Sixth as a Christian fief
she turned the palace into a fortified nunnery and stayed to defend it
context: History records that Jimena held Valencia until 1102 and then, unable to hold on longer against the Almoravids, evacuated the city (burning it as she left, according to some chronicles) and carried her husband's body west to Castile. The legendary phantom-charge belongs to story, not to what really happened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: A mysterious woman comes to live in secret with Crunniuc, a widowed farmer of Ulster. She blesses his home with wealth and swiftness and asks only one thing in return: he must never boast about her to strangers. Which figure of Irish myth is she?
context: Macha is a supernatural woman of Ulster, variously called a goddess of the land or one of the three Morrigna sisters, who comes to live in secret with the widower Crunniuc mac Agnomain. Deirdre is the tragic heroine of a different Ulster tale; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife; Brigid is a Tuatha De goddess of the flame. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: King Conchobar sends for Crunniuc's wife after the farmer boasts, drunk at the royal assembly, that she can outrun the king's chariot-team. Heavy with child, she begs to be spared, but the king refuses and forces her to race his horses on foot. What happens as she crosses the finish line?
answer: she collapses in labour and delivers twins on the field
choices: she collapses in labour and delivers twins on the field
she is trampled under the hooves of the king's team
she runs on past the line and out of Ulster forever
she throws herself on the king's spear in front of the crowd
context: Macha wins the race and, in the same breath, delivers twins on the ground -- a boy named Fir ('True') and a girl named Fial ('Modest'). The double birth in front of the whole assembly is the moment that gives Emain Macha its name: 'the twins of Macha.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: Crunniuc's wife lies dying on the field at King Conchobar's assembly, and she calls down a curse on all the fighting men of Ulster within hearing. In the hour of the province's greatest need, she says, they shall suffer one particular sharp pain. What pain is it?
answer: the pangs of a woman in labour
choices: the pangs of a woman in labour
the fever that comes with the plague of the crows
the palsy that seizes the sword-hand of the perjurer
the thirst that no water in Ireland can slake
context: The Ulstermen must feel the same labour-pain Macha herself has just felt -- for five days and four nights (or five nights and four days, versions vary) whenever the province is invaded, and the curse binds nine generations. It is a wholly unique motif in world myth. Source: storyarchaeology.com/noinden-ulad-the-story-of-macha; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: Queen Medb of Connacht drives her army across the Ulster border in the Tain Bo Cuailnge, the great cattle-raid epic, to seize the Brown Bull of Cooley. The fighting-men of Ulster, king, princes and champions alike, are helpless to stop her. Why can none of them fight?
answer: they are all bedridden by the curse Macha laid on their forefathers
choices: they are all bedridden by the curse Macha laid on their forefathers
they are away at a great feast in Emain Macha and cannot be recalled
they are bound by an oath of peace with Connacht that Conchobar refuses to break
they have all been paralysed by a druid of Medb's court in advance of the war
context: Macha's curse is the mythic pre-condition of the Tain: at the hour of Ulster's greatest need the whole fighting force is on its back in labour-pain, for nine generations, for five days and four nights at a stretch. It is what makes Cu Chulainn's one-man defence necessary and honourable. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: An army marches on Ulster, and as at every invasion a dying woman's curse falls on the province's fighting-men. The weakness does not settle in for good: it comes in bouts of a fixed length, and that is what lets the province survive. How long is a single bout said to last?
choices: one full turning of the moon
context: Each bout of noinden Ulad lasts five days and four nights (or, in some manuscripts, five nights and four days -- the compilers disagree), and the curse binds nine generations of Ulster fighting-men. That the debility comes in short, sharp bouts -- and not as a permanent blight -- is what lets the province survive at all. Source: storyarchaeology.com/noinden-ulad-the-story-of-macha.  (Legend.)

question: Homer's Odysseus led twelve of his best men into a cave on an island of giant shepherds, the Cyclopes, on his way home from Troy. He hoped for a guest-gift from its owner. What was the name of the man-eating giant who lived there?
context: Polyphemus is a Cyclops, a huge one-eyed shepherd giant. His cave is the setting for the most famous single episode of the Odyssey. (Odyssey 9; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: The Cyclops of Homer's Odyssey came home with his flock while Odysseus and his men were waiting in the cave for a guest-gift. He sealed the cave mouth behind him with something no ordinary man could budge. What did he roll across it?
context: Polyphemus seals the cave with a massive stone that no ordinary man could shift. Odysseus and his crew cannot simply kill the giant in his sleep, because then they would never be able to move the stone. (Odyssey 9; cliffsnotes.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus built his whole escape plan around one target on the giant who was eating his crew two at a time. The Cyclops had only one of a feature that every man of the crew had two of. Which feature was it?
context: Cyclopes are one-eyed giants. Blinding that single eye is the crux of Odysseus's escape plan -- with the giant blind, the crew can slip past him when he opens the cave. (Odyssey 9; cliffsnotes.com.)  (Legend.)

question: The surviving crewmen worked in secret with Odysseus while the giant was out with his flocks. They took his own great staff, sharpened it into a huge pointed weapon and hardened its point in the fire. What wood was the staff made of?
context: The staff is olive-wood, the sacred tree of Athena. Odysseus and his men shape and fire-harden the point, then hide it, waiting for the giant to fall asleep. (Odyssey 9; cliffsnotes.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus offered the giant a skin of very strong wine on the evening the Cyclops ate two more of his men. The drunk giant, pleased, asked what his guest was called, so that he could offer a proper gift in return. What name did Odysseus give?
context: Odysseus says: 'Outis is my name; my mother, my father, my friends call me Outis.' 'Outis' is Greek for 'Nobody.' The giant, pleased, promises: 'I will eat Nobody last, after all his friends.' (Odyssey 9.366-367; Wikipedia: Outis.)  (Legend.)

question: Four picked men took up the sharpened stake with Odysseus once the drunk giant had passed out. They heated it red in the fire and drove it home, blinding him. Homer compared their work with the burning stake to a shipwright doing what with a beam?
context: Homer writes that they turn the burning stake in the giant's eye 'as a shipwright bores a beam with a drill' -- one of the most famous similes in the Odyssey. (Odyssey 9.383-388; theoi.com.)  (Legend.)

question: The other Cyclopes on the island heard the giant roaring in agony and came running to the mouth of his cave, shouting in, asking who was hurting him. Because of the name Odysseus had given, the answer the giant shouted back made them turn round and leave. What did they conclude was happening to him?
context: The wounded giant screams 'Nobody is killing me!' The other Cyclopes hear 'no man' and conclude it must be a sickness sent by Zeus that no mortal can help with -- so they leave. (Odyssey 9; Wikipedia: Outis.)  (Legend.)

question: The blind giant rolled back the great stone in the morning to let his flock out to pasture. He sat in the opening and felt each animal with his hands as it passed, to make sure no man rode out on top. How did Odysseus and his men get past those searching hands?
answer: Tied to the bellies of the rams
choices: Tied to the bellies of the rams
Rolled up in the giant's own fleece cloaks
Standing on the shoulders of the biggest sheep
context: Odysseus lashes each surviving man to the belly of one of the giant's rams -- and clings himself to the belly of the biggest ram. The blind Polyphemus feels only wool on the backs of the animals as the flock passes. (Odyssey 9; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus was safely back on his ship and pulling away from the shore when he did the one thing he would regret for the next ten years of wandering. He could not help himself, and he shouted something back across the water to the blinded giant. What did he shout?
choices: A curse on the whole island
context: Odysseus taunts the blinded Polyphemus by shouting his true name across the water -- his one great mistake. Now the giant knows exactly whom to curse. (Odyssey 9; sparknotes.com/lit/odyssey.)  (Legend.)

question: The giant blinded by Odysseus lifted his hands and prayed to his own father to punish the man, in Homer's Odyssey. At last he knew who had done it, and his father was a powerful Olympian who would hear him. Which god was the father of the Cyclops?
context: Polyphemus is a son of Poseidon, god of the sea, and a sea-nymph. That parentage is why his curse has real weight over the whole Odyssey -- Odysseus is at sea, in Poseidon's domain, for another ten years. (Odyssey 9; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outis.)  (Legend.)

question: The Cyclops made a precise prayer against Odysseus, in Homer's telling. He did not ask that Odysseus die on the way home. He asked for two conditions that shaped the rest of the poem's story. How did he pray Odysseus would reach home?
context: Polyphemus prays that Odysseus either never reach home, or if he must, that he reach it LATE and ALONE and find his house in trouble. Poseidon hears, and that prayer is the reason the Odyssey lasts ten years and Odysseus arrives home without a single crewman left. (Odyssey 9; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus met a Cyclops in Book 9 of the Odyssey, and the name of the giant's race described him. One Greek root of the name, kyklo-, meant 'circle' or 'round.' The other named a single part of the body. What did 'Cyclops' literally mean?
context: 'Cyclops' comes from kyklo- ('circle', 'round') plus -ops ('eye') -- so 'round-eye'. The one great circular eye is the defining feature. (cliffsnotes.com.)

question: A huge, red-bearded, big-bellied god in a hooded cloak walks at the head of the Tuatha De Danann in Irish myth. His people praise him, not for kindness but because he is skilled at every craft: war, magic, poetry, husbandry, cooking. Who is he?
context: The Dagda is the father-figure of the Tuatha De Danann -- his name means 'the good god' in the sense of 'good at everything.' Nuada Silver-Arm is the first king of the Tuatha De but loses the throne through his wound; Lugh Lamhfhada is Nuada's grandson, master of every art; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god who later divides the fairy mounds among the Tuatha De. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda drags his club behind him as he walks, and it cuts a long ditch in the ground wherever he goes. Eight ordinary men together cannot lift it. What name do the old tales give this weapon?
context: Lorg Mor means simply 'the great staff' in Old Irish. The Gae Bolg is Cuchulainn's belly-spear; the Claiomh Solais is the Sword of Light belonging to Nuada; the Gai Assail is Lugh's victory-spear -- three other famous Irish weapons, each with its own story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda; worldhistory.org/The_Dagda/.  (Legend.)

question: A company of warriors eats its fill from the Dagda's great cauldron, brought out of the northern city of Murias. Every man draws out as much food as his hunger calls for, and the more the cauldron is emptied the more it fills. What is this cauldron called?
context: Coire Ansic means 'the un-dry cauldron' in Old Irish. The Cauldrons of Ceridwen, Bran, and Annwn all belong to the WELSH branch of Celtic tradition -- real cauldrons from a sister tradition, but not the Dagda's Irish cauldron. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.  (Legend.)

question: The Fomorians drink in their feast-hall after the Second Battle of Moytura, with the Dagda's stolen harp hung on the wall. It will answer to no voice but his. He walks in among them and calls it aloud by its two secret names, and it tears itself free. What happens as it flies through the hall to his hand?
answer: It kills nine Fomorians on its flight
choices: It kills nine Fomorians on its flight
It sings the Fomorians dead where they sit
It turns to gold in mid-air
It calls fire down onto the roof-beams
context: The scene is Cath Maige Tuired sec 162. The Dagda calls 'Come Daur Da Bla, come Coir Cetharchair' and the harp answers, killing nine Fomorians as it flies past them. Only then does he play its three great strains. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T300010.html.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda sits down among the beaten Fomorians with his harp back in his hand and plays three great strains. The first is the Goltrai, the weeping strain, and no man hearing it can hold back tears. The third is the Suantrai, the sleeping strain, and all in earshot fall into a deep sleep. What is the strain between them called?
context: The three great strains of the Dagda's harp are Goltrai (weeping), Geantrai (laughing), and Suantrai (sleeping) -- fixed in Irish tradition as the Three Noble Strains of harp music down to the modern day. The other three names in the list are inventions on the same pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uaithne.  (Legend.)

question: The Fomorians dig a great pit to humiliate the Dagda through his own hunger, in the saga Cath Maige Tuired. Into it go eighty gallons of new milk, an equal weight of meal and fat, and whole herds of sheep, pigs and goats boiled together. Their king tells him he will be killed unless he eats every last drop. How big is the ladle they set beside the pit?
answer: Big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the middle of it
choices: Big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the middle of it
Big enough to carry the head of an ox in one scoop
Big enough to bail a small boat with
Big enough to serve nine warriors at once
context: The line is preserved verbatim from Cath Maige Tuired sec 89: the ladle 'was big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the middle of it.' The Dagda eats the whole pit, and afterwards his belly is 'as big as a house cauldron' and the Fomorians laugh at him. The rude humour of the scene was kept intact by the Christian monk-copyists. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T300010.html.  (Legend.)

question: In the Irish tale Cath Maige Tuired, the Dagda goes to fetch his stolen harp from the Fomorians. It is called Uaithne, but it will not fly to his hand unless he addresses it by both of its secret bynames. One byname is Coir Cetharchair, 'Four-Angled Music.' What is the other?
answer: Daur Da Bla, 'Oak of Two Meadows'
choices: Daur Da Bla, 'Oak of Two Meadows'
context: The two names are preserved together in Cath Maige Tuired sec 162: Daur Da Bla and Coir Cetharchair. The wood-and-tree choices are inventions on Irish-sounding patterns -- yew, hazel, and Nuada's harp all live elsewhere in Irish tradition but none is the Dagda's harp-name. The 'four-angled' name is thought to describe the frame's shape. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uaithne.  (Legend.)
