question: A woman washes bloody armour at a ford on the night before the Second Battle of Moytura, and the Dagda meets her there. It is Samhain, when the walls between worlds grow thin, and a washer at the ford is a sign of death for the men whose armour she scrubs. She lies with him, and in return promises him the destruction of the Fomorian king. Which of the Tuatha De is she?
choices: Danu, mother of the Tuatha De
context: The tryst at the ford of the Unius on Samhain is one of the most famous scenes of Irish myth. The washer-at-the-ford scrubbing the armour of doomed men is the Morrigan's signature image. Brigid is the Dagda's daughter, goddess of the flame at Kildare; Danu is the ancestress the whole Tuatha De are named for; Aine is a sun-and-sovereignty goddess of Munster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda walks the shore of Traigh Eabha after the Fomorians' mocking porridge, with a belly as big as a house cauldron, and there he meets a young woman. She satirises him in verse, blocks his way by turning into obstacles and demands that he carry her on his back. Who is she?
answer: the daughter of the Fomorian king Indech
choices: the daughter of the Fomorian king Indech
the daughter of the Fir Bolg king Eochaid
the daughter of the Milesian druid Amergin
the daughter of the Ulster king Conchobar
context: Indech mac De Domnann is the Fomorian king who served the porridge, and it is his daughter the Dagda meets on the shore afterwards -- a wonderfully rude scene kept intact by the medieval monks. Eochaid, Amergin, and Conchobar belong to other cycles of Irish tradition. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T300010.html.  (Legend.)

question: In the book of Acts, Saul of Tarsus, a strict young Pharisee, set out from Jerusalem with letters from the high priest. They gave him authority to arrest any Christians in the synagogues of one city and drag them back in chains. What city was Saul heading to that day?
context: Acts 9:1-2 (KJV): 'And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest, and desired of him letters to Damascus to the synagogues, that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem.' Damascus at the time held a substantial Jewish community; hunting Christ-followers there was Saul's next planned raid.

question: Saul of Tarsus was on the road at midday, going out to hunt more Christians, when a light shone round him from the sky. It came suddenly, and it did one thing to him at once. What did the light do to Saul in that instant?
answer: It knocked him to the ground
choices: It knocked him to the ground
It set his cloak on fire
It made his horse rear up and bolt
It froze him where he stood
context: Acts 9:3-4 (KJV): 'And as he journeyed, he came near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven: And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him...' The horse everyone remembers from paintings (Caravaggio, Michelangelo) is nowhere in the text -- Acts just says Saul fell.

question: A voice called Saul of Tarsus twice by name as he lay stunned on the road, on his way to arrest Christians. That moment would turn him into the apostle Paul. What did the voice say?
choices: 'Saul, Saul, thy sins be forgiven thee'
context: Acts 9:4 (KJV). The double name -- 'Saul, Saul' -- is a biblical marker of direct divine address (compare 'Abraham, Abraham', 'Moses, Moses', 'Samuel, Samuel'). The point is startling: the voice does not accuse Saul of persecuting the disciples; it says Saul is persecuting the speaker himself.

question: Saul of Tarsus called back into the blinding light, trembling: 'Who art thou, Lord?' He had set out to make arrests in the synagogues, and a voice from the sky had just called to him, asking why Saul was persecuting him. What name did the voice give itself?
context: Acts 9:5 (KJV): 'And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest.' For a Pharisee hunting a heretical sect, hearing that the crucified rabbi is not only alive but identifying himself with the hunted is the whole hinge of the story.

question: Saul's companions took him by the hand and guided him into the city, because he had stood up on the road and opened his eyes and could see nothing. For how long did the blindness last, during which he neither ate nor drank?
context: Acts 9:8-9 (KJV): 'And Saul arose from the earth; and when his eyes were opened, he saw no man: but they led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus. And he was three days without sight, and neither did eat nor drink.' The three-day-in-darkness beat deliberately echoes Jonah in the fish and Jesus in the tomb.

question: Ananias, a disciple already living in the city where the blinded Saul lay, received a vision. It sent him to the house of one Judas to find the man. It even gave him the actual street to look for. What was that street called in the book of Acts?
context: Acts 9:11 (KJV): 'Arise, and go into the street which is called Straight, and enquire in the house of Judas for one called Saul, of Tarsus: for, behold, he prayeth.' The Via Recta ran east-west across Roman Damascus; a stretch of it is still walkable in the old city today.

question: Ananias objected when a vision told him to go and find Saul of Tarsus, for this Saul was the very man jailing his fellow Christians. But he obeyed anyway, entered the house where Saul lay, and laid hands on the blinded persecutor. How did Ananias greet Saul as he did so?
context: Acts 9:17 (KJV): 'And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost.' 'Brother' -- from the disciple whose friends Saul had come to arrest -- is the first word of Christian welcome Saul ever hears.

question: Saul's sight returned to him instantly when the disciple Ananias laid hands on him in a house in the city. The book of Acts describes something visible dropping away from his eyes at that very moment. What did Acts say fell from Saul's eyes?
context: Acts 9:18 (KJV): 'And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized.' The Greek word (lepides) is the ordinary word for fish-scales. The literal image is the point: Saul's spiritual blindness comes off like a fish being cleaned.

question: Saul of Tarsus was baptised, and he did not hide. He began preaching at once in the very synagogues he had come to raid a few days before as a Pharisee. What was the message of the sermons he preached in those first days?
answer: that Jesus is the Son of God
choices: that Jesus is the Son of God
that the Temple in Jerusalem would fall
that the Gentiles need not be circumcised
that the end of the world was at hand
context: Acts 9:20 (KJV): 'And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.' The reversal is total: the man sent to arrest the sect now stands in the same synagogue pulpits proclaiming its central claim.

question: Saul's enemies set watchmen at the city gates day and night to kill him, once his preaching had made him a target. To smuggle him safely out, the disciples took him up onto the city wall at night and lowered him down the outside. What did the disciples lower Saul in?
context: Acts 9:25 (KJV): 'Then the disciples took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket.' The Greek word (spuris) is the big woven hamper used for grain or dung -- the same word used for the seven baskets left over after Jesus fed the four thousand. The dignity of the future apostle to the Gentiles starts with being lowered down a wall in a farm hamper.

question: Paul wrote to the Corinthians about his hardships years later, and he boasted of the humiliating escape from the city he had once set out to raid. In his own words, he was let down by the wall 'and escaped his hands.' Which ruler's officer did Paul name as the one who had been trying to seize him?
context: 2 Corinthians 11:32-33 (KJV): 'In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me: And through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands.' Aretas IV of Nabataea controlled Damascus in the mid-30s AD. Paul lists this escape at the bottom of a boast-list of beatings and shipwrecks, deliberately closing on the least heroic image he can find.

question: A warrior of twenty-seven goes to his last fight in the closing tale of the Ulster Cycle. He trained on the Isle of Shadow and carries the belly-spear, and once held a border alone while a curse left Ulster helpless. Who is he?
context: Conchobar and Fergus are kings of Ulster in the same cycle; Fionn belongs to the later Fenian Cycle. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: One woman raises the war-band that will finally kill Cu Chulainn. He wrecked her famous cattle-raid years before and cost her a champion, and now she calls together the sons of all the men he has killed. Who is she?
context: Medb of Connacht had lost her champion Ferdiad and much of her army in the Tain Bo Cuailnge; she draws the sons of every man Cu Chulainn ever killed into one war-band. Emer is Cu Chulainn's own wife; Deirdre is from the Sons of Uisliu tale; Grainne belongs to the Fenian Cycle. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: An old crone by the roadside offers Cu Chulainn a hospitality-meal on the way to his last fight, and by the ancient rule against refusing a host he cannot say no. Under his geasa, his personal taboos, one meat is forbidden him. What meat does she put in front of him?
context: His name means 'the Hound of Culann' -- eating dog is his forbidden meat. Refusing hospitality is equally forbidden, so the crone traps him coming and going. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn, mortally wounded, refuses to fall before his enemies. He drags himself to a tall granite pillar in a field in County Louth, ties himself upright to it with his own belt and dies on his feet, so that even in death he still seems to stand guard. That ten-foot stone still stands in what has long been called the Field of Slaughter. What is the stone called?
context: Clochafarmore stands in Rathiddy Townland near Knockbridge, County Louth. The Lia Fail is the coronation stone at Tara; the Blarney Stone is in Cork; the Turoe Stone is a decorated La Tene pillar in Galway. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn; Voices from the Dawn.  (Legend.)

question: The men of the war-band stand off at a distance from the dying hero, tied upright with his sword still in his hand. For days they wait for a sign that he is truly dead: a bird on his shoulder, the bird of the war-goddess he once refused. Which bird finally lands?
context: The raven is the Morrigan, the war-goddess in bird-form; her landing to drink his blood is the confirmation his enemies have been waiting for. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: The leader of the war-band finally dares to walk up to the standing corpse and cut off the head, now that the sign has come. As his blade comes down, the sword falls from the hero's grip and takes a price from the killer. Who is the killer, and what does he lose?
answer: Lugaid mac Con Roi -- he loses his own hand
choices: Lugaid mac Con Roi -- he loses his own hand
Erc mac Cairpre -- he loses his shield-arm
Cet mac Matach -- he loses his sword-arm
Ailill mac Mata -- he loses his chariot-horse
context: The falling sword severs Lugaid's hand -- one final blow from a corpse. Wikipedia: Lugaid mac Con Roi.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn's foster-brother tracks down the killer to settle the account. The man has only one hand left, so to keep the fight fair the foster-brother ties one of his own hands into his belt. Even so he cannot finish it until his warhorse takes a bite out of the man's side. Who is the avenger?
context: Conall's fair-fight code -- matching Lugaid's missing hand -- is a standing image in the Ulster Cycle; the horse's bite is his own warhorse Dub-Sainglend. Wikipedia: Lugaid mac Con Roi.  (Legend.)

question: The sculptor Oliver Sheppard shaped the dying Cu Chulainn in bronze in 1911 and 1912, lashed upright to his stone. Eamon de Valera later had the statue set up as the official memorial to one rising. In which building was it installed, and for which rising?
answer: in Dublin's General Post Office, for the 1916 Easter Rising
choices: in Dublin's General Post Office, for the 1916 Easter Rising
in Kilmainham Gaol, for the 1798 Rebellion
in Dublin Castle, for the 1867 Fenian Rising
in Trinity College, for the 1803 Emmet Rising
context: Oliver Sheppard's 'The Death of Cuchulain' was unveiled at the GPO in Easter Week 1935 as the official memorial to the 1916 Rising -- the GPO having been the rebels' headquarters. Wikipedia: Oliver Sheppard.

question: Joshua sent about three thousand men against the small town of Ai, in the book named for him, right after Jericho fell. He expected an easy win. Instead they were routed at the gate, and the book counts the Israelite dead exactly. How many died?
context: Joshua 7:5 KJV: 'And the men of Ai smote of them about thirty and six men.' Six hundred belongs to Samson's slaughter with the jawbone; seventy is a common biblical count (the seventy elders, the seventy nations); twelve hundred is a plausible battle-loss but not the number Joshua 7 records. The thirty-six is famously SMALL -- and that is the sting.

question: A thief in the camp of Israel had secretly taken loot from fallen Jericho, in the Book of Joshua, and Joshua drew lots to find him. He drew for the twelve tribes, then for families inside the guilty tribe, then for houses, then for one man at a time. Who did the lot fall on?
context: Joshua 7:18 KJV: 'and Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.' Nadab is Aaron's son consumed by fire for offering strange incense; Korah leads the wilderness rebellion swallowed by the earth; Zimri son of Salu is pierced by Phinehas at Peor -- all three real biblical judgement-stories on other men.

question: The guilty man stood before Joshua and confessed. He listed the three things he had taken from the sacked city and buried in the dirt floor of his tent: two hundred shekels of silver, a wedge of gold weighing fifty shekels, and one thing more. He called that third thing a 'goodly' what?
context: Joshua 7:21 KJV: 'When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight... I coveted them, and took them.' Persian robes, Egyptian mantles, and Philistine cloaks all appear elsewhere in the Bible as spoil-types, but Achan's specific loot is Babylonish -- a name that would have meant 'foreign luxury from far Mesopotamia' to the hearer.

question: Thirty thousand men lay hidden behind Ai for Joshua's second attack, while he drew the defenders out with a pretended retreat. At the right moment, in the Book of Joshua, God told him to give the signal: 'Stretch out the ___ that is in thy hand toward Ai.' What was he to stretch out?
context: Joshua 8:18 KJV: 'Stretch out the spear that is in thy hand toward Ai; for I will give it into thine hand. And Joshua stretched out the spear that he had in his hand toward the city.' Moses's stretched-out staff parts the Red Sea and defeats Amalek at Rephidim, and Aaron's rod buds in the tabernacle -- both are real staff-signals in scripture, but at Ai the sign is Joshua's spear.

question: Joshua stood before all Israel, years after Ai, defending the men of Gibeon against five Amorite kings, and he asked for something no one had ever asked. The Book of Joshua gives his command: 'Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of ____.' Which valley did he name for the moon?
context: Joshua 10:12 KJV: 'Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.' Elah is where David meets Goliath; Sorek is where Samson meets Delilah; Kidron is the brook Jesus crosses to Gethsemane -- all real biblical valleys, all wrong for this scene. Ajalon is the paired half of the sun-and-moon verse and the half people always forget.

question: Israel's army fought a league of Canaanite kings, and Joshua asked God to hold the sun still in the sky, so that the day of battle would last long enough to win. The next verse of the Book of Joshua breaks off to name an outside record for the moment, an ancient book now lost. Which book was it?
choices: the book of the Wars of the LORD
the book of the Chronicles of the Kings
context: Joshua 10:13 KJV: 'Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven.' The book of Jasher ('the Upright') is quoted twice in scripture (also 2 Samuel 1:18 for David's lament for Saul and Jonathan) and is now lost. The book of the Wars of the LORD is cited in Numbers 21; Chronicles-of-the-Kings is cited throughout Kings; Enoch is a later apocryphal book quoted in Jude.

question: Homer's Odysseus asked a witch for the road home to Ithaca, and she told him he must first reach the edge of the world and speak with the dead. She had turned his men into pigs and kept his crew a year. Who was she?
context: Circe, who had turned Odysseus's men into pigs and then become his lover for a year on the island of Aeaea, gives him the sailing directions for the Halls of Hades: cross the river Ocean to the western edge of the world. Source: Homer, Odyssey 10.487-540.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus reached the dark shore at the edge of the world, drew his sword and dug a small pit to summon the dead, so that he could speak to the ghost of the prophet Tiresias. Into the pit he poured a set of liquids, one after another. What did he pour?
answer: Milk with honey, then wine, then water
choices: Milk with honey, then wine, then water
context: The pit is a libation-trench: sweet milk with honey first, then sweet wine, then plain water, and sprinkled barley on top. Only after the libations does Odysseus cut the throats of the sacrifice animals into the same trench. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.24-28.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus stood over his trench at the edge of the world and cut the throats of his sacrifice, letting the blood pool inside for the thirsty dead. The victims had been chosen with care by their colour. What did he sacrifice at the trench?
answer: A black ram and a black ewe
choices: A black ram and a black ewe
A pure white bull and a pure white heifer
A red rooster and a white dove
context: Black victims were the standard offering for the powers of the underworld, as white victims were for the sky gods. Circe herself had picked out this pair from her own flocks. Source: Homer, Odyssey 10.571-574 and 11.34-36.  (Legend.)

question: The shades of the dead crowded around the trench, and Odysseus had to drive them back with his sword. Homer's dead had lost most of what they were in life, and until a shade had drunk the blood there was one thing it could not do. What was that one thing?
context: Homer's underworld is a place of witless shades who drift without memory or voice; the black blood restores just enough of the living power to hold a conversation. It is the reason Odysseus can even question Tiresias. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.34-50.  (Legend.)

question: The youngest man on Odysseus's ship got drunk on a witch's roof on the crew's last night ashore, in Homer's Odyssey, fell off it and broke his neck. Two days later his was the very first shade to reach the pit at the edge of the world. What was his name?
context: Elpenor is the youngest and least warlike of the crew; his body was left unburied in the rush to leave Aeaea. His shade begs Odysseus to sail back and bury him properly. Source: Homer, Odyssey 10.552-560 and 11.51-83.  (Legend.)

question: A dead crewman's shade came to the pit at the edge of the world and begged Odysseus to sail back and bury him properly, for his body still lay on the witch's island. He also asked that one object be planted upright on the beach as his grave-marker. What object?
context: The oar as grave-marker becomes a small poem inside the epic: the tool a rower spent his life pulling, planted upright over him in the sand. Odysseus does go back and does this. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.71-78 and 12.8-15.  (Legend.)

question: The blind seer Tiresias told Odysseus, at the pit of the dead, that even after he got home he must one day take an oar and walk inland from Ithaca. He was to keep walking until he came to a country where the people had never seen the sea. He would know he was there when a stranger, seeing the oar on his shoulder, mistook it for what?
context: A winnowing fan is the shovel-shaped tool a farmer uses to toss threshed grain into the air so the wind carries off the chaff. When someone that far inland saw Odysseus's oar and called it a winnowing fan, he was to plant the oar there and sacrifice a ram, a bull and a boar to Poseidon -- and the sea god's anger would end. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.121-137.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus's dead mother Anticleia came up to the pit in Homer's Odyssey, and he reached out to fold her in his arms. She had died of grief while he was away at Troy, and now his arms passed through her like mist. How many times did he try to hold her before he understood?
context: Three times he lunged forward to hold his mother Anticleia, and each time -- in the famous simile -- his arms passed through her 'like a shadow, or like a dream' (Lattimore). Anticleia, daughter of Autolycus, told her son she had died of grief waiting for his return. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.204-208 and 11.152-224.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles, the greatest warrior of the Iliad, came up to the pit in Homer's Odyssey, drank the blood and spoke. He told Odysseus he would rather be alive in the meanest, humblest work on earth than hold a crown among the dead. What was the work he named?
answer: A hired hand of a landless man
choices: A hired hand of a landless man
A galley slave on a merchant's oar
A shepherd on a barren mountain
context: The line is Odyssey 11.489-491, in Lattimore's translation: 'I would rather follow the plow as thrall to another man, one with no land allotted him and not much to live on, than be a king over all the perished dead.' Achilles, who chose glory over long life in the Iliad, now saying he chose wrong. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.489-491.  (Legend.)

question: A great Greek warrior's shade came up to the pit in Homer's Odyssey and refused the blood. He had taken his own life at Troy after Odysseus was awarded Achilles' golden armour over him, and he had not forgiven the slight even in death. Odysseus called out to him to make peace. Which shade was it?
context: Ajax son of Telamon had lost the vote for Achilles's armor to Odysseus, and it had driven him mad and then to suicide -- he was still angry in death. His dignified silence at the pit is one of the most famous moments in Greek literature. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.541-565.  (Legend.)

question: Irish nationalists took an old word for their rebel name in the 19th century. It meant a small sworn company, and it was the name of Fionn mac Cumhaill's roving hunter-warriors, pledged to the High King of Ireland. What was the band called in Irish?
context: The Fianna are the warrior-hunter bands of Gaelic Ireland; the 19th-century Fenian Brotherhood of Irish republicans took the name deliberately, borrowing the ancient association with sworn warrior loyalty. The Aos Si are the fairy-folk; the Tuatha De Danann are the old gods; the Fomorians are the sea-born enemies of the gods. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fianna.  (Legend.)

question: Geoffrey Keating wrote in the 17th century that the Fianna spent half the year in the wild hunting for their food. They were not the king's regular army, and they lived outside the normal rules for land and marriage. Their months in the wild ran from Beltane until which other festival?
context: The Fianna are seasonal: from Beltane to Samhain (about May to November) they must live in the wild by hunting; from Samhain to Beltane they are quartered on the nobility. Lughnasadh is the harvest festival of Lugh; Imbolc marks the start of spring; the Newgrange solstice is Neolithic (millennia older than the Fianna). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fianna.  (Legend.)

question: A hopeful young man stood in a hole in the ground so deep it came up to the fold of his belt, while seasoned warriors hurled their spears at him all at once. It was one of the brutal entry-tests of the Fianna, set by the captain, Fionn mac Cumhaill. What two implements was the candidate given to defend himself?
answer: a shield and a fore-arm's length of hazel stick
choices: a shield and a fore-arm's length of hazel stick
a bronze sword and a leather sling
an iron helm and a wooden club
a spear and a woollen cloak
context: The pit-test forces the candidate to defend himself from the waist up while nine warriors cast spears at him. The hazel stick is not a weapon of offence -- it is a length just long enough to beat aside a hurled spear. Hazel is a symbolic wood in Irish tradition, associated with the Fianna's own hero Fionn (who burned his thumb on the Salmon of Knowledge cooked over hazel-wood). Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: In old Irish legend, a line of warriors formed up at a set distance from a young man buried to the belt in a pit, and they hurled their spears at him all at once. He wanted to join the Fianna, and if even one spear touched him he failed. How many warriors, and from what distance?
answer: nine warriors from nine furrows' width away
choices: nine warriors from nine furrows' width away
three warriors from three ridges away
seven warriors from a single bow-shot
twelve warriors from the length of a chariot-run
context: Silva Gadelica gives the numbers: 'nine warriors, having nine spears, with a ten furrows' width betwixt them and him' -- the sources vary between nine and ten furrows, but nine warriors is fixed. Nine is a recurring sacred number in Irish story (the nine hazels of Segais, the nine daughters of Manannan). Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: A war-band pursued a would-be member of the Fianna at full speed through a thick forest. The trial was not of brute strength alone: four small details of his person and gear were checked at the end of the run, and any one of them ruined would fail him. What was one of the four?
answer: not a plait of his hair might come loose in the branches
choices: not a plait of his hair might come loose in the branches
not a fleck of mud might spatter his shield-boss
not a tuft of moss might cling to his cloak-hem
not a smear of sap might mark his bow-stave
context: The braided-hair test measures poise, silence, and control at speed: a runner who bulls through the wood loses his plaits in the branches and fails. The same trial also disqualifies him if he cracks a dry stick underfoot, if his weapons quiver in his hand, or if he is caught or wounded -- four tests inside one run. Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: In the old Irish tales, a candidate for the Fianna leapt over every branch that came level with his brow, running alone through a deep forest with armed men behind him. He could not shake or break a single branch, and he could not slow his pace. He had to obey a second rule at the same time. What was that other rule?
answer: stoop under any bough level with his knee
choices: stoop under any bough level with his knee
shatter any branch level with his ribs
sing a stave of poetry between each stride
unstring and restring his bow one-handed
context: Silva Gadelica lists it in a single breath: 'he jumped a stick level with his brow, and stooped to pass under one even with his knee.' The pair is not choose-one; both had to be performed, mid-run, without any drop in speed. The other choices are invented parallels for testing shape. Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: Warriors of the Fianna chased a would-be member through a forest at a dead run, in the Fenian Cycle of Irish myth. Still at full pursuit, the candidate had one more feat to perform: he had to attend to his own injury without ever losing pace. What did he have to do?
answer: pluck a thorn from his own foot without slowing
choices: pluck a thorn from his own foot without slowing
bind a bleeding wrist one-handed while running
shake the pine-needles out of his eyes without looking down
swap the shield to the wounded arm on the run
context: The thorn-in-the-foot test is the strangest and best-remembered detail of the Fianna tests: a runner in a Gaelic forest picks up thorns constantly, and the candidate must reach down at full speed, extract the thorn cleanly, and never lose a step. All three other choices are shaped from the same run but are not the sourced trial. Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: Two old veterans of the Fianna outlived their band and told its stories to a churchman new to Ireland, in the Colloquy of the Ancients, and most of the Fenian tales survive because of them. One was Fionn's son, the poet Oisin. Who was the other, Fionn's kinsman, known as the swift-footed of the Fianna?
context: Caoilte mac Ronain co-narrates the Acallam na Senorach ('Colloquy of the Ancients,' c. 1200) with Oisin -- the longest surviving work of medieval Irish literature at some 8,000 lines. Diarmuid dies young at the boar-hunt of Ben Bulben; Oscar is Oisin's own son and dies at the Battle of Gabhra; Goll mac Morna is the leader of the rival Connacht Fianna, not Fionn's kinsman. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acallam_na_Sen%C3%B3rach.  (Legend.)

question: A churchman wept at the passing of the Fianna, in the Colloquy of the Ancients, and gave orders that the old veterans' stories be written down and preserved. He was drawn with unexpected warmth, not as a man hostile to the old ways. Which Irish saint was this listener?
context: The Acallam na Senorach frames Oisin and Caoilte as pagan warrior-survivors telling Patrick the old tales place by place across Ireland. Columba is the 6th-century founder of Iona; Kevin is the 6th-century hermit of the Wicklow mountains; Malachy is the 12th-century reformer of the Irish church. Patrick is the traditional 5th-century missionary and the only Irish saint the compiler could plausibly frame as contemporary with the last Fianna survivors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acallam_na_Sen%C3%B3rach.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann landed in Ireland, in the medieval Book of Invasions, and found one older people holding the whole island. They were the fourth of six waves of settlers, and the last before the new arrivals. Who were these people?
context: Lebor Gabala Erenn: the Fir Bolg are the fourth wave (after Cessair, Partholon, and Nemed), followed by the Tuatha De Danann as the fifth. The Milesians come sixth. The Fomorians are the monstrous sea-raiders, not a settler-wave. Danaans is a Greek term.  (Legend.)

question: A handful of survivors fled Ireland, in the Book of Invasions, after raids from the sea had almost wiped out their people. Their descendants later came back as the Fir Bolg. To which earlier wave of settlers did these survivors belong?
context: Lebor Gabala Erenn: after Fomorian raids reduced the people of Nemed to a handful, the survivors scattered; the group that went to Greece became the Fir Bolg and returned. Partholon's people had died of plague long before. Cessair's people all drowned in the Flood. The Fomorians are the sea-raider enemies, not ancestors.  (Legend.)

question: Caesar fought a Celtic confederation in Gaul, and some scholars tie the Fir Bolg to it rather than to any bag. Which people do they link to the Fir Bolg?
context: One scholarly proposal reads 'Bolg' as cognate with Belgae, the Continental Celtic confederation Caesar fought in Gaul and whose name survives in Belgium. The Helvetii were the Swiss-plateau Celts. The Iceni were Boudica's tribe in Britain. The Averni (Arverni) were Vercingetorix's people in central Gaul.

question: A slave of the people later called the Fir Bolg hauled a heavy leather sack up a bare rocky hillside for his master, in a foreign land far to the south. The Book of Invasions tells the story to explain their odd name, 'bag-men.' What did the sacks hold?
context: Lebor Gabala Erenn: the enslaved Nemedians were made to carry leather bags of earth up onto bare rocky hillsides to build soil for the crops of their masters. When they escaped they used the very same bags to stitch hide-boats and sailed home to Ireland. Hence 'men of bags'.  (Legend.)

question: The Fir Bolg broke free of their masters at last, stitched their leather bags into boats of hide and sailed home to Ireland. The Book of Invasions names the country of their slavery, the same land to which many of their scattered people had fled. Which land was it?
context: Lebor Gabala Erenn: the Nemedian survivors went to Greece and were enslaved there for many generations before returning to Ireland as the Fir Bolg. Spain is where the Milesians (the sixth wave) are said to have come from. Egypt and Britain do not figure in this part of the tale.  (Legend.)

question: Slainge mac Dela, king of the Fir Bolg, and his brothers cut the whole island of Ireland into provinces called coigeda, one for each brother. No other thing their people did outlasted that division. How many provinces did they make?
context: The Fir Bolg divided Ireland into five coigeda ('fifths' -- the Irish word 'cuig' still means five today): Ulster, Leinster, Munster, Connacht, and Mide (the sacred centre). Modern Ireland has four provinces because Mide was gradually absorbed into Leinster in the medieval period.  (Legend.)

question: The brothers who carved up Ireland for the Fir Bolg set a sacred middle kingdom at the centre of the island. Ulster, Leinster and Munster are still on the map, but this one was absorbed into Leinster in the Middle Ages, though its name lives on in a modern county. What was it called?
context: Mide (modern Meath) was the sacred central fifth, where the High King's seat at Tara stood. Tara is a hill within Mide, not a province. Brega and Uisneach are smaller sacred sites in the region, not the province itself. Meath survives in Ireland today as a county, not a province.  (Legend.)

question: The victors at Moytura, the Tuatha De Danann, treated the beaten survivors of the Fir Bolg with respect and offered them a single province to keep as their own for ever. To this day many families there proudly claim Fir Bolg ancestry. Which province did the Fir Bolg keep?
context: The surviving Fir Bolg were granted their pick of the five provinces and chose Connacht, the west. In later legend many Connacht families proudly claim Fir Bolg ancestry -- the Fir Bolg do not vanish; they retreat west and quietly persist. Per the Lebor Gabala, Connacht had already been assigned to the brother Genann in the original fivefold division.

question: One woman led the great cattle-raid against Cu Chulainn in the epic Tain Bo Cuailnge, and she ruled from a huge earthen fort in Roscommon, at Cruachan. That royal seat had once belonged to the Fir Bolg. Who was she?
context: Queen Medb (Maeve) of Connacht rules from Cruachan / Rath Croghan in Roscommon, on the site of the old Fir Bolg capital. Deirdre is the tragic heroine of the Sons of Uisnech. Macha is an earlier goddess-queen of Ulster. Emer is Cuchulainn's wife, not a Connacht queen.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod wrote to his brother Perses around 700 BC, in a long complaint about their father's land, and he buried a myth inside it. In it the world grew steadily worse, each race more wretched than the last. How many ages did he count?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 106-201. Hesiod counts five ages: Gold, Silver, Bronze, the Age of Heroes, and Iron. Four are named for metals; the Age of Heroes breaks the metal pattern. Centuries later Ovid compressed the schema down to four (dropping the Heroes); the biblical Book of Daniel 2.31-45 has a four-metal decline too, in Nebuchadnezzar's dream-statue.  (Legend.)

question: A first race of mortals feasted in an endless spring, Hesiod told, living like the gods with no toil, no old age and no winter. This happiest age came before Zeus was king. Which older god held the sky in that golden time?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 109-120. The first age was under Cronus, before Zeus overthrew him. Uranus is even earlier, the primal sky castrated by Cronus. Hades has always been king of the dead, never of heaven. When the golden race died out they did not go to Hades but became daimones -- benevolent spirits watching over the living.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod gave the second race in his myth a strange lifespan: a hundred years as little children at their mothers' side, then a short and foolish adulthood before they died. His first age had been golden, a time of ease and joy. For what metal did he name this second one?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 127-142. The Silver race refused to sacrifice to the gods, and Zeus (now king in place of Cronus) buried them beneath the earth in anger at their impiety. The pattern of the metals -- gold, silver, and then bronze -- is a sequence of decline, each race worse than the last.  (Legend.)

question: A hard warlike people sprang from ash trees, Hesiod said, to be his third race of mortals. They had bronze weapons, bronze armour and bronze tools, and one other thing of bronze that no later people had. What was it?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 143-155. The bronze race even lived in bronze houses -- 'there was no black iron yet' in the world, Hesiod says. They were terrible warriors born from ash-trees, and destroyed themselves by their own violence, going down nameless into the dark house of Hades.  (Legend.)

question: The best of the demigod heroes of Thebes and Troy did not go down to Hades with the others, Hesiod said. They were sent instead to a place at the edge of the world Ocean, where the fields gave grain three times a year and an old dethroned god was king again. What was Hesiod's name for that place?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 166-173. The Isles of the Blessed lie at the edge of Ocean; there Cronus (dethroned by Zeus) reigns quietly and the earth yields three harvests a year. The Fields of Aaru are the Egyptian afterlife; Persephone rules the shades in Hades; the Halls of Bragi (or Valhalla) are Norse. Later Greeks called the same place the Elysian Fields.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod came at last to the age he lived in himself, and he said he wished he had died before it or been born after it. It was the last and worst of his ages, named for a hard, dull metal still fairly new in his day. For what metal was it named?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 174-179. Iron is the fifth age, our own. Steel as a distinct alloy is not named by Hesiod; clay is Nebuchadnezzar's dream-statue in the biblical Book of Daniel; ash is the material of the Bronze race, born from ash-trees. Iron for Hesiod is the metal of toil and grief -- workaday, useful, ordinary, without splendour.  (Legend.)

question: Two goddesses wrapped their faces in white robes and left the earth for Olympus at the close of Hesiod's myth. One was the shame that holds a person back from wrong, the other the righteous indignation that falls on a wrongdoer. Once they had gone, he said, mortals had no defence left against evil. What were their names?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 197-201. Aidos is reverence-that-restrains from within; Nemesis is righteous indignation from without. Themis and Dike are the older law and justice; Hera and Hebe are queen of gods and cupbearer; Iris and Nike are messenger and victory. When Aidos and Nemesis go, Hesiod says, mortals have no defence at all against evil.  (Legend.)

question: Ovid, the Roman poet, retold the ages of the world in the opening book of his Metamorphoses, long after Hesiod, as a straight fall from a golden paradise into violence. To keep that fall unbroken he left one of the old poet's ages out of the sequence. Which age did he leave out?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.89-150. Ovid kept the four metal ages -- gold, silver, bronze, iron -- but dropped Hesiod's inserted Age of Heroes, since he was telling a straight decline from paradise to violence. The biblical Book of Daniel 2.31-45 also has four (Nebuchadnezzar's dream-statue: gold head, silver breast, bronze belly, iron legs with feet of iron and clay). Only Hesiod has five.

question: The first wave of settlers landed in Ireland, in the Book of Invasions, and found a dark, older race already there. These enemies lived on the rocky outer islands and cliffs and made war on every new people to come ashore. What were they called?
context: The Fomorians (Old Irish Fomoire) are Ireland's ancient monstrous race in the Book of Invasions. The Fir Bolg are the fourth wave of settlers (defeated by the Tuatha De at the First Battle of Moytura); the Milesians are the human sixth wave who displace the Tuatha De; 'the Danaans' is another name for the Tuatha De themselves.  (Legend.)

question: A Fomorian warrior came up out of the sea to raid the settlers of Ireland, in the old Irish tales, a misshapen sea-monster of a man. In the most common description he had only one of each of three body parts that a whole man would have two of. Which three?
answer: one eye, one arm, one leg
choices: one eye, one arm, one leg
one hand, one foot, one ear
one shoulder, one hip, one knee
one lip, one nostril, one tooth
context: Wikipedia and Book of Invasions tradition: many Fomorians in the primary tales have one eye, one arm, and one leg -- a mirror-image of the Irish blemish-taboo that put Nuada off the throne when he lost a single hand. Some Fomorians are also given human bodies with goat heads.  (Legend.)

question: Conand, chief of the Fomorians, took his tribute from the people of Nemed at his tower on Tory Island on the eve of Samhain. They were the third wave of settlers in Ireland, and the tax was a heavy one. What share of their children and grain did he take?
context: The Book of Invasions and the Conand-mythology tradition: the Nemedians paid two-thirds of their children, grain, and cattle to Conand's Tower on Tory Island every Samhain. The tribute is the mythic charter for Samhain as the sinister half of the Celtic year. One-half, one-tenth, and nine-tenths are the wrong fractions.  (Legend.)

question: The Nemedians rose up at last against the sea-monster Fomorians and stormed Conand's great tower on Tory Island, off Ireland's north coast. The Fomorian counter-attack nearly wiped them out, and only a tiny group survived to flee Ireland. How many survivors did the tradition count?
context: The Book of Invasions: after the storming of Conand's Tower and the Fomorian counter-attack, only thirty Nemedians survived, and they fled Ireland in different directions -- the ancestors, in tradition, of the Fir Bolg and (through Britain) of the Tuatha De themselves.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann deposed their half-Fomorian king Bres, yet their greatest champion was half Fomorian too. His father Cian was one of their own, and his mother Ethniu was Balor's daughter. Who was this champion?
context: Lugh's father Cian was Tuatha De and his mother Ethniu was Balor of the Evil Eye's daughter, locked in the crystal tower on Tory Island. So the young champion who kills Balor at Moytura is killing his own grandfather. Bres, the Dagda, Ogma, and Nuada are all full Tuatha De by ancestry -- only Bres and Lugh have the mixed line.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir went out at Ragnarok to fight an older, wilder race and die against it. Western myths tell that shape of story more than once, and Ireland tells it of the Tuatha De Danann and the Fomorians, a younger family of gods bringing order. In Norse myth, which race played the Fomorian part?
context: The Jotnar (frost-giants and fire-giants of Jotunheim, Muspelheim, and elsewhere) are the Norse structural parallel to the Fomorians -- an older, wilder race the Aesir must fight and eventually die against at Ragnarok. The Vanir are a second god-family the Aesir reconciled with; the Einherjar are Odin's dead warrior host in Valhalla; the Alfar are the elves.  (Legend.)

question: A young champion of the Tuatha De Danann killed his own grandfather, Balor of the Evil Eye, with a single sling-stone straight through the forehead, in County Sligo. The whole Fomorian host was broken and driven into the sea forever. In which battle did it happen?
context: Cath Maige Tuired ('the battle of the plain of pillars') is the great mythological showdown that ends the Fomorian threat. The FIRST Battle of Moytura was Tuatha De vs Fir Bolg (where Nuada lost his hand). The Battle of Tailtiu is where the Tuatha De later fall to the Milesians; the Battle of the Boyne (1690) and Clontarf (1014) are historical Irish battles, not mythic.  (Legend.)

question: The Fomorians raised the great stone forts on the sea-cliffs of Inishmore, the traditional Aran Islanders said. These are rings of drystone wall at the very edge of the ocean, hundreds of feet above the waves. Which fort is the most famous of them?
context: Dun Aengus (Dun Aonghasa) on Inishmore in the Aran Islands is a semicircle of drystone rampart on a cliff-edge 300 feet above the Atlantic; local tradition assigns it to the Fomorians, though archaeology dates it to the Iron Age. Dun Aluinne is an inland ringfort; the Cashel of the Kings is the seat of the kings of Munster; the Grianan of Aileach is a hilltop ringfort near Derry.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann land in Ireland, the tales say, with a sacred set of treasures. One treasure comes from each of the northern cities of their druid-teachers. How many treasures do they bring?
context: The Four Treasures are one of the great numbered sets of Western myth, alongside the Norse dwarves' six treasures and the twelve Instruments of the Passion. Four is the ritual number of Irish myth -- four cities (Falias, Gorias, Findias, Murias), four teachers, four objects, and later four virtues of kingship attached to them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.  (Legend.)

question: A claimant to the High Kingship of Ireland stands on the Lia Fail, on the Hill of Tara. In the old tales the stone is his test, and under a pretender it does nothing. What does it do under the rightful king?
answer: It cries out with a loud shriek
choices: It cries out with a loud shriek
It splits in two beneath his feet
It gives off a warm golden glow
It sinks a hand's breadth into the ground
context: The Lia Fail's shriek beneath the rightful king is the founding motif of Irish sacred kingship: sovereignty is not chosen but recognised. The same motif is echoed in the Arthurian Sword in the Stone, and (say Scots tradition) survives in the coronation stone taken to Scone and later to Westminster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lia_F%C3%A1il.  (Legend.)

question: A warrior of the Tuatha De plunges a red-hot weapon into a cauldron of dark blood, or of milk, to still it between fights. It burns from its own thirst for battle, it has never been beaten, and no cast of it has ever missed. To whom does it belong?
context: The Spear of Lugh is also called Gai Assail or Slea Bua ('the victory spear'), and it is the weapon Lugh will use to kill his grandfather Balor of the Evil Eye at the Second Battle of Moytura. Nuada owns the Sword of Light, the Dagda owns the club Lorg Mor and the cauldron, and Manannan owns his own sword Fragarach -- all real Tuatha De weapons, but none matches the never-missing thirsty spear. Source: morgynbard.com/post/the-gift-of-the-four-treasures.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann leave the northern cities of their druid-teachers for Ireland, and each city sends a treasure along. One is a spear that burns red-hot from its own thirst for battle and must be cooled between fights in a cauldron of blood or milk. From which city does the spear come?
context: The four cities are always listed in the same order in the medieval sources, each paired to one treasure: Falias (stone), Gorias (spear), Findias (sword), Murias (cauldron). Kids will guess the spear-and-sword pair swapped; the primary text keeps spear at Gorias and sword at Findias. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda, great father-god of the Tuatha De Danann, feasts his people from a great cauldron, the last of their sacred treasures. Two medieval Irish sources give the cauldron one fixed promise, in the same exact words. What does the formula say?
answer: No company ever went away from it unsatisfied
choices: No company ever went away from it unsatisfied
No man who ate from it could ever be poisoned
No warrior who tasted it could be killed by iron
No woman who tasted it could bear a mortal child
context: The formula, straight from Lebor Gabala Erenn and Cath Maige Tuired, is that no company ever leaves the cauldron unsatisfied. The other three would have been fine legendary powers, but none of them is the promise the sources carry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.

question: Morfessa teaches the Tuatha De Danann in Falias and Uiscias in Findias, and the medieval sources preserve the name of the druid-master in every northern city. Who teaches in the city that gives up the spear?
context: The four teachers in the medieval formula: Morfessa, Esras, Uiscias, Semias -- obscure druid-masters whose names are preserved only in this one glossed passage. Amergin is the Milesian druid, Cathbad is Conchobar's druid in the Ulster Cycle, Mog Ruith is the great blind sorcerer of Munster -- three real druid-names of Irish tradition, but from other cycles. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.  (Legend.)

question: Edward I of England, Scottish tradition holds, carried off a stone in 1296 and set it beneath the coronation chair at Westminster. It was said to be the Lia Fail itself, taken east to be used at the coronation of Scottish kings. What is this stone called in English?
context: The Stone of Scone (also called the Stone of Destiny) was taken by Edward I in 1296 and set beneath the wooden coronation chair at Westminster Abbey, where it stayed until 1996. Scots and Irish scholars have disputed for a thousand years whether it is really the Lia Fail. The Blarney Stone (Cork) is a real kissing-luck stone; the Kingston Coronation Stone is the real Anglo-Saxon coronation stone at Kingston-upon-Thames where seven Saxon kings were crowned; the Turoe Stone is a real La Tene decorated stone in County Galway -- three real famous stones of Britain and Ireland, each with a different purpose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_of_Scone.

question: The Dagda eats his way through a whole pit of porridge in one of the two great sagas of Ireland's Mythological Cycle. The same saga carries the killing of Balor and the harp snatched off a Fomorian wall, and it opens with the cities and their treasures. Which saga is it?
answer: Cath Maige Tuired ('The Second Battle of Moytura')
choices: Cath Maige Tuired ('The Second Battle of Moytura')
the Tain Bo Cuailnge ('The Cattle Raid of Cooley')
Togail Bruidne Da Derga ('The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel')
the Acallam na Senorach ('Colloquy of the Ancients')
context: Cath Maige Tuired opens with the four cities and their gifts; the Tain is the Ulster Cycle war-epic (Cuchulainn's world); Togail Bruidne Da Derga is the tragic-king tale of Conaire Mor; the Acallam na Senorach is the huge Fionn-cycle framing dialogue between Oisin and St Patrick. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T300010.html.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn holds the border of Ulster against Queen Medb's army, and one weapon of his frightens her men more than any sword or bow. It is a spear, held back for the fights he is losing. What is it called?
context: Birgha is Fionn mac Cumhaill's spear in the Fenian Cycle; Areadbhar is Lugh's spear in later Tuatha De Danann lists; the Gae Assail is another spear-name in the same Tuatha tradition. The Gae Bolg is Cu Chulainn's alone. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: A charioteer floats the shaft of the great spear down the stream to Cu Chulainn as he stands in the current of a ford. Cu Chulainn must not take it in his hand: his teacher's rule is strict. From what part of the body does he cast it?
answer: from between the toes of the foot
choices: from between the toes of the foot
from the shoulder in an underhand hurl
from the crook of the elbow
from the mouth as a warcry-launch
context: The Gae Bolg is caught between the toes as it floats past and kicked up at the enemy -- a technique some scholars suspect began as spear-fishing. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: An enemy takes Cu Chulainn's great spear in the body, and the point enters like an ordinary javelin, leaving one small wound. The throw is not the horror. The horror is what the spear does next, inside him. What does it do?
answer: it opens into thirty barbs that fill every joint and limb
choices: it opens into thirty barbs that fill every joint and limb
it bursts into a cold blue flame
it splits the enemy's shadow from his body
it calls its twin spear across the battlefield to strike
context: The medieval text says the spear enters as a single wound but opens into thirty barbs inside the flesh, filling every limb and joint. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn's charioteer comes forward after the killing at the ford in the Tain Bo Cuailnge, with the great spear still inside the dead man. Any pull back through the entry wound only hooks it deeper. How is the spear retrieved?
answer: the flesh has to be cut open around it
choices: the flesh has to be cut open around it
it dissolves out of the wound after a day
the wielder whistles it back through the air
it must be pulled by two horses at once
context: In the Tain, Cu Chulainn's charioteer has to come forward after the killing of Ferdiad and cut the body open to take the Gae Bolg back -- the extraction kills the enemy a second time. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: Ferdiad holds the ford against Cu Chulainn for three days. The two trained side by side on the Isle of Shadow, drilled alike in every feat but two. Cu Chulainn alone knows the great spear, and Ferdiad alone has an advantage of his own, the one thing that lets him hold the ford so long. What is it?
answer: his horn-skin that ordinary weapons could not pierce
choices: his horn-skin that ordinary weapons could not pierce
his ability to fight in the warp-spasm ristrad
his geis against striking a foster-brother
his chariot-team that could not be outrun
context: The Tain says the two foster-brothers were equal in all martial feats save two: Cu Chulainn alone knew the Gae Bolg, and Ferdiad alone had impenetrable horn-skin. It is why every ordinary weapon Cu Chulainn tried in the ford failed and why the Gae Bolg had to come out. Wikipedia: Ferdiad, Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn is losing at the ford on the third day, with every ordinary weapon spent against Ferdiad. He calls out for the one weapon he has been holding back. A man standing mid-current floats it down the stream to him. Who is this man?
context: Loeg is Cu Chulainn's lifelong charioteer; he floats the Gae Bolg down the current in the ford and later has to cut Ferdiad open to take the spear back out. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: Ferdiad lies dead, the foster-brother Medb's war has forced Cu Chulainn to destroy, and the hero stands over the body and breaks into a long formal lament. In the Tain the lament opens, 'Ah, Ferdiad, betrayed to death. / Our last meeting, oh, how sad!' What is its third line?
choices: 'The gods have set us at swords.'
context: The lament turns the whole ford-episode from a victory into a wound -- Cu Chulainn is broken by having killed the brother Scathach's fosterage bound to him. Wikipedia: Ferdiad.  (Legend.)

question: Lady Gregory gave 'bolg' in the spear's name one more reading in 1902, in her Cuchulain of Muirthemne, and hers is no medieval gloss at all. Old Irish glossators had left at least three that keep resurfacing in modern editions of the Tain. Which reading is hers?
context: 'Bag' (a bag-full of barbs), 'notch or gap', and 'belly' are the recurring medieval glosses; Eric Hamp reconstructs Proto-Celtic for 'spear of mortal pain'. The sea-monster-bone origin -- the beast of Coinchend -- is a modern addition by Lady Gregory in her 1902 'Cuchulain of Muirthemne', not a medieval gloss. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.

question: Cu Chulainn's enemies tricked him at last into breaking a magical ban, the kind a druid laid on a hero: a single act he must never do, on pain of ruin. What is the old Irish word for such a ban?
context: Plural geasa (roughly 'gaysh' / 'gaysha'). Fian = a warrior-band (compare fianna); fidchell = the Irish board game; filid = a poet. Wikipedia: Geis.  (Legend.)

question: A boy of Ulster killed the guard-dog of a smith and offered to serve in its place until a new hound could be raised. From then on he was called by a name that means 'the Hound' of that smith. Who was this hero?
context: The smith was Culann; the name Cu Chulainn is literally 'the Hound of Culann'. Wikipedia: Cu Chulainn.  (Legend.)

question: Medb's war-band closed in on Cu Chulainn in three factions: a son of Cu Roi, Erc avenging his father Cairbre Nia Fer, and a set of sorcerers. These were the children of a wizard who fell to him years before, raised by their mother for this one purpose. Who were the sorcerers?
context: Cailitin's widow bore his children after his death and trained them in sorcery for revenge. The sons of Uisliu belong to Deirdre's tale; the children of Lir were turned into swans; the Dagda's daughters are from a different cycle. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn rode past an open fire on his way to his last battle. Three old crones, each blind in one eye, were cooking a piece of meat there, and they called to him to share it. The fire and the spits were cut from one tree, the wood the old Irish tales most often name for druidic work and protection against ill. What wood was it?
context: The Aided Con Culainn specifies the crones' fire is of rowan sticks and their spits are of rowan -- rowan (caorthann) is the Irish tree of druidic power. Ash is Yggdrasil in the Norse tradition; oak is the druids' great tree but not the wood named in this tale; hazel is Fionn's Salmon-of-Knowledge tree. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn; Seven Miles of Steel Thistles blog.  (Legend.)

question: The three crones gave Cu Chulainn a piece of roast meat, and he took it in one hand. From that moment the strength drained out of the arm that held it, and out of the whole side of his body that arm served. It was the side he would need most against the war-band waiting for him. What went dead?
answer: his left side, from shoulder to fingertip
choices: his left side, from shoulder to fingertip
his right side, from shoulder to fingertip
context: He took the meat in his left hand; the whole left side goes. He also puts the bone down on his left thigh and the thigh is struck through too. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn; Steel Thistles.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles faced a choice in Greek epic between a short glorious life and a long dim one. Behind it stood no druid's ban, as in Ireland, but a share of destiny handed to a mortal by the gods. What is the Greek word for that share?
context: Norse wyrd is the parallel in that tradition. Arete = excellence; hubris = overreach; kleos = fame. Wikipedia: Moira; Geis.

question: A High King of Ireland broke his geasa one after another on a single unlucky night, in the tale Togail Bruidne Da Derga, each time by a forced act. No hero carried a longer list of bans, and that night ended with him dead in the hostel. Who was the king?
context: Togail Bruidne Da Derga is one of the great tragic sagas of the Mythological Cycle. Cormac mac Airt is a later High King associated with wisdom-tales; Nuada is a Tuatha De Danann king; Diarmait mac Cerbaill is a historical-legendary king. Wikipedia: Togail Bruidne Da Derga.

question: A compiler at a Cistercian abbey in County Laois took down an Old Irish text of the Death of Cu Chulainn about the year 1160. The same great manuscript carries much of the Ulster Cycle, the Fenian Cycle and one main version of the Tain Bo Cuailnge. Which manuscript is it?
context: Lebor Laignech, compiled c.1160 at Terryglass/Oughaval. The Book of Kells is a gospel-book; Ballymote is a later (14th c.) codex; the Cathach is a 6th-c. psalter. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn; Book of Leinster.

question: A folk-hero of Ireland lays a stone road across the sea in the old tale. On the north coast of County Antrim some 40,000 six-sided basalt columns really do march out of the cliff into the sea. What is this flat pavement of columns called?
context: The Irish name is Clochan an Aifir. Geologically the columns are the top of a 60-million-year-old cooled lava flow. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.

question: An Irish giant tears up rocks and sets them across the sea, in the folk-tale, so that he can walk over dry and fight a rival on the far shore. The tale calls the Antrim columns his work. Which hero is the builder?
context: Cu Chulainn is the hero of the Ulster Cycle; Lugh is a Tuatha De Danann warrior; Conall Cernach is a foster-brother of Cu Chulainn. In the folk-tale of the causeway Fionn is treated as a full-sized giant, which drifts from the manuscript Fenian Cycle where he is a human-scale chief of the Fianna. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: A rival on the far shore has been shouting insults across the water for months, in the folk-tale of the Antrim columns, and the Irish giant wants to settle it face to face. So he starts to build his road over the sea. Where does the rival live, and what is his name?
answer: in Scotland -- his name is Benandonner
choices: in Scotland -- his name is Benandonner
in Wales -- his name is Bran the Blessed
in the Isle of Man -- his name is Manannan mac Lir
in Norway -- his name is Ymir
context: Benandonner (the Red Man) shouts across the North Channel; Fionn accepts the challenge and starts building. Bran the Blessed is Welsh; Manannan is Irish; Ymir is Norse. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: The Irish giant is part of the way across the sea on his new stone road when he catches sight of his rival up close for the first time. He stops, looks properly and turns for home. What has he just realised?
answer: the rival is far bigger than he is
choices: the rival is far bigger than he is
the rival has been dead for a year
the rival's causeway is finished first
the rival is his own long-lost brother
context: Fionn had assumed he was the bigger giant; halfway across he sees the size of Benandonner and turns for home to think. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: Oonagh, as the giant's clever wife is usually named, though some tellings call her Sadhbh, takes charge when her husband runs home with his rival close behind him. He has no plan and no time. She tells him to lie still and not speak a word. Under what identity will she pass him off?
answer: her infant son sleeping in the cradle
choices: her infant son sleeping in the cradle
the family's dog-boy tending the hearth
a dead uncle laid out for the wake
a deaf servant sweeping the floor
context: The whole trick turns on the giant thinking he is looking at a baby. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: The giant's wife greets the rival politely when he arrives at her door roaring for a fight, and she says her husband is out hunting. She sits him down to tea and fresh loaves. She has baked something hard into each one, to make him crunch and to let her boast about how tough the men of the house must be. What has she baked into the loaves?
context: In the folk-tale these are iron griddles or 'bakestones' baked right into the bread -- the whole point is that if the men here eat bread this hard, the father must be enormous. Cited in Irish Central and Irish Road Trip retellings.  (Legend.)

question: The visitor sits in the kitchen with his teeth ringing from the bread, and at last he notices the 'baby' asleep by the fire. He stares. He does the arithmetic. Then he panics and runs. What arithmetic sends him bolting for the door?
answer: if the baby is this size, the father must be monstrous
choices: if the baby is this size, the father must be monstrous
if the baby is this loud, the neighbours will come
if the baby is this hungry, the food will not last
if the baby is this ugly, the mother must be his match
context: That inference -- father-must-be-worse -- is the whole hinge of the trick. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: The rival flees back onto the stone road, sure the master of the house is about to come out after him. He does not just run. On the way he does something to the pavement under his feet, and the folk-tale uses it to explain a real fact about the basalt columns. What does he do to the road?
answer: he tears up the stones behind him as he goes
choices: he tears up the stones behind him as he goes
he sinks the middle spans under the sea
he sets fire to the wooden pilings
he calls a storm down to wash it away
context: The tearing-up is the folk-tale's answer to why the real basalt formation survives only at the two ends of the crossing and not in the middle. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: In the Gospel of Luke, a Jewish lawyer asked Jesus, 'Who is my neighbor?' Jesus answered with a story: a man on a real, dangerous road 'from Jerusalem to _______' was jumped by bandits, stripped, beaten and left half dead. Where was he going?
context: Luke 10:30 KJV: 'A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves.' The word 'down' is literal -- Jerusalem sits at about 2,300 feet above sea level and Jericho at about 1,300 feet below, so the road drops more than 3,000 feet in some seventeen miles of desert. Bethany is a village of the same descent but only two miles from Jerusalem; Emmaus is the town of the post-resurrection walk (Luke 24); Nazareth is Jesus's home village up in Galilee, in the wrong direction entirely.  (Legend.)

question: Jesus set the beating in his parable on a real road, seventeen miles long and notorious in his day for bandit ambushes. It dropped steeply from Jerusalem, high in the Judean hills, down to an ancient oasis city on the plain below. By how much did the road drop across those seventeen miles?
context: Jerusalem sits at roughly 2,300 feet above sea level; Jericho, near the Dead Sea, lies about 1,300 feet below -- so the road drops around 3,300 to 3,600 feet in about seventeen miles of desert wadis. The steep descent, isolated terrain, and cliffside caves made it a bandit-country classic. In Arabic the pass carried the name tal`at ed-damm, 'Ascent of Blood', from its ambush reputation; Jerome, writing from Bethlehem in the fourth century, notes the same.

question: A temple priest came along the road in Jesus's parable, in the Gospel of Luke, saw the beaten traveller lying half dead and 'passed by on the other side.' A second respectable man came and did exactly the same. Who was he?
context: Luke 10:32 KJV: 'And likewise a Levite, when he was at the place, came and looked on him, and passed by on the other side.' The Levites were the tribe of Israel set apart for temple service under the priesthood. The point of the pairing is that Jesus is naming the two most respectable religious figures of the day -- the men most trained in the law that the lawyer just quoted -- as the ones who refuse to help. Pharisees, scribes, and temple guards all appear elsewhere in the gospels but are not in this parable.  (Legend.)

question: A third traveller stopped on the road in Jesus's parable, after two respectable men had walked past the robbed and bleeding man. He belonged to a people Jesus's Jewish audience despised so deeply that the lawyer, at the end of the story, would not even speak the name aloud. The gospel names them. Who were they?
context: Luke 10:33 KJV. The Samaritans kept the first five books of Moses but rejected Jerusalem as the true worship-place, holding to Mount Gerizim instead. John Hyrcanus destroyed their Gerizim temple in 109 BCE; a few decades later, at Passover around 8 CE, Josephus (Antiquities 18.29-30) says some Samaritans crept into the Jerusalem Temple courts at night and scattered human bones, desecrating the sanctuary. Sadducees, Idumeans, and Herodians were other first-century Judean factions, but they are not the group at the centre of this parable.  (Legend.)

question: A passing stranger poured oil and wine on the wounded man's cuts and bandaged them, in Jesus's parable. Then he did one more inconvenient thing to get the man to an inn. The King James wording puts it in three plain words. What did he set the man on?
context: Luke 10:34 KJV: 'and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.' 'Beast' in KJV translates the Greek 'ktenos' -- a generic word for a mount, most likely a donkey or a mule; the gospel does not name the species, but the point is that it was his and he gave it up. Carrying on his back would be Christ-on-the-shoulders imagery from a different parable (Luke 15:5, the lost sheep); a cloak on the ground is the Palm Sunday scene; the parable does not use a cart.  (Legend.)

question: The innkeeper took coins in the morning from the stranger who had stopped on the road, to cover the wounded man's care. The King James Bible calls the payment 'two pence,' but 'pence' stands in for a specific coin. What coin did Luke's Greek name?
context: The KJV 'penny/pence' consistently renders the Greek denarion -- the standard Roman silver piece, roughly a labourer's daily wage. Two denarii were roughly two days' wages -- enough for perhaps a week or two of room and board at a modest inn. The drachma was a Greek silver coin; the shekel was Jewish temple currency; the talent was an enormous unit (about 6,000 denarii), the weight-based sum in the parable of the talents (Matthew 25). The Samaritan does not pay a fortune. He pays enough to start, and promises more.  (Legend.)

question: The traveller in Jesus's parable did not just leave his money at the inn and go. He added a promise, the sharpest detail in the whole story. In the King James wording he told the innkeeper, 'Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will _____.' What closed the promise?
context: Luke 10:35 KJV in full: 'Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee.' The wounded man now has an open account at the inn, with a stranger's word for the balance -- unlimited care, guaranteed by a Samaritan the innkeeper will have to trust to come back at all. In the ancient world, before signed contracts or banks, the plain future-tense 'I will repay thee' between two strangers was the whole guarantee. The other choices soften it into a reward, a restitution, or paperwork.  (Legend.)

question: Jesus turned the question back on the lawyer at the end of the parable: 'Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?' The lawyer, apparently unable to name the third man's people aloud, answered with a phrase that Luke records. What did he say?
answer: He that shewed mercy on him
choices: He that shewed mercy on him
context: Luke 10:37 KJV. Jesus's reply is even shorter -- 'Go, and do thou likewise.' The lawyer's refusal to name the Samaritan is the quiet punchline: even having heard the story, he can only describe the hero by his action, not his people. The parable does not overturn Leviticus 19:18 ('love thy neighbour as thyself'); it enlarges the definition of neighbour until it includes the man on the other side of every antagonism.  (Legend.)

question: A poet of medieval France said the Grail was the cup Jesus lifted at a meal in an upper room in Jerusalem. Jesus shared bread and wine there with his twelve disciples on the night before his arrest. Which meal from the Gospels was it?
choices: the Feeding of the Five Thousand
context: The Grail-as-cup identification (Robert de Boron, c.1200) points back to the Last Supper -- the Passover meal in the upper room, source of the Christian Eucharist. Cana is where Jesus turned water into wine; the Feeding of the Five Thousand is the loaves-and-fishes miracle; the Feast of Tabernacles is a Jewish harvest festival.

question: Chretien de Troyes wrote Perceval in the 1180s, and his mysterious 'graal' was only a shining dish carried in a strange procession, not yet a Christian relic. Around the year 1200 another poet was the first to turn it into one: the very cup Jesus lifted in the upper room. Which poet did that?
context: Robert de Boron's verse Joseph d'Arimathie (c.1200) fused the Grail with the Eucharist cup for the first time. Chretien de Troyes wrote the earlier Perceval (c.1181-90) where the graal is only a serving-dish. Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (c.1210) made it a stone from heaven instead. Thomas Malory, writing much later in the 1400s, took the cup version and put it into English.  (Legend.)

question: Joseph of Arimathea stood below the cross at the crucifixion, in the first poem to make the Grail a cup, holding that same cup from the upper-room supper. He used it to catch something that day. What did the cup collect?
context: In Robert de Boron's Joseph d'Arimathie, Joseph catches the blood flowing from Jesus's side after the soldier's lance-thrust. The cup thus carries both the memory of the Last Supper wine and actual drops of blood -- twice hallowed. The shroud is Joseph's linen cloth, wrapping the body. The crown of thorns is a separate relic given to the mocking soldiers. Frankincense is one of the Magi's birth-gifts, not part of this scene.  (Legend.)

question: The leaders of Jerusalem threw Joseph of Arimathea into a dungeon right after the crucifixion for stealing the body of Jesus, in a French Grail legend of about 1200. There he sat, kept alive by the Grail, until the future emperor Vespasian came south, heard of him and set him free. How many years did Joseph sit in that cell?
context: The legend places Joseph in prison for exactly forty-two years, fed each day by a wafer laid in the cup by a dove and by daily visits from the risen Jesus who taught him the 'secrets of the Grail'. Vespasian, later Roman emperor, hears of him and releases him. Seven, twelve, and a hundred are all round biblical numbers but not the one this story uses.

question: Family and companions sailed west with Joseph of Arimathea and the cup in the Grail legend, once he was out of prison. Eventually he landed in a distant country and founded its first Christian community. In which land does the legend place his landing?
context: The Joseph-to-Britain journey is 12th-century French legend, first written down by Robert de Boron and expanded in the Vulgate Estoire del Saint Graal (c.1220). Egypt is where the Holy Family flees from Herod (a different story). Spain is where the apostle James is buried by legend (Santiago). Armenia was the first officially Christian kingdom historically, but not part of the Grail story.

question: The legend has Joseph of Arimathea thrust his walking staff into the ground on a hill outside a small Somerset town. By morning the staff had taken root and grown into a flowering thorn tree. He had come there, medieval legend added, carrying the Holy Grail. In which town does the legend place his staff?
context: The tree, called the Glastonbury Thorn, grew on Wearyall Hill until it was chopped down by Puritan soldiers in the 17th century; a successor stood there until it was vandalised in 2010, but cuttings survive. Canterbury is Becket's cathedral. Winchester is Alfred's royal city. Tintagel is Arthur's Cornish birthplace.  (Legend.)

question: Puritan soldiers cut down the thorn tree said to have grown from Joseph of Arimathea's staff in the seventeenth century, but cuttings survive. The thorn really does bloom twice a year, once in the ordinary spring and once in a season the Christian world already treated as holy. When does the second flowering come?
context: The tree, botanically Crataegus monogyna 'Biflora', really is a rare cultivar that blooms in midwinter as well as in spring -- the Christmas bloom is the source of the miracle-claim. To this day a flowering sprig from a surviving specimen is sent to the British monarch every Christmas. Easter, midsummer, and harvest all have Christian feasts but not the Glastonbury Thorn story.

question: Wolfram von Eschenbach would not have the cup in his Parzival of about 1210. His Grail gave off a light so bright the candles paled, and no one who had seen it could die within the week. What was the Grail in Wolfram's telling?
choices: a mirror sent by the moon
context: Wolfram calls his Grail 'lapsit exillis', usually read as garbled Latin for 'the stone that fell from heaven'. It gives off a light so bright the candles pale, and no one who has seen it can die within the week. Robert de Boron's cup-version was more popular in later English romance (Malory follows the cup); Wolfram's stone-version inspired Wagner's opera Parsifal.  (Legend.)

question: A wounded king of Joseph of Arimathea's line held the cup at the castle of Corbenic, in the later Grail cycle, as one guardian after another had done before him. Each waited, generation after generation, for a destined knight to arrive and ask the right question that would heal the wound. What was this line of guardians called?
context: The Fisher King line, keepers of the Grail at Corbenic, waits generation after generation for the destined knight who will ask the right question and end the wound. Unable to walk from the groin-wound, each king spends his days in a small boat on the castle lake with a rod in his hand -- the source of the name. Galahad finally achieves the healing in Malory Book XVII. Nazarites are Old Testament vow-keepers (Samson). 'Marys of the Sea' is a separate Provencal Grail-adjacent legend of Mary Magdalene landing in France. The Knights Templar were a real 12th-century order later fictionally attached to the Grail story.

question: A young man walked first into the supper hall in Chretien de Troyes's Grail procession, carrying what looked like a plain spear. Its point was white as snow, and from the tip, without stopping, something kept running down over his fingers. What kept falling from the tip?
context: Chretien's opening image: 'a lance whose point was as pure white as snow, and from the point a drop of blood ran down the shaft'. The bleeding lance is one of the strangest images in medieval literature -- centuries of readers have argued what it means. Wax would drip from a candle; oil from a lamp; dew from a plant -- none from a spear-point.  (Legend.)
