question: Two maidens followed the boys with the candelabra through Chretien's supper hall. The first bore the graal itself, which Chretien described as a dish of pure gold set with precious stones, so bright the candles paled. What did the second maiden carry?
context: Chretien's Old French: 'un tailleoir d'argent' -- a silver carving-platter. The four elements of the procession are lance, candelabra, graal, platter. Wolfram's Parzival gives a different set. The horn belongs to Roland's story (Olifant); a crown or cloak would suit a coronation, not the Grail procession.  (Legend.)

question: A Roman soldier stabbed Jesus in the side at Golgotha to make sure he was dead, in the story behind the Grail romances. Later writers said the weapon had bled ever since, and they made it the thing carried through the Grail Castle in procession. Which Passion relic did they make of it?
context: The Christianising of Chretien's original: the anonymous bleeding relic becomes the Lance of Longinus, the Roman soldier's spear that pierced Jesus's side at the crucifixion. Malory keeps this identification. The Sword of Peter is the one Peter drew in Gethsemane to cut off Malchus's ear. The Nails and the Reed are separate Passion relics.  (Legend.)

question: Perceval sat silent all through supper in Chretien de Troyes's Grail Castle, watching the shining graal and the bleeding lance pass in procession before the wounded Fisher King. His old tutor Gornemant once warned him never to ask idle questions of a host. What did Perceval find when he woke the next morning?
answer: the castle empty and every soul gone
choices: the castle empty and every soul gone
the Fisher King healed and standing tall
the Grail waiting on his pillow at last
the maidens returning to explain each relic
context: Perceval's silence at the Grail is the great failure of Chretien's poem. He wakes to an abandoned castle -- the Fisher King, the maidens, the procession, all vanished -- and rides out to find the surrounding land still waste. The moral, that courtesy misapplied can be worse than boldness, runs through the whole Grail cycle. Chretien died before finishing the poem, and other writers took up the ending.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Balin, cornered inside a chapel at Corbenic long before Perceval's visit, snatched the bleeding lance off its wall and drove it through the Fisher King's thighs. He did it in self-defence, but the blow broke the land around him. What name did later writers give this blow?
context: The Dolorous Stroke, developed in the Vulgate Cycle and the Post-Vulgate Suite du Merlin, is the founding wound of the whole Grail geography. Balin acts in self-defence but the misuse of the holy lance breaks everything around him. Camlann is Arthur's final battle where Mordred deals HIS death-wound; Uther is Arthur's father with a different death; the Stroke of Mordred blurs those.  (Legend.)

question: Three knights of the Round Table finished the Grail quest together in Malory's seventeenth book: Perceval, Bors and a third. Only that third knight touched the Fisher King's wound with blood from the lance and healed king and Waste Land alike. Who was he?
context: Malory Book XVII ch.21: Galahad, purest of the three, is the one who anoints the Fisher King's thighs with drops from the Lance -- king is healed, Waste Land restored. Lancelot is Galahad's father but too stained by his love for Guinevere to complete the quest. Gawain fails early. Kay never comes near the Grail. Galahad dies shortly after in ecstasy at the sight of the uncovered cup.  (Legend.)

question: Men from Judea came down to Antioch and told its mostly Gentile (non-Jewish) believers that Jesus was not enough. They could not be saved, the visitors said, without one command from the law of Moses. What did the visitors demand?
context: Acts 15:1 (KJV): 'And certain men which came down from Judaea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.' The demand set off the first great argument inside the Christian church.

question: The local leaders at Antioch could not settle a fight that broke out around AD 49 over whether Gentile Christians had to keep Jewish law. So they sent two of their top missionaries up the road to Jerusalem to ask the apostles for a ruling. Which two men did they send?
context: Acts 15:2 (KJV): '...they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.' Paul and Barnabas had just finished their first missionary journey together and were the two men who had actually been baptising Gentiles in the field.

question: At the Jerusalem council, Peter stood up to argue against forcing the Mosaic law on Gentile converts. He said requiring the whole law would put on the disciples' necks a burden that even the ancestors of Israel had never been able to bear. What single word did Peter use for that burden?
context: Acts 15:10 (KJV): 'Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?' The yoke image is the ox-harness of Jewish tradition -- the ordinary Talmudic phrase for accepting the Law was 'to take the yoke of the commandments upon oneself'.

question: The leaders of the early church gathered in Jerusalem around AD 49 to settle whether Gentile (non-Jewish) converts had to keep Jewish law. Neither Peter nor Paul delivered the verdict. It came from a third man, who by then led the Jerusalem church and who by tradition was the brother of Jesus. Who gave the final ruling?
context: Acts 15:13-19 (KJV): 'And after they had held their peace, James answered, saying, Men and brethren, hearken unto me... Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God.' The James in question is not one of the Twelve but James the Just, brother of Jesus, who ran the Jerusalem congregation and later wrote the epistle.

question: The head of the Jerusalem church gave his ruling around AD 49: Gentile (non-Jewish) converts were not to be troubled over the Jewish rite that visitors from Judea had demanded of them. Instead the decree named only four things they must keep away from, three rules about food and blood and one sexual rule. Which of these stood on the decree's list of four in Acts 15?
context: Acts 15:20 (KJV): '...that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood.' A strangled animal has not had its blood drained; the ban lines up with the older Noahide category. The four together: idol-meat, blood, things strangled, fornication.

question: The apostles at Jerusalem would not send their verdict of AD 49 back to Antioch by word of mouth. They wrote a formal letter, the earliest surviving document produced by the Christian church. What extraordinary opening phrase did the letter use to introduce its own decision?
answer: 'it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us'
choices: 'it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us'
'in the name of the Father and of the Son'
context: Acts 15:28 (KJV): 'For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things.' The phrase gave later church councils their formula for issuing binding decrees; nothing quite like it had been written before.

question: Two men from Jerusalem went back to Antioch with the letter as witnesses, because the apostles would not trust it to the two missionaries alone. Antioch might suspect the pair of softening the wording in their own favour. One of the witnesses was Judas Barsabas. Who was the other?
context: Acts 15:22 (KJV): '...to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren.' Silas -- the same Silas who will shortly become Paul's next travelling partner -- first appears here as a Jerusalem witness to the decree.

question: Paul proposed to Barnabas, not long after the council, that they revisit the churches they had planted together. Barnabas agreed, but he insisted on bringing a young man who had abandoned them mid-mission the first time out, at a place called Perga. Which young companion did Barnabas insist on bringing?
context: Acts 15:37-38 (KJV): 'And Barnabas determined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark. But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work.' John Mark was Barnabas's cousin (Colossians 4:10), which was probably why Barnabas kept defending him.

question: Barnabas would not budge when Paul refused to take the young man who had abandoned them on their first journey. Acts calls their argument 'so sharp' that the two greatest missionaries of the early church split their partnership on the spot. Barnabas and the young man then took ship. To which island did Barnabas sail?
context: Acts 15:39 (KJV): 'And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus.' Cyprus was Barnabas's own homeland (Acts 4:36) and the first stop on the earlier joint journey with Paul.

question: Paul stayed on the mainland after the split, when Barnabas sailed away, and he set out the other way with his own new partner, travelling overland to strengthen the churches. Through which two connected regions did Paul travel on that route?
context: Acts 15:40-41 (KJV): 'And Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God. And he went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches.' Cilicia was Paul's own home province -- Tarsus, his birthplace, sat in Cilicia. He was walking home before going west.

question: Paris, a young prince of Troy raised as a shepherd, was out with his flock when Hera, Athena and Aphrodite appeared before him. Zeus had sent them so that Paris could judge which of them was fairest. On which mountain above Troy was he tending his sheep?
context: Paris had been exposed as an infant and raised by a herdsman on Mount Ida, which overlooks Troy; the three goddesses came to him there. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paris (mythology)' and 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Queen Hecuba of Troy had a frightening dream while she was carrying her son Paris. The seer Aesacus warned that it foretold the ruin of Troy, so the baby was left out on a mountain to die. What did she dream she would give birth to?
answer: A flaming torch that burned the city
choices: A flaming torch that burned the city
A silver wolf that ate the sheep
A great serpent that swallowed the sun
A black bull that gored the king
context: The seer Aesacus read the dream as prophecy of Troy's ruin, so the baby was left on Mount Ida to die. He was rescued and raised as a shepherd. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paris (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus refused to judge between his wife and daughters when Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each claimed the golden apple marked 'For the Fairest'. He sent one divine messenger down to the hills above Troy, to lead the three goddesses to a young shepherd named Paris and let him decide. Whom did Zeus send?
context: Hermes, the wing-sandalled messenger of the Olympians, was Zeus's usual errand-runner between gods and mortals; each goddess then offered Paris a private bribe on the mountainside. Iris was a real divine messenger too (she carried word for Hera), but the Judgement of Paris myth names Hermes as the one who led the three goddesses down to Mount Ida. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Three goddesses came to a young Trojan prince named Paris on a mountainside above Troy, and each offered him a bribe for the golden apple marked 'for the fairest'. Hera offered him rule over Asia. Then Athena made her own offer. What did she promise Paris?
answer: Wisdom and unmatched skill in war
choices: Wisdom and unmatched skill in war
A shield no spear could pierce
The most beautiful woman in the world
A ship that could sail the sky
context: Athena offered what she herself embodies -- craft and battle-wisdom, so no mortal would defeat him. Paris turned it down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Aphrodite went last among the three goddesses who bribed Paris for the golden apple. She offered him a wife: the most beautiful mortal woman alive on earth. Only one problem stood in the way, for the woman was already married to a king. Who was the woman Aphrodite promised him?
answer: Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta
choices: Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta
Andromache, wife of Hector of Troy
Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon of Mycenae
Penelope, wife of Odysseus of Ithaca
context: Aphrodite offered the woman -- and the woman was already married. Helen of Sparta -- soon to be Helen of Troy -- was called the most beautiful woman in the world. Paris chose her, took her back to Troy, and the Greek kings sailed after them; choosing her started the war. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Paris sailed to Sparta as a royal envoy, already promised the most beautiful woman in the world by the goddess Aphrodite. King Menelaus received him as an honored guest. Then Menelaus was called away and left Paris alone in the palace with the queen. Where had Menelaus gone?
answer: To Crete for his grandfather's funeral
choices: To Crete for his grandfather's funeral
To Delphi to consult the oracle
To Athens to fight beside Theseus
To Egypt to buy horses for Sparta
context: Menelaus went to Crete to bury his grandfather Catreus, leaving Helen in Paris's company. Paris carried her home to Troy while he was away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Hera and Athena never forgave Paris for rejecting them on the mountain, and both fought against Troy for the whole war. In Book 5 of the Iliad, Athena even guided a mortal Greek warrior to charge and wound Aphrodite herself in battle. Which warrior did Athena aim at the goddess?
context: In Iliad 5 Diomedes, urged on by Athena, cuts Aphrodite's hand with his spear as she tries to shield her son Aeneas; the wound was the goddesses' revenge for the judgment. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Homer gives the judgment scene only a glance, one brief passage in Book 24 of the Iliad that calls it the folly that came home. The full story of the three goddesses and the bribes belonged to a lost epic poem of the Trojan cycle. What was that poem called?
context: The Kypria (also spelled Cypria) told the events leading up to the Iliad, including the judgment; it survives only in summaries and fragments. Apollodorus and Ovid's Heroides 16 also preserve the scene. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.

question: The Twelve gathered with Jesus in an upper room in Jerusalem to eat the Passover. Partway through the meal he told them that one of those eating with him would betray him. The disciples each began to ask the same short, worried question. What was it?
context: Mark 14:18-19; Matthew 26:22. Each disciple in turn asks whether he himself is the traitor -- none of them yet knows it is Judas. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Supper.

question: Jesus took a loaf on the night before he was crucified, blessed it, broke it and handed the pieces around the table. Over the bread he spoke one short sentence that Christians have repeated for two thousand years. What did he say?
choices: 'Take, eat: this is the bread of heaven.'
'Take, eat: this is the bread of life.'
'Take, eat: this is my flesh, given for you.'
context: Matthew 26:26. The full line: 'And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat: this is my body.' The other three lines are echoes and paraphrases from later liturgy and from John 6, but Matthew's Last Supper wording is this one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Supper.

question: Jesus lifted a cup of wine at the Last Supper, gave thanks and passed it around the upper room. He told the Twelve that what was in the cup was his blood, and he attached a specific purpose to it, what the blood was 'shed for'. What purpose did he name?
context: Matthew 26:28: 'For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.' 'Remission' here means forgiveness -- the wiping-away of sins. The other three phrases are real biblical themes tied to different scenes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Supper.

question: Peter, James and John went a stone's throw further into the garden with Jesus, and he asked them to keep watch while he prayed. Falling on his face, he asked his Father for one thing 'if it be possible', and then, having asked, he submitted. What did he ask for?
answer: that this cup pass from him
choices: that this cup pass from him
that the temple veil be spared
context: Matthew 26:39: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.' The 'cup' is the suffering of the crucifixion; the image echoes the cup he passed around a few hours earlier. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agony_in_the_Garden.

question: Peter woke in the Garden of Gethsemane to a short, wounded question from Jesus, on the first of three times Jesus found his friends fast asleep. Peter, James and John had been told to keep watch while he prayed. How long did Jesus say Peter could not stay awake with him?
context: Matthew 26:40: 'What, could ye not watch with me one hour?' The other choices are all real Gospel-era ways of marking time overnight, but the line Jesus uses is the plain 'one hour'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agony_in_the_Garden.

question: Peter panicked in the Garden of Gethsemane, pulled out a sword and swung at the men who had come to seize Jesus. He sliced off the right ear of one of the servants of the high priest. Three of the four Gospels tell this story but leave the servant nameless, and John's Gospel alone gives him a name. Whose ear did Peter cut off?
context: John 18:10 -- and Luke 22:50 adds that it was specifically the man's right ear. Luke alone then reports that Jesus touched the wound and healed it, his last recorded healing before the resurrection. The other three are all real biblical servants keyed to their masters: Onesimus is the runaway servant returned in Paul's letter to Philemon; Gehazi is the prophet Elisha's servant in 2 Kings; Doeg is King Saul's chief herdsman. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malchus.

question: Jesus stopped Peter at once, after Peter had drawn a sword at the arrest and sliced off a servant's ear. He told Peter to put the weapon away, wrapping the rebuke in one short line that has echoed through every argument about violence and self-defence since. 'They that take the sword shall...' How did the line end?
context: Matthew 26:52. In the same breath Jesus tells Peter he could summon twelve legions of angels if he wished -- and does not. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_of_Judas.

question: Leonardo da Vinci painted his 'Last Supper' on the refectory wall of a Milan convent between 1495 and 1498, without showing the bread and cup being lifted. He picked an earlier moment in the meal, the instant a single line from Jesus sent a shockwave down both sides of the long table. Which moment did he paint?
answer: Jesus saying, 'one of you shall betray me'
choices: Jesus saying, 'one of you shall betray me'
Jesus rising to lead them to the garden
context: The twelve apostles react in four clusters of three -- shock, denial, questioning, calculation -- while Judas alone leans back with the money-bag. All four listed moments happen at the Last Supper in the Gospels; Leonardo picked the betrayal-announcement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Supper.

question: Religious teachers grumble about the company Jesus keeps. In Luke's Gospel he answers them with a short parable. A shepherd with a hundred sheep finds that one of them has wandered off and got lost. What does the shepherd do?
answer: Leaves them in the wilderness and goes after the one that is lost
choices: Leaves them in the wilderness and goes after the one that is lost
Pens them safely in the fold and then goes home for the night
Sends a hired hand out after the missing one and stays himself
Calls his neighbours to help him watch the flock overnight
context: Luke 15:4 KJV: 'What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?' Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: Jesus tells of a poor woman in Luke 15 who loses one small silver coin somewhere in her one-room house. It is a drachma, worth about a day's wages. How many coins does she have altogether before she loses it?
context: Luke 15:8 KJV: 'Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' The coins were drachmas -- Greek silver, each about a day's wages. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: A shepherd in Luke 15 searches the wilderness for one strayed sheep until he finds it. Jesus describes in exact words what the shepherd does the moment he finds it, and how he brings it back home. What does the shepherd do?
answer: He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and carries it home himself
choices: He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and carries it home himself
He ties a rope round its neck and leads it back with his staff
He whistles for his sheepdog to drive it back to the fold
He signals for the other shepherds to help him drive it home
context: Luke 15:5 KJV: 'And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing.' The image of a young man carrying a live lamb across his neck became the very first common picture of Jesus in Christian art. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: In Jesus's second lost-and-found parable in Luke 15, a poor woman loses one of her small silver coins somewhere inside her one-room house. Jesus names the two very ordinary, homely things she does to hunt for it. What are they?
answer: Lights a candle and sweeps the house
choices: Lights a candle and sweeps the house
Wakes her husband and searches the storeroom
Turns out her chest and shakes out the bedding
Sends her servant girl outside to check the courtyard
context: Luke 15:8 KJV: '...doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' Village houses in first-century Galilee had small windows and packed-earth floors -- a coin in the dust really did need a lamp and a broom. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: The shepherd of Luke 15 gets home with his lost sheep and does not just put it in the pen and go to bed. He calls all his friends and neighbours together for what sounds like a small party, and Jesus quotes his exact words in the old King James English. What does the shepherd say?
answer: 'Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost'
choices: 'Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost'
'Blessed be the Lord; he hath restored what was taken from me'
'Come, my friends, and eat with me; my flock is whole again'
'Give thanks to God, who hath spared the least of these'
context: Luke 15:6 KJV. Two verses later the woman with the coin says almost the same line -- 'Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost' (Luke 15:9). The near-identical wording deliberately pairs the two scenes. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: A young man walks home with a lamb across his neck, painted around AD 200 on the ceiling of a burial room in Rome. The scene comes from Luke 15, and it is the first common image of Jesus in Christian art. In which Roman burial place is it?
context: The 'Good Shepherd' fresco sits on the domed ceiling of the Cubiculum of the Veiled Woman in the Catacomb of Priscilla, on the Via Salaria in Rome, around AD 200. The pose deliberately echoes the older Greek statue-type of Hermes Kriophoros, Hermes the ram-bearer -- a shape a Roman viewer would already recognise. Source: Bible Odyssey, 'The Good Shepherd in the Catacomb of Priscilla'.

question: The Pharisees and scribes mutter as they watch Jesus at supper, and the twin parables of the lost sheep and the lost coin are his answer. Both are short stories about someone searching for something small until it is found, and then throwing a party. Luke 15:2 gives the specific complaint he is answering, in the King James wording. What do the Pharisees and scribes say?
answer: 'This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them'
choices: 'This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them'
'By what authority doest thou these things?'
'Master, we would see a sign from thee'
'Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?'
context: Luke 15:2 KJV. The whole of Luke 15 -- lost sheep, lost coin, and the longer Prodigal Son that follows -- is Jesus's reply to that single murmured line. The ratio of loss tightens as he goes: one in a hundred, then one in ten, then one in two. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: Two Greeks came forward to claim the god-made armor of the dead Achilles, which had to go to the best fighter left in the camp. One was clever Odysseus. The other was the strongest fighter still standing, who had carried Achilles's body off the battlefield on his shoulders. Who was he?
context: Ajax the Great, son of Telamon and king of Salamis, was the strongest Greek warrior left after Achilles fell. In the fight around Achilles's corpse it was Ajax who carried the body off while Odysseus covered his back. Source: Sophocles, Ajax, prologue; Little Iliad tradition.  (Legend.)

question: The Greek generals held a contest over the god-forged armor of the dead Achilles. Ajax, son of Telamon, was the biggest and strongest Greek warrior still alive, and his rival Odysseus was a smaller man. The generals awarded the armor to Odysseus. What did Odysseus win it by?
context: The armor of Achilles went to Odysseus for the persuasive speech he made. Ajax, who had physically saved the body, got nothing but the shame of having been beaten by words. Source: Sophocles, Ajax, prologue; Odyssey 11.541-565.  (Legend.)

question: Ajax took up his sword on the night the armor of Achilles went to his rival, and he went out into the darkness in a black rage. He meant to kill the three chief men he blamed: the two brothers who commanded the whole Greek army, and the rival who had beaten him. Which three men did Ajax set out to murder?
choices: Nestor, Ajax the Lesser and Teucer
context: Agamemnon and Menelaus (the two Atreid kings who had allowed the vote) and Odysseus (who had won it) -- the three Greek chieftains Ajax held responsible for his disgrace. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 41-65.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess stopped Ajax in the dark as he crept toward the tents of the Greek leaders to murder his own comrades in their sleep. The Greeks had given the armor of Achilles to Odysseus instead of to him, and he was crushed with rage. She twisted his sight in the darkness. Which goddess turned him aside?
context: Athena, patron of clever Odysseus throughout the Iliad and Odyssey, twists Ajax's sight in the darkness so he cannot tell friend from beast. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 51-65 and 91-117.  (Legend.)

question: Ajax stormed out of his tent one night after losing Achilles's armor, meaning to murder the three men he blamed. A goddess cast a mist of madness on him and made him see the wrong targets in the dark. He hacked and stabbed for hours before he understood what he had done. Instead of the three Greek chieftains, what did Ajax actually slaughter that night?
choices: A group of captive Trojan women
The horses of the Greek chariots
context: Ajax butchered the flocks and herds of the Greek camp, killing them one by one and believing each animal was one of the generals he blamed. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 51-65 and 231-244.  (Legend.)

question: Ajax dragged one big animal back to his tent in the middle of his night of killing, tied it to a post and whipped it with a cord. A goddess had struck him mad, and he thought he had caught his worst enemy alive. Which animal did he tie up, and whom did he think he was whipping?
answer: A ram, thinking it was Odysseus
choices: A ram, thinking it was Odysseus
A bull, thinking it was Agamemnon
A stallion, thinking it was Menelaus
A boar, thinking it was Diomedes
context: The huge ram bound to the tent-post is the play's central emblem of Ajax's madness -- the strongest warrior in the army beating a sheep and mocking it as if it were the man who beat him with words. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 231-244 and 297-330.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess lifted her madness from Ajax at dawn. He stood with wet hands among all he had killed, the bound beast still bawling behind him, and understood what he had done. In the play by Sophocles, two figures came in from the tent and found him weeping. Who were they?
answer: His concubine Tecmessa and their small son
choices: His concubine Tecmessa and their small son
His half-brother Teucer and a herald
The prophet Calchas and a priest of Apollo
His father Telamon and his mother
context: Tecmessa is a captive war-prize turned Ajax's partner; the child is their infant son Eurysaces. Their entrance is the most tender scene in the tragedy -- a father in ruin and a small boy who does not yet understand. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 201-347.  (Legend.)

question: In Sophocles's tragedy, Ajax gathered his small son at his feet before his final act. The boy was his only child, named by his father for the piece of war-gear that had made Ajax famous among the Greeks: a mighty tower-shield of seven layered ox-hides with a bronze layer on top. What was the boy's name?
context: Eurysaces, from Greek eurys (broad) + sakos (shield) -- 'Broad-Shield' -- named for his father's tower-shield, the seven ox-hides with a bronze layer on top that Homer describes in Iliad 7.219-220. He grew up under Teucer's protection after the play. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 574-577.  (Legend.)

question: The two brothers who commanded the Greeks, still furious about Ajax's murder plot, tried to leave his body unburied on the beach as carrion for dogs and birds. One of Ajax's own men had to stand up to them and fight for his right to a proper burial: his half-brother, a famous archer of the Greek army. What was the half-brother's name?
context: Teucer, son of Telamon by a captive Trojan princess, was Ajax's half-brother and the greatest archer in the Greek army. Odysseus himself finally shamed Agamemnon into allowing the burial -- one of the great acts of magnanimity in Greek literature. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 1047-1420.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus journeys to the underworld in Book 11 of Homer's Odyssey and sees the ghost of Ajax, who killed himself in shame after the vote for Achilles's armor went against him. Odysseus tries to make peace, saying that no one, not even he, had wished this on him. How does Ajax's shade answer?
answer: He says nothing and walks away in silence
choices: He says nothing and walks away in silence
He weeps and forgives Odysseus at last
He curses Odysseus by every god of the dead
He asks Odysseus to look after young Eurysaces
context: One of the most famous moments of dignified fury in Western literature: even in death Ajax will not speak to the man who beat him with words. Homer says the shade 'went off into the darkness of Erebus with the other souls of the perished dead'. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.541-565.  (Legend.)

question: Strangers from far away walked into Jerusalem in Matthew's Gospel and went straight to the palace with a question that terrified King Herod: where is the newborn king of the Jews? They explained how they knew to come at all. What had they seen?
context: Matthew 2:2: 'Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.' The pillar of fire is from the Exodus, the moon-to-blood from Revelation, and the white bird echoes Jesus's later baptism dove. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Magi.

question: The wise men of Matthew's Gospel reached the child's house in Bethlehem, knelt down and opened their travel-treasures at his feet. They gave three gifts, the same trio that Christmas carols have listed ever since. Which trio did they give?
context: Matthew 2:11. Frankincense is a fragrant resin burned as incense; myrrh is a bitter resin used to embalm the dead -- which is why the myrrh gift has always struck readers as an odd present for a newborn. The other three trios are all real ancient trade goods along the same caravan routes, but none of them are the magi's gifts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Magi.

question: Travellers from the east came to Bethlehem to see the baby Jesus, in Matthew's Gospel. Later Christmas cards, carols and school plays put three crowned kings on camels, but Matthew never put a crown on them and called them by a different word altogether. What did Matthew call these visitors?
context: The Greek is magoi -- a class of Persian priest-astrologers, students of the stars. The 'three kings' upgrade is medieval, read back into Matthew from Old Testament lines about foreign rulers bringing tribute. Prophets, scribes and shepherds all appear elsewhere in the Nativity story; the magi are their own category. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Magi.

question: Herod pulled the wise men aside before they left Jerusalem and gave them a private instruction: come back this way and tell me exactly where the child is. He gave a friendly reason for asking, a reason that would turn out to be a straight-faced lie. What reason did he give?
answer: 'that I may come and worship him also'
choices: 'that I may come and worship him also'
'that I may send him gifts of my own'
'that I may bless his mother and father'
'that I may guard him against my enemies'
context: Matthew 2:8. Warned in a dream not to trust him, the magi go home 'another way' and never report back -- which is what triggers what happens next in Bethlehem. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: In Matthew's Gospel, King Herod worked out that he had been outwitted when the wise men, warned in a dream, slipped away without reporting back. He did not chase them. He sent soldiers into Bethlehem, six miles south of Jerusalem, with an order to let no rival grow up. Whom did he order killed?
answer: every boy in Bethlehem two years old and under
choices: every boy in Bethlehem two years old and under
every firstborn son in the district of Judea
every priest of the temple who had greeted the magi
every foreign traveller camped outside the walls
context: Matthew 2:16. Christians have kept a feast for these children -- the Holy Innocents -- since at least the second century, marked in the Western church on 28 December, four days after Christmas. The killing of the firstborn is Exodus 12; a temple purge and a foreigner sweep both fit Herod's paranoid style but are not the Matthew story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: Joseph did not wait for Herod's soldiers. Warned in a dream by an angel, he got Mary and the baby up in the middle of the night and fled the country, the scene painters have drawn a thousand times: a woman with a baby and a man on foot walking beside them. Where did they flee to?
context: Matthew 2:13-14. Egypt was the classic hiding-place for a Jewish family in trouble -- a Roman province, but outside Herod's reach, with a large existing Jewish community. Matthew is also quietly echoing the older story of Israel itself coming out of Egypt. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: Joseph heard in another dream that it was safe to go back, for Herod was dead. He started for home in Bethlehem, but news changed the route: Herod's son Archelaus was now the ruler of Judea. So Joseph veered north and settled the family in a small town in Galilee. Which town?
context: Matthew 2:22-23. All four are real Galilean towns Jesus knew: Capernaum will become his adult base of ministry, Bethsaida is the home of Peter and Andrew, and Cana is the site of the wedding-water-into-wine -- but the boyhood home in Matthew is Nazareth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: Herod's soldiers killed the little boys of Bethlehem when they could not find Jesus, and Western churches have kept a feast for them since at least the second century. It falls four days after Christmas, tucked deep inside the Christmas season. What is this feast called?
answer: the Feast of the Holy Innocents
choices: the Feast of the Holy Innocents
context: The Feast of the Holy Innocents falls on 28 December in the Western church. The Feast of the Circumcision is 1 January (eight days after Christmas, as Jewish law required); the Feast of the Presentation is 2 February, when Mary brings the baby to the Temple; the Feast of Stephen is 26 December -- the 'Good King Wenceslas' feast, for the first Christian martyr. All four are real feasts of the Christmas cycle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: Matthew never counted the wise men who came from the east and never gave their names. Long after him, medieval Christian tradition settled on three, one imagined as African, one as Asian and one as European, to stand for all the peoples of the known world. Two of their names are Caspar and Melchior. What is the third?
context: The trio Caspar-Melchior-Balthasar is fixed by the sixth century -- see the Ravenna mosaic at Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, where the three are shown in procession with their names lettered above them. Bartholomew is one of the Twelve, Barabbas the prisoner released at the Passion, and Barnabas the missionary companion of Paul -- all real New Testament figures, none of them a magus. Source: christianiconography.info/Edited%20in%202013/Italy/sApolNuovoLeftNave.magi.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Magi.  (Legend.)

question: In Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, a stranger came to the hall of the Aesir, the Norse gods, and offered to build them a stone wall so tall that no giant could ever break through it. Around which stronghold did he offer to build it?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the stranger offers to build a rampart around Asgard, the home of the Aesir. Valhalla is Odin's hall inside Asgard, not the outer boundary. Midgard is the world of humans. Jotunheim is where the giants live -- what the wall is supposed to keep OUT.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir listened in shock as a stranger at their hall named his price for a giant-proof wall. He wanted no gold or silver. He asked for one of their own goddesses, the fairest, as his wife. Which goddess did the builder demand?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder demanded Freyja the goddess of love. Frigg is Odin's wife. Sif is Thor's wife (the same Sif whose golden hair Loki cut off). Idunn keeps the apples of youth. On top of the goddess, the builder also demanded the sun and the moon.  (Legend.)

question: A mysterious stranger offered to wall in the home of the gods in a single winter, and for pay he named a goddess as his wife. That alone was a monstrous price. Then he demanded two more prizes on top. Besides the goddess, what else did the builder ask for?
choices: the sacred spear and the ship
the golden apples and the mead
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder demanded Freyja, plus the sun and the moon out of the sky. The spear Gungnir and the ship Skidbladnir are dwarf-forged gifts to the gods, not up for wager. Idunn's apples of youth and the Mead of Poetry are other treasures. Yggdrasil the world-tree and Mimir's well are cosmological features, not gifts to give.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir were about to refuse a stranger's wild price for their wall when one of them talked the rest into it with a clause: the builder must work alone and finish in one winter or lose everything. With the wall nearly done, they threatened to kill that same god unless he wrecked the deal. Which god was it?
context: Gylfaginning 42: Loki talked the reluctant Aesir into accepting on the impossible-sounding terms, and because he was the one who had pushed the deal through, the Aesir threatened him with death unless he wrecked it. He did -- by shape-shifting into a mare and luring away Svadilfari. Odin presides but does not push the bargain. Thor is away in the east fighting trolls when the deal is struck. Heimdall watches Bifrost, not the bargaining table.  (Legend.)

question: The gods granted the stranger one thing when he took on their wall: he could bring a single animal to haul the stones. He had one winter and no other helpers. Snorri says this beast did more of the wall-work than its owner. What kind of animal did the builder bring with him?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder brought Svadilfari, a stallion whose stone-hauling did more work than his master. Oxen haul stones in many myths (Rome's plough, Ireland's cattle-raid) but not this one. Freyr's Gullinbursti is a boar, from the Brokkr wager. Bears do not appear in this tale.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri tells how close the builder of the gods' wall came to winning. Working through the winter with only his one hauling beast, he raised walls so high the giants could not have broken them. With three days left before summer's first day, only one part of the fortification still stood unfinished. What was left to build?
context: Gylfaginning 42: with three days before the first day of summer, only the gateway (the doorway through the wall) remained. Snorri does not describe watchtowers, a keep, or a well inside Asgard's outer wall; those are medieval castle features.  (Legend.)

question: The builder of the gods' wall saw the sun rise on his deadline with the work unfinished, knew he had been cheated of his pay and flew into a rage, and in his fury his disguise fell away. Snorri says he had never been the ordinary craftsman he pretended to be. What was the builder truly?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder was a hrimthurs, a frost-giant, in disguise. The dwarves live in Svartalfheim and forge (Brokkr, Sindri, the Sons of Ivaldi). Elves have their own realm (Alfheim) but do not appear in this bargain. Sorcerers are not a Norse category the tale uses.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir looked at the raging builder, his disguise gone, and said an oath to such a creature was worth less than what he had asked for. One of the gods walked up to him and settled the whole matter with a single blow. Which god struck the killing blow?
context: Gylfaginning 42: Thor had been away in the east fighting trolls and came home just in time; he paid the builder with a single hammer-blow that shattered his skull and sent him 'down to Niflhel.' Odin does not do the killing. Tyr fights Garm at Ragnarok. Vidar avenges Odin against Fenrir. Only Thor is the wall-story's executioner.  (Legend.)

question: A poet sailed in from Iberia with the last fleet in the Book of Invasions, after five waves of Irish settlers had come and gone. His people overthrew the Tuatha De Danann and became the Gaels. What was this sixth people called?
context: The Milesians -- sons of Mil Espaine, 'Mil of Spain', led by the poet Amergin -- are the sixth and final wave in Lebor Gabala Erenn, and the ancestors of the historical Gaels of Ireland. The Fomorians are the sea-born enemies of the gods, already beaten by the Tuatha at the Second Battle of Moytura; the Aos Si are the fairy folk (in fact the Tuatha De renamed); the Fianna are the roving warrior-band of Fionn mac Cumhaill, centuries later. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish); Wikipedia, 'Tuatha De Danann'.  (Legend.)

question: Three queens of the Tuatha De Danann came out to the Milesians one after another as they marched inland from the coast. Each made the Milesian druid swear that Ireland would be named after her, and he promised each in turn. The three sisters were Eriu, Fodla and one more. Who was she?
context: The three land-goddesses are Eriu, Banba, and Fodla -- all three still survive as poetic names for Ireland in Irish literature, but Eriu's name became Eire in daily speech. Brigid, Danu, and the Morrigan are three other great Tuatha De goddesses, each with her own domain (flame, ancestry, war) and her own story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish).  (Legend.)

question: The druids of the Tuatha De Danann worked their fiercest magic when the Milesian ships came in sight of the Irish shore. A great storm blew up from the land against the invaders, howling out over the water. How far back out to sea did the magic wind drive the Milesian fleet?
context: 'Nine waves' is the ritual formula in the sources -- the exact distance beyond which the Tuatha De's magic could not reach. Once the Milesians were driven the nine waves out, only Amergin's counter-magic could bring them back. Nine is the great ritual number in Celtic and Norse myth alike. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish).  (Legend.)

question: The chief druid and poet of the Milesians out-magicked the Tuatha De's wind and sang his people onto the Irish shore. His epithet meant 'White-Kneed', and his name is preserved in the Book of Invasions and the Book of Leinster. Who was he?
context: Amergin Gluingel ('white-kneed Amergin') is the founding poet of Irish tradition -- the man whose verse ends the age of the gods and opens the age of the Gaels. Cathbad is Conchobar's druid in the Ulster Cycle; Mog Ruith is the great blind sorcerer of Munster; Tuan mac Cairill is the ancient shape-changing witness who lived through all six invasions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amergin_Gl%C3%BAingel.  (Legend.)

question: The Milesians' poet stepped onto the beach, with the wind calmed by his first poem, and chanted a second poem to claim the land. It started: 'I am a wind on the sea, I am a wave of the ocean, I am the roar of the sea, I am a stag of...' How many tines, or antler points, did he give the stag?
context: 'I am a stag of seven tines' is the fixed formula in every surviving translation of the Song of Amergin. A tine is a point of an antler; seven tines is a magnificent, mature stag. Nine is the ritual number of the wind; three and twelve are the other ritual numbers of Irish myth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Amergin.  (Legend.)

question: Standing on the beach, the druid of the Milesians sang himself into every part of the Irish natural world, in a long chain of images. One line named the fish famous in later Irish myth as the fish of wisdom, the one that would burn Fionn mac Cumhaill's thumb. In which watery place did the druid say he was that fish?
context: 'I am a salmon in a pool' is the fixed line in the surviving translations. The salmon-of-wisdom motif runs all through Irish tradition -- the same fish appears in the Fenian Cycle as the Salmon of Knowledge that Fionn cooks and accidentally tastes, gaining all wisdom. The Song of Amergin is one of the oldest surviving pieces of writing in the Irish language, preserved in the Lebor Gabala Erenn and copied into the Book of Leinster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Amergin.  (Legend.)

question: The Milesians won the war against the Tuatha De Danann, but the sons of Mil knew they had been fighting gods, and they offered a settlement instead. The old gods would not die out. One people would keep one part of Ireland and the other people another. How was Ireland divided?
answer: Milesians take the surface, Tuatha De take the underground
choices: Milesians take the surface, Tuatha De take the underground
Milesians take the south, Tuatha De take the north
Milesians take the coasts, Tuatha De take the mountains
Milesians take the summer, Tuatha De take the winter
context: The famous division: the Milesians (the modern Irish) hold the visible land, sea, and sky; the Tuatha De hold every hollow-hill, fairy-fort, and sidhe mound beneath the ground. The god-people did not perish; they retreated into the hills, and this is how the old gods became the fairy folk who live under Ireland. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish); Myth and Folklore Wiki; godsandmonsters.info, 'Sidhe'.  (Legend.)

question: A dark bird landed on the shields and spears of one side before an old Irish battle, and that side was about to die. The Tuatha De Danann, the old gods of Ireland, said one of their war-goddesses took this shape to mark her chosen dead. Which shape-changing goddess flew over the battle as a crow?
context: The Morrigan ('great queen' or 'phantom queen') is the war-and-prophecy goddess of the Tuatha De Danann; her most famous shape is the crow (badb) settling on the doomed side of a fight. She is often described as a trio (with Badb and Macha, or Badb and Nemain). Brigid is the goddess of poetry, flame, and healing; Danu is the mother-goddess whose name is in Tuatha De Danann itself; Aine is a summer sun-goddess of Munster. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan; Timeless Myths, 'Celtic Gods and Goddesses'.  (Legend.)

question: The Morrigan appeared in the Book of Invasions as three war-sisters, daughters of Ernmas. One was Badb, the Scald-Crow battle-hag. One was Anand, sometimes called Nemain, 'Frenzy'. The third had her name stamped on the ancient royal seat of Ulster and on the modern city of Armagh. Who was she?
context: Macha is the horse-and-sovereignty sister; EMAIN MACHA (Navan Fort, the seat of the Ulster kings) and ARD MACHA ('Macha's Height,' modern Armagh) both bear her name. Brigid, Boann (the goddess of the River Boyne), and Etain are all other great Tuatha De women. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: The chief-god of the Tuatha De came down to a stream in what is now County Sligo on the eve of Samhain, looking for the Morrigan, in the days before his people's great fight with the Fomorians. He found her straddling the water, one foot on the north bank and one on the south, washing. Which of the Tuatha De met her there?
context: The Dagda -- 'the Good God' -- is the chief of the Tuatha De and the Morrigan's partner in the sacred-marriage tryst that seals the Tuatha De's war-alliance with the goddess of the land. Lugh is the war-leader, Nuada the deposed king, Ogma the champion. Source: Cath Maige Tuired section 84; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda.  (Legend.)

question: The Morrigan stood with a foot on each bank of a ford in Corann, near modern Riverstown, on the eve of the great battle of Mag Tuired, and the chief-god of the Tuatha De came to meet her there. The sagas have fixed the place ever since. On which river is that ford?
context: The Unius flows through Corann in County Sligo; the Morrigan's ford is on it, near Riverstown. The Boyne is the river of Newgrange (Aengus's mound); the Shannon is the longest river in Ireland; the Liffey runs through Dublin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan; Cath Maige Tuired section 84.  (Legend.)

question: The Morrigan lay with the chief-god of the Tuatha De at the ford, and in return she pledged to go alone against the Fomorian king before the battle and cripple him from within. In the words of the Cath Maige Tuired she promised to take from him 'the blood of his heart and the kidneys of his valour.' Which Fomorian king did she name?
context: Indech mac De Domnann is the Fomorian king the Morrigan promises to un-man; the pledge is preserved verbatim in Cath Maige Tuired section 84. Balor is the one-eyed champion killed by Lugh; Bres is the half-Fomorian king the Tuatha De once tried and deposed; Elatha is Bres's father. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired section 84.  (Legend.)

question: A ghostly woman keens outside an Irish house on the night the head of the family is about to die. She is the folk descendant of the Morrigan's Washer-at-the-Ford face, and in Ireland she has her own name. What is she called?
context: BEAN-SIDHE means 'woman of the sidhe' (fairy-mound), anglicised as BANSHEE -- the folk-shadow of the Washer at the Ford, an aos si woman heard keening for a coming death. The Puca is a shape-changing sidhe trickster; the Leanan-Sidhe is a fairy-lover; the Cailleach is the old woman of winter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banshee.  (Legend.)

question: The Morrigan chanted a second poem over the field after the Fomorian champion Balor was killed. It cheered the win, then rolled into a dark prophecy: 'summer without blossoms, cattle without milk, women without modesty, men without valour...' At the end of which battle did she chant that prophecy?
context: The prophecy is preserved in Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167 at the close of the SECOND battle of Moytura (Tuatha De vs Fomorians). The First Battle of Moytura was the Tuatha De against the Fir Bolg. The Cattle Raid of Cooley is Cuchulainn's saga. The Battle of Ventry is a Fenian-cycle tale. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167.  (Legend.)

question: 'I shall not see a world which will be dear to me,' the Morrigan chanted over the beaten Fomorians. Her closing poem rolled straight from a battle-cry into a foretelling that stands beside two others of the same shape: the Norse Voluspa, with Odin questioning the seeress, and one book of the Christian Bible whose visions of beasts, seals and a final battle have haunted Western art. Which book is that?
context: REVELATION (the Apocalypse of John) closes the New Testament with the final-days vision -- the Western Christian counterpart to the Morrigan's rosc and to the Voluspa. Daniel and Isaiah contain famous apocalyptic passages of their own; Genesis is the opening book of origins. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Revelation.  (Legend.)

question: In the Tain Bo Cuailnge the Morrigan comes to Cu Chulainn at the ford in her most beautiful young-woman shape, in the middle of the war he is holding off alone. She offers him two things together, one of them a gift no goddess offers lightly. What does she offer?
answer: her love and her aid in the fighting
choices: her love and her aid in the fighting
a magic spear and a golden shield
a chariot and a team of horses
a cauldron of healing and a druid's cloak
context: Tain Bo Cuailnge (Recension I, ed. O'Rahilly 1976): the Morrigan appears to Cu Chulainn as a beautiful young woman in royal dress and offers herself and her supernatural help against the army of Connacht. Lugh's spear, chariots and cauldrons belong to other Irish myths.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn is holding the border of Ulster alone against a whole invading army when a beautiful young woman meets him at a ford with an offer. She is the Morrigan, war-goddess of the Tuatha De Danann, in disguise. He does not recognise her, he cannot afford a distraction, and he refuses her plainly. How does the Morrigan answer his refusal?
answer: she promises to oppose him in the fights to come
choices: she promises to oppose him in the fights to come
she rides away in silence and never returns
she laughs and offers him a second chance the next day
she strikes him blind with a look
context: Tain Bo Cuailnge: when the young warrior turns her down (he does not know she is a goddess), the Morrigan tells him that if he will not have her love he will have her hate -- she will hinder him herself in his next fights. The Tain then delivers exactly that in three animal-shape scenes.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn passes an old woman at the roadside after the last of his fights. She is lame in one leg, blind in one eye and has one arm crushed, the exact three wounds he has just given the eel, the heifer and the wolf. Whatever she is doing, when he blesses her three times, each blessing heals one of those wounds. What is she doing?
answer: milking a cow and offering him three drinks
choices: milking a cow and offering him three drinks
spinning wool and asking him to hold the thread
washing bloody clothes in a stream
carrying firewood and asking him to lift the bundle
context: Tain Bo Cuailnge: the old woman is the Morrigan in disguise, and she is milking a cow at the roadside. Cu Chulainn is thirsty and asks for a drink; she gives him three, and after each one he blesses her -- and each blessing heals one of the wounds he has just inflicted. Washing bloody clothes at a ford is Badb's Washer-at-the-Ford omen, a related but different scene; spinning and firewood belong elsewhere.  (Legend.)

question: The Morrigan already has a job among the older gods long before Cu Chulainn is born: she stands with the Tuatha De Danann against the Fomorians in the Cath Maige Tuired. In the middle of the fight she does something that turns the whole battle. What does she do?
answer: chants a poem that breaks the Fomorian line
choices: chants a poem that breaks the Fomorian line
throws Balor's own eye back at him
wakes the dead of the Tuatha De for one more charge
opens the earth beneath the Fomorian king
context: Cath Maige Tuired (the second Battle of Moytura): the Morrigan promises the Dagda on Samhain eve that she will aid the Tuatha De against the Fomorians, and during the battle she chants a poem -- 'kings rise up to the battle' -- and the Fomorians break and are driven into the sea. Balor's eye is put out by Lugh's sling-stone (a different question); the dead are not raised; the earth-opening motif is not part of this fight.  (Legend.)

question: Three maidens come out of a hall at dawn, beside a holy well at the second root of the world-tree Yggdrasil. Anything dipped in that well comes out white as an eggshell, and the fate of the nine worlds lies in the maidens' hands. What are these three maidens called?
context: The Norns come out of their hall beside the well of Urd and carve on wood, setting the fate of every being in the nine worlds. The Valkyries are the choosers-of-the-slain who carry fallen warriors up to Valhalla. The Disir are a broader class of protective female spirits, tied to family lines. The Idisi are the Old High German equivalent, mentioned in the Merseburg Charms -- close cousins but a different name.  (Legend.)

question: The speaker of the Voluspa names the three fate-women of Norse myth in stanza 20, and their names are just three Old Norse words for three ordinary things a Norse-speaker used every day. The three words together mean 'Was', 'Being' and 'Shall-Be'. What are the three names?
context: Urd = 'was / has-become' (past); Verdandi = 'becoming / that-which-is' (present participle); Skuld = 'shall-be / debt-owed-to-the-future' (future). Frigg / Freyja / Sif are three Aesir goddesses. Modi / Magni / Vidar are three sons of the gods who survive Ragnarok. Nott / Dag / Sol are Night, Day, and Sun.  (Legend.)

question: The three fate-women come out of their hall beside the well at the foot of the world-tree to set the life of one newborn child, stanza 20 of the Voluspa says. They do the same for every child born into the nine worlds, and once it is done not even Odin, chief of the gods, can undo the doom. How do they set a child's fate?
answer: they carve runes on a stave of ash
choices: they carve runes on a stave of ash
they weave a thread on a great loom and cut it at death
they spit into the well and read the ripples
they whisper a secret name over the cradle
context: Voluspa 20: the three Norns 'scored' -- they carve the runes that decide fate onto wood. Once cut, the rune stands: no god, not even Odin, can un-carve it. The loom-and-thread image is real too, but it belongs to the Greek Moirai and later medieval retellings; the older Poetic-Edda picture is knife-on-wood. Spitting-into-a-well is the mead-of-poetry story, not a fate-rite. Whispering a name is Anglo-Saxon nam-giefu, not Norse.  (Legend.)

question: One woman speaks the whole of the Voluspa, the great fate-poem at the head of the Old Norse Poetic Edda, sung in Iceland in the 10th or 11th century. She says she has watched the three fate-women at their well, and she carries the story all the way to its end at Ragnarok. What kind of speaker is she?
context: The Voluspa (literally 'the volva's prophecy') is spoken by a volva, a seeress, who claims first-hand sight of the Norns at Urdarbrunnr. Her testimony -- what she saw them carve -- is the frame for the whole poem, up through Ragnarok. A skald is a court-poet who composes praise-verse for kings. A godi is a chieftain-priest who ran temple sacrifices. A thul is a reciter of wisdom-verse (Odin is called Fimbulthul, 'great thul', in Havamal).  (Legend.)

question: Odin and the Aesir came into their power only after the three fate-women had laid down the law of fate, stanza 20 of the Voluspa says, so even Odin acts inside a story someone else has already written. The Old Norse word for it is not one of the god-names but an ancient noun meaning literally 'ancient-law' or 'primal-layer'. What is the Norse word for fate itself?
context: Orlog (Old Norse orlog / urlag) literally means 'primal-law' or 'that-which-was-laid-down-first' (or- 'ancient' + log 'law, layer'). It is above the gods; even Odin acts inside it. Urdr is the eldest Norn's own name (and 'that which was'). Skop means 'shaping / doom-shape' -- what fate does to a person. Aldr means 'lifespan / age' -- how long a person lives, not fate itself.  (Legend.)

question: In Mark's Gospel, four men carried a paralysed friend on his sleeping mat to a house in Capernaum where Jesus was teaching. The crowd was packed so tight around the door that no one else could squeeze in, so the four found another way. Where did they take their friend to reach Jesus?
choices: Around to a side courtyard opening
context: Mark 2:1-4. First-century Galilean houses had flat roofs made of wooden beams overlaid with thatch and packed mud -- soft enough to dig through, sturdy enough to walk on. The stairs to the roof were usually on the outside of the house.

question: Jesus turned back to the paralysed man on the mat after the scribes objected, and he gave him a short three-part command: get up, then do something with the bed, and go home. He proved his point by healing the man in front of the whole crowded room. What was the middle instruction Jesus gave about the bed?
choices: Leave thy bed for the poor
Burn thy bed in the fire
Sell thy bed at the market
context: Mark 2:11 -- 'Arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house'. The man immediately rose, picked up his mat, and walked out through the crowd (Mark 2:12); this was the proof-in-action for the scribes.

question: Jesus was leaving the city of Jericho on the road when a blind beggar by the roadside heard who was passing and started shouting for help. Mark is the only gospel that gives this beggar a name, and it stops to explain what the name means. What is the name Mark gives him?
context: Mark 10:46 places Bartimaeus by the roadside as Jesus leaves Jericho. Zacchaeus was a tax collector Jesus met in Jericho going the OTHER direction (Luke 19); Lazarus was raised from the dead in Bethany; Malchus was the servant whose ear Peter cut off in Gethsemane.

question: Mark stops to translate the blind beggar's Aramaic name, Bar-Timaeus, for his readers. The prefix Bar- names a family tie. Hebrew Ben-, as in Benjamin, names the same tie, and Gaelic Mac-, as in MacDonald, names it too. What family tie do all three prefixes name?
context: Bar in Aramaic, ben in Hebrew, and mac in Gaelic all mean 'son of'. Bartimaeus = son of Timaeus; Benjamin = son of the right hand; MacDonald = son of Donald. Mark 10:46 spells the meaning out for Greek-speaking readers who didn't know Aramaic.

question: A blind beggar sat by the road outside the gates of Jericho, hearing a huge crowd move past him. When he learned that Jesus of Nazareth was in the middle of it, he shouted at the top of his lungs, 'Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me.' The people around him told him to be quiet, for he was making a scene. What did the beggar do next?
answer: Shouted the same words even louder
choices: Grabbed at the cloaks of the passers-by around him
Shouted the same words even louder
Called out the names of the disciples one by one
Begged a bystander to lead him closer to Jesus
context: Mark 10:48 -- 'many charged him that he should hold his peace: but he cried the more a great deal, Thou son of David, have mercy on me'. This persistence is what Mark uses to show his faith: he refuses to be shushed. It is only after this second, louder cry that Jesus stops and calls for him.

question: Jesus stopped at last on the Jericho road and called the blind beggar over. The beggar probably owned nothing more valuable than his cloak, and Mark records deliberately what he did with it before he ran to Jesus. What did the beggar do with his cloak?
answer: Threw it off into the road
choices: Threw it off into the road
Tore it up as a sign of grief
context: Mark 10:50 -- 'And he, casting away his garment, rose, and came to Jesus.' For a beggar the outer cloak served as coat by day and blanket by night; discarding it before he could see was the risk of a man expecting to be healed.

question: The blind beggar stood face to face with Jesus outside Jericho, after shouting for mercy until Jesus stopped and called him over. Before healing him, Jesus asked one deliberate question. Mark keeps the question because its answer sounds so obvious: the man was blind, so of course he wanted his sight, and yet Jesus made him say it out loud. What did Jesus ask, in the King James wording?
answer: What wilt thou that I should do unto thee
choices: Believest thou that I am able to do this
What wilt thou that I should do unto thee
Who do men say that I am
context: Mark 10:51. All four are REAL questions Jesus asks in the gospels ('wilt thou be made whole' to the paralytic at Bethesda in John 5, 'believest thou' to the blind men in Matthew 9, 'who do men say' to the disciples at Caesarea Philippi in Mark 8). The Bartimaeus question is the one that makes the beggar name his desire out loud.

question: A woman with a twelve-year haemorrhage came forward trembling and admitted she was the one who had touched Jesus's cloak in the crowd. Jesus did not scold her. He gave her a single line that Mark records word for word, the same line he later said to a blind beggar outside Jericho. What did Jesus tell her had made her whole?
context: Mark 5:34 -- 'Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace'. Jesus uses the exact same phrase to Bartimaeus at Mark 10:52: 'thy faith hath made thee whole'. In both scenes it is the person's trust, not the physical touch or the shouted words, that Jesus names as the healer.

question: Moses did not lead the Hebrews out of Egypt alone, the book of Exodus says. God went before them in a visible sign that changed with the time of day: a tall column of one thing during the day and a tall column of another thing at night. What were the two forms of the guiding column?
answer: Cloud by day and fire by night
choices: Cloud by day and fire by night
Smoke by day and ash by night
Rain by day and lightning by night
Mist by day and moonlight by night
context: Exodus 13:21. The pillar is one continuous presence; only its appearance changes with the hour. Later at the sea it moves from before them to behind them and stands between the two camps overnight.

question: Pharaoh, king of Egypt, let the Hebrew slaves go after ten plagues struck his land, and then his heart hardened again. He wanted to drag them back by force. Exodus says he mustered six hundred of Egypt's finest, each with a captain, the fastest and deadliest force on an ancient battlefield. Six hundred of what did Pharaoh muster?
context: Exodus 14:7. 'Six hundred chosen chariots, and all the chariots of Egypt, and captains over every one of them.' Egyptian chariots of the New Kingdom were fast, light, two-wheeled, carrying a driver and an archer.

question: The Hebrews saw Pharaoh's army bearing down on them, with nothing but water behind them, and they turned on Moses with a bitter, sarcastic question. In the King James wording, they cried: 'Because there were no --- in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?' What is the missing word?
context: Exodus 14:11. Egypt was famous for its tombs (the pyramids and rock-cut tombs of the Valley of the Kings). The Hebrews' sneer is that Egypt had plenty of graves; Moses did not need to drag them to the desert to bury them.

question: Moses stood with the Hebrews on the shore of the Red Sea, Pharaoh's army closing in fast behind them. The people panicked and cried out that he had led them out only to die. Moses answered with a famous three-verb command that the King James Bible records exactly, three things to do while God himself fought for them. What did Moses command?
answer: Fear not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD
choices: Fear not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD
Kneel, cry out, and wait for the LORD to answer
Trust, obey, and follow the pillar of cloud
Draw your swords, form up, and charge the sea
context: Exodus 14:13. Moses forbids both flight and combat: the Hebrews are to hold their line and watch. In the next verse he adds, 'The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.'

question: In Exodus, Moses stretched his rod over the water that night. God drove the sea back with a wind, and the King James verse says two things about it: God sent it 'all that night', and it blew from one specific direction. From what direction did it blow?
context: Exodus 14:21. 'The LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land.' The east wind is a recurring instrument of God's judgment in the prophets (Jonah, Hosea, Ezekiel).

question: In the book of Exodus, Pharaoh's army came thundering down onto the dry seabed after the Hebrews, between the standing walls of water. In the middle of the crossing, God stopped the pursuit by ruining one specific part of its war-machines, so that the drivers could not go forward. What part of the war-machines broke?
context: Exodus 14:25. 'And took off their chariot wheels, that they drave them heavily; so that the Egyptians said, Let us flee from the face of Israel; for the LORD fighteth for them.' The chariots bog down; Moses then stretches out his hand again and the water returns.

question: Jesus opens one of his most famous parables with a plain, one-line setup: 'A certain man had two sons' (Luke 15:11). The younger boy walks up to his father one morning with a demand that would have shocked every listener at the time. What does he ask for?
choices: the deed to the family land
context: Luke 15:12: 'Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me.' In first-century terms this is close to telling his father, 'I wish you were already dead' -- a son normally only asks for his portion after the funeral. A blessing over the herd (Isaac to Jacob), a deed to land (Naboth's vineyard), and a dowry chest all belong to other Bible scenes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: A younger son leaves home for 'a far country' with his money in hand, in a parable Jesus tells in Luke's Gospel. Luke sums up what happens to the money there in one memorable phrase that gets quoted whenever the parable is retold. What does the boy do with it?
choices: buries it in a field for safekeeping
lends it to strangers at interest
pays it into the local temple
context: Luke 15:13: 'wasted his substance with riotous living.' The Greek behind 'riotous' means unrestrained, dissolute -- the kind of spending that leaves no trace. Burying money in a field is what the third servant does in Jesus's Parable of the Talents; lending at interest and paying into the temple both figure in other Gospel scenes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: The younger son of Jesus's parable hires himself out to a local man once his money is gone and a famine hits the far country. Broke and hungry, he takes the lowest job available in that world, one a young Jewish man would have found humiliating on top of miserable. What is the job?
context: Luke 15:15. Pigs are unclean animals in the Mosaic law -- the equivalent of hiring yourself out to shovel something ritually filthy every day. That is Jesus's point: rock bottom for a Jewish audience. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: A starving young man in a far country comes to himself in Luke's parable, snaps out of it and decides to go home. He rehearses a short, humble speech to say to his father, and the first line names two audiences he has wronged. What does the speech begin with?
answer: 'I have sinned against heaven, and before thee'
choices: 'I have sinned against heaven, and before thee'
'I have wasted thy silver and my name'
'I have shamed thy house and my mother's memory'
'I have broken every commandment given to Moses'
context: Luke 15:18-19, continued: 'and am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants.' The boy has planned it out -- but as it turns out, he never gets to finish the speech. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: A young man comes home starving from a far country in Jesus's parable in Luke 15, to beg his father for a servant's place. He begins his rehearsed apology, but before he can finish, his father is already shouting orders to the servants. Three specific things are to be brought out and put on the boy at once. Which three?
answer: the best robe, a ring, and shoes
choices: the best robe, a ring, and shoes
a crown, a rod, and a golden chain
linen bands, oil, and a lamp
context: Luke 15:22. Each token means something specific: the robe is the honoured guest's mantle, the ring carries the father's seal (authority over the household), and shoes mark him as a free son and not a barefoot slave. Sackcloth and ashes are mourning wear (Job, Nineveh); linen bands and oil are burial gear (Lazarus). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: A father runs out to meet his son on the road in the parable of the Prodigal Son, throws his arms around him and cuts him off mid-apology. In the same breath, still holding the boy, he shouts to the servants to kill one specific animal at once for a welcome-home feast. Which animal does the father call for?
context: Luke 15:23: 'And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry.' The 'fatted calf' was a young beast penned apart from the herd and grain-fed for the biggest occasion the family would ever mark -- the household's showpiece meat. The Passover lamb, the two turtledoves (poor family's temple offering), and the ram of consecration (Aaron's priesthood, Exodus 29) are all real biblical animals sacrificed for particular occasions -- but the parable's feast animal is the calf. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: The elder brother of Luke's parable comes in from the fields, hears music and dancing, refuses to go inside and starts listing his own long years of service to his father. In the middle of the rant he complains that his father has never once given him a young animal to roast for a party with his friends, a much smaller beast than the one being killed inside. What smaller animal does he name?
context: Luke 15:29: 'yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends' -- a kid, a young goat, the everyday party meat, versus the fatted calf being killed for his brother. The elder brother's fury is exact and petty: 'you never gave me even the cheap one.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: Jesus tells three parables in a row in Luke 15 to a crowd of grumbling scribes and Pharisees. Each story is about something valuable being lost and then found, and about the joy of finding it. The Prodigal Son is the third of the three. What are the other two parables about?
answer: a lost sheep and a lost coin
choices: a lost sheep and a lost coin
a lost ring and a lost letter
a lost donkey and a lost cloak
a lost bride and a lost harp
context: Luke 15:3-7 (a shepherd leaves 99 sheep to find one that has wandered off), Luke 15:8-10 (a woman sweeps the whole house for one lost silver coin from her string of ten), and Luke 15:11-32 (the Lost Son). Together the three parables form Luke's 'lost-and-found' set. The other lost-object pairings in the choices are not from Jesus's parables. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: The father of Luke's parable goes out to his sulking elder son and answers the whole complaint in one line that the story turns on. He tells him everything the father has is already his, but they had to celebrate, because his brother had been counted as one thing and now was another. In what pair does he put it?
answer: was dead, and is alive again
choices: was dead, and is alive again
was in shadow, and is in light
context: Luke 15:32. The father repeats a version of the same line from earlier in the scene: 'this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.' The other three pairs are all real Gospel formulas -- blind-now-sees is John 9, shadow-and-light is the Isaiah quotation over Galilee, silenced-and-speaks is Zechariah after John the Baptist's birth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: A young warrior of Ulster holds the border alone in the Tain Bo Cuailnge, the greatest of the Old Irish sagas, and falls into a strange body-change in battle until his shape stops being human at all. Which hero goes through it?
context: Fionn belongs to the later Fenian Cycle and never undergoes ristrad; Beowulf and Sigurd are heroes of other traditions listed here as wrong choices. Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn falls into a terrifying body-change in battle, and his shape stops being human. The Tain uses one Old Irish word for it each time the change hits him, and English translators call it 'the warp-spasm' or 'the distortion'. What is the Old Irish word for that battle-change?
context: Also spelled riastradh. Geis = a magical prohibition; imbas = poetic inspiration; dinnshenchas = the lore of place-names. Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: The young hero of the Tain goes into the warp-spasm, his body twisting and swelling, and a tall column rises straight up above his head. It stands higher than a ship's mast, it is made of dark blood or black smoke, and every warrior on the field can see it. The Irish call it the lon laith. What is that in English?
context: Lon laith, sometimes 'warrior's moon'. A single black column above the crown -- his mark on any battlefield. Mythical Archives; Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: One of Cu Chulainn's eyes sinks so deep in the warp-spasm that the Tain says a wild crane could not probe it out. That detail has become one of the most-quoted images in Irish literature. What happens to the other eye?
answer: it bulges out onto his cheek
choices: it bulges out onto his cheek
it turns red as a hot coal
it closes and does not open
context: One eye in, one eye out. One of the most reprinted passages in early Irish literature. Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: The young Ulster hero's lower jaw strikes the upper with 'a lion-killing blow' when the warp-spasm is on him, the Tain says. Out of his mouth come objects each as large as a ram's fleece. What comes out?
context: The image is of the hero literally spitting fire the size of ram-fleeces. Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn comes back to Emain Macha from his first raid, a boy still in the warp-spasm, and the men of Ulster are so afraid he will slaughter them all that they will not open the gates. Conchobar's queen Mugain leads the women of the fort out to the plain. What do they do to shame him out of the frenzy?
