answer: they walk out to meet him naked, baring their breasts
choices: they walk out to meet him naked, baring their breasts
they set fire to their own hair in front of him
they lay their infant sons at his feet
they sing his mother's death-lament together
context: Mugain leads the women out; Cu Chulainn covers his face at the sight -- the shame breaks the frenzy long enough for the warriors to seize him. Cuchulainn's Boyish Deeds (Tain Recension I).  (Legend.)

question: The warriors of Ulster seize the boy Cu Chulainn, his face covered from the women, and plunge him into a series of vats of cold water to cool the frenzy off him. In the first, the water bursts the wooden staves. In the second, it boils with bubbles the size of a fist. What happens in the third?
answer: the water heats only to a comfortable bath
choices: the water heats only to a comfortable bath
the water freezes solid around him
the water is thrown out untouched
context: First bursts, second boils, third tempers -- and the boy is himself again. Mugain then puts a blue mantle and silver brooch on him and seats him at Conchobar's knee. Cuchulainn's Boyish Deeds (Tain).  (Legend.)

question: Scribes copied the longest and best surviving version of the Tain, the great cattle-raid tale of old Ireland, into one particular medieval Irish manuscript. Into which of these great old Irish books did they copy it?
choices: the Annals of the Four Masters
context: Lebor Laignech, c.1160. The Book of Kells is a gospel-book; the Cathach is a 6th-c. psalter; the Annals are 17th-c. history. Recension I is in the Lebor na hUidre. Wikipedia: Tain Bo Cuailnge.

question: Cu Chulainn remakes himself into a fighting shape in the warp-spasm, and scholars set that Irish scene beside a related Norse battle-state: a trance-frenzy of certain warriors of Odin, chief of the Norse gods. Those warriors are said to fight without pain of wound or fire, and to remember nothing of it after. What is the Norse word for that state?
context: 'Going berserk'. Scholars note the ristrad is more monstrous and more visually elaborate than berserkergangr -- a physical melting into a fighting-shape, not merely a fury. Wergild = blood-price; einherjar = Odin's chosen dead in Valhalla; seidhr = Norse magic. Wikipedia: Berserker; Riastrad.

question: In Malory's stories, King Arthur would not sit down to eat until he had heard of some wonder, on the one day each year when his knights rode back to Camelot. They feasted at his round table as equals and renewed their vows. Which church feast was it?
context: Pentecost (Whitsunday) falls fifty days after Easter and was the high feast of the Round Table year in Malory. It was Arthur's great gathering day, and he would not sit down to eat until he had heard of some wonder or adventure. The knights gathered, feasted, and renewed the oath together; scribes recorded what each had done in the year past. Malory's Book III opens the pattern. It is at Pentecost that Galahad arrives and the Grail quest begins. Christmas and Easter were the two greatest feasts of the church year but did not have this special Round Table meaning; All Hallows (November 1) was a solemn feast for the dead, not for oath-renewal.  (Legend.)

question: The knights of the Round Table gathered at Camelot for the great feast and repeated their oath together. They swore never to commit murder or treason, always to help ladies and widows, and never to fight in a wrongful quarrel. One more rule in the oath concerned a defeated enemy. What was that rule?
answer: always to give mercy to any who asked mercy
choices: always to give mercy to any who asked mercy
always to hang defeated foes as a warning to others
always to hold captured knights for ransom
always to demand a public confession before sparing life
context: The mercy clause is the heart of the Pentecostal Oath: to spare any beaten foe who called for mercy, upon pain of forfeiture of his lordship and worship as an Arthurian knight. Hanging defeated foes was the crime of Malory's villains, such as the Red Knight of the Red Launds who had hanged nearly forty. Ransom was normal in real medieval war but was not written into the Round Table oath. Public confession is not there either.  (Legend.)

question: Agravaine and Mordred brought an accusation before King Arthur against Queen Guinevere, in Malory's twentieth book. No invading army broke the Round Table; Arthur's own law forced him to send her to the stake, and the fellowship went to war with itself. What accusation did the two knights bring?
answer: that she had lain with Sir Lancelot
choices: that she had lain with Sir Lancelot
that she had plotted with Morgan le Fay to poison the king
that she had taken the treasury of Camelot in secret to Benoic
that she had been born the daughter of a witch
context: Agravaine and Mordred trapped Lancelot in the queen's chamber and forced the accusation into the open; by his own laws Arthur had to condemn her to burn. Morgan le Fay's poisoning schemes belong to earlier books and did not touch the queen. The Benoic treasury and witch-birth accusations are inventions and do not appear in Malory.  (Legend.)

question: The Greeks hid their finest warriors in the belly of a huge wooden horse and left it outside Troy as a fake gift. The Trojans dragged it in. At nightfall the men inside climbed down, opened a gate from the inside and let the whole army pour in. What did the Greeks then do to Troy itself?
context: The night the wooden horse trick pays off. The city is torched and the royal family destroyed one by one -- the dark counterweight to the cleverness of the horse. Sources: Virgil, Aeneid 2 and the Iliou Persis summary in Proclus.  (Legend.)

question: Old King Priam of Troy pulled on his armor on the last night of the war and fled for safety to a family altar standing in his own courtyard. One Greek warrior chased him down and killed him right there at the altar. Who was that Greek warrior?
context: Neoptolemus (also called Pyrrhus) came to Troy as a teenager, after Achilles was already dead. He becomes the face of the sack. Source: Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-558.  (Legend.)

question: In Virgil's Aeneid, one Greek warrior hunted down Priam, old king of Troy, at a family altar in the palace courtyard on the last night of the war. Before killing Priam himself, he first cut down one of the old king's other sons right in front of him, to make him watch. Which of Priam's sons did he kill at his father's feet?
context: Polites ran wounded through the palace and died at his father's feet. Priam then threw a spear at Neoptolemus that harmlessly bounced off the shield, and Neoptolemus dragged him to the altar and cut his throat. Deiphobus (who married Helen after Paris died) and Helenus (the prophet-son) also survived into the last night of Troy. Source: Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-558.  (Legend.)

question: The Trojan princess Cassandra ran up to the citadel on the last night of the war and clung to a wooden cult image inside a goddess's temple, begging the goddess for sanctuary. A Greek warrior dragged her away from the image anyway, a sacrilege the goddess would punish years later. Which goddess's temple was it?
context: The temple was Athena's, which is why the sacrilege about to happen matters so much: Athena had helped the Greeks the whole ten years and is about to switch sides. Source: Iliou Persis summary; Euripides, Trojan Women prologue.  (Legend.)

question: A Greek warrior stormed into a temple on the night Troy fell, seized the princess Cassandra, a doomed prophetess of Apollo, and dragged her out so violently that the goddess's sacred wooden statue tipped over. She had been clinging to it for sanctuary. It was one of the most infamous sacrileges of the whole Trojan War. Which Greek dragged her out?
answer: Ajax the Lesser, son of Oileus of Locris
choices: Ajax the Lesser, son of Oileus of Locris
context: There are two Ajaxes in the Greek army and children mix them up: Ajax the Great (Ajax son of Telamon) killed himself in a rage before Troy fell, after the armour of the dead Achilles was awarded to Odysseus instead of to him. Ajax the Lesser (son of Oileus) is the one at Athena's altar. Source: Iliou Persis summary; Odyssey 4.499-511.  (Legend.)

question: In Euripides's tragedy Trojan Women, the Greeks divide up the enslaved royal women of Troy, and Andromache, widow of the Trojan prince Hector, keeps her infant son with her. But the victors are afraid: if Hector's boy grows up, he might one day come back and avenge his father. What do the Greeks do to the child?
answer: They throw him from the walls of Troy
choices: They throw him from the walls of Troy
They cut his throat over Achilles's tomb
They drown him in the harbor of Troy
They bury him alive in the palace foundations
context: In Trojan Women, the herald Talthybius tells Andromache that the Greek council, at Odysseus's urging, has decided the child cannot be allowed to live. Source: Euripides, Trojan Women 719-739.  (Legend.)

question: Hecuba washes the small body of Hector's son in Euripides's play Trojan Women, when it is carried back into ruined Troy, and she lays the child out for burial upon a single object. What object serves as his bier?
choices: The topmost tile of the citadel
context: The shield that had covered Hector in battle now covers the child in the grave -- one of the most piercing images in Greek tragedy. Source: Euripides, Trojan Women 1133-1206.  (Legend.)

question: The Greek captains divided the captured royal women of Troy among them as slaves, after ten long years of siege. The commander of all the Greek forces chose for himself Cassandra, the daughter of King Priam whose warnings were fated never to be believed. Which Greek captain took Cassandra as his prize?
context: Agamemnon and Cassandra were both cut down in the bath at Mycenae by his wife Clytemnestra (with Aegisthus) -- the opening scene of Aeschylus's Oresteia. Source: Aeschylus, Agamemnon; Odyssey 11.405-434.  (Legend.)

question: The ghost of Achilles appeared to the Greek fleet after the sack of Troy and demanded King Priam's youngest daughter Polyxena as his share of the plunder, before the ships would be granted a fair wind home. Achilles's son carried out the demand. What did he do to her?
choices: Burned her alive on Achilles's pyre
Buried her beside Achilles in his tomb
Gave her as slave to Odysseus
context: The ghost of Achilles had demanded a bride from the Trojan spoils, and Neoptolemus carried out the demand on his father's behalf. Polyxena is the Trojan counterpart to Iphigenia, the girl sacrificed by the Greeks before the war began. In Euripides's Hecuba she asks to die standing, refusing to be treated as a slave. Source: Euripides, Hecuba; Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.  (Legend.)

question: Euripides staged Trojan Women before Athenian audiences in 415 BCE, the year after Athens had massacred the men of a small island and enslaved its women. The play's grief-drenched sympathy for the losing side reads as protest. Which island's fate stood behind it?
context: The Melian Dialogue in Thucydides 5 records Athens's ultimatum to Melos in 416 BCE: submit or be destroyed. When Melos refused, Athens killed the men and enslaved the women and children. Trojan Women premiered the following spring. Source: Thucydides 5.84-116; Euripides, Trojan Women (415 BCE).

question: Jesus climbed a low hill above the Sea of Galilee to give what later readers called the Sermon on the Mount, his longest teaching in Matthew's Gospel. Before he began, he took the exact pose that a Jewish rabbi used with students who came to be taught. What did Jesus do?
context: Matthew 5:1 -- 'seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him'. A rabbi taught SITTING; the audience stood or sat lower. This is why the whole discourse is called the Sermon on the Mount.

question: Jesus opened the Sermon on the Mount with a set of blessings called the Beatitudes. Each one began 'Blessed are...' and named a group of people who would receive a great reward from God. The very first promised the Kingdom of Heaven itself. Which group did Jesus say it belonged to?
context: Matthew 5:3 -- 'Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven'. Each of the other three groups also gets a promise: the pure in heart shall see God, the peacemakers shall be called children of God, those who mourn shall be comforted.

question: The crowd on the Galilean hillside heard Jesus call them the salt of the earth, in Matthew's Gospel. In the very next line he gave them a second image and paired it with a picture of something built high up that everyone could see for miles. What did Jesus say cannot be hid?
answer: A city set on a hill
choices: A lamp lit on a hilltop
A city set on a hill
context: Matthew 5:14 -- 'Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.' The pairing (salt + light) is the point; the city is the picture Jesus uses to make the light-image concrete.

question: Jesus's disciples learned a short prayer from him halfway through the Sermon on the Mount, one that Christians would go on repeating for two thousand years. It had seven petitions and began with a direct address. What were its opening words in the King James wording?
answer: Our Father which art in heaven
choices: Blessed be the name of God forever
Our Father which art in heaven
Hear O Israel the Lord our God
Almighty God unto whom all hearts
context: Matthew 6:9-13 -- 'After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done...' This is the Lord's Prayer.

question: King Solomon of Israel, in all his royal glory, was never dressed as splendidly as one wild flower of the meadow, Jesus told his listeners on the hillside. He was telling them not to worry about food or clothing, because God would provide for them as he did for the wild things. Which flowering plant did Jesus tell them to consider?
context: Matthew 6:28-29 -- 'Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.'

question: Jesus gave one single instruction near the end of the Sermon on the Mount, so famous that later readers named it the Golden Rule. He said this one line summed up 'the law and the prophets', that is, the whole Hebrew Scripture in one sentence. Which of these is the Golden Rule as the King James Bible gives it?
answer: Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them
choices: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you
Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them
Owe no man any thing, but to love one another
Do good to them that hate you, and pray for them that despitefully use you
context: Matthew 7:12. All four choices are real ethical teachings -- the first is the older 'silver rule' Rabbi Hillel gave, the third is from Paul in Romans 13:8, the fourth is from Jesus earlier in the same sermon at Matthew 5:44. The POSITIVE form 'do unto others' is what makes the Golden Rule distinctive.

question: Two builders put up houses in the last parable of the Sermon on the Mount. One set his house on solid rock and it stood. The other built on a different foundation, and when the rain descended and the floods came and the winds blew, Jesus said, 'great was the fall of it'. What did the foolish man build his house on?
context: Matthew 7:24-27. The wise man's house on the rock stands; the foolish man's house on the sand collapses when the rain, floods and winds beat on it. This is the very last image before the sermon ends.

question: In Luke's Gospel, Jesus came down and stood on level ground for a shorter parallel to the Sermon on the Mount, which is why Luke's version is called the Sermon on the Plain. Luke matched each of its four blessings with a paired counterline in the same rhythm, opening with a single sharp English word. What word opened each of Luke's four paired lines?
context: Luke 6:17-26 -- often called the Sermon on the Plain because Luke has Jesus come down and stand 'in the plain' (a level place). Luke gives four blessings (poor, hungry, weeping, hated) each answered by a matching 'Woe unto you' (rich, full, laughing, well-spoken-of).

question: In the old English ballads, a royal officer sent his men into Sherwood Forest again and again to catch the outlaw Robin Hood and his merry men. He hanged the outlaws he caught from the walls of his stone castle. Which town was that castle in?
context: The Sheriff of Nottingham is Robin Hood's chief enemy across the whole cycle. Robin's greenwood may be Barnsdale or Sherwood depending on the ballad, but the Sheriff is always tied to Nottingham. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Monk.  (Legend.)

question: A monk who had once been robbed by Robin Hood spotted the outlaw kneeling alone in prayer inside a church, in the oldest surviving Robin Hood ballad. The monk slipped out through the door and ran down the street to fetch the one man in town powerful enough to put Robin in chains. What was that man's title?
context: In Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119, earliest surviving Robin Hood ballad, c.1450) the monk fetches the Sheriff, who captures Robin in the church. Little John and Much the Miller's Son later rescue him. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Monk.  (Legend.)

question: An Old English king set his officer over a shire, centuries before the first Robin Hood ballad. The man's title was two words squashed together, one for 'shire' and one for the king's officer in it, and the modern word 'sheriff' comes from it. What was that older Old English title?
context: 'Sheriff' is a worn-down form of Old English 'scir-gerefa' -- shire-reeve, the king's reeve (officer) over a shire. Thanes were noble landholders, wardens and marshals were later Norman-French titles. Source: Wikipedia, Sheriff of Nottingham (position).

question: One sheriff handed the royal treasury, the Exchequer, the fixed lump sum his shire owed for the year, then pocketed as pure profit whatever he had squeezed out of the countryside above it. This arrangement had its own name in medieval finance. What was the practice called?
context: Sheriffs 'farmed' their shires -- paid a set farm (firma) to the Exchequer and pocketed everything squeezed above it. Gleaning was picking up leftover grain, reeving was general officer-work, tithing was the church tenth. Tax-farming is what made the office one of the most hated in the shires and gave rise to the Sheriff of Nottingham as a story-villain. Source: Wikipedia, Sheriff of Nottingham (position).

question: Robin Hood's enemy proclaimed a grand public contest in the town square, in the ballad A Gest of Robyn Hode, with a rich prize for the winner. The whole event was really a trap to lure Robin out of hiding, and Robin walked right into it in disguise, and won. What kind of contest was it?
context: In Fytte 5 of A Gest of Robyn Hode the Sheriff offers a prize arrow of gold and silver; Robin wins the shoot, is ambushed, Little John is wounded, and they take refuge at Sir Richard at the Lee's castle. Source: Wikipedia, A Gest of Robyn Hode.  (Legend.)

question: The Sheriff hunted Robin Hood through the oldest surviving ballads, A Gest of Robyn Hode and Robin Hood and the Monk among them, all first written down in the 1400s. He gave orders, set traps, led hunts and died badly. But in those medieval poems, one thing about the Sheriff was missing. What was missing?
context: The Sheriff is only 'the Sheriff' or 'the high Sheriff of Nottingham' in the earliest ballads -- no first name, no family name, no coat of arms. His villainy is his office. Later Victorian retellings invented names ('Sir Reginald', 'Sir Guy') that are not in the medieval texts. Source: Robbins Library, The Sheriff.  (Legend.)

question: One real sheriff under King John threatened arson against anyone who would not pay him protection money. His wrongful seizures were so notorious that the 1215 Magna Carta named him outright, in a clause ordering him and his kin expelled from royal office. What was his name?
context: Philip Marc, a Touraine-born supporter of King John, held Nottingham from 1208. Clause 50 of Magna Carta orders him, his brothers, and his nephew Geoffrey removed from office and out of England -- one of very few individuals singled out by name in the charter. He is probably the closest historical model behind the ballad villain. Source: Wikipedia, Philip Marc.

question: Patroclus could not stand watching Greeks die while his friend Achilles refused to fight, in Homer's Iliad. He borrowed Achilles's own armor, led the men out and was killed on the battlefield, and the armor was stripped off his body. Who killed Patroclus and took the armor?
context: Iliad 16 -- Patroclus, wearing Achilles's armour to scare the Trojans, is killed by Hector and stripped. Achilles's rage at this drives the rest of the poem. Source: Homer, Iliad 16.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles had lost his armor to the Trojans, so his sea-goddess mother Thetis climbed Mount Olympus in the Iliad to have new armor made for her son. She went to the forge of the smith of the Olympian gods, the crippled god who hammered out divine armor, thunderbolts and winged sandals for the others. Which god was she visiting at his forge?
context: Hephaestus was the smith of Olympus; the Romans called him Vulcan. He also forged Zeus's thunderbolts, Poseidon's trident, and Hermes's winged sandals. Source: Homer, Iliad 18; Hephaestus in Hesiod, Theogony.  (Legend.)

question: Homer lists the star-groups one by one at the center of the shield of Achilles, after earth, sky, sea, sun and full moon. He names the Pleiades, the Hyades, mighty Orion, and one more that he says men also call 'the Wain.' What is that last one?
context: 'The Bear, whom men also call the Wain' -- Iliad 18.487-489, Lattimore's translation. The Wain (wagon) is the old English name for the same constellation Americans call the Big Dipper. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.483-489.  (Legend.)

question: The smith-god laid a great world-encircling river around the very outer rim of the new shield of Achilles, in Book 18 of Homer's Iliad. Inside it he had hammered ploughed fields, dancers, the sun, the moon and the stars. Homer named the river as the boundary of everything. What was its name?
context: Okeanos (Ocean) was, for Homer, not the sea but a river that circled the flat disc of the world. Styx and Acheron are rivers of the underworld; Eridanos is a river of the far north. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.607-608.  (Legend.)

question: Thetis asked the smith-god for new armor for Achilles in the Iliad, and he made a huge round shield covered in scenes of the whole living world. Farther out from the cosmic center he inlaid two cities. One was a city at peace, with a bridal procession winding through the streets by torchlight and elders judging a quarrel in the market. What was the other city's condition?
context: The two-cities scene is Iliad 18.490-540. The besieged city has an ambush laid at the river outside its walls -- a snapshot of war to answer the snapshot of peace. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.509-540.  (Legend.)

question: Two predators pulled down an ox on one pastoral panel of Achilles's shield, in Homer's Iliad. The herdsmen and their dogs could not drive them off, and the beasts gorged on its black blood. What two predators were shown?
context: Iliad 18.573-586. The lions are gorging on the ox's black blood; the men and dogs stand back. Homer's world had lions, though they had gone extinct in Greece by classical times. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.573-586.  (Legend.)

question: Young men and young women danced hand in hand in the last scene before the outer river, on a great dancing-floor hammered into the shield of Achilles. Homer compared it to a legendary dancing-floor built long ago at a palace where a certain famous princess once danced. Which princess?
context: Iliad 18.590-592 -- the dancing-floor Daedalus built at Knossos for Ariadne (Minos's daughter, later the giver of the thread that saves Theseus in the Labyrinth). Source: Homer, Iliad 18.590-606.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles marries a princess of Calydon, in western Greece, long after his twelve labours. She is the sister of Meleager, leader of the great boar-hunt, and a dying centaur's lie will one day make her the cause of her husband's death. What is her name?
context: Sophocles's Trachiniae and Apollodorus 2.7 name Deianira as Heracles's Calydonian wife. Megara was his first wife, whom he killed in his madness; Alcmene is his mortal mother; Iole is the captive girl whose arrival triggers the tragedy.  (Legend.)

question: Nessus the centaur, shot down by Heracles for bolting with the hero's wife on his back, calls her close and lies to her. She should hide some of his blood in a jar; smeared on her husband's clothes, he promises, it will work a certain kind of magic. What does Nessus claim the blood is?
context: Sophocles, Trachiniae 570-587. The blood is really soaked in Hydra-venom from the arrow just fired; Nessus knows perfectly well he has handed her a delayed murder-weapon disguised as a love-charm.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles's wife sits at home and sees a captive princess arrive, years after the river-crossing. He has sacked a city and sent the young woman on ahead of him, and his wife fears he is about to leave her for a younger bride. Panicking, she remembers the dying centaur's advice. What is the captive girl's name?
context: Sophocles, Trachiniae. Iole, daughter of King Eurytus of Oechalia, is the fresh bride who triggers Deianira's panic. Omphale is the Lydian queen Heracles once served in women's clothing; Auge and Chalciope are other Heracles-women from earlier episodes.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles puts on his wife's gift at Cape Cenaeum in Euboea, where he is making a sacrifice, and wears the tunic for the rite. As his body warms the cloth something horrific begins. He panics and tears at the shirt to rip it off. What comes off with the cloth?
context: Sophocles, Trachiniae 1046-1075. The Hydra-venom in the soaked blood, activated by body-heat, fuses the fabric to Heracles's skin and eats through muscle; when he rips at the shirt his own flesh tears away with it, and in his agony he uproots trees on the mountainside.  (Legend.)

question: A messenger reaches the wife of Heracles with the truth about the jar she has kept for years. The dying centaur's gift is Hydra-poison, and the tunic she smeared with it is burning her husband alive. She has wanted only to hold on to him. What does she do in that same hour?
choices: she flees to a temple for sanctuary
she runs to warn her son Hyllus
she throws the empty jar into the sea
context: Sophocles, Trachiniae 812-946. Deianira takes her own life the moment she understands what she has done; in Sophocles she uses a sword on her marriage-bed. The horror of the play is that she is innocent of intent -- she meant only to keep her husband.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles has his companions carry him up a mountain, burning from the skin inward in a robe soaked with the poison of the Hydra. He knows no cure exists for it. He orders a great pyre of oak logs built and lies down on it to end his agony. What is the mountain called?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.229-272; Sophocles's Trachiniae ends with Heracles carried toward Oeta. Ida is Zeus's Cretan mountain; Pelion is the mountain of Chiron's cave; Cithaeron is where the infant Heracles was said to have strangled the twin lions.  (Legend.)

question: Every companion of Heracles refuses in horror when he orders them to set fire to the great pyre and end him. Finally one man agrees, but only in exchange for the bow of Heracles and the last of the poisoned arrows. Which companion strikes the flame?
context: Sophocles's Philoctetes. Iolaus is Heracles's chariot-nephew who cauterised the Hydra-stumps; Hylas is his young companion carried off by nymphs at a spring; Theseus is the Athenian hero of another cycle. Philoctetes is specifically the one who lights the pyre and earns the bow.  (Legend.)

question: The man who lit Heracles's pyre is fetched to Troy at last, carrying the bow he was paid with. A Greek oracle has warned that the city cannot be taken until that bow comes to the war. He shoots one of King Priam's sons dead outside the walls. Which Trojan prince does he kill?
context: Sophocles's Philoctetes and the Little Iliad. The oracle's condition is that Troy cannot fall without Heracles's bow. Hector is killed earlier by Achilles; Aeneas escapes the city and founds the Roman line; Deiphobus, another son of Priam, is killed later at the sack. Paris is the prince whose theft of Helen began the war, and Philoctetes with Heracles's bow shoots him down.  (Legend.)

question: Hera reconciles at last with the stepson she has hounded his whole life, once the pyre has consumed the mortal part of Heracles and only his Zeus-half has gone up to Olympus. She gives him her own daughter as his bride. Which daughter of Hera does Heracles marry on Olympus?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.229-272. Hebe, daughter of Zeus and Hera, is cup-bearer of the gods until she marries the deified Heracles. Eileithyia is Hera's daughter of childbirth (the goddess who delayed Heracles's own birth); Enyo is a war-goddess sometimes called Hera's daughter; Angelos is an obscure daughter of Hera in local tradition.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann went down into the hollow hills. Later Irish stories dropped their old name. The old gods took a new Irish name from the mounds, the one English speakers just turn into 'the fairies' or 'the Good Folk'. What is that Irish name?
context: AOS SI (pronounced roughly ees-shee, literally 'folk of the mounds') is the Irish name for the fairy folk -- the Tuatha De Danann in retreat underground. When later stories talk of the sidhe or the good people or the gentry of the hills, they are talking about the diminished Tuatha De Danann. The Fianna are the roving warrior-band of Fionn mac Cumhaill; the Fir Bolg are the fourth wave in the Book of Invasions; the Sons of Mil are the Milesians (the modern Irish) themselves. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aos_Si; godsandmonsters.info, 'Sidhe'; Sharon Wray, 'A Brief History of the Aos si'.  (Legend.)

question: The aos si walk out through the open barrier of the sidhe mounds, it is said, as the ghosts of the dead walk in. That happens on one night of the year, and much of the world now keeps the eve of that old Irish festival as Halloween. Which festival is it?
context: SAMHAIN (November 1) is the direct ancestor of Halloween -- the night the sidhe open. Bealtaine (May 1) opens summer; Lughnasadh (August 1) is the harvest festival; Imbolc (February 1) is spring's opening. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samhain.  (Legend.)

question: One of the Tuatha De took charge of the underground kingdom once the settlement with the Milesians had been struck, and he handed out one mound to each of his fellow gods. He gave Aengus the mound at Newgrange and Midir the mound of Bri Leith, then raised a magical mist called the Feth Fiada to hide the aos si from mortal eyes. Which of the Tuatha De did this?
context: Manannan mac Lir ('son of the sea') is the Tuatha De sea-god who links the visible world to the Otherworld across the water; he assigned the mounds, giving each god one, and raised the FETH FIADA, the magical mist that hides them from human sight (as in Altram Tige Da Medar, the Fosterage of the House of the Two Vessels). Lugh Lamhfhada is the long-armed spear-god, Nuada Silver-Arm is the first Tuatha De king, Ogma is the champion who invented the ogham script -- all Tuatha De heroes but not the divider. Sources: irishmyths.com/2025/08/27/god-map-fairy-mounds-tuath-de-danann; Wikipedia, 'Manannan mac Lir'.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn mac Cumhaill's son Oisin rode away with the Otherworld princess Niamh and spent what he believed was one long happy stay in the Land of Youth. When he finally rode back and set his foot on Irish soil, he turned at once into a withered old man and died. How long, by the counting of the story, had Oisin actually been gone?
context: Oisin is gone THREE HUNDRED YEARS while it feels to him like a short stay; the classic 'time-in-fairyland' story. Time in the sidhe mounds and Tir na nOg does not run at the same rate as time above ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oisin.  (Legend.)

question: An Irish farmer steered his plough carefully around a lone tree standing in the middle of his field, attached to no hedge or woodland, rather than cut it down. Irish folk tradition held that tree sacred to the aos si. Which tree was it?
context: The lone HAWTHORN (whitethorn) is the classic fairy-tree; to cut one down is to invite the aos si's wrath. Yew is the graveyard tree of Ireland; rowan is planted against fairy mischief (a protection, not a mound); ash is one of the sacred five 'guardian trees' but not the specifically-fairy tree. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aos_Si; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorn.  (Legend.)

question: Eddie Lenihan, an Irish folklorist, told the papers in 1999 that one small whitethorn on the route of a brand-new County Clare motorway was a rendezvous-point for the Kerry aos si on their way to fight the Connacht aos si. The construction workers refused to touch it, and the engineers altered the route around it. The story made the international news and the tree still stands. Where does it stand?
context: The LATOON FAIRY BUSH in County Clare -- a lone whitethorn on the route of the new M18 -- was spared in May 1999 after Lenihan's letter to the Irish Times went viral (CNN, BBC, New York Times all picked it up). Tara is the High Kings' hill in Meath; Skellig is the monastic sea-crag in Kerry; Uisneach is the mythic centre of Ireland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latoon_fairy_bush.

question: The apostle Paul rented a lecture hall in the Greek port of Ephesus and taught in it daily for two full years, reasoning with anyone who came in. The book of Acts names the schoolmaster who owned the room. What was the schoolmaster's name?
context: Acts 19:9-10 (KJV): '...disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus. And this continued by the space of two years; so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus.' The Greek name tyrannos originally meant a ruler who had seized power outside the constitution -- it is the root of the English word 'tyrant'. The schoolmaster himself is just the person whose lecture-room Paul rented daily for two years.

question: A pilgrim reached the Greek port of Ephesus and stood before a huge marble temple to one goddess. It rose on more than a hundred columns and counted as one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Which goddess did the temple honor?
context: Acts 19:27 (KJV) calls her 'the great goddess Diana' -- the Latin name the King James translators used for Artemis. The Ephesian version of the goddess was pictured with rows of what look like breasts, eggs, or dates across her chest; the temple was the biggest structure in the Greek world of its day, and one of the Seven Wonders alongside the pyramids, the Hanging Gardens, the Lighthouse at Alexandria, and others.

question: Owners of magic spellbooks in Ephesus, converted by Paul's teaching, carried their scrolls out and set them on fire in public. Acts gives the counted value of the burnt pile in coins. What was it worth?
context: Acts 19:19 (KJV): 'Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.' If those pieces were drachmas (a day's wages), the burnt library was worth about 137 years of a labourer's pay.

question: A craftsman beside the great temple at Ephesus sold a visiting pilgrim a keepsake: a tiny model of the temple front, with a row of columns and a peaked roof. The craftsmen of the city hammered these little shrines out for worshippers from all over the ancient world. What metal did the craftsmen mostly use?
context: Acts 19:24 (KJV): 'For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen.' Small terracotta and metal facade-models have been dug up around the Ephesus site by modern archaeologists, matching the Acts description.

question: One of the Ephesian craftsmen called his fellow workers of the trade together and gave them a warning speech. This man Paul, he said, was turning people away from idols not just in Ephesus but across all of Asia, and their whole trade was in danger. Who was the craftsman who called the meeting?
context: Acts 19:24-27 (KJV). Demetrius is careful to mix commercial self-interest with civic-religious pride: he warns that Paul is not only shrinking their profits but 'the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed'. The playbook of a threatened guild has not changed in two thousand years.

question: A mob in Ephesus rushed into the great open-air stone theatre, roaring for its goddess, and dragged two of Paul's travelling companions in with it. The people roared the same line for two hours before the town clerk could quiet them. Both captives were men of Macedonia, and one was Aristarchus. What was the other man's name?
context: Acts 19:29 (KJV): 'And the whole city was filled with confusion: and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre.' The Ephesus theatre still stands today, cut into the slope of Mount Pion, with about sixty rows of seats and room for around 25,000 people. A visitor can sit where the crowd sat.

question: Odysseus, sailing home to Ithaca after the ten-year Trojan War, heard a warning about a stretch of sea near a rocky coast. Certain women sang there so beautifully that any sailor who heard them steered onto the rocks and died. What were they called?
context: The Sirens sat on a meadow-shore heaped with the bones of dead sailors their song had drawn to death. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12; Wikipedia, 'Siren (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: The witch Circe warned Odysseus of the women whose singing drove sailors onto the rocks. His crew had to be deafened for the passage, so she told him to soften one substance in the sun and press it into each man's ears. What did she tell him to use?
context: Odysseus kneaded a great lump of beeswax warm in his hands and stopped his crewmen's ears one by one, so they could not hear the Sirens at all. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.170-180; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: Circe, the witch who warned Odysseus of the deadly singers, allowed him only one way to hear the song and live, as no mortal ever had. His crew would pass with stopped ears, and before the ship reached the singers they had to do one thing to him. What did the crew have to do?
answer: Bind him standing upright to the mast
choices: Bind him standing upright to the mast
Chain him inside the hold below decks
Blindfold him and lash his hands
Lock him inside a wooden chest
context: Circe's rule was that Odysseus could listen only if he was bound hand and foot to the ship's mast, unable to steer or leap overboard. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus added one strict order of his own before the ship sailed past the singers. He would be bound, his men would be deaf to the song, and he alone would hear it and survive. If he begged to be released while the singing lasted, they must not let him go. What exactly were they to do?
choices: Row on and ignore all his signals
Turn the ship out to open sea
context: Odysseus told them that begging would be a sign of the song's power, not a real command; if he pleaded to be released, the crew was to bind him TIGHTER. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.160-165; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: The singers on the shore called out to Odysseus as his ship passed, in Homer's Odyssey, and their song was not about love at all. The love-songs are a later invention. Homer's singers aimed at a curious mind rather than a lonely one. What did they promise him if he would come ashore and listen?
answer: All that comes to pass on the fertile earth
choices: All that comes to pass on the fertile earth
The road home to Ithaca in three days
The song that raises the dead from Hades
The name of the god who cursed his voyage
context: The Sirens promise KNOWLEDGE -- omniscient understanding of everything that happens on the earth, and of all the Greeks and Trojans suffered at Troy. It is a lure aimed at Odysseus's cleverness. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.184-191.  (Legend.)

question: Two of the crew got to their feet as the ship glided past the meadow of bones, while Odysseus strained against his ropes and threw his eyebrows up as the signal to be freed. They did the opposite of what he asked. Homer remembers both men by name. Who were they?
context: Homer names Perimedes and Eurylochus as the two crewmen who obeyed the standing order and bound their captain tighter to the mast (Odyssey 12.195-200). Source: Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: Homer counted two of the singing women who lured sailors to the rocks, and he gave neither of them a name. Later Greek writers settled the count at three and gave each one her own proper name, and one of those names became the ancient name of the city of Naples. What three names did the later writers supply?
context: Homer counts only two Sirens and never names them. Post-Homeric Greek tradition fixed the count at three and named them Parthenope, Ligeia, and Leucosia. The other triads are the three Fates, the three Furies, and the three Graces. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siren (mythology)'.

question: One of the earliest Greek vase-painters gave Homer's deadly singer a human head and, below it, no fish tail at all. The fish-tailed mermaid of modern pictures came much later, in the Middle Ages. What did the earliest Greek artists give the singers instead of fish tails?
context: Early Greek vase-painting portrays the Sirens as bird-bodied creatures with human heads. The fish-tailed mermaid form is a medieval and Renaissance development. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siren (mythology)'.

question: Odysseus sailed past the singers and lived, though steersmen who heard them drove onto the rocks reaching for the song. The scene outlived Homer's poem as an everyday English idiom. If a speaker today calls a new proposal a 'siren song', what does the phrase mean?
choices: A warning cry before a battle
A promise from a dying friend
A tune sung only by children
context: 'Siren song' names anything alluring that leads the follower to ruin -- the phrase comes straight from Odysseus's episode with the Sirens. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siren (mythology)'.

question: An Irish monk put together the Lebor Gabala Erenn, the 'Book of the Taking of Ireland,' around the year 1100. In it wave after wave of settlers takes the land from the wave before. How many such waves did he count?
context: The book is the LEBOR GABALA ERENN, and it counts six waves: Cessair, Partholon, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha De Danann, and the Milesians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebor_Gabala_Erenn.  (Legend.)

question: A granddaughter of Noah, refused a place on the Ark, set sail with fifty women and only three men to outrun the coming Flood, in the medieval Irish Book of Invasions. She reached Ireland forty days before the waters came. What was her name?
context: CESSAIR is the leader of the first wave in the Book of Invasions -- fifty women, three men, one ship, forty days before the Flood. Every one of the fifty women is named in the manuscripts. Eriu is the Tuatha De queen whose name became Eire; Danu is the mother-goddess of the Tuatha De Danann; Boann is the goddess of the River Boyne. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessair.  (Legend.)

question: Noah's granddaughter lost her whole company to the Flood in Ireland, all but her husband, who lived by changing his shape. He came through the year of the water that way and went on to see every later wave of settlers land. What shape did he take first?
context: FINTAN MAC BOCHRA turned into a SALMON to survive the Flood -- the same salmon-of-wisdom motif that runs through Irish story into the Fenian Cycle. He later took the shapes of an eagle and a hawk (and finally a man again) to live on as witness through every wave of the six. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fintan_mac_Bochra.  (Legend.)

question: A man came ashore in Ireland with his wife before the waters of the Flood, in the Book of Invasions, and lived through them by changing his shape. He went on to watch every wave of settlers land, and Irish tradition returns to him again and again as 'the witness of all Ireland.' What was his proper name?
context: FINTAN MAC BOCHRA is Cessair's husband who lives through all six invasions. Tuan mac Cairill is a parallel shape-changing witness from the wave of Partholon (with the same job); Mog Ruith is the great blind druid of Munster; Amergin Gluingel is the Milesian poet -- the man of the sixth wave, not the first. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fintan_mac_Bochra.  (Legend.)

question: Partholon led the second wave of settlers to Ireland roughly three hundred years after the Flood, in the medieval scribes' reckoning. His people cleared new plains for farming and brought in the first cattle. Then, in a single week, they were wiped out to a man, all but one shape-changer, Tuan mac Cairill. What killed them?
context: Partholon's people are wiped out by a PLAGUE in one week, leaving only Tuan mac Cairill as a shape-changing sole survivor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partholon.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann, the people of the goddess Danu and the fifth wave in the Book of Invasions, rolled in over Ireland hidden in dark clouds of fog. They beat the earlier settlers, the Fir Bolg, in a great fight, one of the two great Battles of Moytura. Which one was it?
context: The FIRST Battle of Moytura (Cath Maige Tuired Cunga) was Tuatha De against the Fir Bolg. The SECOND Battle of Moytura, later, was Tuatha De against the Fomorians. Clontarf (1014) is a historical battle -- Brian Boru against the Vikings. The Battle of Ventry is a Fenian-cycle tale of Fionn mac Cumhaill. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cath_Maige_Tuired.  (Legend.)

question: Mil's people set sail for Ireland as the sixth wave in the Book of Invasions, the wave that stayed, the one the modern Irish descend from. Their leader's own name doubles as an epithet: Mil of somewhere. From which land did he take it?
context: MIL ESPAINE -- 'Mil of SPAIN' -- gives his name to the MILESIANS, the sixth wave. The medieval Irish schools placed the launching-point in Iberia (specifically Galicia in the north-west). Egypt, Greece, and Sicily are all launching-points for other, earlier waves in the same book (Partholon's people, for instance, are said to pass through Sicily and Greece). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish).  (Legend.)

question: Amergin, a druid-poet, led the last wave of settlers ashore in the Book of Invasions, singing them onto Irish soil with a claiming-poem so powerful the land itself yielded to it. The manuscripts give him an unusual nickname pointing to a part of his own body: Gluingel. What does that epithet mean?
context: AMERGIN GLUINGEL -- 'White-Kneed Amergin' -- is the founding poet of Irish tradition. 'Silver-Armed' is Nuada (Nuada Airgetlam) of the Tuatha De; 'Swift-Footed' is a Homeric epithet (Achilles); 'Sharp-Eyed' is a general Celtic hero-epithet but not Amergin's. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amergin_Gluingel.  (Legend.)

question: An anonymous Irish monk, writing around the year 1100, set the old gods of his island and its wave upon wave of settlers inside a wider history of the world he knew from his monastery library. Which biblical frame did he fit them into?
context: The compiler works from a GENESIS-and-FLOOD frame -- which is exactly why the first wave is a granddaughter of Noah trying to outrun the deluge. The whole scheme is designed to give Ireland an origin story to rival Rome and Israel. Exodus, the fall of Jerusalem, and Revelation are all later biblical events. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebor_Gabala_Erenn.  (Legend.)

question: Crowds press around Jesus by the Sea of Galilee, so he speaks from a fishing boat a short way from shore. He opens a parable on one plain picture of a farmer at work. What is the farmer doing?
choices: Threshing wheat on a stone floor
Digging a well beside his field
context: Matthew 13:3 KJV: 'Behold, a sower went forth to sow.' The parable of the Sower opens Matthew 13 -- a chapter-long teaching Jesus delivers seated in a boat, using seven parables in a row. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: A Galilean farmer in a parable of Jesus walks across his field scattering handfuls of seed. Some of it lands on the beaten footpath alongside the ploughed ground, packed hard by passing feet. Jesus says in one short sentence what happens to that seed almost at once. What happens to it?
answer: The birds come and eat it up
choices: The birds come and eat it up
The rain washes it into the ditch
The oxen tread it into the dust
The wind blows it back into the sack
context: Matthew 13:4 KJV: 'And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up.' The 'way side' is the packed footpath at the edge of a Galilean field where seed could not sink in. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: Jesus tells of a farmer scattering seed, and some of it falls on stony ground, where only a thin layer of soil lies over solid rock. That seed springs up quickly and green, and then something goes wrong with it. What goes wrong?
answer: It withers in the sun because it has no root
choices: It withers in the sun because it has no root
It is trampled flat by the shepherd's flock
The stones grow warm and scorch the young shoot
The seed cracks apart before it can send up a stalk
context: Matthew 13:5-6 KJV: '...forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.' Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: Jesus tells in Matthew of the seed that bears fruit at last on the good ground, and he gives three figures for the yield. Mark sets the same three down in the reverse order. In what order does Matthew give them?
context: Matthew 13:8 KJV: 'But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.' Mark 4:8 reverses the order to ascending -- thirty, sixty, hundred. Source: KJV Matthew 13, Mark 4.

question: Jesus explains the farmer's parable to his disciples afterwards, as he does for very few of his parables. Some seed falls on the path, some on rock, some among thorns. The thorns, he tells them, choke the word until the hearer brings forth nothing. What does Jesus say the thorns are?
answer: The care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches
choices: The care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches
The false teaching of the elders and the scribes
The pride of learning and the boast of knowledge
The hunger and the thirst and the labour of the field
context: Matthew 13:22 KJV: 'He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful.' The Sower is one of the very few parables Jesus explains rung by rung. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven with the smallest seed a Galilean farmer works with, one he can barely see between his fingers. This comes in the same chapter of Matthew as the farmer and his four kinds of ground. It grows, Jesus says, into a tree big enough for birds to nest in. Which seed does Jesus name?
context: Matthew 13:31-32 KJV: 'The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.' Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: Jesus builds a parable in Matthew 13 on the least of seeds, which botanists identify as that of Brassica nigra, a seed only about one to two millimetres across. The plant is a one-season herb, no true tree, yet it forms a woody bush where small birds can shelter. In good Galilean soil, how tall can it grow in a single season?
context: Black mustard (Brassica nigra) really does grow eight to ten feet tall in the fertile soil of the Levant in a single growing season, forming a woody bush -- large enough for small birds to perch and shelter in. It is botanically an herbaceous annual, not a true tree, so Jesus's 'becometh a tree' is rhetorical scale, but the plant is genuinely dramatic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustard_seed ; biologyinsights.com/how-big-is-a-mustard-seed-tree.

question: Mark sets down one seed parable of Jesus that no other Gospel has. A farmer scatters his seed, and then he 'sleepeth, and riseth night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how.' Nothing he does can hurry it, and at last he reaps. What is this parable called?
context: Mark 4:26-29 is the only parable unique to Mark's gospel. Its picture of the stages of growth -- 'first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear' -- shows a farmer who cannot force the growth, only wait and reap. Source: KJV Mark 4 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_Growing_Seed.

question: James and John were mending nets in a boat with their father Zebedee when Jesus called them. Simon and his brother Andrew fished the same water. Jesus later slept through a storm there, and on another night he walked out across its waves. On what body of water did the four men fish?
context: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long. It sits some 210 metres below sea level, which is one reason the temperature contrast with the ring of hills around it drives such abrupt storms. The disciples Peter, Andrew, James and John were commercial fishermen from its shore. James and John were sons of Zebedee, a Galilean fisherman; Jesus called them from their boat as they mended nets (Mark 1:19-20). Source: Mark 1:19-20; Wikipedia: James, son of Zebedee.

question: Jesus and his disciples were crossing the lake at night when a fierce squall struck the boat. Waves nearly swamped it, and the disciples, many of them fishermen who knew this water well, fought to keep it afloat. Mark keeps one small homely detail about Jesus that Matthew and Luke drop. What was Jesus doing?
choices: Bailing out water with the others
context: Mark 4:38 -- 'he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow'. Only Mark keeps the pillow detail -- Matthew and Luke both say 'asleep' but drop the cushion. It is one of the small vivid touches that tradition says Peter (Mark's source) remembered from the actual boat.

question: The disciples shook Jesus awake in the stern of the boat, with the waves swamping the deck. They were sure the boat was going down. Mark preserves their panicked words exactly. In the King James wording, what did they say to him?
answer: Master, carest thou not that we perish
choices: Lord, if it be thou, save us
Master, carest thou not that we perish
Peace be still, we are undone
Have mercy on us, son of David
context: Mark 4:38. All four choices are real gospel lines -- 'Lord, if it be thou' is Peter on the water in Matthew 14, 'peace be still' is what Jesus SAYS a moment later, and 'son of David, have mercy' is Bartimaeus in Mark 10. The reproach ('carest thou NOT') is the mark of this specific scene.

question: The disciples were alone in the boat on the lake at night, rowing against a headwind, when they saw a figure approaching them across the water. They felt neither joy nor recognition. They were terrified. What did they think the figure was?
context: Matthew 14:26 -- 'they were troubled, saying, It is a spirit; and they cried out for fear'. Mark 6:49 uses the same word (phantasma). Jesus called back at once: 'Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.'

question: A figure came walking toward the disciples' boat on the lake toward dawn, and they cried out in fear until Jesus called back that it was he. Matthew alone then adds a scene the other gospels leave out: one man in the boat called back and asked to be told to come out onto the water too. Which disciple did this?
context: Matthew 14:28 -- 'Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water'. Only Matthew records this. Mark and John both cut straight from Jesus reassuring the disciples to Jesus getting into the boat and the wind dropping.

question: One disciple climbed out of the fishing boat late one stormy night and took several steps across the lake toward Jesus, who was walking on the water. Then something specific broke his concentration and he began to sink. Matthew's gospel names it exactly. What did the disciple notice around him that made him afraid?
choices: The waves against the far shore
context: Matthew 14:30 -- 'when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me'. Matthew is careful: it isn't the WATER that scared Peter (he was already walking on it), it's the wind he suddenly noticed.

question: Jesus caught the sinking disciple and lifted him back to standing on the water, and he gave him a two-part sentence, one nickname and one question. The nickname was tender and ironic: 'O thou of little faith.' Then Jesus asked a single question about what had just happened. What did he ask?
context: Matthew 14:31 -- 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?' The other three are real Jesus/Paul lines -- 'why hast thou forsaken me' is the cry from the cross (Matthew 27:46), 'believest thou this' is to Martha at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:26), 'who did hinder you' is Paul to the Galatians (Galatians 5:7).

question: Jesus sent his disciples across the lake one evening and went up the mountain alone to pray, before walking out to them over the water late that night. A miracle earlier the same evening, one all four gospels record, gave him his reason to dismiss them. Which miracle was it?
answer: The feeding of the five thousand
choices: The feeding of the five thousand
context: Matthew 14:13-33; Mark 6:30-52; John 6:1-21. Every gospel places the walking-on-water on the crossing right after the feeding -- Jesus dismissed the fed crowd (about 5,000 men fed with five loaves and two fish), sent the disciples over the lake, and stayed alone on the mountain until the fourth watch of the night, when he came to them across the water.

question: Odysseus went unrecognised into his own hall on Ithaca and counted the young noblemen feasting there, pressing his wife Penelope to remarry. Not all of them were Ithacans; some had sailed in from nearby islands. How many islands in all did the suitors come from?
context: Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, and Ithaca itself -- 52 from Dulichium, 24 from Same, 20 from Zacynthus, 12 from Ithaca, 108 in all. Source: Homer, Odyssey 16.245-253.  (Legend.)

question: Penelope faced a crowd of young noblemen in her husband's palace on Ithaca, all pressing her to give up on Odysseus and pick a new husband. They ate his food and drank his wine while he was away. The Odyssey gives an exact count. How many suitors were there in all?
context: 52 from Dulichium, 24 from Same, 20 from Zacynthus, 12 from Ithaca -- the number matters because Odysseus, his son, and two servants have to kill every one of them. Source: Homer, Odyssey 16.245-253.  (Legend.)

question: Penelope promised her suitors she would choose one of them the moment she finished weaving a burial shroud on her loom. Every night she quietly undid what she had woven that day, and the trick held them off for three years. Whose burial shroud was she pretending to weave?
context: Odysseus's aged father Laertes was still alive, living on a small farm outside town; Penelope claimed she owed him the shroud out of duty. A palace maid named Melantho eventually betrayed the trick. Source: Homer, Odyssey 2.93-110; 19.137-156.  (Legend.)

question: Penelope, cornered by her suitors, announced a contest in the palace at Ithaca. Whoever could string Odysseus's own great old bow and shoot one arrow through a line of iron axe-heads standing in a row would be her new husband. How many axe-heads did the arrow have to pass through?
context: Twelve is a specific and famously puzzling number -- Homer describes the axes lined up in a straight row and Odysseus sending one arrow through all the sockets. Source: Homer, Odyssey 21.75-79; 21.420-423.  (Legend.)

question: Young Odysseus took a great bow as a guest-gift, long before the war at Troy, and gave a sword and spear in return. He left the bow behind, and it lay unstrung in the palace storeroom the whole time he was away. Which friend had given Odysseus the bow?
context: Iphitus and the young Odysseus had exchanged guest-gifts -- Iphitus giving the great bow, Odysseus giving a sword and spear. The bow was too precious to carry to Troy and had waited in the storeroom for the whole span of the Iliad plus the whole span of the Odyssey. Source: Homer, Odyssey 21.11-41.  (Legend.)

question: The suitors tried the bow one by one. They even softened its horn at the fire and oiled it, but not one of them could bend it enough to slip the string on. Then the disguised beggar in the corner quietly asked to try. Who in the hall commanded that the stranger be given the bow?
context: Telemachus was in on the plan. He commands the servants to hand the bow across and tells his mother to go to her chamber -- the men will handle what comes next. Source: Homer, Odyssey 21.343-358.  (Legend.)

question: The old beggar took the bow and, Homer writes, strung it as easily 'as when a man skilled in the lyre easily stretches a string to a new peg.' He plucked it once and it sang like a bird. Then he shot one arrow clean through every socket in the row of axe-heads. What did he do next, before the suitors could react?
answer: Threw off the rags and leapt onto the great threshold of the hall
choices: Threw off the rags and leapt onto the great threshold of the hall
Called for a herald to announce his true name
Turned the bow on Penelope to test her loyalty
Ran to the palace gate to bar it against the town
context: 'Now for another mark,' he says -- Odyssey 22.5-6, Fagles's translation. From the raised stone threshold he has a clear line of fire over the whole hall. Source: Homer, Odyssey 22.1-8.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus and his son prepared to kill the suitors in the great hall at Ithaca, two men against the whole crowd. Two loyal household slaves helped them bar the doors and shoot the suitors down from the shadows. What were the two slaves' jobs on Odysseus's farm?
context: Eumaeus the swineherd (whose hut had been Odysseus's first shelter on Ithaca) and Philoetius the cowherd. Both had proved their loyalty when Odysseus tested them. Source: Homer, Odyssey 21.188-244; 22.  (Legend.)

question: Melanthius the goatherd was caught in the middle of the fight, sneaking a fresh load of weapons and armour to the surviving suitors. He was a traitor of Odysseus's own household, who had kicked the disguised beggar in the road and fed the suitors the best of the herd. What did Odysseus's men do to Melanthius?
answer: Hoisted him up from the beams of the storeroom
choices: Hoisted him up from the beams of the storeroom
Threw him from the palace roof
Sold him overseas the next morning
context: Eumaeus and Philoetius bind his feet and hands behind him and haul him up to the rafters on a rope, to leave him hanging until the fight is over. Homer's later description of his end -- nose and ears cut off, hands and feet chopped -- is one of the grimmest passages in the poem. Source: Homer, Odyssey 22.187-193; 22.474-477.  (Legend.)

question: Telemachus turned to a second reckoning inside the palace once the suitors were dead: the household maids who had gone willingly to the suitors' beds during his father's absence. Odysseus told him to kill the maids cleanly with the sword. Telemachus refused that and did something else. What did he do to them?
answer: Hanged them from a ship's cable in the courtyard
choices: Hanged them from a ship's cable in the courtyard
Sold them into slavery in Egypt
Sent them into exile on Zacynthus
Bricked them into the storeroom walls
context: Odyssey 22.457-473. Homer's simile is brutal: they hang 'like doves caught in a net.' The ancient Greeks called this whole massacre -- suitors and maids together -- the Mnesterophonia, 'the suitor-slaying'. Source: Homer, Odyssey 22.437-473.  (Legend.)

question: One adviser goes to the Archbishop of Canterbury in Malory's book, with King Uther Pendragon dead and the barons ready to fight for the crown. He says to call every lord to London by Christmas, so God can show a sign. Who is the adviser?
context: Malory Book I ch.5. Merlin is the counsellor at every hinge of the early Arthur story. Sir Ector will turn out to be Arthur's foster-father. Sir Bedivere is the knight who will one day return the sword to the lake. Sir Kay is Ector's son and Arthur's foster-brother.  (Legend.)

question: The great lords come out of a London church after praying for a sign and find a huge marble block in the yard. On it sits a steel anvil with a fair sword driven through it. Letters run around the blade. What colour are they?
context: Malory Book I ch.5: 'letters there were written in gold about the sword.' Silver, black and blood-red letters do not appear on the sword; Malory names the letters gold and only gold.  (Legend.)

question: William Caxton, printing Malory's book in 1485, gives the letters on the London churchyard sword almost word for word. The great lords gather around it on Christmas Day, where it stands driven through an anvil and a stone. The letters speak of whoever pulls the sword free. What do they say the puller shall be?
answer: rightwise king born of all England
choices: rightwise king born of all England
chosen champion of the Round Table
servant to the Archbishop of Canterbury
sworn defender of the Holy Grail
context: Malory Book I ch.5, near-verbatim Caxton 1485: 'Whoso pulleth out this sword of this stone and anvil is rightwise king born of all England.' The Round Table, the Archbishop's service and the Grail defence are all real later Arthurian ideas but not what the inscription promises.  (Legend.)

question: All the great barons and knights in the kingdom come to a London churchyard on Christmas morning and take turns at a sword standing in an anvil on a great stone. The letters on the blade tell them what is at stake. In Malory, what happens when they pull?
answer: not one of them can move the sword
choices: not one of them can move the sword
the sword cuts every hand that touches it
the stone sinks into the ground when they touch it
the sword shatters at the first strong pull
context: Malory Book I ch.5: 'not one of them all might stir the sword nor move it.' The sword hurts no hand, the stone stays put, and the sword does not break in this scene -- it will break much later in Arthur's own hand.  (Legend.)

question: The young squire Arthur gallops back at New Year for his foster-brother's forgotten sword and finds the inn locked. He will not return empty-handed. He remembers the blade stuck in the stone in the churchyard, rides there alone, and takes hold of it. What does the sword do when Arthur puts his hand to it?
choices: it burns his palm and holds fast
it names him aloud in a great voice
it will not move until he prays
context: Malory Book I ch.5: Arthur 'pulled it out of the stone lightly and fiercely.' No burning hand, no speaking sword, no prayer -- Malory's Arthur simply lifts it out as if the stone had never held it.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Kay hurries to his father Sir Ector with the blade from the London churchyard in his hand, knowing at once what it is, and he claims to be the rightful king himself. Ector does not believe his son and questions him hard. In Malory, what does Kay finally admit?
answer: that his young brother Arthur brought him the sword
choices: that his young brother Arthur brought him the sword
that a stranger on the road handed it to him
that he pulled a copy the Archbishop had made
that Merlin had put it into his hand
context: Malory Book I ch.5: pressed by Ector, Kay confesses his younger foster-brother Arthur drew and brought the sword. The other three stories -- a road stranger, a copy, a gift from Merlin -- appear nowhere in the passage.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Ector takes the boy Arthur back to the churchyard and makes him set the sword in the anvil again and draw it a second time, to be sure. Ector himself tries and fails, and so does Sir Kay. Arthur draws it out again, as lightly as ever. What do Ector and Kay do the instant he stands holding it?
choices: they seize him and lock him in the church
they ride at once for the coast
they hide the sword under the altar
context: Malory Book I ch.5: Ector and Kay kneel before Arthur, and Ector tells him that Uther Pendragon was Arthur's true father and that he, Ector, is only his foster-father. Weeping, Arthur begs Ector to remain his father in his heart.  (Legend.)

question: The great barons refuse to accept the Christmas result and demand the sword-test again. Malory stages it at three more feasts of the Christian year: Candlemas, Easter, and a last one where the commons cry at last that Arthur shall be king and put in no more delay. What is that final feast?
context: Malory Book I ch.5-7: Candlemas, Easter and Pentecost mark the three delayed tests. At Pentecost the commons cry 'we will have Arthur unto our king, we will put him no more in delay.' Michaelmas, All Hallows and Epiphany are real medieval feasts but not this sequence.  (Legend.)

question: The Archbishop of Canterbury sets a guard over the sword in the London churchyard once the great lords have tried it and failed. He wants it kept from being stolen or moved between their attempts, day and night. In Malory, how large is this guard?
context: Malory Book I ch.5: 'the Archbishop ordained ten knights, men of good fame, that they should watch the sword.' Three bishops, a hundred squires and a lone hermit do not appear in the passage.  (Legend.)

question: Geoffrey of Monmouth crowns Arthur with no stone, no anvil and no test at all, in his Historia Regum Britanniae of about 1136. The boy simply takes the crown as Uther's son as soon as his father dies. The sword-test comes later, from Robert de Boron, a French poet. How old is Geoffrey's Arthur when he is crowned?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1136): Arthur is crowned at fifteen, with no sword-test. The stone-and-anvil episode was invented by the French poet Robert de Boron in his Merlin (c.1200), and that later version is what Malory follows.

question: A rich man in a parable Jesus tells in Matthew 25 calls three servants before a long journey and hands each of them some of his money. How much does he give the first, the second, and the third?
answer: Five talents, then two talents, then one talent
choices: Five talents, then two talents, then one talent
Three talents, then three talents, then three talents
Ten talents, then five talents, then one talent
Two talents, then two talents, then two talents
context: Matthew 25:15 KJV: 'And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.' Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: Two servants of a rich man trade with the silver he has left them, in a parable Jesus tells in Matthew 25, and they double what they were given. The third, afraid of his strict master, does something very different with his share. What does the third servant do with it?
answer: He digs a hole in the ground and buries it
choices: He digs a hole in the ground and buries it
He lends it out to moneychangers for interest
He gives it away to beggars in the marketplace
He hides it inside a hollow beam in the roof
context: Matthew 25:18 KJV: 'But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money.' Later in the same parable the master rebukes him precisely because he did not even lend it to the exchangers to earn interest (Matthew 25:27). Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: A rich master comes home from his long journey to his three servants. Two of them have traded and doubled what he gave them. The third, frightened, brings back his single talent and confesses. The master rebukes him for not even lending it out at interest and takes it back. What does the master order done with it?
answer: Given to the servant who now has ten talents
choices: Given to the servant who now has ten talents
Thrown into the fire so no one could use it
Divided equally between the two other servants
Kept in the master's own strongbox from then on
context: Matthew 25:28 KJV: 'Take therefore the talent from him, and give it unto him which hath ten talents.' The line that follows -- 'unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance' -- has been quoted for two thousand years as the Matthew Effect. Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: Ten young women go out at night with their lamps to meet a bridegroom, in a parable Jesus tells in Matthew 25. Five of them carry spare oil and five do not, and the parable gives each group its own name. What does it call the five with no spare oil?
context: Matthew 25:2 KJV: 'And five of them were wise, and five were foolish.' The wise five brought extra oil in vessels alongside their lamps; the foolish five brought only what was already in the wick. Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: A bridegroom is late to his own wedding in a parable Jesus tells in Matthew 25. All ten of the young women who have gone out with oil lamps to meet him and light his way fall asleep waiting. Then a shout wakes them all. At what hour of the night does the shout come, according to Matthew?
choices: At the first watch, just after sundown
At cockcrow, near the third watch
At dawn, as the sky was reddening
context: Matthew 25:6 KJV: 'And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him.' The midnight timing is why the wise women's SPARE oil matters -- the ordinary wick oil has burned all evening and is running low just as the bridegroom finally arrives. Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: Five young women with no spare oil run out to buy more for their dying lamps, and while they are gone the bridegroom arrives and the door is shut. They get back at last and pound on it, crying 'Lord, Lord, open to us.' What answer comes back from inside?
context: Matthew 25:12 KJV: 'But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not.' It is the parable's punchline -- the door already shut, the answer as flat as the shut door itself. Bonus: the English word 'talent' meaning a natural ability came out of the OTHER parable in this same chapter -- Old English 'talent' meant only a weight of silver; the sense of a gift entrusted for use developed by the mid-1400s from medieval preaching on Matthew 25. Source: KJV Matthew 25 ; etymonline.com/word/talent.

question: Pharaoh answered Moses's first demand by making the Hebrews' work harder. His overseers still demanded the same number of bricks a day, but they stopped giving the slaves one thing they had been given for free. What did the Hebrews now have to gather for themselves in the fields?
context: Exodus 5:7-8. Pharaoh says, 'Ye shall no more give the people straw to make brick, as heretofore: let them go and gather straw for themselves.' Source: Wikipedia, Plagues of Egypt.

question: Moses warned Pharaoh to free the enslaved Hebrews, and when Pharaoh refused, the second of ten plagues fell on Egypt in the book of Exodus. Creatures came swarming up out of the river Nile into the houses, into the bedchambers and the wooden troughs where bread was being kneaded. What creatures were they?
context: Exodus 8:3. The frogs come up and 'cover the land of Egypt,' entering ovens, bedrooms, and kneading-troughs before Pharaoh begs Moses to remove them. Source: Wikipedia, Plagues of Egypt.

question: Moses stood before Pharaoh during the sixth plague of Egypt, and the court magicians could not stand in front of Moses. The same men had copied the first two plagues by their enchantments. Now their bodies were covered in the same thing as every Egyptian's. What was the sixth plague?
context: Exodus 9:11 KJV: 'And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians, and upon all the Egyptians.' The magicians match plagues 1 and 2 with their enchantments, fail at 3, and are physically laid low by 6. Source: Wikipedia, Jannes and Jambres.

question: A Hebrew household killed its lamb at twilight before the last plague, to be spared the death of the firstborn. The blood went on the lintel and the two side posts of the door, painted on with a bunch of one specific plant dipped in the blood in the basin. What was the plant?
context: Exodus 12:22 KJV: 'And ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel and the two side posts with the blood.' Hyssop returns at the crucifixion in John 19:29, sponge of vinegar lifted on a hyssop stalk. Source: Bible Gateway, Exodus 12 KJV.

question: Moses told the Hebrew slaves in Goshen to eat their lamb roast with fire on the night the tenth plague was to strike Egypt. They ate it dressed to leave that very hour: loins girded, shoes on their feet, staff in hand. The same verse of Exodus names two other foods served with the lamb. Which two?
context: Exodus 12:8, 11 KJV: 'they shall eat the flesh in that night, roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it... with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand.' The unleavened bread and the bitter herbs (maror) are still eaten every Passover seder today. Source: Bible Gateway, Exodus 12 KJV.

question: Pharaoh cried out for Moses to leave on the night the firstborn died, and the Hebrews carried raw dough on their shoulders because there was no time to let it rise. They took away jewels of silver and gold as they went. What single word does the King James Bible use for what they did to the Egyptians?
context: Exodus 12:35-36 KJV: 'they borrowed of the Egyptians jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment... and they spoiled the Egyptians.' Pharaoh's summons that same night: 'Rise up, and get you forth from among my people' (Exodus 12:31). Source: Bible Gateway, Exodus 12 KJV.

question: A rooster crows in the dark forest of Gagalvidr as Ragnarok opens, in the old Norse poem the Voluspa, mustering the giants of Jotunheim against the gods. Two more birds crow in two other worlds. His Old Norse name means 'hider' or 'deceiver.' What is the giants' rooster called?
context: Voluspa stanza 42. Fjalar the rooster is one of Voluspa's eerier names -- a bird whose crowing HIDES the safety of the old world and DECEIVES no one about what is coming. Vidofnir is a completely different named rooster who sits atop the tree Mimameidr in the poem Fjolsvinnsmal -- not the Ragnarok rooster.
