Salgofnir ('hall-crower') is the rooster that wakes the einherjar of Valhalla in some skaldic verse -- again NOT the Jotunheim doom-rooster. Vindsvalr ('cold-wind') is the father of Winter in Vafthrudnismal -- a wintry-sounding Norse name that would fit a doom-rooster but is not one. Fjalar is the specific gallows-wood rooster. There is a completely separate Fjalar in Norse myth -- the murderous dwarf who killed the wise Kvasir to make the Mead of Poetry -- but the two Fjalars are unrelated; the name is simply reused.  (Legend.)

question: The dead of Hel wake to a rooster's crow when Ragnarok begins, in the old Norse poem the Voluspa, as birds in Jotunheim and Asgard rouse the giants and the gods. Each of those two birds has a name. This one has none in the poem, only a single colour. What colour is Hel's rooster?
context: Voluspa stanza 43. Sotraudr (sot 'soot' + raudr 'red') -- 'soot-red' -- is the whole description we get of the Hel rooster. He has no proper name, only that color. The nameless-ness is part of the horror: the roosters of Asgard and Jotunheim have names because their worlds have names; the dead in Hel have no such dignity, and neither does their bird.  (Legend.)

question: Galar and his brother murder the wise being Kvasir, drain his blood into vessels and brew the Mead of Poetry from it. The brother bears the same name as the rooster who crows for the giants at Ragnarok, but the two are wholly unrelated. What kind of creature is this brother?
context: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal (the Mead of Poetry story) vs. Voluspa 42. The dwarves Fjalar and Galar killed Kvasir -- the wisest being ever made, born from the gods' spit -- and drained his blood into three vessels, mixed it with honey, and brewed the Mead of Poetry that gives anyone who drinks it the gift of verse. The dwarf-Fjalar and the rooster-Fjalar are completely unrelated; the Norse simply reused the name, the way English reuses 'John'. Scholars flag this kind of name-reuse as evidence that Norse myth was assembled from many local traditions, not written by one hand.  (Legend.)

question: A rooster crows at an odd hour in Scandinavia, long after the land has turned Christian, and folk tradition counts it very unlucky. The fear is an echo of the three doom-cocks of the Voluspa, a thousand years earlier. What kind of rooster is it?
context: Scandinavian folk-belief. A black rooster crowing at midnight or another wrong hour kept its association with the underworld cock of Hel long after the Christianisation of Iceland and Scandinavia. The image of doom announced by a bird-cry survives in bits of the folk-tradition even now.  (Legend.)

question: Cronus overthrew his own father and took the throne of the world, long before Zeus. He was the youngest of twelve, born of Gaia and Ouranos, and his brothers and sisters shared power with him. By what group name are the twelve remembered?
context: Named in Hesiod's Theogony 133-138. Cronus was the youngest of the twelve. Wikipedia: Cronus, Titans.  (Legend.)

question: Rhea watched her husband Cronus take the newborn from her arms. A prophecy said one of his own children would overthrow him, and he did one terrible thing to stop it. What did Cronus do to each newborn child?
answer: swallowed the newborn on the spot
choices: swallowed the newborn on the spot
cast the newborn into the sea
chained the newborn to a rock
burned the newborn on an altar
context: Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon all went down one after another. Wikipedia: Cronus.  (Legend.)

question: Cronus had taken each baby his wife Rhea bore until she hid her sixth pregnancy from him and gave birth in a hidden cave. The baby was Zeus, raised there in secret until he could fight back. On which great Mediterranean island was the cave?
context: The cave is set on Mount Ida (or Mount Dikte in other versions). Wikipedia: Cronus.  (Legend.)

question: Rhea handed her husband Cronus a bundle wrapped in her baby's swaddling-clothes, so that he would think the child was gone. He gulped it down without looking, and the real baby stayed hidden. What did Cronus actually gulp down that day?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 485. The stone bundle is one of the most famous single images in Greek myth. Wikipedia: Cronus.  (Legend.)

question: The baby Zeus cried like any newborn in his hidden cave, and Cronus was a listening god. A band of young warrior-spirits danced at the mouth of the cave and clashed their spears against their bronze shields to drown out the crying. What were these dancing warrior-spirits called?
context: The armed dance of the Kouretes was still performed at festivals of Zeus on Crete centuries later. Wikipedia: Amalthea.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus and his freed brothers and sisters fought his father Cronus and the older gods, and the war went on a long time before either side broke through. Hesiod gives it a memorable length that later poets kept as a fixed number. How long did the Titanomachy last?
context: The ten-year Titanomachy is a deliberate poetic mirror of the ten-year Trojan War. Wikipedia: Titanomachy.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus freed the three one-eyed giant smiths called the Cyclopes from the pit of Tartarus, deep under the earth, and they repaid him and his two brothers with a forged gift each. The thunderbolt went to Zeus and the trident to Poseidon. What did the Cyclopes forge for Hades, lord of the dead?
context: The Cap of Hades (or Cap of Darkness) let its wearer become unseen. Perseus later borrowed it to sneak up on the sleeping Medusa. Wikipedia: Titanomachy.  (Legend.)

question: Three brothers, Zeus, Poseidon and Hades, divided the world between them, once the old gods were locked away in Tartarus behind bronze gates. They did not fight over it. One simple method settled who ruled the sky, who ruled the sea and who ruled the underworld. How did the three brothers decide the split?
context: Iliad 15.187-193, where Poseidon tells the story: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the underworld, and all three shared earth and Olympus. Wikipedia: Titanomachy.  (Legend.)

question: In the gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke, Jesus led a small group of his closest disciples up a high mountain, away from the others. There they watched his face shine like the sun, in the scene later called the Transfiguration. How many disciples did he take with him?
context: Peter, James, and John -- the same 'inner three' Jesus later takes deeper into the garden at Gethsemane and into the room where he raises Jairus's daughter (Matthew 17:1; Mark 5:37; Mark 14:33).

question: Matthew described Jesus on the mountaintop before his closest disciples, his face shining like the sun itself. Then he added a specific line about what happened to Jesus's clothing at the same moment. What did Matthew say happened to the clothing?
answer: It became white as the light
choices: It became white as the light
It became white as fresh snow
context: Matthew 17:2 KJV: 'his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.' The three other choices are also real biblical light-imagery -- Mark 9:3 compares the garments to snow, Daniel 7:9 describes the Ancient of Days with 'garment white as snow' and hair 'like the pure wool', and Revelation 1:15 gives Christ's feet 'like unto fine brass' -- but Matthew's specific line here is 'white as the light'.

question: Jesus climbed a high mountain with Peter, James and John, and there they watched his face and clothes shine bright as the sun. Then two great figures out of the Hebrew Bible, from centuries before, appeared beside him and spoke with him. Who were the two visitors?
context: Matthew 17:3; Mark 9:4; Luke 9:30. Moses represents the Law and Elijah the prophets -- the two great Hebrew traditions standing together with Jesus. The same inner three -- Peter, James, John -- also alone accompanied Jesus into the inner garden at Gethsemane.

question: Peter was still offering to build shelters on the mountaintop, one for Jesus and one for each visitor, when a bright cloud came down and overshadowed the whole summit. Out of the cloud a voice spoke. Matthew records exactly what it said. What were the words from the cloud?
answer: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him
choices: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him
Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-jona: flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee
Fear not: for I am with thee, and will bless thee
Behold, I stand at the door, and knock
context: Matthew 17:5 KJV. The same voice from heaven spoke almost identical words at Jesus's baptism (Matthew 3:17) -- but on the mountain 'hear ye him' is added, a direct command to the three disciples.

question: Jesus shone like the sun before his closest disciples on a mountain, Mount Tabor by tradition. The Eastern Orthodox churches keep that day as a great feast on 6 August. At the end of the liturgy the people bring the first fruits of one particular harvest to be blessed by the priest. In the Byzantine custom, which fruit is it?
context: In Orthodox practice the first grapes of the harvest are brought to be blessed at the Transfiguration liturgy on 6 August -- tying the mountaintop light-scene to the yearly turning of the vineyards. In some regional traditions apples or other early fruit are blessed instead where grapes do not yet ripen; grapes are the classical Byzantine custom.

question: One Greek leader proposed a way into Troy without a battle at all, after ten straight years of siege had failed. His plan turned on a giant wooden gift big enough to hide warriors inside. Which Greek hero came up with it?
context: Odysseus, the cleverest of the Greeks, proposed the trick after force had failed for ten years. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: The Greek craftsman Epeios built a huge hollow wooden gift for the army outside Troy, big enough to hide picked warriors in its belly. It looked like a farewell offering to the gods. In the shape of what animal was it built?
context: Epeios built the enormous wooden horse with the help of the goddess Athena; the shape gave the whole story its name. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: The Greeks left a great hollow gift on the beach at Troy, with thirty warriors hidden inside and writing cut into its flank. Its builder Epeios had carved words that would read as an innocent religious offering, naming one goddess who had helped him build it. Which goddess was named?
context: The inscription dedicated the horse to Athena as if the Greeks had left it behind as a peace-offering for a safe journey home. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: The Greek fleet slipped away from the beach at Troy, so that the army would look as though it had given up and sailed for home. The ships never went home. They hid just out of sight of the Trojan shore, behind a small island nearby. What was that island called?
context: The Greek fleet hid behind Tenedos, an island just off the Trojan coast, waiting for the signal from inside the walls. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: The Trojans came out one morning to find the Greek camp gone and a huge hollow gift standing on the empty beach. One man was deeply suspicious: a priest of Apollo, who cried out 'I fear Greeks even bearing gifts' and hurled his spear at the wooden flank so hard that the whole hollow thing boomed. What was the priest's name?
context: Laocoon, priest of Apollo, threw his spear and heard the boom -- yet the Trojans refused to believe him. Source: Wikipedia, 'Laocoon'.  (Legend.)

question: A single Greek was dragged in front of King Priam in tears, claiming he had been left behind on the beach because his own side had wanted to kill him. He swore the great wooden gift was a peace-offering, and Priam took pity and cut him loose. What was the weeping prisoner's name?
context: Sinon was the planted liar -- his tears convinced Priam to spare him and drag the horse inside. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: A priest of Apollo hurled his spear at the great wooden gift and warned Troy not to bring it inside. Moments later two huge sea-serpents rose out of the water and crushed him and his two sons to death in their coils. The moment survives in a famous ancient marble of a bearded man and two boys wrestling the coils. Where is this sculpture kept today?
context: The Laocoon Group was unearthed in a Roman vineyard in 1506 and is now displayed in the Vatican Museums; Pliny credited three Rhodian sculptors -- Agesander, Athenodoros, and Polydorus. Source: Wikipedia, 'Laocoon'.

question: The freed Greek prisoner lit a beacon on the wall that night, once the Trojans had feasted and fallen asleep, to signal the fleet hidden behind the island. The men inside the great wooden gift then came down onto the street below by one specific means. How did the Greeks get out?
answer: By a rope-ladder from a trapdoor in the belly
choices: By a rope-ladder from a trapdoor in the belly
By hacking the horse apart from inside with axes
By waiting for slaves to open a hatch in the back
By sliding down the tail through a hidden gap
context: The picked warriors came down a rope-ladder through a trapdoor cut into the horse's belly, opened the city gates, and let the returning army in. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: Homer ends the Iliad before the city falls, and he never tells of the great wooden gift in that poem at all. The fullest ancient telling came much later, in a Latin epic, put into the mouth of a Trojan survivor who saw it happen. Which epic tells the story at length in the survivor's own voice?
context: In Aeneid Book 2, Aeneas himself tells Dido the story of the horse and the fall of the city. Homer's Odyssey Book 8 has a shorter version sung by the bard Demodocus. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.

question: Helen, by then inside the walls of Troy, was said to walk around the great wooden gift at night, in Odyssey Book 4. She imitated one specific set of voices, trying to get the men hidden inside to call back. Whose voices did Helen imitate?
answer: The voices of their wives back home
choices: The voices of their wives back home
The voices of their own commanders
context: In Odyssey 4.271-289, Helen called out to the hidden men in the exact voices of each man's wife; Odysseus had to physically hold his hand over each man's mouth to keep the men silent. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: Irish myth tells of a magic people who came to Ireland long before the modern Irish, the closest thing the tradition has to a family of gods. The name they carried means the people of one goddess. Which goddess do they take their name from?
context: Danu (also called Anu) is the mother-goddess whose name the Tuatha De Danann ('the people of the goddess Danu') carry. Almost no story about Danu herself survives -- she is a name behind a name. Brigid is the poetry-and-smithcraft goddess inside the Tuatha De Danann. Macha is one of the three faces of the Morrigan. Aine is a summer sun-goddess of Munster. Source: Irish Myths, 'Who Are the Tuatha De Danann?' -- https://irishmyths.com/2023/11/15/tuatha-de-danann/  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland by sea, and the Lebor Gabala Erenn, the Book of Invasions, says the sky went completely black for three days as they landed. Watchers on the shore could not see the sun at all. What was the real source of the darkness?
answer: the smoke of their own ships burning on the beach
choices: the smoke of their own ships burning on the beach
a storm the Fomorians raised to stop them landing
a plague of ravens the Morrigan sent before them
a cloud of ash from a mountain in the north
context: The moment the Tuatha De Danann stepped ashore they set fire to every vessel that had carried them, so that they could never think of retreating. The smoke of the burning ships was what darkened the sky for three days. Source: Celtic Life International, 'The Tuatha de Danann'; Book of Invasions redaction on the fifth invasion.  (Legend.)

question: The true king of Ireland set his foot on a stone at Tara, and the stone cried out. It was one of four great treasures the Tuatha De Danann had brought to Ireland, one from each of the four northern cities where they trained. From which of the four cities did that crying stone come?
context: The Stone of Fal (Lia Fail) came from Falias, one of the four northern cities where the Tuatha De Danann trained. It stood at Tara and cried out under the foot of the rightful king. The other three cities each gave a different treasure: Gorias gave the Spear of Lugh, Findias gave the Sword of Nuada, and Murias gave the Cauldron of the Dagda. Source: Wikipedia, 'Four Treasures of the Tuatha De Danann'.  (Legend.)

question: The first king of the Tuatha De Danann in Ireland lost his hand fighting the Fir Bolg at the First Battle of Moytura, and by the old Irish law a mutilated man could not sit as king. A healer made him a new hand out of one metal, and he went back to the throne with a new royal name. Out of what was the hand made?
context: Nuada lost his hand at the First Battle of Moytura against the Fir Bolg. Dian Cecht the healer-god crafted him a working hand of silver, and from that day he was called Nuada Airgetlam -- Nuada of the SILVER HAND. Later Miach, Dian Cecht's son, grew him a hand of living flesh, and Dian Cecht killed his own son in jealousy. Source: Timeless Myths, 'Celtic Gods and Goddesses'.  (Legend.)

question: The chief god of the Tuatha De Danann, a huge bearded figure, swung a great club that killed with one end and healed with the other. He owned a bottomless cauldron of plenty as well. His epithet simply called him 'the good god', meaning good at everything rather than good in a moral sense. Which of the Tuatha bore that epithet?
context: The Dagda -- 'good god' in the sense of 'competent at every art' -- is chief of the Tuatha De Danann and owner of both the bottomless cauldron of Murias and the double-ended club. Lugh is the young sun-god and master of all arts, but the 'good god' epithet is not his. Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god who later assigns the fairy-mounds. Aengus is the god of love, and in one story tricks the Dagda out of his hall at Bru na Boinne. Source: Mythopedia, 'Dagda'.  (Legend.)

question: The queen of Connacht counts her possessions against her husband Ailill's and comes up short on one thing: his magnificent white-horned bull. She marches on Ulster with an army to steal a rival for it. Who is the queen?
context: The pillow-talk of Medb and Ailill counting their possessions opens the Tain; the great bull is the one thing on which Ailill outmatches her. Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife; Deirdre is from a different Ulster tale; Grainne belongs to the later Fenian Cycle. Wikipedia: Tain Bo Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: King Ailill of Connacht, in the west of Ireland, outmatches his queen's wealth with one mighty white-horned bull in the Irish epic the Tain Bo Cuailnge. The beast's Old Irish name means simply 'the White-Horned'. What is the bull called?
context: Finn = 'white/fair', bennach = 'horned'. Donn Cuailnge is the OTHER bull, from Ulster (another question). Liath Macha is Cu Chulainn's grey horse; Enbarr is Manannan's horse. Wikipedia: Donn Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: Friuch and Rucht, two supernatural swineherds, fight each other through one shape after another in the tale De Chophur in da Muccida. Their last change before the two great bulls of the Tain is into a pair of the same tiny thing, swallowed by two cows and reborn. What are they in that last shape?
context: The cows that drank the worms then gave birth to Donn Cuailnge and Finnbennach. The Tain war is the LAST stage of this quarrel. Wikipedia: Donn Cuailnge; De Chophur in da Muccida.  (Legend.)

question: The raiders of Connacht drive the brown bull of Ulster off to the west, the one thing the whole war is for, though Cu Chulainn has held the ford single-handed until the men of Ulster rally. The raiders bring the bull back to the royal seat of the queen and her husband Ailill, where the two king-bulls are put in a single enclosure. What is the name of that royal seat?
context: Cruachan (modern Rathcroghan, County Roscommon) is Medb and Ailill's capital. Emain Macha is the seat of Conchobar and the Ulstermen; Tara is the High King's seat; Dun Aengus is a stone fort on Inishmore. Wikipedia: Rathcroghan.  (Legend.)

question: The two king-bulls attack the moment they see each other in the pen, and the whole assembly comes out to watch. The fight does not stay there. It rages across the whole of Ireland, tearing up ground, with bellowing so loud that no one sleeps. How long does the combat last?
answer: a full day and a full night
choices: a full day and a full night
the seven nights of a wake
context: Recension I closes with this all-Ireland running battle from noon to noon. The 'three summers and three winters' echoes older Indo-European fight-formulas but is not this text. Wikipedia: Tain Bo Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: The brown bull of Ulster still stands in the morning, and he runs for Cooley with the remains of his white-horned rival on his horns. Pieces drop off as he goes, and Irish tradition says each one names the place where it falls. Modern Athlone, on the river Shannon, is said to be one of them. Which piece is said to have fallen there?
context: The tale reads Ath Luain as 'Ford of the Loin', since the Old Irish luan is the loin or thigh, though scholars more often take Luan as a personal name; the school-lore collection at Dúchas.ie preserves the tradition that the bull's loin-bone dropped there. Wikipedia: Donn Cuailnge; Dúchas.ie schools collection, Christian Brothers, Athlone.  (Legend.)

question: The winning bull reaches his own country in Ulster at last, with the whole war behind him and the remains of his white-horned rival carried home on his horns. He stops, sets his back against a hill, gives a great bellow, and does not walk away from his victory. What kills him?
choices: Medb's men catch up and spear him
the Morrigan takes him in raven-form
context: The exertion, the fury, the grief for a rival -- the story leaves the exact cause unsettled; the heart simply bursts. Wikipedia: Donn Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: Loki cut off the golden hair of Thor's wife as a prank, then went down to the dwarf-quarter for new hair to save his life. There he bragged about his hired smiths and staked a part of his body on them. What did he wager?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki bet his own head that no other dwarves could match the Sons of Ivaldi. Odin gives an eye at Mimir's well. Tyr loses a hand in the wolf Fenrir's mouth. Bragi speaks with a rune-carved tongue but does not wager it. Loki is the head-wagerer.  (Legend.)

question: A dwarf overheard Loki boasting about the Sons of Ivaldi and refused to let his own brother be called second-best. He and his brother took up Loki's wager and set out to forge three treasures of their own. Which dwarf took the bet?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Brokkr took the wager on his brother's behalf. Alviss is the all-wise dwarf whom Thor keeps talking until sunrise turns him to stone. Andvari owns the cursed gold ring of the Volsung cycle. Regin fosters Sigurd and urges him to kill Fafnir. Only Brokkr bets against Loki.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr took his place at the bellows and left the smithing to his brother, the master craftsman who stood at the anvil with the hammer. Brokkr's whole task was to keep the fire at just the right heat. What was the name of Brokkr's smith-brother?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri (also called Eitri) is the master smith and Brokkr the bellows-worker. Ivaldi is the FATHER of the rival dwarves who made Sif's hair, Skidbladnir, and Gungnir. Dvalinn is a dwarf-name that appears in Volundarkvida and Havamal. Fjalar (with Galar) murdered Kvasir for the Mead of Poetry.  (Legend.)

question: Loki shape-shifted into a small biting thing and attacked the dwarf at the bellows, knowing that if the forge fire faltered for a single moment the metal would spoil. Snorri names the insect he became. What insect was it?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki became a fly (fluga, sometimes translated 'gadfly'). Wasps and mosquitoes and moths do not appear in the tale. Loki's other famous shape-changes are the mare who bore Sleipnir, the salmon caught in his own net, and the old woman Thokk who refused to weep for Baldr.  (Legend.)

question: Loki bit Brokkr's hand while the first treasure took shape in the forge, but the dwarf never broke rhythm. The piece came out as a living animal that could run through air and water and light up the sky around it. What was the first treasure?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: the first treasure was Gullinbursti, the golden-bristled boar, given to Freyr -- his bristles lit the air around him and he ran across sea and sky. Fenrir the wolf is a child of Loki and Angrboda, not a dwarf-forged treasure. Tanngrisnir is one of the goats that pulls Thor's chariot. Jormungandr the world-serpent circles Midgard.  (Legend.)

question: Loki gave up on Brokkr's hand and neck at the third and hardest treasure and struck for the dwarf's face, biting him hard enough that blood flowed. Brokkr had to raise one hand for the space of a heartbeat to wipe it away. Where did Loki bite him this final time?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: the third bite was on the eyelid; blood ran into Brokkr's eye and he lifted a hand to wipe it, breaking the bellows-rhythm for one moment. The lip, ear, and forehead do not appear in Snorri's version. That one flinch would have consequences.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr lifted his hand from the bellows for a single instant, and the third treasure came out of the forge with one defect that no amount of hammering could fix. Thor took it up anyway, but he could never wield it the way a great warrior wields a normal weapon. What was wrong with the third treasure?
answer: the handle was too short to grip in two hands
choices: the handle was too short to grip in two hands
one face was cast from ordinary iron
the head was too heavy to swing at all
one side of the head was left unhardened
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Mjolnir came out with a haft so short that Thor could only manage it one-handed, and needed the iron gauntlets Jarngreipr (and the belt Megingjord) to wield it at full strength. The other defects are plausible smith-faults but not the one Snorri names.  (Legend.)

question: Both pairs of dwarves carried the six treasures up to Asgard, the three from the Sons of Ivaldi and the three from the brothers Loki had bet against, and everything Loki had staked hung on the verdict. Three gods sat in judgement to decide which pair of dwarves had won the wager. Which three gods sat as judges?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Odin, Thor, and Freyr are the judges, one for each pair of Ivaldi/Sindri gifts (Odin gets Gungnir/Draupnir, Thor gets Sif's hair and Mjolnir, Freyr gets Skidbladnir and Gullinbursti). The other combinations are real gods but not the judging panel.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr stood over Loki with the wager won and the forfeit his by the terms of the bet. Loki dodged death by pointing to one word in the bargain: he had bet one part of his body, but not the joint that connected it to the rest. In fury Brokkr gave up the forfeit, but he silenced that boasting mouth for a while. What did Brokkr do to Loki?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki argued that the neck was not part of the head he had wagered, so Brokkr could not behead him. In frustration Brokkr sewed Loki's lips shut with awl and thong to silence his boasting -- until Loki tore the stitches out. Cutting the tongue, iron gags, and branding do not appear in the tale.  (Legend.)

question: Peleus, a mortal king of the Myrmidons in Phthia, married the sea-nymph Thetis on Mount Pelion, and every Olympian god came with a gift. From that marriage came the greatest warrior of the Trojan War, the hero Homer sings about in the Iliad. Who was their son?
context: The mortal king was Peleus; the sea-nymph was Thetis. Their son Achilles was the central figure of Homer's Iliad. Peleus won Thetis by holding onto her tightly through every one of her sea-shape transformations, as the sea-god Proteus had instructed him. Source: Wikipedia, 'Peleus'.  (Legend.)

question: In Greek myth, the sea-nymph Thetis married the mortal king Peleus on the wooded slopes of Mount Pelion. Every god and goddess of Olympus was invited to the feast except one, and the whole Trojan War began with her revenge. Which goddess was left off the guest list?
context: Eris's name means simply 'Strife'. The apple's inscription read 'to the fairest', and Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite each claimed it. The other three are real Greek goddesses but the wrong ones here -- Nemesis in particular is a goddess of divine payback, but Nemesis was NOT the one snubbed at the wedding. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Eris (mythology)'; Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: The one goddess left off the guest list for the wedding of Peleus and Thetis came anyway, insulted, and sent a single object into the middle of the banquet hall. In the myth's own logic, the whole Trojan War began with it. What did she send into the hall?
context: The apple was inscribed with a single Greek word -- KALLISTEI, 'for the fairest' (or 'to the most beautiful'). Later Greek and Roman writers called it 'the Apple of Discord'. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Apple of Discord' and 'Eris (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: Gods and mortals feasted together at the wedding of Thetis and Peleus for one of the last times, until the uninvited goddess took her revenge. The object she sent into the hall carried one Greek word, and that word set the three greatest goddesses quarrelling and would eventually start the Trojan War. What did the word mean?
context: The Greek is 'tei kallistei' -- 'to the most beautiful' or 'for the fairest'. The Latin sources render it 'formosissima'. It was designed to force a beauty contest among the goddesses at the feast. Source: Wikipedia, 'Apple of Discord'.  (Legend.)

question: Three goddesses reached at once for the object the uninvited guest had sent into the hall, at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis on Mount Pelion, each claiming it was meant for her. Two of them were Athena, goddess of wisdom, and Aphrodite, goddess of love. Who was the third?
context: Hera was queen of the gods and wife of Zeus. Athena was gray-eyed goddess of wisdom and war-craft; Aphrodite was goddess of love and desire. The other choices are real Olympian goddesses too -- Artemis, Demeter, and Persephone are honestly wrong here. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus refused to choose between the three goddesses who claimed the prize at the wedding, and he sent a messenger to fetch a mortal to decide the quarrel. The messenger went to the slopes of Mount Ida above the plain of Troy, where the chosen judge was tending sheep. Who was that young herdsman?
answer: Paris, son of Priam king of Troy
choices: Paris, son of Priam king of Troy
Ganymede of the house of Tros
context: Paris had been exposed at birth because of a prophecy that he would bring ruin to Troy, and he was raised as a herdsman on Mount Ida. The other choices are real Trojan-cycle figures too -- Aeneas, Ganymede, and Tithonus are all really tied to Troy's royal house. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: In the prose summary of the Kypria, the lost Greek poem that begins the whole Trojan War cycle, Zeus himself was said to have arranged the discord at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. What reason did the Kypria give for his doing so?
answer: The earth was overburdened with too many mortals
choices: The earth was overburdened with too many mortals
The Fates had ordered him to end the age of heroes
Prometheus had warned him a great hero would soon rise
Hera had begged him for revenge on the Trojans
context: The Kypria (a lost early poem of the Epic Cycle, preserved only in a prose summary) says Zeus arranged the discord because the earth was groaning under too many mortals; the Trojan War was his way to thin their numbers. This makes Eris's apple part of a divine plan, not a random insult. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eris (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: Peleus went to the shape-shifting sea-god Proteus for help, because the sea-nymph Thetis did not want a mortal husband. Whenever he seized her arm she turned into fire, water, a lion and a snake. Proteus told him the one thing he had to do to win her. What did Proteus tell Peleus to do?
answer: Hold onto her tightly until she stopped
choices: Hold onto her tightly until she stopped
Speak her true name three times
Cut a lock of her hair with a bronze knife
Bind her wrists with a rope of kelp
context: Thetis turned into fire, water, a lion, and a serpent trying to escape him, but Peleus held on until she gave in. Later Greek and Roman art shows him gripping her through all the transformations. Source: Wikipedia, 'Peleus'.  (Legend.)

question: The seeress of the Voluspa watches Ragnarok undo the Norse gods: Odin swallowed by the wolf, Surt burning the world, the sea rising over every land. She does not stop there. In stanza 59 she sees something happen a second time. What does she see?
answer: a new earth rise from the sea, green anew
choices: a new earth rise from the sea, green anew
a great feast set in Valhalla
the ships of the dead sail out again
the giants build a hall on the ash
context: Voluspa 59 in the Poetic Edda: 'She sees rise up a second time earth from the ocean, green anew.' After Surt's fire and the drowning of the world, a new green earth surfaces from the flood -- the surprise of Norse eschatology is that the ending is also a beginning. The other three choices are real Norse motifs (Valhalla-feasting, Naglfar the ship of the dead, giants and their halls) but none is the second-rising of stanza 59.  (Legend.)

question: A man and a woman hide in Hoddmimir's Wood while the fire-giant Surt burns the earth at Ragnarok, the end of the Norse world. When the world is green again, all new humans will come from the two of them. What is the man's name?
context: Vafthrudnismal 45 and Snorri's Gylfaginning 53. The Old Norse name Lif means simply 'life, the life of the body.' Ask is the FIRST man of Norse myth (carved from an ash tree by Odin, Vili, and Ve at the beginning of the world) -- not the survivor at the end. Bor is Odin's father, one of the primordial line. Bergelmir is the frost-giant who survived the FIRST flood (of Ymir's blood) at the world's beginning, not Ragnarok. The two Ragnarok-survivor humans are Lif and Lifthrasir.  (Legend.)

question: Two humans hide in a wood from the burning of Ragnarok with no bread and no meat, none of the food of Midgard. The poem Vafthrudnismal says what keeps them alive while the world burns. What do the two survivors live on inside the wood?
choices: the milk of a hidden cow
context: Vafthrudnismal 45. Their sustenance is morgindoggvar -- the morning dew. The image is that after the fire and the flood, the very first food of the new humanity is the drops that gather at dawn on the leaves of Yggdrasil itself. Audhumla the cow feeds the frost-giant Ymir at the world's BEGINNING, not its end; sap and hoarded honey belong to other Norse strands.  (Legend.)

question: The surviving gods come together on a grassy plain after Ragnarok, in stanza 61 of the Voluspa, and sit down in the grass. It is the same plain where the Aesir first held their meetings in the world's youth, so their end brings them back to where they started. What is this grassy plain called?
context: Voluspa 61 (and Voluspa 7, at the world's dawn). Idavoll is where the Aesir first raised their halls and forges in the beginning; and it is where the small band of surviving gods -- Baldr, Hodr, Vidarr, Vali, Modi, Magni, and Honir -- meet again after the fire. Vigrid is the OTHER plain, the battlefield of Ragnarok itself. Folkvangr is Freyja's field; Glasir is the golden-leaved grove outside Valhalla.  (Legend.)

question: The gods who outlive the world's end sit talking on the fresh grass when they reach down and find something there. The Aesir owned it in the world's dawn and lost it when the trouble first started. What do the gods find lying in the grass?
context: Voluspa 61: 'In the grass shall the wondrous golden tables be found, which they possessed in ancient days.' In Old Norse, gullnar toflur -- the golden playing-pieces from the gods' board-game in the world's youth. It is one of the strangest and gentlest images in all of Norse myth: gods sitting in fresh grass after the end of the world, picking up the toys they had lost when they were young. Gungnir is Odin's spear (broken with him inside Fenrir's mouth at Ragnarok); Heimdall's Gjallarhorn has already been blown; Odroerir is the vat that held the Mead of Poetry, kept by Odin in Asgard. None of those three are found lying in the grass at Idavoll.  (Legend.)

question: Modi and Magni come through Ragnarok alive, with their father Thor lying dead beside the world-serpent. The poem Vafthrudnismal says Vidarr and Vali will inhabit the temples of the gods when Surt's fire is slaked, and that Thor's two sons will inherit one very specific thing from him. What do Modi and Magni inherit?
context: Vafthrudnismal 51: 'Modi and Magni shall Mjollnir possess.' The two brothers -- Modi ('the wrathful,' Thor's son by Sif) and Magni ('the strong,' Thor's son by the giantess Jarnsaxa) -- carry the hammer forward into the new world. Thor's iron gauntlets (Jarngreipr), his iron chariot pulled by the goats Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjostr, and his belt of strength (Megingjord) are Thor's other named gear; the poem singles out MJOLNIR as the sons' inheritance.  (Legend.)

question: The seeress sees a hall standing on the new earth after Ragnarok, in stanza 64 of the Voluspa, and she calls it 'more beautiful than the sun, better than gold.' The trustworthy troops shall dwell there, she says, and have joy for evermore. What name does she give this hall?
context: Voluspa 64: 'She sees a hall standing, more beautiful than the sun, better than gold, at Gimle -- there shall the trustworthy troops dwell, and joy shall have for evermore.' Voluspa 37 names two other post-Ragnarok halls in the same eschatological cluster: Brimir's beer-hall on Okolnir ('never-cold'), and Sindri's hall of red gold in the Nidafjoll mountains. All three stand on the new earth after Surt's fire; Gimle is the one the seeress calls more beautiful than the sun.  (Legend.)

question: Nidhoggr the dark dragon comes flying up out of Nidafjoll, the Moon-wane Hills, in the very last stanza of the Voluspa, and he is carrying something in his wings over the plain. The seeress has just seen a golden hall, but the poem will not end on it. What is the dragon carrying in the poem's final image?
context: Voluspa 66: 'Then comes there the dark dragon flying, the glittering serpent, up from Nidafjoll -- he bears in his feathers dead bodies as he flies over the plain, and now the seeress sinks.' Nidhoggr ('Spite-striker'), the same dragon who gnaws at Yggdrasil's root through the whole poem, flies up carrying corpses in his wings, and that is the last thing the seeress sees before her prophecy ends. Scholars are split on whether it is a last dark note or a strange redemption -- but corpses in the wings is what she sees.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson retells most of the Voluspa's ending in his thirteenth-century Prose Edda. His surviving gods also gather on a plain and sit together in the grass, in the new world after the fire. What is the first subject Snorri says they talk about there?
answer: the runes and events of the past
choices: the runes and events of the past
the road up to the new hall
the ships that survived the flood
the fate of the missing Aesir
context: Gylfaginning 53. Snorri: the survivors 'come together and talk of things and remember their runes and speak of the events that had happened before, of the Midgard-Serpent and of the Fenris-Wolf.' In Snorri's telling the very first thing the new world does is REMEMBER -- the gods hand the memory of the old world down through their talk on the grass. It is what turns Ragnarok from an ending into a beginning.

question: Agamemnon, the Greek high king at Troy, took a captive girl away from his greatest warrior Achilles, in Homer's Iliad. She had been given to Achilles as his prize of war. What was the girl's name?
context: Briseis was Achilles's war-prize, taken when he sacked her city of Lyrnessus. The other choices are real women of the Trojan cycle too: Cassandra was Priam's prophet-daughter, Andromache was Hector's wife, Iphigenia was Agamemnon's own daughter. Source: Wikipedia, 'Briseis'.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles went down in the dirt when the news reached the beach at Troy, in Homer's Iliad: his closest friend was dead. The friend had grown up beside him in the house of King Peleus. What was the friend's name?
context: Patroclus and Achilles were raised together as boys in the household of Achilles's father Peleus. Homer's word for their bond is 'hetairos' -- companion. The other choices are real Greek heroes at Troy too. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: Homer opened the Iliad, his epic of the ten-year Greek siege of Troy, on a single word that names what the whole story is about. 'Sing, goddess, the ______ of Achilles son of Peleus.' What is the missing word?
context: The Greek word is 'menin' -- 'wrath' or 'rage'. Richmond Lattimore's translation opens: 'Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles son of Peleus, and its devastation, which put pains thousandfold upon the Achaeans.' The Iliad is, from its first breath, a poem about anger. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: Agamemnon, leader of the Greek host at Troy, seized the captive woman of his great warrior Achilles to punish him. Achilles answered with a choice that shaped the whole rest of the poem and turned a personal quarrel into a disaster for the whole army. What did Achilles do?
answer: Refused to fight for the Greek army
choices: Refused to fight for the Greek army
Sailed home to Phthia that night
context: Achilles pulled his Myrmidons back to their tents and would not fight. His plan: let the Greeks lose without him, until Agamemnon learned what Achilles was worth. That withdrawal is what turns a personal quarrel into the disaster of the whole war. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess climbed Mount Olympus and begged Zeus to let the Trojans push the Greeks back to their ships, until the honour of her son Achilles was restored. King Agamemnon had insulted him and stripped him of his prize. Who was Achilles's divine mother?
context: Thetis was the sea-nymph Peleus had married; Achilles was her only surviving son. She went up to Zeus and begged him -- so that Agamemnon would learn how badly he needed her son. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: The Trojans pushed the Greeks all the way back to their ships on the beach, in Book 15 of Homer's Iliad, and set fire to the very first hull. After nine years of siege the Greeks were still camped there, with the great warrior Achilles in his tent. Who led the Trojan charge that reached the ships?
context: Hector was the greatest of the Trojan warriors and Priam's eldest son. The other choices are real Trojan captains too -- Paris was Hector's brother, Aeneas the greatest ally, Sarpedon a Lycian ally and son of Zeus himself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles's dearest friend ran to him weeping, with the Greek ships burning on the beach and the Trojans about to win the war. He did not beg Achilles to fight. He begged for a loan, something that would trick the Trojans into thinking the great warrior had returned. What did the friend ask to borrow?
context: Patroclus's plan was to wear Achilles's own armour into the fight so that the Trojans would think Achilles had returned and would run. Achilles agreed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles finally agreed to send his best friend out at the head of the Myrmidon soldiers, to save the burning ships from the Trojan attack. Before the friend rode into battle, Achilles gave him one strict order. Once the Trojans were pushed back from the ships, what was the friend to do?
answer: Stop, and do not chase them to the walls of Troy
choices: Stop, and do not chase them to the walls of Troy
Wait for Achilles himself to arrive in battle
Bring back Hector's helmet as a token
Set fire to the Trojan camp in return
context: Achilles warned him plainly: drive them from the ships, then come back. Patroclus disobeyed. He pressed the Trojans all the way to the Scaean Gates of Troy itself -- and that was where he was killed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: Three foes brought down Achilles's friend at the Scaean Gates of Troy, one after another, in Book 16 of Homer's Iliad. A god struck him first and dazed him, a Trojan named Euphorbos speared him, and a Trojan prince killed him. Which god was it who first struck the friend at the gate?
context: Homer writes that Apollo himself came down and struck Patroclus, dazing him and knocking the borrowed armour loose. Then Euphorbos speared him, and Hector delivered the killing blow. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: Antilochus had to hold Achilles's hands on the beach at Troy, to stop him cutting his own throat, when the news came of his dearest friend's death. Achilles had collapsed on the ground, and he did one thing there before he howled so loud that his mother heard it under the sea. What did he do on the ground?
answer: Poured black ashes on his own hair
choices: Poured black ashes on his own hair
Broke his father's spear across his knee
Cut off his own long hair with a knife
Threw his golden shield into the sea
context: Achilles took the black ashes of the mourning fire and poured them over his golden hair, and he howled -- Homer says his mother Thetis heard it in her father's halls beneath the sea and came up to him. Antilochus had to hold his hands to keep him from cutting his own throat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles stood among his men in the Greek camp on the beach and swore a terrible mourning oath, with his dearest friend lying dead. There were things he would refuse to do until the Trojan prince who killed the friend was dead by his own hand. Which vow did Achilles never swear?
answer: He would not sail home to Phthia
choices: He would not sail home to Phthia
context: Achilles swore he would neither eat, nor sleep, nor bury Patroclus's body, until Hector was dead by his hand. Sailing home was never part of the oath -- Achilles had already been told by Thetis that if he killed Hector, he himself would die soon after. He killed Hector anyway. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus of Athens and his sworn friend Pirithous each vowed to wed a daughter of Zeus. They began with Theseus's choice, a Spartan girl still a child, and he left her with his mother Aethra in Attica. Whom did the two carry off for Theseus?
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23; Plutarch, Life of Theseus 31: Theseus carried off Helen -- the future Helen of Troy -- while she was still a child and left her with his mother Aethra in Attica. Persephone was Hades's wife (and would be Pirithous's fatal target next); Ariadne is the Cretan princess who gave Theseus the thread through the Labyrinth; Iphigenia is Agamemnon's daughter.  (Legend.)

question: Pirithous, king of the Lapiths in Thessaly, swore to carry off a goddess already married to another Olympian, under his pact with Theseus to marry daughters of Zeus. He had lost his own first wife Hippodamia in the great brawl at his wedding feast. Which goddess did he swear to take from her husband?
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24; Diodorus Siculus 4.63: Pirithous set his sights on Persephone, wife of Hades and queen of the dead. Amphitrite is wife of Poseidon; Hera wife of Zeus; Aphrodite wife of Hephaestus (but lover of Ares) -- all married Olympian goddesses. Pirithous's first wife Hippodamia had been the woman a centaur tried to abduct at the wedding-feast, starting the great Lapith-vs-centaur brawl in Ovid's Metamorphoses 12.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus had sworn to help his friend Pirithous take a wife, however wild the choice, so he went down alive with him into the underworld itself to fetch the queen of the dead. Where did the two friends enter the underworld to begin their descent?
answer: through a cave at Cape Tainaron
choices: through a cave at Cape Tainaron
through the crater of Mount Etna
through a well at the oracle of Dodona
through the sea-gate of the Bosporus
context: Pausanias, Description of Greece 3.25.4; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24: the descent was at Cape Tainaron on the southern tip of the Peloponnese, one of the ancient Greek entrances to Hades. Aeneas descends by Cumae in Italy in Virgil; Odysseus reaches the shore of the dead across Ocean.  (Legend.)

question: Hades came out politely to meet Theseus and Pirithous, with no drawn weapon in his hand, and welcomed them into his hall. Then the king of the underworld did one thing that seemed the kindest reception they could have hoped for. What did Hades do?
answer: offered them seats at his table
choices: offered them seats at his table
poured them cups of dark wine
sent for Persephone to greet them
led them to the fires of Tartarus
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24: Hades welcomed the two friends and, on the pretence of a feast, invited them first to sit down. It was the trap.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus and Pirithous, down alive in the hall of Hades to steal his queen, sat down on two waiting stone seats. The moment they sat, their bodies grew fast to the stone and they could not rise from the table. By what name are those seats known in the story?
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24: the seats were the Chairs of Forgetfulness -- thronoi lethes in Greek -- and the two heroes grew into the stone and were held there. Their memories faded and they forgot why they had come. Apollodorus is the only ancient source that names the chairs explicitly this way. Diodorus 4.63 tells the trap without the name.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles came down to the underworld on his final labour, gripped Theseus by the arm and tore him bodily off the stone seat. So violent was the pull that some pieces of Theseus stayed behind, and Athenians afterwards joked that this was why their men had a peculiar body-feature. Which part of Theseus did Heracles leave stuck to the chair?
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24; scholia on Aristophanes, Knights 1368: pieces of Theseus's thighs stayed on the stone, and Athenian men afterwards were said to have unusually narrow thighs because of it -- a comic folk-etymology from the Athenian comic stage.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles tore Theseus loose from the stone in Hades and reached next for Pirithous, meaning to free him the same way. The earth shook underfoot, and the queen of the dead herself forbade the rescue. Both men had come down together and sat trapped for years. Why was Pirithous refused release when Theseus had been allowed to go?
answer: Pirithous had planned the outrage against Persephone
choices: Pirithous had planned the outrage against Persephone
Pirithous had killed a suppliant in Hades
Pirithous had cursed Cerberus at the gate
context: Diodorus Siculus 4.63; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24: Persephone forbade Pirithous's release because he was the one who had conceived the plan to carry her off. Theseus had only come along in oath-loyalty to his friend. Pirithous is left stuck to the chair in Hades forever.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus made it back to the upper world, but his long absence had broken his kingship in Athens. In the end he was driven into exile on an Aegean island, where the local king pretended to receive him as a guest and then pushed him off a cliff to his death. On what island was Theseus murdered in exile?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 35: Theseus was killed on Scyros by King Lycomedes, who pushed him off a cliff. Naxos is where Theseus abandoned Ariadne; Delos is the sacred birth-island of Apollo and Artemis; Aegina is the island of Aeacus. Later the Athenian general Cimon recovered what were said to be Theseus's bones from Scyros in 475 BCE and brought them home to Athens.  (Legend.)

question: Aethra kept the stolen Spartan child-bride in Attica while her son Theseus sat stuck in Hades. Then two great warriors marched an army into Attica to recover their sister and take her home, and they carried Aethra off as the girl's servant. Who were the brothers who invaded Attica?
context: Herodotus, Histories 9.73; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23: Helen's brothers Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, invaded Attica, freed Helen, and carried off Theseus's own mother Aethra as a captive-servant to Helen -- who was still with Helen years later in Homer's Iliad. Menelaus and Agamemnon are the Atreid brothers of the Trojan War; Ajax and Teucer are sons of Telamon.  (Legend.)

question: King Minos of Crete ordered a great maze built under his palace to hide the Minotaur, a monster with the head of a bull and the body of a man. His own master craftsman did the work. Who was that craftsman?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.1.4; Plutarch, Life of Theseus 15-19. Daedalus was an Athenian by birth who had fled to Crete after killing his nephew Perdix out of jealousy. Icarus is his own son; Hephaestus is the divine smith; Prometheus was the fire-bringer. The maze is called the LABYRINTH.  (Legend.)

question: King Aegeus gave the pilot a second sail, folded away below decks, when his son Theseus sailed from Athens for Crete under a black one. If Theseus was still alive, the pilot must raise this sail on the way home, so that Aegeus, watching from the cliffs, would know. What colour was it?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 17.4-5: Aegeus 'gave the pilot another sail, a white one, ordering him, if he returned with Theseus safe, to hoist the white sail, but otherwise to sail with the black one.'  (Legend.)

question: Ariadne, daughter of King Minos, gave Theseus a ball of thread on Crete before he went in to kill the Minotaur in the Labyrinth. She had fallen in love with him, and she told him one exact thing to do with the thread so that he could find his way back out. What did she tell him to do?
answer: Tie one end to the door of the Labyrinth and let the ball unwind as he walked in
choices: Tie one end to the door of the Labyrinth and let the ball unwind as he walked in
Hold the ball tightly in his fist and let it unspool as he pushed on through the passages
Tie one end firmly around his own wrist and cut it loose once the beast was dead
Trail the thread quietly behind him without touching it, letting it fall as he passed
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.9. Ariadne 'gave him a clue of thread' and told him to fasten one end to the door of the labyrinth as he entered, and to unwind it as he penetrated the maze. It is Ariadne's engineering, not just her love, that saves Theseus -- Theseus follows the taut thread back to the door and out. The English word 'clue' comes directly from this 'clew' of thread.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus sailed home from the island of Naxos grieving over the loss of Ariadne, with the Minotaur dead behind him and his father King Aegeus watching from the cliff at Athens. He had made his father one solemn promise before leaving, and on that voyage he broke it. What had he forgotten to do?
answer: He forgot to raise the white sail in place of the black one
choices: He forgot to raise the white sail in place of the black one
He forgot to pour a libation of wine to Poseidon before setting off
He forgot to return the sword Ariadne had given him
He forgot to bury the Minotaur's body in the sea
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 22.1. This is the promise from another question -- broken, and about to cost his father his life. Grief for Ariadne, in some tellings, is why the change of sail slipped his mind.  (Legend.)

question: King Minos of Crete crushed Athens in war and demanded a living tribute, after Prince Androgeus died at the Panathenaic games. Every nine years Athens had to send a fixed number of young men and an equal number of young women to Crete, to be fed to the Minotaur in the Labyrinth. How many youths were in each shipment, all told?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 15.1: 'they sent heralds and made their supplication and entered into an agreement to send him every nine years a tribute of seven youths and as many maidens.' Seven plus seven -- fourteen. Some later sources say every year instead of every nine years.  (Legend.)

question: A detective in an English story follows a clue, and the word itself has a story behind it. Its older spelling was 'clew', from Old English cliewen. From what famous mythic escape did the modern sense, the thing that guides a person out of a puzzle, come?
answer: Ariadne's thread guiding Theseus out of the Labyrinth
choices: Ariadne's thread guiding Theseus out of the Labyrinth
Odysseus escaping the Cyclops's cave beneath the belly of the ram
Perseus using Athena's mirrored shield to escape the gaze of Medusa
Orpheus climbing back from the Underworld with Eurydice behind him
context: OED and etymonline.com trace the sense-shift precisely to Ariadne's clew of thread; by the 17th century 'clue' had come to mean any hint that leads you out of a puzzle. Every time an English detective story uses the word, it is quietly retelling this myth.

question: The craftsman who had designed the maze built two pairs of wings, for himself and for his son, to escape from Crete. King Minos had thrown him into prison for having helped Ariadne after Theseus got away. What became of the son during their flight to freedom?
answer: Icarus flew too near the sun, whose heat melted the wax, and he fell into the sea
choices: Icarus flew too near the sun, whose heat melted the wax, and he fell into the sea
Icarus was struck by an arrow of Apollo who mistook him for a bird
Icarus was blown out to sea by a sudden storm and was never seen again
Icarus grew tired mid-flight and drowned before reaching the mainland
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.183-235; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.12. The stretch of sea where he fell is called the Icarian Sea to this day, off the island of Icaria. His father Daedalus flew on and landed safely in Sicily.  (Legend.)

question: Aethra leads her son Theseus to a great boulder in Troezen and tells him to lift it. The boy has grown up not knowing his father. Underneath lie two objects the absent man left as tokens years before. What two things does Theseus find?
answer: a sword and a pair of sandals
choices: a sword and a pair of sandals
a bow and a quiver of arrows
a crown and a golden ring
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 3-4. The tokens belong to Aegeus, king of Athens; when Theseus reaches the city and lays them before Aegeus, the king recognises his son. Pausanias 2.32.7 records that the boulder was still shown to travellers in his day.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus rolls a great boulder aside at Troezen and lifts out what his absent father left beneath it. Only then does his mother Aethra name the man, a king ruling a great walled city to the north. What is his father's name?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 3-6. Aegeus is king of Athens. In another tradition Theseus is also son of the god Poseidon on the same night, so he is treated as doubly-fathered. Laius is Oedipus's father at Thebes; Menelaus rules Sparta and is Helen's husband; Peleus is Achilles's father.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus leaves Troezen to find his father in Athens and refuses the safe, short ship-passage across the water. He insists on going the long way on foot, on a road famous for bandits and monsters, so that he can prove himself a hero on the way. Which route does he take?
answer: the overland road around the Saronic Gulf
choices: the overland road around the Saronic Gulf
the ridge above the vale of Tempe
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 6-7. The choice is deliberate: Theseus wants a career of his own before he arrives at his father's court. The stretch of coast between Troezen and Athens (the modern Isthmus of Corinth) was famous in myth for road-monsters.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus kills a road-monster on his dangerous walk from Troezen to Athens, then five more, and he dispatches every one of them by a single memorable rule. Greek storytellers love it above all others. What is the rule?
answer: he kills each one by that killer's own method
choices: he kills each one by that killer's own method
he lets each one strike first and disarms him
he offers each one mercy and kills only those who refuse
he binds each one and hands him over to Aegeus
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 8-11. The pattern is the point of the cycle: the club-bearer's club, the pine-bender's pines, the cliff-kicker's cliff, the wrestler's grip, and the bed-stretcher's bed each turn on their owner.  (Legend.)

question: A giant near Epidaurus swings a great brass club at young Theseus, the first road-monster on his way to Athens. Theseus wrests it away, beats the giant dead with his own weapon, and carries the club for the rest of his life as a trophy. What is this club-swinger called?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 8. Periphetes is nicknamed Corynetes, 'the Club-Bearer'. Antaeus is the Libyan wrestler Heracles crushes; Cacus is the Aventine fire-thief; Talos is the bronze automaton of Crete -- all real Greek strongmen, none of them the Epidaurus bandit.  (Legend.)

question: A bandit on the coast road to Athens bends two pine trees down to the ground, ties a traveller's arms and legs to the trunks, then lets the trees spring apart and tear the man in half. Theseus ties him between his own two pines and lets them go. What name is this pine-artist known by?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 8. Sinis is nicknamed Pityocamptes, 'the Pine-Bender'. Nessus is the centaur of the Deianira story; Amycus is the boxer of the Argonauts; Diomedes is the Thracian who feeds his mares on strangers.  (Legend.)

question: A giant beast is terrorising the farmers near the town of Corinth when Theseus turns aside to hunt it on his road to Athens. He is making a name by killing every bandit and monster he meets. The beast is known as the Crommyonian. What kind of animal is it?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 9. She is the Crommyonian Sow, sometimes named Phaea after the old woman who raised her. A many-headed serpent is Heracles's Hydra; a bronze-hooved bull recalls the Cretan Bull; a fire-breathing goat is part of the Chimera.  (Legend.)

question: On a narrow clifftop path above the sea Theseus finds a robber who has a favourite trick: he forces passing travellers to kneel and wash his feet, and while they are kneeling he kicks them off the cliff into the water below. Theseus lets him take up his usual seat, then kicks him over the edge. What is this cliff-robber's name?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 10. Sciron sits on the Sceironian Rocks on the road between Megara and Attica. Busiris is the Egyptian king who sacrifices foreign guests; Lityerses is the reaper-tyrant of Phrygia; Antaeus is Heracles's Libyan wrestler.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus reaches a lonely roadside inn near Athens, the lair of the last and most famous bandit on his road. The innkeeper offers every traveller an iron bed for the night and then makes each guest fit it. Theseus ties him to the same bed and finishes him the same way. What is the innkeeper's fitting-trick?
answer: short guests get stretched, tall guests get chopped down
choices: short guests get stretched, tall guests get chopped down
guests get bound in chains until they starve to fit
guests get force-fed until they burst to fit
guests get frozen with cold iron until they shrink to fit
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 11. The innkeeper is Procrustes ('the Stretcher'), also called Damastes. The trick's mechanical honesty -- fit the person to the bed, never the bed to the person -- is why it survives as a proverb.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus turns the Athens innkeeper's trick on its owner, and that scene outlasts every other episode of his road-trip. It lives on as a single English phrase for a rigid framework forced on things that do not fit it, still used in statistics, editing, law and philosophy. Which two-word phrase carries the tale into everyday speech?
context: The innkeeper is named Procrustes ('the Stretcher'). The phrase 'Procrustean bed' entered English via Latin and is used in statistics, editing, law, and philosophy for any standard imposed by amputation or stretching. The Gordian knot means an intractable problem cut through; the Trojan horse a deceptive gift; the Damoclean sword a hanging danger over privilege.

question: The students at Cologne in the 1240s mocked a huge, heavy, almost silent young friar named Thomas Aquinas with an animal nickname. He had escaped from his own noble family, who had locked him up for a year to stop him joining the Dominicans, and he had come to study under Albert the Great. What did the students call him?
context: His teacher was Albertus Magnus, Albert the Great. Thomas's massive silence at the back of the hall convinced classmates he was slow-witted; they had no idea what was going on inside his head. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: Albert the Great stopped his class at Cologne in the 1240s when he heard his students laugh at Thomas Aquinas, the huge, silent young friar they had nicknamed an ox. He defended his student and warned them about the name they had given him. One day, Albert said, this ox would do what to the whole world?
choices: plough its fields to the sea
context: The line survives in several forms: 'You call him the Dumb Ox; I tell you that this Dumb Ox will one day fill the world with his bellowing.' Albert had spotted the theological giant hidden inside the heavy young Sicilian. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: Thomas Aquinas began his huge masterwork of Christian thought around 1265, while he taught first in Rome and later in Naples. It is built from thousands of questions, each with objections, replies and quotes from Aristotle and the early church fathers, arguing every side of a problem before answering it. He worked on it for years and never finished. What is this work called?
context: He had already finished the Summa Contra Gentiles, aimed at non-Christian readers. The Summa Theologiae was meant as a full teaching guide for beginners in theology, and Thomas never lived to finish it. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: Thomas Aquinas cited the ancient Greek thinker Aristotle so constantly in his great book that he no longer bothered to name him at all. He wove Aristotle's philosophy together with Christian doctrine and called him only by a single title. What did Aquinas call Aristotle?
context: In parallel, Aquinas called the Muslim writer Averroes simply 'the Commentator' because his line-by-line reading of Aristotle was without rival. Both nicknames were casual medieval scholar-slang and treated as obvious. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: Witnesses at the Dominican house in Naples watched Thomas Aquinas say Mass on December 6, 1273, when he was still at work on his huge unfinished book. Something happened during the service that changed him for good. They said the Mass was broken up by an unusually long what?
context: From the moment of that long ecstasy Thomas laid down his pen and stopped adding to the great Summa Theologiae. He was working on the sacrament of Penance in Part III. He never wrote another article. Christian History Institute, 'I can write no more'.

question: Reginald of Piperno, the friar who was secretary and companion to Thomas Aquinas, begged him to take up his great work again. Thomas had set down his pen after a strange Mass at Naples in December 1273 and would not write another line. He gave one reason. Everything he had ever written, he said, seemed to him like what, next to what he had seen?
context: Aquinas said, in effect: 'Reginald, I cannot; all that I have written seems like straw to me compared with what I have seen.' He never dictated another article of the Summa. Christian History Institute, 'I can write no more'.

question: A low branch struck Thomas Aquinas hard on the head in early 1274, on the road to a great church council at Lyons in France. He had laid down his pen for good a few months before. He fell ill, died on March 7, 1274, aged about forty-nine, and never reached Lyons. At which abbey did he end his journey?
context: Fossanova, a Cistercian house on the road between Naples and Rome, took the sick Dominican in. He died there and was later canonized by Pope John XXII in 1323. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: King Henry II of England gave his old friend Thomas Becket a great post in the English Church in 1162. The two had hunted and drunk together, and Becket already served as the king's Chancellor. Which post did Becket get?
context: Henry had already made Becket his Chancellor. He assumed the new archbishop would sign whatever the crown wanted. He was very wrong. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: Thomas Becket shocked his old friend Henry II by turning strict churchman as Archbishop and blocking royal courts from trying priests and monks. Henry answered in 1164 with sixteen articles meant to bring the church under the crown, named after the palace where he issued them. What were they called?
context: The heart of the fight was 'criminous clerks': clergy accused of murder or theft, whom Henry wanted judged in the king's courts, not the bishops'. Becket refused to sign; the quarrel drove him into exile in France for nearly six years. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: A visiting monk from Cambridge stood right next to Thomas Becket when four knights of King Henry II attacked him inside Canterbury Cathedral in December 1170, and he was cut on the arm defending him. About ten years later the monk wrote down the fullest eyewitness account of the killing. What was the monk's name?
context: Grim's Vita S. Thomae, written around 1180, is the source for almost every famous detail: Becket's last words, the sword shattering on the pavement, the parting taunt of Hugh of Horsea. Wikipedia, 'Edward Grim'.

question: Four knights of King Henry II's household crossed the Channel and rode hard for Canterbury, taking the king's Christmas outburst as an order to deal with Thomas Becket. Their names are still remembered: Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, and one more. Who was the fourth?
context: Le Breton would strike the last and most terrible blow of the four. All four knights were later exiled to the Holy Land as penitents by the pope for fourteen years. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: Thomas Becket ordered the doors of Canterbury Cathedral opened again late on December 29, 1170, when the monks tried to bar them against the four knights. He had come down from vespers, and he would not run. In which part of the great cathedral did the knights finally catch him?
context: Becket had come down from vespers. He refused to hide or run, telling the monks it was wrong to make a fortress out of the house of prayer. The eyewitness Edward Grim, a visiting monk from Cambridge, was standing beside him. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'; Edward Grim, 'Vita S. Thomae' (c. 1180).

question: Thomas Becket faced four armed knights inside his own cathedral on December 29, 1170, and he refused to run or draw a weapon. A wounded monk beside him wrote down his dying answer word for word. For whose name and for what did Becket say he was ready to die?
answer: for the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church
choices: for the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church
for the name of King Henry and the peace of the realm
for the name of Rome and the honor of the pope
for the name of England and the safety of the monks
context: Grim's Vita S. Thomae records the exact line: 'For the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church I am ready to embrace death.' Becket made no move to defend himself. Edward Grim, 'Vita S. Thomae' (c. 1180).

question: The last of four knights struck Thomas Becket with such force inside Canterbury Cathedral that the sword shattered against the stone pavement. A piece of the broken tip became a relic. According to the eyewitness monk at Becket's side, that same downward stroke did something terrible to his head. What did the blow do?
answer: sliced off the crown of his skull
choices: sliced off the crown of his skull
drove a nail into his temple
context: Grim writes that the blow 'shattered the sword on the stone pavement and separated the crown of Becket's head, which was large, from his skull.' A fragment of the broken sword-tip was preserved for centuries as a relic. Edward Grim, 'Vita S. Thomae' (c. 1180).

question: Hugh of Horsea, a cleric who had come with the four knights, stepped over the body of Thomas Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral on December 29, 1170. He set his foot on the archbishop's neck and used a sword for one final horror. What did he do?
answer: drove the sword-tip into his skull
choices: drove the sword-tip into his skull
carved a cross on his cheek
context: Grim records Hugh's parting taunt: 'Let us away, knights; this fellow will arise no more.' Within hours the monks were gathering the blood and brains into vessels as relics. Edward Grim, 'Vita S. Thomae' (c. 1180).

question: The monks of Canterbury lifted away Thomas Becket's fine outer robes, after the four knights had cut him down in the cathedral on December 29, 1170, and they gasped. Next to his skin lay a secret undergarment of hidden penance, crawling with vermin. What was it?
context: The old friend of the king had turned in private into a rough-cloth ascetic. Along with Grim's eyewitness murder, the shocking hair shirt convinced Rome: Pope Alexander III canonized Becket in 1173, barely two years after his death. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: King Henry II of England walked into Canterbury in July 1174 barefoot, in the rough shirt of a pilgrim, nearly four years after his own knights had murdered Thomas Becket. He had come to do public penance at Becket's tomb, and he submitted there to something no English king before him had endured in public. What did he submit to?
context: Every monk of the cathedral chapter struck the kneeling king with a rod. It was one of the most humbling scenes ever staged by a medieval king. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: Thomas More published a little Latin book in 1516 describing an imaginary island of perfect politics. The London lawyer, a friend of the Dutch humanist Erasmus, called it by a word he had just coined from Greek roots meaning 'no place'. What was the word?
context: The Greek OU + TOPOS becomes Utopia, 'no place'. The joke in the name is that More's ideal island is nowhere real. The book gave English a word we still use every day. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'.

question: King Henry VIII set about divorcing Queen Catherine of Aragon and becoming Supreme Head of the Church of England instead of the pope, and his Lord Chancellor, Thomas More, would not back him. More was the king's highest legal officer. In 1532, rather than sign, he did something no one expected. What did More do?
answer: resigned his office and went home
choices: resigned his office and went home
led an army into the north
married a second wife in secret
context: More gave up the great seal and retired to his Chelsea house with his large learned family, hoping to be left alone. Henry would not leave him alone. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'.

question: A royal official swore under oath at Sir Thomas More's trial for treason in July 1535 that More had told him Parliament could not make the king head of the Church. More had refused to swear the oath supporting King Henry VIII's claim. His story was a lie, and More told the man so to his face. Who was the perjurer?
context: More denied Rich's account under oath, calling him a liar to his face. The jury convicted More anyway, in about fifteen minutes. Rich, later Lord Rich, went on to a long and notorious career. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; famous-trials.com, 'Trial of Sir Thomas More'.

question: An officer stood at Sir Thomas More's elbow on Tower Hill on the morning of July 6, 1535, as the condemned man climbed to his death for refusing King Henry VIII's Oath of Supremacy. The wooden scaffold looked unsteady, so More made a wry remark. What did he ask the officer?
answer: to see him safe up, and let him shift for himself coming down
choices: to see him safe up, and let him shift for himself coming down
to strike quickly, for his neck was but a little one
to lend him a strong arm as he was an old man
to say a Requiem Mass at St Paul's that afternoon
context: William Roper, More's son-in-law, records the words: 'I pray you, Master Lieutenant, see me safe up; and for my coming down let me shift for myself.' The joke was that More would be coming down as a corpse and would manage the descent one way or another. William Roper, 'Life of Sir Thomas More' (c. 1557).

question: The executioner waited on Tower Hill in 1535 while Thomas More, kneeling at the block, carefully arranged his own long beard over the wood, out of the way of the axe. More was condemned for refusing to swear the King was head of the Church of England. According to his son-in-law William Roper, what did More say as he did it?
answer: This hath not offended the King
choices: This hath not offended the King
Do thy work and fear not
context: It is the last recorded joke of a man famous for jokes. The beard, at least, was innocent of treason and should not lose its head. William Roper, 'Life of Sir Thomas More' (c. 1557).

question: Thomas More spoke a final sentence on Tower Hill just before the axe fell: 'I die the King's good servant, but God's first.' The line survives because two independent sources wrote it down within weeks. One was his son-in-law William Roper's memoir. What was the other?
choices: the diary of the Spanish ambassador Eustace Chapuys
the Acts and Monuments of John Foxe
context: A newsletter sent from London to Paris that August carried a full account of the execution, including the last words, to readers on the Continent. Together with Roper's 'Life of Sir Thomas More' (c. 1557), it is why we can still quote the line today.

question: Margaret Roper bribed the keeper of London Bridge about a month after her father Thomas More's beheading, and she rescued his head from its pike. It had been parboiled and stuck up there, the standard treatment for traitors. What did the keeper's job usually involve doing with old heads?
choices: burying them in an unmarked pit
carting them out to the city gates
returning them to the Tower for storage
context: Margaret paid the keeper to give her father's head to her instead of into the river. It was a brave and dangerous thing to do; the Crown considered it treason to honour the traitor's remains. Wikipedia, 'Margaret Roper'.

question: King Henry VIII beheaded Sir Thomas More in 1535 for refusing to swear the king was head of the English church, and More's head went up on a spike on London Bridge as a warning. His devoted daughter Margaret Roper carried it home and preserved it for the rest of her own life. How did she keep it?
