context: Margaret kept the head until her own death in 1544 at about thirty-nine. It eventually came to rest in the Roper family vault beneath St Dunstan's church in Canterbury, where visitors can still see the grate over the vault today. Wikipedia, 'Margaret Roper'.

question: Thomas More refused to accept King Henry VIII's break with Rome and went to his death for it in London in 1535. There is an honest complication in the story. As Lord Chancellor of England, More had aggressively prosecuted Protestants he considered heretics, and six of them were burned at the stake during his time in office. At which London execution ground were they burned?
context: Smithfield, just outside the London wall, was the burning-ground for heretics under the Tudors. More is remembered as a martyr for his own conscience, but as Lord Chancellor he sent Protestants to the fire for theirs. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'.

question: Thomas, one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, refused to believe until he could touch the wounds himself, and English remembers him as Doubting Thomas. The Gospel of John, written in Greek, gives him a different nickname, one that means 'twin.' What is that Greek nickname?
context: John 11:16 KJV: 'Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples...' John 20:24 KJV: 'But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.' Didymus is Greek for 'twin' (no one knows who Thomas's twin was). Boanerges ('sons of thunder') was James and John; Iscariot was Judas's byname; Cephas ('rock') was Simon Peter's.

question: Jesus told his apostles he meant to go back to Bethany in Judea and raise his dead friend Lazarus, though enemies there had tried to stone him once before. One apostle said grimly, 'Let us also go, that we may die with him.' Which apostle?
context: John 11:16 KJV. Thomas -- the same apostle later called 'Doubting' -- is the one who volunteers to walk into danger with Jesus here. Peter is the impulsive one at other moments, Andrew is the quiet brother, Philip asks about the loaves.

question: Jesus appeared again inside the locked upper room, in the Gospel of John, eight days after Thomas had refused to believe his friends' story. Thomas had said he must see the wounds himself. Jesus turned straight to him. What did Jesus say to him first?
answer: Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands
choices: Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands
Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these
Get thee behind me, Satan, thou art an offence unto me
Whom seek ye? I am he: if therefore ye seek me, let these go
context: John 20:27 KJV: 'Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.' The other quotes are Jesus to Peter on the shore (John 21:15), Jesus to Peter about the cross (Matt 16:23), and Jesus in the garden at his arrest (John 18:7-8).

question: In the tradition of the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, in southwest India, the apostle Thomas landed on their Malabar coast around AD 52. He founded a fixed number of churches along the shore before moving inland to preach, and together those churches are called the Ezharappallikal. How many churches does the tradition count?
context: The Ezharappallikal are traditionally called 'the seven and a half churches' of Kerala -- seven full churches plus one small one -- attributed to Thomas's Malabar mission. Twelve is the number of apostles; forty is Jesus's wilderness days; three is a general biblical number.  (Legend.)

question: By the account of the Saint Thomas Christians of India, the apostle Thomas preached along both coasts after AD 52 and was eventually killed at Mylapore, on the east coast near what is now the city of Chennai. How does the tradition say he died?
answer: Stabbed with a spear while at prayer
choices: Stabbed with a spear while at prayer
Crucified upside-down at his own request
Beheaded by a Roman sword outside the city walls
Boiled alive in a cauldron of oil
context: The Mylapore tradition (San Thome, Chennai) holds Thomas was speared at prayer. The upside-down crucifixion belongs to Peter (Rome, tradition); beheading by Roman sword belongs to Paul (Ostian Way); the cauldron of oil belongs to John the Beloved (Rome, tradition -- who survived it).  (Legend.)

question: A vast sea-monster grips his own tail in his teeth, coiled around the whole world under the ocean. He is one of three monstrous children Loki fathered on the giantess Angrboda, with Hel and Fenrir the wolf. What is this Midgard Serpent's own name?
context: Jormungandr is the world-encircling sea-serpent, the eternal enemy of Thor. Nidhogg is the dragon at Yggdrasil's third root, gnawing at the world-tree's root and chewing corpses in Hel. Garm is the great hound chained at the gates of Hel. Fafnir was a dwarf who turned into a dragon, killed by Sigurd the Volsung.  (Legend.)

question: Thor pays the giant Hymir a visit on an errand: the sea-god Aegir has agreed to host a feast for all the Aesir, and Hymir owns the only cauldron big enough to brew ale for every god at once. Hymir agrees to lend it, but on one condition. What does Hymir make Thor do first?
answer: row out to sea and help catch enough fish for supper
choices: row out to sea and help catch enough fish for supper
sing three drinking-songs before the whole hall
wrestle Hymir's champion in the yard for a day
drink from Hymir's great horn without a breath
context: Hymiskvida and Gylfaginning 48: Hymir agrees to the loan only if Thor helps him catch enough fish to feed the household that night. The three wrong choices are real motifs from other Thor-among-the-giants stories -- the horn-drinking is Utgardaloki's contest (where the horn turns out to be the sea itself), and wrestling and drinking-song feats belong to other giant-halls.  (Legend.)

question: Hymir tells Thor to fetch his own bait before the boat can go out, because the giant will not spare any. Thor walks into Hymir's cattle-pasture, chooses the biggest black bull in the herd, and does one shocking thing to get his bait. What does Thor do to Hymir's biggest ox?
answer: rips its head off with his bare hands
choices: rips its head off with his bare hands
cuts a thick steak from its shoulder
chases it into the sea and drowns it
hurls Mjolnir at it and pulps the skull
context: Gylfaginning 48 and Hymiskvida: Thor walks up to the biggest black bull in the herd and tears the head off with his bare hands, then carries the head down to the boat as bait. Hymir, watching from the doorway, says nothing but goes very pale.  (Legend.)

question: Thor drops an ox-head over the side of the giant Hymir's boat, as bait for the world-serpent. The head has come from no ordinary beast: the bull's name in Old Norse means 'Sky-Bellower' or 'Heaven-Bellower'. What is the ox's name?
context: Himinhrjot means 'Heaven-Bellower' -- Old Norse himin ('sky, heaven') + hrjot- ('roarer, bellower'). Audhumla is the primeval cow who licked the ice to free the first god at the world's beginning. Sanngrid is a Valkyrie. Saehrimnir is the boar in Valhalla who is butchered every night and whole again every morning to feed the einherjar.  (Legend.)

question: The Midgard Serpent takes Thor's baited hook in the deep. Thor braces his feet against the hull of the little boat to heave, and he puts so much of his god-strength into the pull that one shocking thing happens. What happens when Thor braces?
answer: his heels punch through the planks and he stands on the sea-floor
choices: his heels punch through the planks and he stands on the sea-floor
the boat splits down the middle and both men fall in
the mast snaps and drops across his shoulders
the oars break in his hands like dry twigs
context: Gylfaginning 48: Thor pulls so hard that his feet drive straight through the bottom of the boat, and he ends up bracing against the SEA-FLOOR itself as he heaves the serpent's head up out of the water. It is the most famous 'Thor's strength' image in the Prose Edda.  (Legend.)

question: Thor and Hymir sit in a boat on a broken tenth-century cross-shaft in an English churchyard, with an ox-head bait dangling on a line and a serpent-mouth rising from the waves below. The fishing trip is one of the most-carved scenes in Viking-age stone, and Vikings settled this corner of England. In which English county does this stone stand?
context: The Gosforth Fishing Stone was found in the churchyard of St Mary's, Gosforth, in Cumbria in March 1882 by C. A. Parker, while he was measuring the taller Gosforth Cross beside it. It is a fragment of what was probably a second cross-shaft, from the first half of the 10th century -- Anglo-Norse, from a Viking-settled region of England. The Ilkley Cross, Rothbury Cross, and Sutton Hoo are all real English early-medieval sites but do not carry this scene.

question: Thor the thunder-god stands in the hall of the giant-king Utgard-Loki, challenged to lift a huge grey cat off the floor. He does not know that the cat is really the world-serpent Jormungandr in disguise. He heaves with all his strength. How much of the cat does Thor manage to lift off the floor?
context: Gylfaginning 47. At Utgard-Loki's court Thor is tricked into an unwinnable challenge: the cat is Jormungandr in disguise and lifting the world-serpent off Midgard is impossible. Thor pours in every ounce of god-strength and manages exactly ONE paw off the floor. Utgard-Loki tells him afterwards that even that terrified the giants -- Thor came close to breaking the world in half by lifting the serpent that holds it.  (Legend.)

question: The giant Hymir sits in a small boat on the open sea with Thor, who drops an ox-head over the side as bait. The world-serpent takes it. When the serpent's head rises out of the water beside the boat, Hymir panics. What does he do?
answer: cuts the line with his knife
choices: cuts the line with his knife
drops his oar into the sea
screams a warding spell at the serpent
hurls the ox-head back at the serpent
context: Gylfaginning 48 and the Eddic poem Hymiskvida. Hymir sees the world-serpent's head come up out of the sea beside the boat, drops his knife on the line, and cuts Thor's catch loose. The serpent sinks back into the deep with Thor's ox-head bait still in his mouth -- and Thor swings Mjolnir at Hymir's head in fury, but the giant dives overboard and swims for shore. The score between god and serpent is left unfinished for ages.  (Legend.)

question: The world-serpent Jormungandr rises out of the ocean at Ragnarok, the last battle at the end of the world, and comes ashore with the frost-giants. They meet Odin and the gods on one great plain, a hundred leagues each way, to fight the final battle. What is that plain called?
context: Voluspa 55 and Gylfaginning 51. Vigrid is the great plain where the gods and the giants meet for the last battle at Ragnarok -- Snorri gives it a hundred leagues on every side. Bifrost is the rainbow-bridge that Surt and his fire-host shatter as they cross into Asgard. Idavoll is the meadow at the CENTER of Asgard where the surviving gods will meet again in the new world after Ragnarok. Folkvangr is Freyja's own field, where she takes half the battle-dead. As Jormungandr comes ashore he sprays so much venom that the sea itself is fouled before the two hosts even meet.  (Legend.)

question: Jormungandr closes with Thor for the third and last time, on the great plain of the final battle. This time Thor does what he has never been able to do before, not in Utgard-Loki's hall and not in Hymir's boat. What does Thor do to the serpent?
choices: hurls him back into the sea
context: Voluspa 55-56 and Gylfaginning 51. Thor strikes with Mjolnir and CRUSHES the world-serpent's head -- the killing blow that the ox-head bait at sea and the cat-lift at Utgard-Loki both pointed toward. Binding, sea-return, and burning belong to other Norse fights (the wolf Fenrir was bound with the ribbon Gleipnir; Balder's body was set on the burning ship Hringhorni; nothing is 'thrown back into the sea' at Ragnarok because the sea itself has risen). The hammer to the head is the specific end.  (Legend.)

question: The poet of the Voluspa will not use Thor's own name in the stanza where he kills Jormungandr. The poet calls him 'the son of Hlodyn' instead, and Hlodyn is a name for Thor's mother, the goddess of one very specific thing. Hlodyn is the goddess of what?
context: Voluspa 56 in Bellows: 'Fares Hlodyn's son to fight the serpent.' Hlodyn (also Jord, also Fjorgyn) is Thor's mother, the goddess of the earth herself -- so at the moment Thor kills the serpent who wraps the earth, the poet calls him by his EARTH-mother's name. Nott (Night), Ran (sea), and Sif (Thor's wife, associated with grain and golden hair) are other Norse goddesses -- Hlodyn is specifically the earth.  (Legend.)

question: Thor brings the hammer down and kills the world-serpent, but the serpent's venom is already in his lungs. He staggers forward from the corpse, and Snorri and the Voluspa both give the same famous count of the paces he manages before he falls dead. How many paces does Thor walk?
context: Gylfaginning 51: 'Nine paces will Fjorgyn's son [Thor] step, then fall to the earth dead, from the venom of the serpent.' Voluspa 56 says the same. The number is not incidental -- nine is one of Norse myth's sacred numbers (see another question in this story). The serpent's venom kills him, but only after he has walked away from the body he beat.  (Legend.)

question: Thor walks his last paces from the dead world-serpent at Ragnarok, and the count of them is no random number. Norse myth uses it for its most sacred images throughout the Eddas: the ring Draupnir drips every ninth night. Which of these is also counted by that number?
answer: the worlds held up by Yggdrasil
choices: the worlds held up by Yggdrasil
the wolves that chase the sun
the ravens that fly around Odin
context: The world-tree Yggdrasil holds up NINE worlds -- Asgard, Midgard, Jotunheim, Alfheim, Svartalfheim, Vanaheim, Muspelheim, Niflheim, Helheim. Odin also hangs on Yggdrasil for nine nights to win the runes; Draupnir the ring drops eight new gold rings every ninth night; Thor walks nine paces to die. Only TWO wolves chase the sun and moon (Skoll and Hati); only TWO ravens fly around Odin (Huginn and Muninn); Thor's hammer-strokes aren't counted. Nine is the number of the worlds.  (Legend.)

question: Thor and his companions crawl inside what looks like a huge empty hall on the first night of their journey east. At dawn they find it is a piece of a giant's clothing, dropped in the road. What have they slept inside?
answer: the thumb of a giant's glove
choices: the thumb of a giant's glove
the hood of a giant's cloak
the toe of a giant's boot
the sleeve of a giant's shirt
context: Gylfaginning 45. The 'hall' was the empty thumb of the glove of the sleeping giant Skrymir, whose snoring shook the ground. The other three items are the sort of thing you might expect a giant to drop; the glove-thumb is the specific detail in Snorri's Prose Edda.  (Legend.)

question: Thor's travelling party reaches Utgard, a giants' castle in Jotunheim so huge that its front gate is barred with iron taller than a full-grown man. They cannot open it. What do they do to get inside?
answer: slip in sideways between the bars
choices: slip in sideways between the bars
climb the wall on the north side
shout until a guard opens a side door
smash the lock off with Mjolnir
context: Gylfaginning 46. The bars of Utgard's gate are so widely spaced that even Thor and his companions can walk through them sideways. It is the first hint that this castle is not what it seems: the king inside is scaling everything up to make his guests feel small.  (Legend.)

question: Loki brags at the feast in Utgard that he can out-eat any man alive. The giant-king Utgardaloki seats no one who cannot do some feat. Two long troughs of meat are set out, and Loki is matched against a man called Logi. Loki picks his trough clean and still loses. What did Logi do?
answer: ate the meat, the bones, AND the trough
choices: ate the meat, the bones, AND the trough
swallowed his trough in a single gulp
finished before Loki had taken a bite
ate a second trough while Loki chewed
context: Gylfaginning 46. Logi chews trough and all -- because Logi, as Utgardaloki reveals the next morning, is Wildfire itself, and fire consumes everything it touches.  (Legend.)

question: Thialfi, Thor's servant and a farm boy who can outrun any man in the human world, steps onto a courtyard track at Utgard against a slim boy called Hugi. Three times they run, and three times Thialfi loses badly. When Thialfi finishes, what is Hugi already doing?
context: Gylfaginning 46. Hugi finishes so fast that he has time to turn round and jog back before Thialfi arrives. Hugi turns out to be Thought itself, and nothing in any world can outrun thought.  (Legend.)

question: Utgardaloki turns to Thor and offers a drinking test: any real man at his court drains this horn in one swallow, or at worst two, or three at the most shameful. Thor puts his lips to the rim and pulls, and pulls, and pulls a third time, and the level has barely dropped. Why can Thor not empty the horn?
answer: its far end opens into the sea
choices: its far end opens into the sea
a giant kept refilling it from behind
the mead grows back as fast as he drinks
the horn has no bottom at all
context: Gylfaginning 46-47. Utgardaloki reveals the trick the next morning: the horn was set with its lower end in the ocean.  (Legend.)

question: Thor, furious at failing the drinking test, demands another at Utgard. The giant-king points to a large grey cat curled on the flagstones and tells him to lift it. Thor stoops, gets his arm under its belly and heaves with all his god-strength. What is the most he can manage?
answer: one paw comes off the floor
choices: one paw comes off the floor
the cat sits upright but does not rise
he raises the cat above his head
the cat purrs and does not move at all
context: Gylfaginning 46. The cat merely arches its back until one paw lifts; Thor cannot get more than that. What kind of creature the cat truly was, Utgardaloki will reveal the next morning outside the castle.  (Legend.)

question: Utgardaloki laughs when Thor, twice beaten and furious, calls for a wrestling match against any man in the hall. No one there wants to fight the god at grips, he says, but perhaps his old nurse will oblige. She hobbles out, and the harder Thor pulls, the firmer she stands. How does the wrestling end?
answer: Thor is brought down onto one knee
choices: Thor is brought down onto one knee
Thor is thrown flat on his back
Thor breaks free and storms out
the nurse tosses him across the hall
context: Gylfaginning 46. Utgardaloki calls the match. The old nurse's name is Elli, and Utgardaloki later says of her: 'none such has ever been, and none shall be, if he becomes so old as to abide her, that she shall not cause him to fall.' What Elli truly is he saves for the morning reveal.  (Legend.)

question: Utgardaloki leads Thor's party from the castle the morning after the contests and admits what each opponent had really been. The large grey cat that lay on his flagstones and beat the thunder-god, he says, was no cat at all. What was it?
context: Gylfaginning 47. The 'cat' was the world-serpent that circles the earth; by lifting one paw Thor had lifted the serpent's coil out of the ocean, an almost impossible feat. Fenrir will fight Odin at Ragnarok; Nidhogg gnaws at Yggdrasil's third root; Garm guards the gates of Hel.  (Legend.)

question: Thor leaves Utgard believing he has failed at the drinking horn, after three great pulls barely lowered its level. Outside the castle the giant-king Utgardaloki tells him the swallows were not wasted after all, for they did something the whole world can see. What did his three swallows do?
answer: they created the tides in the sea
choices: they created the tides in the sea
they drained the biggest fjord dry
they hollowed the sea-caves of Norway
they froze the northern sea for winter
context: Gylfaginning 47. The lower end of the horn opened into the ocean itself; Thor's three great swallows drew sea-level down so far that the whole ocean has ebbed and flowed ever since. It is Snorri's mythic origin of the tides.  (Legend.)

question: Utgardaloki owns up about the wrestling match outside his castle the next morning. The nurse who fought Thor is called Elli, and he calls the god's showing the most astonishing feat of all, since no living thing has ever come off that well against her. What is Elli in truth?
context: Gylfaginning 47. The nurse Elli is Old Age herself. Utgardaloki tells Thor: no one has ever been who did not fall entirely to Elli in the end, if only he lived long enough to meet her; that Thor came down onto only one knee is a marvel. Elli appears in no other extant Norse source, only in this scene.  (Legend.)

question: Thor hears the last of Utgardaloki's tricks and, incandescent, spins on his heel and lifts Mjolnir to smash the giant-king where he stands. But when the hammer comes up there is nothing to swing at. What has happened to Utgardaloki, his castle and everything in it?
answer: they have all vanished; only empty plain remains
choices: they have all vanished; only empty plain remains
they have shrunk to the size of an anthill
they have been swallowed by the earth
they have been carried off in a fog-bank
context: Gylfaginning 47. The whole illusion drops: castle, king, horn, cat, nurse, hall -- gone. Thor stands with Mjolnir raised over an empty grass plain. Utgardaloki, the reader learns, was Skrymir on the road as well; the three deep valleys Thor had left in a mountainside during the journey were where the giant had slipped a mountain between himself and Mjolnir while pretending to sleep.  (Legend.)

question: Thor rides across the sky behind two enormous goats, and Snorri Sturluson, writing in Iceland around 1220, names them Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjostr. Both names are built on one Old Norse word for a body part the goats are famous for. Which body part is it?
context: Gylfaginning 21. Both names carry the element tann- ('tooth'): Tanngrisnir means 'tooth-barer' or 'snarler', Tanngnjostr means 'tooth-grinder' or 'tooth-gnasher'. The teeth of the chariot-goats are front and centre in the name-pair.  (Legend.)

question: Thor halts his goat-chariot for the evening on the road east into Jotunheim, the land of the giants. However many nights his party camps along the way, he never runs out of meat. What does Thor do with his two chariot-goats each evening?
answer: slaughter and eat them, then wake them at dawn
choices: slaughter and eat them, then wake them at dawn
milk them for a river of ale each night
shear their wool into a fresh cloak each night
ride them one day and eat them the next
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thor slaughters the goats, roasts and eats the meat, then blesses the hides at dawn with Mjolnir. Provided every bone has been laid whole on the hide, the goats stand up alive and ready to be harnessed again.  (Legend.)

question: Thor holds his hammer Mjolnir over two goat-hides at first light, and everything depends on one strict condition kept overnight. If it is broken, the goats still come back alive, but they come back damaged. What is the condition?
answer: every bone must be laid whole on the hide
choices: every bone must be laid whole on the hide
no fire may touch the hide overnight
the goats' names must not be spoken
the meat must be finished before midnight
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thor gives strict instructions before dinner: eat all the meat you like, but every single bone goes intact on the hide. What comes back in the morning is exactly what was laid on the hide the night before -- damaged bones make a damaged goat.  (Legend.)

question: Thor stops at a poor farmhouse one night on the road east into Jotunheim, with Loki at his side. The household has nothing to feed the god's party, so he solves the problem himself: he kills both his own goats and roasts the meat on the hearth. Who does he then invite to share the meal?
choices: only Loki, apart from the others
the farmer alone at his own table
no one; the meat is for him
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thor turns the empty farmhouse into a feast: he brings the meat, the family brings the hearth. He gives them the same strict warning he always gives -- eat what you like, but leave every bone whole on the hide.  (Legend.)

question: The farmer's hungry son takes his knife to one of the goats' thigh-bones at Thor's supper, then lays it back on the hide with the rest. Thor has warned the family about the bones, for in the morning he will swing Mjolnir over the hides to make the goats live again. What does the boy do to the bone?
answer: splits it lengthwise to suck the marrow
choices: splits it lengthwise to suck the marrow
gnaws a notch off the end of it
snaps it in two across his knee
carves his initials along its side
context: Gylfaginning 44. The boy takes his knife to a thigh-bone and splits it lengthwise to get at the marrow inside, then lays the split halves back on the hide with the rest of the bones. He thinks nobody will notice.  (Legend.)

question: Both goats stand up at dawn when Thor raises his hammer Mjolnir over the hides and blesses them back to life. But the farmer's son has not kept the rule about the bones, and one of the goats is not quite whole. What is wrong with it?
answer: it is lame in a hind leg
choices: it is lame in a hind leg
one of its horns has snapped off
it has lost the sight in one eye
it will not answer to its name
context: Gylfaginning 44. The split thigh-bone becomes a lame hind leg. The boy's midnight snack has broken a chariot-goat for good.  (Legend.)

question: The whole farm family throws itself to the floor when Thor's face goes dark at the sight of the damaged goat. Snorri says his brows drop low over his eyes and his knuckles turn white on Mjolnir. The family offers to pay any price for mercy. What price does Thor take?
answer: their two children as his servants forever
choices: their two children as his servants forever
every animal in the farm's stables
the farm and the fields it stands on
seven years of the farmer's own labour
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thor forgoes destroying the family and takes their son and daughter as bond-servants. The exchange is stark: one goat-leg for two lives.  (Legend.)

question: The farmer's son leaves home at Thor's side that morning, the same boy who broke the rule of the bones. He will run with the god across the giant-country and one day lose a foot-race at Utgardaloki's court. What is the boy's name?
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thialfi becomes Thor's fastest human servant, famed as the swiftest runner among men. Bragi is the god of poetry; Ullr is a god of the bow and skis; Vidar is Odin's silent, avenging son.  (Legend.)

question: The sister of the boy who cracked the goat-bone leaves the farmhouse with him that morning and enters the service of the thunder-god Thor. She travels on with his party into Jotunheim, the land of the giants. What is her name?
context: Gylfaginning 44. Roskva is named in the Prose Edda alongside her brother as the second of the two children given to Thor. Sif is Thor's own wife (of golden hair); Idunn keeps the apples of youth for the Aesir; Skadi is the giantess who married Njord after her father's death.  (Legend.)

question: Thor's two chariot-goats drag the thunder across the sky, and in his Prose Edda Snorri Sturluson builds both their names on one old root, tann-. One goat is Tanngnjostr, the 'grinder of teeth.' The other is Tanngrisnir. What does that name mean?
context: Gylfaginning 21. Tanngrisnir translates as 'tooth-barer' or 'snarler'; Tanngnjostr as 'tooth-grinder' or 'tooth-gnasher'. Both names put the goats' teeth front and centre, which fits creatures that pull the thunder-god's chariot through the sky.  (Legend.)

question: Thor's swift servant, the farm boy who spoiled the goat-bone, is pitted in a foot-race at the giant-king Utgardaloki's court against a small boy called Hugi, and Hugi beats him badly. Outside the castle afterwards, Utgardaloki confesses that his contests have all been illusions. What does Hugi really turn out to be?
context: Gylfaginning 46-47. Hugi is the personification of Thought; nothing in any world can outrun thought, and Thialfi's defeat is no shame. In the same reveal Loki's eating opponent Logi is unmasked as Wildfire, and the horn Thor could not drain has its far end in the sea.  (Legend.)

question: Thor wakes one morning in Asgard and reaches for his weapon, in the Norse poem Thrymskvida, and finds it gone. The giants have stolen it in the night. He shakes his beard in rage and calls for the trickster Loki. What weapon has been stolen?
context: Thrymskvida 1-2: Thor wakes to find his hammer gone. Gungnir is Odin's spear. Tyrfing is the cursed sword of the Hervarar Saga. Gram is the sword Sigurd will one day reforge from his father's broken blade to kill Fafnir.  (Legend.)

question: Loki agrees to help Thor find his stolen weapon, and he goes first to the goddess Freyja to borrow one of her magical treasures for the long journey. The giants have hidden the weapon away in Jotunheim. What does Loki borrow from Freyja?
context: Thrymskvida 3-5: Freyja lends Loki her feather-cloak (fjadrhamr) and he flies in falcon shape to Jotunheim. All four items belong to Freyja -- her boar Hildisvini, her chariot drawn by cats, and her dwarf-forged necklace Brisingamen -- but Thrymskvida specifically names the falcon-cloak as what Loki borrows.  (Legend.)

question: Thrym the giant names his price to Loki in Jotunheim: Thor's weapon comes back only if the gods send him Freyja as his bride. Meanwhile no god can just dig it up, for Thrym has buried it far under the earth. How deep does the poem say he buried it?
context: Thrymskvida 8: Thrym boasts that Mjolnir is buried eight leagues (about eight miles) below the ground. The other depths are the sort of round numbers a listener might guess; the poem is exact about eight.  (Legend.)

question: The gods gather in assembly when Freyja refuses to go to the giant Thrym, who holds Thor's weapon. One of the Aesir proposes the plan that will actually work: dress Thor himself in a bride's clothes and send him to Jotunheim to marry Thrym. Which of the Aesir proposes it in Thrymskvida?
context: Thrymskvida 15: Heimdall the watchman speaks up with the plan to disguise Thor. Odin is silent in this poem. Bragi is the god of poetry. Tyr will lose his hand in Fenrir's mouth. Heimdall alone proposes the bridal disguise.  (Legend.)

question: The veiled bride sits down at the wedding-feast in Thrym's hall and, before anyone else has taken a bite, clears the table set for the whole wedding-party. She eats a whole ox and all the dainties meant for the women, and she drains three vats of mead. The poet counts the fish as well. How many salmon does the poem say she swallows?
context: Thrymskvida 24: the bride ate one ox and eight salmon and all the dainties meant for the women, and drained three vats of mead. The poet loves the number eight in Thrymskvida -- eight leagues to the buried hammer earlier, eight salmon on the plate here.  (Legend.)

question: Thrym stares in astonishment at his veiled bride, who has just cleared the wedding table alone. The bride is Thor in Freyja's gown, and Loki has come along disguised as his maidservant. Loki leans in and whispers a smooth lie in the giant's ear. What reason does Loki give for the bride's hunger?
answer: she has fasted eight nights for eagerness
choices: she has fasted eight nights for eagerness
she has traveled eight days without food
brides of her people always eat before the vows
she is carrying an unborn heir and eats for two
context: Thrymskvida 26: Loki tells Thrym that Freyja was so eager for Jotunheim that she has not eaten for eight nights. The number matches Thrym's earlier boast that the hammer is buried eight leagues down; the poet loves the number eight in this poem.  (Legend.)

question: Thor sits in Freyja's veil at his own wedding to the giant Thrym, with Loki at his side as a maidservant. Thrym leans in for the wedding kiss and reaches to lift the bridal veil. He gets one look and springs back the length of the hall in terror. What has Thrym seen under the veil?
context: Thrymskvida 27-28: Thrym recoils from Freyja's terrible eyes, which burn like fire. Loki covers again -- 'she has not slept for eight nights either, in her longing for Jotunheim.' The specific tell that gives Thor away in Thrym's own hall is his EYES, not his beard or his hands.  (Legend.)

question: A young knight of Lyonesse sails for Ireland at the command of his uncle the king, in the old Cornish tale. He must bring back the princess Iseult the Fair as a bride, but not for himself. What is the knight's name?
context: The Tristan legend survives from Beroul (c.1170) and Thomas of Britain (c.1175). Lancelot is Arthur's champion and Guinevere's lover in Chretien and Malory. Gawain is Arthur's nephew. Perceval is the Grail knight. Only Tristan sails to Ireland for a bride.

question: The King of Cornwall sends Tristan across the water to Ireland to fetch him a bride. Tristan is his nephew and his champion, and the whole tragedy of the legend turns on the loyalty Tristan owes this uncle. What is the king's name?
context: King Mark of Cornwall, Tristan's uncle, is the wronged husband in the romance. Arthur is Britain's high king in the parallel cycle. Uther is Arthur's father, generations earlier. Ryence is a rival king in Malory's early books.  (Legend.)

question: Iseult's mother brews something in a gold flask on the day the ship sails, and gives it to Iseult's maid Brangaine. Tristan is carrying the princess home from Ireland to marry his uncle, the King of Cornwall, and Brangaine is to serve it to the couple on their wedding night. What is in the flask?
context: The queen's flask is a love potion meant for King Mark and his bride on their wedding night, so they will love one another forever. Sleeping draughts, salves and truth-serums are stock medieval story-devices but not what the queen sends.  (Legend.)

question: Tristan and Iseult, alone below decks on the ship from Ireland to Cornwall, find the golden flask Brangaine has been guarding. The summer heat has left the two of them thirsty, so they uncap it and drink from it together. What do they think they are drinking?
context: Tristan and Iseult mistake the flask for wine, share a cup, and are bound in love from that moment. Water, medicine and ale do not appear -- the mistake in the story is specifically wine.  (Legend.)

question: Beroul sets a limit on the magic drink that binds Tristan and Iseult, in his Anglo-Norman verse around 1170: after a set span, the two may at least consider parting. Thomas of Britain's later, courtly version makes the drink bind them forever. In Beroul, how long does its power last?
context: Beroul (c.1170) sets the potion's power at three years, after which the lovers can at last consider parting. Thomas of Britain and the courtly branch make the love last a lifetime. One hundred days, seven winters and a single moon are not attested spans.  (Legend.)

question: Iseult marries the king as planned, but she and Tristan go on meeting in secret until at last they are found out. To escape, the lovers run into a great forest. They sleep in bowers of tree-boughs and eat deer that Tristan hunts. What is this forest called?
context: The Forest of Morois is where Tristan and Iseult live in exile in Beroul and later versions. Broceliande is Merlin's enchanted wood in the Arthurian cycle. The Forest Perilous is a name for various dangerous woods. Camelot is a court, not a forest.  (Legend.)

question: Iseult's royal husband tracks the lovers to their forest hut and finds them asleep. He spares them both and does not shout the camp awake, but he leaves one quiet signal that he was there. In Beroul, what does he do before he slips back out into the trees?
answer: he swaps his own sword for Tristan's on the bed
choices: he swaps his own sword for Tristan's on the bed
he cuts a lock from Iseult's hair
he sets his crown at Tristan's feet
he stabs the hut's roof with an arrow
context: Beroul c.1170: Mark exchanges his own sword for Tristan's and his ring for Iseult's, so when they wake they will know he came, saw, and forbore. The lock of hair, the laid-down crown and the pierced roof do not appear in the passage.  (Legend.)

question: Exiled from Cornwall, Tristan marries a second princess in Brittany, and he never loves her. She shares a first name with Iseult the Fair, the woman he cannot forget, but the legend gives her a different epithet. What is she called?
context: Iseult of the White Hands (Isolde of Brittany) marries Tristan in the Brittany section of Thomas of Britain and Malory Book XII. The Green Isle, Silent, and Lyonesse epithets are not attached to this second Iseult.  (Legend.)

question: Tristan lies wounded and dying in Brittany, and he sends a messenger by ship for the only healer who can save him, Iseult the Fair, back in Cornwall. He tells the crew to raise sails of one colour on the return trip if she is coming, and another colour if she has refused him. Which colours does Tristan set for the two signals?
answer: white for yes, black for no
choices: white for yes, black for no
gold for yes, grey for no
red for yes, blue for no
green for yes, black for no
context: Thomas of Britain c.1175: white sails if Iseult the Fair comes, black sails if she refuses. This same white/black-sails device is directly borrowed from the Greek myth of Theseus's father Aegeus.  (Legend.)

question: Tristan's wife stands at the window as the ship comes back over the water. Iseult the Fair is aboard, so the sail on the mast is the colour Tristan asked for if she came. His wife tells him it is the other colour. He hears her before Iseult the Fair can even step onto shore. What does Tristan do?
answer: he dies of grief on the spot
choices: he dies of grief on the spot
he calls for a priest and takes the sacrament
he curses his wife with his last breath
he crawls to the harbour to see for himself
context: Thomas of Britain c.1175: Tristan hears the lie and dies at once of grief; Iseult the Fair steps off the ship, finds him already dead, lies down beside him and dies of grief also. Sacrament, curse and crawl-to-harbour appear in no early version.  (Legend.)

question: An old father stands on a cliff watching his son's ship come home under the wrong sail, and he throws himself off. The son, a Greek hero, had sailed off to kill a monster, promising a change of sail if he lived, and he forgot. That story is centuries older than Tristan's signal. Which Greek hero's story is this?
context: Theseus sailed from Athens to Crete to kill the Minotaur; his father Aegeus, watching from the cliff, saw the black sails still up and drowned himself in the sea now called the Aegean. Perseus, Jason and Bellerophon are Greek heroes but not the sail story.  (Legend.)

question: Fenrir the wolf smelled a trick when the gods came to bind him with a magic ribbon. He would be tied only if a god put a hand in his jaws as a pledge of good faith. When the ribbon held, he bit the hand off at the wrist. Which god lost his hand?
context: Snorri's Gylfaginning 34 names Tyr as the only god brave enough to make the pledge. When Fenrir realised the ribbon Gleipnir would not break, he bit off Tyr's right hand. Baldr is Odin's shining son killed by mistletoe; Bragi is the god of poetry; Forseti is the god of justice at Glitnir.  (Legend.)

question: Tyr, the Norse god of single combat and oath-keeping, lost a hand in the jaws of the wolf Fenrir. The Anglo-Saxons of old England worshipped this same one-handed war-god under a different name, and it survives today in the day-name Tuesday. What was his Anglo-Saxon name?
context: Old English Tiwesdaeg means Tiw's Day, later worn down to Tuesday. Woden is the Anglo-Saxon Odin (Wednesday). Thunor is Thor (Thursday). Frige is Frigg (Friday).

question: Snorri Sturluson gathered the old Norse tales around 1220 AD of Ragnarok, the last battle at the end of the world, fought on the plain called Vigrid. On that field the war-god Tyr and the hell-hound Garmr struck each other down together. Snorri named a second pair of enemies who also killed each other. Which pair?
context: Snorri writes in Gylfaginning 51: Loki has battle with Heimdall, and each is the other's slayer. Heimdallr is the watchman of Bifrost with the Gjallarhorn; the two had an old grudge from the fight over Freyja's necklace. Thor's Ragnarok fight is with Jormungandr the world serpent; Odin's is with Fenrir the wolf; Vidar avenges Odin by killing Fenrir, and himself survives to see the new world.  (Legend.)

question: A king of Britain sits at a great banquet at his court and sees the beautiful wife of one of his own dukes. He falls violently in love on the spot, and the whole legend of Arthur begins there. What is this king's name?
context: Malory Book I ch.1-2 and Geoffrey of Monmouth Historia Book VIII: Uther Pendragon is Arthur's father. Aurelius Ambrosius is Uther's elder brother who ruled before him. Vortigern is the earlier king who brought the Saxons in. Cadwallader is a much later Welsh king. Only Uther falls for Igraine.  (Legend.)

question: The wizard Merlin helps the king of Britain take a woman who is not free, for she is married to Gorlois, one of the king's own dukes. She becomes the mother of Arthur. What is her name?
context: Igraine (Igerna in Geoffrey) is Arthur's mother, wife of Gorlois of Cornwall. Guinevere is Arthur's own queen a generation later. Morgan le Fay is Igraine's daughter and Arthur's half-sister. Nimue is the enchantress who traps Merlin. Only Igraine is Arthur's mother.  (Legend.)

question: Duke Gorlois sees how the king looks at his wife and does not stay at court to argue. He carries her away that very night and shuts her up in his safest castle, a stronghold on a great crag cut off from the mainland by sea on almost every side. What is this fortress called?
context: Tintagel on the Cornish coast is Gorlois's stronghold in Geoffrey Historia VIII.19 and in Malory; it is also a real 5th-6th c. archaeological site. Camelot is Arthur's own court city, later. Camlann is the field of Arthur's last battle. Astolat is the town of Elaine the Lily Maid.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin agrees to help Uther reach the duke's wife, but sets a hard price. Merlin does not want gold, or land, or a favour at court. He wants one thing Uther does not yet have, and Uther must swear an oath on it before Merlin will act. What does Merlin demand?
answer: the child Uther will father that night
choices: the child Uther will father that night
the crown itself when Uther is dead
context: Malory Book I ch.2: Merlin makes Uther swear that the child conceived that night shall be given to Merlin to be raised as he sees fit -- and that child is Arthur. The crown, Gorlois's head, and Tintagel are all things Uther could have offered but not what Merlin asks.  (Legend.)

question: Uther rides up to the duke's castle that night with two men at his side, each wearing the likeness of one of Duke Gorlois's own two chief companions, so the guards will not question them. In Malory, one of the two is Sir Ulfius, who takes the likeness of Sir Jordanus. The other is Merlin himself. Whose likeness does Merlin wear?
context: Malory Book I ch.2: Sir Ulfius rides as Sir Jordanus, and Merlin himself takes the shape of Sir Brastias, Gorlois's chief knight. Bedivere, Kay and Lucan are famous later Round Table knights but do not appear in the Tintagel-night trick.  (Legend.)

question: Uther rides in through the open gate in the duke's shape, and the duke's wife welcomes him as her own husband home from war. That same night, miles away at his other castle of Dimilioc, the real Duke Gorlois leads a sortie against the besieging army and is killed in the fighting. Word of his death does not reach her until when?
context: Geoffrey Historia VIII.19: Gorlois falls in his sortie the same night; the messengers reach Tintagel at dawn. That is when Igraine begins to wonder how the man in her bed could have been her husband, since Gorlois was already dead. The other timings would collapse the whole story.  (Legend.)

question: Geoffrey of Monmouth sets his shape-change story on a Cornish crag around 1136, and for centuries scholars dismiss the place as pure legend. Then archaeologists dig the headland and find that its sub-Roman layer is not empty. Out of it comes something that shows the site was a high-status stronghold in the very century Uther and Arthur are set. What do they find in the dirt?
choices: a stone throne carved with a dragon
a hoard of Saxon silver coins
context: Excavations on the Tintagel headland uncovered large quantities of 5th-6th century imported pottery from the eastern Mediterranean -- amphorae for wine and oil, fine tablewares -- the sort of luxury goods only a high-status stronghold could pull in that far west. No Roman eagle, no dragon throne, no Saxon hoard have been found there. Geoffrey's Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1136) invented the shape-change scene, but he set it on a site that really was a big deal in the sub-Roman age.

question: Jesus was invited to a village wedding in Galilee, early in the Gospel of John, along with his mother Mary and his first disciples. John names one small Galilean village as the place. Which village was it?
context: John 2:1-2. Nazareth is where Jesus grew up; Capernaum becomes his ministry base; Bethsaida is Peter and Andrew's hometown. The wedding is at Cana, a small village whose exact site scholars still debate.

question: Mary noticed a small but embarrassing crisis partway through a wedding feast in a Galilean village: something the hosts needed for the celebration had run out. She quietly pointed it out to her son Jesus. Which practical thing had run out?
context: John 2:3. A village feast running dry of wine would have shamed the host family for a generation; Mary flags it to Jesus without ceremony.

question: Jesus answered his mother with a question when she told him the hosts of a village wedding in Galilee had run short, in John's gospel. 'Woman, what have I to do with thee?' he said, and he added one more short line. What was that line?
answer: Mine hour is not yet come
choices: Mine hour is not yet come
context: John 2:4, King James Version. In John's gospel Jesus repeatedly puts off his 'hour' until the Passion; here he seems to push back, then acts anyway.

question: Mary did not argue when her son Jesus brushed her off at a wedding in Galilee, where the feast had run short. She turned to the servants and gave them one short instruction. What did she tell them?
answer: Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it
choices: Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it
Fetch the master of the feast
Send for more from the village
context: John 2:5, King James Version. These are Mary's last recorded words in any gospel -- a full stop of trust before the first miracle.

question: Jesus pointed the servants to six large jars standing near the door, at a village wedding in the Gospel of John. They were the kind Jewish households kept so guests could wash their hands and cups in the ritual way before eating. What material were those six large jars made of?
context: John 2:6. Under Jewish purification custom, stone vessels were considered easier to keep ritually clean than clay ones, so the household kept large stone jars ready for hand-washing and vessel-washing at feasts.

question: The servants filled six huge jars with water at Jesus's order, at a wedding feast in Galilee. The jars stood at the door for the guests' ritual hand-washing, and the Gospel of John gives their size in an old unit, saying each held 'two or three firkins apiece.' Roughly how much water did each jar hold?
context: John 2:6. A firkin was about nine to ten gallons; six jars at the top end works out to well over a hundred and fifty gallons of wine for a village party -- an absurd, superabundant amount.

question: In the Gospel of John, Jesus told the servants at a village wedding to draw from six huge jars they had just filled with water. The hosts had run short and shame threatened the family. He said to carry the first cup to one particular guest to taste. Whom did he send it to?
context: John 2:8. The 'governor of the feast' was a kind of head steward who supervised the meal and its wine. He tastes the cup without any idea where it came from -- only the servants who drew it know.

question: A servant carried a cup to the steward in charge of a wedding feast in Galilee, in John's gospel. It came from six great jars that had held plain water. The steward tasted it, not knowing where the drink had come from, and called the bridegroom over to compliment him. What did the steward say?
answer: Thou hast kept the good wine until now
choices: Thou hast kept the good wine until now
Thou hast poured out the wine of gladness
A finer vintage I have not tasted in Galilee
This wine shames the vineyards of Judah
context: John 2:10, King James Version. The custom, he says, is to serve the good wine first and the cheap wine after the guests are past noticing -- the bridegroom, he thinks, has flipped the order. The bridegroom has done nothing at all. The other lines here are invented parallels, not scripture.

question: A runaway slave stumbles into a barrow-mound on a headland and steals one bright thing from a hoard guarded by a sleeping monster. Beowulf, hero of the Old English poem, is old now and king of this land. What does the slave steal?
context: Beowulf 2214-2231. The fleeing slave picks up a single golden cup from the pile and creeps back out of the mound. When the monster wakes and counts his gold and finds the cup gone, he goes berserk. Every other detail is a real Anglo-Saxon treasure motif -- helmets, rings, and daggers all appear elsewhere in the poem -- but the specific stolen item is the cup.  (Legend.)

question: A dragon wakes on its hoard in a barrow, counts the gold and finds one treasure gone. That very night it flies out over the land of the Geats breathing fire, and it burns one building to the ground. What does the dragon burn down?
context: Beowulf 2302-2323. The dragon burns Beowulf's own royal hall to the ground -- the poet marks it as the personal insult that drives Beowulf, now old, to arm one last time and ride out. The watchtower, the ships, and the forge all fit Migration-era Geatland, but the dragon's first burning is the king's hall.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf rides out in his old age to face a dragon at the barrow-mound where it hoards its treasure. He takes a war-band with him. The poet gives the count exactly, so the coming shame will land hard when most of the band breaks and runs. How many thanes does Beowulf take to the mound?
context: Beowulf 2401-2405. He takes eleven thanes with him -- twelve fighters counting the king himself. The number is set up carefully so that the poet can later tell you EXACTLY how many run (ten) and exactly how many stay (one), and the arithmetic is the shame. Seven, thirteen, and nine are all common war-band counts in Old English and Norse verse, but this specific ride to the mound is eleven.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf shouts a war-cry down into the mouth of the barrow, and the dragon comes rushing out breathing fire. He swings his old sword against its scaled head, but the sword lets him down. One of Beowulf's most-quoted lines says 'the blade failed him in the fight; his old iron was not fated to help him.' What is the name of Beowulf's own sword?
context: Beowulf 2679-2687. Naegling is Beowulf's own famous blade -- and it shatters in his grip when it bites too shallow on the dragon's scales. Hrunting was Unferth's sword, which had failed Beowulf earlier against Grendel's mother in the mere; the giant-forged wall-sword in that mere-cave was unnamed and melted in the monster's blood. Nothung and Balmung are the German sword-names from Wagner's Ring cycle and the Nibelungenlied for Sigurd's / Siegfried's sword, not Beowulf's.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf stands before a fire-breathing dragon with his iron sword shattered on its scales. The old king of the Geats has seen most of his men flee into the woods. The beast closes in for the strike that will kill him. What does the dragon do?
answer: fastens his fangs in Beowulf's throat
choices: fastens his fangs in Beowulf's throat
lifts him into the air by the shield
context: Beowulf 2688-2705. The dragon sinks his fangs into Beowulf's neck -- and along with the bite comes the venom that will kill the king even after the dragon is dead. Everything else the dragon does in the poem (breathing fire, coiling on the hoard, flying with wings) is real, but the specific killing wound is the fanged bite to the throat.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf's thanes turn and run into the woods when the dragon's flame comes, all but one. That one, a young kinsman of Beowulf who has never fought a battle before this day, runs into the fire beside his falling king and helps him kill the dragon. What is the loyal thane's name?
context: Beowulf 2596-2601. Wiglaf, son of Weohstan, of the Waegmunding clan and Beowulf's own kinsman, is the one thane who does not flee. His Old English name means 'battle-remnant' or 'battle-heir' -- the one who stays behind after the others are gone. Hondscioh was the Geat Grendel devoured first in Heorot fifty years earlier; Aeschere was Hrothgar's counsellor, killed by Grendel's mother; Hygelac was Beowulf's own late king back in Geatland. The one who stays with Beowulf against the dragon is Wiglaf.  (Legend.)

question: A young kinsman of Beowulf drives his sword up into the dragon's softer lower body, where the scales are thin, and the flames drop. Then Beowulf himself, dying of his wound but still on his feet, draws a shorter weapon from his belt and finishes the beast. What does Beowulf do with his belt-knife?
answer: cuts the dragon in half at the middle
choices: cuts the dragon in half at the middle
drives it through the dragon's eye
buries it in the dragon's tongue
wedges it in the dragon's jaws
context: Beowulf 2699-2705. With Wiglaf's sword-thrust already inside the dragon, Beowulf pulls his war-knife and cuts the beast in two at the belly. The dragon dies between them. The eye-thrust belongs to Odysseus and Polyphemus in the Greek Odyssey; the tongue and the jaws are common dragon-slaying motifs but not Beowulf's move. The specific finish is the knife across the middle.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf lies dying beside the fire-breathing dragon he has just killed, with its venom spreading through him. One warrior stood by him, a young kinsman who helped land the death-blow. As the poison finishes him, the old king asks the young man for one thing before he goes. What does Beowulf ask him to do?
answer: bring out some of the treasure so he can see it
choices: bring out some of the treasure so he can see it
raise a mound high on the headland
carry his ring-mail back to the queen
send word to the ten who fled
context: Beowulf 2743-2820. The old king asks Wiglaf to go into the barrow and bring out some of the dragon's hoarded gold so he can look on the treasure he won for his people before he dies. Wiglaf does it -- he carries out cups and standards and lays them at his king's feet, and Beowulf sees the gold and gives thanks and dies. The headland-mound is arranged by the Geats LATER, after his death; the ring-mail stays with the body; the ten cowards are dealt with by Wiglaf, not by Beowulf.  (Legend.)

question: A picked band of warriors, sons of noblemen and brave in battle, ride round and round Beowulf's finished burial-mound at Hronesnaess, singing dirges and reciting his praises. The poet gives their exact number. How many horsemen ride around the mound?
context: Beowulf 3169-3177. Twelve of the best Geat warriors ride round the mound, voicing their grief and speaking Beowulf's deeds aloud so the sound would rise. The circling-praise image is one of the most-copied endings in Old English studies. Seven, three, and twenty-four all appear in other Anglo-Saxon and Old Norse ceremonies but the number of horsemen at this specific mound is twelve.  (Legend.)

question: The poet of Beowulf ends his poem on one word, lofgeornost, one of the most-quoted words in all of Old English literature. His closing line calls the dead king the mildest of the world's kings, the gentlest and the kindest to his people, and in that last word keenest for one thing more. What is that thing?
context: Beowulf 3182: 'lofgeornost' -- Old English lof ('praise, fame') + geornost ('most eager'). The line says Beowulf was 'of the world's kings the mildest of men and gentlest, kindest to his people, and keenest for praise.' Scholars still argue whether that final word is admiring (a hero's rightful hunger for lasting fame) or a small pointed criticism (a king who cared what people said of him too much); either way, praise is what the last word names, not gold or peace or wisdom.

question: The monk Bede, writing a generation later, described an odd split in the palace of King Oswiu of Northumbria. Oswiu, raised by Irish monks, kept the Celtic date of Easter, and his queen Eanfled, raised in Kent, kept the Roman date. What did this cause in some years?
answer: The king feasted Easter while the queen still fasted Lent
choices: The king feasted Easter while the queen still fasted Lent
The king's household ate meat while the queen's household kept Lent fast
The queen's chaplain refused to share the vigil table with the king's
The two royal chapels lit the paschal candle a week apart
context: King Oswiu of Northumbria kept the Ionan Easter; his queen Eanfled, raised in Kent, kept the Roman date. Bede reports (Historia Ecclesiastica III.25) that in some years one royal faction was celebrating Easter while the other was still fasting Lent. The other three household frictions are the kind of thing a divided-calendar palace would face, but Bede's specific complaint is the feast-and-fast overlap. This mismatch is what pushed Oswiu to call the synod.

question: A powerful Anglo-Saxon abbess opened her double monastery on the North Sea cliffs to King Oswiu's great church meeting in 664. The meeting was called to settle the Easter question. She personally preferred the Celtic side but still hosted the debate. Who was that abbess?
context: The Synod of Whitby (664) was held at Streanaeshalch, Hilda's double monastery of monks and nuns. Hilda favored the Ionan tradition but presided as host. Etheldreda founded Ely; Aebbe ruled the double monastery at Coldingham; Hildelith later led Barking. All four are real 7th-century English abbesses -- only Hilda hosted Whitby.

question: The bishop of Lindisfarne, an Irish monk, argued the Celtic side at King Oswiu's synod at the cliff-top abbey of Whitby in 664. He cited the tradition of Saint Columba and John the Evangelist for the old reckoning of Easter, against the Roman reckoning being spread from Rome. Who spoke for the Celtic Easter?
context: Colman, bishop of Lindisfarne, defended the Ionan 84-year Easter cycle. Cedd was present as a translator between Old English and Irish. Agilbert was the Frankish bishop on the Roman side. Cuthbert, the great Lindisfarne saint, came later and accepted the Roman decision.

question: King Oswiu ruled for the Roman date of Easter at Whitby in 664, and for the Roman way of shaving a monk's head. The Irish-trained bishop of Lindisfarne lost the debate, refused to change his practice, gathered his monks and left the Northumbrian coast for good. What did the bishop carry away with him, by Bede's account?
answer: Some of the relics of Aidan
choices: Some of the relics of Aidan
The abbey's copy of the four Gospels
context: Bede reports that Colman carried away some of the relics of Aidan (his predecessor and founder of Lindisfarne) when he withdrew to Iona after 664. The other three items are plausible-sounding but not what Bede records.

question: A whole band of outlaws shared Robin Hood's fire under the trees of Sherwood Forest, in the old English ballads. They hid and fought beside him. What were Robin Hood's followers called together?
context: 'Merry Men' is the traditional name for Robin Hood's outlaw band. The earliest ballads name a core of them individually: Little John, Will Scarlet, and Much the Miller's Son. Source: Wikipedia, Merry Men.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood tried to cross a narrow log bridge over a stream in Sherwood, and a giant on the far side would not step aside. They fought with quarterstaves, and Robin ended up in the water. Who was the giant who beat him?
context: The log-bridge fight is the traditional first-meeting between Robin and Little John: Little John's staff knocks Robin into the stream, and the giant then joins the band. The earliest ballads name Robin's core companions as Little John, Will Scarlet, and Much the Miller's Son; later broadsides bring in Alan-a-Dale. Source: Wikipedia, Merry Men.  (Legend.)

question: A later ballad-maker dropped the usual name of one of Robin Hood's oldest companions and called him 'Midge', so small was the man. He was one of the three the earliest ballads named. Which of Robin's men was this small companion?
context: Much the Miller's Son is one of Robin's three earliest ballad-companions (with Little John and Will Scarlet). In Robin Hood and Queen Katherine he is called Midge -- a name that suggests small stature and hints that Much was traditionally imagined as short. Source: Wikipedia, Much the Miller's Son.  (Legend.)

question: A young man sat weeping under a great oak when Robin Hood came across him, in the old English ballad Robin Hood and Allen a Dale. His beloved was being forced to marry a rich old knight in the morning, and he begged the outlaws for help. Robin asked what he did for a living. What was his trade?
context: Alan-a-Dale is a wandering minstrel who joins the Merry Men in Child 138. His beloved is being forced by her father to marry an old knight for money. Alan carries a lute or harp, which lets Robin's later disguise as a harper work. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and Allan-a-Dale.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood walked into the church on the wedding morning dressed as a harper and stopped the marriage, in Robin Hood and Allen a Dale. The bishop refused to marry Alan and his sweetheart, saying consent must be asked. Robin put the bishop's cloak on one of his outlaws, who asked the question seven times until it counted. Which outlaw took the bishop's place?
context: In Child 138 Robin robes Little John in the bishop's cloak; Little John asks the consent question seven times (in mockery of the bishop's 'three times' rule) and marries Alan-a-Dale to his sweetheart on the spot. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and Allan-a-Dale.  (Legend.)

question: Friar Tuck, one of the best-loved of Robin Hood's men today, came late to the story. The fifteenth-century ballads do not have him at all. A brief play from about 1475 gave him his first entrance, and another of 1560 brought him back. Through which kind of performance did he come into the legend?
context: Friar Tuck appears in a c.1475 play, Robyn Hod and the Shryff off Notyngham, and again in a 1560 May-games play. He probably comes into the Robin Hood tradition through the jovial-friar figure of English May-games and morris dances, not through the earliest ballads. Maid Marian arrives the same way, from the French Jeu de Robin et Marion and English May Day festivities. Source: Wikipedia, Friar Tuck.  (Legend.)

question: A Bavarian knight-poet picked up an unfinished French Grail-poem in the early 1200s and retold the whole story in Middle High German. His huge poem became the greatest German Arthurian tale, and centuries later Wagner based an opera on it. What was the poet's name?
context: Wolfram von Eschenbach was a Bavarian knight who wrote around 1200-1210. Hartmann von Aue wrote Erec and Iwein; Gottfried von Strassburg wrote Tristan; Walther von der Vogelweide is the great Middle High German lyric poet. All four are real 13th-century German poets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parzival.

question: The widow Herzeloyde raised her son alone in a forest to keep one word from him: knight. His father was the wandering knight Gahmuret. A huge German Arthurian romance of the early 1200s follows the boy from his birth onward. What was the boy's name?
context: Parzival is Wolfram's version of the French hero Perceval. Erec and Iwein are the two Arthurian heroes Hartmann von Aue wrote about; Tristan is the hero of Gottfried von Strassburg's rival epic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parzival.  (Legend.)

question: The old hermit Trevrizent told the knight Parzival the true origin of the Grail, in Wolfram's poem of about 1210. Wolfram's Grail was no cup but a mysterious stone, and the hermit said it had not begun on earth. A certain company of angels had carried it down out of heaven. Which angels were those?
answer: the ones who stayed neutral in Lucifer's war
choices: the ones who stayed neutral in Lucifer's war
the guardians of Eden's eastern gate
the seraphim around the throne of God
context: Wolfram's Grail is guarded by NEUTRAL angels -- a bold and strange invention, since medieval theology usually had NO neutral angels (Dante later flatly rejected the idea in Inferno III). It is one of the reasons Wolfram's poem was read as touched by heresy for centuries afterwards. Michael's host, the cherubim at Eden's gate (Genesis 3:24), and the seraphim around the throne (Isaiah 6) are all real biblical angelic groups, but none of them brought down the Grail in Wolfram. Source: premieretat.com/wolframs-parzival-the-esoteric-metaphysics-of-the-grail.  (Legend.)

question: In Wolfram's poem, a white dove came down from heaven to the Grail-stone and laid a Communion wafer on it, renewing its power. The stone gave all who looked on it whatever food and drink they most desired and preserved their youth. The dove came once a year. On what day of the year did it come?
context: Good Friday is the day the church remembers the Crucifixion, and Wolfram places the wafer-descent there for that reason. Easter Sunday, Christmas Eve, and Pentecost are all major days of the church year and would be natural guesses, but Wolfram specifies Good Friday. The bird is a white dove. Source: swordandcup.substack.com/p/the-grails-secret-origin-and-sacred.  (Legend.)

question: Wolfram gave his Grail a wonder no French Grail had. His Grail was no cup but a magical stone kept at the castle of Munsalvaesche, and mysterious writing appeared on it all by itself. Once someone had read the words, they faded away again. What did the writing say?
answer: the names of new Grail Knights
choices: the names of new Grail Knights
the sins of the dying king
the year of the world's ending
the words of a hidden prayer
context: Whenever a new knight is to be summoned to serve the Grail, his name appears on the stone; once someone has read it, the writing vanishes. The stone effectively RECRUITS its own knights. Robert Eisler and other 20th-century scholars pointed to the parallel with the alchemists' philosopher's stone; others compare it to the Book of Life in Revelation. Source: premieretat.com/wolframs-parzival-the-esoteric-metaphysics-of-the-grail.  (Legend.)

question: Parzival came back to the Grail Castle at last and stood before the wounded Grail-King, his own uncle Anfortas. On his first visit he had failed by saying nothing. This time he asked a single question, and the question itself healed Anfortas and made Parzival the new Grail-King. What did Parzival ask?
context: Compassion is the whole moral engine of Wolfram's version: the young Parzival's first failure was that, taught to be a courteous knight, he stayed silent about his host's obvious pain. Years later he finally asks the compassionate question -- and that is what wins the Grail. The Middle High German is 'oeheim, waz wirret dier?' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parzival.  (Legend.)

question: Gahmuret, the hero's father in Wolfram's Parzival, went east and married the black queen Belacane of Zazamanc. Their son, Parzival's older half-brother, was born with skin patched black and white, and Wolfram said it looked like a magpie or a written-on parchment. What was this half-brother's name?
context: Feirefiz means 'piebald son' (from Old French 'vaire fiz'). He is one of the most striking figures in medieval European literature -- a black-and-white African-European Grail-knight, presented by Wolfram with full dignity. Gawan is Wolfram's version of the Arthurian Gawain; Anfortas is the wounded Grail King; Trevrizent is Parzival's hermit uncle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feirefiz.  (Legend.)

question: Repanse de Schoye, who carried the Grail, married Parzival's half-brother once he was baptised, and went east with him in the closing pages of Wolfram's poem. Wolfram made their son the founder of a half-legendary Christian kingdom in the far East, beyond the Muslim world, one that medieval Europe spent centuries trying to find. Who was that son said to be?
context: Prester John was a real medieval legend -- letters purporting to be from a great Christian king in India or Ethiopia circulated across Europe from the 1160s onward, and expeditions were actually sent to find him. Wolfram folds that legend into the Grail-story, tying the Grail lineage to the far East. Charlemagne, Saladin, and Baldwin of Jerusalem are real historical rulers of the crusading era, not sons of Feirefiz. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feirefiz.

question: Snorri told how a single vast world-tree, Yggdrasil, held the whole Norse cosmos together, with nine worlds set into its branches and roots. He and the Voluspa both made it a hardwood common in the forests of the north. What kind of tree was it?
context: Voluspa 19 and Gylfaginning 15 both call the world-tree an ash. Zeus's sacred tree at Dodona was an oak; the yew was sacred to some Celtic sites; birch is the sacred tree of certain Siberian traditions. The Norse tree is an ash specifically.  (Legend.)

question: Odin rode no trees, and he never put a saddle on the great world-tree that held up the nine worlds. Yet the tree's own name meant Odin's horse. Why was the world-tree called that?
answer: it was his gallows the night he hanged himself for the runes
choices: it was his gallows the night he hanged himself for the runes
he tied his eight-legged horse to it every morning
he rides its branches down from Asgard to Midgard
its roots grew where his horse first pawed the earth
context: The kenning 'gallows' = 'horse of the hanged' is a common Old Norse metaphor: a hanged man 'rides' the gallows. Odin hanged himself on the world-tree for nine nights, pierced with his own spear, and won the runes; the tree became Ygg's-horse ever after.  (Legend.)

question: The three Norns, the goddesses of fate, sat at the bottom of the world-tree Yggdrasil and drew water from a well to keep the tree alive. It was the well where the fates of gods and men were decided and spoken. What was the Norns' well called?
context: Gylfaginning 15-16 and Voluspa 20. Urd's well feeds one of Yggdrasil's three roots and is where the three Norns -- Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld -- draw water to keep the tree alive. Mimir's well is where Odin traded his eye for wisdom; Hvergelmir bubbles up in cold Niflheim under the third root; Byrgir is the well from which Bil and Hjuki were fetching water when the moon-god Mani caught them up into the sky.  (Legend.)

question: The poet of Grimnismal named four harts in a single verse, four male deer pacing round the branches of the world-tree Yggdrasil and cropping its leaves and bark. The tree had many creatures living on it, and these four were named together. What were the four harts called?
context: Grimnismal 33. The four hart-names all begin with D. Sleipnir/Grani/Gullfaxi/Hofvarpnir are famous horses (Odin's, Sigurd's, Gunnar's, Frigg's). Skoll/Hati/Fenrir/Garm are the four great wolves. Odin/Vili/Ve/Bor are Odin and his family.  (Legend.)

question: Heidrun the she-goat stood on the roof of Valhalla, the great hall of Odin for warriors slain in battle, grazing the leaves of the tree over the hall. From her udder flowed an endless supply of one certain drink for the fighters inside. What drink poured from Heidrun's udder?
context: Grimnismal 25. Heidrun the goat gives mead, not milk, and the mead never runs out; the Einherjar in Valhalla drink from it forever. The other three are the drinks a real Norse hall might have poured -- but the goat on Valhalla's roof pours only mead.  (Legend.)

question: A serpent-dragon lay coiled in the dark beneath the third root of the world-tree Yggdrasil, gnawing at it to bring the whole tree crashing down. He kept at it day and night, and his name meant 'Malice-Striker'. What was the dragon's name?
context: Grimnismal 32 and Gylfaginning 16. Nidhogg gnaws at the root and, in Voluspa, also chews the corpses of oath-breakers in Hel. Fafnir is the dwarf-turned-dragon killed by Sigurd for the ring-hoard; Jormungandr is the Midgard Serpent that circles the sea; Fenrir is the wolf of Ragnarok.  (Legend.)

question: A creature called 'Drill-Tooth' or 'Bore-Tooth' scurried up the trunk of Yggdrasil with an insult from the dragon gnawing at the root for the eagle perched at the crown. Then he ran back down with another, keeping the quarrel between the two ends of the world-tree going. What was his name?
context: Grimnismal 32; Gylfaginning 16. Ratatoskr's name breaks down as rata- ('boring, gnawing') + -toskr ('tusk, tooth') -- and yes, he is a squirrel. Nagelfar is the ship built from dead men's nails that will sail at Ragnarok; Hraesvelg is the giant in eagle-shape whose wing-beats stir the winds of the world; Vidofnir is a golden cockerel that perches at the top of the mythic tree Mimameid in Fjolsvinnsmal.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus kept one weapon for himself and let no other god wield it, ruling the Olympian gods from the cloud-wrapped summit of Mount Olympus. Ancient kings and armies swore their most binding oaths by this weapon. What weapon was it?
context: The trident belongs to Poseidon, the caduceus to Hermes, and the golden bow to Apollo. Wikipedia: Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus, king of the Olympian gods, kept a sacred bird of his own, as Athena kept the owl, Hera the peacock and Aphrodite the dove. His bird appeared again and again on Greek and Roman standards and coins as his emblem. Which bird was it?
context: The eagle is Zeus's sacred bird throughout Greek myth and later Roman iconography (it later became the emblem of the Roman legions). Wikipedia: Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus freed three grateful giant smiths from Tartarus during the great war of the gods, and they forged a great weapon for him as a gift. Each was named for what a thunderstorm sounds and looks like: Brontes, Steropes and Arges. What kind of monsters were these three smiths?
context: The three Elder Cyclopes: Brontes ('Thunder'), Steropes ('Lightning'), and Arges ('Bright'). Wikipedia: Zeus, Cyclopes.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus came down from Mount Olympus to visit Leda, the mortal queen of Sparta, in a disguise that Renaissance painters returned to again and again on huge canvases. Their mortal daughter grew up to be Helen of Troy, whose beauty would launch a thousand ships. In what shape did Zeus come to Leda?
context: From the union came two eggs. From one hatched Helen of Troy and Pollux (Zeus's), and from the other Castor and Clytemnestra (Tyndareus's). Wikipedia: Leda.  (Legend.)

question: A Phoenician princess was picking flowers on the beach at Tyre when a majestic white beast, gentle as a house pet, knelt beside her. She climbed on its back to play, and it stood up, walked into the surf and swam all the way to Crete. There it turned back into Zeus. In what shape had he carried her off?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.836-875. On Crete she bore him Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon. Wikipedia: Europa.  (Legend.)

question: A priestess stood beneath a single enormous sacred tree in the mountains of Epirus and listened to its leaves and branches for the god's answer. This was Zeus's oracle at Dodona, one of the oldest in Greece, older than Delphi. Which tree was his oracle-tree?
context: The oak at Dodona was Zeus's alone. Compare Athena's olive at Athens, Apollo's laurel at Delphi. Wikipedia: Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus sent his own sacred bird down to a mountainside where a prince of Troy was tending sheep, a boy famous as the handsomest young man in the world. It snatched the boy up alive into the sky and set him at the Olympian table to pour the gods' wine forever. What was the boy's name?
context: Ganymede replaced Hebe as cupbearer to the gods. The largest moon of Jupiter is named for him. Wikipedia: Ganymede.  (Legend.)
